Election Division Dispatch 
 Brad King & Angie Nussmeyer, Co-Directors | January 2018  
NEWS & UPDATES 
Indianavoters.com Updates 
If you visit indianavoters.com, you’ll see a refreshed   
website with new content and features, including a ﬁlter to 
idenƟfy if a person is already registered to vote to reduce 
duplicate registraƟons coming through the online portal. 
Duplicate registraƟons may sƟll occur, especially if users 
aren’t searching with an exact match to their registraƟon 
name, but the site will provide beƩer informaƟon to the 
user, including conﬁrmaƟon of registraƟon and an opƟon to 
update, if the registraƟon address is incorrect. 
 
Many improvements go live by January 10, 2018, and will 
conƟnue to be made to the site over the next several 
months, including enhancements to idenƟfy elecƟon day 
polling locaƟons and allow counƟes to provide more data 
regarding early voƟng dates, Ɵmes, and sites. If you visit the 
site aŌer January 10, and believe you have found an error, 
please let us know so we can share with our partners. 
 
Don’t Forget the CAN‐5! 
When a DemocraƟc or Republican candidate runs for 
oﬃce in the primary elecƟon, counƟes must hand‐
deliver or mail the CAN‐5 (Candidacy Filing  
ConﬁrmaƟon for 2018) no later than one day aŌer  
receiving the candidate’s ﬁling. You can use the form 
provided on the 2018 forms disc (or found on the  
portal), or use SVRS to generate the document aŌer 
creaƟng the candidate’s proﬁle in the system.  
QuesƟons? Contact the Quest Help Desk or visit the 
online training portal for a step‐by‐step guide. 
 
Oﬃce Naming Standards & SVRS 
Recently the state launched an ElecƟon Night Re‐
porƟng (ENR) website that pulls data from SVRS to dis‐
play on indianavoters.com on elecƟon night. To ensure 
consistency with candidate and oﬃce names, all oﬃce 
names across all counƟes were updated to display uni‐
formly in SVRS and an SOP was created. As candidate 
ﬁling season is underway it is important to use upper 
and lower case characters when entering candidate 
names in SVRS and, if any oﬃces need to be added, 
please consult the SOP (found on the training portal 
site) to ensure the proper format is used.

2017 Annual Report 
In a few short days, county elecƟon 
oﬃcials will have a steady stream of 
candidates visiƟng their oﬃces to ﬁle 
paperwork to run for oﬃce. Every 
DemocraƟc and Republican candidate 
running for local oﬃce in the primary 
elecƟon must ﬁle a CAN‐12 statement 
of economic interest and a CAN‐2  
declaraƟon of candidacy. 
(A reminder that for this purpose,  
candidates for prosecutor and judge 
are not running for “local oﬃce.” Both 
are state oﬃces and these candidates 
must ﬁle their candidate paperwork 
with the ElecƟon Division. However, 
campaign ﬁnance ﬁlings made by 
these candidates are managed by the 
county elecƟon board.) 
County elecƟon oﬃcials are not 
“candidate police” and may not reject 
a candidate ﬁling except for these 
FOUR reasons speci ﬁed in statute: 
1) Candidate running for state oﬃce 
(federal, statewide, state legislaƟve, 
judge, prosecutor) presents candidate 
ﬁling incorrectly to county. IC 3‐5‐4‐
1.2 
2) Filed aŌer the noon, prevailing local 
Ɵme candidate ﬁling deadline. IC 3‐5‐4
‐1.9 
3) Filing made on a form NOT  
approved by the state. IC 3‐5‐4‐8 
4) DeclaraƟon of candidacy is not  
accompanied by the required state‐
ment of economic interest (CAN‐12). 
IC 3‐8‐2‐11; 3‐8‐9‐6 
Some candidates may fail to include 
required informaƟon on their ﬁling or 
jot down the wrong precinct, for  
example. Only a registered voter of 
the elecƟon district or the county  
party chair may ﬁle a challenge (CAN‐
1) with the county clerk by the noon, 
February 16, 2018, deadline to  
quesƟon the inaccuracy of a form or 
the candidate’s qualiﬁcaƟons to run 
for elected oﬃce. 
The County ElecƟon Board must hold a 
hearing inviƟng the challenged candi‐
date and the challenger to present the 
facts of the case. The Board will  
review the facts, apply the law, and 
determine if the candidate will remain 
on the ballot (or not). 
One last reminder: county elecƟon 
administrators must mail the CAN‐5 
Candidacy Filing ConﬁrmaƟon to each 
DemocraƟc or Republican candidate 
ﬁling for nominaƟon in the primary 
elecƟon within 24‐hours of receiving 
the ﬁling paperwork. 
For more informaƟon, please review 
pages 5‐20 of the 2018 Indiana  
Candidate Guide OR review the chap‐
ter speciﬁc to the oﬃce found in the 
Guide. 
VR CORNER 
Don’t Forget to File the VRG‐21! 
Federal law (NVRA) and state law requires a 90‐day 
“freeze” period on nearly all voter list maintenance 
(VLM) acƟviƟes before each primary, general, municipal, 
or special elecƟon. To conﬁrm your county has complied 
with voter list maintenance requirements, a VRG‐21 
(Aﬃdavit of County Voter RegistraƟon Oﬃcer  
Concerning Voter List Maintenance) must be ﬁled with 
the Indiana ElecƟon Division. 
 
The deadline to ﬁle the VRG‐21 with the ElecƟon Divi‐
sion is close of business, Tuesday, February 20, 2018. 
 
While most VLM acƟvity must be put on “pause” during 
this period (and counƟes will not have access to some 
hoppers within SVRS as a result), counƟes may conƟnue 
to: 
1) process voter registra Ɵon forms; 
2) Remove deceased voters; 
3) Remove voters who are imprisoned a Ōer being con‐
victed of a crime; and 
4) Remove a voter if the voter submits a wri Ʃen  
request to cancel their voter’s registraƟon. 
 
In addiƟon, no voter may be marked “inacƟve” during 
the 90‐day freeze period. 
QUESTIONS OF THE MONTH 
Q. Do candidates for Judge and Prosecutor need to 
ﬁle a CAN‐12 Statement of Economic Interest?  
A. No. Candidates for judicial oﬃce or prosecutor do 
not ﬁle a CAN‐12 with the county elecƟon board. 
Instead, these candidates ﬁle a statement of  
economic interest with the Commission on Judicial 
QualiﬁcaƟons before ﬁling the declaraƟon of  
candidacy with the ElecƟon Division. 
Q. I’m the elected Clerk and plan to run for  
re‐elecƟon in 2018. What, if any, special steps do I 
need to take to manage elecƟons? 
A. The only restricƟon you should be concerned 
about relates to absentee ballots. A county clerk  
running for re‐elecƟon or another oﬃce on the  
ballot may not print their signature on the absentee 
ballot and must use the generic county seal on it. 
(Your county’s generic seal can be found on the SVRS 
county portal in the “Shared Documents” folder.) 
State law does not require the clerk’s signature or 
county seal be printed on elecƟon day ballots, but if 
the county does so, then it’s our best advice to apply 
the same ballot prinƟng rule.

the ElecƟon Division can serve as an interpreƟve source. However, where important legal rights are concerned, you must consult with your own aƩorney to be fully and properly advised.

AdministraƟvely Opening Candidate

A candidate running for oﬃce that pays more than

Candidate ﬁling for the DemocraƟc 
and Republican party primary closes

DemocraƟc or Republican county chair 
within the elecƟon district may ﬁle a

CAN‐1 form to challenge a county

The form requires the person making 
the challenge to provide facts   
indicaƟng why the candidate is not

Ɵon of the County ElecƟon Board 
meeƟng and it is recommended a copy 
of the CAN‐1 be enclosed. 
Our best advice is to mail the wriƩen 
noƟce in a way that includes postal 
service tracking like cerƟﬁed or  
priority USPS mail. Tracking  
informaƟon is oŌ
en helpful to CEB 
members if either person fails to 
aƩend the hearing. (Sending noƟce by 
email can be a helpful alternaƟve, too, 
if the person acknowledges receipt.) 
At the hearing, the county elecƟon 
board may establish procedures that 
can help move along the challenge 
hearing and, at the same Ɵme, give 
each side the opportunity to present 
their arguments to the board. While 
each side is enƟtled to be heard on

case and rebut claims made by the

AŌer each side makes their argu‐

should debate the challenge and vote

have to be conducted at a public hear‐
ing of the elecƟon board, all debate on

VR CORNER 
Federal VR Forms 
In addiƟon to the state’s VRG‐7 and VRG‐11 voter 
registraƟon forms, counƟes may receive federal 
voter registraƟon applicaƟons from Ɵme‐to‐Ɵme.  
 
The federal voter registraƟon form was designed by 
the ElecƟon Assistance Commission (EAC) to meet 
the needs of all 50 states, so it looks a liƩle  
diﬀerent than the Indiana form. Plus, the federal 
form is translated in to several languages, which  
are available to download from its website 
(www.EAC.gov). 
 
County voter registraƟon oﬃcials are to give the 
same consideraƟon to the federal VR form as they 
would an Indiana VR form. While the federal VR 
form does not have the “receipt” or “custodian  
aﬃdavit” like the state form, a person who takes 
custody of another person’s federal voter  
registraƟon form is required to submit the VR form 
no later than noon, ten days aŌer taking custody of 
it.
 
QUESTIONS OF THE MONTH 
Q. Do I have to put uncontested candidates for  
precinct commiƩeeman or state convenƟon  
delegate (party oﬃces) on the ballot? 
A. No—but the Democra Ɵc or Republican member of 
the county elecƟon board can submit a wriƩen  
request to print names of uncontested party oﬃce 
candidates on the ballot. The deadline to do so is 
noon, Friday, February 16. (IC 3‐10‐1‐5(d)) 
Q. Can a ﬁreﬁghter run for oﬃce? 
A. Candidates should consult IC 3‐5‐9, which  
sƟpulates a government employee may not serve as 
an elected oﬃcial in the same unit of government. 
(Volunteer ﬁreﬁghters are exempt from this rule if 
they are not full‐Ɵme, paid employees.) This doesn’t 
mean the individual can’t run for oﬃce; rather, the 
person resigns from government employment when 
they assume elected oﬃce. For example, Sarah has 
the job of town dogcatcher, runs for town council, 
and assumes elected town oﬃce. By doing so, she 
resigns her job as dogcatcher. Had she run for  
county council, she could conƟnue being employed 
as town dogcatcher and be a elected county oﬃcial.

QUESTIONS OF THE MONTH 
Q. Do the candidate names on the ballot have to be 
capitalized? 
A. Yes. IC 3‐10‐1‐14.1 requires the names on the  
ballot to be printed in uniform capital leƩers. 
Q. Do uncontested candidates go on the primary 
elecƟon ballot? 
A. For elected oﬃces in 2018, yes.  Because there is 
at least one contested elecƟon in any party’s primary 
elecƟon this year, all candidates and oﬃces, even 
those that are uncontested, must  appear on the 
ballot. (IC 3‐10‐1‐5) BUT,  uncontested candidates 
for party oﬃces—precinct  commiƩeeman or state 
convenƟon delegate—do  not appear on the ballot 
unless the DemocraƟc or Republican ElecƟon Board 
member ﬁles a request for uncontested party  
candidates to appear on the ballot. The deadline to 
submit such a request has passed, however. 
Q. I have an oﬃce where no candidate has ﬁled. Am 
I required to print “No Candidate Filed” as the  
candidate name? 
A. No, but you may do so if you choose.

InformaƟon in this newsleƩer is provided by the Indiana ElecƟon Division as a courtesy to county elecƟon administrators. If a person is unclear concerning elecƟon law provisions,  
the ElecƟon Division can serve as an interpreƟve source. However, where important legal rights are concerned, you must consult with your own aƩorney to be fully and properly advised. 
The May primary elecƟon allows the  
DemocraƟc and Republican parƟes to 
nominate their candidates for the  
November elecƟon. For the November 
elecƟon, Libertarian, independent and 
other minor party candidates also have 
methods for ballot access, and counƟes 
should be planning for ﬁlings from these 
candidates.  
 
Below are reminders for Libertarian  
candidate ﬁlings. Next month we’ll  
highlight independent candidate and  
other minor party ballot access. To learn 
more, you are encouraged to review the 
2018 ElecƟon Calendar Guide (yellow 
book) and the 2018 Candidate Guide for 
more speciﬁc informaƟon. 
 
Libertarian Candidates  
The Libertarian Party of Indiana (LPIN) is 
holding its state convenƟon on May 5, 
2018. Candidates nominated at this  
convenƟon are those for federal, state 
legislaƟve, statewide, judicial oﬃce, and 
prosecuƟng aƩorney.  
 
LPIN has also begun to hold county  
convenƟons across the state  to nominate 
county and township candidate for the 
general elecƟon and may conƟnue to do 
so through early summer. Their local  
candidates ﬁle the CAN‐22(Candidate Cer‐
ƟﬁcaƟon) and CAN‐12 (Local Candidate 
Statement of Economic Interest) with the 
county elecƟon board no later than noon, 
July 3, 2018.  
 
AddiƟonally, the Libertarian Party may ﬁll 
ballot vacancies. AŌer the county LPIN 
convenƟ
ons, the LPIN state commiƩee 
may ﬁll local oﬃce ballot vacancies across 
the state. AŌer a local candidate is  
selected the state chair must ﬁle the CAN‐
22 and CAN‐12 with your oﬃce to ﬁll the 
vacancy. Ballot vacancies caused by no 
candidate being nominated at the LPIN 
county convenƟon must be ﬁlled by noon, 
July 3. 
 
Libertarian, Independent, and other minor 
party candidates are also held to the same 
campaign ﬁnance rules. However, some 
Libertarian candidates may need to ﬁle a 
pre– or post‐convenƟon CFA‐4 report. A 
pre‐convenƟon report is needed IF the 
LPIN candidate has ﬁled a CFA‐1 form with 
your oﬃce; a post‐convenƟon report is 
needed IF the LPIN candidate does not 
have a CFA‐1 form on ﬁle and the oﬃce 
pays more than $5,000 in a calendar year. 
 
If the LPIN candidate ﬁlls a ballot vacancy 
and the oﬃce pays more than $5,000 in a 
calendar year, then a CFA‐1 must be ﬁled 
no later than noon, seven days aŌer the 
ﬁling period closes or July 10, 2018, for 
this elecƟon cycle. More details on these 
reports can be found in the 2018  
Campaign Finance Manual. 
VR CORNER 
VR ApplicaƟons & Postmarks 
The statewide voter registraƟon deadline for the May 
primary elecƟon is Monday, April 9, 2018. Before your 
team delays processing a VR applicaƟon received by 
mail aŌer this deadline, please be sure to check the 
postmark on the envelope. The postmark is a criƟcal 
piece of informaƟon to determine whether or not a VR 
form can be processed  for the May elecƟon. 
 
If a VR form is mailed to your oﬃce, received aŌer April 
9, 2018, and includes a legible postmark dated on or 
before April 9, 2018, then your county must process the 
form. (IC 3‐7‐33‐4) 
 
If a VR form is mailed to your oﬃce, includes an illegible 
or NO postmark, and is received aŌer April 9, 2018 but 
on or before Monday, April 16, 2018, then your county 
must to process the forms. (IC 3‐7‐33‐4; IC 3‐7‐33‐3.7) 
 
These same rules apply to VR forms received by the  
Indiana ElecƟon Division, and forwarded to your county.  
Review pages 7‐10 of the 2018 Indiana Voter  
RegistraƟon Guidebook for more details, including the 
deadlines for online voter registraƟon and hand‐
delivery. 
QUESTIONS OF THE MONTH 
Q. Can an absentee voter requesƟng a DemocraƟc 
ballot in the primary change their mind and re‐ﬁle 
an applicaƟon or otherwise request a Republican 
ballot (or vice versa)? 
A. No, a voter may not change their mind and  
request a diﬀerent parƟsan absentee ballot to  
replace the one they’ve already requested.  
 
Q. Can a candidate be a poll worker? 
A. It depends. In a non‐voter center county, a  
candidate may be a poll worker in a precinct where 
their name does not appear on the ballot, such as 
another township. In a vote center county, a  
candidate may not serve as a poll worker since all 
precincts vote at each vote center. See IC 3‐6‐6‐7 for 
details.  Please note: an uncontested candidate for 
party oﬃce (precinct commiƩeeman or state  
convenƟon delegate) may  serve as a poll worker in 
any precinct or vote center. 
 
Q. My newspaper failed to publish my noƟce for a 
public test. Do I have to reschedule? 
A. Not necessarily. State law and permits a county 
where the newspaper failed to Ɵmely publish a no‐
Ɵce to allow the county to either 1) display the no‐
Ɵce prominently in three locaƟons in the county or 
2) post on the county’s website (IC 5‐3‐1‐2(k)).

Election Division Dispatch 
 Brad King & Angie Nussmeyer, Co-Directors | May 2018  
NEWS & UPDATES 
ElecƟon Night ReporƟng 
We are delighted to report a new ElecƟon Night  
ReporƟng site was recently released as part of the  
refresh to the look, feel, and funcƟonality of  
indianavoters.com. Visitors can access statewide elecƟon 
results at indianavoters.com/elecƟonresults aŌer 6PM 
(Indy Ɵme) elecƟon night. 
This new funcƟonality includes an SVRS module to allow 
counƟes to enter unoﬃcial elecƟon night results so that 
they may be modiﬁed during canvassing and made 
“ﬁnal” when it comes Ɵme to ﬁle cerƟﬁcaƟon paperwork 
in SVRS. In fact, the results will carry over to your CEB‐23 
and CEB‐24 (Statement of Votes cast for DemocraƟc and 
Republican Party candidates, respecƟvely) to streamline 
your reporƟng requirements by prevenƟng “double  
entry” of the same data. 
Step‐by‐steps are  available on the county portal, and the 
Quest/GCR Help Desk is available to assist you. 
CerƟﬁcaƟon of ElecƟon Results 
There isn’t much Ɵme to rest following elecƟon day! 
Your county elecƟon boards must canvass the results of 
your elecƟon no later than noon, ten days aŌer the  
elecƟon, and process any provisional ballots or late  
arriving overseas ballots by 3PM that same day. You’ll 
then need to ﬁle the CEB‐23, CEB‐24, and CEB‐25 (if you 
had a public quesƟon) using SVRS, and separately send 
your precinct level results to IED by noon, Monday, May 
21, 2018. The CEB‐9 is due Tuesday, May 22. Web  
training on these post elecƟon processing pieces will be 
held, so please aƩend if you’re unsure of the process. 
State ConvenƟon Delegates 
The state DemocraƟc and Republican ParƟes are holding 
their state convenƟons in June, and cerƟfying the names, 
addresses, convenƟon delegate district, and congression‐
al district of each elected delegate is criƟcally important 
to the process. The parƟes must use this list to send no‐
Ɵce to delegates at least 30‐days before the convenƟon. 
The Indiana ElecƟon Division will be compiling the infor‐
maƟon provided by the counƟes in order for the Secre‐
tary of State to cerƟfy the ﬁnal list of delegates to the 
state party chairs.

InformaƟon in this newsleƩer is provided by the Indiana ElecƟon Division as a courtesy to county elecƟon administrators. If a person is unclear concerning elecƟon law provisions,  
the ElecƟon Division can serve as an interpreƟve source. However, where important legal rights are concerned, you must consult with your own aƩorney to be fully and properly advised. 
Last month we touched on milestones for 
Libertarian Party candidate ﬁlings in  
preparaƟon of the November 2018  
general elecƟon. Below are reminders for  
independent and other minor party ballot 
access. To learn more, you are  
encouraged to review the 2018 ElecƟon 
Calendar Guide (yellow book) and the 
2018 Candidate Guide for more speciﬁc  
informaƟon. 
 
Independent and minor parƟes have two 
ways to access the ballot—through the 
peƟƟon process or to be a write‐in  
candidate. 
 
If an independent or minor party  
candidate wants to have their name  
printed on the ballot, then they must go 
through the peƟƟon process. Beginning 
January 10, 2018,  candidates may collect 
peƟƟon signatures using the CAN‐19 form. 
The individual signing the peƟƟon must be 
a registered voter in the elecƟon district 
of the oﬃce the candidate is seeking. At 
the Ɵme the peƟƟon is processed.  
 
In order to gain ballot access, the  
candidate must collect signatures totaling 
at least 2% of the total votes cast in the 
2014 Secretary of State race in the  
precincts of the elecƟon district. This 
means county elecƟon oﬃcials will need 
to pull out the November 2014 precinct 
level results and calculate the signature 
threshold for local oﬃces. (Countywide 
totals can be found in the back of the 
2018 Candidate Guide.) State legislaƟve or 
federal candidates should contact  IED  for 
this informaƟon. 
 
CAN‐19 peƟƟons must be ﬁled with the 
county VR oﬃcial by noon, July 2, in order 
to be reviewed and cerƟﬁ
ed. The  
candidate must also submit their CAN‐20 
consent and CAN‐12 statement of  
economic interest to the county no later 
than noon, July 16, 2018. 
The county clerk must send by cerƟﬁed 
mail a leƩer to the candidate if the  
individual does NOT achieve the signature 
threshold for ballot access. If the  
candidate did collect enough signatures, 
then there is no need to cerƟfy this  
informaƟon to the person.  
 
Some individuals want to be a write‐in 
candidate. WRITE‐IN CANDIDATES ARE 
NOT PRINTED ON THE BALLOT! This  
individual must submit the CAN‐3 not  
earlier than January 10, 2018, and no later 
than noon, July 3, 2018, along with the 
proper statement of economic interest. 
 
Independent and minor party candidates 
may be challenged using the CAN‐1 form. 
The deadline to ﬁle a challenge in this  
scenario is noon, August 24, 2018. 
 
NOTE: School Board candidates have a 
slightly diﬀerent peƟƟon process, which 
will be covered at a later date.  
VR CORNER 
VR Form Types 
When doing voter registraƟon data entry in SVRS, a 
county user must select the proper form number to 
help track the form type used to register. The drop 
down menu in SVRS has a variety of opƟons, so 
which number or name is to be used?  
 
For state forms like the VRG‐7, the form number 
can be found in the upper leŌ corner or lower right 
number of the form. 
 
 
 
The VRG‐6 is NOT a publicly available VR form, and 
is used by full service agencies like the BMV, FSSA, 
and DWD. If you are unsure which VRG‐6 form 
number is correct, use the forms master list, which 
highlights which public agency uses that form. 
 
“Federal” means the federal mail‐in registraƟon 
form, “military” is the designaƟon for the FPCA, 
“NCOA” is used if you receive an update on an 
NCOA mailer, and “VLM Card” is used with updates 
made on the statewide postcard mailer.
 
QUESTIONS OF THE MONTH 
Q. Can a media watcher ﬁlm inside a polling place? 
A. Yes, but they may not capture how an individual 
voted. Likewise, they may not photograph a voter 
who objects. 
 
Q. Can we process absentee by mail applicaƟons 
postmarked on or before the deadline of April 30 
but received aŌer the deadline? 
A. Generally, no. The CEB must have physical custody 
of the applicaƟon by the deadline date to process an 
ABS applicaƟon as Ɵmely. The excepƟon would be an 
ABS‐Mail applicaƟon Ɵmely received by another 
county or IED that is forwarded to your county. 
Those are to be processed and an ABS ballot mailed, 
even if its just before the elecƟon. 
 
Q. Where can I ﬁnd elecƟon deadlines for military 
and overseas (UOCAVA) voters?  
A. Page 6 of the 2018 Military & Overseas Handbook 
published by IED has all of the relevant dates for this 
elecƟon cycle. There are special excepƟons to voter 
registraƟon and absentee ballot deadlines for 
UOCAVA voters, and this calendar is a great tool.

2. GCR / Quest Help Desk will have extended hours on Election Day from 5am to 8pm at 1-888-467-8771 and 
can be reached by email at helpdesk@Questis.com. 
3. Voting Information Project – A final update of precinct polling location data to the VIP program will be sent 
Sunday night. Please ensure your precincts all have polling locations assigned. You can check this using the

’ report in the Poll Category of the SVRS report library.

.

- The token is associated to a username and therefore can be used on any computer. If a token has been

usernames.  
- Computers used for election day should have Google Chrome installed.

Election Division Dispatch 
 Brad King & Angie Nussmeyer, Co-Directors | June 2018  
NEWS & UPDATES 
August Build Preview 
Below are a few highlights of the upcoming August Build 
in SVRS :  
1)Polling LocaƟon Updates in SVRS 
Any change to an ElecƟon Day polling locaƟon in SVRS 
will default to the hours of 6A to 6P, prevailing local 
Ɵme. This will help streamline county data entry, but also 
ensure indianavoters.com correctly reﬂects the hours 
polls are open on ElecƟon Day. 
2) Time/Date Stamps on OVR Submissions 
Once implemented, central Ɵme zone counƟes will no 
longer need to subtract an hour to determine if an online 
voter registraƟon submission was Ɵmely received. This 
change will not impact most county users, but should be 
helpful to our colleagues in the central Ɵme zone. 
3) Streamlined Voter Response Card Mailers 
Currently SVRS has two voter response card mailers—the 
NCOA and Interstate— that serve similar purposes and 
share language. To help with training  and to streamline 
operaƟons, the NCOA and Interstate mailers will be  
combined into one document. 
4) Duplicate Hopper Expansion 
Today when a county user enters a registraƟon in SVRS, 
potenƟal duplicates (those with a conﬁdence factor of 50 
or more points) within the county are presented, and the 
county makes a decision to merge the records (or not). 
AŌer the August Build, county users will see potenƟal 
duplicates statewide. If a potenƟal duplicate in another 
county is found (again hiƫng at least the 50‐point  
conﬁdence factor), the voter’s former county would have 
to approve the match in order for the records to merge. 
JUNE WEB TRAINING 
Web training for June has passed; stay tuned for dates/
Ɵme of refresher training in July! 
 
Dates are subject to change; check the 2018 INSVRS  
Training Schedule on the county portal to conﬁrm.

InformaƟon in this newsleƩer is provided by the Indiana ElecƟon Division as a courtesy to county elecƟon administrators. If a person is unclear concerning elecƟon law provisions,  
the ElecƟon Division can serve as an interpreƟve source. However, where important legal rights are concerned, you must consult with your own aƩorney to be fully and properly advised. 
IN FOCUS: Ballot Vacancies 
For the DemocraƟc and Republican ParƟes, Ɵme is running out to ﬁll ballot  
vacancies where no candidate ran in the primary elecƟon. The two major parƟes 
have the following opƟons available to ﬁll the ballot vacancy 
 
1) Direct Appointment (LOCAL o ﬃces only, including judge/prosecutor) 
County party commiƩee (PCs, vice PCs) can adopt a resoluƟon or pass a moƟon 
to permit the county chair to make a direct appointment to ﬁll a ballot vacancy. 
The resoluƟon or moƟon can be open‐ended; in other words, there is no legal 
requirement for an end date. The appointment must be made by noon, June 30, 
with the paperwork (CAN‐29, CAN‐31, CAN‐12, meeƟng minutes/resoluƟon) 
ﬁled with the county clerk by noon, July 3, 2018. (State legislaƟve ballot  
vacancies are NOT to be ﬁlled by direct appointment; the state chair or his  
designee calls the caucus and all paperwork is ﬁled with IED.) 
 
2) Caucus 
Chair must mail the call to caucus (CAN‐30) to  all eligible PCs AND ﬁle a second 
CAN‐30 with the clerk no later than ten‐days before the caucus is to be held. 
The caucus must be held no later than noon, June 30, 2018, which means the 
latest a call to caucus must be mailed and ﬁled is noon, June 20, 2018.  
Candidates interested in ﬁlling the ballot vacancy must also ﬁle the CAN‐31 and 
CAN‐12 no later than 72‐hours before the caucus is held with the chair of the 
caucus AND the county clerk. AŌer the caucus is held, the chair has unƟl noon, 
July 3, 2018, to ﬁle the CAN‐29 with the clerk’s oﬃce. 
 
Note: paperwork to ﬁll a ballot vacancy by direct appointment or caucus for 
judge/prosecuƟng aƩorney is ﬁled with IED. Candidates should stop at the  
Commission on Judicial QualiﬁcaƟons to ﬁle their statement of economic  
interests form, which is available on the agency’s website. Online ﬁling of the 
economic interest statement is now an opƟon.  
 
The Libertarian Party may also ﬁll ballot vacancies, but must ﬁrst ﬁle a noƟce of 
intent with the Indiana ElecƟon Division for federal or state oﬃces, including 
judge and prosecuƟng aƩorney, or with the clerk for a local oﬃce. The  
Libertarian state party the makes the selecƟons and ﬁles the CAN‐22 and the 
appropriate statement of economic interest with the Indiana ElecƟon Division or 
the county clerk, depending on the oﬃce sought. 
 
Finally, candidates ﬁlling a ballot vacancy where no candidate ran in the primary 
and where the oﬃce pays more than $5,000 per year have campaign ﬁnance 
obligaƟons. A CFA‐1 must be ﬁled no later than noon, July 10, 2018, unless the 
candidate has an open commiƩee, and a post‐nominaƟon CFA‐4 is ﬁled no later 
than noon, July 24. The reporƟng period begins the date the individual opened 
their commiƩee through July 17, 2018. AŌer this report is ﬁled, the candidate 
syncs with the “standard” reporƟng schedule, with the next being a pre‐elecƟon 
report. 
VR CORNER 
Changes in ElecƟon LegislaƟon  
ImpacƟng VR 
The retenƟon schedule for cancelled voter 
registraƟons has been a source of many 
quesƟons from county oﬃcials over the 
years. A recent change in state law pro‐
vides more clarity on this issue.  
 
IC 3‐7‐33‐8 requires a county VR oﬃcial to 
maintain the acƟve voter’s current  
registraƟon, assuming it’s a paper record, 
in perpetuity. This now includes scanning 
the paper record and aƩaching it to the 
voter’s informaƟon in SVRS.  
 
If at any point the voter moves within or 
out of your jurisdicƟon, paper forms 
corresponding to the cancelled registraƟon 
address must be 1) scanned in to SVRS and 
2) retained for at least 24‐months  
following the next general elecƟon. AŌer 
this 24‐month period, the county may  
destroy the paper document by following 
the proper protocols. 
 
For example, Jane moves within Boone 
County from Main Street to First Avenue, 
and submits the update on a VRG‐7 on 
June 14, 2018. Boone County must scan 
the new record with the First Avenue  
address into SVRS.  The paper VRG‐7 form 
with the old Main Street address must also 
be scanned and stored in SVRS, and it  
becomes eligible for destrucƟon on or 
aŌer November 7, 2020, or 24‐months 
aŌer the November 6, 2018, general  
elecƟon. (Before this change, the county 
would need to maintain both of Jane’s  
records unƟl her voter status moved to 
cancelled in Boone County.) 
 
Paper documents include, but are not  
limited to, the VRG‐7, VRG‐11, federal VR 
form, VR forms submiƩed by full‐service 
agencies, and the “paper chaser” BMV VR 
form. There is no requirement to print oﬀ 
online voter registraƟon forms or  
electronic submissions from the BMV. 
However, if your county creates a paper 
record for the electronic submission, then 
you must follow the retenƟon schedule as 
noted above for the printed copy of the 
electronic record. 
QUESTIONS OF THE MONTH 
Q. Does return postage need to be provided by the county on the 
NCOA Mailer? 
A. Yes, state law requires return postage to be paid for by the county 
on the NCOA mailer. This is a requirement for vote‐by‐mail absentee 
ballots, too. 
 
Q. Can we accept absentee ballot applicaƟons for the November 
elecƟon? 
A. Yes. Absentee ballot applicaƟons for the November 2018 elecƟon 
can be received by the county as early as May 22 (date VR opened 
for the November 2018 elecƟon).

Election Division Dispatch 
 Brad King & Angie Nussmeyer, Co-Directors | July/August 2018  
NEWS & UPDATES 
New Election Forms  
Counties will be receiving a few new forms for the  
November 2018 election, including the new form (PRE-
16) for those counties using touch screen (DRE) voting 
equipment. If you recall from the summer conferences, 
we discussed the new requirement for poll workers to 
complete an audit after the polls close to compare the 
signatures on the poll book and votes cast at the polls on 
the electronic voting system. The PRE-16 form is the  
correct document for the poll workers to complete and 
deliver with election materials in a precinct or for each 
precinct of a vote center.   
We also have updates to the IEC-9 (certification of public 
test of DREs) and the IEC-10 (certification of public test of 
optical scan systems), which should be used in November 
2018. These three forms updates are included in this 
packet for easy reference, and will be posted to the SVRS 
county portal. 
 
BMV Update 
As noted at the IVRA conference, the BMV is offering  
voter registration through its kiosks and other self  
service interfaces, printing the VRG-6 (the paper chaser), 
and sending those to county offices from a centralized 
site in Indianapolis. These are no different than the VRG-
6 paper forms sent to you by local branch offices. At the 
conference, several counties asked if the VRG-8 needs to 
be sent to the BMV main office for these  “new” forms. 
The answer is “no.” The VRG-8 is only used if the BMV or 
other full service agency sends an employee to hand-
deliver the VRG-6 forms to your office. There is no need 
to send a VRG-8 to the BMV if the “paper chaser” forms 
are mailed to your office.

Information in this newsletter is provided by the Indiana Election Division as a courtesy to county election administrators. If a person is unclear concerning election law provisions,  
the Election Division can serve as an interpretive source. However, where important legal rights are concerned, you must consult with your own attorney to be fully and properly advised. 
Noon, July 16 was the deadline for any can-
didate to withdraw from the November 
ballot for any reason. Now that this dead-
line has passed, a candidate may only  with-
draw if the candidate 1) is convicted of a 
felony, or 2) moved out of the election dis-
trict. A candidate may also be removed due 
to death.  
 
If a Democratic, Republican or Libertarian 
candidate must withdraw now, the candi-
date must file a CAN-24 with the county 
election board. The resulting vacancy from 
withdrawal or death may be filled by the 
political party. For Democratic or Republi-
can candidates, the ballot vacancy may be 
filled by caucus or direct appointment of 
the chair, if the party has authorized her or 
him to do so. The  Libertarian Party state 
committee fills all ballot vacancies. While 
independent candidates cannot fill a vacan-
cy, it is possible for a minor party to do so.  
 
Vacancies occurring up to 31-days before 
the election are considered “early.” After 
October 6, any vacancy is considered “late.” 
While the party may be able to fill the va-
cancy,  its possible the ballot may not be 
reprinted, depending on the timing. Please 
be in touch with our office if you experience 
a late ballot vacancy, and need direction on 
next steps. 
 
Many counties have small towns, which are 
defined as having  a population of less than 
3,500 persons. In some cases, the town has 
decided not to hold a primary election and 
instead, the parties may conduct town con-
ventions to choose Democratic, Libertarian, 
and Republican candidates. The town 
should have any ordinance requiring a pri-
mary on file with your office. 
 
In small towns where the town convention 
is the preferred model, the deadline for a 
Democratic, Libertarian, or Republican can-
didate to file a CAN-16 (declaration of can-
didacy) and CAN-12 with the county clerk’s 
office  is noon, August 1, 2018. 
 
A town convention is only called by the 
party if a person is opposed for the same 
office  by someone from the same party. 
For example, if Tom and Sally both file to 
run as a Libertarian Party candidate for 
dogcatcher, then a Libertarian Party town 
convention must be called. However, if  
Tom is the only person running in the Liber-
tarian Party for dogcatcher, then he is auto-
matically placed on the ballot and the party 
does not need to hold a convention for this 
particular office. Neither of the other par-
ties is required to conduct their own con-
vention in this case.  
 
 
Town conventions are conducted by the 
town party chair and secretary. The town 
party chair is appointed by the county chair, 
and the town party chair appoints the sec-
retary. The notice of convention must be 
posted in three prominent locations, includ-
ing the office of town clerk-treasurer,  with-
in the small town no later than 48-hours 
before the convention is held. 
 
All eligible persons are entitled to vote in a 
convention to nominate the party’s candi-
dates. Once the nominees are selected, the  
town chair files the CAN-18 (town conven-
tion certificate of nomination)  with the 
county clerk no later than noon, Tuesday, 
August 28.  
 
Independent , minor party, and write-in 
candidates may run for small town office. 
However, the deadline to file the petition of 
nomination for their name to appear on the 
ballot (or in the case of a write-in candi-
date, the CAN-3) has passed.  
 
The blue Election Administrator’s manual 
and red Candidate Guide go into greater 
detail on these issues, if you would like to 
learn more.  
 
 
IN FOCUS: Candidate Withdrawals & Small Town Offices 
VR CORNER 
Federal Freeze Period 
August 8 is the LAST DAY for counties to complete Voter List  
Maintenance (VLM) work before the 90-day federal freeze period  
begins. Starting August 9, a county VR official may not change a voter’s 
status from active to inactive. This work may resume the next day  
following the fall election, or November 7, 2018, though will require a 
county VR official to first confirm whether or not the person voted in the 
election or otherwise updated their voter registration information be-
fore changing a voter’s status. 
 
During the federal freeze period, county VR officials may accept new 
registrations, make updates to a voter’s registration, and move a  
registration to cancelled if the voter has died, is imprisoned following 
criminal conviction, or has submitted written authorization to cancel 
their registration. See IC 3-7-38.2-3 for details. 
 
Once VLM work concludes, county VR officials are asked to complete the 
VRG-21, and file it with IED no later than Thursday, August 21. 
Don’t Forget! 
Recently, several counties 
were asked to review the 
office names in SVRS and 
correct any that do not 
meet the naming standards 
found in SOP EM4.4 on the 
county portal. 
 
This review is important as it 
impacts how commissions 
and oaths of office are print-
ed and how the information 
is presented on  
indianavoters.com. 
 
The deadline to complete 
this work is August 1. 
QUESTIONS OF THE MONTH: 
School Board Filing Focus 
Q. Do school board candidates have to open a  
campaign finance committee? 
A. Maybe. A school board candidate must open a 
campaign finance committee and file required  
reports if and when they raise or spend $500 toward 
running for office. Until then, there is no need to file 
a CFA-1.  
 
Q. Who can sign a school board petition? 
A. Registered voters within the boundaries of the 
community school corporation. School board  
information should be part of your county’s precinct 
key matrix and included in the voter’s record. If not, 
reach out to your GIS department or the school  
corporation for a map. (Some metropolitan school 
districts exist throughout Indiana  in these cases, 
voters signing the petition must be in the school 
board district.)  
 
Q. Does a candidate for school board need to  
submit multiple candidate consent forms? 
A. No. The CAN-34 form is designed to capture the 
10 signatures of registered voters on the front of the 
form, while the back of the form includes the  
candidate’s consent. While the candidate can submit 
multiple CAN-34 documents to ensure he or she has 
enough petition signatures, only one “back” side 
needs to be completed by the candidate. 
 
Q. Where is the CAN-34 petition filed? 
A. In most Indiana counties, the county clerk is the 
county’s voter registration official, so the CAN-34 
and CAN-12 is filed with the clerk’s office no later 
than noon, August 24.  
 
In the few counties where the county has a separate 
VR board, the CAN-34 is filed with the VR board by 
noon, August 24, so the VR board can certify  the 
number of  signatures on the petition. The certified 
petition is then delivered to the clerk. The candidate 
must also file the CAN-12 with the county clerk no 
later than noon, August 24. 
 
In both cases, the clerk has a responsibility  to inform 
the candidate if the petition was approved or denied  
either in person or by certified mail. If denied, the 
candidate may file a CAN-1 challenge by noon,  
August 31 to contest the denied signatures. 
SAVE THE DATE! 
2019 Election Administrator’s Conference will be held 
Monday, December 10 to Wednesday, December 12 in 
downtown Indianapolis. Once the hotel contract is  
finalized, invitations will be sent out to reserve your space 
at the conference. 
 
Our office will also be reaching out to the county clerks to 
get the names and addresses of your county election 
board members and candidates for clerk of the circuit 
court so that they, too, are aware of the conference. 
 
Under state law, the county clerk, clerk-elect, board of 
voter registration, and county election board members 
are entitled to certain reimbursements under IC 3-6-4.2-
14(d) to attend.

Election Division Dispatch 
 Brad King & Angie Nussmeyer, Co-Directors | September 2018  
NEWS & UPDATES 
New PRE‐16 Form 
(Pollbook & DRE ElecƟon Day Audit) 
Last month we shared the PRE‐16 with this newsleƩer. 
The form is to be used by counƟes that use DRE voƟng 
systems as its main voƟng system on ElecƟon Day. The 
PRE‐16 does not apply to counƟes using an opƟcal scan 
ballot card voƟng system as its main system on ElecƟon 
Day. 
Legislators recently required poll workers to record the 
number of signatures on the poll list and the number of 
votes cast on the DRE on the form at the precinct, and  
provide an explanaƟon for any discrepancies.  
The CEB must then compile into a single document lisƟng 
for each precinct or vote center the number of votes cast 
on each DRE and the number of voters signing the poll 
book and compute the diﬀerence. No later than noon, 
the second Friday following ElecƟon Day, the document 
must be discussed at a CEB hearing and report made 
publicly available. 
The CEB or Secretary of State may order an audit of all 
votes cast in the precinct if the number of votes cast on 
the DRE and the number of signatures on the poll list 
exceed the statutory audit threshold numbers found in  
IC 3‐12‐3.5‐8.  
New IEC‐6, IEC‐22 Forms  
(VoƟng System Disposal) 
Included in this packet are two new forms, which 
will be included on the 2019 forms disc: 
IEC‐6: Indiana VoƟng System or ePollbook Disposal 
Plan. This is used if your county decides to dispose 
of a voƟng system or ePollbook, and requires the 
county to include important informaƟon about the 
device. The plan is then forwarded to the IED for 
review and approval.  
 IEC‐22: County CerƟﬁcaƟon of VoƟng System & ePoll‐
book Inventory. No later than January 31 of each year, 
the county must conﬁrm the accuracy of VSTOP’s  
inventory of its ePollbooks and voƟng systems to the 
Secretary of State.

InformaƟon in this newsleƩer is provided by the Indiana ElecƟon Division as a courtesy to county elecƟon administrators. If a person is unclear concerning elecƟon law provisions,  
the ElecƟon Division can serve as an interpreƟve source. However, where important legal rights are concerned, you must consult with your own aƩorney to be fully and properly advised. 
With school board ﬁlings in the rear view 
mirror and the state’s list of candidates 
cerƟﬁed to you, ballot building has begun 
in earnest around the state. The 2018 
ElecƟon Administrator’s Guide goes into 
great detail about the required elements 
in building your ballot. See pages 71‐78 of 
the blue book. 
 
Our oﬃce has received several calls about 
voƟng straight party and recent changes in 
state law aﬀecƟng “at‐large” type races.  
 
As a reminder, straight party no longer 
applies to all parƟsan races on the ballot. 
State law requires tabulaƟon of the votes 
containing the straight party device on 
“vote for 1” parƟsan races. For any race 
that allows a voter to vote for more than 1 
person (usually “at large”), then the voter 
must mark their choices individually and 
straight party does not apply. 
 
For example, the town dogcatcher is on 
the ballot and it’s a “vote for no more 
than 3” race. Sally gets her ballot, and 
uses the DemocraƟc Party straight party 
device. The machine will tabulate the re‐
sults of her ballot as vote for every  
DemocraƟc candidate on the ballot in a 
“vote for 1” race but will not tabulate  
results  in the town dogcatcher race. 
 
Doug goes to his polling place, and he uses 
the Republican Party straight party device 
AND individually marks two candidates 
running for dogcatcher. The machine will 
tabulate the results of his ballot as a vote 
for every Republican candidate in a “vote 
for 1” race and for the two candidates he 
picked for dogcatcher. (In this  example, 
Doug “under‐voted” in the dogcatcher 
race, which is OK.) 
 
Of course, using the straight party device 
would not cast votes for any public  
quesƟon, school board candidate, or  
judicial retenƟon quesƟon. Those races or 
quesƟons must be individually marked. 
 
To help voter’s navigate these changes, 
state law  requires “vote for no more than 
X” races to appear at the end  of the ballot 
order for parƟsan races, just above school 
board elecƟons. It also requires addiƟonal 
instrucƟons to be printed below the “vote 
for not more than X” direcƟon: 
 
 “Vote for not more than X for this 
 o ﬃce. To vote for this oﬃce, you 
 must make a vo Ɵng mark for 
 each candidate you wish to vote  
 for. A straight party vote will not 
 count as a vote for any candidate 
 for this o ﬃce.” 
 
These instrucƟons under the oﬃce name 
must be printed for each “at‐large” type 
race on your ballot. This is in addiƟon to 
the general instrucƟons that can be  
printed above the names of the poliƟcal 
parƟes on the ballot or hung inside the 
voƟng booth on elecƟon day for voters to 
read. Pages 76 and  73  of the blue  
Administrator’s Manual include these  
details. 
IN FOCUS: Changes to Straight Party Device & Your Ballot 
VR CORNER 
Voter’s Request to Cancel RegistraƟon 
SomeƟmes a voter will contact your oﬃce to  
request their voter registraƟon record to be moved 
to cancelled status. State and federal law requires 
this request to be in wriƩen form made by the  
voter. Voter registraƟon oﬃcials may not accept a 
verbal cancellaƟon from the voter or any person 
associated with the voter, like a family member.  
 
CounƟes create the cancellaƟon request form 
through SVRS. Navigate to the voter’s name, click 
“voter overview > “voter reports” and select the 
“registraƟon” category. This allows you to click the 
“AuthorizaƟon to Cancel RegistraƟon” link and  
generate the form  in .pdf or excel format to mail to 
the voter.
 
QUESTIONS OF THE MONTH  
Q. Can a candidate withdraw from the ballot at this 
point in the process? 
A. Generally speaking, no. However, if the candidate 
moves out of the elecƟon district, is convicted of a 
felony, dies, or is otherwise disqualiﬁed (IC 3‐8‐7‐
28), then the candidate must withdraw.  The county  
party is able to ﬁll the vacancy within the 30‐day 
window pursuant to the procedures in IC 3‐13‐1. If 
ballots have been printed, the county must re‐print 
the ballot with the new candidate’s name and send 
noƟce and an ABS‐5 to votes that have already sub‐
miƩed a ballot. 
 
Q. Can a candidate withdraw in the ﬁnal 30‐days 
before an elecƟon? 
A. Yes, but only for the reasons noted above. Howev‐
er, any vacancy occurring on or aŌer the 30‐days 
before the elecƟon is considered a late vacancy. 
While the county party may ﬁll the vacancy, the 
county elecƟon board has discreƟon in some cases 
on whether or not the ballot is to be re‐printed, and 
tabulaƟon may be impacted if the ballot is not cor‐
rected. See IC 3‐11‐13‐29.5 and IC 3‐13‐2 for these 
details.

Election Division Dispatch 
 Brad King & Angie Nussmeyer, Co-Directors | October 2018  
NEWS & UPDATES 
ePB Report & CAN‐39 Reminders 
Currently ePollbook counƟes receive emails for Web  
Service Framework (WSF) transacƟons (i.e. “put” and 
“get” calls). While those emails will conƟnue, ePB  
counƟes can run a report to compile daily transacƟon 
details. This should help counƟes stay on top of issues 
with ePB data transmission to SVRS. You can  ﬁnd the 
report “ePollBook WSF Transaction Call Tracking” in the 
INSVRS Reports Library under the elecƟons category. 
 
For those counƟes that have not yet published the Legal 
NoƟce of ElecƟon (CAN‐39) a reminder that counƟes are 
able to generate the CAN‐39 through SVRS via the  
Reports Library under the “ElecƟon” category. A remind‐
er that the CAN‐39 is to be placed in the minutes of a 
CEB meeƟng and providing the names and addresses of  
candidates are opƟonal. 
 
Voter InformaƟon Project (VIP) 
IED is again partnering with Democracy Works, a non‐
parƟsan non‐proﬁt, to increase visibility of early voƟng 
and polling place informaƟon. A baseline data set and 
frequent updates will be shared with them soon. Please 
make sure your ElecƟon Day locaƟons are up to date in 
SVRS on or before October 9 as our elecƟon informaƟon 
will be shared on many websites.  
ABS Central Count LegislaƟve Changes 
Recent changes in Indiana law permit a CEB in a 
county that counts absentee ballots at a central  
locaƟon to adopt unanimous resoluƟons to 1)  
eliminate elecƟon day ABS signature review of ABS 
ballots received by travel board or in‐person absen‐
tee (IC 3‐11.5‐4‐12) and 2) begin processing & 
counƟng ABS ballots at 6AM on elecƟon day, if the 
county has updated their ePollbooks no later than 
12:01A on elecƟon day. (IC 3‐11.5‐4‐11). 
Please note: A signature review must be conducted 
by the CEB or absentee voter board before ElecƟon 
Day on ABS mail ballots and ABS counters must  
perform a signature review on ABS mail ballots on 
ElecƟon Day. (IC 3‐11‐10‐4; IC 3‐11.5‐4‐12) 
OCTOBER WEB TRAINING 
Oct. 11 & 15 | CerƟﬁcate of Error Processing 
Oct. 23 & 25 | County ENR Data Entry  
 
Dates are subject to change; check the 2018 INSVRS  
Training Schedule on the county portal to conﬁrm. 
InformaƟon in this newsleƩer is provided by the Indiana ElecƟon Division as a courtesy to county elecƟon administrators. If a person is unclear concerning elecƟon law provisions,  
the ElecƟon Division can serve as an interpreƟve source. However, where important legal rights are concerned, you must consult with your own aƩorney to be fully and properly advised. 
CALENDAR 
October 8, 2018 
IED closed for Columbus Day Holiday 
October 8, 2018 
Deadline for county commissioners to designate poll‐
ing locaƟons for November elecƟon, for those coun‐
Ɵes with precinct‐based polling sites 
October 9, 2018 
Statewide VR Deadline

In‐person early voƟng begins statewide

Campaign Finance reporƟng period ends (Pre‐
ElecƟon Report)

Large ContribuƟon (CFA‐11) reporƟng period begins 
October 16, 2018 
NOON Deadline for D & R party chairs to ﬁle nomina‐
Ɵons for precinct elecƟon oﬃcers 
October 18, 2018 
Travel Board begins visiƟng conﬁned voters 
October 19, 2018 
NOON deadline to ﬁle pre‐elecƟon reports 
October 27, 2018 
All Clerk’s oﬃces must be open for in‐person  
absentee voƟng 
October 29, 2018 
ABS Mail ApplicaƟon deadline (11:59P) 
VR CORNER 
VR ApplicaƟons & Postmarks 
The statewide voter registraƟon deadline for the  
November general elecƟon is Tuesday, October 9, 2018. 
Before your team processes a VR applicaƟon received by 
mail aŌer this deadline, please be sure to check the 
postmark on the envelope.  
 
If a VR form is mailed to your oﬃce, received aŌer  
October 9, 2018, and includes a legible postmark dated 
on or before October 9, 2018, then your county must 
process the form. (IC 3‐7‐33‐4) 
 
If a VR form is mailed to your oﬃce, includes an illegible 
or NO postmark, and is received aŌer October 9, 2018 
but on or before Monday, October 15, 2018, then your 
county must to process the forms. (IC 3‐7‐33‐4; IC 3‐7‐33
‐3.7)  
 
These same rules apply to VR forms received by the  
Indiana ElecƟon Division, and forwarded to your county.  
Review pages 7‐10 of the 2018 Indiana Voter  
RegistraƟon Guidebook for more details. 
 
Online Voter RegistraƟon (OVR) 
A reminder that a recent update to INSVRS now Ɵme‐
stamps the date an OVR applicaƟon was received by the 
proper Ɵme zone. This change does not impact Eastern 
Ɵme zone counƟes; instead, Central Ɵme zone counƟes 
can now rely on the Ɵme‐stamp to reﬂect when the  
applicaƟon was received according to local prevailing 
Ɵme. 
QUESTIONS OF THE MONTH 
Q. Can a candidate be a poll worker? 
A. It depends. In a non‐voter center county, a  
candidate may be a poll worker in a precinct where 
their name does not appear on the ballot, such as 
another township. In a vote center county, a  
candidate may not serve as a poll worker since all 
precincts vote at each vote center. See IC 3‐6‐6‐7 for 
details.  Please note: This applies to unopposed  
candidates as well. 
 
Q. My newspaper failed to publish my noƟce for a 
public test. Do I have to reschedule? 
A. Not necessarily. State law permits a county where 
the newspaper failed to Ɵmely publish a noƟce to 
allow the county to either 1) display the noƟce 
prominently in three locaƟons in the county or 2) 
post on the county’s website (IC 5‐3‐1‐2(k)). 
ABS App Scanning & “ALERT ME” on 
County Portal 
IED has been scanning absentee ballot applicaƟons and 
posƟng to the county portal since September 22. The 
scanning eﬀort is to get informaƟon to counƟes more 
quickly, since mail oŌen runs several days behind and 
creates a delay for your county elecƟon board to review 
the applicaƟons and send absentee ballots to eligible  
voters. 
Of course your county may wait for the originals to come 
by mail before processing; the scanned images are posted 
as a convenience to counƟes who wish to use them. All 
scanned images should have a watermark noƟng it’s an 
IED scan so you can diﬀerenƟate between the hard copy 
and the scan when matching the two. 
Scanned absentee applicaƟons are placed daily in the 
“IED PosƟngs” secƟon of the INSVRS county portal. In 
your county’s folder, you’ll ﬁnd a “2018 General ABS  
ApplicaƟons” folder, and the ﬁles are posted there. 
A reminder that at “alert me” funcƟon exists on your fold‐
ers to alert you to new posƟngs. When you log in to the 
portal, there is a tool bar with speciﬁc funcƟons noted. If 
you click the “…” bu Ʃon, a new drop down box appears 
(see image below). 
 
 
 
 
 
Select “Alert Me” and a new screen will appear, giving 
you opƟons to manage your alerts and the frequency 
they are sent to you. Below is a parƟal screen shot of  
opƟons available for your alerts.

Election Division Dispatch 
 Brad King & Angie Nussmeyer, Co-Directors | November 2018  
NEWS & UPDATES 
ElecƟon Night ReporƟng 
In addiƟon to state and federal elecƟon results, counƟes 
can leverage indianavoters.com/elecƟonresults to dis-
play the results of their local elecƟons aŌer 6P elecƟon 
night. Plus, this reporƟng funcƟonality will carry over and 
can be updated throughout cerƟﬁcaƟon before it’s made 
“ﬁnal” when you ﬁle cerƟﬁcaƟon paperwork in SVRS. In 
other words, the work done on elecƟon night to enter 
unoﬃcial results will streamline your reporƟng  
requirements and prevent “double entry” of ﬁnal data. 
Step-by-steps are  available on the county portal, and the 
Quest/GCR Help Desk is available to assist you. 
CerƟﬁcaƟon of ElecƟon Results 
There isn’t much Ɵme to rest following elecƟon day! 
Your county elecƟon boards must canvass the results of 
your elecƟon no later than noon, ten days aŌer the  
elecƟon, and process any provisional ballots or late  
arriving overseas ballots by 3PM that same day. You’ll 
then need to ﬁle the CEB-11, CEB-12, CEB-13 and CEB-25 
using SVRS, and separately send your precinct level  
results to IED by noon, Monday, November 19, 2018. The 
CEB-9 is due Tuesday, November 20.  
 
County clerks must also begin issuing cerƟﬁcates of  
elecƟon aŌer 12P local prevailing Ɵme on November 26.  
These reporƟng funcƟons are managed through SVRS, so 
please contact the Quest Help Desk with quesƟons, 
aƩend online training, or review step-by-steps found on 
the county portal. 
BMV Open on ElecƟon Eve & ElecƟon Day 
State law requires BMV branches that issue credenƟals 
like driver’s licenses or state ID cards to be open from 
8:30A to 8P, local prevailing Ɵme, Monday, November 5 
and from 6A to 6P, local prevailing Ɵme, Tuesday,  
November 6, to assist individuals in geƫng ID required to 
vote. As a reminder, state law requires a photo ID to  
include a photo of the voter, be issued by the state or 
federal government, be current or expired since 11/8/16, 
and include the voter’s name that conforms (not be  
exact!) to their registraƟon record. (IC 3-5-2-40.5)  
Further, an address on a state ID does not need to match 
the person’s registraƟon record. ExcepƟons exist for  
military and veterans’ IDs. 
NOV WEB TRAINING 
Nov. 13 & 14 | Post ElecƟon Processing 
 
Dates are subject to change; check the 2018 INSVRS  
Training Schedule on the county portal to conﬁrm. 
CALENDAR

Must make in-person ABS early voƟng available 
November 5, 2018 (ElecƟon Eve): 
Check yellow calendar book for mulƟple deadlines 
November 6, 2018 (ElecƟon Day): 
Poll are open from 6A to 6P, local prevailing Ɵme

Deadline for town council to adopt an ordinance creaƟng 
or modifying town council districts for the 2019 elecƟon

Deadline to register for Dec. conference to avoid late fee!

postmarked on or before November 6, 2018; Deadline for 
voter to bring ID to the clerk’s oﬃce to count provisional 
ballot for lacking proper ID 
November 16, 2018 (3PM): 
Deadline for county elecƟon board to determine whether 
or not to count a provisional ballot 
November 19, 2018 (NOON, Indy Time): 
Deadline to cerƟfy elecƟon results to IED

Deadline by noon for a candidate to ﬁle a recount or  
contest acƟon with county clerk or IED, depending on 
oﬃce sought 
November 26, 2018 (NOON): 
Deadline by noon for a county or state party chair to ﬁle

InformaƟon in this newsleƩer is provided by the Indiana ElecƟon Division as a courtesy to county elecƟon administrators. If a person is unclear concerning elecƟon law provisions,  
the ElecƟon Division can serve as an interpreƟve source. However, where important legal rights are concerned, you must consult with your own aƩorney to be fully and properly advised. 
Besides voters and poll workers, very few 
others are permiƩed inside a polling  
locaƟon on ElecƟon Day. To gain entry 
most will need a credenƟal through the 
county elecƟon board or county chair of a 
bona ﬁde poliƟcal party with a candidate 
on the ballot. (For November’s elecƟon, 
independent candidates can also request 
challenger credenƟals.)  
 
CredenƟaled challengers, watchers and 
poll book holders may NOT be a candidate 
on the ballot. In addiƟon, a recent change 
in state law does NOT permit precinct 
elecƟon oﬃcers (inspector, clerk, judge, 
etc.) to be poll book holders, challengers 
and watchers though poll clerks can  
mantain a “scratch list” for their poliƟcal 
party. 
 
AddiƟonally, party chairs can only appoint 
one challenger, one watcher and one poll 
book holder for each precinct where  
candidates of their poliƟcal party appear 
on the ballot. In other words, two  
DemocraƟc Party challengers cannot be in 
the same precinct at the same Ɵme; one 
person must leave. The excepƟon to this 
rule are watchers. Because state and 
county chairs can each make those  
appointments, there may be up to two 
watchers appointed by the same poliƟcal 
party in a precinct at the same Ɵme.  
 
Also, if the polls have more than one  
precinct in the same locaƟon, then each  
precinct can have its own challenger, 
watcher or poll book holder. Further, in 
vote center counƟes, there may be a  
challenger, watcher, or poll book holder 
for each electronic poll book staƟon  
present in the voter center or the number 
of ePollbook staƟons speciﬁed in the voter 
center plan, whichever is greater. 
 
County chairs can produce their own  
credenƟals, and those include the name of 
the person, type of credenƟal (watcher, 
challenger, poll book holder), name of the 
person making the appointment and their 
Ɵtle (state or county chair), and the name 
of the poliƟcal party. 
 
 
 
 
Here are the types of credenƟaled persons 
a poll worker may encounter on ElecƟon 
Day: 
 
1) Challengers must be at least 18 years 
old and a registered voter of the county.  
(IC 3-6-7-5)  2) Members of the press can 
be issued media watcher credenƟals and 
enter the polling place to ﬁlm or take pho-
tographs. Voters can require the reporter 
not to photograph them, and no member 
of the press should be ﬁlming in such a 
way to capture how a person voted. (IC 3-
6-10)  3) State AND county chairs can ap-
point watchers, who must be registered 
voters of the county. State law outlines 
their powers and duƟes  in IC 3-6-8-4. 4) 
Pollbook holders are deﬁned and their 
duƟes found in IC 3-6-7 et. seq.  5) County 
elecƟon board members and mechanics 
may also enter a polling site.  
 
OŌen county chairs and precinct  
commiƩeepersons believe they have  
authority to enter a polling locaƟon  
without a credenƟal. This is not true. Any 
person entering the chute and the voƟng 
area besides a voter must have a valid 
credenƟal!  
VR CORNER 
Voter Fail Safes 
State law has several voter “fail-safe” statutes that 
may be helpful to a voter if they’ve recently moved 
or an error is made by the county, which leaves the 
person oﬀ of the poll list.  
 
Perhaps the most frequent quesƟon asked by voters 
is: “I moved. Can I sƟll vote at my old address?” Poll 
workers should ask when and where the voter 
moved, and used the ﬂow chart found in the 2018 
ElecƟon Day Handbook can inform their decision-
making. 
 
There are other voter fail-safes like how to manage a 
person in cancelled status, or a voter who doesn’t 
appear on the poll list but has a receipt from the 
BMV showing they registered before the 10/9 dead-
line, or a voter who doesn’t appear on the poll list 
because of a mistake by the county. 
 
Please take Ɵme to review the details in the purple 
2018 VR Guidebook to ensure the proper laws and 
procedures are being followed. 
QUESTIONS OF THE MONTH 
Q. Can I remake a military or overseas voter’s fax/email 
ballot using the DRE voƟng system? 
A. NO. A faxed/emailed ballot must be made on a ballot card 
and tabulated on the opƟcal scan voƟng system. (IC 3-12-3-5) 
Do not forget to serialize your remade ballots! The remake 
team must  include a serial number on the voter’s ballot and 
use the same number on the remade ballot. This is important in 
the event there is a recount. The folks involved should be able 
to look at the original ballot and the remade ballot to  
ensure the remake team captured the intent of the voter  
appropriately. Don’t forget a qualiﬁed voter using the FPCA can 
request a faxed/emailed ballot through noon, November 5. 
 
Q. Can a voter who was sent an ABS ballot vote a  
regular ballot on ElecƟon Day? 
A. While state law changed several years ago to not allow an 
absentee voter to “beat their ballot” to the polling site, it may 
be permissible for an individual who requested, but did not  
return their ABS ballot, to vote a regular ballot on ElecƟon Day.  
An absentee voter could 1) surrender their uncompleted ballot 
to the Inspector, who would write “cancelled’ on the ABS bal-
lot , store it with the rejected ballots, and issue a regular ballot, 
if the voter is otherwise eligible; or 2) complete the PRE-5  
aﬃdavit to aﬃrm the ballot was not received by the ballot and 
then be issued a regular ballot, if otherwise eligible.

Election Division Dispatch 
 Brad King & Angie Nussmeyer, Co-Directors | December 2018 & January 2019  
NEWS & UPDATES 
Don’t Forget the CAN‐5! 
When a DemocraƟc or Republican candidate ﬁles a 
CAN‐42 to run in the primary elecƟon, counƟes must 
hand‐deliver, email or mail the CAN‐5 (Candidacy Filing  
ConﬁrmaƟon for 2019) no later than one day aŌer  
receiving the candidate’s ﬁling. You can use the form 
found in the shared documents folder of the SVRS 
County Portal or use SVRS to generate the document 
aŌer creaƟng the candidate’s proﬁle in the system.  
QuesƟons? Contact the Quest Help Desk or visit the 
online training portal for a step‐by‐step guide. (NOTE: 
The CAN‐5 is not used when a candidate ﬁles a CAN‐16, 
CAN‐44, CAN‐45, or CAN‐51.) 
 
CAN‐16 & PublicaƟon Updates 
A few sharp eyes caught an error on the CAN‐16 form. 
Instead of the CAN‐19 & CAN‐20, independent and  
minor party candidates ﬁling peƟƟons and consent 
forms use the CAN‐44 & CAN‐45 in 2019. A new version 
of the CAN‐16 has a revision number of (R20/12‐18), 
and can be found on the INSVRS county portal or the 
elecƟon forms webpage. Candidates required to use 
the CAN‐16 to run in a small town convenƟon may use 
the CAN‐16 (R19/6‐18) or the CAN‐16 (R20/12‐18).  
 
At the December conference, we were alerted to an 
error on page 129 of the blue ElecƟon Administrator’s 
Manual about the rules regarding the expiraƟon date 
of a person’s photo ID. An ID that is current or expired 
since the date of the November 6, 2018, general elec‐
Ɵon may be used if the other three criteria are met. 
 
In the orange 2019 Town ElecƟon Guidebook on page 
16, it notes the CAN‐16 may be ﬁled through noon  
February 8, 2019. This is incorrect. The period for a 
DemocraƟc, Libertarian, or Republican candidate to ﬁle 
a CAN‐16  is January 9, 2019, through noon, August 1, 
2019. 
 
Both publicaƟons have been updated and are available 
on the Indiana ElecƟon Division’s website. The printed 
manuals have not been corrected, so please make 
those edits, if you are able.

CANDIDATE QUALIFICATIONS 
County elecƟon administrators are not 
the candidate police! Candidates must 
be fully and properly advised before 
running for oﬃce.  
The red 2019 Candidate Guide is an 
invaluable resource for candidates to 
beƩer understand the requirements 
to run for a speciﬁc oﬃce. Require‐
ments to run may include, but are not 
limited to, residency, voter registra‐
Ɵon status, felony convicƟon re‐
stricƟon, and other consideraƟons 
such as how government employment 
may impact their ability to assume 
oﬃce and retain their job. 
CITY & “LARGE” TOWN OFFICES 
Candidate ﬁling in ciƟes and “large” 
towns (those with a populaƟon of 
more than 3,500 as of the 2010  
census) in 2019 is similar to the pro‐
cess used in 2018. However, the form 
names are diﬀerent and the  
municipaliƟes pay for their elecƟons. 
DemocraƟc and Republican party  
candidate ﬁling for the 2019 primary 
elecƟon started January 9, 2019, and 
ends at noon, February 8, 2019. These 
candidates use the CAN‐42 and  
CAN‐12 with the county clerk. 
Libertarian candidates in ciƟes and 
large towns are nominated by  
convenƟon in order for their  
candidates to appear on the  
November ballot. 
In a future newsleƩer we’ll address 
how the parƟes ﬁll ballot vacancies 
when no candidate ﬁles or a candidate 
withdraws from the November ballot. 
“SMALL” TOWN OFFICES 
For elecƟon purposes, a “small” town 
has a populaƟon of less than 3,500 as 
of the 2010 decennial census. By de‐
fault, a “small” town does not hold a 
May primary elecƟon. Instead, the 
DemocraƟc, Republican, and  
Libertarian candidates are nominated 
at a town convenƟon held in August if 
there is a contest within a party for a 
nominaƟon. The voters aƩending the 
town party’s nominaƟng convenƟon 
will decide which candidate will  
ppear on the November ballot to face 
other party and independent candi‐
dates running for the same oﬃce. 
Candidate ﬁling for the town party 
convenƟon began January 9, 2019, 
and ends at noon, August 1, 2019. The 
forms to ﬁle are the CAN‐16 and the 
CAN‐12, and are ﬁled with the county 
clerk. The orange 2019 Town ElecƟon 
Guide is the best resource to beƩer  
understand the small town  
nominaƟng convenƟon process. 
Some town councils in a “small” town 
adopted an ordinance by January 1, 
2019, for the county elecƟon board to 
conduct a primary elecƟon for the 
DemocraƟc and Republican parƟes. If 
so, the DemocraƟc and Republican 
candidates ﬁle the CAN‐42 and  
CAN‐12, and the ﬁling period is  
January 9, 2019, through noon,  
February 8, 2019. 
Under this scenario where a small 
town has a primary elecƟon, the  
Libertarian party will have a town  
convenƟ
on to nominate their  
candidates, if there is a contest for 
that party’s nominaƟon. 
In a future newsleƩer we’ll address 
ballot vacancies and what happens 
when a town council of a “small” town 
adopts an ordinance for a town  
elecƟon board to conduct the  
November elecƟon. 
INDEPENDENT & MINOR PARTY 
CANDIDATES 
An independent or minor party  
candidate gains ballot access through 
the peƟƟon process (CAN‐44) in order 
for their name to be printed on the 
ballot.  Candidates must collect signa‐
tures of registered voters in precincts 
contained in their elecƟon district to‐
taling at least 2% of the total votes 
cast in the 2018 Secretary of State’s 
elecƟon.  
The CAN‐44 may be ﬁled as early as 
January 9, 2019, and no later than 
noon, July 1, 2019. The county voter 
registraƟon oﬃcial cerƟﬁes the  
individuals are registered voters of the 
elecƟon district. The candidate then 
ﬁles the CAN‐45 consent and CAN‐12 
no later than noon, July 15, 2019, to 
qualify for the ballot. 
To be a declared write‐in candidate 
where the person’s name is NOT  
printed on the ballot, a candidate 
must ﬁle the CAN‐51 and CAN‐12  
earlier than January 9, 2019, and no 
later than noon, July 3, 2019. 
STATEMENT OF ECONOMIC  
INTERESTS (CAN‐12) 
The CAN‐12 is required of every  
person running for a local oﬃce in 
2019. The candidate should ﬁll it out 
looking through the lens of 2018, and 
this should be the year the candidate 
includes near the top of the black box 
where the “20___” appears. You must 
reject a candidate ﬁling if a CAN‐12 is 
not aƩached to the CAN‐16, CAN‐42, 
CAN‐45, CAN‐49, CAN‐50, or CAN‐51. 
FOUR REASONS TO REJECT A  
CANDIDATE FILING 
County elecƟon oﬃcials are not the 
“candidate police” and may ONLY  
reject a candidate ﬁling for these 
FOUR reasons, speci ﬁed in state 
statute: 
1) Candidate running for state oﬃce 
(federal, statewide, state legislaƟve, 
judge, prosecutor) presents candidate 
ﬁling incorrectly to county (Doesn’t 
apply in 2019). IC 3‐5‐4‐1.2 
2) Form ﬁled aŌer the noon, prevailing 
local Ɵme of candidate ﬁling deadline.  
IC 3‐5‐4‐1.9 
3) Filing made on a form NOT  
approved by the state. IC 3‐5‐4‐8 
4) DeclaraƟon of candidacy is not  
accompanied by the required  
statement of economic interest (CAN‐
12). IC 3‐8‐2‐11; 3‐8‐9‐6 
Once a ﬁling has been accepted, it 
may not be rejected. A qualiﬁed indi‐
vidual may ﬁle a CAN‐1 challenge to 
bring the maƩer before the county 
elecƟon board, however. 
InformaƟon in this newsleƩer is provided by the Indiana ElecƟon Division as a courtesy to county elecƟon administrators. If a person is unclear concerning elecƟon law provisions,  
the ElecƟon Division can serve as an interpreƟve source. However, where important legal rights are concerned, you must consult with your own aƩorney to be fully and properly advised.

VR CORNER 
Voter RegistraƟon Records RetenƟon 
IC 3‐7‐33‐8 requires a county VR oﬃcial to maintain the 
acƟve voter’s current registraƟon, assuming it’s a paper 
record, in perpetuity. This now includes scanning the  
paper record and aƩaching it to the voter’s informaƟon in 
SVRS.  
If at any point the voter moves within or out of your  
jurisdicƟon, paper forms corresponding to the cancelled 
registraƟon address must be 1) scanned in to SVRS and 2) 
retained for at least 24‐months following the next general 
elecƟon. AŌer this 24‐month period, the county may de‐
stroy the paper document by following the proper proto‐
cols. 
For example, Jane moves within Tipton County from Main 
Street to First Avenue, and submits the update on a VRG‐7 
on January 10, 2019. Tipton County must scan the new 
record with the First Avenue address into SVRS.  The  
paper VRG‐7 form with the old Main Street address must 
also be scanned and stored in SVRS, and it becomes  
eligible for destrucƟon on or aŌer November 4, 2022, or 
24‐months aŌer the November 3, 2020, general elecƟon. 
(Before this change, the county would need to maintain 
both of Jane’s records unƟl her voter status moved to can‐
celled in Tipton County.) 
Paper documents include, but are not limited to, the VRG‐
7, VRG‐11, federal VR form, VR forms submiƩed by full‐
service agencies, and the “paper chaser” BMV VR form. 
There is no requirement to print online voter registraƟon 
forms or electronic submissions from the BMV. However, 
if your county creates a paper record for the electronic 
submission, then you must follow the retenƟon schedule 
as noted above for the printed copy of the electronic  
record. 
QUESTIONS OF THE MONTH 
Q. When I enter candidate names into SVRS, do I use all 
CAPS or mixed case? And how do we change the oﬃce 
Ɵtles?  
A. To ensure consistency on reporƟng documents and on 
indianavoters.com, mixed case is preferred when entering 
candidate names in SVRS. We also updated SVRS a few 
years ago to ensure all oﬃce names in the 92‐counƟes 
aligned with the statutory name of the oﬃce. SOP 
“EM04.4. Naming Standards in SVRS” was created to 
share these naming standards with counƟes. If you need 
an oﬃce name change to conﬁrm with state law, please 
reach out to the HAVA Administrator 
(HAVAadministrator@sos.in.gov), who will need to make 
it for you; however, the name change must align with the 
oﬃce naming standards. 
 
Q. I have an independent candidate running for a town 
council district, but the district is smaller than one pre‐
cinct. How do I compute the 2% signature requirement? 
A. Our best advice is to calculate the 2% against the total 
votes cast for 2018 SOS in the whole precinct, even 
though the elecƟon district might be smaller than the  
precinct itself. As a reminder, if the resulƟng number is a  
fracƟon like 2.67, then you round down the signature  
requirement to 2. 
EAC SURVEY 
AŌer each even‐numbered November general elecƟon, 
the U.S. ElecƟon Assistance Commission asks states for 
speciﬁc data related to the federal elecƟon. While much 
of the data can be pulled from SVRS, our oﬃce does need 
input from county elecƟon administrators. 
 
Many thanks to those counƟes that have completed the 
EAC surveys. The deadline to submit responses to the  
survey is January 18, 2019. If you have ques Ɵons, please 
be in touch with Tom White, who is managing the project 
for us, at Thomas.white@bakerƟlly.com. 
CAMPAIGN FINANCE REMINDERS 
If an elected oﬃce pays $5,000 or more in a calendar year, 
then a candidate must ﬁle a CFA‐1: 
1) no later than noon, ten days a Ōer raising or spending 
more than $100 toward running for oﬃce; or 
2) a Ōer ﬁling a declaraƟon of candidacy (for example, CAN‐
16, CAN‐42) or consent (for example, CAN‐45), no later 
than noon, ten days aŌer ﬁling the declaraƟon or no later 
than noon, seven days aŌer the ﬁling deadline, whichever 
comes sooner. 
 
As an example, Sally ﬁles for mayor on January 9, and the 
oﬃce pays more than $5,000 a year. She needs to ﬁle the  
CFA‐1 no later than noon, ten days aŌer January 9 to comply 
with state law. Michael ﬁles for mayor on February 8, which is 
the candidate ﬁling deadline. He has to ﬁle his commiƩee’s 
CFA‐1 no later than noon, seven days, since February 8 is the 
ﬁling deadline for the May primary elecƟon. 
 
If an elected oﬃce pays less than $5,000 a calendar year, then 
the candidate ﬁles a CFA‐1 no later than noon, ten days aŌer 
raising or spending  more than $500 toward running for oﬃce. 
For example, MarƟn ﬁles to run for dogcatcher on January 10, 
2019. He spends $750 on t‐shirts on June 1. He has to ﬁle a 
CFA‐1 no later than noon, ten days aŌer the June 1st  
expenditure. 
OTHER KEY RESOURCES 
 
2019 ElecƟon Forms 
Forms can be found in two places: 
1) SVRS County Portal. County SVRS users can ﬁnd the 2019 forms in the “Shared Documents” folder on the 
portal. This folder can also be downloaded in its enƟrety and saved to your work computer. If you need 
assistance in learning how the portal works, please contact the Quest Help desk. 
2) Indiana Elec Ɵon Division website: hƩps://www.in.gov/sos/elecƟons/4564.htm. The web page is public 
facing, and can be a resource to your candidates and other public and party oﬃcials. 
 
Brochures & PublicaƟons 
CounƟes can order addiƟonal printed guidebooks by submiƫng an IEC‐7 form with the required payment. 
Those same publicaƟons can be access through the ElecƟon Division’s website under the “ElecƟon  
Administrator’s Portal.” 
 
“ElecƟon Day” Outreach Materials 
Materials produced by the Help America Vote Administrator (HAVA) like the 2019 ElecƟon Day Handbook 
oŌen used by poll workers, Military & Overseas Voters Guide, and other materials like the Voters’ Bill of 
Rights can be found on the ElecƟon Division’s website in the Help America Vote Act Outreach Library. Printed 
versions of these materials will be available to county elecƟon administrators this spring. Please be sure to 
reach out to Brandon Kline (HAVAadministrator@sos.in.gov) to place your order for the primary elecƟon! 
SVRS RESOURCES FOR NEW STAFF

 Do you know your SVRS county admins?

 If you are a token county, do you have all of the tokens your staﬀ needs to access the system?  
(NOTE: All counƟes will be required to use tokens in 2019) 
 
Quest Help Desk 
Don’t know the answers to the checklist quesƟons? Contact the Quest Help Desk:  
PHONE: 888 467 8771 EMAIL: helpdesk@QuesƟs.com 
 
New User Training for SVRS 
Quest has scheduled a third new user online training on January 21, 2019. This training lasts about 2 ‐hours, 
and will walk through the key features of the statewide voter registraƟon system. The 2019 web training cal‐
endar is also posted to the county portal. The webinars highlight key processes and walk through the step‐by‐
steps training materials. 
On‐Site SVRS Training 
Want a hands‐on experience? Reach out to the Quest Help Desk and ask for a county authorizaƟon form, 
which is submiƩed to the state for review. Once approved, Quest staﬀ will visit your oﬃce to provide on‐site 
SVRS training to your team.
