Election Division Dispatch 
 Brad King & Angie Nussmeyer, Co-Directors | February 2019 
NEWS & UPDATES 
Regular Party CommiƩee Reports Due 3/1 
Regular party commiƩees (that is, commiƩees 
opened using the CFA‐3 and are usually county party 
commiƩees) are required to ﬁle the 2018 Annual  
Report not later than noon (prevailing local Ɵme), 
March 1, 2019. 
Where the party commiƩee ﬁles their CFA‐4 depends 
on where the CFA‐3 (statement of organizaƟon) was 
ﬁled. Some party commiƩees choose to ﬁle with the 
ElecƟon Division because they support statewide or 
state legislaƟve commiƩees and are therefore  
required to ﬁle with the state. Others who do not 
support state or legislaƟve candidates ﬁle the CFA‐4 
with the county clerk. 
A reminder that regular party commiƩees will have to 
ﬁle pre‐primary and pre‐elecƟon reports this year, 
but are exempt from ﬁling the CFA‐11 large  
contribuƟon reports. (The CFA‐11 reports are only 
ﬁled by candidate commiƩees.) Further, a regular 
party commiƩee only needs to itemize contribuƟons 
or expenditures that exceed $200 in a calendar year. 
March Build 
Though updates are pushed regularly to SVRS, larger 
projects are called a “build” and occur a few Ɵmes a 
year. A few updates coming next month should be of 
interest to county users: 
 
The Ballot Names ﬁeld format has been changed to 
allow for standardizaƟon, and names will now appear 
in the correct format. For example, John A Smith not 
JOHN A SMITH. 
“Get Winners” funcƟonality will now be available to 
county users, and will allow you to copy winners from 
the Primary to the General ElecƟon to help avoid  
unnecessary duplicate data entry. 
Currently, peƟƟon reports are only available in the 
peƟƟon module. Everyone will soon be able to access 
the informaƟon in the “ElecƟon” category of  the  
Reports Library.

primary ordinance was passed, some “Small” Towns 
Under Indiana law a candidate is required to meet speciﬁc qualiﬁcaƟons to run 
for oﬃce or to claim party aﬃliaƟon when running in a primary elecƟon or small 
town convenƟon. A county chair or a voter in the elecƟon district may have  
informaƟon that alleges a candidate does not meet those qualiﬁcaƟons. If so, the 
individual may ﬁle a challenge using the CAN‐1 form not later than the deadline 
set forth in state law.  
Each ﬁling type has its own unique challenge period, which is further complicated 
in a municipal elecƟon year due to “small” town elecƟons where no primary  
elecƟon is held: 
1) DeclaraƟon of Candidacy (CAN‐42) for Primary ElecƟon. A CAN‐1 challenge 
must be ﬁled by noon, February 15, 2019, and the CEB must decide the  
validity of the challenge not later than February 28, 2019. 
2) PeƟƟon of NominaƟon (CAN‐44) for candidates running in a city or “large” 
town elecƟon. A CAN‐1 challenge must be ﬁled by noon, August 23, 2019, 
and the CEB must decide the validity not later than noon, September 6, 2019. 
NOTE: If a candidate does not qualify for the ballot and wishes to dispute any 
rejected signatures on the peƟƟon, then the candidate ﬁles a CAN‐1  
challenge to be aﬀorded an opportunity for a hearing. 
3) CerƟﬁcate of NominaƟon to Fill a Ballot Vacancy (CAN‐44) for candidates 
running in a city or “large” town. A CAN‐1 challenge must be ﬁled by noon, 
August 23, 2019, and the CEB must decide the validity not later than noon, 
September 6, 2019 
4) DeclaraƟon of Intent to be a write‐in candidate (CAN‐51). A CAN‐1 chal‐
lenge must be ﬁled no later than noon, August 9, 2019, and the CEB must 
decide the validity of the challenge not later than noon, August 16, 2019. 
5) Small Town Oﬃces. This applies to the declara Ɵon of Candidacy (CAN ‐16) 
for a Small Town Oﬃce where No Primary was Conducted; a peƟƟon of  
nominaƟon (CAN‐44); or a cerƟﬁcate of nominaƟon (CAN‐48). A CAN‐1  
challenge must be ﬁled by noon, September 4, 2019, and the CEB must  
decide the validity not later than noon, September 11, 2019. 
Should a CAN‐1 challenge be ﬁled, the CEB must schedule a hearing and give best 
possible noƟce to the challenger and the challenged candidate of the date, Ɵme 
and locaƟon of the hearing. Both parƟes, if present, must be aﬀorded the  
opportunity to present their facts and evidence supporƟng or dispuƟng the  
challenge. Once tesƟmony has concluded, the CEB members must review the 
facts, apply the law, and take a vote at the public meeƟng to determine if the 
candidate will remain on the ballot. The CEB should take acƟon on the challenges 
not later than the dates noted above. 
VR CORNER 
Sheriﬀ & Dept. of Health 
Quarterly Reports 
State law requires the county 
sheriﬀ to provide, at minimum, a 
quarterly report of individuals 
who are imprisoned following 
convicƟon. (IC 3‐7‐46‐6) Those 
reports are due to the county VR 
oﬃcial not later than January 31, 
April 30, July 31, and October 31, 
of each year. The sheriﬀ must 
aƩach the VRG‐1 form to the 
quarterly report.  
 
The reporƟng systems used by 
the sheriﬀs vary from county, so 
the individual county reports 
may not be uniform across the 
state. CounƟes will need to  
evaluate the informaƟon 
provided by the sheriﬀ to  
conﬁrm that an individual is  
currently imprisoned following 
convicƟon of a crime.  
 
If the individual is awaiƟng  
sentencing or has been released 
before the voter registraƟon 
oﬃce received the sheriﬀ’s  
report, then the individual’s  
record may not be cancelled. If 
the individual’s record is eligible 
for cancellaƟon, the county 
sends noƟce to the alleged  
disfranchised person at their last 
known address not later than the 
day aŌer their registraƟon status 
was moved to cancelled. (IC 3‐7‐
46‐9) 
 
The local department of health is 
required to ﬁle quarterly “death” 
reports with the county auditor. 
The county VR oﬃcial is required 
to request a copy of this report, 
and if a person is idenƟﬁed as 
being deceased, then the  
person’s registraƟon status is to 
be moved to cancelled. (IC 3‐7‐45
‐2.1(e))

the ElecƟon Division can serve as an interpreƟve source. However, where important legal rights are concerned, you must consult with your own aƩorney to be fully and properly advised. 
IN FOCUS: CANDIDATE CHALLENGES 
Candidate Set‐Up in SVRS 
In preparing for the 2019 Municipal Primary ElecƟon please be sure to set 
up your candidates in SVRS. The “Candidate Summary” and “Candidate 
Detail” reports available in the “ElecƟon” category of the reports library 
are helpful with this project. If this is an oﬃce that has not been added to 
SVRS, please submit a county authorizaƟon form to Brandon Kline  
requesƟng that he set up the oﬃce. (BrKline@sos.in.gov). If you have 
quesƟons about candidate or oﬃce set up please reach out to the Quest 
Help Desk at 888‐467‐8771 or helpdesk@quesƟs.com. 
QUESTIONS OF THE MONTH 
Q. Can in‐person early voƟng hours in the Clerk’s Oﬃce be 
reduced in a municipal elecƟon year? 
Yes. State law allows for the county elec Ɵon board (CEB) 
to reduce “early” voƟng hours in a municipal elecƟon year, 
if the board unanimously agrees to do so. However, should 
such a resoluƟon be adopted, the CEB may not mail ABS‐
mail ballots unƟl the ﬁrst day of “early” voƟng begins. In 
other words, if a CEB restricts “early” voƟng to the 7‐days 
before an elecƟon, then ABS‐mail ballot would be mailed  
7‐days before elecƟon day. (NOTE: Military/overseas voters 
with a Federal Postcard ApplicaƟon (FPCA) on ﬁle must 
have their ballots sent not later than 45‐days before an 
elecƟon.) (IC 3‐11‐10‐26.5) 
Further, all vote center counƟes are required to have at 
least one vote center open the two Saturdays before an 
elecƟon. This requirement cannot be eliminated from a 
vote center plan in a municipal elecƟon year. (IC 3‐11‐18.1‐
4(17)) 
 Q. Our city elecƟon has a contested race for mayor, but all 
of the other races are uncontested in that party’s primary. 
Do all names need to appear on that party’s primary bal‐
lot? 
Yes. State law requires that if there is one contested race 
in a municipal primary elecƟon, then all oﬃces and  
candidate names for that party must appear on the ballot. 
However, if the contested race is limited to a council  
district seat, then the CEB can unanimously agree to only 
print the contested council district race and conduct a  
primary elecƟon in only those precincts within the elecƟon 
district. This excepƟon does not apply to other oﬃces or to 
a contest in a council at‐large seat. (IC 3‐10‐6‐4) 
Q. Are candidate ﬁlings like a declaraƟon of candidacy 
public informaƟon? 
Yes. With the excep Ɵon of full social security numbers, all 
informaƟon contained  in a candidate ﬁling is public  
informaƟon, including phone numbers and addresses. In  
fact, the noƟce of primary elecƟon must be published in a 
newspaper not later than Saturday, April 27, 2019,  and it is 
to include, among other things, the name, address, and 
oﬃce sought of each candidate seeking nominaƟon. A  
recent change in state law does make it possible for certain 
candidates to withhold their address informaƟon from  
publicaƟon, if they peƟƟon the county assessor to redact 
their address from the property tax online database and if 
approved, ﬁle a document with the county elecƟon board 
to restrict their address from newspaper publicaƟon.  
(IC 36‐1‐8.5) 
No Primary Election Needed?  
 
In a municipal elecƟon year, it is possible that a 
city or town will not hold a May primary elecƟon 
because there are no contested races, and the  
party chair has not requested that the county  
conduct a primary by the deadline. (IC 3‐10‐6‐4) 
 
If this occurs in your county, the county elecƟon 
board sƟll needs to cerƟfy the city and town  
winners for the November municipal elecƟon. 
There is no prescribed form to do so; instead, our 
best advice is to list all of the nominated candi‐
dates on oﬃce leƩerhead and read it into the 
minutes of your county elecƟon board meeƟng. 
There is no requirement to ﬁle a list with the  
ElecƟon Division.  
Public Questions 
Indiana law authorizes only certain public quesƟons 
to appear on primary, municipal, general, and special 
elecƟon ballots. The Indiana ElecƟon Division  
publishes a referendum brochure, which goes into 
more detail about the types of quesƟons that might 
be cerƟﬁed to the county elecƟon board, and is  
available at  hƩps://www.in.gov/sos/elecƟons/
ﬁles/2019%20Referendum%20Brochure.ﬁnal.pdf. 
 
The most common types are school tax levy and  
controlled project referendums, which are brought 
about by local units of government or school  
corporaƟons. A school tax levy, if approved, would 
create a new funding stream for the school  
corporaƟon for a speciﬁc period of Ɵme. The school 
board would approve a public quesƟon at a public 
meeƟng, and must cerƟfy the quesƟon to the CEB 
not later than 60‐days before a primary elecƟon or 
not later than August 1 for the municipal elecƟon. 
 
A capital project referendum would allow a school 
corporaƟon or local unit of government to issue 
bonds to service debt or enter into lease agreements 
for certain construcƟon projects. There are a few 
ways for this type of quesƟon to be placed on the 
ballot. The Department of Local Government  
Finance (in.gov/dlgf) has a very helpful referendum 
web page that provides these steps. A capital project 
referendum quesƟon must be cerƟﬁed to the CEB 
not later than noon, 74‐days before a primary  
elecƟon, or not later than noon, August 1 for the  
municipal elecƟon.

Election Division Dispatch 
 Brad King & Angie Nussmeyer, Co-Directors | March 2019 
NEWS & UPDATES 
User Audit 
To help to maintain the security of SVRS, an audit of  
users accounts in SVRS is performed each year. Any  
accounts that are no longer in use should be expired.  
In addiƟon to the methods employed to harden access to 
our systems, the user audit is a criƟcal element in  
maintaining the security of our statewide voter  
registraƟon system. The person serving as the county’s  
SVRS administrator is to review and update user accounts 
on an ongoing basis; however, this audit conﬁrms all  
counƟes are being vigilant on the managing user access. 
The “Password Reset Management Step‐by‐Step” is  
available on the SVRS county portal. This document walks 
you through the process of perform the audit. If you have 
quesƟons or require addiƟonal assistance an SVRS User  
Audit Training will be held on Wednesday, March 13 from 
3:00‐4:30 pm ET and Thursday, March 14 from 10:30am – 
12:00pm ET. The deadline to complete this audit and  
survey is Friday, March 15, 2019.  
AŌer compleƟng the audit, please navigate to the “user  
audit” message in your SVRS hopper and complete the  
survey to conﬁrm compliance with this request. Failure to 
complete this acƟvity by the deadline may result in a  
temporary loss of SVRS access.  
Municipal Primary ElecƟon Survey 
In the coming weeks county elecƟon administrators will  
be asked to complete a survey to document which  
municipaliƟes will be conducƟng primary elecƟons in 2019. 
Please keep an eye out for an email from the co‐directors. 
 
Absentee Ballot Ready Date 
SVRS includes a “ballot ready date” to note when  
absentee ballots are to be mailed by your county. Since the 
deadline to mail absentee ballots is 45‐days before each 
elecƟon, the ballot ready date for this elecƟon will default 
to March 23. If you would like to move up this date (for  
example, March 21), please submit a county  
authorizaƟon form to the HAVA Administrator with your 
preferred date. For those counƟes with reduced in‐person 
early voƟng dates and Ɵmes, you may not mail ballots to 
“domesƟc” voters earlier than the ﬁrst date of in‐person 
early voƟng; however, you must mail your military /
overseas ballots by the March 23 deadline.

Special Ballot Styles 
In a primary elecƟon, a county must 
print one ballot style for the Demo‐
craƟc Party and one ballot style for 
the Republican Party. (Of course this 
year it is possible no primary elecƟon 
will be held because a party has no 
contested races, and prinƟng a ballot 
is not necessary.) 
However, some jurisdicƟons will have 
a public quesƟon cerƟﬁed to them for 
the May primary, which requires its 
own special “non‐parƟsan” ballot style 
for those voters who do not want to 
vote in a party’s primary elecƟon but 
do want to vote on the referendum. 
If your municipality is having a primary 
elecƟon AND there is a public  
quesƟon that appears in some or all of 
the precincts in the municipality, then 
you must 1) print the public quesƟon 
on the D & R primary ballots, 2) create 
a non‐parƟsan ballot with only the 
public quesƟon for the reason stated 
above, and 3) print a special 17‐year 
old D & R ballot that does NOT include 
the public quesƟon but does include 
the candidates. 
Don’t forget that primary elecƟon  
ballots should have the name of each 
party printed near the top of the  
ballot, and it’s also permissible to in‐
clude color coding to allow for beƩer 
visual idenƟﬁcaƟon for poll workers to 
pull the proper party’s ballot  
requested by the voter.  
Ballot PrinƟng Orders for May  
Primary ElecƟon 
1) Be sure to es Ɵmate the number of 
provisional and absentee ballots 
your county will need not later 
than March 8, 2019. 
2) Order the number of ballots your 
county will need for absentee 
voƟng by March 18, 2019. (If your 
county uses a ballot‐on‐demand 
printer, then the CD or equivalent 
with the ballot ﬁles should be  
delivered by this date.) 
3) Coun Ɵes using opƟcal scan paper 
ballot cards or tradiƟonal hand‐
counted paper ballots need to 
order ElecƟon Day ballots. The 
print order should arrive on Ɵme 
for your county to organize the 
ballots for pick‐up by Inspectors 
the Saturday before the elecƟon. 
To order ElecƟon Day ballots for the 
May primary elecƟon, a county needs 
to review its 2018 November elecƟon 
precinct level results and idenƟfy 
which DemocraƟc candidate was the 
top vote geƩer in each precinct, and 
which Republican  candidate was the 
top vote geƩer in each precinct to set 
forth the minimum ballot order. 
 
Figure 1 below is an example of how 
many ballots and of which party type 
should be ordered for each precinct 
on ElecƟon Day. (No, state law does 
not permit counƟes to back out any 
absentee voters; you must follow this 
law for ordering in the primary.) 
 
Some counƟes use a voƟng system 
where a blank ballot card is inserted 
into a ballot marking device, the voter 
makes their selecƟons, and a complet‐
ed ballot card is printed for the voter 
to insert into the opScan tabulator. 
You would sƟll follow the ballot order‐
ing rules, though instead of having 
printed ballots, you would be ordering 
blank ballot stock at this minimum 
threshold. 
 
If you are a vote center county using 
printed ballot cards or blank ballot 
card stock, then you’ll want to go 
through this same exercise and sum

a total minimum to deliver to each

Please note: in the November elecƟon 
a county is required to have enough

precinct. This would include printed 
opScan ballot cards or paper ballots or 
blank opScan ballot stock. Again, a 
county elecƟon  board is not

17‐year old Voters 
Indiana law allows a 17‐year old to register and vote if they turn 
18 on or before the date of the municipal elecƟon, November 5, 
2019 and the person lives within a municipality OR the date of 
the November 3, 2020 elecƟon if the person lives in an  
unincorporated part of the county. In these cases, the person 
should answer “yes” to the quesƟon “Will you be 18 on ElecƟon 
Day” if their birthday falls on or before the date of the Novem‐
ber elecƟon applicable to them. 
 
An “underage” voter can also parƟcipate in the May primary. 
However, if a public quesƟon has been cerƟﬁed to appear on the 
May primary ballot, the county must create a special “17‐year 
old” ballot for each party’s primary that lists the candidates but 
excludes the public quesƟons.  
 
The reason for the special ballot is needed is that an “underage” 
voter can nominate which candidates from their poliƟcal party 
that they want to appear on the November ballot, but cannot 
vote in an elecƟon where the outcome is determined, such as a 
referendum elecƟon. 
Statewide VLM Project Preview 
The ElecƟon Division is required to engage in a statewide voter list 
maintenance project in each odd‐numbered year under state law, 
which means the project will launch right aŌer the May 2019 pri‐
mary elecƟon. The project’s implementaƟon follows federal elec‐
Ɵon law guidelines and consists of two mailers: 
1) Card 1: Sent to the mailing address of every acƟve voter in 
Indiana via USPS non‐forwardable mail. In 2019, the ﬁrst card 
should be mailed in late May. If the card is returned  
undeliverable pursuant to IC 3‐5‐2‐49.7, then card 2 is sent to 
the voter. 
2) Card 2: Sent by USPS forwar dable mail to the mailing address 
of a person whose card 1 is returned undeliverable. Card 2 
allows the person to a) conﬁrm their residence address is their 
registraƟon address or b) update their registraƟon within the 
county or c) cancel their registraƟon if they’ve moved out of 
county. 
Card 2 is the main focus for county VR oﬃcials. The vendor will 
enter InformaƟon from the “response card.” If the  response is 
unclear, then the county VR oﬃcial makes the determinaƟon in the 
VLM ExcepƟons hopper. County VR oﬃcials must also review the 
other VLM related hoppers to conﬁrm the returned voter cards 
with the voter’s request were correctly categorized. 
If a voter does not respond to card 2 or card 2 is returned  
undeliverable, then the voter is placed in the county’s VLM inacƟve  
hopper and should be marked inacƟve on or before the 90‐day 
freeze deadline of August 7, 2019. More details about the project 
will be shared as the contract is ﬁnalized. 
Upcoming Public Notices 
 
Before each elecƟon there are a minimum of three 
public noƟces that must be published in a  
newspaper in accordance with IC 5‐3‐1, generally. 
Those noƟces include: 
 
1) NoƟce of Public Test. NoƟce must be  
published in the newspaper not later than 48‐
hours before the county’s public test of voƟng 
equipment. The CEB is required to pay for its 
publicaƟon, and there is no prescribed state 
form  (IC 3‐11‐14.5‐2; IC 3‐11‐13‐22)  
2) CAN‐9 NoƟce of Primary ElecƟon. NoƟce 
must be published not later than 10 calendar 
days before the elecƟon. The CEB is required 
to pay for its publicaƟon, and counƟes are to 
use the CAN‐9 form. A copy of this noƟce is to 
be ﬁled with IED. (IC 3‐8‐2‐19)  Note: If  
candidates were entered into SVRS, a CAN‐9 
can be generated through the SVRS Reports 
Library. 
3) NoƟce of Polling LocaƟons (including Vote 
Centers). This noƟce must be published not 
later than 10 calendar days before the  
elecƟon. The county commissioners are  
required to pay for its publicaƟon, and there is 
no special state form. (IC 3‐11‐8‐3.2) 
 
Please note: unless speciﬁcally noted in statute 
like those above, CEB meeƟngs do not need to be 
published in the newspaper, though a CEB may do 
so if desired. Be certain to follow the state’s Open 
Door Law to post proper noƟce as required.  
QUESTIONS OF THE MONTH 
Q. Do I need to update polling locaƟons, including 
vote center sites, in SVRS? 
A. Yes! If you have quesƟons about candidate or 
oﬃce set up please reach out to the Quest Help 
Desk at 888‐467‐8771 or helpdesk@quesƟs.com. 
Q. If a candidate ﬁles a CAN‐42 to run in the May 
primary elecƟon and the city or town is NOT 
holding a primary elecƟon because one or both 
poliƟcal parƟes do not have a contested primary, 
does the candidate in this case have to ﬁle a pre‐
primary CFA‐4 report and comply with the 48‐
hour CFA‐11 reporƟng requirements? 
A. Yes! If a candidate has ﬁled a CAN‐42 to run in 
the primary and is required to open a campaign 
ﬁnance commiƩee, then the candidate must ﬁle a 
pre‐primary report and report any “large”  
contribuƟons during the CFA‐11 reporƟng window.

InformaƟon in this newsleƩer is provided by the Indiana ElecƟon Division as a courtesy to county elecƟon administrators. If a person is unclear concerning elecƟon law provisions,  
the ElecƟon Division can serve as an interpreƟve source. However, where important legal rights are concerned, you must consult with your own aƩorney to be fully and properly advised. 
Independent and minor party candidates have two ways to 
access the ballot—through the pe ƟƟon process or to be a 
write‐in candidate. 
 
If an independent or minor party candidate wants to have 
their name printed on the ballot, then they must go through 
the peƟƟon process. The candidate must collect signatures 
of registered voters within the elecƟon district totaling at 
least 2% of the total votes cast in the 2018 Secretary of 
State race in the precincts of the elecƟon district. This 
means county elecƟon oﬃcials will need to pull out the  
November 2018 precinct level results and calculate the  
signature threshold for local oﬃces to be elected in 2019.  
 
CAN‐44 peƟƟons must be ﬁled with the county VR oﬃcial 
not earlier than January 9, 2019, and not later than noon, 
July 1, 2019, in order to be reviewed and cerƟﬁed. The can‐
didate must also submit, along with their cerƟﬁed CAN‐44 
peƟƟons, a CAN‐45 consent and CAN‐12 statement of eco‐
nomic interest to the county elecƟon board not later than 
noon, July 15, 2019, to complete their ﬁling.  
 
The county clerk must send, by cerƟﬁed mail, a leƩer to the 
candidate if their ﬁling is not approved. A candidate may ﬁle 
a CAN‐1 challenge no later than noon, Friday, August 23, 
2019, to contest the decision to reject a peƟƟon of nomina‐
Ɵon. If the candidate’s ﬁling is approved, then there is no 
need to noƟfy the individual. Pages 59‐66 of the 2019 Voter 
RegistraƟon Guidebook go into great detail on peƟƟon  
review, including the peƟƟon carrier aﬃdavit requirement 
and compleƟon of the cerƟﬁcaƟon found on the back of the 
CAN‐44 form. 
 
Some individuals want to be a write‐in candidate. WRITE‐IN 
CANDIDATES ARE NOT PRINTED ON THE BALLOT! Instead, 
a write‐in line must be printed on the ballot, and poll work‐
ers canvass to determine and count a write‐in vote based 
on the list of declared write‐in candidates provided by the 
CEB. To be a declared write‐in candidate, the person must  
submit the CAN‐3 not earlier than January 9 2019, and not 
later than noon, July 3, 2019, along with the CAN‐12  
statement of economic interest. 
QUESTIONS OF THE MONTH 
Q. Can an absentee voter requesƟng a Demo‐
craƟc ballot in the primary change their mind 
and re‐ﬁle an applicaƟon or otherwise request 
a Republican ballot (or vice versa)? 
A. No, a voter may not change their mind and  
request a diﬀerent parƟsan absentee ballot to re‐
place the one they’ve already requested.  
 
Q. My newspaper failed to publish my noƟce 
for a public test. Do I have to reschedule it? 
A. Not necessarily. State law permits a county 
where the newspaper failed to Ɵmely publish a no‐
Ɵce to allow the county to either 1) display the no‐
Ɵce prominently in three locaƟons in the county or 
2) post on the county’s website (IC 5‐3‐1‐2(k)). 
 
Q. What am I required to publish on the CAN‐
9? Do I need to do anything more with it be‐
sides publishing in the newspaper? 
A. The CAN‐9 should include the names, addresses, 
poliƟcal party, and oﬃce sought for each candidate 
ﬁling a CAN‐42 with your oﬃce. If the county is not 
conducƟng a primary for one or both poliƟcal par‐
Ɵes, then it is not necessary to publish the AƩach‐
ment “A” (DemocraƟc Party candidates) or AƩach‐
ment “B” (Republican Party candidates) unless your 
county elecƟon board chooses to do so. AƩachment 
“C” of the CAN‐9 would include any text of a public 
quesƟon, if a special elecƟon were called to vote on 
a referendum quesƟon. As a reminder, there is a 
report in the SVRS library that will create your CAN‐
9 (and in the fall, CAN‐39). The CAN‐9 does need to 
be published in the newspaper not later than April 
27, 2019, and a copy ﬁled with the Indiana ElecƟon 
Division and in the minutes of a county elecƟon 
board meeƟng. (IC 3‐8‐2‐19) 
 
Q. Can a candidate withdraw before the  
primary elecƟon? 
A. Yes, but only if the person moves out of their 
elecƟon district or is convicted of a felony. Other‐
wise, a candidate who is seeking their party’s nomi‐
naƟon in May must remain on the ballot. If nomi‐
nated, the person may ﬁle a CAN‐46 to withdraw for 
any reason on or aŌer May 8 and up to noon, July 
15. If a candidate withdraws aŌer the primary, the 
party may ﬁll the vacancy and has up unƟl 30‐days 
from the date of the vacancy to do so. 
IN FOCUS: Independent &  
Minor Party Candidate Filings 
VR CORNER 
VR in Municipal ElecƟons 
A few counƟes do not have municipal elecƟons in 2019, 
and therefore, statewide voter registraƟon deadlines 
would not apply to their voters. In this case, the county 
VR oﬃcial will review and process voter registraƟon 
forms year‐round. 
 
However, most counƟes will conduct elecƟons within 
their municipaliƟes this year, which means the statewide 
voter registraƟon deadline would only apply to some  
voters.  For those individuals living in the unincorporated 
porƟons of the county (in other words, not in a munici‐
pality), there likely will be no registraƟon deadline in 
2019.  The statewide VR deadline would only apply to 
voters living within the municipality. 
 
In some ciƟes and “large” towns (and “small” towns, if 
the town council passed an ordinance for the CEB to hold 
a primary elecƟon) the CEB may not be holding a primary 
elecƟon for the DemocraƟc and Republican parƟes under 
IC 3‐10‐6‐4. If no primary is being held for both poliƟcal 
parƟes within a municipality, then county VR oﬃcials do 
not need to enforce the April 8, 2019, statewide voter 
registraƟon deadline within this speciﬁc municipality 
where no elecƟon is held.  
 
VR ApplicaƟons & Postmarks 
The statewide voter registraƟon deadline for the May 
primary elecƟon is Monday, April 8, 2019 for voters  
living within a municipality. Before your team delays  
processing a VR applicaƟon received by mail aŌer this 
deadline, please be sure to check the postmark on the 
envelope. The postmark is a criƟcal piece of informaƟon 
to determine whether or not a VR form can be  
processed  for the May elecƟon. 
 
If a VR form is mailed to your oﬃce and received aŌer 
April 8, 2019, and includes a legible postmark dated on or 
before April 8, 2019, then your county must process the 
form. (IC 3‐7‐33‐4) If a VR form is mailed to your oﬃce, 
includes an illegible or NO postmark, and is received aŌer 
April 8, 2019, but on or before Monday, April 15, 2019, 
then your county must to process the forms. (IC 3‐7‐33‐4; 
IC 3‐7‐33‐3.7) 
 
These same rules apply to VR forms received by the  
Indiana ElecƟon Division, and forwarded to your county.  
Review pages 10‐11 of the 2019 Indiana Voter  
RegistraƟon Guidebook for more details, including the 
deadlines for online voter registraƟon and hand‐delivery. 
Ballot Vacancies Several counƟes have asked about the process for the DemocraƟc or Republican parƟes to ﬁll 
a ballot vacancy, if the party did not have a candidate ﬁle a CAN‐42 to seek nominaƟon in a  primary elecƟon. Details 
about the process to ﬁll ballot vacancies are found on pages 25‐28 of the 2019 ElecƟon Administrator’s Manual. NOTE: 
These procedures do not apply to a candidate ﬁling a CAN‐16 to become the nominee for the DemocraƟc & Republi‐
can parƟes in a “small” town oﬃce, as the nominaƟng convenƟons (if needed) are held in August 2019. 
ConducƟng ElecƟons for MunicipaliƟes 
in more than One County  
There was a recent change in law that may impact those 
counƟes where boundaries of a municipality are in more 
than one county. IC 3‐6‐5‐15 states that the county con‐
taining the greatest percentage of the populaƟon may 
designate the polling places for the elecƟon, which may be 
located in any county in which the poliƟcal subdivision is 
located, and shall appoint poll workers to conduct the 
elecƟon upon nominaƟon by the county chair of the coun‐
ty where the precinct is located or by ﬁlling a vacancy if a 
nominaƟon is not Ɵmely made. 
 
However, each county elecƟon board must provide poll 
lists, receive and approve absentee ballot applicaƟons, 
issue cerƟﬁcates of error or other documents for the vot‐
ers of that county, print ballots, and canvass results.  
For example, “Indiana City” has 5 precincts in Wayne 
County and 3 precincts in Randolph County, where the 
greatest populaƟon is in Wayne County. The Wayne  
County CEB can establish polling places exclusively in 
Wayne County or in both counƟes. The Wayne and  
Randolph county party chairs would nominate their poll 
workers to the Wayne County ElecƟon Board. However, 
each CEB would conduct poll worker training, produce poll 
lists, build ballots, code voƟng systems, and manage  
ElecƟon Day for their speciﬁc precincts. AŌer canvassing 
the results, Randolph County would cerƟfy their results to 
Wayne County, who would then determine the winners 
and issue cerƟﬁcates of elecƟon, if required.  
 
Randolph County would need to determine their costs to 
conduct the elecƟon as would Wayne County, and  
“Indiana City” would need to reimburse both counƟes for 
the apporƟoned costs. 
FEDERAL POST CARD APPLICATION (FPCA) 
The Federal Post card ApplicaƟon (FPCA) is used by military and overseas voters to 1) register to vote and 2) request 
an absentee ballot. An FPCA is good for one calendar year (January 1 to December 31). This means if a military or 
overseas voters submits an FPCA on March 1, 2019, then an absentee ballot is sent to the individual for the May 
primary elecƟon and November municipal elecƟon. While the absentee applicaƟon expires aŌer December 31, the 
voter’s registraƟon remains on the voter rolls and can be updated in a future elecƟon via the FPCA or a state or  
federal voter registraƟon form. 
 
To use the FPCA in Indiana, the 
voter must mark one of these 
four reasons: 
 
 
 
 
 
 If a voter marks boxes 1, 2, or 3, then 
a regular ballot is sent. 
 If a voter marks box 4, a federal only 
ballot is sent AND the voter is  
registered to vote at the address of 
the VR oﬃce. (NOTE: there are no  
federal only ballots in 2019; a voter 
should not receive a ballot in 2019) 
 If a voter marks box 5, the FPCA is  
rejected. 
 
The FPCA is the only absentee applicaƟon that  
allows a military or overseas voter to vote by fax or email. If a military or overseas voter wants to vote by fax or 
email, then they must be sent an ABS‐9 along with their ballot to waive their right to secret ballot. An email or faxed 
ballot is then remade by a bi‐parƟsan team on ElecƟon Day, paying careful aƩenƟon to serialize the original ballot 
AND remade ballot with the same set of numbers in the event a recount is ordered. 
 
What about the FWAB? 
The Federal Write‐In Absentee Ballot (FWAB) looks very similar to an FPCA, but it includes a separate “ballot” that 
allows a military or overseas voter to write their candidate selecƟons and submit to county elecƟon oﬃcials. BUT, in 
Indiana, the FWAB does NOT replace the FPCA. Instead, the voter must submit an FPCA ﬁrst and then the county 
can accept the FWAB. Think of the FWAB as the back‐up absentee ballot that is only used if the ballot sent from the 
original request (FPCA) does not arrive by the appropriate deadline (noon, ElecƟon Day for email/fax ballots; noon, 
ten days aŌer ElecƟon Day for overseas or overseas military ballots that are postmarked on or before the date of 
the elecƟon). If the original ballot is NOT received, then the FWAB can be opened and a ballot can be remade  
according to the text wriƩen by the voter on the FWAB. 
 
Federal and state law have a number of “special” rules for military and overseas voters.  
The 2019 Military & Overseas Voters’ Guide is a terriﬁc resource for more details.

Election Division Dispatch 
 Brad King & Angie Nussmeyer, Co-Directors | May 2019  
NEWS & UPDATES 
ElecƟon Night ReporƟng 
On ElecƟon night don’t forget to enter your preliminary 
elecƟon results in SVRS! Unoﬃcial results will be  
displayed on indianavoters.com/elecƟonresults  Before 
elecƟon day, please visit the site and conﬁrm races are 
displaying correctly. Please contact the Help Desk about 
any errors or issues. 
 
CerƟﬁcaƟon of ElecƟon Results 
There isn’t much Ɵme to rest following elecƟon day! 
Your county elecƟon boards must canvass the results of 
your elecƟon no later than noon, ten days (May 17) aŌer 
the elecƟon, and process any provisional ballots or late  
arriving overseas ballots by 3PM that same day. In SVRS 
you’ll complete and ﬁle the CEB‐25 (if you had a public 
quesƟon), and separately send your precinct level results 
to IED by noon, Monday, May 20, 2019. The CEB‐9 is due 
Tuesday, May 21. Web training on these post elec Ɵon 
processing pieces will be held, so please aƩend if you’re 
unsure of the process. 
 
PRE‐16 Form 
Adopted by law in 2018, the PRE‐16 form was ﬁrst used 
in the November 2018 elecƟon and may be new for 
many counƟes. This form is ONLY for counƟes using a 
direct record electronic (DRE) voƟng system on ElecƟon 
Day. (A ballot marking device is not a DRE!) Poll workers 
are to complete this form aŌer the polls close to report 
any discrepancy between the number of voters signing 
the poll list and the number of ballots cast on the DRE 
system. AŌer the elecƟon, the county elecƟon board 
must compile the informaƟon and not later than noon, 
the second Friday aŌer the elecƟon, discuss and publish 
the document at an elecƟon board meeƟng. AddiƟonal 
reporƟng requirements may be necessary. See IC 3‐12‐
3.5‐8 for more details (NOTE: The pink code book does 
not have the updated language of this law. Rely on the 
supplement OR go online at iga.in.gov) 
 
Updates to Current Forms 
Changes in state elecƟon law this legislaƟve session will 
require a forms update for the November 2019 elecƟon. 
We anƟcipate changes to the PRE‐1 Oath Book (including 
updates to aid vote center counƟes), CFA‐1, CFA‐4, CFA‐
11, and potenƟally a few others. Most of the new forms 
will be available on or aŌer July 1. 
MAY WEB TRAINING 
May 9 & 13 | Post ElecƟon Processing  
May  29 & 30 | Statewide VLM Project 
 
Dates are subject to change; check the 2019 INSVRS  
Training Schedule on the county portal to conﬁrm. 
CALENDAR 
 
May 6, 2019 (Primary ElecƟon Eve): 
Check yellow calendar book for mulƟple deadlines 
May 7, 2019 (ElecƟon Day): 
Poll are open from 6A to 6P, local prevailing Ɵme 
May 8, 2019: 
First day D or R party may ﬁll a primary elecƟon 
ballot vacancy (see IC 3‐13‐1 for details) 
May 17, 2019 (NOON): 
Deadline to receive overseas absentee by mail 
ballots postmarked on or before May 7, 2019; 
Deadline for voter to bring ID to the clerk’s oﬃce 
to count provisional ballot for lacking proper ID 
May 17, 2019 (3PM): 
Deadline for county elecƟon board to determine 
whether or not to count a provisional ballot 
May 20, 2019 (NOON, Indy Time): 
Deadline to cerƟfy elecƟon results to IED;  
Card 1 of Statewide VLM Postcard Mailing drops 
May 21, 2019: 
Voter RegistraƟon Opens;  
Deadline by noon for a candidate to ﬁle a recount 
or contest acƟon with the clerk  
May 24, 2019: 
Deadline by noon for a county chair to ﬁle a re‐
count or contest acƟon with county clerk  
May 27, 2019:

Statewide VLM Hoppers go “live” 
InformaƟon in this newsleƩer is provided by the Indiana ElecƟon Division as a courtesy to county elecƟon administrators. If a person is unclear concerning elecƟon law provisions,  
the ElecƟon Division can serve as an interpreƟve source. However, where important legal rights are concerned, you must consult with your own aƩorney to be fully and properly advised. 
NOTE: The 2019 ElecƟon Administrator’s 
Manual included incorrect forms used in 
ﬁlling ballot vacancies (on pages 26‐28). 
The pages are updated in the online  
ediƟon of the Manual, and are noted in 
the text below. 
 
Last month the newsleƩer touched on  
ballot access rules for independent and 
minor party candidates. In addiƟon to this 
group of “summer” ﬁlings, it is possible for 
the DemocraƟc and Republican parƟes to 
ﬁll ballot vacancies where no candidate 
ﬁled to run in the primary elecƟon or 
withdrew aŌer the primary, and for the 
Libertarian Party to ﬁll ballot vacancies 
where a state or county convenƟon was 
not held.  
 
It’s important to note that the following 
does not apply to “small” town 
(populaƟon of less than 3,500) oﬃces 
where a primary elecƟon was not  
conducted. The DemocraƟc, Republican, 
and Libertarian parƟes follow a speciﬁc 
process to nominate their candidates, 
which will be reviewed in the newsleƩer 
next month or by consulƟng the orange 
“Small” Town Guide. 
 
DEMOCRATIC & REPUBLICAN PARTIES 
For local oﬃces, the DemocraƟc and  
Republican parƟes have two opƟons to ﬁll 
a ballot vacancy where no person ran in 
the primary elecƟon: 1) Caucus of eligible 
precinct commiƩeemen; OR 2) Direct  
appointment. 
 
1. CAUCUS 
The county chair must send wriƩen noƟce 
(CAN‐47) 
to all eligible precinct  
commiƩeemen via ﬁrst class mail not later 
than ten days before the caucus is to be 
held. In addiƟon, the CAN‐47 must be ﬁled 
with the county clerk not later than noon,  
ten days before the caucus is held. 
 
Candidates for the caucus are required to 
ﬁle the CAN‐48 with the chair of the  
caucus not later than 72‐hours before the 
caucus is held. The CAN‐48 must also be 
ﬁled with the county clerk not later than 
72‐hours before the caucus. 
 
The caucus is held according to the  
procedures in IC 3‐13‐1, and must be held 
not later than noon, June 30, 2019. The 
nominated candidate’s CAN‐12 statement 
of economic interest AND the CAN‐49 
consent must be ﬁled with the county 
clerk not later than noon, July 3, 2019. 
 
2. DIRECT APPOINTMENT 
The county party organizaƟon can pass a 
resoluƟon or otherwise vote to give  
authority to the county chair or the  
county commiƩee (chair, vice chair,  
secretary and treasurer) to ﬁll a ballot 
vacancy by direct appointment. State law 
does not prescribe the form of the  
resoluƟon; some are very speciﬁc to an 
elecƟon, while others are open‐ended. It’s 
ulƟmately up to the party organizaƟon to 
decide the form of their resoluƟon or  
other authorizaƟon.  
 
The direct appointment must be made not 
later than noon, June 30, 2019. The  
candidate’s CAN‐12 and CAN‐48, and the 
CAN‐49 along with a copy of the meeƟng 
minutes, resol
uƟon or other document 
granƟng the direct appointment authority 
must be ﬁled  with the county clerk not 
later than noon, July 3, 2019. (NOTE: If the 
party is ﬁlling mulƟple vacancies by direct 
appointment, the resoluƟon or meeƟng 
minutes must be aƩached to EACH  
CAN‐49.) 
 
AlternaƟvely, if only one precinct  
commiƩeeman is eligible to parƟcipate in 
the caucus, the county chair is required to 
ﬁll a ballot vacancy by direct appointment. 
The CAN‐49 form has a box for the chair to 
mark and indicate this reason. 
 
LIBERTARIAN PARTY 
The Libertarian Party generally ﬁlls their 
city and large town oﬃces at a city  
convenƟon. Instead of ﬁling declaraƟons 
of candidacy with the county elecƟon 
board, the Libertarian Party chair and  
secretary will cerƟfy the Party’s nominees 
to the county elecƟon board using the 
CAN‐22 cerƟﬁcate of nominaƟon along 
with the candidate’s CAN‐12 statement of  
economic interests. The city convenƟon 
for the Libertarian Party must be held not 
later than noon, June 30, 2019. 
 
If aŌer the Libertarian Party holds its city 
convenƟon and fails to ﬁll a posiƟon, its 
state party commiƩee may ﬁll the ballot 
vacancy not later than noon, June 30, 
2019.  The Libertarian Party State chair 
will ﬁle noƟce with the county elecƟon 
board of their party’s intent to ﬁll a ballot 
vacancy, which must be ﬁled not later 
than ten days before the vacancy can be 
ﬁlled. The CAN‐22 and CAN‐12 must be 
then be ﬁled with the county elecƟon 
board not later than noon, July 3, 2019. 
 
FINAL NOTE. Filling a ballot vacancy is 
NOT the same as ﬁlling an elected oﬃce 
vacancy, where an individual is no longer 
serving. Elected oﬃce vacancy procedures 
can be found on pages 28‐34 of the blue 
2019 ElecƟon Administrator’s Manual. 
QUESTIONS OF THE MONTH: Last Minute Election Reminders 
Q. Are people who are in line (or on ElecƟon Day, entering the chute) allowed to vote? 
A. If otherwise eligible, yes. Individuals in line at noon, Monday, May 6 (last day of in‐person early voƟng) and those in 
line at 6PM on elecƟon day, even if the line extends beyond the chute, must be allowed to vote. However, poll workers 
should determine the end of the line and use one of the following methods to denote who may vote: (1) write down 
name of each voter; (2) stamp each voter’s hand; or (2) stand or designate another person to stand immediately be‐
hind the last voter who may vote. A person entering the polling site aŌer 6PM on ElecƟon Day is not eligible to vote, 
unless a judge issues a court order on ElecƟon Day. If the judge extends the hours of the polling site, all voters must 
vote a provisional ballot. See IC 3‐11‐8‐11 and IC 3‐11‐10‐29.2 for more details. 
IN FOCUS: Filling Ballot Vacancies After Primary Election 
Statewide VLM Project Updates 
We noted in our March 2019 newsleƩer that the 
statewide VLM Project was underway and launching a 
short Ɵme aŌer the May 7 primary elecƟon. As a refresher, 
the project’s implementaƟon follows federal elecƟon law 
guidelines and consists of two mailers, included in this 
packet: 
1) Card 1: Sent to the mailing address of every ac Ɵve vot‐
er in Indiana via USPS non‐forwardable mail. If the 
card is returned undeliverable pursuant to IC 3‐5‐2‐
49.7, then card 2 is sent to the voter. 
2) Card 2: Sent by USPS forwardable mail to the mailing 
address of a person whose card 1 is returned undeliv‐
erable. Card 2 allows the person to a) conﬁrm their 
residence address is their registraƟon address or b) 
update their registraƟon within the county or c) cancel 
their registraƟon if they’ve moved out of county. 
Card 2 is the main focus for county VR oﬃcials. The vendor 
will enter InformaƟon from the “response card.” If the  
response is unclear, then the county VR oﬃcial makes the 
determinaƟon in the new VLM ExcepƟons hopper. County 
VR oﬃcials must also review the other VLM related hop‐
pers to conﬁrm the returned voter cards with the voter’s 
request were correctly categorized. 
Training 
Your raining will be criƟcal to the success of counƟes  
compleƟng the statewide VLM project on Ɵme, and all 
counƟes are encouraged to aƩend one of the two “live” 
webinar sessions: 
 Wednesday, May 29 at 2:30P (ET) 
 Thursday, May 30 at 2:30P (ET) 
The sessions will be recorded and posted to the county 
portal along with the step‐by‐step instrucƟons on using 
the modules within SVRS. 
 
There will be new informaƟon to learn, even for veteran 
elecƟon administrators! For example, the “image” viewer 
is now integrated with SVRS, which gives counƟes more 
opƟons for clipping signatures and storing card images. 
Plus, duplicaƟve processing steps have been eliminated to 
further streamline your work, and a new VLM ExcepƟons 
Hopper has been implemented. 
 
Key Dates: 
May 23: Card 1 drops 
May 29: Online Webinar Training 
May 30: Online Webinar Training 
June 4: Card 2 beings to drop on a rolling basis unƟl June 
25, as cards are returned undeliverable 
June 4: Data may begin to appear in SVRS VLM Hoppers  
August 7: Deadline to ﬁnish VLM work to change voter 
status to “inacƟve” 
August 8: Freeze period begins so no voter status may be 
changed to inacƟve

QUESTIONS OF THE MONTH: Last Minute Election Reminders, con’t. 
Q. Can a media watcher ﬁlm inside a polling place? 
A. Yes, but they may not view which candidates an individual votes for. They may not photograph a voter who objects. 
 
Q. How do we help a voter on ElecƟon Day who never received their absentee by mail ballot? 
A. Ask the voter to complete a PRE‐5 at their polling site and issue them a regular ballot, if otherwise eligible. The PRE‐5 
is the voter’s wriƩen aﬃrmaƟon that they did not receive their absentee by mail ballot. 
 
Q. Can a voter who returned their absentee ballot to the elecƟon board vote on ElecƟon Day? 
A. Generally, no. State law does not permit a person who already submiƩed an absentee ballot to vote again in person 
that would “supersede” their absentee ballot. The excepƟon would be a person who’s absentee ballot was rejected on 
ElecƟon Day. In a central count county, the county elecƟon board has to give best possible noƟce to the individual that 
their ballot was rejected and issue them a cerƟﬁcate that would allow them to vote at the polling site on ElecƟon Day. (IC 
3‐11.5‐4‐18) 
 
Q. Does a person who moves in or out of a municipality qualify for a fail‐safe to vote at their old precinct one last 
Ɵme, if the person did not update their registraƟon by the statewide deadline? 
A. No. The fail‐safe provision that allows a person to vote at their old precinct one last Ɵme does not apply to a person 
who moved in/out of a municipality  (even within the same precinct—if the precinct is split by a municipal boundary—
under new state law) during a municipal elecƟon year like 2019. (IC 3‐10‐11‐4(b); 3‐10‐12‐3.4(d))

2019 CARD 2 EXAMPLE
Voter List Maintenance Talking Points 
The Secretary of State’s Election Division is conducting voter list maintenance to update 
Indiana’s voter registration information. Required by Indiana law, the process will identify 
outdated and inaccurate voter registration information to help counties improve the accuracy 
and integrity of Indiana’s voter registration list.  
 
In May 2019, all “active” Hoosier voters will receive a postcard sent by non-forwardable, first-
class mail to the voter’s mailing address. In June, Hoosier voters whose first postcard was 
returned as “undeliverable for unknown or insufficient address” as addressed will receive a 
postcard in the mail from the Secretary of State Election Division asking them to update their 
voter registration information. This second “voter response card” will be sent by forwardable, 
first-class mail to the voter’s mailing address. Voters who receive a second postcard asking for 
updated information should fill out the postage pre-paid response card, sign it, and return it to 
the Secretary of State Election Division.  
Voters who received a second postcard asking for their current address have until July 27, 2019, 
to return the postcard to confirm their registration address or update their voter information. 
The Election Division must receive the postcard by August 2, 2019. Voters who do not respond 
by confirming their current address or updating their information will have their voter 
registration record at that address moved to “inactive” status.  
Being marked “inactive” does not mean a voter cannot vote. It simply means a voter did not 
update or confirm their registration record address. The voter will still be eligible to vote in 
November 2019, if otherwise qualified. If the voter casts a ballot in November 2019 from that 
address, their status will be reclassified as an “active” voter. If they do not vote in November, 
they can still vote in the federal elections of 2020 and 2022 and if applicable, a special election 
in 2021.  If they do not vote in any election prior to January 2023, the county voter registration 
office may move their voter’s registration record status to “cancelled,” which will remove the 
name from Election Day poll lists but will remain in the statewide voter registration system. 
 
Indiana Voter List Refresh Facts 
• In May 2019, all active voters received a postcard reminding them that Election Day is 
November 5, 2019. 
• In June 2019, a second mailing with a postage pre-paid voter response card will be 
distributed to those whose original mailing was returned via the postal service asking for 
updated information.  
• Voters who received a second mailing have until July 27, 2019, to return the postcard to 
update their voter information using the postage pre-paid, voter response card on the 
second mailing.  
• Failing to update voter registration information by July 27, 2019, will result in the voter’s 
registration record being moved to “inactive” status.    
• As an inactive voter, the voter is still eligible to vote at their registration address in the 
upcoming November election.   
• If the voter votes in November 2019 at their registration address, he or she will be 
reclassified as an active voter.   
• If the voter does not vote in November, he or she can still vote at their registration 
address in the Primary and General Elections of 2020 and 2022, and, if applicable, any 
special election held in 2021.   
• If the voter fails to respond to the second mailing but has moved, they should update 
their Indiana registration by submitting a state or federal voter registration form to their 
county clerk or Indiana Election Division or going online to update it at 
indianavoters.com. This update to their registration will change their status to “active,” 
if the voter is otherwise eligible. If the voter does not update their information or vote 
in any election prior to 2023, the county voter registration office will change the voter’s 
registration record status to “cancelled,” which results in the person not appearing on 
Election Day poll lists. However, their registration record is not deleted or otherwise 
removed from the statewide voter registration system. 
• Indiana Code 3-7-38.2 requires county voter registration offices to perform voter list 
maintenance on a regular basis, which includes the statewide postcard mailing program 
performed by the Indiana Election Division.  
• Since 2013, the General Assembly has fully funded the statewide mailing to all voters.  
• Uniform and non-discriminatory voter list maintenance is mandatory pursuant to the 
federal National Voter Registration Act (NVRA) of 1993 signed into law by President Bill 
Clinton.   
• The National Voter Registration Act requires that a voter registration record must be 
inactive for two federal election cycles (up to 4 years) before the voter registration 
record can be cancelled, as part of this specific type of voter list maintenance process.  
 
Frequently Asked Questions 
Q: What happens if I receive a postcard? 
A: You do not need to do anything to respond to the first postcard.  If you receive a second 
postcard asking for a response, you need to fill out the postage pre-paid response card, sign 
it, and return it to the Indiana Election Division by July 27, 2019.   
Q: What happens if I don’t respond to the second postcard before the due date of July 27, 
2019? 
A: This does not mean you can’t vote! If you do not respond to the second postcard by July 
27, your voter registration status may be changed to inactive by your county. If you have 
not moved, then there is no action for you to take except to vote once in any Indiana 
election between November 2019 and November 2022. Voting at your registration address 
confirms you continue to reside there, and will result in your registration record status 
being moved to “active.” 
However, if you have moved from your registration address, then you will need to update 
your information using a state or federal voter registration form or register to vote online at 
indianavoters.com. The statewide voter registration deadline for the November 2019 
election is October 7, 2019. A person who does not update their registration record address 
may still be able to vote a regular ballot in an election if certain “fail safe” conditions are 
met. 
If you respond to the second postcard after July 27, the postcard will be forwarded to your 
county voter registration office. The county can continue to process late arriving postcards 
to update registration information, but may not change the voter’s registration status to 
“inactive” during the 90 day “freeze” period before each  Election (August 8-Nov. 5, 2019). 
This is due to federal and state law.  
Q: What happens if my record becomes “inactive” and I don’t vote in any of these 
elections, including the November 2022 General Election?  
A: If your record is inactive and you do not update your address or voter registration 
information nor do you vote or appear to vote from that address in any election before 
2022, the county will change your registration status to “cancelled;” however, your record 
remains in the statewide voter registration system. 
Q: If I don’t need to update my information until the November 2022 General Election, 
why are you doing the mailing and public outreach campaign now? 
A: Federal law requires a voter list maintenance process that takes several years to 
complete, and state law requires the Election Division perform this task in every odd-
numbered year. We have to start now. Our goal is to make sure that every Hoosier voter 
has ample time and information to correct any errors and make his or her voter registration 
record accurate.  
Q. How do I check my current registration information?  
A. You can check to see if you are registered to vote online at www.indianavoters.com. You 
can call the Hoosier Voter Hotline at 866-IN-1-Vote or at 866-461-8683.  You may also check 
at your county clerk’s office or county board of registration.  
Q. How do I register to vote? 
A. If you have an Indiana’s driver’s license or ID card, you can register to vote online 
at www.indianavoters.com
 or you can pick up a voter registration form at your county 
clerk’s office, county board of registration, Indiana Election Division, license branch, local 
family and social services office, WorkOne center or department of health. State and federal 
paper voter registration forms are available for download at in.gov/sos/elections  
Q. How do I update my existing voter registration? 
A. If you have an Indiana driver’s license or ID card, you can update your voter registration 
online at www.indianavoters.com or you can pick up a registration form at your county 
clerk’s office, county board of registration, Indiana Election Division, license branch, local 
family and social services office, WorkOne center or department of health.  State and 
federal paper voter registration forms are available for download at in.gov/sos/elections 
Q. How do I cancel my outdated voter registration? 
A. You can cancel your voter registration by filling out an Authorization to Cancel. A voter 
must cancel their registration in writing. The cancellation form is available online 
at http://www.in.gov/sos/elections/files/VRG-14.pdf or at your county clerk’s office. If you 
print and fill out the online form, you must mail in the signed form to the Indiana Election 
Division or your county clerk. 
Q. Where can I find contact information for my county clerk or county board of 
registration? 
A. The mailing and contact information for your county clerk or county board of registration 
is available online at www.indianavoters.com
 or by calling the Hoosier Voter Hotline at 866-
IN-1-VOTE or 866-461-8683.  
Q: Why is it important to do voter list maintenance? 
A: This is first about cleaning up our voter lists. We need to help county clerks perform 
much needed maintenance to outdated voter registration information and protect the 
integrity of elections. Inaccurate voter information can affect public confidence in the 
integrity of our voting process. Candidates and voters can question the integrity of our 
voting process when they know we have inaccurate registrations. It can discourage citizen 
participation in the election process when we have artificially low voter turnout statistics. 
Plus, it’s the law. The Indiana General Assembly requires voter list information maintenance 
every two years and voter list maintenance is a continuous, ongoing federal requirement of 
the National Voter Registration Act of 1993. 
Q: How big of a problem is this for counties?   
A:   Counties often struggle with having enough resources to accomplish all of the important 
work they have to do.  Voter list maintenance can be one of those tasks that is put off to 
another time.  As each election cycle begins, different groups conduct drives to register 
people to vote. Some people may register to vote not realizing they are still registered at an 
old address. After each election, counties do not always have enough information to 
contact the voter’s previous county of residence to have the former voter registration 
record canceled in accordance with the law. And as each election cycle passes without 
comprehensive maintenance, the voter rolls grow since this old information is still an active 
record.    
Q: What kind of voter list maintenance is done at the county level? 
A: Counties conduct voter list maintenance in several ways.  This includes receiving 
information from the Social Security Administration and the State Department of Health to 
determine if someone has passed away. This also includes removing voters convicted of a 
crime and put in jail following their conviction based on information from the Indiana 
Department of Correction and County Sheriffs, and voters who cancel their registration 
through a cancellation request.   
Some counties send a first postcard to all active voters; others may send a first postcard to 
voters to notify them that polling places or precinct boundaries have changed or to follow 
up a jury duty summons when a jury notice is returned by the US postal service. If the 
postcard comes back as “undeliverable due to an unknown or insufficient address,” then 
the county may send the voter a second voter response postage pre-paid card by 
forwardable mail to the voter’s mailing address. If the second postcard is also returned as 
undeliverable, then the voter registration record may be made inactive.  
Q: What kind of progress has been made by the counties in removing inaccurate 
registrations? 
A: The National Voter Registration Act requires two federal election cycles (up to 4 years) to 
pass before a county can move an inactive voter registration record to cancelled status.  
This means even the most proactive county that does regular maintenance will have 
inactive voters during this 4 year process.  This is why it is so important that counties 
perform regular voter list maintenance. 
Q: Doesn’t this cleaning up of voter rolls have the potential to remove legitimately 
registered voters, therefore preventing them from exercising their right to vote? 
A: A voter is never “purged.” Likewise, voter’s registration record is never removed or 
deleted from the statewide voter registration system. Instead, the voter’s registration 
record status is updated to reflect active, inactive, or cancelled status. Even if a voter 
registration record is cancelled in error, that voter can still cast a regular ballot by simply 
affirming to the poll workers that they have continuously resided at their registration 
address. A voter can also cast a provisional ballot, which gives voter registration officials 
time to sort out the facts in that voter’s case, so that their vote can be counted if they are 
still eligible.

InformaƟon in this newsleƩer is provided by the Indiana ElecƟon Division as a courtesy to county elecƟon administrators. If a person is unclear concerning elecƟon law provisions,

Now that the ﬁrst postcard has been 
mailed to all acƟve Hoosier voters, a 
few hundred thousand of those “card 
1” postcards are being returned as  
undeliverable. This return requires IED 
to mail a Card 2, which includes a  
detachable, postage‐paid voter  
response card (VRC).  
 
The VRC allows the voter to conﬁrm 
their registraƟon is correct (oval 1),  
authorize cancellaƟon due to a move 
out of county (oval 2), and update their 
registraƟon within the county (oval 3). 
When the VRC is received by IED  on or 
before the July 27, 2019 deadline, it is 
reviewed and placed in the proper data 
“silo” so that the informaƟon can be 
made available to counƟes in one of the 
following four hoppers: 
 
1)  CANCEL HOPPER: if a voter has 
marked oval 2 to authorize  
cancellaƟon of their registraƟon 
record and signed the VRC, the  
person’s name will appear in the 
cancel hopper. Records in the  
cancel hopper may be reviewed  
individually or processed in a batch.  
2)  INACTIVE HOPPER: If a voter does 
not respond to the second mailing 
by July 27, 2019, OR Card 2 is  
returned as undeliverable, OR the 
voter fails to sign the VRC to make 
their changes eﬀecƟve, the record 
will appear in the inacƟve hoper. 
This hopper will have records early 
in the process, but expect the bulk 
to come on or aŌer July 28, 2019, as 
the “no response” individuals will 
be loaded in bulk. Records in the 
inacƟve hopper can be reviewed 
individual or processed in batch. 
3)  UPDATE HOPPER: If a voter marked 
oval 3 to update their registraƟon 
address within the county,  
answered the age & ciƟzenship 
quesƟon, and signed the VRC, then 
the record is placed in the update 
hopper. Records in the update hop‐
per must be reviewed individually 
by a county user. Special aƩenƟon 
should be made to review the card 
for a name change, which is a new 
addiƟon to the VRC card for the 
2019 mailing.  
4)  EXCEPTION HOPPER: SomeƟmes a 
VRC will be returned with  
conﬂicƟng informaƟon, like a ovals 
2 & marked or oval 3 is marked for 
an update, signed, but the  
voter failed to answer the age & 
ciƟzenship quesƟons. Records like 
these go to the NEW excepƟon  
hopper and require a county admin 
to review the record to determine 
the best path forward based on 
state and federal law. (County  
Admins are the only persons that 
will have access to this hopper & 
will appear on their dashboard!)  
 
The Step‐By‐Step document includes 
the business rules adopted by the state 
to direct how a response on a VRC 
should be categorized in the data “silos” 
and may be helpful to a county user to 
beƩer understand why a record ended 
up in a hopper. 
 
So what happens to a voter who marks 
oval 1 (address conﬁrmaƟon) and signs 
the VRC? No acƟon is taken on their 
record and will not be directed to any 
hopper for county review. However, 
you can view the VRC in the Image 
Viewer and an image of the VRC will be 
aƩached to the voter’s documents in 
SVRS. 
 
In fact, you can search the image  
viewer for scanned images of the VRC 
or cards returned as undeliverable and 
those images will be aƩached to the 
individual’s voter record in SVRS.  
However,  there will be a message 
staƟng that no image is available when 
a person does not respond to the  
second mailing. 
QUESTIONS OF THE MONTH 
Q. When a caucus is called to ﬁll a ballot vacancy, does a 
CAN‐12 need to be ﬁled with the CAN‐48,  
declaraƟon of candidacy to ﬁll a ballot vacancy? 
A. No. The CAN‐12 is not ﬁled with the CAN‐48 when a  
candidate comes to ﬁle the CAN‐48 with the clerk’s oﬃce

vacancy). 
 
Q. A candidate nominated in the primary ﬁled a CAN‐46 
withdrawal form. How long does a party chair have to ﬁll 
the ballot vacancy? 
A. The chair has 30‐days to ﬁll a ballot vacancy from the date 
the CAN‐46 form is ﬁled and following the procedures in IC 3
‐13‐1, generally. The CAN‐49 & CAN‐12 must be ﬁled by 
noon,  three days aŌer the appointment is made.

NOTE: The VRG‐6 is NOT a publicly available form as it is

InformaƟon in this newsleƩer is provided by the Indiana ElecƟon Division as a courtesy to county elecƟon administrators. If a person is unclear concerning elecƟon law provisions,

This summer poliƟcal parƟes and

calendar year. It also assumes the  
candidate does NOT have an open

Q. What’s the retenƟon schedule for campaign ﬁnance 
forms? 
A. Campaign ﬁnance reports and statements are kept four 
years from December 1, following the elecƟon to which they 
pertain. (IC 3‐9‐4‐6). The excepƟon to this rule are

are kept for six years from December 1 following the elecƟon 
to which they pertain. 
 
Q. Does the June 30 deadline for the parƟes to ﬁll a ballot 
vacancy where no one ran in the primary elecƟon rollover 
to Monday, July 1? 
A. No. The party chairs must take acƟon (either hold the  
caucus or make the appointment) to ﬁll a ballot vacancy 
where no one ran in the primary elecƟon by noon, June 30. 
The deadline for the paperwork required to be ﬁled aŌer the 
party’s acƟon is noon, July 3.   
IN FOCUS: Campaign Finance & “Summer” Filings 
VR CORNER 
The statewide VLM Mailing Project conƟnues this month 
through August 7, 2019. More than 4.25 million postcards 
were mailed to acƟve voters in Indiana, and more than

This smaller universe of acƟve voters were mailed a

to send back the voter response card to conﬁrm their

Data from the second card is being loaded into county SVRS
 
hoppers. A reminder: the ExcepƟons Hopper is only visible to

mine how best to manage the change requested by the voter.

In Indiana, the DemocraƟc, Libertarian, 
and Republican parƟes in “small” towns 
(populaƟon of less than 3,500) may 
need to nominate candidates for the 
November ballot at a town convenƟon 
held in late summer.  
 
This convenƟon replaces the May  
primary elecƟon, unless the small 
town’s council
 passed an ordinance for 
the county elecƟon board to conduct a 
May primary. A “small” town  
nominaƟng convenƟon is not a caucus 
nor a primary elecƟon nor the  
municipal elecƟon. Instead, it’s how the 
DemocraƟc, Republican, and Libertarian 
parƟes nominate their candidates for 
the November ballot where all  
candidates go head‐to‐head to  
determine who is elected to serve a 
speciﬁc term in oﬃce. 
 
The candidate ﬁling deadline for “small” 
town oﬃces (where no primary elecƟon 
was held) is noon, August 1, 2019. This 
is also the deadline 
for a candidate who 
ﬁled the CAN‐16/CAN‐12 to withdraw 
to be a candidate for “small” town 
oﬃce with one excepƟon noted later. 
 
The county’s poliƟcal parƟes will then 
determine if a nominaƟng convenƟon is 
necessary. A convenƟon is only held if 
more individuals from the same  
poliƟcal party ﬁle to run for the same 
oﬃce than is permiƩed. 
For example,  
town dogcatcher is one race. Two  
Democrats ﬁled to run; one Republican 
ﬁled. The DemocraƟc Party must hold a 
town convenƟon, while the Republican 
Party does not. 
 
SomeƟmes more than one person can 
be elected to a posiƟon, usually in at‐
large council seats. Let’s say in a vote‐
for‐three small town oﬃce that four 
Republicans ﬁle and two Democrats ﬁle. 
In this example, the Republican Party 
would hold a convenƟon to determine 
which of their four candidates will be 
one of three nominees; the DemocraƟc 
Party would not hold a convenƟon since 
fewer than three people ﬁled. 
 
The orange 2019 Town ElecƟon  
Guidebook contains the steps in con‐
ducƟng a small town convenƟon. In a 
nutshell, the county party chair  
nominates a registered voter of the 
town who is not a candidate or an  
elected oﬃcial of the town to serve as 
the town party chair. The town party 
chair then selects a registered voter of 
the town to serve as the party’s  
secretary. The secretary will also serve 
as secretary of the “small” town  
convenƟon. 
 
The town chair and secretary must then 
post the
 call to convenƟon (CAN‐15) 
noƟce in at least three prominent  
locaƟons, including the town clerk‐
treasurer’s oﬃce, at least three days 
before the convenƟon is to be held. 
 
Any registered voter within the town 
may parƟcipate in one party’s  
convenƟon, as long as the person meets 
the requirements under state law and 
the poliƟcal party’s rules. 
 
The orange guidebook walks through 
many of the steps to help town party 
chairs conduct their convenƟon. The 
town chairs should also consult state  
party rules, as Indiana elecƟon law does 
defer to 
party rules in some instances. 
(Sample rules are in the orange book, 
but our best advice is to get the infor‐
maƟon directly from the state party.) 
 
All small town nominaƟng convenƟons 
must be held not later than August 21, 
2019. AŌerward, the town party chair 
and
 town party secretary will cerƟfy the 
nominees to the county clerk’s oﬃce 
using the CAN‐18 form. The CAN‐18 
must be ﬁled for each candidate not 
later than noon (local prevailing Ɵme), 
August 28, 2019. 
 
A candidate nominated at a small town 
convenƟon may withdraw not
 later 
than noon (local prevailing Ɵme), three 
days following the adjournment of the 
convenƟon. The poliƟcal party may ﬁll 
the ballot vacancy if this occurs, but 
otherwise, no other ballot vacancies 
for “small” town oﬃce can be ﬁlled. 
For example, the DemocraƟc Party only 
ﬁlls two of the three at‐large council 
seats. The party is 
not able to ﬁll the 
remaining open seat aŌer the noon, 
August 1, 2019, ﬁling deadline. 
 
The county clerk must then ﬁle a copy 
of each CAN‐18 with the town clerk‐
treasurer not later than noon (local  
prevailing Ɵme), September 4, 2019.  
IN FOCUS: Small Town Nominating Conventions 
VR CORNER 
What roles does the county voter registraƟon oﬃcial play in a small town  
convenƟon? The county does not play a formal role if the county party determines 
that a convenƟon is necessary to determine who will be the party’s nominee for 
“small” town oﬃce on the November ballot. 
 
BUT, the county VR oﬃcial does need to provide to the town party chair and town 
party secretary a report with the name and registraƟon date of each individual  
within the municipality. Those reports can be pulled from SVRS.  
 
The county VR oﬃcial does not upload any voƟng history from the town convenƟon. 
This may seem confusing, but the county would not upload voƟng history from a 
state or naƟonal party convenƟon held in even‐numbered years, and the “small” 
town convenƟon is a similar type of nominaƟng process. 
QUESTIONS OF THE MONTH 
Q. Can a candidate nominated in the May primary elecƟon 
be challenged now? 
A. No. The opportunity to ﬁle a CAN‐1 challenge against a  
DemocraƟc or Republican candidate who ﬁled a CAN‐42 to 
run as a local candidate for the May primary elecƟon has 
passed. There may be other legal opƟons for an individual to 
explore, but the CAN‐1 hearing is no one of them. 
 
Q. Can candidates who ﬁlled a ballot vacancy or those who 
were cerƟﬁed as an independent/minor party candidate be 
challenged? 
A. Yes, though the deadlines to ﬁle a CAN‐1 challenge are 
staggered depending on the type of ﬁling. Please consult the 
yellow calendar guide for those details, as some of those 
dates go into September. 
 
Q. Does our county need to hold an elecƟon in November? 
A. Maybe. Similar to the May primary elecƟon, a November 
elecƟon may not be required. Please see IC 3‐10‐6‐7.5 for 
ciƟes and “large” towns; IC 3‐10‐7‐6 for “small” towns. Your 
CEB may need to pass a resoluƟon on this. 
 
Q. When does a small town council need to pass a  
resoluƟon to conduct its own November elecƟon and when 
does it need to be ﬁled? 
A. A “small” town council must adopt a resoluƟon to conduct 
its own November elecƟon not later than August 8, 2019, 
and ﬁle it with the county clerk not later than noon (local 
prevailing Ɵme), August 21, 2019. (IC 3‐10‐7‐5.5) The  
resoluƟon expires on December 31, 2019. 
 
Q. Our small town adopted a resoluƟon in 2011 to conduct 
its own November elecƟon. Can that be used in 2019? 
A. No. A resoluƟon adopted by a “small” town council to 
conduct its own November elecƟon expires on December 31 
in the year it was adopted.  An outdated resoluƟon cannot 
be used by the town as jusƟﬁcaƟon to conduct their  
November elecƟon with the excepƟon of a few small towns 
that have special procedures in its town charter.  
 
Q. What happens if a “small” town doesn’t pass a resolu-
Ɵon to conduct its own November elecƟon or ﬁles it with 
the clerk aŌer noon, August 21, 2019? 
A. In this scenario, state law requires the county elecƟon 
board to conduct the November elecƟon. The “small” town 
will reimburse the county for the cost of the elecƟon. 
 
Q. Is there anything the clerk’s oﬃce needs to do aŌer the 
August 1, 2019, small town oﬃce ﬁling deadline? 
A. Yes. Immediately following candidate ﬁling, the county 
clerk will need to post a list of candidates who ﬁle for “small” 
town oﬃce on your oﬃce’s public noƟce board, cerƟfy to the 
town clerk‐treasurer and release a list to the public each 
candidate who ﬁled, and provide a copy of each CAN‐16 to 
the respecƟve town clerk‐treasurer. (IC 3‐8‐5‐10.5) 
HOLDOVERS 
On occasion, no one ﬁles to run for an oﬃce on the  
November ballot. In these cases, the current oﬃceholder 
“holds‐over” for a new term of oﬃce pursuant to ArƟcle 
15, SecƟon 3 of the Indiana ConsƟtuƟon. 
 
For example, Cardinal Town Council District 1 is on the 
ballot in November 2019. Julie is the currently elected 
councilor for district 1, who is serving a four‐year term. 
Not only did Julie not ﬁle paperwork to be a candidate on 
the November ballot, no one else in Cardinal Town did 
either. Julie conƟnues serving as the town council member 
for district 1 for another four‐year term, unƟl her  
successor is elected and qualiﬁed. Because she is a 
“holdover” under state law, she does not ﬁle a new oath of 
oﬃce. 
 
CounƟes oŌen ask what happens if Julie didn’t ﬁle because 
she doesn’t want to conƟnue serving ? Julie may resign 
from elected oﬃce by ﬁling a wriƩen resignaƟon with the 
county clerk, and the elected oﬃce vacancy would be ﬁled 
according to statute. (IC 3‐13‐9, generally, for town oﬃces) 
The individual selected is a “pro‐tem appointment” for the 
remainder of the term. 
VLM PROJECT UPDATE 
The statewide VLM Mailing Project ﬁnishes this month 
with records being loaded for county review up to August 
7, 2019. The “freeze” period begins August 8, which means 
counƟes cannot move a voter’s registraƟon status to 
“inacƟve” unƟl aŌer the November 2019 elecƟon. 
 
However, counƟes may consider a late arriving voter  
response as a voter’s wriƩen authorizaƟon to update or 
cancel a voter’s registraƟon. County VR oﬃcials are to 
follow general voter registraƟon processes when  
considering these requests.  
 
Since counƟes are to give priority to the VLM InacƟve  
hopper before it closes on August 8, 2019, the VLM Update 
and ExcepƟon hoppers will remain open to allow counƟes 
to conƟnue making the changes requested by the voter. 
 
IED will also be mailing leƩers to individuals who returned 
a voter response card and indicated a move out of county 
or who landed in the ExcepƟons hopper. This leƩer will 
include a state VR form so that the person can ensure their 
registraƟon is updated in Ɵme for next elecƟon. 
 
Finally, the paper copies of scanned cards will be delivered 
to counƟes on or around August 30, 2019. Our vendors will 
contact your oﬃce at least 24‐hours ahead of Ɵme to alert 
you to the delivery. Stay tuned for more updates on  
delivery of unscanned cards, some of which will start to 
arrive in early September.

Election Division Dispatch 
 Brad King & Angie Nussmeyer, Co-Directors | September 2019 
NEWS & UPDATES 
 
Precinct ElecƟon Results Survey 
A survey was emailed to counƟes asking if they intend to use 
the new SVRS precinct level results upload module in the  
November 2019 elecƟon.  
 
While the tool was designed for counƟes to upload ﬁnal  
cerƟﬁed results to SVRS to eliminate paper ﬁling during  
cerƟﬁcaƟon, an added beneﬁt is counƟes may use the module 
to upload unoﬃcial results that can be viewed and  
downloaded from the state’s ENR website. The ENR website 
can be leveraged by counƟes to share early precinct level  
results  with interested parƟes and aŌer cerƟﬁcaƟon, a  
public‐facing website to point to for ﬁnal precinct level results 
when requested. 
 
Please respond to this survey not later than Friday, September 
27, 2019. We’ll use this informaƟon to reach out to counƟes 
interested in using the module to provide extra support map‐
ping the data, if needed. 
 
NoƟce of Public Test of VoƟng Systems 
State law requires a county elecƟon board to begin its test of  
voƟng systems not later than the day before in‐person voƟng 
occurs in the clerk’s oﬃce. (CounƟes are to follow the 28‐day 
start date, even if the CEB passed a resoluƟon to reduce hours 
under IC 3‐11‐10‐26.5 in 2019.)  
 
NoƟce of the public test under the Open Door Law requires 
noƟce to be posted not later than 48‐hours before the public 
test, or Thursday, October 3, 2019, for a test conducted on 
October 7, 2019. Because the Open Door Law views the 48‐
hours in business days and not calendar days, then a county 
may not count the weekend in its calculaƟon for posƟng no‐
Ɵce. 
 
AddiƟonally, state elecƟon law requires noƟce of the public 
test to be published in the newspaper not later than 48‐hours 
before the test begins. This deadline is October 5, 2019, for a 
public test held on October 7, 2019. In this case, the  statute 
relies on calendar days, so the 48‐hours may include the week‐
end. There is never a penalty for publishing early! 
 
SomeƟmes a newspaper fails to publish noƟce of a public test. 
A CEB need not reschedule the test as a result. Instead, state 
law permits a county where the newspaper failed to Ɵmely 
publish a noƟce to either 1) display the noƟce prominently in 
three (3) locaƟons in the county or 2) post on the county’s 
website (IC 5‐3‐1‐2(k)).
