With absentee ballots being delivered to 
counƟes and mailed to voters this week, a 
common quesƟon our oﬃce receives is 
what do we do if we spot an error (or  
omission) or we have a candidate withdraw 
aŌer ballots are printed and the elecƟon 
coded on our voƟng systems. 
 
ERROR OR OMISSION 
If the CEB is alerted to an error or omission 
on a ballot, then one of two things can  
occur: 
 
1/ The CEB conducts a public meeƟng,  
discusses the issue, and agrees to re‐print 
the ballot; OR 
2/ The CEB conducts a public hearing,  
noƟﬁes the parƟes that may have an  
interest in the error or omission, discusses 
the issue, takes tesƟmony, and decides if  
re‐prinƟng is necessary.  
 
If the hearing is conducted under #2 and no 
person ﬁles a wriƩen request to re‐print the 
ballots before the hearing ends, then the 
CEB may choose to reprint the ballots or 
not. 
 
However, if a person ﬁles a wriƩen request 
before the close of the hearing in opƟon #2, 
then the CEB must re‐print the ballot. 
There are a number of requirements to  
follow, if the county chooses to hold the 
hearing noted in opƟon #2. Please be cer‐
tain to consult IC 3‐11‐2‐16 for those de‐
tails. 
 
CANDIDATE WITHDRAWAL 
As noted below, ballot vacancies can be 
ﬁlled by county chairs up to the day before 
an elecƟon, if certain criteria are met. 
 
A CEB MUST re‐print a ballot if the county 
chair ﬁlls the vacancy not later than 5‐days 
before the elecƟon. If no replacement or 
“successor” candidate is found, then the 
CEB may re‐print the ballot to include the 
term “Candidate Deceased” or “No  
Candidate” or may simply remove the  
withdrawn candidate’s name. (IC 3‐11‐3‐
29.5) 
 
If a ballot vacancy is ﬁlled within the last 5‐
days before the elecƟon, then the CEB may 
re‐print the ballot but is not required to do 
so. (IC 3‐11‐3‐29.5) 
 
If a successor candidate’s name in NOT 
printed on the ballot, then only the straight 
party votes recorded for that oﬃce may be 
counted for the successor candidate. If the 
name is re‐printed on the ballot, then 
straight party votes AND the ballots where 
the successor candidate’s name appears 
may be counted. (In other words, any “old” 
ballots with the withdrawn candidate’s 
name may not be counted for the successor 
candidate, unless the voter used the 
straight party device.) 
 
This assumes the oﬃce is a “vote for 1” and 
not at‐large where more than one person 
can be elected. Straight party selecƟons do 
not apply to at‐large candidates where 
more than 1 person is elected. (IC 3‐12‐1‐
15) 
 
VOTER OUTREACH 
A CEB is not required to inform voters of a 
defecƟve ballot, but are encouraged to do 
so. A voter has the right to complete an ABS
‐5 to request a new absentee ballot. State 
law was updated this legislaƟve session to 
provide more opƟons as to how the  
replacement ballot may be issued. 
 
If in‐person “early voƟng” has begun in the 
oﬃce, the voter may complete the ABS‐5, 
complete an ABS‐In Person applicaƟon (or 
sign ePollbook), and complete an in‐person 
ABS ballot. Or the person may receive a 
new ballot by mail or if needed, by travel 
board. If travel board is needed and the 
voter meets the travel board requirements, 
then the voter should complete a ABS‐
Travelling Board applicaƟon before sending 
the bi‐parƟsan team to  deliver the  
replacement ballot . 
IN FOCUS: Ballot Re-Printing 
Early Ballot Vacancy v. Late Ballot Vacancy 
For context, ballot vacancies are created because a person did not run for an oﬃce in the Dem. or Rep. party primaries, not ﬁlled by 
the Libertarian Party at their convenƟon, or a candidate withdrew for any reason up to noon, July 15, in an elecƟon year. State law 
does limit candidate withdrawal aŌer the July 15 deadline to the following: candidate dies, moves out of the elecƟon district, was 
convicted of a felony, or ordered oﬀ the ballot. However, it does not set a deadline by which this “late” withdrawal can occur. 
 
Therefore, state law contemplates two types of ballot vacancies: early and late. An “early” vacancy occurs at any point in the  
elecƟon cycle up to day 31 before the elecƟon. A “late” vacancy occurs in the ﬁnal 30‐days before an elecƟon. CounƟes are likely 
more familiar with early vacancies, which are ﬁlled pursuant to IC 3‐13‐1. The method by which an “early” vacancy is ﬁlled is for the 
chair to either call a caucus of PCs or ﬁll by direct appointment if authorized by the party (or there’s only one eligible PC to vote in a 
caucus) not later than 30‐days aŌer the vacancy was created. The chair then ﬁles the required paperwork with the county clerk. 
(CAN‐47, CAN‐48, CAN‐49)  
 
Ballot vacancies created in the last 30‐days before an elecƟon may be ﬁlled by county chairs ﬁll the vacancy using the procedures in 
IC 3‐13‐2. A “late” vacancy created in the last 30‐days for a local oﬃce is to be ﬁlled by direct appointment by the county chair and 
the cerƟﬁcate of candidate selecƟon immediately ﬁled. The Ɵming of when the cerƟﬁcate of candidate selecƟon is ﬁled will impact 
whether or not a ballot is re‐printed (see above). (CAN‐48, CAN‐50) 
 
NOTE: Independent candidates who withdraw are not eligible to ﬁll a ballot vacancy, since independent candidates by deﬁniƟon do 
not aﬃliate with a poliƟcal party. 
QUESTIONS OF THE MONTH 
Q. Do we need to include the names of candidates and their 
address on the CAN‐39 noƟce of general elecƟon? 
A. No. Unlike the noƟce of the primary elecƟon, state law 
only requires the oﬃces on the November ballot to be  
published in the newspaper not later than 10 days from the 
elecƟon. CounƟes using SVRS to create the CAN‐39 noƟce 
will ﬁnd that the system does not include the candidate  
informaƟon. Finally, don’t forget that a copy of the CAN‐39 
must be included in the CEB meeƟng minutes. 
 
Q. We’re a vote center county. Are we able to eliminate 
one or both Saturdays from the requirements in IC 3‐11‐
18.1, if our CEB passes a resoluƟon under IC 3‐11‐10‐26.5 to 
reduce early voƟng dates and Ɵmes? 
A. No. While IC 3‐11‐10‐26.5 does allow a CEB to  
unanimously agree to reduce “early voƟng” at the Clerk’s 
oﬃce, it does not eliminate the requirement under the vote 
center statute (IC 3‐11‐18.1‐4) to have at least one vote  
center used on ElecƟon Day to be available to voters the two 
Saturdays before ElecƟon Day. 
 
Q. Can an ABS‐Mail applicaƟon used in the November  
elecƟon exclude the party choice box needed in a primary 
elecƟon? 
A. Yes. in the forms order signed by the co‐directors and  
noted on the forms master list provided to counƟes, it’s  
noted that a printer may remove the primary party choice 
box on the ABS‐Mail applicaƟon (both English and Spanish) 
used in a November elecƟon and renumber the secƟons. 
Further, the printer may print the ABS‐Mail applicaƟon  
portrait or landscape. 
 
Q. Does the CEB enforce where yard signs are to be placed 
in and around our community? 
A. No. The CEB would enforce whether or not a yard sign 
includes the proper “paid for” disclaimer language. If this is 
missing, then the CEB may ask that the signs be removed, 
disclaimer language added, or ﬁnd other approach the CEB 
believes is appropriate. 
 
Q. Where are at‐large candidates where more than one 
person can be elected  placed on the ballot? 
A. At‐large candidates are placed at the end of the “parƟsan” 
secƟon of the ballot. A reminder: straight party selecƟons in 
the Nov. elecƟon do not apply for at‐large candidates where 
more than one person is elected. (NOTE: A few jurisdicƟons 
in Indiana use ‘at‐large’ for an oﬃce where only one person 
is elected. In this case, the at‐large candidate would be listed 
with the district oﬃces.) 
 
Q. How many ballots do we provide to each precinct or vote 
center on ElecƟon Day? 
A. For opƟcal scan counƟes, the county must provide blank 
ballot cards for ballot marking devices or printed opScan  
ballots totaling 100% of the total acƟve registered voters for 
each precinct. If your county has mulƟple precincts reporƟng 
to one polling locaƟon or are a vote center, then you must 
plan accordingly. (IC 3‐11‐3‐11) 
VR CORNER 
In 2019, not every jurisdicƟon in the state is holding an  
elecƟon. Those individuals “in the county” technically don’t 
have a voter registraƟon deadline, assuming there is no  
special elecƟon being conducted in their precinct. 
 
So what about those ciƟes and towns that are scheduled to 
hold an elecƟon, but the CEB or town elecƟon board (TEB) 
passes a resoluƟon to not conduct a November elecƟon 
because there are no contests? In our view, the elecƟon is 
sƟll considered to have occurred in those precincts and the 
voter registraƟon deadline should sƟll be enforced. 
 
County voter registraƟon oﬃcials also have some  
responsibiliƟes to a “small” town where the town elecƟon 
board is conducƟng the fall elecƟon. First, the county VR 
oﬃcial must provide a list of all voters in the “small” town to 
the TEB not later than 24‐days before the elecƟon in order 
to conduct absentee voƟng. (IC 3‐10‐7‐30) However, the 24‐
day deadline may not comport with the TEB’s hours for  
in‐person early voƟng, and counƟes should discuss with the 
town their need for this list before this deadline. 
 
Further, to prepare for ElecƟon Day, the county VR oﬃcial  
must print a list of all voters in the “small” town and provide 
it to the TEB not later than ten days before the elecƟon. (IC 
3‐7‐29‐1; IC 3‐10‐7‐30) NOTE: CounƟes using ePollbooks 
cannot provide their ePollbooks to the TEB for use. 
 
Further, county VR oﬃcials must also issue cerƟﬁcates of 
error on ElecƟon Day in those small towns where the town 
is conducƟng their own elecƟon. The CoE does not need to 
be printed and delivered; instead, the SVRS code can be 
provided and documented in the town’s precinct poll book. 
ALERT ME The SVRS County Portal has an “alert me”  
funcƟon that will send an email when documents are posted 
to a county’s folder. Below is an image where you can ﬁnd 
this funcƟonality along the top navigaƟon bar on the far right 
side. 
 
IED is scanning ABS‐Mail applicaƟons and posƟng them  
under IED PosƟngs in the speciﬁc county’s folder each day, so 
the “alert me” funcƟon might be helpful to county users. 
Uploading scanned images of the ABS‐Mail applicaƟons is a 
convenience to the counƟes for those that want to print and 
get ballots out the door. The original hard copies will follow 
by regular mail.

Recent changes in state law have changed 
how voƟng systems and ePollbooks are to 
be delivered for use on ElecƟon Day. 
ePOLLBOOKS 
ePollbooks are to be given to the inspector 
(or a person authorized in wriƟng by the  
inspector) on the Saturday before the  
elecƟon at the same Ɵme other elecƟon 
materials are picked up for use on ElecƟon 
Day. Under the new law,  the county  
elecƟon board will seal ePBs  and provide a 
list of seal numbers with the elecƟon  
materials. (GCR is working on an update to 
allow counƟes to record seal numbers in 
SVRS and generate a report by precinct - 
stay tuned for updates!) 
On ElecƟon Day, the inspector and opposite 
party judge will complete step #4 of the  
PRE‐1 Oath Book to conﬁrm the seal num‐
bers listed in the oath book (or SVRS report, 
if applicable) are the same as the seal n 
umbers on the ePBs used at their polling 
place and that the seals are not otherwise 
broken or tampered with. 
AlternaƟvely, if the county elecƟon board 
wants to secure their ePB in a diﬀerent 
manner than a plasƟc seal, state law allows 
them to unanimously agree to adopt a  
resoluƟon staƟng its policy and procedures 
for securing ePBs. However, the PRE‐1 Oath 
Book will sƟll be completed by poll workers 
to conﬁrm the ePB has not been tampered 
with prior to the polls opening. 
VOTING SYSTEMS 
A few years ago state law changed to  
require county elecƟon boards to either 
adhere to statutory requirements to seal 
voƟng systems aŌer the elecƟon results 
canvass unƟl the public test or other  
speciﬁc cases where access is necessary OR 
adopt a  resoluƟon that sets forth its policy 
to secure voƟng systems from tampering 
throughout the year.  (IC 3‐11‐15‐46) 
This year state law changed on how voƟng  
systems are to be delivered to the polling 
place or vote center before elecƟon day. (IC 
3‐11‐3‐10) VoƟng systems (DRE, opScan, 
ballot marking devices) are to be delivered 
by the county elecƟon board, a bi‐parƟsan 
team OR a commercial delivery enƟty. The 
teams or commercial enƟty delivering the 
equipment must complete the CEB‐1A and 
the individual at the polling place must be 
present  to sign the acceptance form. 
Unlike the other statutes, state law doesn’t 
give the county elecƟon board discreƟon in 
adopƟng an alternate policy as to who may 
deliver the voƟng system. However, several 
counƟes have raised quesƟons about using 
a county highway department or an inspec‐
tor/judge combo to deliver  the equipment.  
As long as the county highway department 
or other delivery service has bi‐parƟsan 
representaƟon approved by the enƟre 
county elecƟon board membership, then 
the standards under the law are met in the 
ElecƟon Division’s view.

QUESTIONS OF THE MONTH 
Q. Do candidates who ﬁled a CAN‐16 for small town oﬃce 
need to ﬁle a pre‐elecƟon report? 
A. Maybe! If the oﬃce pays more than $5,000 in a calendar 
year, then a person ﬁling a CAN‐16 must open a campaign 
ﬁnance commiƩee (CFA‐1) not later than noon, 7‐days aŌer 
the candidate ﬁling deadline. Those candidates will have a 
pre‐elecƟon report due not later than noon, October 18, 
2019. 
Q. What about candidates who ﬁle d to run in the primary 
elecƟon but lost? Do they need to ﬁle a pre‐elecƟon report? 
A. No. DemocraƟc and Republican candidates, who ﬁled  to 
run in the primary elecƟon and ﬁled a CFA‐1 and do not  
appear on November’s ballot because they lost the May  
elecƟon, are not required to ﬁle a pre‐elecƟon report.  
Instead, they ﬁle an annual report in Jan. 2020 unless a ﬁnal/
disbands report is ﬁled before the annual report deadline. 
Q. How about a candidate who ﬁle d to run for oﬃce who 
ﬁled a CFA‐1 but is not on the ballot because the oﬃce is 
uncontested? Do they need to ﬁle a pre‐elecƟon report? 
A. Yes. State law requires a pre‐elecƟon report to be ﬁled in 
this instance. 
Q. How are voted absentee ballots & applicaƟon s to be 
stored before elecƟon day? 
A. Under bi‐parƟsan lock and key in the clerk’s oﬃce. Each 
key is controlled by its appointed elecƟon board member.  
(IC 3‐11‐10‐10) 
VR CORNER 
State law requires each county sheriﬀ to provide, at  
minimum, a quarterly report to county voter  
registraƟon oﬃcials with a list of persons who are  
currently imprisoned following convicƟon of a crime. 
These reports will vary from county‐to‐county  
depending on the type of soŌware the sheriﬀ’s  
department uses to create them. However, the VRG‐1 
cover sheet should be aƩached. 
County VR oﬃcials are only to move a person’s  
registraƟon record status to “cancelled” if there is 
enough informaƟon on the report to determine that 
the person is currently imprisoned following convicƟon 
of a crime. A person is being held in jail awaiƟng  
sentencing or a person who is not longer incarcerated 
does not meet the threshold requirements to be  
disenfranchised pursuant to IC 3‐7‐13‐4; IC 3‐7‐46‐2. 
A reminder that a person who is on probaƟon, parole, 
home d
etenƟon, or some community correcƟons  
programs may be registered to vote. Further, a person 
who is released from jail or prison and who had their 
registraƟon status moved to cancelled must re‐register 
to vote.
 More informaƟon can be found in the 2019 
Indiana Voter RegistraƟon Guidebook on starƟng on 
page 39.

Election Division Dispatch 
 Brad King & Angie Nussmeyer, Co-Directors | November 2019  
NEWS & UPDATES 
CerƟﬁcaƟon of ElecƟon Results 
There isn’t much Ɵme to rest following elecƟon day! Your 
county elecƟon boards must complete the canvass the results 
of your elecƟon no later then ten days aŌer the elecƟon, and 
process any provisional ballots or late arriving overseas ballots 
by 3PM that same day. You’ll then need to ﬁle the CEB series 
of forms using SVRS, and separately send your precinct level 
results to IED by noon, Monday, November 18, 2019, unless 
your county has opted to send precinct level results through 
SVRS. The CEB‐9 is due Tuesday, November 19, 2019.  
 
Don’t forget! CounƟes cerƟfy elecƟon results, including those 
from small towns holding their own elecƟons. The town  
elecƟon board should be reminded to get their results to the 
county asap. Further, the town is required to ﬁle all of its  
elecƟon materials with the county elecƟon board to comply 
with retenƟon laws. 
  
County clerks may begin issuing cerƟﬁcates of elecƟon to  
newly elected oﬃcials aŌer 12P local prevailing Ɵme on  
November 22, 2019.   
BMV Open on ElecƟon Eve & ElecƟon Day 
State law requires BMV branches that issue credenƟals like 
driver’s licenses or state ID cards to be open from 8:30A to 8P, 
local prevailing Ɵme, Monday, November 4, 2019, and from 6A 
to 6P, local prevailing Ɵme, Tuesday, November 5, 2019, to 
assist individuals in geƫng ID required to vote. As a reminder, 
state law requires a photo ID to include a photo of the voter, 
be issued by the state or federal government, be current or 
expired since 11/8/16, and include the voter’s name that  
conforms (not necessarily be exact!) to their registraƟon  
record. (IC 3‐5‐2‐40.5)  Further, an address on a state ID does 
not need to match the person’s registraƟon record. ExcepƟons 
exist for  military and veterans’ IDs. 
 
Conference Reminders 
 If you haven’t registered for the December conference, 
Friday, November 8, 2019, is the deadline to avoid a $50 
per person late fee added to the registraƟon fee. 
 The HyaƩ room block was expanded to include a few 
more rooms at the reduced rate, but room block is  
nearing capacity. Make your reservaƟons soon! 
 NominaƟons for the annual awards luncheon are also due 
to IED not later than noon, November 8, 2019. Please 
make sure include background as to why you’ve  
nominated this person for the award.

InformaƟon in this newsleƩer is provided by the Indiana ElecƟon Division as a courtesy to county elecƟon administrators. If a person is unclear concerning elecƟon law provisions,  
the ElecƟon Division can serve as an interpreƟve source. However, where important legal rights are concerned, you must consult with your own aƩorney to be fully and properly advised. 
LAST MINUTE ELECTION QUESTIONS OF THE MONTH 
Q. Can I remake a military or overseas voter’s fax/email ballot using the DRE voƟng system? 
A. No. A faxed/emailed ballot must be made on a ballot card and tabulated on the opƟcal scan voƟng system. (IC 3‐12‐3‐5) Do not forget to 
serialize your remade ballots! The  remake team must  include a serial number on the voter’s ballot and use the same number on the remade 
ballot. This is important in the event there is a recount. Don’t forget a qualiﬁed voter using the FPCA can request a faxed/emailed ballot 
through noon, Monday, November 4, 2019! 
 
Q. Can a voter who was sent an ABS ballot vote a regular ballot on ElecƟon Day? 
A. While state law changed several years ago that does not permit an absentee voter to “beat their ballot” to the polling site, it may be per‐
missible for an individual who requested, but did not return their ABS ballot, to vote a regular ballot on ElecƟon Day.  An absentee voter may 
1) surrender their uncompleted ballot to the Inspector, who would write “cancelled’ on the ABS ballot , store it with the rejected  ballots, and 
issue a regular ballot, if the voter is otherwise eligible; OR 2) complete the PRE‐5 aﬃdavit to aﬃrm the ballot was not received by the voter 
and then be issued a regular ballot, if otherwise eligible.  
 
Q. Can any person hand‐deliver a completed absentee ballot to the county elecƟon board? 
A. No. Only the voter, a member of the voter’s immediate household, a bonded courier, or aƩorney in fact may hand‐deliver a completed 
absentee ballot to the CEB. (IC 3‐11‐10‐1) A reminder, a completed absentee ballot may be hand‐delivered or otherwise received by the CEB 
in all Indiana counƟes not later than noon on ElecƟon Day. (Note: the county clerk or his designee must go to the post oﬃce at noon to en‐
sure there are no absentee ballots to be collected. See IC 3‐11.5‐4‐7) The excepƟon to this rule are overseas voters who requested an absen‐
tee ballot and the ballot security envelope has a postmark on or before November 5, 2019. The CEB must count this universe of absentee 
ballots ONLY if the ballot is received not later than noon, Nov. 15, 2019. 
 
Q. Do absentee ballot security envelopes need to have the postage pre‐paid for the voter? 
A. Yes. Indiana law requires it. (IC 3‐11‐4‐
20) 
 
Q. Are ﬁrearms allowed in polling places on ElecƟon Day? 
Except for polls located on school property, there is no state law that prohibits ﬁrearms in a polling place. So, as long as the person carrying a 
weapon is observing the general laws regarding carrying, it may be permissible to carry in a polling locaƟon. However, even one who lawfully 
possesses a ﬁrearm can run afoul of the law if they act carelessly (or with any other weapon for that maƩer, including a knife or bat). There 
are voter inƟmidaƟon laws on the books at both the federal level (18 U.S.C. §§ 241, 245(b)(1)(A) and the state level (IC 3‐14‐3‐21.5).  
However, mere lawful possession of a ﬁrearm does not violate these statutes.  
 
Q. Does a voter in “inacƟve” status need to complete a VRG 4/12 or other document if they come to vote? 
A. No. Only “inacƟve” or “acƟve” voters are included in the poll book and voters should be issued a regular ballot, if otherwise qualiﬁed. In 
fact, voƟng is a cure for an “inacƟve” voter to have their voter status moved to “acƟve” status, if they vote in any elecƟon between when the 
person was made inacƟve through two federal elecƟon cycles. By signing the poll book and casƟng a ballot, an “inacƟve” voter aﬃrms they 
reside at the address on the poll book and no addiƟonal steps are required.  
 
Q. What is elecƟoneering? 
A. ElecƟoneering is deﬁned in IC 3‐14‐3‐16. Generally, a person may not wear an arƟcle of clothing or otherwise express the support of a 
candidate, poliƟcal party, or public quesƟon. A person wearing such an arƟcle of clothing or holding a sign may be asked to take o
ﬀ the 
buƩon or cover up the clothing. However, a person not complying with this request may not be turned away or prevented from voƟng, if 
otherwise eligible. Instead, the poll workers may forward the non‐compliant voter’s name to the county elecƟon board, who may determine 
if an elecƟon law violaƟon occurred. 
 
Q. Can a voter bring material into the voƟng booth with them? 
A. Yes. Indiana law allows a person to bring in materials with them to assist them in voƟng, whether it’s a list on a sheet of  
paper or a slick piece created by a candidate or poliƟcal party. (IC 3‐11‐8‐18.5) This wriƩen assistance is not considered elecƟoneering, if not 
displayed to others. 
 
Q. Can a voter take a “selﬁe” with their ballot? 
A. Yes. Although the statute has not been repealed (IC 3‐11‐8‐17.5) and remains “on the books,” a federal court has ruled the Indiana law 
unconsƟtuƟonal and it cannot be enforced. 
 
Q. Can I release absentee ballot totals before 6PM on ElecƟon Day in Indiana? 
A. No. Absentee ballot totals may not be released unƟl aŌer the polls close. Even county elecƟon board members are not permiƩed to 
 review or otherwise view the absentee totals tape before 6PM. 
 
Q. Who can enter the polling place on ElecƟon Day? 
A. A comprehensive list of who may be in the polling place can be found in IC 3‐11‐8‐15. Remember, most of these individuals require some 
type of credenƟal to enter a voƟng site!

Election Division Dispatch 
 Brad King & Angie Nussmeyer, Co-Directors | December 2019  
NEWS & UPDATES 
State ConvenƟon Delegates 
The DemocraƟc and Republican state parƟes have cerƟﬁed to 
the Indiana ElecƟon Division the number of delegates to be

their respecƟve state convenƟons to be held in the summer of

the ElecƟon Division can serve as an interpreƟve source. However, where important legal rights are concerned, you must consult with your own aƩorney to be fully and properly advised. 
QUESTIONS OF THE MONTH 
Q. When do we need to complete the CEB‐35 (precincts) 
or CEB‐39 (vote center) and ﬁle with the county auditor? 
A. Unless a small town entered into a ﬁxed price  
agreement with the county elecƟon board, the county 
auditor must submit the elecƟon expenses calculated by 
the county elecƟon board to the town ﬁscal body not later 
than 30‐days aŌer the November 5, 2019, elecƟon, or  
December 5, 2019. 
 
Q. Do we have to issue cerƟﬁcates of elecƟon? 
A. The statute says that you only have to issue a cerƟﬁcate 
of elecƟon when requested by a candidate. However, our 
oﬃce encourages you to do provide each elected oﬃcial 
with the documentaƟon. (IC 3‐12‐5‐2) NOTE: City and 
town judges do not receive a cerƟﬁcate of elecƟon;  
instead, they will receive a commission from the governor. 
 
Q. Do elected oﬃcials have to submit the oath of oﬃce 
included with the state form such as the CEB‐27? 
A. No. The oath of oﬃce included with the cerƟﬁcates of 
elecƟon prescribed by IED is provided as a convenience. 
An oath of oﬃce is to be in wriƟng, which could be  
leƩerhead from an elected oﬃcial or another person  
authorized to give the oath of oﬃce. The text of the oath 
is to be substanƟally similar to the text found on page 34 
of the blue ElecƟon Administrator’s Manual. 
 
Q. Who can give an oath of oﬃce? 
A. A person who is authorized to perform notarial acts 
may give an oath of oﬃce. See IC 33‐42‐9‐7 for the full list. 
 
Q. What is the deadline to ﬁle an oath of oﬃce? 
A. The deadline to take and ﬁle an oath of oﬃce with the 
county clerk is January 31, 2019. This includes elected  
oﬃcials in small towns where a town elecƟon board  
conducted the November elecƟon. NOTE: City or town 
judges ﬁle the oath of o ﬃce with the Secretary of State. 
 
Q. What happens if a person fails to ﬁle the oath of oﬃce 
by the deadline? 
A. The oﬃce becomes vacant when an oath of oﬃce has 
not been properly ﬁled by the deadline. (IC 5‐4‐1‐1.2) The 
incumbent oﬃceholder would then “holdover” pursuant 
to the Indiana ConsƟtuƟon. This would include city and 
town judges because those oﬃces are created by statute. 
(ConsƟtuƟonal oﬃce holders such as superior or circuit 
court judges, prosecuƟng aƩorney, county clerk, etc. are 
exempt from this rule.)  
 
Q. Are oaths of oﬃce public records? And how long are 
those to be retained? 
A. Yes. Please refer to the county’s general retenƟon poli‐
cy established by State Archives as to when you may move 
or otherwise destroy oaths of oﬃce. 
VR CORNER 
Vote History Updates 
If you haven’t already, counƟes may begin updaƟng SVRS 
with informaƟon from the November 5, 2019, elecƟon. 
State law requires updates, including vote history and  
registraƟon informaƟon like name or address, be  
completed not later than 60‐days aŌer the elecƟon or  
January 6, 2020. However, in those areas where a recount 
is being conducted, this deadline is 60‐days from when the 
judge concludes the legal maƩer. 
 
Voter List Maintenance 
State and federal law allow for VLM acƟvity to begin aŌer 
the general, municipal, primary, or special elecƟon. If your 
county has work in the statewide VLM mailing hoppers or 
statewide address mailing conﬁrmaƟon noƟces (SAMC) 
sent by your oﬃce that were put on hold, then VLM  
acƟvity may resume up to February 5, 2020, which is the 
last day to perform VLM work before the primary elecƟon. 
IN FOCUS: Holdovers 
SomeƟmes no one ﬁles to run for an elected oﬃce during 
an elecƟon cycle. The state consƟtuƟon has a remedy for 
those scenarios—holdovers. Generally, if no one ﬁles to 
run for an oﬃce OR an individual who was elected does 
not qualify to assume oﬃce for the new term, then the 
previous oﬃceholder “holds over” and conƟnues in oﬃce 
unƟl such a Ɵme their successor is elected and qualiﬁed or 
the holdover oﬃcial resigns that would allow for the  
elected oﬃce vacancy to be ﬁlled under IC 3‐13, generally. 
 
Determining who holds over when more than one person 
can be elected to the posiƟon is a liƩle more complicated. 
Depending on the unit of government,  the legislaƟve body 
holds a meeƟng to determine which of the incumbent “at‐
large” members will hold over. This year, city common 
councils or town councils may make this determinaƟon. 
 
SomeƟmes its an easy decision where two out of the three 
current “at‐large” members ﬁled to run, leaving the third 
posiƟon vacant. The third member who did not ﬁle would 
then hold over. Other Ɵmes, perhaps none of the  
incumbent members ﬁle but two other community  
members were elected. Then the body would have to pick 
which of the three current oﬃceholders will holdover.  
 
These details can be found in IC 3‐13, but you’ll have to 
ﬁnd the correct arƟcle that corresponds to the unit of  
government. IC 3‐
13‐9, for example, are procedures for 
elected oﬃce vacancies for town oﬃces. Finally, a person 
who holds over does not need a cerƟﬁcate of elecƟon and 
does not complete a new oath of oﬃce. (IC 5‐4‐1‐1.2)

Election Division Dispatch 
 Brad King & Angie Nussmeyer, Co-Directors | January 2020  
NEWS & UPDATES 
2020 Forms 
The Forms Master List and all 2020 forms can be 
found on the INSVRS County Portal, found under the 
“calendar and links” secƟon of the site. The forms on 
the portal replace the forms disc formerly given out at 
past annual conferences, as you’ll ﬁnd the word 
and .pdf versions of each form there. AddiƟonally, you 
can ﬁnd forms on forms.in.gov or the IED  
website (in.gov/sos/elecƟons). These forms are  
ﬁllable .pdf, but are locked down to avoid tampering 
by the public. 
 
Don’t Forget the CAN‐5! 
When a candidate ﬁles to run for oﬃce, counƟes must 
hand‐deliver or mail the CAN‐5 (Candidacy Filing  
ConﬁrmaƟon for 2020) not later than one day aŌer 
receiving the candidate’s ﬁling. You can use the form 
found on the INSVRS or use SVRS to generate the  
document aŌer creaƟng the candidate’s proﬁle in the 
system. QuesƟons? Contact the Quest Help Desk or 
visit the online training portal for a step‐by‐step 
guide. 
 
INSVRS Proﬁciency Standards 
To comply with changes to state law, all SVRS users 
must complete proﬁciency standards approved by the 
Secretary of State. VSTOP & the Secretary’s oﬃce sent 
emails out around the holidays about VRAPSA and 
how to log‐in to Ball State’s CANVAS system. All coun‐
ty users are expected to take module A for cybersecu‐
rity awareness; all county oﬃcials with VR duƟes must 
also take modules B&C. These are “open book” tests, 
and the 10‐page study guide is a great resource for 
those who are new to SVRS and need assistance. 
 
2019 Annual Report 
ALL open candidate and poliƟcal acƟon commiƩees 
are required to ﬁle a 2019 Annual Report not later 
than noon, January 15, 2020. Regular party  
commiƩees are the excepƟon to this deadline; these 
commiƩees have unƟl noon, March 2, 2020, to ﬁle the 
annual report.

In a few short days, county elecƟon 
oﬃcials will have a steady stream of 
candidates visiƟng their oﬃces to ﬁle 
paperwork to run for oﬃce. Every 
DemocraƟc and Republican candidate 
running for local oﬃce in the primary 
elecƟon must ﬁle a CAN‐12 statement 
of economic interest and a CAN‐2  
declaraƟon of candidacy. 
(A reminder that for this purpose,  
candidates for judge are not running 
for “local oﬃce.” It is a judicial oﬃce 
and these candidates must ﬁle their  
candidate paperwork with the ElecƟon 
Division. However, campaign ﬁnance 
ﬁlings made by judicial candidates are 
managed by the county elecƟon 
board.) 
County elecƟon oﬃcials are not 
“candidate police” and may not reject 
a candidate ﬁling except for these 
FOUR reasons speciﬁed in statute: 
1) Candidate running for state oﬃce 
(federal, statewide, state legislaƟve, 
judge, prosecutor) presents candidate 
ﬁling incorrectly to a county elecƟon 
administrator instead of the state.  
IC 3‐5‐4‐1.2 
2) Candidate forms ﬁled aŌer the 
noon (prevailing local Ɵme) candidate 
ﬁling deadline. IC 3‐5‐4‐1.9 
3) Filing made on a form NOT  
approved by the state. IC 3‐5‐4‐8 
4) DeclaraƟon of candidacy is not  
accompanied by the required  
statement of economic interest  
(CAN‐12). IC 3‐8‐2‐11; 3‐8‐9‐6 
Some candidates may fail to include 
required informaƟon on their ﬁling or 
jot down the wrong precinct, for  
example. Only a registered voter of 
the elecƟon district or the county  
party chair may ﬁle a challenge (CAN‐
1) with the county clerk by the noon, 
February 14, 2020, deadline to  
quesƟon the inaccuracy of a form or 
the candidate’s qualiﬁcaƟons to run 
for elected oﬃce. 
The County ElecƟon Board must hold a 
hearing inviƟng the challenged  
candidate and the challenger to  
present the facts of the case. The 
Board will review the facts, apply the 
law, and determine if the candidate 
will remain on the ballot (or not). 
For more informaƟon, please review 
the 2020 Indiana Candidate Guide. 
VR CORNER 
VRC Cards from 2019 Statewide VLM Mailing  
Several counƟes have inquired what, if anything, can be done 
with the “late” voter response cards from the 2019 statewide 
VLM mailing. All of these individuals should be in “inacƟve” 
status, as the card was not received by the August 8, 2019, 
noƟce deadline. (This assumes the county performed its  
hopper work before the freeze period hit.) 
 
Before reviewing these cards, please be sure vote history from 
the November 2019 elecƟon is applied. A person in “inacƟve” 
status who voted at their registraƟon address in November 
2019 is moved back to “acƟve” status in SVRS. 
 
Next, take a moment to review the voter response card. If the 
person marked oval 1 to conﬁrm they reside at the  
registraƟon address, signed the card, and did not vote in the 
November 2019 elecƟon or otherwise make an address  
update to their registraƟon record, then the voter must be 
manually moved from “inacƟve” to “acƟve” status. 
 
If the person marked oval 3 to note a move within the county 
AND the person answered the age & ciƟzenship quesƟons 
AND signed the card AND did not otherwise update their  
registraƟon, then you should update the person’s registraƟon 
at their wriƩen request. This update will move their status to 
“acƟve” aŌer the 7‐day “pending” period. 
 
If the person marked oval 2 to request cancellaƟon of their 
Indiana voter registraƟon in wriƟng AND signed the card, then 
their registraƟon status should be manually moved to 
“cancelled.” However, it’s important that this document be 
signed by the voter and not any other person.  
QUESTIONS OF THE MONTH 
Q. I’m the elected Clerk and plan to run for re‐elecƟon or 
for another oﬃce in 2020. What, if any, special steps do I 
need to take to manage elecƟons? 
A. The only restricƟon you should be concerned about 
relates to absentee ballots. A county clerk running for re‐
elecƟon or another oﬃce on the ballot may not print their 
signature on the absentee ballot and must use the generic 
county seal on it. (Your county’s generic seal can be found 
on the SVRS county portal in the “Shared Documents” 
folder.) State law does not require the clerk’s signature or 
county seal be printed on elecƟon day ballots, but if the 
county does so, then it’s our best advice to apply the 
same ballot prinƟng rule. 
Q. Do candidates for U.S. House need to collect peƟƟon 
signatures? 
It depends. DemocraƟc, Libertarian, and Republican  
candidates do not, but Independent and minor party  
candidates who want their names printed on the ballot 
do.  The independent and minor party candidates must 
collect signatures of registered voters within their  
Congressional district totaling 2% of ALL votes cast in the 
2018 Secretary of State’s race. 
Q. Does a Republican running for precinct commiƩee‐
man need to ﬁle a separate CAN‐37 to run for state  
convenƟon delegate? 
A. Yes. Because she is running for two diﬀerent party 
oﬃces, a Republican who wants to seek both posiƟons 
must ﬁle two separate CAN‐37 forms—one for each o ﬃce. 
InformaƟon in this newsleƩer is provided by the Indiana ElecƟon Division as a courtesy to county elecƟon administrators. If a person is unclear concerning elecƟon law provisions,  
the ElecƟon Division can serve as an interpreƟve source. However, where important legal rights are concerned, you must consult with your own aƩorney to be fully and properly advised. 
IN FOCUS: FOUR REASONS TO REJECT A CANDIDATE FILING 
CounƟes should expect 2020 to be a heavy peƟƟon ﬁling year. 
You have a few opƟons if you need a quick refresher  before 
candidate ﬁling begins. The purple VR guidebook includes a  
secƟon on peƟƟon processing. AddiƟonally, PCC hosted an 
online webinar to cover peƟƟon set‐up, and the “PeƟƟon  
Processing” PowerPoint from the December conference will be 
on the IED website under “ElecƟon Administrator’s Portal” soon.  
Here are a few reminders based on quesƟons our oﬃce is  
ﬁelding from your colleagues: 
 IC 3‐5‐6, generally, is the chapter in Indiana Code that sets 
forth the standards to cerƟfying documents signed by  
registered voters, including substanƟal and minor variaƟon 
in a person’s name or address.  Remember, IC 3‐5‐6‐2 notes 
that resoluƟon of reasonable doubt is to be in favor the  
registered voter.  
 A person’s residence address on the peƟƟon must conform 
to their registraƟon address at the Ɵme the peƟƟon is  
processed by county VR oﬃcials. SubstanƟal and minor  
variaƟons in address are covered in IC 3‐5‐6‐4 and  
IC 3‐5‐6‐5. 
 The master peƟƟon in SVRS for state and federal candidates 
will need to be set up by the HAVA administrator. When you 
get a peƟƟon and don’t ﬁnd it in SVRS, please email 
HAVAadministrator@sos.in.gov and Brandon Kline will get 
the oﬃce set up as soon as possible. (Have a local minor 
party or independent candidate ﬁle? If so, then the county 
user sets up the master peƟƟon.) 
 With one excepƟon related to school board oﬃces, the 
county VR oﬃcial may only review signatures of voters  
within their county. 
 Please do NOT forget to complete the cerƟﬁcaƟon on the 
back of each candidate form. It’s also important that the 
number of signatures out of each Congressional district be 
noted on the front and back of the form in the spaces  
provided. (The peƟƟons ﬁled with IED are the oﬃcial count 
of signatures, not SVRS, so the county’s cerƟﬁcaƟon plays a 
vital role in this process!) 
 Please try not to mark through a signature line on the  
peƟƟon, if the signature is rejected. The Indiana  
ElecƟon Commission may need to review the forms if a  
challenge is ﬁled, and marking through a name may prevent 
the commissioners from performing their due diligence. 
 PeƟƟons may be mailed to the county VR oﬃce for review 
and cerƟﬁcaƟon. However, you must receive and ﬁle stamp 
the peƟƟ
on form by the stated deadline. Any peƟƟon  
received aŌer the noon deadline, even if it’s postmarked 
before, must be rejected. 
 Make sure the peƟƟon is on the current version of the form. 
You can ﬁnd the Forms Master List in the INSVRS portal, 
which will note the current version of the form.  
 Before a peƟƟon ﬁler leaves the oﬃce, take a moment to 
review the aﬃdavit of peƟƟon carrier. If the requested  
informaƟon of the peƟƟon carrier is missing or incomplete, 
the county VR oﬃcial may not process the peƟƟon. BUT, the 
county VR oﬃcial must aƩempt to reach out to the peƟƟon 
carrier to alert them of their omission. The person has unƟl 
the ﬁling deadline (noon, Jan. 28, 2020 for US PresidenƟal 
candidates; noon, February 4, 2020 for Governor  
candidates) to correct the error. Failure to perfect the  
peƟƟon carrier aﬃdavit by this deadline will result in the 
peƟƟon being rejected by the county VR oﬃcial. 
Petition Review Reminders 
State Convention Delegates 
In 2020, the DemocraƟc and Republican parƟes will have state con‐
venƟon delegates on the primary elecƟon ballot for their party 
oﬃce elecƟons. (The Republican Party will also have  
precinct commiƩeemen on the ballot in 2020; the DemocraƟc Party 
will have PCs on the ballot in 2022.) 
 
State law requires the state party chairs to ﬁle with IED the  
number of delegates to be elected in each county and how the 
county will elect their delegates, either at‐large or by district.  The 
plans from the state parƟes can be found under “Candidate Infor‐
maƟon” on the in.gov/sos/elecƟons website. 
 
At‐large means the voter will vote for no more than the number of 
elected delegates in the ﬁled plan. However, if the county chair 
wants to elect delegates by district, then the chair must ﬁle not 
later than December 31, 2019, a descripƟon of each district and the 
number of delegates to be elected from each district. 
 
State law does not address how the districts are to be created; they 
can change every two years if the chair decides elecƟng delegates 
by district is the way to go. BUT, if the chair fails to ﬁle their district 
descripƟon by this deadline, the county elecƟon board must create 
the districts not later than the day candidate ﬁling opens, or January 
8, 2020. 
 
County users may need to revisit the elecƟon set‐up in SVRS to con‐
ﬁrm the delegate districts are set up appropriately. If they are not, 
please submit a county authorizaƟon request to ensure those oﬃc‐
es are created in Ɵme for candidate ﬁling.   
 
CreaƟng the delegate oﬃces and ensuring their accuracy  will be 
important not just for producing the CAN‐5 noƟ
ce, but also to ﬁle 
post‐primary paperwork since counƟes are now required to ﬁle the 
CEB‐9 and other cerƟﬁed elecƟon results through SVRS. This  
includes a complete list of elected delegates with their name,  
address, and Congressional District, which is gathered through data 
entered by the county. 
 
Finally, uncontested precinct commiƩeemen  and delegates are not 
required to be printed on the ballot UNLESS the appointed  
DemocraƟc or Republican member of the CEB ﬁles, in wriƟng, a 
request that the names of uncontested candidates for party  
oﬃces be printed on the ballot. The deadline to ﬁle such a request 
is noon, local prevailing Ɵme, February 14, 2020. (IC 3‐10‐1‐5)

than January 31, 2020, which is the deadline to ﬁle 
the IEC‐22 with the SOS oﬃce Please send a signed 
copy to Brandon Kline—brkline@sos.in.gov—and, if 
possible, copy VSTOP@bsu.edue on the email. 
 
If you have quesƟons about the VSTOP inventory  
database, please email VSTOP@bsu.edu. Their team 
can assist counƟes with logging in to the system. 
Upcoming VLM Projects 
County voter registraƟon oﬃcials will have access to 
at least two pieces of informaƟon from other county 
oﬃcials to assist with voter list maintenance at the 
end of January. 
At minimum, the county sheriﬀ must ﬁle on a  
quarterly basis a list of each Indiana resident who has 
been convicted of a crime and placed in a county  
correcƟonal facility during the previous quarter. The 
ﬁrst list for 2020 is due to the county VR oﬃcial not 
later than January 31, 2020. The VRG‐1 cover sheet is 
to be aƩached to any list provided to the county from 
the sheriﬀ’s oﬃce.  
Using the sheriﬀ’s list, the county VR oﬃcial may 
move a person’s registraƟon status to “cancelled” if 
the person is currently imprisoned following  
convicƟon of a crime. If the individual is no longer  
imprisoned, then the person’s registraƟon is not to be 
moved to “cancelled” status. (IC 3‐7‐46‐6; IC 3‐7‐46‐1) 
AddiƟonally, the local health department ﬁles a copy 
of death records with the county Auditor pursuant to 
IC 16‐37‐3‐9(d). CounƟes may request this list from 
the auditor and use it to move a registered voter’s 
status to “cancelled” as the individual is cerƟﬁed as 
deceased. (IC 3‐7‐45‐2.1(d); IC 3‐7‐45‐1) 
Later this spring counƟes will be hearing from IED 
about a project using data from the U.S. Northern and 
Southern District Courts. Stay tuned!

Candidate ﬁling for the DemocraƟc 
and Republican party primary closes

Cyber Term: Malware 
Malware is a collecƟve name for any type of 
malicious soŌware. Malicious soŌware  
includes but is not limited to viruses,  
spyware, worms, and ransomware.  
Malware’s main purpose is to invade,  
damage, or disable computers, computer 
systems, networks, tablets, mobile devices 
and data.  
Malware tradiƟonally consists of code that 
has been developed by cyber‐aƩackers to 
cause extensive damage to data and systems 
or to gain access to an unauthorized  
network or system.  
TradiƟonally, malware is delivered to an  
unknowing user through phishing aƩempts 
via email. The user unknowingly clicks on a 
link or opens a ﬁle to execute the malware. 
“Ransomware” is an example of malware.
 
Incident Response Plan (IRP) 
During the 2020 Indiana ElecƟon Administrators’ Conference, Indiana University’s Center for Applied  
Cybersecurity Research (IU‐CACR) reviewed incident response fundamentals and the importance of having an 
incident response plan in place. An incident response plan (IRP) is a set of instrucƟons to help detect,  
respond to and recover from incidents. An IRP facilitates eﬀecƟve and repeatable management of emergency 
situaƟons or incidents through the use of situaƟon speciﬁc IRPs or playbooks. These types of plans are used 
to address issues such as cybercrime, breaches, data loss, service outages, natural disasters, etc. The main 
components of an IRP are:  
 response team establishment 
 Incident analysis; decision to invoke a speciﬁc IRP or playbook 
 Incident management and containment  
 Incident recovery

 The Belfer Center: ElecƟon Cyber Incident CommunicaƟons Plan Template

On a related note, a reminder that state law recently changed

CAN‐9: NoƟce of Primary ElecƟon 
For the May primary elecƟon, each county elecƟon board must

along with their address and oﬃce sought. (Addresses must be

maƟon.

Every elecƟon cycle we’re all asked  
quesƟons about yard signs and when/
where/what Ɵme can they be placed. IED  
publishes a Disclaimer brochure with 
more detailed informaƟon, but here are 
some FAQs: 
1/ Is there a state law that dictates when 
yard signs can be put out before an  
elecƟon? No, state law doesn’t  
speciﬁcally address when campaign yard‐
signs can go out in people’s yards. This 
decision is leŌ to local ordinance or 
homeowner associaƟon policies.  
However, there is a state law that states 
IF there is a local ordinance prohibiƟng 
yard signs, then the ordinance is not  
enforceable for 60‐days before an  
elecƟon and 5‐days aŌer. (IC 36‐1‐3‐11) 
AddiƟonally, a homeowner’s associaƟon 
policy prohibiƟng yard signs cannot be 
enforced 30‐days before an elecƟon and 
5‐days aŌerward. 
2/ can yard signs be placed in the right of 
way? No. However, the county elecƟon 
board doesn’t enforce placement of yard 
signs. Instead, your county or city  
highway department, planning dept., or 
equivalent would enforce this rule. 
3/ Are disclaimers required on yard 
signs? In most cases, yes. A disclaimer in 
at least 7 size font with who paid for the 
sign is required to be included on the sign 
in indelible ink that contrasts with the  
background. (IC 3‐9‐3‐2.5) However, signs  
supporƟng or opposing a referendum do 
not require the use of a disclaimer. (IC 3‐9
‐3‐2.5)  The county elecƟon board would 
address complaints about yard signs that 
appear to not be compliant with state’s  
disclaimer law. 
4/ A non‐incumbent printed on their 
yard sign “Sam Smith Dogcatcher.” This 
implies they are the incumbent. Is this 
allowable? In the view of the Indiana 
ElecƟon Commission, yes. The bi‐parƟsan 
IEC issued an advisory opinion (2015‐01) 
that interprets IC 3‐9‐3‐5. A copy of this  
advisory opinion is included in the  
appendix of the green Campaign Finance 
Manual. 
5/ A person calls to ask if she can remove 
a yard sign placed in the highway right‐of
‐way without permission. What do I tell 
her? Only those with legal authority over 
the property can remove the yard sign 
from the county right‐of‐way. Any other 
person without such authority may be 
liable for criminal conversion. She should 
ﬁle a complaint with the proper authori‐
Ɵes to make them aware of the yard 
sign’s placement. If the sign is located on 
the owner’s property outside of any right‐
of‐way, then the owner may remove it.

ReƟring the Indianavoters Mobile App  
The Indianavoters Mobile App will no longer be available 
in the Apple and Android store aŌer March 13, 2020, 
and the app will no longer be supported. Instead, users 
should visit indianavoters.com, which is now mobile 
phone‐friendly, using their phone’s web browser. 
 
The mobile website has the same features as the app, 
but also integrates funcƟonality for persons with  
disabiliƟes to beƩer serve everyone. Further, the mobile 
website has the same security features as those 
 accessing the site through a desktop computer. 
 
Military & Overseas Voters VR Deadline 
Military & overseas voters using the Federal Post Card 
ApplicaƟon (FPCA) have an extended voter registraƟon 
deadline before each elecƟon. Rather than the standard 
29‐day statewide cut‐oﬀ, individuals eligible to use the 
FPCA may use this form to register to vote unƟl eight 
days before the elecƟon. The  voter registraƟon cut‐oﬀ 
for FPCA‐eligible voters is April 27, 2020. An FPCA can be 
emailed or faxed, so it is not necessary for a military or 
overseas voter to be held to the same “wet” or original 
signature standard on a VR form as a civilian voter  
submiƫng the state or federal voter registraƟon form. 
InformaƟon in this newsleƩer is provided by the Indiana ElecƟon Division as a courtesy to county elecƟon administrators. If a person is unclear concerning elecƟon law provisions,  
the ElecƟon Division can serve as an interpreƟve source. However, where important legal rights are concerned, you must consult with your own aƩorney to be fully and properly advised. 
IN FOCUS: Campaign Yard Signs & Using “For” 
MARCH BUILD 
1) VRG forms sent electronically from BMV and OVR 
hoppers will now automaƟcally associate to the  
Document’s secƟon of the voter records in SVRS. 
 
2) StarƟng with the May 2020 primary elecƟon post‐
elecƟon cerƟﬁcaƟon, counƟes will noƟce a second  
secƟon of the CEB 9. This addiƟonal informaƟon will  
collect more elecƟon data and assist in compleƟng the 
bi‐annual EAC Survey. In the past the informaƟon had 
been collected through an online survey and now this 
informaƟon will be submiƩed through SVRS through 
post‐elecƟon acƟviƟes. 
 
3) For ePB counƟes only, a noƟﬁcaƟon email will be  
received if WSF execuƟons have not taken place. This 
will serve as a noƟce to county users as well as their 
vendors and help to ensure data is as up to date as  
possible. 
 
4) Two factor code validaƟon will be extended to  
indianavoters.com as an opƟon for members of the  
public to enable when they are registering or changing 
their voter registraƟon record. This is similar to two‐
factor authenƟcaƟon measures currently employed for 
SVRS users. Enrolling in 2FA on the indianavoters.com 
site is NOT a requirement, but is an added layer of  
security available to those voters who wish to acƟvate it. 
Cyber Term: Ransomware 
“Ransomware” is an example of malware, a term 
covered in last month’s Dispatch. It demands some 
sort of payment from the vicƟm in order to recover 
control of their computer or data. Some types of 
ransomware include scareware, screen lockers, and 
encrypƟng ransomware.  
While there are several ways ransomware can infect 
a computer or network, one of the most common 
methods is through malicious spam. SomeƟmes 
spam is harmless, but every person should remain 
guarded when receiving an email from an unknown 
individual or organizaƟon, especially if it contains a 
link to a website or document. 
If your county experiences a ransomware aƩack, 
please noƟfy the state so that our federal and state 
partners can be alerted and security protocols for 
SVRS can be deployed.
 
QUESTIONS OF THE MONTH 
Q. Do candidate names appear in CAPITAL leƩers 
on the ballot? And do I use “” or () around a  
candidate’s nickname? 
A. Yes, a candidate’s name is printed in ALL CAPS on 
the ballot. (IC 3‐10‐1‐14.1) State law changed to  
require parentheses () around a candidate’s  
nickname, not quotaƟon marks. (IC 3‐5‐7‐5) 
Q. A candidate ﬁled their declaraƟon of candidacy 
but their name designaƟon is out of order. Can I 
change the order to comply with law? 
A. No. The ballot name as indicated on the  
declaraƟon of candidacy must be used on the ballot 
in the order requested by the candidate, unless a 
CAN‐1 challenge was ﬁled contesƟng how the  
candidate’s ballot name was ordered. More  
informaƟon about the ﬁrst, second, third, and fourth 
designaƟon can be found in the red Candidate’s 
Guide or in IC 3‐5‐7‐5. 
Q. Do I need to change a candidate’s name on their 
voter registraƟon record if their ballot name on 
their declaraƟon of candidacy doesn’t match their 
voter registraƟon name? 
A. Yes. State law requires county VR oﬃcials to  
adjust the voter registraƟon name of a candidate to 
match the candidate’s ballot name. The declaraƟon 
of candidacy and candidate consent forms note this 
statute and give permission to counƟes to make this 
change. (IC 3‐5‐7‐6) 
Q. What’s a federal only absentee ballot? 
A. A federal only ballot is ONLY used for an overseas 
voter who marks on the FPCA that they are an  
overseas voter and their return to the U.S. is  
uncertain. These voters must be registered to vote at 
the address of the county voter registraƟon oﬃce, 
even if they provide a residence address within  
Indiana  (IC 3‐
11‐4‐8). Under federal law , these  
voters can vote only for federal oﬃces in even‐
numbered general elecƟon years. Every Indiana 
county must have a federal only DemocraƟc and  
Republican ballot with the oﬃces of U.S. President 
and U.S House for the May 2020 primary elecƟon. 
(U.S. Senate is not on the ballot in Indiana in 2020). 
As noted above, only certain overseas voters are  
enƟtled to cast a federal only ABS ballot; no other 
persons are eligible to use this ballot and it should 
not be included with ElecƟon Day materials. 
ABSENTEE BALLOT REMINDERS 
 ABS‐Mail ballots must be delivered to the county by 
their vendor not later than March 16, 2020, for the 
primary elecƟon. 
 State law and the federal MOVE Act require counƟes 
to send absentee ballots to voters with approved 
ABS‐Mail and FPCA applicaƟons not later than 45‐
days before each elecƟon, or March 21, 2020. 
 March 21, 2020, is the default “ballot ready” date in 
SVRS. CounƟes can request the deadline to be 
moved up to an earlier date by submiƫng a county 
authorizaƟon form in INSVRS. 
 Expect IED to follow‐up on the March 21, 2020, 
deadline as each state is required to report back to 
the U.S. Department of JusƟce on compliance with 
this important federal law. 
 Once counƟes begin sending absentee ballots out on 
or around March 21, 2020, state law requires an 
absentee ballot be sent on the same day the  
applicaƟon is approved. (IC 3‐11‐4‐18) 
 ABS‐Mail and FPCA applicaƟons for a mailed  
absentee ballot must be received not later than 
11:59PM, April 23, 2020. 
 Absentee and FPCA forms can be mailed, hand‐
delivered, faxed, or emailed.

Election Division Dispatch 
 Brad King & Angie Nussmeyer, Co-Directors | Late April/Early May 2020  
NEWS & UPDATES 
ABS ApplicaƟons 
Included with this newsleƩer is an updated Forms Master List, 
as there has been a number of changes to absentee forms due 
to IEC Orders and county requests. To clarify: 
 
ABS‐Mail 
The R28/11‐19 version of the ABS‐Mail ApplicaƟon for an

AddiƟonally, Order 2020‐41 permits the ABS‐Mail ApplicaƟon

ABS‐Por Correo

updates made to this version of the form. 
 
ABS‐Mail Primary 2020

the reason box. The form was just updated to remove  
language for #4 Reason, and instead says “Read & Sign Below” 
based on feedback from our county colleagues. BOTH versions 
of this form are OK to use in the primary elecƟon.

‐Mail Primary 2020 form in English and the

approved.) 
 
Online ABS Portal 
Beginning this week, registered voters may use indianavot‐
ers.com to ﬁle an absentee by mail (English & Spanish) and 
absentee by traveling board form. County users will have two 
new INSVRS hoppers, and are encouraged to aƩend training or 
review training once posted in the INSVRS county portal. 
APRIL/MAY WEB TRAINING

CALENDAR

for June 2, 2020 primary elecƟon

‐6‐10)

systems

person early voƟng; vote center counƟes must have 
the clerk’s oﬃce AND one vote center used on

As you know, the Indiana ElecƟon  
Commission unanimously agreed to IEC 
Order 2020‐37 and Order 2020‐40, which 
modiﬁed some procedures in state law 
but also restated porƟons of current law 
to provide addiƟonal context.  
Our oﬃce has received a number of calls 
and emails looking for guidance and  
clarity. Below are some commonly asked 
quesƟons from counƟes.  
POLL SITES IN NON‐VOTE CENTER  
COUNTIES 
Q/ I’m a non‐vote center county. Can we 
move to the vote center model now for 
the primary elecƟon? 
No. The Orders did not alter state law 
requiring a county to ﬁle a vote center 
plan with IED not later than 60‐days from 
the date of the primary elecƟon. This 
deadline has passed. Any non‐vote center 
county must assign a polling locaƟon to 
each precinct, but there is an allowance 
for consolidaƟng adjoining precincts to 
report to one polling place (more below). 
Q/Do the county commissioners select 
polling locaƟons? 
Yes. The Orders did not alter state law 
requiring the county execuƟve 
(commissioners) from selecƟng ElecƟon 
Day polling places and ﬁling the list with 
the CEB not later than 29‐days before the 
elecƟon, or May 4, 2020. (Note: in Lake 
and Porter counƟes, the Board of  
ElecƟons and RegistraƟon makes these 
selecƟons by the same deadline date.) 
Q/ If our county wants to open fewer 
elecƟon day polling places, how would 
we do that? 
The Orders did not alter state law. Non‐
vote center counƟ
es should rely on IC 3‐
11‐8‐4.3. This allows the CEB, through 
unanimous consent, to assign ONE polling 
locaƟon to adjoining precincts. For  
example, precinct 1, 2, 3 go to site A;  
precinct 4, 5 go to site B. All voters in  
precinct 1, 2, or 3 must go to site A, which 
is their assigned polling place. While it 
may sound the same as a vote center, it’s 
not. A vote center allows any voter go to 
any locaƟon. Non‐vote center counƟes do 
not have this ﬂexibility, and voters must 
go to their assigned polling place on  
elecƟon day. 
 
Q/ OK—so our CEB unanimously agreed 
to consolidate precincts at fewer polling 
places. How do we manage voƟng  
systems and poll books? 
Let’s ﬁrst discuss voƟng systems. For 
counƟes using DRE systems (and DRE  
systems are NOT ballot marking devices 
used with some opScan systems!) each 
precinct may be loaded on one (or more 
machines). For example, if precinct 1 & 2 
go to site A, then precinct 1 & 2 may be 
loaded on the same DRE unit, and the CEB 
may have mulƟple DRE units with those 
two precincts at site A. 
For opScan counƟes, you must have one 
tabulator for each precinct at the  
locaƟon. Using the above example, the 
site would have two opScan tabulators—
one for precinct 1 and one for precinct 2. 
The voter would need to cast their ballot 
on the tabulator assigned to their pre‐
cinct. 
Some opScan counƟes use a ballot  
marking device (BMD) in conjuncƟon with 
the tabulator. Each BMD assigned to the 
polling place may have all precincts for 
the site loaded on to it. Using the above 
example,  each BMD may have precinct 
1&2 loaded on it for voters to use (but 
the voter has to cast their ballot on the 
proper tabulator). 
If your county uses an ePollbook on  
ElecƟon Day, then each precinct assigned 
to the polling place may be on each unit. 
Using the above example, precinct 1&2 
may be on one or more ePBs used at site 
A. 
If your county prints poll lists for ElecƟon 
Day, you must have a printed poll list for 
each precinct assigned to the polling  
locaƟon. Using the above example, this 
means precinct 1 has its own poll list, as 
does precinct 2.  
POLL SITES IN VOTE CENTER COUNTIES 
For the June 2, 2020 primary elecƟon 
only, IEC Order 2020‐37 did alter state 
law for counƟes with 25,000 ac
Ɵve voters 
or more. Rather than requiring one vote 
center for every 10,000 acƟve voters and 
one for any remaining number, a vote 
center county with 25,000 acƟve voters 
or more may amend their plan to have, at 
minimum, one vote center for every 
25,000 acƟve voters and one for any  
remainder. For example, county A has 
67,000 acƟve voters. Order 37 requires 
the county to have, at minimum, three 
ElecƟon Day vote centers. 
State law currently allows vote center 
counƟes with fewer than 25,000 acƟve 
voters to have only one ElecƟon Day vote 
center, at minimum. 
Again, the county’s vote center plan 
would need to be amended through 
unanimous agreement of the CEB to  
reduce or otherwise modify ElecƟon Day 
sites. 
ELECTION DAY POLL WORKERS 
Q/ We’re a non‐vote center county, but 
concerned about recruiƟng enough poll 
workers. Are we able to reduce poll 
worker posiƟons? 
Current law provides for some ﬂexibility 
here. IC 3‐11‐8‐4.3 allows a CEB, through 
unanimous consent, to have one precinct 
elecƟon board (Inspector and two judges 
of opposite poliƟcal party) manage the 
enƟre polling place.  
AlternaƟvely, IC 3‐6‐6‐38.5 allows the CEB 
to have only one Inspector manage a  
polling place with the support of bi‐
parƟsan judges.  
AddiƟonally, non‐vote center counƟes 
can eliminate poll clerk and sheriﬀ  
posiƟons. (IC 3‐6‐6‐38) 
Q/ I’m a vote center county. Are we able 
to reduce the number of poll workers at 
a site? 
Current law allows a vote center county 
to determine how many poll workers 
each site has through its vote center plan. 
The minimum requirement is one  
precinct elecƟon board (inspector and 
two judges of opposite poliƟcal party) at 
each site. Any changes to the vote center 
plan require unanimous consent. 
Q/ Did the Orders change anything 
about who can be a poll worker? 
Yes. Order 2020‐40 altered the  
requirement that a poll worker be a  
resident of Indiana rather than a resident 
of the county for the June 2, 2020  
primary only. The other  requirements 
found in IC 3‐6‐6‐7 (general  
requirements) and IC 3‐6‐6‐39 (student 
poll worker) sƟll apply. 
InformaƟon in this newsleƩer is provided by the Indiana ElecƟon Division as a courtesy to county elecƟon administrators. If a person is unclear concerning elecƟon law provisions,  
the ElecƟon Division can serve as an interpreƟve source. However, where important legal rights are concerned, you must consult with your own aƩorney to be fully and properly advised. 
IN FOCUS: Changes to Election Procedures due to IEC Orders 
PUBLIC TEST OF VOTING EQUIPMENT 
Q/ Our Courthouse is closed, so do we 
have to hold the public test? 
Yes. The Orders did not alter state law. 
CounƟes must sƟll conduct a public 
meeƟng to perform the public test of 
voƟng equipment. However, Order 37 did 
reference the governor’s execuƟve order 
to allow for public meeƟngs to be  
conducted by video or telephonic  
conferencing. 
However, since state law (IC 3‐11‐13‐22 & 
3‐11‐14.5) requires the public be allowed 
to request addiƟonal machines to be  
tested, the virtual meeƟng must allow for 
public parƟcipaƟon in real‐Ɵme. 
Q/ When does the public test need to be 
performed by? 
The Orders did not alter state law. State 
law simply notes the public test must be 
performed before in‐person absentee 
voƟng begins (IC 3‐11‐13‐22; IC 3‐11‐14.5‐
1). This would be Monday, May 25, 2020, 
but since IED is closed for the Memorial 
Day holiday, the deadline to begin the 
public test is Tuesday, May 26, 2020. 
Q/ Do we have to publish noƟce of the 
public test in the newspaper? 
Yes. The Orders did not change this  
requirement. The publicaƟon deadline is 
48‐hours before the public test is held. If 
you hold the public test on the last  
possible day, May 26, this means the 
newspaper must publish the noƟce not 
later than Saturday, May 24. 
BUT, since the public test is a public 
meeƟng, counƟes must also publish  
noƟce on its general noƟce board. For a 
meeƟng held at 10AM on May 26, the 
public test no
Ɵce must be posted not 
later than 10A, Thursday, May 22. Slightly 
diﬀerent rules due to the state’s Open 
Door Law. 
IN‐PERSON ABSENTEE VOTING 
Q/ The Courthouse is closed, and I’m not 
sure it will be open before early voƟng 
begins on May 26. What can I do? 
The Orders did not alter state law, which 
requires under IC 3‐11‐10‐26 for one  
locaƟon of the circuit court clerk’s oﬃce 
as designated by the circuit court clerk to 
be available for the abbreviated early 
voƟng schedule.  
It is possible for the clerk to designate a 
space in an alternaƟve locaƟon, as long as 
it’s designated as the ONE oﬃce of the 
circuit court clerk for purposes of in‐
person absentee voƟng. CEBs can have 
more satellite locaƟons under IC 3‐11‐10‐
26.3, but it must have at least this ONE 
locaƟon of the circuit court clerk available 
to voters. 
Q/What days are we to conduct in‐
person absentee voƟng? 
At the one locaƟon of the clerk’s oﬃce, 
Thursday, May 26 to Friday, May 29;  
Saturday, May 30; Monday, June 1 unƟl 
noon, local prevailing Ɵme. In‐person 
absentee voƟng must be available during 
regular business hours of the clerk’s oﬃce 
during the week, with the Saturday and 
Monday excepƟons (see below). 
For vote center counƟes, the clerk’s oﬃce 
AND at least one vote center used on 
ElecƟon Day must be open on Saturday, 
May 30. AddiƟonal sites can be added, 
but this is the minimum requirement. 
For non‐vote center counƟes, addiƟonal 
satellite sites may be open by unanimous 
consent of the CEB pursuant to IC 3‐11‐10
‐26.3. 
ALL counƟes with a populaƟon of 20,000 
or more must have early voƟng available 
for at least seven hours on Saturday, May 
30, which is consistent with current state 
law. 
CounƟes with a populaƟon of less than 
20,000 may reduce the hours to at least 
four on Saturday, May 30, which is con‐
sistent with state law. (IC 3‐11‐10‐26(i)) 
Q/ Must we use the same satellite  
absentee locaƟons in the November 
elecƟon as we had in the primary? 
Current state law requires the satellite 
sites used in the primary elecƟon to be 
used in November. You can have more 
sites in November, but at least must have 
the same ones from the primary. 
HOWEVER, Order 37 made adjustments 
to this requirement. A county does not 
need to have the same satellite locaƟons 
in the spring and fall for the 2020 elecƟon 
cycle. 
Q/ In‐person absentee voƟng ends at 
noon, June 1. Do we have to allow  
people in line to vote? 
Yes. Whether it’s the ﬁrst day, deadline 
day, or a day in‐between when in‐person 
absentee voƟng is conducted, a person 
who is in line when the oﬃce closes or at 
noon on June 1 must be allowed to vote, 
if otherwise eligible. The county should 
put a staﬀ person at the end of the line, 
take down names, or mark the voter’s 
hand in some way. (IC 3‐11‐10‐29.2) 
TRAVELING BOARD 
Order 37 eased some rules relaƟng to 
traveling board. The April Dispatch  
covered those items.  
CENTRAL COUNT OF ABS BALLOTS 
Q/ How did Order 40 impact the central 
count? 
Recognizing a county may need to use 
more space to conduct its central count, 
Order 40 allows counƟes with fewer than 
50,000 acƟve voters to have up to three 
central count locaƟons. 
For counƟes with 50,000 acƟve voters or 
more, the CEB may have one central 
count locaƟon for every 50,000 acƟve 
voters. 
HOWEVER, each CEB member (appointed 
members AND clerk) must have a proxy 
assigned to each central count locaƟon to 
adjudicate issues that may be brought 
before them or to make residency chal‐
lenges. 
Q/ Can we use 16– and 17– year olds for 
the central count? 
Yes. State law already allows for this. See 
IC 3‐11.5‐4‐23.  
AddiƟonally, state law allows a 16– or 17– 
year old to serve as a judge or poll clerk at 
elecƟon day polling sites by following IC 3
‐6‐
6‐39.  
Order 37 also permits a 16– or 17– year 
old to be an absentee voter board  
member for in‐person absentee or to 
assist with ABS‐mail requests. 
Q/ When can we start counƟng absentee 
ballots on ElecƟon Day? 
Under Order 37, the CEB may begin the 
central count at 6AM. 
Please be reminded that absentee results 
may NOT be released to the public or 
even members of the CEB before 6P on 
elecƟon night! (IC 3‐14‐4‐10) 
IN FOCUS: Changes to Election Procedures due to IEC Orders 
VR CORNER 
ABS ApplicaƟons & Changes in Residence  
State law allows a voter to change their name using the absentee ballot applicaƟon. Only voters who move within their precinct 
may use the form to update their residence address. If the voter is found to have moved within their precinct, then the residence 
address change is to be made in INSVRS and the applicaƟon scanned and aƩached as the registraƟon document. The update to 
the voter’s record would be automaƟc and their registraƟon status must stay “acƟve” since they moved within the precinct. 
 
Pending Voters & ABS VoƟng 
A voter must be in acƟve or inacƟve status to have their absentee applicaƟon reviewed of approved. A voter in pending status 
may bring their acknowledgement card and present themselves to VR oﬃcials within the 7‐day period to have their registraƟon 
moved to acƟve status.  
Q/ Can we scan or otherwise manage or 
prep absentee paperwork before  
ElecƟon Day? 
No. The Orders did not alter state law on 
these points. A county is not permiƩed to 
pre‐scan opƟcal scan ballot cards. Before 
elecƟon day, all counƟes must perform 
the ﬁrst of two signature review. In this 
case the signatures on the absentee  
applicaƟon and on the ballot security  
envelope must be reviewed by the CEB or  
bi‐parƟsan ABS voter board following the 
procedures in state law (IC 3‐11‐10‐4). 
On ElecƟon Day, the central count teams 
must also perform a second signature 
review, unless the CEB unanimously  
passes a resoluƟon to eliminate the sec‐
ond review of ABS‐Travel Board and ABS‐
In Person ballots. (Teams must sƟll do a 
second review of ABS‐Mail signatures). 
See IC 3‐11.5‐4‐12 for more details. 
Q/ The CEB can count the ABS ballots on 
ElecƟon Day by themselves, right? 
No. The Orders did not alter state law on 
this point. State law requires central 
count teams to manage the ballot review 
process under IC 3‐11.5‐4‐11. If the bi‐
parƟsan central count team disagrees on 
whether or not to reject an absentee  
ballot, then the issue must be brought 
forward to the CEB who makes the ﬁnal 
decision to count or reject the absentee 
ballot, before the ballot envelope is 
opened. 
Q/ When are absentee ballots due on 
ElecƟon Day? 
Noon, local prevailing Ɵme. The Orders 
have not made changes to this deadline. 
Further, the county clerk or her designee 
must go to the post oﬃce at noon to  
collect any ABS ballots that may be in the 
facility. 
A reminder that overseas voters (civilian 
and military) using the FPCA can have 
their ballot envelope postmarked on or 
before ElecƟon Day and received not later 
than noon, ten days aŌer the primary 
(Friday, June 12, 2020). The ballot is to be 
counted, if the voter is otherwise eligible. 
DEFECTIVE ABS APPS/BALLOT  
ENVELOPES 
Order 40 includes advice IED has given 
counƟes in the past. While a county is not 
required to give noƟce to the voter if 
their applicaƟon or security envelope is 
defecƟve or rejected, a county may 
choose to do so in a uniform and  
consistent manner. In other words, what 
you do for one, you must do for all. 
The absentee applicaƟon and the  
absentee ballot envelope is to NEVER 
leave the possession of the CEB. Instead, 
ask the voter to complete a new  
applicaƟon or if the ballot envelope is 
defecƟve, the voter should complete the 
ABS‐5 to have a ballot re‐issued to them 
because they failed to sign the security 
envelope or their partner signed their 
envelope by mistake, for example. 
Remember, if an FPCA is rejected, noƟce 
IS required to be given to the voter, and 
this noƟce can be generated in INSVRS. 
Q/ A voter selected a D ballot on their 
absentee app, but now wants an R  
ballot. Can we switch? 
No. State law was clariﬁed on this point a 
few years ago. The party indicated on the 
absentee applicaƟon or marked on the 
poll list for in‐person absentee voƟng or 
on ElecƟon Day is the party’s ballot the 
person receives in the primary elecƟon. 
(IC 3‐11‐4‐17.7;IC 3‐10‐1‐24) 
EMERGENCY ELECTION DAY SITE 
CHANGE 
Q/ What if a site decides last minute it 
isn’t able to be a polling place due to an 
emergent reason? Can we change it? 
The Orders did not alter state law in this 
regard except on one minor point. 
The CEB in a vote center county may 
unanimously agree to alter its vote center 
plan, even on ElecƟon Day. The plan must 
be ﬁled with IED in order to be eﬀec
Ɵve. 
The CEB must give best possible noƟce to 
the voters, and must update the change 
in INSVRS as soon as possible. 
The CEB in a non‐vote center may  
unanimously agree to move a polling 
place, if an emergency within 2 days of 
elecƟon day occurs. The CEB must give 
best possible noƟce to the voter, and  
Order 40 requires the resoluƟon be ﬁled 
with IED. CounƟes must also make the 
change in INSVRS as soon as possible. 
 
IN FOCUS: Changes to Election Procedures due to IEC Orders

Election Division Dispatch 
 Brad King & Angie Nussmeyer, Co-Directors | May 2020  
NEWS & UPDATES 
Public Test of VoƟng Systems 
CounƟes must begin the public test of voƟng systems not later 
than May 26, 2020. (The deadline is impacted by IEC Order 
2020‐40 and the Memorial Day holiday.)  Please do not forget 
to ﬁle the IEC‐9 (DRE) and IEC‐10 (opƟcal scan) when the test is 
completed. All counƟes will have an IEC‐10 to ﬁle; counƟes 
using a DRE voƟng system are also required to ﬁle the IEC‐9. 
 
Candidate Lists & Polling LocaƟon NoƟces 
Don’t forget to publish the CAN‐9 noƟce of the primary  
elecƟon in the newspaper at least 10‐days before the June 2, 
2020, elecƟon. A copy of the CAN‐9 is to be ﬁled with IED, too. 
 
For non‐vote center counƟes, the county elecƟon board must 
publish a list on polling locaƟons not later than 10‐days before 
the elecƟon. (IC 3‐11‐8‐3.2) The county commissioners are 
required to publish noƟce in vote center counƟes at least 10‐
days before the elecƟon. (IC 3‐11‐18.1‐9)  
MAY WEB TRAINING

Dates are subject to change; check the 2020 INSVRS 
Training Schedule on the county portal to conﬁrm.

period ends 
May 9, 2020 CFA‐11 “Large ContribuƟon”  
Supplemental Period begins for candidate  
commiƩees  
May 12, 2020 (NOON) Deadline for D&R chairs to 
nominate poll workers for the primary; aŌer 12P 
local Ɵme, the CEB may begin ﬁlling vacancies (IC 3‐6
‐6‐10) 
May 14, 2020 Travel Board begins 
May 15, 2020 (NOON) Pre‐Primary CFA‐4 Campaign 
Finance Report due for all candidate commiƩees, 
PACs & regular party commiƩees 
May 23, 2020 Deadline to publish polling place list, 
CAN‐9  in newspaper

May 26, 2020 Deadline to begin public test of voƟng 
systems 
May 26, 2020 First day of in‐person early voƟng 
May 30, 2020 All counƟes must be open for in‐
person early voƟng; vote center counƟes must have 
the clerk’s oﬃce AND one vote center used on  
ElecƟon Day open

Supplemental ﬁling period ends
