VR CORNER 
Statewide VR Deadline Reminder 
Monday, May 4, 2020, is the VR deadline for the June 2, 
2020, primary elecƟon.  As noted in the purple VR 
Guidebook:  
1/ Voter registraƟon forms are to be hand‐delivered not 
later than the Ɵme your local VR oﬃce closes on  
Monday, May 4, 2020. 
2/If mailed, the envelope must be postmarked on or 
before May 4, 2020, for the county to review and  
process the applicaƟon—even if it’s received on June 1! 
If the postmark on the envelope containing the VR  
applicaƟon is missing or illegible, then the county may 
process it if received by May 11, 2020.  
3/ If received through INSVRS (i.e. BMV, OVR), then the 
date/Ɵme stamp must be before 11:59PM (local  
prevailing Ɵme), Monday, May 4, 2020. A reminder the 
Ɵme/date stamp in INSVRS is now reﬂecƟve of your 
county’s Ɵme zone.  
County chairs are responsible for  
recruiƟng ElecƟon Day central count 
team members and poll workers. The 
deadline for the CEB to noƟfy the 
chairs of the number of ElecƟon Day 
central count team members needed 
and the chair to nominate has passed. 
 
Non‐vote center AND vote center 
counƟes should have an Inspector 
and two judges (one Democrat and 
one Republican) working at each site. 
These three poll workers make up the 
precinct elecƟon board and make  
decisions on certain issues arising at 
the polling place.  
 
In addiƟon to having at least one  
precinct elecƟon board, vote center 
counƟes have addiƟonal support staﬀ 
as outlined in the county’s vote  
center plan. Non‐vote center counƟes 
may also have poll clerks and sheriﬀs, 
one from each poliƟcal party, and 
possibly assistant poll clerks, if a  
resoluƟon is passed by the county 
elecƟon board.  
 
Don’t forget—vote center and non ‐
vote center counƟes are able to have 
fewer workers, though one  
precinct board per locaƟon should be 
the baseline. Vote center counƟes can 
amend their plan to have fewer  
workers, though that plan has to be 
unanimously approved by the CEB. 
Non‐vote center counƟes can turn to 
IC 3‐11‐8‐4.3 to consolidate precinct 
boards; IC 3‐6‐6‐38 to eliminate poll 
clerks or sheriﬀs; and IC 3‐6‐6‐38.5 to 
allow one inspector to serve at the 
enƟre locaƟon. 
 
The county chairs can nominate  
individuals to ﬁll a poll worker  
posiƟons unƟl NOON (local prevailing 
Ɵme), Tuesday, May 12, 2020. AŌer 
noon, the CEB is authorized to ﬁll poll 
worker vacancies if the county chair 
fails to ﬁll the posiƟons. This deadline 
applies to vote center and non‐vote 
center counƟes.  
Requirements to Serve as a Poll 
Worker or Central Count Team  
Member 
Generally speaking, a voter of the 
county may serve as an ElecƟon Day 
poll worker or central count team 
member. For the June 2, 2020, IEC 
Order 40 relaxed this rule and will 
allow for any person who is registered 
to vote in Indiana to be nominated 
and appointed to be a poll worker. IC 
3‐6‐6‐7 sets forth the poll worker  
requirements; IC 3‐11.5‐4‐22 sets for 
the central count team requirements. 
However, there are a few excepƟons 
to this rule: 
 
‐ An unopposed candidate for state 
convenƟon delegate or precinct  
commiƩeeman may serve as a poll 
worker or central count team  
member, even if their name appears 
on the ballot. 
 
‐ In non‐vote center counƟes,  
opposed candidates for state  
convenƟon delegate or precinct  
commiƩeeman may be appointed to 
serve in precincts where their name 
does not appear in the ballot. (See 
note below for vote center counƟes.) 
 
‐ Candidates (opposed or unopposed) 
for local, state, and federal oﬃce may 
not serve as a poll worker in the  
precinct where their name appears on 
the ballot. In non‐vote center  
counƟes, it is possible to reassign a  
candidate to a precinct outside of 
their elecƟon district to work on  
ElecƟon Day. Because a voter can 
vote anywhere in a vote center  
county, it is not possible to reassign a 
candidate to another precinct to 
serve on ElecƟon Day. 
 
‐ Candidates may not serve as an  
ElecƟon Day central count team 
member, unless the candidate is  
running for a non‐county wide oﬃce 
and is assigned absentee work that 
avoids the precincts where the  
candidate’s name appears on the  
ballot or is an unopposed candidate 
for delegate or PC. (IC 3‐11‐10‐36(d); 
IC 3‐11.5‐4‐22(d)) 
 
‐ Family members of candidates, as 
deﬁned in IC 3‐6‐6‐7, IC 3‐11‐10‐36, 
and IC 3‐11.5‐4‐22, generally may not 
serve as a poll worker or absentee 
voter board member, unless the  
candidate is unopposed on the ballot 
where their name appears. (IC 3‐6‐6‐7
(a)(4); IC 3‐11‐10‐36(c)(4); IC 3‐11.5‐4‐
22(c)(4)) 
 
Poll workers and central count team 
members must also be able to read, 
write, and speak the English language 
and cannot have any property bet or 
wagered on the result of the elecƟon. 
Individuals nominated to serve as  
Inspector must aƩend training, and 
may not be the chair or treasurer of a 
candidate’s commiƩee where the 
candidate appears on the ballot. 
 
16 and 17 year old nonvoters may be 
appointed to serve as a poll worker 
(other than inspector) if allowed by a 
unanimous vote of the CEB. The 16 or 
17 year old must be: 
 a U.S. ciƟzen and resident of the 
county; 
 has a 3.0 out of 4.0 GPA; 
 has wriƩen permission to serve 
from a parent or guardian; and 
 meet all other poll worker  
qualiﬁcaƟons and aƩends required 
training. 
 
State law also allows a 16– or 17‐year 
old to be a central count team  
member. (IC 3‐11.5‐4‐23(d)) As a  
reminder, IEC Order 37 waived the 
requirement that the student’s school 
principal has to give wriƩen approval 
if the school is not in session on  
primary elecƟon day. 
InformaƟon in this newsleƩer is provided by the Indiana ElecƟon Division as a courtesy to county elecƟon administrators. If a person is unclear concerning elecƟon law provisions,  
the ElecƟon Division can serve as an interpreƟve source. However, where important legal rights are concerned, you must consult with your own aƩorney to be fully and properly advised. 
IN FOCUS: Election Day Poll Workers & Central Count Teams 
QUESTIONS OF THE MONTH 
Q. Do the voter fail safe procedures apply to  
absentee voters? 
A. Yes. An absentee applicaƟon can serve as a voter 
registraƟon document, even aŌer the statewide  
voter registraƟon deadline, for voters who move 
within their precinct ONLY. Voters who qualify for a 
voter fail safe and are able to vote in their old pre‐
cinct one last Ɵme, the VRG 4/12 may be used but it 
should be ﬁled at the same Ɵme as their absentee 
applicaƟon. IC 3‐11‐10‐4(a)(3). CounƟes should  
follow the “when did the voter move and where did 
the voter move” analysis found in the purple 2020 
VR guidebook in the appendix. 
Q. Can we begin counƟng absentee ballots on  
ElecƟon Day at 6AM? 
Under IEC Order 37, all counƟes may begin counƟng 
absentee ballots at 6AM for the June 2, 2020  
elecƟon, but this order does not cover the  
November elecƟon. CounƟes will need to follow  
current state law, which is detailed in IC 3‐11.5‐4‐11. 
EssenƟally, vote center counƟes or non‐vote center 
counƟes using an ePb can begin counƟng at 6AM on 
ElecƟon Day, if the CEB unanimously agrees to it and 
the absentee voter data is pushed to ePBs not later 
than 12:01A on elecƟon day. Of course, counƟes 
may have absentee ballots delivered up unƟl noon 
on ElecƟon Day, and the addiƟonal data would be 
pushed out to the polling sites as those ballots are 
received. 
Q. Do we go to the post oﬃce on elecƟ
on day? 
A. Yes. State law requires the clerk or her designee 
to go to the local post oﬃce at noon to conﬁrm all 
ballots have been delivered. (IC 3‐11.5‐4‐7) 
Q. Has the deadline changed for the two major  
parƟes to ﬁll ballot vacancies where no one ran in 
the primary? Or for minor party/independent  
candidates/Libertarian candidates to ﬁle for the 
November elecƟon? 
No. Please see revised 2020 Calendar: ElecƟon  
Administrator’s Guide on the website. 
ABS Election Day Troubleshooting 
Did the voter complete their absentee ballot?  
If yes, bring the completed ballot, which is sealed in 
their signed security envelope, to the county elecƟon 
board’s central locaƟon by noon on ElecƟon Day for it to 
be processed and counted. (IC 3‐11.5‐4‐3)  
IEC Order 2020‐37 allows for caregivers, family  
members, members of the immediate household,  
aƩorney‐in‐fact, USPS, or a bonded courier to deliver a  
completed ballot in the primary elecƟon. If it’s not the 
voter, USPS, or a bonded courier returning the  
completed ballot, don’t forget to provide the individual 
with the ABS‐19 form. 
Did the voter decide to not complete the absentee   
ballot?  
A voter can bring the ballot to their ElecƟon Day polling 
place; surrender it to the Inspector, who will spoil the 
ballot and issue a regular ballot to the voter, if otherwise 
eligible. The absentee ballot MUST be surrendered, or 
else the voter will only be able to vote provisionally.  
(IC 3‐11.5‐4‐18)  
Did the voter not receive their absentee ballot?  
The voter is to complete the PRE‐5 aﬃdavit at the  
polling place, which aﬃrms the voter did not receive the 
ballot issued to them. AŌer compleƟng the aﬃdavit, the 
voter may vote a regular ballot if otherwise eligible.  
(IC 3‐11.5‐4‐18) 
Was the voter’s absentee ballot rejected or delivered 
aŌer noon on ElecƟon Day?  
The voter may appear before the CEB not later than 
5PM (local prevailing Ɵme) on ElecƟon Day, and request 
an ABS‐21. The ABS‐21 will allow the voter to go to their 
ElecƟon Day polling locaƟon and vote a regular ballot 
before the polls close, if the voter is otherwise eligible. 
(IC 3‐11.5‐4‐13 & 3‐11.5‐4‐21)   
While not required the CEB may inform a voter when 
their absentee ballot has been rejected and how they 
can cast a ballot on elecƟon day so long as the CEB does 
so in a uniform and nondiscriminatory way. EssenƟally if 
the CEB informs one voter, they must inform all similarly 
situated voters.

Election Division Dispatch 
 Brad King & Angie Nussmeyer, Co-Directors | June 2020  
NEWS & UPDATES 
NEW! Primary CerƟﬁcaƟon Deadline 
A reminder that counƟes must cerƟfy their ﬁnal elecƟon  
results from the June 2, 2020, primary elecƟon to not later 
than 3P (local prevailing Ɵme), FRIDAY, JUNE 12! This is an 
earlier deadline than required by statute. CounƟes are to ﬁle 
all their required forms in INSVRS and either upload precinct 
results in INSVRS or provide a hard copy of those results to IED 
not later than the 3P (local prevailing Ɵme), deadline of June 
12, 2020. 
 
Recount & Contests 
With the June 2 primary nearing cerƟﬁcaƟon, candidates may 
be asking about recount and contest acƟons. IC 3‐12‐6,  
generally, walks through the procedures and candidates 
should secure their own aƩorney to be properly advised. The 
deadline for a candidate to ﬁle a recount or contest acƟon 
stemming from the June 2, 2020 elecƟon is noon (local  
prevailing Ɵme), Tuesday, June 16, 2020. The deadline for a 
county chair to do so is noon (local prevailing Ɵme), Friday, 
June 19. 
 
A recount or contest acƟon is a court acƟon, meaning a civil 
complaint is ﬁled with the county clerk. The person ﬁling the 
case pays the court ﬁling fee. For a recount, the individual 
must also pay a minimum $100 bond at the Ɵme of ﬁling. The 
$100 bond allows for the person to request up to 10 precincts 
to be recounted. If the person wants more than 10 precincts 
counted, then the bond increases by: 
 $10 per precinct if the diﬀerence in the vote totals  
between the candidates is not more than 1%; OR 
 $100 per precinct if the diﬀerence in the vote totals  
between the candidates is more than 1%.
 
 
The case is ﬁled with a court assigned randomly to civil or  
circuit courts in your county. The judge will appoint a local  
recount commission, consisƟng of a Democrat, Republican, 
and mechanic. The CEB plays no oﬃcial role beyond making 
requested elecƟon material available. Please note: original poll 
lists may be impounded due to the court acƟon. CounƟes may 
make copies of poll lists to update vote history, but the  
deadline to update vote history is extended to end 60‐days 
aŌer the date the recount ends. 
 
US District Court Data VLM Project 
State law requires IED to provide jury return informaƟon from 
the US Northern and Southern District Courts in Indiana not 
later than 24‐days aŌer the primary, or June 26, 2020. County 
VR oﬃcials must then act on the informaƟon and complete 
work before the August 5, 2020, 90‐day federal freeze  
deadline. More informaƟon to come on this project. 
JUNE WEB TRAINING 
June 3 & 9 | Post ElecƟon Processing 
Dates are subject to change; check the 2020 INSVRS Training 
Schedule on the county portal to conﬁrm.

elecƟon results

make an appointment to ﬁll a local oﬃce ballot  
vacancy where no D/R candidate ran in the primary

vacancy resulƟng from a vacancy for an oﬃce  
nominated at its state/county convenƟon

independent candidates who want their name  
printed on the ballot to ﬁle peƟƟons & CAN‐12 with 
county VR oﬃcial to review and cerƟfy (NOTE: for 
the few counƟes with a separate VR board, see July 
15, 2020 entry) 
July 3, 2020 IED Closed

cerƟﬁcate of  candidate selecƟon nominaƟng  
candidates to ﬁll ballot vacancies resulƟng in no  
person running in the primary elecƟon

minor party candidate who wants their name

‐20 consent (and for

12 and cerƟﬁed peƟƟons with clerk/CEB)

paperwork for those candidates nominated at  
county or state convenƟon 
InformaƟon in this newsleƩer is provided by the Indiana ElecƟon Division as a courtesy to county elecƟon administrators. If a person is unclear concerning elecƟon law provisions,  
the ElecƟon Division can serve as an interpreƟve source. However, where important legal rights are concerned, you must consult with your own aƩorney to be fully and properly advised. 
While the primary was moved 28‐days to 
June 2, the IEC Orders did not change 
dates for preparaƟons for the November 
elecƟon, including ﬁlling ballot vacancies 
by the DemocraƟc, Republican and  
Libertarian parƟes. 
DEMOCRATIC & REPUBLICAN PARTIES 
For local oﬃces, the DemocraƟc and  
Republican parƟes have two opƟons to ﬁll 
a ballot vacancy where no person ran in 
the primary elecƟon: 1) Caucus of eligible 
precinct commiƩeemen; OR 2) Direct  
appointment. The deadline to ﬁll a ballot 
vacancy where no person ran in the  
primary elecƟon is NOON, June 30, 2020. 
Caucus 
The county chair must send wriƩen noƟce 
(CAN‐30) to all eligible precinct  
commiƩeemen via ﬁrst class mail not later 
than ten days before the caucus is to be 
held. In addiƟon, the CAN‐30 must be ﬁled 
with the county clerk not later than noon,  
ten days before the caucus is held. 
Candidates for the caucus are required to 
ﬁle the CAN‐31 with the chair of the  
caucus not later than 72‐hours before the 
caucus is held. The CAN‐31 must also be 
ﬁled with the county clerk not later than 
72‐hours before the caucus. 
The caucus is to be held according to the  
procedures in IC 3‐13‐1, and must be held 
not later than noon, June 30, 2020. The 
nominated candidate’s CAN‐12 statement 
of economic interest AND the CAN‐29 
cerƟﬁcaƟon must be ﬁled with the county 
clerk not later than noon, July 6, 2020. 
Direct Appointment 
The county party organizaƟon can pass a 
resoluƟon or otherwise vote to give  
authority to the county chair or the  
county commiƩee (chair, vice chair,  
secretary and treasurer) to ﬁll a ballot 
vacancy by direct appointment. State law 
does not prescribe the form of the  
resoluƟon; some are very speciﬁc to an 
elecƟon, while others are open‐ended. It’s 
ulƟmately up to the party organizaƟon to 
decide the form of their resoluƟon or  
other authorizaƟon.  
The direct appointment must be made 
not later than noon, June 30, 2020. The  
candidate’s CAN‐12 and CAN‐31, and the 
CAN‐29 along with a copy of the meeƟng 
minutes, resoluƟon or other document 
granƟng the direct appointment authority 
must be ﬁled with the county clerk not 
later than noon, July 6, 2020. (NOTE: If the 
party is ﬁlling mulƟple vacancies by direct 
appointment, the resoluƟon or meeƟng 
minutes must be aƩached to EACH  
CAN‐29.) 
AlternaƟvely, if only one precinct  
commiƩeeman is eligible to parƟcipate in 
the caucus, the county chair is required to 
ﬁll a ballot vacancy by direct appointment. 
The CAN‐29 form has a box for the chair to 
mark and indicate this reason. 
NOTE: The DemocraƟc and Republican 
parƟes may ﬁll state legislaƟve vacancies, 
but those are handled by the state parƟes 
and calls directed to their oﬃce and IED.  
LIBERTARIAN PARTY 
The Libertarian Party generally ﬁlls their 
federal, state, and local oﬃces at a state 
or county convenƟon. Instead of ﬁling 
declaraƟons of candidacy with the county 
elecƟon board, the Libertarian Party chair 
and secretary will cerƟfy the Party’s  
nominees to the county elecƟon board 
using the CAN‐22 cerƟﬁcate of nominaƟon 
along with the candidate’s CAN‐12  
statement of economic interests. The 
state and county convenƟon for the  
Libertarian Party must be held not later 
than noon, June 30, 2020. 
If aŌer the Libertarian Party holds its state 
or county  convenƟon and fails to ﬁll a 
ballot posiƟon, its state party commiƩee 
may ﬁll the ballot vacancy not later than 
noon, June 30, 2020.  The Libertarian  
Party State chair will ﬁle noƟce with the 
county elecƟon board of their party’s  
intent to ﬁll a ballot vacancy, which must 
be ﬁled not later than ten days before the 
vacancy can be ﬁlled. The CAN‐22 and 
CAN‐12 must be then be ﬁled with the 
county elecƟon board not later than noon, 
July 6, 2020. 
INDEPENDENT & MINOR PARTY  
CANDIDATES 
Filing PeƟƟons 
Independent and minor party candidates 
for local oﬃce who want their names 
printed on the ballot ﬁle in two‐parts. 
Step 1: The candidate must ﬁle CAN‐21 
peƟƟons and the CAN‐12  with the county 
VR oﬃcial not later than noon, June 30, 
2020.  (NOTE: In the few counƟes with a 
separate board of voter registraƟon, the 
CAN‐12 is ﬁled in step 2.) 
To qualify, the candidates must have  
cerƟﬁed signatures of registered voters in 
their elecƟon district totaling at least 2% 
of the total votes cast for all candidates in 
the 2018 Secretary of State’s race 
Step 2: Not later than noon, July 15, the 
candidate supplements the cerƟﬁed  
peƟƟ
ons with the CAN‐20 candidate con‐
sent. (Note: in the few counƟes with a 
separate board of voter registraƟon, the 
CAN‐12 is ﬁled with the county elecƟon 
board at the Ɵme the cerƟﬁed peƟƟons 
and CAN‐20 consent form is ﬁled.) 
Important! The peƟƟon form for local  
candidates is the CAN‐21; the form for 
federal, statewide, and state legislaƟve 
oﬃce is the CAN‐19 form. Though county 
VR oﬃcial cerƟfy peƟƟons signatures for 
federal, state, and state legislaƟve candi‐
dates, the ﬁling of the cerƟﬁed documents 
is managed at IED. 
Declared Write‐in Candidates 
Independent or minor party candidates 
may ﬁle to run as a local candidate by  
submiƫng the CAN‐3 & CAN‐12 not later 
than noon, July 6, 2020. The candidate’s 
name is NOT printed on the ballot. 
SCHOOL BOARD CANDIDATES 
Most candidates for school board need to 
collect at least 10 signatures from  
registered voters in their elecƟon district 
using the CAN‐34. For most school board 
candidates, the elecƟon district is the en‐
Ɵre school corporaƟon area. For those in 
metropolitan school district who are re‐
quired to run in a district, the signatures 
are limited to those individuals within that 
small district. The candidate completes 
the consent found on the back of the CAN‐
34 and 
ﬁles the peƟƟons along with the 
CAN‐12 beginning July 22, 2020, and not 
later than noon, August 21, 2020. 
IN FOCUS: SUMMER CANDIDATE FILINGS 
QUESTIONS OF THE MONTH 
Q. When are our ﬁnal, cerƟﬁed precinct level re‐
sults and elecƟon reports required to be ﬁled with 
IED? 
A. Pursuant to IEC Order 2020‐37, not later than 
3PM (local prevailing Ɵme), Friday, June 12, 2020. 
ALL reports cerƟfying the vote total for each oﬃce 
and public quesƟon on the ballot are to be ﬁled  
electronically through SVRS by this deadline. (The 
CEB‐9 can be ﬁled by noon, June 16.) This reporƟng 
is especially criƟcal as the state convenƟon delegate 
informaƟon is needed for the parƟes to conduct 
their convenƟons.  
CounƟes using the precinct upload via mapping can 
upload their ﬁnal results using this feature. CounƟes 
not using the precinct upload via mapping can aƩach 
the ﬁnal precinct‐level results in SVRS to upload OR 
email them to elecƟons@iec.in.gov. 
VR CORNER 
VRG 4/12 Updates 
County voter registraƟon oﬃcials can have access to the VRG 
4/12 once the elecƟon materials are returned to the county 
elecƟon board, and updates to the voter’s record may be 
made. Please be sure to forward any completed VRG 4/12 
that indicates a move to another county to the proper county 
not later than August 3, 2020. (IC 3‐10‐1‐31.1(f) and IC 3‐10‐1‐
31.2) 
 
VoƟng History 
County VR oﬃcials may begin immediately updaƟng vote  
history from the June 2 primary into INSVRS, once the poll lists 
have been delivered. (IC 3‐10‐1‐31.1; IC 3‐10‐1‐31.2)  If  
materials are impounded due to a recount, poll books may be 
copied to conƟnue work. (IC 3‐12‐6‐19.5) However, ePB data 
may be uploaded into SVRS, even if a recount is occurring. 
Unless there is a recount/contest acƟon, he deadline to  
complete vote history is 60‐days from the date of the elecƟon, 
or August 3, 2020. 
AN (ALMOST) FINAL NOTE ON SUMMER CANDIDATE FILINGS… 
Candidate Withdrawal 
A candidate may withdraw for ANY reason unƟl noon, July 15, 2020. A candidate for local oﬃce ﬁles the CAN‐24 form 
with the county elecƟon board not later than this deadline. The county chair then has thirty days to ﬁll the ballot va‐
cancy, using the same forms and procedures noted above. (IED manages withdrawals for federal, statewide, and state  
legislaƟve oﬃces, though the deadline of noon ET, July 15, sƟll applies.) AŌer noon, July 15, 2020, a local candidate 
may withdraw ONLY if the person passes away, is convicted of a felony, moves out of their elecƟon district, or is or‐
dered oﬀ the ballot by the courts. Should that occur, the ballot vacancy may be ﬁlled by the county chair not later than 
30‐days from the date the vacancy occurred.  
 
Don’t Forget the CAN‐5! 
State law recently changed and requires the county to provide the CAN‐5 noƟce to all candidate ﬁlings, even ballot 
vacancies, within one business day of accepƟng the document. This can be generated in INSVRS aŌer entering the  
candidate informaƟon in the elecƟon module. 
 
Rejected PeƟƟon Filings 
If an independent/minor party candidate ﬁles peƟƟons with the clerk, it’s the clerk’s responsibility to ensure the candi‐
date met the signature threshold requirement of 2% of the total votes cast in the 2018 Secretary of State’s race in 
those precincts within the elecƟon district. If the candidate ﬁled at least the minimum cerƟﬁed signatures, then cerƟfy 
the peƟƟon. If not, then the clerk must reject the candidate ﬁling and send noƟce to the candidate by cerƟﬁed mail. 
The candidate may appeal the decision by ﬁling a CAN‐1 by noon, August 21, 2020, and the CEB would conduct a 
“hearing on the ma
Ʃer. School board rejecƟons are handled a liƩle diﬀerently, and this will be covered next month.

Election Division Dispatch 
 Brad King & Angie Nussmeyer, Co-Directors | July 2020  
NEWS & UPDATES 
Online Absentee Portal Updates 
The online absentee portal for the November 2020 went live 
on June 16, the ﬁrst day counƟes can begin receiving absentee 
applicaƟons for the fall elecƟon. One noƟceable chance on the 
public‐facing site is the addiƟon of buƩons on the main page 
of the voter’s portal page. 
 
While a voter can select absentee voƟng from the gray  
navigaƟon bar to access the applicaƟon, larger ABS buƩons 
can be found under the “Update my RegistraƟon” and lead the 
voter to the proper applicaƟon ‐ ABS‐Mail; ABS Por Correo; 
ABS‐Traveling Board. 
 
Other enhancement requests are logged and will be deployed 
throughout the summer, including adding Avery labels as a 
prinƟng choice for the ballot envelope and further reﬁning the 
signature rendering on the printed document. We are also 
looking to improve the main web page to beƩer direct voters 
to the services contained within the voter portal. Stay tuned! 
 
Reminder: 
US District Court Data VLM Project 
AŌer the primary elecƟon, the ElecƟon Division circulated  
informaƟon about accessing the US District Court Data in the 
INSVRS county portal. County voter registraƟon oﬃcials must 
complete the project and send out SAMC noƟces, if required, 
not later than July 14, 2020. A reminder that a postage  
pre‐paid return envelope must be included with the SAMC 
pursuant to state law. 
 
AddiƟonally, at least 30‐days must pass aŌer mailing the SAMC 
or the SAMC returned as undeliverable (as deﬁned in IC 3‐5‐2‐
49.7) before a voter’s registraƟon can be moved to “inacƟve” 
status. A voter’s status cannot be moved to “inacƟve” between 
August 6 and November 3, 2020, due to the 90‐day federal 
freeze period. However, a county may treat a SAMC the same 
as a voter registraƟon form should a voter use it to conﬁrm, 
update, or cancel their registraƟon in wriƟng during this 
“freeze” window. 
CALENDAR 
July 3, 2020 IED Closed 
July 6, 2020 (NOON) Deadline for D/R to ﬁle  
cerƟﬁcate of candidate selecƟon nominaƟng  
candidates to ﬁll ballot vacancies resulƟng in no  
person running in the primary elecƟon OR in cases of 
a direct appointment, the CAN‐12, CAN‐29, CAN‐31 
and copy of meeƟng minutes/resoluƟon giving chair 
the authority to ﬁll ballot vacancy 
July 6, 2020 (NOON) Deadline for L party to ﬁle  
cerƟﬁcaƟon of nominaƟon exisƟng as a result of no 
person being nominated at convenƟon 
July 6, 2020 (NOON) Deadline for minor party/
independent candidate to ﬁle CAN‐3 to be a  
declared write‐in candidate 
July 15, 2020 (NOON) Deadline for a candidate to 
withdraw for any reason 
July 15, 2020 (NOON) Deadline for an independent/
minor party candidate who wants their name  
printed on the ballot to ﬁle CAN‐20 consent (and for 
the few counƟes with separate VR board, the CAN‐
12 and cerƟﬁed peƟƟons with clerk/CEB) 
July 15, 2020 (NOON) Deadline for L party to ﬁle  
paperwork for those candidates nominated at  
county or state convenƟon 
July 22, 2020: First day for school board candidates 
to ﬁle CAN‐34 & CAN‐12 
August 3, 2020 (NOON): Deadline for a D, R, or L 
candidate in a “small” town (less than 3500 person) 
to ﬁle CAN‐16 & CAN‐12 where no primary was held 
August 3, 2020 (NOON): Deadline for a public  
quesƟon to be cerƟﬁed to a county elecƟon board 
for the November elecƟon 
August 3, 2020: Deadline to update voƟng history 
from the June 2, 2020, primary elecƟon, unless 
county has a local recount or contest acƟon 
August 5, 2020: Deadline to complete VLM work to 
move a voter’s registraƟon status to “inacƟve” 
August 21, 2020 (NOON): Deadline for school board 
candidates to ﬁle CAN‐34 & CAN‐12 
August 21, 2020: Deadline for a “small” town to con‐
duct a town convenƟon, if it’s necessary to do so

chair to ﬁle CAN‐18 with county clerk to cerƟfy who 
won the town party convenƟon, if applicable 
JULY WEB TRAINING 
July 14 & 16 | ElecƟon & Candidate Set‐up 
July 21 & 23 | Refresher Training 
Dates are subject to change; check the 2020 INSVRS Training 
Schedule on the county portal to conﬁrm. 
InformaƟon in this newsleƩer is provided by the Indiana ElecƟon Division as a courtesy to county elecƟon administrators. If a person is unclear concerning elecƟon law provisions,  
the ElecƟon Division can serve as an interpreƟve source. However, where important legal rights are concerned, you must consult with your own aƩorney to be fully and properly advised. 
Summer candidate ﬁling season is about 
at its mid‐point with school board ﬁlings 
ramping up and most other types of ﬁlings  
winding down. 
Candidate withdrawals are part of this 
process that are oŌen overlooked and can 
be confusing to candidates, party oﬃcials, 
and elecƟon administrators. 
Vacancies ON or BEFORE Noon,  
July 15, 2020 
July 15 is the most important date for  
purposes of candidate withdrawing for the 
November elecƟon. Any candidate can 
withdraw for any reason unƟl noon, July 
15, 2020. The candidate simply ﬁles the 
CAN‐24 form with the county elecƟon 
oﬃcial (or IED, for federal, state, state 
legislaƟve, and judicial oﬃces) by this 
deadline and their name is removed from 
the November ballot. It does not maƩer if 
this candidate was selected to ﬁll a ballot 
vacancy, was nominated at the primary 
elecƟon, or ﬁled a form to be a write‐in 
candidate. Again, a candidate needs no 
reason to withdraw up to noon, July 15, 
2020. 
Should a D, R, or L candidate withdraw, 
then a party chair is able to ﬁll the vacancy 
not later than 30‐days aŌer the CAN‐24 
was ﬁled. The clerk does not need to give 
noƟce to the chair of the vacancy; instead, 
state law assumes the candidate is  
coordinaƟng with the poliƟcal party.  
Independent and write‐in candidates are 
not able to ﬁll a ballot vacancy, but minor 
party candidates who gain ballot access by  
peƟƟon can. 
D/R party leaders follow procedures found 
in IC 3‐13‐1, generally, to ﬁll the vacancy 
through direct appointment or caucus and 
uses forms county oﬃcials are already 
familiar with (CAN‐29, CAN‐30, CAN‐31, 
CAN‐12). L party leaders should review IC 
3‐13‐1
‐20 for speciﬁc procedural details. 
The party chair then has unƟl noon, three 
days aŌer ﬁlling the vacancy to ﬁle their 
paperwork with the county elecƟon  
oﬃcial. 
Vacancies AFTER Noon, July 15, 2020 
AŌer noon, July 15, a candidate can only 
withdraw if they move out of the elecƟon 
district, die, are convicted of a felony, or 
ordered oﬀ the ballot by the court. 
Should this occur, then a CAN‐24 is to be 
ﬁled and the ballot vacancy may be ﬁlled. 
For the D/R party, the vacancy is ﬁlled by 
caucus or direct appointment of the chair. 
With the excepƟon noted in the coming 
paragraphs, the D/R parƟes follow the 
procedures in IC 3‐13‐1, generally, and use 
the CAN‐29, CAN‐31, CAN‐30, and CAN‐12.  
An L candidate would withdraw using the 
CAN‐24, and their party follow procedures 
in IC 3‐13‐1‐20. Similarly, it is possible for 
a minor party who gained ballot access by 
peƟƟon to ﬁll a ballot vacancy, but an  
independent or write‐in candidate cannot. 
The second important date on the  
withdrawal “calendar” is the 30‐day mark 
before the November elecƟon, or October 
4, 2020. ParƟes who experience any  
vacancy occurring before October 4 are to 
follow the procedures in IC 3‐13‐1. Ballot 
vacancies occurring on or aŌer October 4 
(that is, within the 30‐day window before 
an elecƟon) follow the procedures under 
IC 3‐13‐2, generally. 
While the party may be able to ﬁll the 
“late” ballot vacancy,  its possible that the 
ballot may not be reprinted, depending on 
the Ɵming.  
IC 3‐
11‐3‐29.5 is the guiding principle on  
whether or not a ballot is to be re‐printed. 
Further, IC 3‐12‐1‐6 notes how to tabulate 
results should a late ballot vacancy be 
ﬁlled but the ballot is not re‐printed.  
Please be in touch with our oﬃce if you 
experience a late ballot vacancy, and need 
direcƟon on next steps. 
Finally, the blue ElecƟon Administrator’s 
manual and red Candidate Guide go in to 
greater detail on these issues, if you 
would like to learn more.  
IN FOCUS: Candidate Withdrawals & the November Ballot 
NOVEMBER BALLOT BUILDING REMINDERS 
1/ IED will cerƟfy a list of federal, state, and judicial candidates to counƟes not later than August 21, 2020, but... 
2/ IED will cerƟfy the candidates for U.S. President & Vice President separately and not later than September 10, 2020. 
3/ALL ballots MUST include a write‐in opƟon for each federal oﬃce (US President, US House in 2020), even if IED does 
not cerƟfy a declared write‐in candidate to counƟes. Federal law requires the write‐in line to be present for federal 
oﬃces. 
4/ Should a public quesƟon be cerƟﬁed to the county elecƟon board by noon, August 3, 2020, the public quesƟon will 
be the ﬁrst thing printed on your ballot, above the straight party secƟon. 
5/ NEW! See 2020 LegislaƟve Summary for more details about requirement to add language to straight party voƟng 
instrucƟons that straight party voƟng is not required. 
6/ All ballots ‐ even federal only or presidenƟal only ballots ‐ must include the straight party secƟon. At minimum, your 
county will display the DemocraƟc, Libertarian, and Republican party symbol and name. The DemocraƟc or Republican 
party name/symbol will be displayed in the order on the ballot as to which candidate for the 2018 SOS race came in 
ﬁrst in the county. The Libertarian Party will be third, and it is possible to have more parƟes to include on your ballot in 
the straight party secƟon.  
QUESTIONS OF THE MONTH: 
School Board Filing Focus 
Q. Do school board candidates have to open a  
campaign ﬁnance commiƩee? 
A. Maybe. A school board candidate must open a 
campaign ﬁnance commiƩee and ﬁle required  
reports if and when they raise or spend $500 toward 
running for oﬃce. UnƟl then, there is no need to ﬁle 
a CFA‐1.  
Q. Who can sign a school board peƟƟon? 
A. Registered voters within the boundaries of the 
community school corporaƟon. School board  
informaƟon should be part of your county’s precinct 
key matrix and included in the voter’s record. If not, 
reach out to your GIS department or the school  
corporaƟon for a map. (The only metropolitan 
school district in Indiana is in Indianapolis, and the 
voters signing the peƟƟon must be in the school 
board district.)  
Q. Does a candidate for school board need to  
submit mulƟple candidate consent forms? 
A. No. The CAN‐34 form is designed to capture the 
10 signatures of registered voters on the front of the 
form, while the back of the form includes the  
candidate’s consent. While the candidate can submit 
mulƟple CAN‐34 documents to ensure he or she has 
enough peƟƟon signatures, only one “back” side 
needs to be completed by the candidate. 
Q. Where is the CAN‐34 peƟƟon ﬁled? 
A. In most Indiana counƟes, the county clerk is the 
county’s voter registraƟon oﬃcial, so the CAN‐34 
and CAN‐12 is ﬁled with the clerk’s oﬃce not later 
than noon, August 21, 2020.
 
In the few counƟes where the county has a separate 
VR board, the CAN‐34 and CAN‐12 is ﬁled ﬁrst with 
the elecƟon board by noon, August 21, but the CAN‐
34 is to be forwarded to the VR Board. Only the 
county VR board can cerƟfy  the number of  
signatures on the peƟƟon. The cerƟﬁed peƟƟon is 
then delivered to the clerk. 
In both cases, the clerk has a responsibility  to inform 
the candidate if the peƟƟon was approved or denied  
either in person or by cerƟﬁed mail. If denied, the 
candidate may ﬁle a CAN‐1 challenge by noon,  
August 28 to contest the denied signatures. 
CAMPAIGN FINANCE REMINDERS: 
Vacancy Reports 
 
DemocraƟc and Republican candidates who ﬁlled a ballot  
vacancy may have a CFA‐1 and CFA‐4 report due at the local 
level soon. If the oﬃce pays more than $5,000 in a calendar 
year, then a CFA‐1 is required to be ﬁled not later than 7‐days 
aŌer the CAN‐29 was ﬁled. A “vacancy” CFA‐4 report is due not 
later than 21‐days aŌer the CAN‐29 is ﬁled. The reporƟng period 
will be from the date the candidate ﬁlled the vacancy through 14 
days from that date. 
Libertarian candidates who were nominated at a state or county 
party convenƟon may have a pre– or post‐convenƟon CFA‐1 and 
CFA‐4 report due, assuming the oﬃce pays more than $5,000. 
Any Libertarian candidate who ﬁlled a ballot vacancy would  
follow the same rule as their D & R counterparts as noted above. 
Independent and minor party candidates who are seeking an 
oﬃce paying more than $5,000 a year would ﬁle a CFA‐1 not 
later than 7 days aŌer ﬁling the CAN‐29 form and a “post‐
nominaƟon” report not later than 21 days aŌer the CAN‐29 was 
ﬁled. The ﬁling period would be the date the candidate ﬁled the 
CAN‐29 form through 14 days following that date. 
 
More informaƟon can be found in the 2020 Campaign Finance 
Manual. 
CANDIDATE CHALLENGES 
Candidates Filling Ballot Vacancies, Nominated at 
ConvenƟon, Gaining Ballot Access by PeƟƟon &  
Declared Write‐In 
For candidates falling into this broad category, the deadline to ﬁle 
a CAN‐1 challenge by a voter or county chair in the elecƟon  
district is noon, August 21, 2020. The CEB has unƟl noon, Sept. 4, 
2020, to determine its validity. 
 
NOTE: An independent candidate who ﬁled peƟƟons and did not 
qualify for the ballot can ﬁle a CAN‐1 challenge to dispute  
rejected signatures not later than noon, August 21, 2020. 
 
School Board Candidates 
The deadline for a voter in the elecƟon district to ﬁle a CAN‐1 
challenge a school board candidate OR for a school board  
candidate to dispute rejected signatures is noon, Aug. 28, 2020. 
The deadline for CEB to determine its validity is noon, September 
10, 2020. 
CDC/COVID-19 Polling Place Updates 
The US CDC recently updated its advice on polling place safety 
related to the COVID‐19 virus. For more details, visit: 
hƩps://www.cdc.gov/coronavirus/2019‐ncov/community/
elecƟon‐polling‐locaƟons.html

Election Division Dispatch 
 Brad King & Angie Nussmeyer, Co-Directors |  August 2020  
NEWS & UPDATES 
August Build 
Targeted for the week of August 20th, the Build will include a 
number of enhancements to the Online Absentee module. 
Thank you for the great suggesƟons to help us improve its 
funcƟonality now and in future builds. Items that will be  
included in this project include : 
 
 UpdaƟng the conﬁrmaƟon message voters see indicaƟng 
their ABS app has been submiƩed to the county and voter 
does not need to take further acƟon (i.e. do not print/
sign/mail electronic submission). 
 Adding a warning message to the Online ABS Hopper

InformaƟon in this newsleƩer is provided by the Indiana ElecƟon Division as a courtesy to county elecƟon administrators. If a person is unclear concerning elecƟon law provisions,  
the ElecƟon Division can serve as an interpreƟve source. However, where important legal rights are concerned, you must consult with your own aƩorney to be fully and properly advised. 
With the elecƟon just around the corner, 
county elecƟon oﬃcials are ramping up 
their absentee operaƟons. CriƟcal to its 
success are absentee voter boards. 
Each county elecƟon board must noƟfy 
the D/R county chairs of the number of 
absentee voter boards needed to support 
absentee operaƟons—mail, travel board, 
and in‐person voƟng—not later than 50 ‐
days before the elecƟon, or September 
14, 2020. (IC 3‐11.5‐4‐23) 
The D/R county chairs have unƟl noon, 46‐
days before the elecƟon (Sept. 18) to ﬁle, 
in wriƟng, their nominaƟons for those 
absentee voter board posiƟons. Of course, 
CEBs can request ABS voter boards more 
than 50‐days out and county chairs can 
ﬁle nominaƟons before their noon  
deadline, but these dates are the very 
latest to make the request or nominate 
folks. 
Individuals serving as ABS voter board 
members must meet the qualiﬁcaƟons 
under IC 3‐11.5‐4‐22. While contested and 
uncontested candidates cannot work in 
this capacity, it may be possible to assign 
their family members to work with ABS 
ballots in those precincts where their 
“candidate” family member is not on the 
ballot. 
State law requires the CEB or the ABS  
voter board to review and approve all ABS 
applicaƟons. (IC 3‐11‐4‐17.5) AŌer the 
clerk’s oﬃce enters the apps into the  
system, the D/R appointed members of 
the CEB or the ABS voter board must aﬃx 
their iniƟals to the back of the ABS ballot. 
(IC 3‐11‐4‐19) 
ABS voter boards OR the CEB also perform 
the ﬁrst absentee signature review, com‐
paring the signature on the voter’s ABS 
applicaƟon against the ABS ballot security 
envelope. This work must be performed 
before ElecƟon Day and then the apps/
ballots (sealed in the ballot envelope) are 
ﬁled by precinct in a cabinet/oﬃce/
receptacle with a bi‐parƟsan lock. The D/R 
CEB member or their designee is to  
maintain custody of their key at all Ɵmes. 
In‐person absentee voƟng is voƟng that 
occurs before an absentee voter board, 
much like traveling board. ABS voter 
boards are to be present during in‐person 
absentee voƟng at the clerk’s oﬃce or 
other satellite locaƟons to perform work 
like approving applicaƟons, checking a 
voter’s ID, or assisƟng voters with the 
voƟng equipment or ballot. 
Traveling board is a speciﬁc funcƟon of 
the ABS voter board, where a two‐person 
team travels to the voter to assist them 
with compleƟng a ballot or to bring a DRE 
unit to allow the voter to vote privately 
and independently. (The DRE resoluƟon 
has to be approved by the CEB ﬁrst; see| 
IC 3‐11‐10‐26.2) 
ABS Ballot PrinƟng. Not later than 60
‐
days before the elecƟon, the clerk or the 
board of elecƟons & registraƟon in Lake, 
Porter, and Tippecanoe counƟes must 
esƟmate the number of absentee ballots 
needed for the elecƟon. 
Those absentee ballots must be delivered 
not later than 50‐days before the elecƟon. 
And not later than 5‐days aŌer receiving 
the printed ballots, counƟes must begin 
mailing ABS ballots to those voters with 
approved applicaƟons. 
Using 50‐days as the rule of thumb,  
counƟes receiving their ABS ballots on day 
50 have unƟl Saturday, September 19, 
2020 (or 45‐days before the elecƟon) to 
begin mailing ABS ballots. However, if 
your county receives ballots on day 55, 
then your deadline to begin mailing  
ballots is day 50 to comply with the “5‐
day” rule found in IC 3‐11‐4‐18(c)). More 
informaƟon can be found in the blue  
ElecƟon Administrator’s Manual. 
IN FOCUS: ABSENTEE VOTER BOARDS & ABS-Mail PRINTING DEADLINES 
HOLDOVERS & UNCONTESTED RACES ON THE NOV. BALLOT 
HOLDOVERS. On occasion, no one ﬁles to run for an oﬃce on the November ballot. In these cases, the current oﬃceholder 
“holds‐over” for a new term of oﬃce pursuant to ArƟcle 15, SecƟon 3 of the Indiana ConsƟtuƟon. 
For example, County Auditor is on the ballot in November 2020. Mia is the currently elected county auditor, who is serving her 
second four‐year term*. No one—not even Mia— ﬁled for the oﬃce. Therefore, Mia will conƟnue serving as the county  
auditor for another four‐year term, unƟl her successor is elected and qualiﬁed. Because she is a “holdover” under state law, 
Mia does not ﬁle a new oath of oﬃce and will not receive a Commission from the Governor. 
CounƟes oŌen ask what happens if Mia didn’t ﬁle because she doesn’t want to conƟnue serving ? Mia may resign from  
elected oﬃce by ﬁling a wriƩen resignaƟon with the governor (as she is a consƟtuƟonal oﬃce holder), and the elected oﬃce 
vacancy would be ﬁled according to statute. (IC 3‐13‐3 through IC 3‐13‐11, generally) The individual selected is a “pro‐tem  
appointment” for the remainder of the term. 
UNCONTESTED RACES. Unlike the odd‐numbered municipal elecƟon years, ALL candidates appear on the November general 
elecƟon  ballot, even if only one person ﬁles. CounƟes may use “No Candidate Filed” for races where no person ﬁled to run OR 
for those parƟes that did not ﬁnd a candidate to run for a speciﬁc oﬃce.  
* Yes, even consƟtuƟonal oﬃce holders that are “term‐limited” will holdover. Think of the holdover as a conƟnuaƟon of her 
service rather than a “new” four‐year term. She’ll serve unƟl December 31, 2024, unless she resigns OR unƟl her successor is 
elected and qualiﬁed in the 2024 elecƟon. 
QUESTIONS OF THE MONTH  
Q. Do the new straight party instrucƟons go to the 
right of the party devices on the ballot? 
A. If your county is using hand‐counted paper  
ballots, then yes, the new straight party instrucƟons 
would go to the right of the straight party devices. 
(IC 3‐11‐2‐10(b)) For opƟcal scan balloƟng systems 
and direct recording electronic voƟng systems, the 
new straight party instrucƟons can go with the other 
instrucƟons at the top OR between the public ques‐
Ɵon (if, applicable) and the straight party secƟon of 
the ballot. However, for opScan these new  
instrucƟons MUST be printed on the ballot. CounƟes 
may NOT print and post them in the voƟng booth, 
for example. (IC 3‐11‐13‐11(l)) For DREs, these  
InstrucƟons may sƟll be posted inside the voƟng 
booth. (IC 3‐11‐14‐3.5(l)). 
Q. Anything else special to include in the  
instrucƟons in a presidenƟal elecƟon year? 
A. Yes. Every ballot must contain a statement in the 
instrucƟons found at the top of the ballot that a vote 
for the presidenƟal Ɵcket is a vote for the electors. 
See IC 3‐10‐4‐3 for speciﬁc details. 
Q. Do voter fail‐safes apply to absentee voters? 
A. Yes. Voter fail‐safes apply to an absentee voter in 
the same way it would apply to an ElecƟ
on Day  
voter. The only diﬀerence is the VRG 4/12 would be 
ﬁled at the same Ɵme as their ABS applicaƟon or 
during in‐person absentee voƟng  before signing an 
ePollbook. 
Q. What is the presidenƟal only ballot? 
A. This ballot is ONLY used for voters who moved out 
of the state of Indiana on or aŌer October 5, 2020, 
and did not register to vote in their new state.  
Federal and state law allow this speciﬁc voter to  
return to their old state and vote for president only 
one last Ɵme at their old polling place (or by  
absentee ballot). The voter is to complete the VRG‐
15 form at the polling place or, if requesƟng an  
absentee ballot, the VRG‐15 form should be ﬁled 
with their ABS applicaƟon. The voter is then given 
the presidenƟal only ballot to complete and return 
to elecƟon oﬃcials. AŌer the elecƟon, the voter’s 
registraƟon is cancelled, as authorized by VRG‐15 
form . NOTE: Please do NOT instruct your poll  
workers or absentee voter  boards to use this ballot 
for voters who express interest in only voƟng for 
president. This is not the proper use for this ballot! 
VR CORNER 
FPCA & Voter Residency 
On the FPCA, military and overseas voters are asked to  
provide as much of their Indiana address where the  
individual person last lived in Indiana before moving  
overseas or being deployed.  In some cases, the voter may 
not intend to return to this address. However, there are 
special allowances in state and federal law that permit the 
person’s registraƟon address  to be reﬂecƟve of the last 
locaƟon where they personally lived in Indiana. 
 
In Indiana, an overseas voter may mark the “I am a US  
ciƟzen, but my return is uncertain.” These voters must have 
lived in Indiana for at least 30 consecuƟve days at some 
point in their life from birth to  their current age. They may 
elect to enter the address of the VR oﬃce in the county, or 
preferably, include as much of their last Indiana residence 
address as they recall and then the county oﬃcial registers 
the person to vote at their VR oﬃce address. Remember, 
overseas voters who mark “my return is uncertain” are  
provided the Federal Only ballot style.

ElecƟon during the COVID‐19 pandemic. Many of the  
pracƟces highlighted in this guide may not be allowable 
under Indiana’s elecƟons laws, and should be viewed as 
sharing best pracƟces from elecƟon oﬃcials around the 
country. 
For more informaƟon about CISA and #Protect2020 eﬀorts 
and guides, visit hƩps://www.cisa.gov/protect2020. 
President/VP & Electors 
On November 3, voters are not selecƟng their presidenƟal 
and vice presidenƟal candidates, who run as a Ɵcket.  
Technically, voters are voƟng for the electors who will cast 
their vote for the Ɵcket at a meeƟng of the electoral college 
held in December 2020.  PoliƟcal parƟes or minor party/
independent candidates ﬁle the names and mailing  
addresses of their electors with IED. The electors of the 
state’s winning Ɵcket then cast their votes, which are  
recorded and are the oﬃcial elecƟon results for the oﬃce 
of president and vice‐president for our state. Please  
remember your ballot instrucƟons MUST include 
“electors” language found in IC 3‐10‐4‐3 this year!

InformaƟon in this newsleƩer is provided by the Indiana ElecƟon Division as a courtesy to county elecƟon administrators. If a person is unclear concerning elecƟon law provisions,  
the ElecƟon Division can serve as an interpreƟve source. However, where important legal rights are concerned, you must consult with your own aƩorney to be fully and properly advised. 
In Indiana, “elecƟoneering” is deﬁned as 
expressing support or opposiƟon to any 
candidate or poliƟcal party or expressing 
approval or disapproval of any public 
quesƟon in any manner that could  
reasonably be expected to convey that 
support or opposiƟon to another person. 
This would include the wearing of  
clothing, buƩons, or displaying signs, etc. 
that states the name of any poliƟcal party 
or includes the name, picture, photo, or 
other likeness of any currently elected 
federal, state, county, or local oﬃcial in 
spaces where this speech is curtailed.  
(IC 3‐14‐3‐16) 
Our state law speciﬁcally requires that the 
candidate be clearly idenƟﬁed. Therefore, 
slogans like “I’m with her” would not be 
considered elecƟoneering but “Sam Smith 
for Dogcatcher” would be considered be. 
However, the elecƟoneering statute does 
not prevent a voter from receiving  
informaƟon about a candidate or public 
quesƟon or bringing in material with  
candidate/PQ informaƟon to assist them 
with voƟng. 
While poll workers or absentee voter 
boards, for example, would be within their 
rights to ask the voter to remove the 
clothing or cover it up, the voter is not 
required to do so and may vote a regular 
ballot, if otherwise qualiﬁed to do so.  
BUT, elecƟon workers are within their 
rights to forward the issue of  
elecƟoneering to the CEB or the county 
prosecutor for violaƟng state law. 
Before ElecƟon Day “ElecƟoneering”  
cannot occur in the space where in‐person 
absentee voƟng is taking place. There is 
no “chute” for early voƟng; instead, it  
cannot occur within the voƟ
ng area. The 
county commissioners would control 
whether or not signs can be posted on the 
courthouse lawn. This is a ﬁrst  
amendment issue, where all candidates 
can post a sign or no candidates can post a 
sign. The Commissioners should consult 
their county aƩorney on this maƩer.  
No person can “elecƟoneer” to an  
absentee voter while the voter is  
compleƟng their vote‐by‐mail ballot, but 
there is an excepƟon for the person’s 
spouse or member of the voter’s  
household in state law. 
On ElecƟon Day No elecƟoneering can 
occur within the chute or inside the voƟng 
area. The chute is deﬁned in IC 3‐5‐2‐10 as 
the 50 foot area leading to the entrance to 
where voƟng occurs. 
Unlike “early” voƟng, similar limitaƟons 
are not placed on yard signs unless the 
sign is placed within the “chute” or inside 
the polls. 
Voters & Masks Before the primary elec‐
Ɵon, the IED Co‐Directors sent out a 
memo about requiring voters to wear 
masks or to have their temperature taken 
before being able to vote. 
In this memo, the co‐directors noted that 
wearing a mask or taking a temperature 
cannot be a pre‐condiƟon to vote. In other 
words, county elecƟon oﬃcials cannot 
turn those persons away from being able 
to cast their ballot, if otherwise qualiﬁed 
under Ɵtle 3 to do so. However, a voter 
may not wear a mask that expresses  
support or defeat of the candidate as the 
elecƟoneering statutes apply to it as well. 
Much like wearing a T‐shirt or hat, a  
person does not need to remove a mask 
that does not comply with the  
elecƟoneering statute but may be subject 
to invesƟgaƟon or prosecuƟon. 
This memo also addressed whether poll 
workers or absentee voter board  
members can be required to wear a mask. 
In IED’s view, the appointed oﬃcials are 
independent contractors and may be  
subject to addiƟonal employment  
requirements like wearing PPE. CEBs are 
advised to discuss this with their county 
aƩorneys. 
IN FOCUS: ELECTIONEERING & PPE 
VR CORNER 
Forwarding Voter RegistraƟons 
A voter may ﬁle state and federal voter registraƟon forms or an FPCA in a county where the voter doesn’t reside. If that 
occurs, county voter registraƟon oﬃcials must forward the VR document to the appropriate county. The forwarding 
count is able to email the document to the correct county, but the hard copy must be sent to the correct county.  
(IC 3‐7‐34‐9) AddiƟonally, IED can receive voter registraƟon forms from any person, and our oﬃce will forward them to 
the appropriate county.  
 
Timely Voter RegistraƟons 
A reminder that any Ɵmely received voter registraƟon form will be sent with a “Ɵmely” memo as we near the statewide 
VR deadline. A “Ɵmely” VR form is either hand‐delivered by the registraƟon deadline, or postmarked on or before  
October 5, 2020. If the postmark is missing or illegible, then those registraƟons can be processed up to and including 
Tuesday, October 13, 2020 (deadline moved due to holiday). A legible postmark date on or before October 5 must be 
processed for November. 
 
Pending RegistraƟons & Auto‐AcƟvate FuncƟonality 
CounƟes may choose to auto‐acƟve pending voƟng registraƟons before each elecƟon. You’ll want to sign the auto‐
acƟvate request document found on the INSVRS County Portal and aƩach it to your County AuthorizaƟon Request ﬁled 
through INSVRS. Signing this document acknowledges your county understands the state’s policy relaƟng to acƟvaƟng 
registraƟons in a batch seƫng. 
QUESTIONS OF THE MONTH  
Q. Can a voter cancel their absentee ballot applicaƟon 
once submiƩed to the county? 
A. State law does not address cancelling an ABS app once 
received by the county. For that reason, the absentee 
ballot must be sent to the voter, assuming the app is  
reviewed and approved. A voter can surrender their  
absentee ballot to the Inspector on ElecƟon Day and vote 
a regular ballot, if qualiﬁed. Or, if the voter’s absentee 
ballot is lost, spoiled, or defecƟve, it can be re‐issued aŌer 
the voter ﬁles an ABS‐5. Or, if the voter never received 
their absentee ballot, on ElecƟon Day, the voter com‐
pletes the PRE‐5 and votes a regular ballot, if qualiﬁed. 
Q. We’re a non‐vote center county. Are we able to  
consolidate polling locaƟons for November? 
A. Yes. In non‐vote center counƟes, state law allows  
adjoining precincts to be co‐located at the same site. See 
IC 3‐11‐8‐4.3 for more details. 
Q. Can we modify in‐person “early” absentee voƟng 
hours in the clerk’s oﬃce? 
A. At minimum, early voƟng must be oﬀered for the same 
hours as the clerk’s oﬃce is open. If the clerk’s oﬃce is 
open 8A to 5P, for example, then early voƟng must be 
oﬀered from 8A to 5P during the weekday. State law sets 
forth minimum hours on the two Saturdays before  
elecƟon day. See IC 3‐11‐10‐26 for more informaƟon. 
Q. A school board candidate wants to purchase yard 
signs, but hasn’t met the threshold to require opening a 
candidate’s commiƩee. What should her disclaimer be? 
A. School board candidates have special rules under  
Indiana’s Campaign Finance Act and are not required to 
open a candidate’s commiƩee unƟl  the candidate raises 
or spends more than $500 toward running for oﬃce. 
However, the candidate is required to have a disclaimer 
on purchased goods, such as: Paid for by Mia Marshall. 
Mia would need to keep records of the purchase as it 
would be an in‐kind contribuƟon and may be reportable IF 
she raises/spends more than $500 for school board oﬃce. 
Q. Could a family member or other individual complete a 
PRE‐3 and assist a voter with compleƟng their absentee‐
by‐mail ballot? 
A. No. State law requires the voter to be able to  
personally mark their own vote‐by‐mail ballot. If they  
cannot, then state law speciﬁcally requires the person to 
vote before a travel board. See IC 3‐11‐10‐24(b). But, if 
the voter wants to vote in‐person at the clerk’s oﬃce or 
other early voƟng site or on ElecƟon Day, then any person 
other than the voter’s employer or union representaƟve 
can assist a voter with disabiliƟes or who cannot read or 
write the English language if the PRE‐3 form is ﬁlled out 
before going to the voƟng booth. (IC 3‐11‐9‐2) 
“Late” Ballot Vacancies 
Occasionally there will be instances where a candidate must 
withdraw as a candidate from an elecƟon due to a felony  
convicƟon, a move out of the elecƟon district, or the candidate 
dies. Any vacancy occurring on or before October 3, 2020, is 
considered an “early” vacancy (even though this may seem 
late in the  elecƟon season to elecƟon administrators). For 
“early”  vacancies, the parƟes follow IC 3‐13‐1, generally, to ﬁll 
those ballot vacancies through caucus or, if the county party 
has  authorized it or there is only one eligible PC to vote in the  
caucus, by direct appointment. 
 
However, “late” ballot vacancy procedures found in IC 3‐13‐2, 
generally, are followed for any ballot vacancy occurring on or 
aŌer October 4, 2020. The procedures to ﬁll a “late”  ballot 
vacancy are streamlined to allow for direct appointment in 
some cases. Please be sure you and the appropriate county 
chair review IC 3‐13‐2, if a vacancy occurs during the ﬁnal 30‐
days leading up to the elecƟon. The blue ElecƟon Administra‐
tor’s Guide goes in to more detail on the forms used for ﬁling 
with the clerk (or IED, if it’s a state or federal oﬃce). 
 
Ballot Re-Printing? 
Despite all the hours and eyes on ballot proofs, mistakes  
happen. In this scenario of a defecƟve ballot due to error or 
omission, the CEB can choose to 1/ reprint the ballot OR 2/ 
hold a hearing to determine if ballot re‐prinƟng is necessary. 
(IC 3‐11‐2‐16)  
 
Before the hearing, the CEB must noƟfy the party(ies) or  
candidate(s) who may have an interest in the maƩer. At the 
hearing, the CEB must discuss the number of ballots, if any, 
containing the error or omission that have been cast; the cost 
of correcƟng the error; whether the error would cause  
confusion or mistakes by the voter; and whether any voter 
objects to using the ballot. 
 
If no voter objects to using the defecƟve ballot AND the CEB 
determines that the error or omission will not cause confusion, 
then the defecƟve ballots may conƟnue to be used. However, 
if any voter objects to using a defecƟve ballot OR the CEB  
determines the error or omission will create confusion, then 
new ballots shall be printed.  
 
AlternaƟvely, a candidate may pass away aŌer the ballot is 
printed . In this scenario, the procedures in IC 3‐11‐3‐29.5  
apply. The CEB must re‐print ballots unless 1/ the party ﬁlls the 
ballot vacancy within the ﬁnal ﬁve days before the elecƟon OR 
2/ the candidate dies and noƟce of the death is received aŌer 
noon, the ﬁnal seven days before the elecƟon. The CEB can 
also unanimously agree a candidate has died without noƟce 
and re‐print the ballot.  
 
Absentee voters must ﬁle an ABS‐5 to have an absentee ballot 
reissued, if the ballot is found to be defecƟve. While there is 
no requirement for the CEB to proacƟvely send the ABS‐5, the 
CEB could choose to send uniform noƟce to impacted voters.

Election Division Dispatch

NEWS & UPDATES 
Public Test: IEC‐9 & IEC‐10 
AŌer conducƟng your public test of voƟng equipment, 
don’t forget to send in your IEC‐9 & IEC‐10 forms to the 
ElecƟon Division. All counƟes will submit the IEC‐10,

CAN‐39: NoƟce of General ElecƟon 
Not later than ten days before the elecƟon, the CAN‐39 
must be printed in your local newspaper and included in 
your CEB meeƟng minutes. Unlike the primary elecƟon,  
the public noƟce for the general elecƟon does not need

law only requires the oﬃce names and any public or  
judicial retenƟon quesƟons to be printed. Of course, a 
county can elect to include the names. However, if you 
create the CAN‐39 out of SVRS, only the oﬃce names and

app/esa/how‐to‐use 
 
The agency also released a new CISA Insights: AcƟons to

EnƟƟes in light of increased sophisƟcated phishing

InformaƟon in this newsleƩer is provided by the Indiana ElecƟon Division as a courtesy to county elecƟon administrators. If a person is unclear concerning elecƟon law provisions,  
the ElecƟon Division can serve as an interpreƟve source. However, where important legal rights are concerned, you must consult with your own aƩorney to be fully and properly advised. 
State law is very speciﬁc about the people 
permiƩed into a polling place besides a 
voter. You can ﬁnd the list in state law:  
IC 3‐11‐8‐15. 
Poll workers are nominated by the D/R 
county chairs not later than noon, 21‐days 
before the elecƟon, or October 13, 2020 
for the upcoming November elecƟon. Any 
vacancies aŌer the deadline are to be 
ﬁlled by the county chair. All poll workers 
must meet the qualiﬁcaƟons found in IC 3‐
6‐6‐7. 
Generally, watchers are appointed by the 
state or county party chair of the D/R/L 
parƟes. This means it’s possible to have 
two watchers from the same poliƟcal  
party: one nominated by the state chair 
and one nominated by the county chair. 
There are speciﬁc qualiﬁcaƟons to be a 
party watcher, including being a  
registered voter of the county.  See IC 3‐6‐
8‐2.5 for the details on qualiﬁcaƟons. 
Before elecƟon day, the parƟes may have 
watchers at early voƟng locaƟons though 
are limited to 2 people per site. On  
ElecƟon Day, watchers can be present at 
the central count locaƟon: one watcher 
nominated by the state and county chair 
for each bi‐parƟsan team counƟng ballots. 
(IC 3‐11.5‐3‐
2) 
At the elecƟon day polling places in non‐
vote center counƟes, the state and county 
party chair can appoint one watcher for 
each precinct. (IC 3‐6‐8‐1) In vote center 
counƟes, a state and county party chair 
can appoint one watcher for each ePBs at 
the vote center site. Some minor party 
and independent candidates might also 
appoint watcher, though the statute for 
them is a liƩle diﬀerent. See IC 3‐6‐8‐1 for 
details. 
The media can also appoint watchers,  
generally following the same rules as 
above for party watchers. Before elecƟon 
day, a media watcher can enter an early 
voƟng locaƟon and on elecƟon day, enter 
a polling place or central count “ﬂoor.” 
More details about media watchers can be 
found in IC 3‐6‐10, generally. 
Challengers and poll book holders are  
appointed by the county parƟes. If a  
challenge is made, then the challenger the 
PRE‐4 and once the voter completes their 
aﬃdavit on the PRE‐4, the poll workers 
issue the voter a provisional ballot. The 
voter then places their provisional into the 
PRO‐2 envelope and signs the aﬃdavit 
found on it.  
Poll book holder credenƟals allow a  
person to enter the polling place and mark 
who has voted already at the precinct on 
what’s oŌen called a “scratch” list. A clerk 
cannot be a pollbook holder for a party, 
but can keep a scratch list for poll book 
holders to see. See IC 3‐6‐7, generally, for 
the qualiﬁcaƟons for serving in either of 
these roles.  
All persons other than a voter must have 
a credenƟal to enter a polling site! Poll 
workers credenƟals are issued by the CEB. 
Watchers, challengers, and poll book  
holders have credenƟals issued by their 
poliƟcal party or in the case of media 
watchers, by their news organizaƟon. 
(Note: if a news organizaƟon is in more 
than one county, IED issues the creden‐
Ɵals). CEBs should read the statutes noted 
above closely, as they may be required to 
issue credenƟals in cases where there is a 
public quesƟon on the ballot, for example. 
IN FOCUS: POLL WORKERS, WATCHERS, CHALLENGERS & POLL BOOK HOLDERS 
VR CORNER 
Polling Place & Early VoƟng InformaƟon 
County elecƟon oﬃcials are asked to enter their early voƟng 
and polling place informaƟon into SVRS by Sept. 30, 2020.  
Understanding that some counƟes may not yet have a ﬁnal list 
of polling places by early October, all ﬁnalized sites should be 
entered. Not only does this informaƟon display on indianavot‐
ers.com, but the polling place data is shared with Democracy 
Works, who posts to geƩothepolls.com. This website is then 
ampliﬁed by other organizaƟons to assist people in ﬁnding 
their voƟng locaƟons before and on elecƟon day. 
 
Incomplete Voter RegistraƟons 
SomeƟmes a voter misses boxes on their VR form before  
turning it in. In these cases, county VR oﬃcials are to call the 
voter, if a number is available, and mail noƟce to a voter if 
their VR form is incomplete. Voters not checking the age/
ciƟzenship quesƟon have unƟl Oct. 5, 2020, to put in wriƟng 
the answer to those quesƟons. For any other reason, the voter 
can cure the incomplete not later than 10‐days before the 
elecƟon, when the VR oﬃcial must reject the applicaƟon and 
send those names to the CEB. (IC 3‐7‐34‐4) More info is in the  
purple VR Guide. 
SEPTEMBER BUILD 
Updates to SVRS will be pushed later this month, such as: 
1/ UpdaƟng the public site online absentee applicaƟon  
portal to require voters to enter their IN DLN  or last 4SSN 
before being granted access to online ABS app. 
2/ Allowing voter to add their DLN to their registraƟon  
record as a correcƟon rather than an update. This should 
resolve the issue where adding DLN to 2FA, for example, 
was updaƟng the VR record and moving the voter’s  
record to “pending.”   
3/ PrevenƟng ABS  ballots from having a Received Date  
prior to the Sent Date. 
4/ Adding more info to the “ABS Portal Part” on indianavot‐
ers.com to display the receipt and approval date for ABS 
applicaƟons and displaying a status for returned ABS ballots 
(like received or rejected). 
5/ Improving the focus of the “Update Voter Info” secƟon 
on a mobile phone to beƩer display its funcƟonality. On 
some phones currently, the “update” secƟon appears not 
to be on the screen but the voter  needs to scroll up.  
Changing the focus will improve the experience
. 
QUESTIONS OF THE MONTH  
Q. Are we able to process absentee applicaƟons to 
vote‐by‐mail if the envelope is postmarked on or  
before Oct. 22 and received aŌer the deadline? 
A. No. State law requires any absentee ballot  
applicaƟon to be received not later than the  
speciﬁed deadline. Any applicaƟon that is received aŌer 
the deadline for ﬁling is to be rejected. 
Q. Can independent candidates appoint watchers? 
A.  Only statewide or federal candidates can appoint 
watchers, who must meet the qualiﬁcaƟons under state 
law to be appointed. The chair of the candidate’s cam‐
paign ﬁnance commiƩee would issue the  
credenƟal. See IC 3‐6‐8‐1 and IC 3‐6‐8‐3 for details.  
Q. Can independent candidates appoint poll book 
holders or challengers? 
A. Yes. The poll book holder and challenger are  
nominated by the independent candidate, but again, 
these individuals must meet the qualiﬁcaƟons under 
state law to serve. See IC 3‐6‐7‐1 for details. 
Q. Can school board candidates appoint watchers? 
A. Yes. School board candidates or group of school 
board candidates can appoint watchers by ﬁling a 
wriƩen statement with the clerk. The contents of this 
statement must include their aƩorney‐in‐fact and the 
list of precincts where the watchers will be present. The 
clerk then issues the credenƟal to the individuals on the 
wriƩen request.  See IC 3‐6‐9, generally, for the speciﬁc 
procedures. NOTE: School board candidates are not 
enƟtled to appoint challengers or poll book  
holders. 
Q. Can a commiƩee supporƟng or opposing a public 
quesƟon appoint watchers? 
A. Yes. The chair of the PAC can appoint watchers, but 
must ﬁrst collect signatures equal to 2% of the total 
votes cast for SOS in 2018 and ﬁle the peƟƟon with the 
county elecƟon board. Once the number of signatures 
is determined to equal this threshold hold, the CEB will 
issue a credenƟal to the watchers. See IC 3‐6‐8,  
generally, for these details. 
Q. Do we have to organize our ABS applicaƟons and 
ballot envelopes by precinct before elecƟon day? 
A. YES! State law requires this organizaƟon to perform 
the central count of absentees on elecƟon day. See IC 3
‐11.5‐4‐5 for details. CounƟes might also consider run‐
ning the ABS Ballot AcƟvity Report to use as a checklist 
for the central count teams to conﬁrm all ballots  
received are present in their precinct pack. 
Q. Can a candidate be a poll worker? 
A. It depends. In a non‐vote center county, a candidate may 
be a poll worker in a precinct where their name does not 
appear on the ballot, such as another township. In a vote 
center county, a candidate may not serve as a poll worker 
since all precincts vote at each vote center. See IC 3‐6‐6‐7 
for details. Please note: This applies to unopposed candi‐
dates as well. 
Q. My newspaper failed to publish my noƟce for a public 
test. Do I have to reschedule? 
A. Not necessarily. State law permits a county where the 
newspaper failed to Ɵmely publish a noƟce to allow the 
county to either 1) display the noƟce prominently in three 
locaƟons in the county or 2) post on the county’s website 
(IC 5‐3‐1‐2(k)). 
Q. Can we remove ballot cards from the ABS security  
envelope before elecƟon day to prepare for tabulaƟon? 
A. No. State law does not permit an absentee ballot  
envelope to be opened prior to the start of the central 
count of absentee ballots. State law also explicitly states 
that a ballot card cannot be pre‐scanned prior to elecƟon 
day. (IC 3‐11.5‐4‐6(b)) 
Q. Do we have to perform the second signature review  for 
absentee ballots? 
A. State law allows a county elecƟon board to unanimously 
agree to forego the second signature review on travel board 
and in‐person absentee ballots. See IC 3‐11.5‐4‐12 for  
details. 
Q. If we have a line at the end of the day during in‐person 
absentee or “early” voƟng, are we required to allow  
individuals waiƟng in line to vote if our oﬃce is closed? 
A. Much like elecƟon day, if there are voters in line waiƟng 
to vote during any day of “early” voƟng at the clerk’s oﬃce 
or satellite locaƟon, then those individuals are allowed to 
vote, if otherwise eligible. Staﬀ should either write down 
each person’s name who is waiƟng, mark their hands with a 
stamp, or designate a staﬀ person to wait at the end of the 
line to mark the end. (IC 3‐11‐8‐11 and IC 3‐11‐10‐29.2) 
Q. If a voter comes to early voƟng and doesn’t have the 
correct photo ID, do they vote provisionally? 
A. Yes. The voter should be issued a provisional ballot, given 
the PRO‐9 form. The voter then has unƟl noon, ten days 
aŌer the elecƟon to bring their ID to the CEB or sign the 
PRO‐10 aﬃdavit to indicate the person is indigent or whose 
religion bars them from being photographed. 
Q. Does a voter’s ID need to have a matching address to 
their registraƟon record? 
A. No. The photo ID law does not require a matching ad‐
dress. Instead, it must be issued by the state of Indiana or 
federal government, be current or expired since the last 
general elecƟon (11/6/18), and include a photo and name 
that conforms with the registraƟon. (IC 3‐5‐2‐40.5)

Election Division Dispatch 
 Brad King & Angie Nussmeyer, Co-Directors | Nov. 2020  
NEWS & UPDATES 
CerƟﬁcaƟon of ElecƟon Results 
There isn’t much Ɵme to rest following elecƟon day! Your 
county elecƟon boards must complete the canvass the results 
of your elecƟon no later then ten days aŌer the elecƟon, and 
process any provisional ballots or late arriving overseas ballots 
by 3PM that same day. You’ll then need to ﬁle the CEB series 
of forms using SVRS, and separately send your precinct level 
results to IED by noon, Monday, November 16, 2020 unless 
your county has opted to send precinct level results through 
SVRS. The CEB‐9 is due Tuesday, November 17, 2020.  
 
County clerks may begin issuing cerƟﬁcates of elecƟon to  
newly elected oﬃcials aŌer 12P local prevailing Ɵme on  
November 20, 2020.   
 
BMV Open on ElecƟon Eve & ElecƟon Day 
State law requires BMV branches that issue credenƟals like 
driver’s licenses or state ID cards to be open from 8:30A to 8P, 
local prevailing Ɵme, Mon., Nov. 2, 2020  and from 6A to 6P, 
local prevailing Ɵme, Tues., Nov. 3, 2020, to assist individuals 
in geƫng ID required to vote. As a reminder, state law requires 
a photo ID to include a photo of the voter, be issued by the 
state or federal government, be current or expired since 
11/6/18, and include the voter’s name that conforms (not nec‐
essarily be exact!) to their registraƟon record. (IC 3‐5‐2‐40.5)  
Further, an address on a state ID does not need to match the 
person’s registraƟon record. ExcepƟons exist for  military and 
veterans’ IDs. 
 
#Protect2020 
CISA has a new ElecƟon Rumor control in support of our

www.cisa.gov/rumorcontrol. This webpage can answer ques‐
Ɵons about the security of an individual’s vote and preemp‐
Ɵvely debunks potenƟal areas for disinformaƟon.  
The US Centers for Disease Control & PrevenƟon has also add‐
ed Ɵps for voters to reduce spread of COVID‐19. You can learn 
more by visiƟng hƩps://www.cdc.gov/coronavirus/2019‐ncov/
daily‐life‐coping/going‐out/voƟng‐Ɵps.html

InformaƟon in this newsleƩer is provided by the Indiana ElecƟon Division as a courtesy to county elecƟon administrators. If a person is unclear concerning elecƟon law provisions,  
the ElecƟon Division can serve as an interpreƟve source. However, where important legal rights are concerned, you must consult with your own aƩorney to be fully and properly advised. 
PROVISIONAL BALLOTS  
(IC 3‐11.7, generally) 
County elecƟon boards must review each 
provisional ballot  aŌer elecƟon day at a 
public hearing. The hearing must be  
conducted not later than noon, ten days 
aŌer the elecƟon and ballots found to be 
valid are to be counted not later than 3P 
by the same 10‐day deadline. 
The board will need to review the facts 
and apply the law to determine if a voter’s 
provisional ballot is to be counted.  
Generally, if the voter is found not to be a 
qualiﬁed voter of the precinct, then the 
provisional ballot should not be counted. 
However, state law was clariﬁed this last 
legislaƟve session to provide more  
guidance (see IC 3‐11.7‐5‐1.7 in the  
supplement). If the voter is found to be a 
qualiﬁed voter of the precinct by the CEB, 
and there is only the PRE‐4 aﬃdavit  
before the CEB to consider, then the  
provisional ballot is counted unless the 
provisional ballot was cast as a result of: 
1/ a court order extending polling locaƟon 
hours (court will provide direcƟon on this 
group of voters); 
2/ being omiƩed from a poll list and the 
voter applied at a voter registraƟon  
agency like the BMV or FSSA;  
3/ failing to produce required ID by the 
noon, ten‐day post elecƟon deadline; or  
4/ failing to provide proof of residency if 
required to do so not later than noon  
elecƟon day for absentee ballots or 6P 
elecƟon day for voƟng at the polls. 
If the provisional ballot was issued for any 
of the four reasons above then there is a 
speciﬁc procedures the CEB must follow to 
determine if the voter’s provisional ballot 
can be counted. 
LOCAL RECOUNTS (IC 3‐12‐6, generally) 
All CEBs must cerƟfy their elec
Ɵon results 
to IED not later than noon (Indy Ɵme), 
November 16, 2020. (The CEB‐9 can be 
sent as late as noon, November 17, 2020.) 
A candidate can ﬁle for a recount not later 
than noon, November 17, 2020. For local 
oﬃces, a county chair can ﬁle for a  
recount as late as noon, Nov. 20, 2020. 
There are no automaƟc recounts in  
Indiana! Instead, the vote margin between 
the candidates dictates the amount of the 
bond the individual pays. The person ﬁling 
the recount, at minimum, must pay the 
ﬁling fee for a civil court case and a bond 
amount of at least $100.  
The $100 bond allows for up to ten  
precincts to go through the recount  
process. If the vote margin is 1% or less, 
then each addiƟonal precinct is $10. If the 
vote margin is more than 1%, then the 
price per precinct is $100.  
For example, the person ﬁling the recount 
peƟƟon wants to recount 15 precincts. If 
the vote margin is 1% or less, her bond 
will be $150. If the vote margin is more 
than 1%, then her bond is $600. 
The judge assigned to the civil  
miscellaneous case will set up a recount 
commission made up of one DemocraƟc 
and one Republican member and a  
mechanic, a person familiar with the 
voƟng system. The local recount  
commission manages the process and 
brings the ﬁndings back to the judge, who 
makes the ﬁnal determinaƟon. 
(Statewide and state legislaƟve candidates  
use diﬀerent procedures, so please direct 
those inquiries to IED.) 
More informaƟon about both topics can 
be found in the blue 2020 ElecƟon  
Administrators’ Manual. 
IN FOCUS: Provisional Ballots & After Certification, Recounts 
VR CORNER 
VoƟng History 
County voter registraƟon oﬃcials can begin 
updaƟng vote history from the November 3, 
2020 elecƟon once the poll lists are returned 
to the CEB. If a state or local recount is going 
to be conducted, your elecƟon materials will 
be impounded. For those counƟes using  
paper poll lists, this means you will not have 
access to the poll lists to make updates.  
However, you can make copies of the poll lists 
if copies are made in the presence of the 
agency impounding the materials. (IC 3‐12‐6‐
19) Vote history must be uploaded to SVRS 
not later than sixty days following the  
elecƟon. Should a recount be conducted, this 
deadline is extended to sixty days following 
the conclusion of the recount. (IC 3‐10‐1‐31.2) 
 
DON’T FORGET! 
VR Re‐Opens Dec. 1, 2020 
QUESTION OF THE MONTH  
Q. How should we manage voters who asked for an absentee ballot 
and now want to vote on ElecƟon Day? 
A. Because all voters who asked for an absentee are to be ﬂagged in 
the poll list, there are a couple of paths for the voter & CEB to address 
issues where an absentee voter appears in person at the polls: 
1/ Complete the PRE‐5 ONLY if the voter’s absentee ballot was mailed 
and not received by the voter. AŌer compleƟng the PRE‐5, the voter 
votes a regular ballot if otherwise qualiﬁed. 
2/ Before signing the poll list, voter surrenders their ballot to the In‐
spector, who cancels it and issues a regular ballot to the voter, if other‐
wise qualiﬁed. 
3/ Before signing the poll list, voter discloses they forgot their ballot or 
it was lost at home. Voter can go to CEB before 5P to request an ABS‐
21, which will allow them to vote at their polling locaƟon. 
4/ If the voter signed the poll list, then oﬀer a provisional ballot to the 
voter. The CEB will determine if the voter was a qualiﬁed voter of the 
precinct.
