Election Division Dispatch 
 Brad King & Angie Nussmeyer, Co-Directors | Dec. 2020  
NEWS & UPDATES 
Thank You! 
CongratulaƟons on a successful elecƟon year, despite all 
of the hardships and obstacles. For those of you reƟring 
at the end of 2020, thank you for your service and  
fellowship. We are grateful to your commitment to 
Hoosier voters and wish you the very best for whatever 
comes next! 
Filing Provisional Ballot Aﬃdavits with SOS 
State law requires copies of all PRE‐4 aﬃdavits,  
regardless if the provisional was counted, to be ﬁled with 
the Secretary of State following the elecƟon. Now that 
the recount and contest deadline has passed and  
assuming your county does not have a pending local or 
state recount or contest, the original provisional ballot 
PRE‐4/PRO‐2 envelopes (sealed or unsealed and ballot 
counted) are to be delivered to the foreman of your 
county’s grand jury. See IC 3‐14‐5‐2 for more details. 
ElecƟon Materials 
A reminder all elecƟon materials are to be retained for at 
least 22‐months following the elecƟon. While ballots and 
provisional ballots are conﬁdenƟal, other materials like 
provisional ballot aﬃdavits, poll lists, tally tapes, etc. are 
public record. (IC 3‐10‐1‐31.1) Please note voter  
registraƟon documents follow a diﬀerent schedule. The 
purple VR Guidebook has more informaƟon. 
No December Conference or New Printed Materials 
A few counƟes have reached out to the oﬃce about the 
annual December ElecƟon Administrator’s Conference. 
TradiƟonally, no conference has been held aŌer the  
presidenƟal elecƟon and as a result, there will not be one 
held in December 2020. The yellow Calendar Guidebook 
does have a few key dates for 2021, though new  
publicaƟons—and a new Code Book—will be made  
available at the December 2021 Conference. Stay tuned 
for updates on that event in mid‐2021!

InformaƟon in this newsleƩer is provided by the Indiana ElecƟon Division as a courtesy to county elecƟon administrators. If a person is unclear concerning elecƟon law provisions,  
the ElecƟon Division can serve as an interpreƟve source. However, where important legal rights are concerned, you must consult with your own aƩorney to be fully and properly advised. 
CANDIDATE COMMITTEES 
With the elecƟon now behind us,  
candidates may be approaching you 
about campaign ﬁnance next steps. 
Whether a candidate is elected or  
defeated, the commiƩee can remain 
open or be disbanded. Unless a  
candidate disbands their commiƩee, 
their campaign ﬁnance commiƩee is 
considered to be open and acƟve. This 
will require the candidate’s commiƩee 
to ﬁle an annual report EACH YEAR 
unƟl their commiƩee is disbanded. 
CANDIDATE COMMITTEES ARE NOT 
CLOSED AUTOMATICALLY AT THE 
END OF THE ELECTION CYCLE!  
To disband a campaign ﬁnance  
commiƩee, their ﬁnal report MUST 
have a $0 balance and may NOT have 
any debts or loans owed to or by the  
commiƩee. CommiƩee funds can be 
donated to another regular party 
commiƩee, another candidate’s  
commiƩee, the elecƟon division, or 
certain non‐proﬁts. AlternaƟvely,  
contribuƟons can be returned to  
donors on a pro rata basis. (Pages 31‐
32 of the green Campaign Finance 
Manual has more details.) 
To communicate their commiƩee is 
disbanded, commiƩees will need to 
mark on their ﬁnal CFA‐4 summary 
sheet the “Final/Disbands” box under 
the “Type of Report” SecƟon.  
It is possible for a commiƩee to mark 
both “Annual” and “Final/Disbands” 
to saƟsfy both their annual report  
ﬁling and their ﬁnal report ﬁling. 
REGULAR PARTY/PACs 
Similar to candidate commiƩees, it is 
possible for a regular party commiƩee 
or PAC to disband. The same  
procedures—$0 balance, no debts or 
loans, mark “ﬁnal/disbands” ‐ apply to 
these commiƩee types, too.  
If the commiƩees remain open, then 
their reporƟng requirements are 
diﬀerent in that PACs & regular party 
commiƩees ﬁle a pre‐primary, pre‐
elecƟon, and annual report. However, 
in 2021, commiƩees are only required 
to ﬁle an annual report since there are 
no scheduled elecƟons held. 
ALL OPEN CANDIDATE COMMITTES & 
PACs MUST FILE THEIR 2020 ANNUAL 
REPORT NOT LATER THAN NOON, 
JANUARY 20, 2021!  REGULAR PARTY 
COMMITTEES MUST FILE  THE 
ANNUAL REPORT NOT LATER THAN 
NOON, MARCH 1, 2021! 
Failure to do so is a $50 per calendar 
day ﬁne, up to $1,000. County elecƟon 
boards must enforce delinquent  
campaign ﬁnance reporƟng.

VR CORNER 
VRG 4/12 from November General ElecƟon 
AŌer elecƟon day, state law requires county voter  
registraƟon oﬃcials to make updates to a voter’s 
registraƟon records as requested by a voter who ﬁled a 
VRG‐4/12 during elecƟon season. There is no speciﬁc 
Ɵmetable set forth in state law beyond requiring the  
update to be made. 
 
Our best advice is to ﬁrst post vote history from the 
November 2020 elecƟon to each voter’s record in 
INSVRS and then make the update to the registraƟon  
informaƟon. This will ensure the voter gets credit for 
voƟng in the elecƟon, which is important if the voter’s 
change results in their record being transferred to  
another county. 
 
If the voter updated their registraƟon address using the 
VRG‐4/12 to an address outside the county then you 
should scan a copy of the VRG‐4/12 into the vote’s SVRS 
record so the voter registraƟon oﬃcial where the voter 
now resides has an electronic copy for their records. 
 
DON’T FORGET! Voter RegistraƟon Opened on  
Dec. 1, 2020 
QUESTIONS OF THE MONTH  
Q. What happens if an oﬃceholder fails to take and ﬁle 
their oath of oﬃce by February 1? 
A. For non‐commissioned local oﬃce holders, their oﬃce 
would be considered vacant for failure to be sworn into 
service (IC 5‐4‐1‐1.2) unless they are enƟtled to hold over 
under the Indiana ConsƟtuƟon. Any dispute would be 
resolved by a judge ruling on a court case. 
Q. Can a new oﬃceholder be sworn in and ﬁle their oath 
before January 1? 
A. Yes. See IC 33‐42‐9‐7 for who can perform swearing‐in. 
Q. Does the oath included with the state’s CerƟﬁcate of 
ElecƟon form need to be used or can it be crated on a 
separate document? For example, can the oath be print-
ed on a judge’s leƩerhead? 
A. The oath found with commissions or with the  
cerƟﬁcate of elecƟon is included as a courtesy. It’s OK if a 
new oﬃceholder wants to create their own document 
using the text found on pages 45 & 46 of the blue  
ElecƟon Administrator's Manual. 
Q. Where are oaths ﬁled? 
A. Judges ﬁle their oath with SOS/IED. All other  
oﬃces, even commissioned local oﬃceholders, ﬁle their 
oath with the county clerk.

Election Division Dispatch 
 Brad King & Angie Nussmeyer, Co-Directors | Jan. 2021 
NEWS & UPDATES 
County Trainings with IED 
Since we were not able to meet much in person in 2020, IED is 
looking at hosting monthly online seminars on election  
administration, generally. We are shooting for monthly,  
hour-long presentations, and will do our best to honor this 
commitment. Stay tuned for details. 
For those of you who are new, the state partners with Civix to 
help manage our statewide voter registration system (SVRS). 
Civix hosts online training opportunities to train on SVRS, and 
the training calendar is found in SVRS. If you need help  
accessing the calendar, please contact the Help Desk. These 
trainings will continue in 2021. You can also request a  
customized online training with Civix, though the team is not 
traveling for hands-on instruction, due to the pandemic. 
Campaign Finance: Administratively Disband 
As you and your county election board (CEB) become more 
familiar with the state’s campaign finance act (CFA), you’ve 
likely found committees who fail to file required reports de-
spite best efforts to contact them about delinquent reports. 
Each year, not later than the last Friday of January (January 29, 
2021) state law requires the CEB to review its list of open  
committees and determine if any committee has not 1/ filed a 
report  of receipts and expenditures (CFA-4) in the last 3 years, 
has $1000 or less cash on hand, AND has no outstanding debts 
noted on their most recent CFA-4 filing. If those three things 
are true, then the CEB can send notice of a hearing to the chair 
and treasurer of the committee that the CEB intends to admin-
istratively disband the committee. At the hearing the CEB will 
make its determinations and follow the procedures found in IC 
3-9-1-12.  
December Hotfix 
Last month the following improvements were made to  
indianavoters.com (IV.com) or SVRS: 
• Added a printer icon to the ABS hopper grid to allow  
county users to reprint current online ABS apps  
• Clarified mailing address section of the online ABS app on 
IV.com. “Mailing address is same as residence address” 
checkbox text was changed to “DIFFERENT mailing  
address.” A voter must click “Different Mailing Address” to 
enter the address where their ballot is to be mailed. 
• Provided more context on IV.com for voters in “pending” 
status to explain counties must take action on the change 
request and the 7-day pending period must expire before 
site reflects updates. 
• Allow public users to edit their phone number and email 
address on the online ABS app. If info is contained in their 
registration record, the app will pre-populate these fields

Information in this newsletter is provided by the Indiana Election Division as a courtesy to county election administrators. If a person is unclear concerning election law provisions,  
the Election Division can serve as an interpretive source. However, where important legal rights are concerned, you must consult with your own attorney to be fully and properly advised. 
For most counties, no elections will be 
conducted in 2021. But like much of 
our state’s election laws, there are 
exceptions to this rule. 
A handful of municipalities will have 
an election in 2021 pursuant to their 
town charter. The town of Vernon, for 
example, is required to hold its  
election in March 2021 as their  
charter dating back to 1851 requires 
them to do so. Their town holds a  
simple paper ballot election at their 
county courthouse on election day to 
determine who leads their town for 
the next term. 
It’s also possible for a special  
referendum election to be held for 
controlled projects or certain property 
tax increases. While the general 
framework of administering elections 
is to be followed, the rules to call for 
these types of election generally  
involve the Indiana Department of 
Local Government Finance (DLGF). 
The DLGF website (in.gov/dlgf) is a 
great resource. When on the main 
page, look for the “Referendum” tab 
in the left toolbar navigation. It  
explains the types of public questions 
and offers current and past public 
question elections. 
Some public questions qualify for the 
ballot via petition process, where a 
specific signature threshold must be 
met. Those petitions are not created 
by IED; instead, you will contact DLGF 
for the document to make available in 
your office. 
Additionally, referendum elections 
held in 2021 must be held on the 
“normal” election days: the first  
Tuesday after the first Monday in May 
or November. Therefore, a special 
election may be conducted on May 4, 
2021 OR November 2, 2021. 
Specific deadlines must also be met by 
the unit of government to certify the 
question to the county clerk in order 
for the election to be held. Controlled 
project questions must be certified 
not later than noon, February 19, 
2021; & noon, March 5, 2021 is the 
deadline to certify a school tax levy or 
school safety public questions.  
Finally, unlike a year where an  
election is normally conducted, a unit 
of government requesting a special 
referendum election in the “off-year” 
must pay for the full cost of the  
election. (IC 6-1.1-20-3.6 & 20-46-1-
14) 
To learn more about authorized public 
questions please see our brochure: 
https://www.in.gov/sos/elections/ 
files/2020%20Referendum%
20Brochure.FINAL.pdf 
IN FOCUS: Special Elections & 2021 
VR CORNER 
2021 Redistricting 
This year the Indiana General Assembly will be tackling  
redistricting by establishing the boundaries for state legislative 
and Congressional districts using data from the 2020 Census 
called census blocks.  
While election administrators are accustomed to precincts, the 
census block is an even smaller unit as a precinct is made up of 
one or more census blocks. Further, state law does not permit 
a federal or state legislative boundary to “split” a census block. 
It’s also  possible a new district will be described in legislation 
as X township plus blocks A, B, C. 
When this occurs, the county commissioners (for most  
counties) will need to re-draw precinct boundaries in 2021 to 
incorporate the census blocks into a new or existing precinct, 
as the precinct also cannot be “split” for state and federal  
election districts. (Also true for most local units of govern-
ment.) 
More information about reprecincting will be coming in the 
months ahead, though IED and its partners are currently  
working to incorporate GIS tools into SVRS to assist with this 
work. Stay tuned! 
 
2021 Statewide VLM Postcard Mailing 
In addition to redistricting, state law also requires IED to  
conduct the statewide voter list maintenance (VLM) project. 
This project is expected to launch in late Spring 2021. More  
information to come. 
QUESTIONS OF THE MONTH  
Q. Are all election deadlines “NOON” deadlines? 
A. Unless otherwise stated in the specific statute, election 
deadlines are “noon” deadlines. See IC 3-5-4-1 for more 
details. If a deadline for filing falls on a weekend or a day 
when the office is closed, then the deadline does roll-over to 
the next business day at noon. (IC 3-5-4-1.5) 
Q. Do all committees file an annual campaign finance  
report in January 2021? 
A. All OPEN candidate and political action committees are 
required to file a 2020 Annual Report not later than noon, 
January 20, 2021. The green Campaign Finance Manual goes 
in to more detail on this subject. Regular party committees 
(i.e. your county, district, and state parties) have an  
extended deadline: noon, March 1, 2021. 
Q. A candidate lost their election in November 2020. They 
no longer have to file campaign finance reports, right? 
A. All committees must file a final/disbands CFA-4 report 
with the county (or with IED if their committee was set-up 
with the state) in order to have a CLOSED committee. The 
final report must show a $0 balance and have no loans/
debts owed to or by the committee. If the candidate did not 
file their final/disbands report with your office, then the 
committee must file required reports until it officially  
disbands and are subject to fines if delinquent.

InformaƟon in this newsleƩer is provided by the Indiana ElecƟon Division as a courtesy to county elecƟon administrators. If a person is unclear concerning elecƟon law provisions,  
the ElecƟon Division can serve as an interpreƟve source. However, where important legal rights are concerned, you must consult with your own aƩorney to be fully and properly advised. 
ALPHABET SOUP: EAC 
EAC = US ElecƟon Assistance Commission 
Bi‐parƟsan federal agency that supports voƟng system  
cerƟﬁcaƟon at the naƟonal level and compiles best pracƟces 
in elecƟon administraƟon. Visit eac.gov for more informaƟon 
All OPEN candidate commiƩees had an 
annual report due not later than noon, 
January 20, 2021. Every CEB must enforce 
the campaign ﬁnance act, which includes 
holding a hearing by the CEB to give late 
ﬁlers the chance to ask for a reduced  
penalty. 
First, what’s an OPEN COMMITTEE? An 
open commiƩee is one that has not 
marked the ﬁnal/disbands box on the CFA
‐4 Summary Sheet aŌer spending down 
their funds to $0 and has no debts owed 
to or by the commiƩee. The commiƩee is 
open unƟl it meets these legal  
requirements. 
Unlike other elecƟon‐related ﬁlings, a 
campaign ﬁnance report is only rejected if 
it’s on an old version of the form. You can 
use “Forms Master List” found on the 
SVRS County Portal to see which forms or 
current. If the report is late, it’s  
considered delinquent.  
A report received by the county elecƟon 
board aŌer the noon deadline is  
considered DELINQUENT and incurs a $50 
per calendar day ﬁne, up to $1,000. The 
ﬁrst $50 is assessed on the deadline date, 
if the commiƩee did not ﬁle by noon. Let’s 
say the commiƩee ﬁled the Monday aŌer 
the Wednesday deadline. This would be a 
$300 ﬁne or $50 Ɵmes six days. 
To ﬁle, the CFA‐4 report must be received 
by the county clerk by mail, fax, email, or 
hand‐delivery. In all cases, the report 
must be in the oﬃce. Mailing a CFA‐4  
report with a postmark date of 1/19 and 
received on 1/21 is late! 
Not later than 30‐days aŌ
er the ﬁling 
deadline (for 2020 Annual, this is Feb 19, 
2021), the county elecƟon board must 
send noƟce to each commiƩee that failed 
to ﬁle their required report. See IC 3‐9‐4‐
14 or see sample in the CFA Enforcement 
Toolkit in the green CFA Manual.  
Next, the CEB MUST hold a campaign  
ﬁnance hearing. NoƟce of the hearing 
must be sent to all commiƩees with a late 
report to be aﬀorded the commiƩee’s 
right to due process.  
The CEB will listen to tesƟmony, review 
the facts, and apply the law. It can  
unanimously agree to waive or reduce the 
ﬁne for each commiƩee that makes the 
request.  
AŌer the hearing, the CEB must send  
orders to each commiƩee that was  
assessed a full ﬁne or a waived or reduced 
ﬁne. This is the document the commiƩee 
should keep for its records and use to pay 
their ﬁne, if applicable. 
Fines associated with CFA reports go into 
a non‐reverƟng fund that can be used by 
the CEB for elecƟon purposes. See IC 3‐9‐
4‐17(k) for those details. 
More details are in the green 2020 CFA 
Manual, which includes a toolkit with 
sample leƩers and noƟces to assist CEBs 
with this process. 
 
IN FOCUS: Campaign Finance Enforcement 
VR CORNER 
Sheriﬀ’s Department Quarterly Reports 
State law sets forth a requirement that your county sheriﬀ 
provide a list of individuals who are currently imprisoned ‐
following convicƟon of a crime. The VRG‐1 should be aƩached 
to the report as well. The reports, at minimum, should be ﬁled 
with your oﬃce on Jan. 31, April 30, July 31, Oct 31. See IC 3‐7‐
46‐6 for more details. 
 
A person’s name on the list is not an automaƟc move to a  
cancelled registraƟon status!  This is why it is important that 
the sheriﬀ’s report give the county VR oﬃcial insight if the 
person is currently imprisoned following convicƟon of a crime.  
 
For example, a person who was imprisoned and released  
before the date of the report would no longer meet the 
threshold requirement of being currently imprisoned to be 
disenfranchised under state law. Further, a person being held 
but not yet convicted also does not meet the threshold  
analysis of being imprisoned AND convicted of a crime. 
 
County Department of Heath Reports 
Your county health department is likely ﬁling quarterly reports 
with your county Auditor. You can request these quarterly 
reports and use this informaƟon to move deceased voters to 
cancelled status within SVRS, assuming the county VR oﬃcial 
agrees the person on this list is the same on the registraƟon 
record. See IC 3‐7‐45‐2.1(e). 
QUESTIONS OF THE MONTH  
Q. Can we destroy 2018 elecƟon materials? 
A. Yes. Be sure to review the retenƟon schedule and  
related procedures found on the State Archives website 
under the “record management” tab! 
Q. An elected oﬃcial resigned and the county party is 
holding a caucus to ﬁll the vacancy. Does the candidate 
need to ﬁle the CEB‐5 with the county clerk? 
A. No. Unlike ballot vacancies, the candidate’s declaraƟon 
of candidacy (CEB‐5) is ONLY ﬁled with the chair of the 
caucus not later than 72‐hours before a caucus is held. 
Q. What paperwork needs to be ﬁled aŌer a caucus is 
held for an elected oﬃce vacancy? 
A. The CEB‐3 or the CEB‐4, depending on how the elected 
oﬃce was ﬁlled. The CEB‐3 is ONLY used if there was only 
ONE eligible precinct commiƩeeman to vote in a caucus or 
a Ɵe vote at the caucus. (The ballot vacancy law has  
diﬀerent rules on direct appointment!) The CEB‐4 is ﬁled if 
a caucus was held. The CEB‐3 or CEB‐4 is to be ﬁled not 
later than noon, ﬁve days aŌer the oﬃce vacancy is ﬁlled. 
Q. When is the CAN‐12 due aŌer a person ﬁlls a local 
elected oﬃce vacancy? 
A. The CAN‐12 is to be ﬁled with the clerk not later than 
60‐days aŌer the person assumes the elected oﬃce.

InformaƟon in this newsleƩer is provided by the Indiana ElecƟon Division as a courtesy to county elecƟon administrators. If a person is unclear concerning elecƟon law provisions,  
the ElecƟon Division can serve as an interpreƟve source. However, where important legal rights are concerned, you must consult with your own aƩorney to be fully and properly advised. 
ALPHABET SOUP: COTS 
COTS = Commercial‐Oﬀ‐The‐Shelf 
This abbreviaƟon is likely not seen much by counƟes, though 
you might come across it when looking at new voƟng systems 
or tune in to Commission recerƟﬁcaƟon this fall.  
 
When used to deﬁne a voƟng system or ePollbook, COTS are 
those soŌware, ﬁrmware, device or component that can liter‐
ally be found “on the shelf” where such components are sold.  
 
COTS components can be used by many diﬀerent people or 
organizaƟons for many diﬀerent applicaƟons other than  
cerƟﬁed voƟng systems and that is incorporated into the 
voƟng system with no manufacturer‐ or applicaƟon‐speciﬁc 
modiﬁcaƟon. See eac.gov for more informaƟon. 
Our oﬃce has ﬁelded a few quesƟons 
about retenƟon of elecƟon materials in an 
eﬀort to take advantage of this “oﬀ‐year.”  
Be sure to follow the retenƟon schedule, 
which can be found online at the State 
Archivist’s website:  hƩps://www.in.gov/
iara/ﬁles/county_general.pdf 
You’ll also need to work closely with your 
Local Records Commission. You may be 
asked to ﬁle addiƟonal forms and aƩend 
meeƟngs before having your records  
destroyed. 
ElecƟon Materials 
This category includes everything stored 
following each elecƟon, such as ballots, 
paper poll lists, machine tapes, etc. This 
does NOT include voter registraƟon and 
campaign ﬁnance, however. 
Federal and state law requires elecƟon 
materials to be retained for a period of  
22‐months. Therefore, materials from 
May 2019 elecƟon and earlier are eligible 
for destrucƟon in Mar. 2021; Nov. 2019 
materials in September 2021. 
AddiƟonally, state law requires the county 
elecƟon board to maintain all elecƟon 
results and at least ONE unvoted regular 
and provisional ballot from each township 
in perpetuity. These are generally ﬁled 
with your board’s meeƟng minutes. 
Voter RegistraƟon Forms 
ALL paper registraƟon forms MUST be 
ﬁled and maintained by county VR  
oﬃcials. While you are not required to 
print electronic records from your hopper, 
if your county chooses to do so, then it 
must ﬁle the paper record and maintain it. 
A paper VR registraƟon may be destroyed 
aŌer the person’s registraƟon is cancelled 
at their former residence address AND 
following two years aŌer the next general 
elecƟon. This retenƟon schedule is set in 
federal and state law. 
For example, a voter moves and updates 
their registraƟon to a new Indiana  
residence address using a paper VR form. 
The form was submiƩed on Mar. 1, 2021. 
The county must maintain the “new”  
registraƟon unƟl the “new” registraƟon is 
cancelled. But, assuming the “old” VR 
form was also submiƩed on paper, the 
“old” VR form can be destroyed on or 
aŌer Nov. 8, 2024. (The next general  
elecƟon aŌer the registraƟon is canceled 
is Nov. 8, 2022; the second general  
elecƟon is Nov. 8, 2024)  
Remember, state law requires all paper 
registraƟons to be scanned and uploaded 
to the voter’s documents in SVRS. 
Campaign Finance Reports 
Generally, campaign ﬁnance records ﬁled 
with your oﬃce must be kept for 4 years 
following Dec. 1 aŌer the elecƟon when 
they were ﬁled. For instance, the 2020  
pre‐elecƟon CFA‐4 report ﬁled by most 
commiƩees in Oct., 2020, must be kept 
unƟl Dec. 1, 2024. 
For any judicial candidates commiƩee, the 
records must be kept for 6 years following 
Dec, 1 aŌer the elecƟon the elecƟon 
when they were ﬁled for, since circuit and 
superior court judges serve 6 year terms. 
IN FOCUS: Spring Cleaning 
VR CORNER 
NVRA Form Numbers 
In SVRS, county users are prompted to enter an NVRA form 
number when entering a voter’s registraƟon. These numbers 
can be found in the upper leŌ corner of each state form.  
 
Below is the VRG‐7 form. Under the bolded form Ɵtle, State 
Form 50504 (R20/4‐20) is printed: 
 
 
 
 
The NVRA number is 50504, and entered in SVRS for data 
tracking purposes. The (R20/4‐20) is the revision number (R20) 
and the month/year it was updated (4/20).  
 
Auto Cancel 
Auto Cancel funcƟonality in SVRS is available, which moves 
eligible  “inacƟve” registraƟons to “cancelled” status in bulk. 
Before performing this task, be certain your county has applied 
vote history from the Nov. 2020 elecƟon!  
 
Vote history is important to idenƟfy those “inacƟve”  
registrants that can legally be moved into “cancelled” status 
aŌer 1/ receiving noƟce and 2/ not voƟng in any elecƟon over 
two general elecƟon cycles.  
 
NOTE: if your county has a special elecƟon in May 2021,  
complete this task not later than 29‐days before the elecƟon. If 
not, then you must wait unƟl aŌer the May elecƟon. 
QUESTIONS OF THE MONTH  
Q. Will there be new absentee forms for 2021? 
A. Yes, but only for ABS‐Mail in English and Spanish. These 
forms are only needed in those communiƟes with special 
elecƟons in 2021. The other ABS forms do not include  
ﬁling deadlines and are to be used for any special elecƟon.  
Indianavoters.com will include the new online ABS‐Mail & 
current ABS‐Traveling Board applicaƟon links in those 
counƟes holding special elecƟons. If the voter is eligible to 
ﬁle an ABS request, then the system will display the  
applicaƟon; if not, it will inform the voter that they are not 
eligible to vote in the elecƟon. 
Q. If we don’t have a special elecƟon in May or  
November 2021, can we accept absentee forms now? 
A. No, at least for state forms. State law allows a voter to 
begin ﬁling ABS apps for the May 2022 elecƟon as early as 
Dec. 1, 2021. For Nov. 2022, ABS forms can be ﬁled 
starƟng late May 2022, the same day VR re‐opens. 
However, military and overseas voters can ﬁle a Federal 
Postcard ApplicaƟon (FPCA) in 2021. Be sure the voter’s 
registraƟon is updated and the ABS app noted, though the 
oﬀ‐year in Indiana means the voter will not likely receive 
an ABS ballot. The absentee porƟon of an FPCA ﬁled in 
2021 expires on Dec. 31, 2021. If the voter wants to vote 
in 2022, they must re‐apply on or aŌer Jan. 1, 2022.

Election Division Dispatch 
 Brad King & Angie Nussmeyer, Co-Directors | April 2021 
NEWS & UPDATES 
Census Data Update III 
The US Census Bureau recently reported their team may be 
able to release “old format” 2020 census data for purposes of 
redrawing Congressional and state legislaƟve districts by Aug. 
2021. However, the “new format” ﬁle is sƟll expected to be 
released in late Sept. 2021. Since county acƟviƟes to re‐
precinct and redraw local oﬃce boundaries will start later  
than usual (but likely to maintain current deadlines), here are 
some ways to prepare: 
 
 Share news of the redistricƟng data delay with county and 
municipal leadership 
 Gather annexaƟons that may be part of reprecincƟng 
 Look at reprecincƟng plans and commissioner minutes 
from previous years for familiarity with both the process 
and the purpose behind the current precinct boundaries 
 Review current Indiana reprecincƟng  laws, but anƟcipate 
changes in pending legislaƟon (IC 3‐11‐1.5) 
 
 
Public Comment on FPCA & FWAB 
In the near future, the Federal Voter Assistance Program 
(FVAP) will be submiƫng a draŌ version of proposed updates 
to the Federal Post Card ApplicaƟon (FPCA) and the Federal 
Write‐In Absentee Ballot (FWAB) to the Federal Register for a 
public comment period. Their March newsleƩer notes that 
only comments made through the OMB website will be consid‐
ered by the FVAP staﬀ.  
 
For those not familiar yet, the FPCA is a dual VR and absentee 
applicaƟon form for military and overseas voters and in  
Indiana, the FWAB is the voter’s back‐up absentee ballot if the 
FPCA is returned. If adopted, the improved FPCA and FWAB 
will be likely be used beginning in 2022.

but in an oﬀ‐year like 2021, candidates eager for the new cycle 
are looking for informaƟon. IED tradiƟonally releases our

InformaƟon in this newsleƩer is provided by the Indiana ElecƟon Division as a courtesy to county elecƟon administrators. If a person is unclear concerning elecƟon law provisions,  
the ElecƟon Division can serve as an interpreƟve source. However, where important legal rights are concerned, you must consult with your own aƩorney to be fully and properly advised. 
ALPHABET SOUP: VLM 
VLM = Voter List Maintenance 
Federal and state law sets forth voter list maintenance rules 
and procedures. In federal law, you’ll ﬁnd the VLM statues in 
52 USC sec. 20507; in state law, these requirements are found, 
generally, in IC 3‐7‐38.2. 
 
VLM is conƟnual work, using resources from the Department 
of Health, Social Security AdministraƟon, Department of  
CorrecƟon, and other valid sources like the statewide postcard 
mailer. 
 
Before each elecƟon in even‐numbered years, VLM work to 
move registraƟons to “inacƟve” status must “freeze” 90‐days 
before the elecƟon. In odd‐numbered years, the “freeze”  
29‐days before the elecƟon. Unless your county has a special 
elecƟon in 2021, there is no “freeze” period this year.  
 
Certain list maintenance  tasks to move registraƟons to 
“cancelled” may occur at any Ɵme, like cancellaƟon due to 
death or incarceraƟon following convicƟon of a crime. 
 
State law requires the Indiana ElecƟon 
Division to manage a statewide voter list 
maintenance project in each odd‐
numbered year. In accordance with state 
and federal law, speciﬁcally IC 3‐7‐38.2‐
16.1, this project consists of two mailers: 
Card 1: Sent to the mailing address of  
every acƟve voter in Indiana via USPS non‐
forwardable mail. If the card is returned 
undeliverable pursuant to IC 3‐5‐2‐49.7, 
then card 2 is sent to the voter. 
Card 2: Sent by USPS forwardable mail to 
the mailing address of a person whose 
card 1 is returned undeliverable as  
deﬁned by state law. Card 2 allows the 
person to return a postage paid response 
card to:  
a) conﬁrm their residence address is their 
registraƟon address;  
b) update their registraƟon within the 
county; or  
c) cancel their registraƟon if they’ve 
moved out of county. 
The card templates are being draŌed 
now, and IED will share examples of the 
cards with counƟes and Hoosier voters 
before the project launches. 
Card 2 is the main focus for county VR 
oﬃcials. Our vendor will scan the 2nd 
mailer or “response card” and enter the 
update from the voter for county review. 
County VR oﬃcials will review the update 
in the respecƟve VLM hopper and make 
decision to approve, reject, or research 
the change. 
If the response from the voter is unclear, 
then the county VR oﬃcial makes the  
determinaƟon. The records in the VLM 
ExcepƟons hopper allow a county user to 
approve, reject, or research. 
Voters who do not respond to Card 2 by 
the August 27, 2021 deadline are loaded 
into an SVRS hopper to move the all of 
these records to “inacƟve” status in batch.  
Please note, there is a 29‐day freeze  
period in those precincts that may have a 
special elecƟon on Nov. 2, 2021, meaning 
a county cannot move a VR record to 
“inacƟve” during this Ɵme. The county 
user can conƟnue this work aŌer the  
elecƟons but before the 90‐day freeze 
deadline ahead of the May 2022 primary. 
TRAINING 
Training on using SVRS & its integrated 
VLM Image Viewer will be held in May. 
The sessions will be recorded and posted 
to the county portal along with the step‐
by‐step instrucƟons on using the modules 
within SVRS. 
KEY DATES 
May 17, 2021: Card 1 mailed by state 
June 1 to July 13, 2021: Card 2 mailed, if 
Card 1 is returned as undeliverable 
July 13, 2021: Last day for state to mail 
out Card 2 to provide voter with at least 
30‐days noƟce to respond 
August 27, 2021: Deadline for voter to 
return the Card 2 response card 
October 4, 2021: Deadline for counƟes to 
move registraƟons to “inacƟve,” if there is 
a special elecƟon in your county 
February 2, 2022: Deadline for counƟes to 
move registraƟon to “inacƟve,” before the 
2022 Indiana primary elecƟon 
IN FOCUS: Statewide VLM Postcard Mailing 
VR CORNER 
“InacƟve” Voters 
In Indiana, a voter is moved to “inacƟve” status ONLY if the 
voter fails to respond to speciﬁc noƟce required by law. For 
counƟes, the noƟce is the SAMC (Statewide Address Mailing 
ConﬁrmaƟon NoƟce) generated in SVRS; for our statewide 
mailing, it’s Card 2 or the “response” card. (To learn which 
items may be used to create a SAMC, see IC 3‐7‐38.2‐2.)  
 
VR oﬃcials are required to give voters at least 30‐days to  
respond to the noƟce, which allows the voter to update their 
registraƟon, cancel it, or conﬁrm their address on the noƟce. 
Failure to respond within 30‐days means the voter can then be 
moved into “inacƟve” status, if outside the “freeze” period. 
 
An inacƟve voter IS a registered voter and eligible to vote in an 
elecƟon. In fact, voƟng in any elecƟon over a two federal  
elecƟon cycle is one way to move back to “acƟve” status.  For 
example, a voter is marked “inacƟve” in August 2019.  
Assuming the voter conƟnues to reside at the registraƟon  
address, she can vote in any of the following elecƟons and 
move back to “acƟve” status: Nov 2019, May 2020, Nov 2020, 
special elecƟon in 2021, May 2022, OR Nov 2022.  
 
If an inacƟve voter does not vote in a qualifying elecƟon, then 
their registraƟon shall be moved to “cancelled” status. If the 
voter votes absentee or on ElecƟon Day and indicates a move,  
QUESTION OF THE MONTH  
Q. Do county parƟes need to ﬁle their CFA‐3 and campaign 
ﬁnance reports with the county elecƟon board? 
A. It depends. Indiana’s campaign ﬁnance act requires  
poliƟcal acƟon commiƩees and regular party commiƩees to 
ﬁle with the Indiana ElecƟon Division IF the PAC or party 
commiƩee ﬁnancially supports state legislaƟve or statewide 
candidates. If their commiƩee only ﬁnancially supports local 
candidates, then campaign ﬁnance docs are ﬁled with the 
county elecƟon board. 
To conﬁrm if the PAC or regular party commiƩee is ﬁled with 
IED, go to campaignﬁnance.in.gov. A PAC or regular party is 
NOT required to ﬁle courtesy copies! It’s best they don’t do 
so to avoid confusion over which body enforces defecƟve or 
delinquent reports, for example. 
then the fail‐safe opƟons may allow them to vote one last Ɵme 
in their “old” precinct. The VRG 4/12 will serve as an update and 
move their registraƟon to “acƟve” status again. 
 
Finally, VR oﬃcials cannot move an “acƟve” voter’s record to 
“cancelled” status for simply failing to vote. Instead, speciﬁc 
VLM procedures must be followed to move the registraƟon from 
“acƟve” to “inacƟve,” which may lead to cancellaƟon aŌer a 
period of Ɵme previously noted.

InformaƟon in this newsleƩer is provided by the Indiana ElecƟon Division as a courtesy to county elecƟon administrators. If a person is unclear concerning elecƟon law provisions,  
the ElecƟon Division can serve as an interpreƟve source. However, where important legal rights are concerned, you must consult with your own aƩorney to be fully and properly advised. 
ALPHABET SOUP: TACS 
TACS = Title, ArƟcle, Chapter, SecƟon 
Indiana
 law is organized by Title, ArƟcle, Chapter, and SecƟon—
or TACS. We oŌen refer to the state’s elecƟon law as Ɵtle 3, as 
most of our elecƟon laws are found in this Ɵtle. The arƟcle is 
usually the theme of statutes contained within the subheading. 
For example, IC 3‐7 is where you’ll ﬁnd voter registraƟon laws or 
IC 3‐9 the campaign ﬁnance act. 
The chapter further breaks down the “theme” of the arƟcle. For 
example, IC 3‐13‐7 is where you’ll ﬁnd informaƟon on ﬁlling an 
elected oﬃce vacancy for most local oﬃces. IC 3 (elecƟons) ‐ 13 
(ballot and elected oﬃce vacancies) ‐ 7 (ﬁlling some county 
oﬃce vacancies). 
The secƟon is the granular detail. IC 3 (elecƟons) ‐ 13 (ballot & 
elected oﬃce vacancies) ‐ 7 (some county oﬃce vacancies) ‐ 1 
(requires a D/R vacancy to be ﬁlled by caucus under IC 3‐13‐11). 
SubsecƟons can be even more speciﬁc, like IC 3‐13‐7‐2(a)(1). 
Occasionally an elected oﬃcial in a local 
oﬃce will resign from oﬃce before their 
term ends and the oﬃce will need to be 
ﬁlled as a pro tempore appointment. 
NoƟce of resignaƟon and procedures to 
noƟfy chairs of a death of an oﬃce holder 
can be found in IC 5‐8‐3.5 and IC 5‐8‐6, 
respecƟvely. Most local oﬃce holders will 
ﬁle their resignaƟon leƩer with the county 
clerk, who then must noƟfy the chair in 
wriƟng within 72‐hours. 
CerƟfying the death of a local oﬃceholder 
is also a responsibility of the clerk, once 
she receives informaƟon about the death. 
A caucus cannot be called unƟl the chair 
receives noƟce of the local oﬃcial’s death 
from the clerk. 
However, please read the statutes closely 
as some local oﬃces will ﬁle a resignaƟon 
with the governor or the governor will 
cerƟfy the death of an oﬃceholder. 
IC 3‐13‐6 is the ﬁrst chapter in the vacancy 
statutes that directly applies to local  
oﬃces. While it is important to read the 
enƟre chapter, beginning with IC 3‐13‐7, 
the ﬁrst secƟon notes that a vacancy in a 
local oﬃce that was last held by a person  
elected or selected as a candidate of a 
major poliƟcal party (D or R) of the state 
shall be ﬁlled by a caucus under IC 3‐13‐
11.  
The other procedures outlined in the rest 
of the chapter usually apply only if the 
oﬃcial was elected as a Libertarian,  
Independent, or other minor party. In 
these instances, a unit of government will 
hold a public meeƟng to ﬁll the vacancy, 
though there are special excepƟons with 
some local oﬃces where the unit is able 
to ﬁll the vacancy if the chair fails to ﬁll 
within the 30‐day period. 
A caucus is required for D or R elected 
oﬃce vacancies with three excepƟons: 
1/ there is only ONE eligible PC that can 
parƟcipate in the caucus (IC 3‐13‐11‐5(c); 
IC 3‐13‐11‐5(a) sets forth PC eligibility 
requirements);  
2/ there is a Ɵe at the caucus (IC 3‐13‐11‐8
(a)); OR  
3/ quorum at the caucus is not estab‐
lished (IC 3‐13‐11‐8(b)). 
Please do NOT conﬂate ballot vacancy 
rules with elected oﬃce vacancy rules. In 
2022, a chair may ﬁll a BALLOT vacancy by 
direct appointment if the party gives the 
chair permission to do so. This is NOT  
allowed for elected oﬃce vacancies but 
for the three excepƟons. 
For elected oﬃce vacancies, there is no 
state form for noƟce of a caucus. Instead, 
chairs send wriƩen noƟce under IC 3‐13‐
11‐4, which includes the date, Ɵme,  
locaƟon, purpose, and name of the caucus 
chair, to all eligible PCs by ﬁrst class mail. 
Candidates are required to submit the  
CEB‐5 to the caucus chair not later than 
72‐hours before the caucus is held (IC 3‐
13‐11‐7), and must meet the same gen‐
eral qualiﬁcaƟons to run for the elected 
oﬃce. The caucus adopts rules of proce‐
dures, which should include some basic 
rules found in IC 3‐13‐11, such as estab‐
lishing the deﬁniƟon of quorum or requir‐
ing a secret ballot if more than one candi‐
date ﬁles. 
The chair ﬁles the CEB‐4 (if it’s a direct 
appointment, the chair uses the CEB‐3) 
not later than noon, ﬁve days aŌer the 
caucus. Clerks are to give the new oﬃcial 
the CEB‐22. The oath is ﬁled not later than 
30‐days aŌer assuming oﬃce while the 
CAN‐12 is ﬁled not later than sixty days.  
IN FOCUS: Elected Office Vacancies 
VR CORNER 
Registering Underage Voters in the Oﬀ‐Year 
In Indiana, an “underage” voter is permiƩed to register to vote 
as long as the person turns 18 on or before the next Nov. mu‐
nicipal or general elecƟon, or Nov. 8, 2022. This means any 
voter who will turn 18 on or before this date can register to 
vote now and parƟcipate in in the May ’22 primary elecƟon, if 
they desire. 
 
But, in 2021, special elecƟons can throw a wrench into this 
Ɵmeline. If a special elecƟon is called for your county in 2021, 
a registrant residing in a precinct within the elecƟon district 
must be 18 on or before the date of the special elecƟon to 
process a registraƟon. 
 
Again, the impact is limited to those precincts that make up 
the elecƟon district involved in the special elecƟon. This may 
mean you can process an underage voter’s registraƟon in a 
part of the county not involved in the elecƟon, but would need 
to hold the registraƟon form and process aŌer elecƟon day for 
those underage voters living in the special elecƟon district who 
submiƩed a voter registraƟon form. 
 
Already registered “underage” voters in the special elecƟon 
district for oﬀ‐years like 2021 are not to be printed in the poll 
list. Of course, a VR oﬃcial would reject a VR form from a  
person answering “no” to the age or ciƟzenship quesƟon. 
QUESTIONS OF THE MONTH  
Q. Can a county clerk receive addiƟonal pay for  
serving as the chief VR oﬃcial for the county? 
A. In a county where the circuit court clerk serves as 
voter registraƟon oﬃcer, the clerk is enƟtled to per 
diem compensaƟon, which is paid out of the general 
fund. (IC 3‐7‐12‐22) In other words, the county council 
would determine what, if any, pay can be provided to 
the clerk for serving as the chief VR oﬃcial and the 
county commissioners would approve the budget line 
item. (IC 3‐5‐3‐1) 
Q. Can the county elecƟon board receive pay in the 
oﬀ‐year when no elecƟons are held? 
A. The county ﬁscal body determines the pay schedule 
for the two appointed members and secretary of the 
CEB. (IC 3‐6‐5‐9) There is no statute that prohibits pay 
in an “oﬀ‐year;” in fact, many counƟes are busy with 
administraƟve tasks put oﬀ during the busy elecƟon 
cycles. Further, the CEB is required to propose its 
budget esƟmate each year (IC 3‐6‐5‐16), which may be 
an opportunity to explore changes to compensaƟon. 
The State Board of Accounts might also have  
recommendaƟons if this is a concern of your board.

InformaƟon in this newsleƩer is provided by the Indiana ElecƟon Division as a courtesy to county elecƟon administrators. If a person is unclear concerning elecƟon law provisions,  
the ElecƟon Division can serve as an interpreƟve source. However, where important legal rights are concerned, you must consult with your own aƩorney to be fully and properly advised. 
ALPHABET SOUP:  
OCD = Oﬃce of Census Data 
 
In the coming months, you’ll be hearing the term “OCD” a lot 
more as their team coordinates with staﬀ at the Indiana Elec‐
Ɵon Division on re‐precincƟng details. 
The Oﬃce of Census Data is a bi‐parƟsan team (one D and one 
R director) that is part of the LegislaƟve Services Agency or 
LSA. LSA works with legislators to draŌ bills, and OCD plays a 
criƟcal role in the upcoming redistricƟng eﬀort. In fact, their 
staﬀ maintains the oﬃcial precinct shapeﬁle for the state and 
gathers and records precinct‐level elecƟon result data. 
IED works with OCD and shares the IEC‐8 re‐precincƟng  
paperwork ﬁled by counƟes . This ensures that the oﬃcial  
precinct boundaries, as established by the IEC‐8s, are properly 
recorded for purposes of redistricƟng. Plus, each precinct is 
made up of census blocks, which are smaller units that contain 
demographic data provided by the US Census Bureau.  
Several counƟes have reached out to ask 
what candidates ‐ or people thinking 
about being candidates ‐ can do in 2021 to 
prepare for the 2022 elecƟon cycle. 
In 2021 state law is preƩy straighƞorward. 
Any person who is thinking about running 
for an oﬃce must open up a campaign 
ﬁnance commiƩee when a threshold  
dollar amount is raised or spent. This is a 
universal requirement, regardless of the 
oﬃce sought or the year the person is 
thinking about being on the ballot. 
If the person is thinking of running for an 
oﬃce paying more than $5,000 in a calen‐
dar year, then a candidate MUST ﬁle a 
CFA‐1 not later than noon, ten days aŌer 
raising or spending $100 toward running 
for oﬃce. 
If the oﬃce pays less than $5,000 in a  
calendar year (or it’s a school board 
oﬃce), the CFA‐1 is ﬁled not later than 
noon, ten days aŌer raising or spending 
$500 toward running for oﬃce. 
The CFA‐1 will ask a candidate if this is a 
principal or exploratory commiƩee. If the 
person isn’t sure which oﬃce they want to 
pursue, the “exploratory” box would be 
marked. The commiƩee would need to 
amend their CFA‐1 at a future date to 
switch from “exploratory” to “principal” 
when a decision is made on the oﬃce for 
which he or she intends to run. 
Marking “principal” means the candidate 
has intenƟons to run for a parƟcular 
oﬃce, though the CFA‐1 can be amended 
at a future date to change the oﬃce 
sought or move it to an “exploratory” 
commiƩee. 
To be clear, ﬁling a CFA‐1 to open a cam‐
paign ﬁnance commiƩee in 2021 does 
NOT commit a person to running for that 
oﬃce in 2022 or beyond. Instead, the 
commiƩee is meeƟng its requirement 
under state law to open a commiƩee and 
ﬁle required reports unƟl such a Ɵme the 
Final/Disbands CFA‐4 report is ﬁled. 
Of course the candidate will want to pay 
aƩenƟon to the ﬁling deadlines in 2022 to 
make sure their declaraƟon of candidacy, 
peƟƟon of nominaƟon, and statement of 
economic interests are Ɵmely ﬁled to 
have their name printed on the ballot. 
The “CAN” series of forms are needed to 
get onto the ballot; the “CFA” series of 
forms are used for campaign ﬁnance  
reporƟng purposes only. 
If a local candidate opens a commiƩee in 
2021, then they’ll likely ﬁle the 2021  
annual report in January 2022. However, 
if the treasurer changes in 2021, then an 
outgoing treasurer’s report must also be 
ﬁled along with the amended statement 
of organizaƟon (CFA‐1). 
Next year, the requirements to open a 
commiƩee are more complicated since 
the act of ﬁling for oﬃce means some 
candidates must open a commiƩee. Those 
details will be covered in a future  
Dispatch. For now, you simply need to 
remember this basic raise/spend thresh‐
old requirement to get you through 2021.   
For more informaƟon, review the 2020 
Campaign Finance Manual OR access the 
PowerPoint & recording of a training  
session IED oﬀered on this topic in the 
“Shared Documents” folder of the County 
Portal.  
IN FOCUS: Candidate Committees & Planning for 2022 
VR CORNER 
Public Access to VR Info 
State law sets for the public access rules as it relates to voter 
registraƟon documents. The purple VR Guidebook is a more 
detailed source, but below are some references that may be 
helpful to county VR oﬃcials. 
 
1/ IC 3‐7‐26.4 does NOT apply to county elecƟon boards. This 
chapter in statute gives direcƟon to the ElecƟon Division as to 
how it can provide statewide voter ﬁle informaƟon. 
 
2/ The county elecƟon board must adopt a uniform and non‐
discriminatory policy to allow a person to request the county 
voter registraƟon informaƟon from SVRS. The county policy 
cannot “pick and choose” which ﬁelds from the ﬁle to provide; 
it’s an all or nothing decision point. However, this statute does 
not include individual registraƟon records or SVRS report. See 
IC 3‐7‐27‐6 for those details and the Public Access Counselor 
opinion found in the appendix of the VR Guidebook. 
 
3/ At the county level, a person can request reports out of

4/ Unless enrolled in the AG’s address conﬁdenƟality program, 
an individual’s voter registraƟon record is public informaƟon! 
A county VR oﬃcial may only redact a 9‐digit SSN to the last 4 
digits, if the full SSN is on ﬁle. 
QUESTIONS OF THE MONTH  
Q. Do Libertarian candidates need to ﬁle peƟƟons of  
nominaƟons like Independent or minor party candidates? 
A.No. The Libertarian Party has diﬀerent ballot access rules 
than DemocraƟc, Republican, Independent, and minor party 
candidates. Below is a simplisƟc view of statute; the 2020 
Candidate Guide oﬀers more details. 
The D & R parƟes are considered “major” parƟes because 
their Secretary of State candidates were the top 2 vote‐
geƩers in previous elecƟons. Therefore, D & R parƟes  
nominate most candidates for the Nov. elecƟon in the May 
primary and a few others at a state convenƟon.  
At one point the Libertarian Party was considered a “minor” 
party, but ﬁelded a candidate to run for Secretary of State 
who achieved not less than 2% and not more than 10% of 
the total votes cast for the oﬃce. As a result, their party 
nominates candidates for the fall elecƟon at a state or  
county convenƟon. Unless there is a change in state law, 
their party will conƟnue to have this level of ballot access 
assuming future Libertarian candidates for SOS earn at least 
2% of the total votes cast for that race in its elecƟon year. 
Other minor parƟes can achieve this level of ballot access, 
but it all starts with ﬁelding a candidate for the SOS race 
who earns a 2% vote share. (Independent candidates could 
not since “Independent” is not a poliƟcal party.)

InformaƟon in this newsleƩer is provided by the Indiana ElecƟon Division as a courtesy to county elecƟon administrators. If a person is unclear concerning elecƟon law provisions,  
the ElecƟon Division can serve as an interpreƟve source. However, where important legal rights are concerned, you must consult with your own aƩorney to be fully and properly advised. 
ALPHABET SOUP:  
VTD = VoƟng District 
VTD is Census Bureau slang for “precinct.” You will see this 
term in Census Bureau publicaƟons and data releases, and 
someƟmes hear it from IED and the Indiana Oﬃce of Census 
Data (OCD) at the state level, too.  
VTDs with updated 2020 Census data are currently available 
on the Census Bureau’s website <www.census.gov> as  
shapeﬁles, which are images used with mapping soŌware to 
digitally record and display boundaries and map features.  
However, in about a month, the Indiana OCD will be releasing 
a newer version with updated precinct names (those which 
have been updated since the U.S. Census Bureau received our 
state’s precincts in early 2020). Expect to see more info from 
our oﬃce when the updated shapeﬁle is available for county 
review. 
UpdaƟng and drawing new precinct 
boundaries is an eﬀort counƟes can  
undertake every year, but the maƩer is 
more acute in each of the two years  
following the decennial census. 
The decennial census updates informaƟon 
within and the boundaries of census 
blocks. Census blocks are the smallest 
geographic units that contain demograph‐
ic and populaƟon staƟsƟcs. In nearly all  
cases, precinct boundary lines “snap” to 
census block boundaries to form precincts 
in each county. 
One of the major drivers of redrawing 
precinct lines is redistricƟng at the state 
level for state legislaƟve oﬃces and  
Congressional districts. Indiana House and 
Senate and US House districts cannot split 
a precinct. But, legislators also have to 
ensure that the populaƟon between the 
districts is nearly equal.  
As a result, the bills adopted by the legis‐
lature will include many of current names 
of counƟes, townships, and precincts, but 
also speciﬁc census blocks. Those census 
blocks cannot stand alone and create a 
split in a precinct where some voters in 
precinct A vote for district 1 and the other 
voters in precinct A vote for district 2. The 
county execuƟve must decide how to  
redraw the precinct boundaries so that 
the precinct is not split by a district line. 
Some local units of government must also 
redistrict in the year following the  
decennial census (or 2021), and in some 
cases, those new districts may not split a 
precinct. Therefore, new precinct lines 
may be warranted. On the horizon,  
municipaliƟes will have to redraw elecƟon 
districts in the second year following the 
decennial census (or 2022) though it will 
not impact work for 2021. 
Because the decennial census revises  
census blocks, it is possible your precinct 
boundaries won’t change but the census 
blocks making up the district will. It’s also 
possible that the geography or mapping 
soŌware has improved the boundaries of 
census blocks. This may create a “sliver” 
of land between the old and new maps 
that may be incorrectly assigned to a  
precinct. In some cases, these issues can 
be addressed through technical  
correcƟons; however, some counƟes may 
opt to draw new precinct boundaries to 
address this issue. 
Another major factor to decide to  
reprecinct is annexaƟons, which may split 
an exisƟng precinct where one porƟon is 
in the “city” and the other porƟon is in the 
“township.” Local oﬃcials may want to  
redraw precinct lines to avoid a split to 
reduce poll worker or voter confusion. 
AnnexaƟon ordinances are to be ﬁled with 
the clerk and can drive a decision to  
create new precinct lines. 
Finally, part of balancing all of these  
compeƟng needs is ensuring your precinct 
does not exceed 2,000 acƟve voters and 
has more than 600 acƟve voters. There 
are excepƟons to these “min‐max” limits, 
but checking your acƟve voter counts to 
ensure compliance with statute might also 
drive the need to draw new precinct lines. 
IED will release a formal noƟce for  
reprecincƟng this month, which will  
include more detailed informaƟon about 
this process. County users can also ﬁnd on 
the INSVRS County Portal a training IED 
held in June to introduce these concepts 
to counƟes. 
IN FOCUS: Ramping Up to Fall Reprecincting 
VR CORNER 
ReprecincƟng & VR 
While county execuƟves manage the process to draw pre‐
cinct boundaries in most counƟes, county voter registra‐
Ɵon and elecƟon oﬃcials may be asked to  
assist with this process or act as the liaison between the 
county and IED. 
 
As we wait for the General Assembly to convene and pass 
legislaƟon with the new state legislaƟve and  
Congressional district boundaries, there is some early 
work that can be accomplished. Finding annexaƟon  
ordinances and running reports in SVRS to determine how 
many acƟve registered voters are currently in each pre‐
cinct will help determine if precinct boundaries need to be 
redrawn. 
 
AddiƟonally, if your county has a GIS expert on staﬀ, going 
to the U.S. Census Bureau to view Indiana’s 2020 precincts 
with new 2020 census data loaded into them will drive 
whether precinct descripƟons need to be updated. 
 
There are a lot of moving parts to this process, which is 
diﬃcult to accomplish in a normal year. But, the delay in 
census data will condense what would take more than 6‐
months to accomplish into a 6‐week period. Any advance 
planning this summer would beneﬁt your team and ours. 
QUESTIONS OF THE MONTH  
Q. Does the county clerk or the elecƟon board provide a cam-
paign ﬁnance commiƩee an EIN? 
A. No. The statement of organizaƟon (CFA‐1 for candidates; CFA‐2 
for PACs; CFA‐3 for parƟes) does ask where the commiƩee intends 
to bank, but county elecƟon oﬃcials do not play any role in what  
informaƟon the bank may require of the commiƩee to open an  
account. The IRS assigns EINs, and the commiƩee must contact the 
federal agency to determine their next steps. 
Q. Do candidates who express interest in ﬁlling an elected oﬃce 
vacancy need to meet the same qualiﬁcaƟons that a candidate 
seeking elecƟon on the ballot? 
A. Yes.  State law requires a candidate to be a registered voter of 
the elecƟon district whether through an elecƟon by all eligible  
voters or selecƟon by a caucus of party oﬃcials. The person should 
be registered and no longer in “pending” status not later than the 
deadline to ﬁle a CEB‐5. Length of residency may also apply to an 
oﬃce, and would require a person seeking to ﬁll an elected oﬃce 
vacancy to reside within the district not later than the date of the 
caucus. In the rare instance where a county chair can ﬁll an elected 
oﬃce vacancy through direct appointment, the person selected 
should be a registered voter and a resident by the Ɵme the CEB‐3 is 
ﬁled. Other requirements to qualify for oﬃce may need to be met, 
and those can be found in state law. The 2020 Candidate Guide is 
helpful but does not include informaƟon for all oﬃces.

Election Division Dispatch 
 Brad King & Angie Nussmeyer, Co-Directors | January 2022 
NEWS & UPDATES 
Candidate Entry into SVRS 
State law now requires all candidates, even those running for party 
oﬃces (delegate and PCs), to be entered into SVRS. CounƟes will 
want to conﬁrm their elecƟon is set up for all oﬃces down to  
delegate and PC for 2022 in SVRS. The Help Desk can provide some 
support and point you to the appropriate step‐by‐step resources if 
you are unfamiliar with the process to set‐up an elecƟon. 
 
Once the candidate informaƟon is entered into SVRS, you can use it 
to create your CAN‐5 noƟce. The CAN‐5 is required to be provided to 
the candidate within one business day of ﬁling pursuant to state law. 
Keeping up on candidate entry, daily, means you can leverage SVRS 
to manage the CAN‐5 process and mail them by batch each day. 
Plus, it should help on and aŌer ElecƟon Day to ensure all candidates 
are in the system for precinct results mapping and creaƟng  
cerƟﬁcates of elecƟon, a feature coming soon to SVRS for county 
users. 
 
IEC‐22 Due by Jan. 31 
Don’t forget to ﬁle your county’s IEC‐22 before January 31, 2022. 
This is a state form that acknowledges the voƟng system and ePB 
inventory database managed by VSTOP is up‐to‐date with your  
county’s inventory. 
 
AdministraƟve Disband of Campaign Finance CommiƩees 
Not later than January 28, 2022, the CEB may review its campaign 
ﬁnance records to determine if a commiƩee is subject to the  
administraƟve dissoluƟon procedure. To move forward with  
dissoluƟon, the commiƩee must have not ﬁled any CFA‐4 or CFA‐11 
during the previous three calendar years AND the cash on hand on 
their last ﬁled report is $1,000 or less. If both condiƟons are met, 
then the CEB may move forward with the process found in IC 3‐9‐1‐
12, including providing noƟce by cerƟﬁed mail to the treasurer and 
making addiƟonal ﬁndings by the CEB.  
 
VLM Hoppers 
The VLM Hoppers for the Statewide Mailing were disabled on Dec. 1, 
2021, as most counƟes completed their work. However, if your 
county had records leŌ to process, you may submit a CAF in SVRS to 
request the hoppers be turned back on. The VLM Hoppers will be 
accessible through Feb. 2, 2022, the last day to move voters to  
inacƟve status before the freeze begins on Feb. 3. 
 
Poll Worker Survey 
Recently the state released surveys to beƩer understand challenges 
for recruiƟng poll workers by elecƟon administrators, party chairs, 
and interested voters. The survey closes on January 12, 2022, and 
we’d love for more people to parƟcipate! On indianavoters.com, 
there is a “Take Survey” buƩon on the home page. Clicking it will 
direct people to the survey monkey to complete. Thanks in advance 
for sharing the informaƟon with others!

InformaƟon in this newsleƩer is provided by the Indiana ElecƟon Division as a courtesy to county elecƟon administrators. If a person is unclear concerning elecƟon law provisions,  
the ElecƟon Division can serve as an interpreƟve source. However, where important legal rights are concerned, you must consult with your own aƩorney to be fully and properly advised. 
QUESTIONS OF THE MONTH  
Q. Does the candidate need to personally ﬁle their declaraƟon of candidacy and other paperwork? 
No. A third party can deliver the candidate’s paperwork before the deadline. AlternaƟvely, the candidate may mail their forms 
but the forms must be received and ﬁled by the deadline date and Ɵme. 
Q. What year does a candidate use on the CAN‐12 to disclose ﬁnancial interests when running for local oﬃce? 
The year preceding the elecƟon. (IC 3‐8‐9‐8) For 2022, candidates will note 2021 on the top of the form and disclose related 
informaƟon for the year 2021. 
Q. Sally is an county employee and also wants to run for county dogcatcher. I thought she couldn’t be a candidate if she’s 
employed by the same unit of government? 
Sally can run for county dogcatcher, if otherwise qualiﬁed, and conƟnue to work for the county government. The restricƟons 
under IC 3‐5‐9, generally, come in to play IF she is elected to oﬃce. If Sally is elected as the county dogcatcher and is qualiﬁed to 
hold that oﬃce, then she eﬀecƟvely has resigned from her employed posiƟon within county government.  
VR CORNER 
PETITION PROCESSING  
REMINDERS 
 
DemocraƟc and Republican candidates for 
U.S. Senate must gather at least 500  
cerƟﬁed signatures of registered voters in 
each of the nine Congressional districts in 
order to qualify for the primary elecƟon 
ballot. The CAN‐4 is used for the peƟƟon 
gathering process for these candidates. 
 
Independent and minor party candidates 
who want their name printed on the  
November ballot must also collect  
signatures of registered voters in their 
elecƟon district totaling at least 2% of the 
total votes cast in the 2018 SOS race in 
their elecƟon district. The CAN‐19 is used 
by candidates in this category for federal, 
state, state legislaƟve, and judicial oﬃce; 
the CAN‐21 is used by these candidates for 
all other local oﬃce. 
 
PeƟƟons are ﬁrst ﬁled with the county VR 
oﬃcial for review and cerƟﬁcaƟon.  
Originals must be ﬁled on the current  
version of the form, and peƟƟons cannot 
be ﬁled by the oﬃce before candidate 
ﬁling. If someone presents a peƟƟon for 
ﬁling before January 5, it must be rejected. 
 
The purple VR Guidebook details what to 
look for when reviewing peƟƟons and  
processing them for cerƟﬁcaƟon. Some 
common issues include: 
 
1) The voter must be registered to vote at 
the address on the peƟƟon at the Ɵme the 
peƟƟon is processed. If they signed the 
peƟƟon with an address on Main Street 
but you reviewed the peƟƟon and found 
that they updated their registraƟon  
address to First Avenue, then the  
signature would be rejected. State law 
does allow for some minor variaƟons in 
address, too. 
 
2) The signature on the peƟƟon must be 
substanƟally similar to the signature on 
ﬁle with the VR record. In this instance, 
you can use some discreƟon due to age or 
inﬁrmity. You should also look to whether 
the aﬃdavit of assistance was completed 
on the back of the form, as the voter may 
have had help prinƟng or signing their 
name. 
 
3) DOB is not a required element. It’s  
included on the form to help you ﬁnd the 
voter in SVRS, but the person signing the 
form does not need to include it. 
 
4) It’s helpful if the peƟƟon has the  
candidate’s ballot name, but the name on 
the peƟƟon does not need to be an exact 
match to their declaraƟon of candidacy. 
The CAN‐2 (or equivalent) will set forth 
the oﬃcial ballot name. 
 
5) Do NOT forget to complete the county 
cerƟﬁcaƟon on the back of the peƟƟon! 
This is the oﬃcial count of cerƟﬁed  
signatures in each congressional district, 
not the report pulled from SVRS. 
 
6) The peƟƟon carrier aﬃdavit must be 
completed (in other words, all requested 
info present). If anything is missing in the 
peƟƟon carrier aﬃdavit, then you cannot 
process the peƟƟon and must aƩempt to 
contact the carrier. The carrier can  
complete the aﬃdavit on the original  
document, but must do so before the  
ﬁling deadline with the county. If the  
aﬃdavit is not perfected, the peƟƟon is 
rejected. 
 
7) The Congressional District for the 2022 
elecƟon is the Congressional District  
associated to the voter on the peƟƟon. It’s 
possible someone formally lived in the 5th 
Congressional District when they signed 
the peƟƟon, but the district lines changed 
and the person now lives in the 7th. The 
7th CD is what will be noted on the  
cerƟﬁcaƟon. 
 
When you’ve ﬁnished review of the  
peƟƟon, it’s helpful to ask the campaign 
representaƟve for U.S. Senate candidate if 
they intend to pick up the peƟƟons from 
your oﬃce. If not, you can mail them to 
IED but the cerƟﬁed peƟƟons would need 
to be received by IED not later than noon 
(Indy Ɵme), February 4, 2022. For inde‐
pendent and minor party candidates re‐
quired to ﬁle cerƟﬁed peƟƟons with IED, 
it’s helpful to ask for contact info to set 
expectaƟons on the pick‐up and delivery 
of cerƟﬁed peƟƟons. 
 
Finally, please email elecƟons@iec.in.gov 
and mƟmperman@sos.in.gov to request a 
master peƟƟon be set‐up for federal and 
state candidates. Providing the  
candidate’s name on the peƟƟon, their 
party, and oﬃce are helpful to complete 
our work. Once a peƟƟon is set‐up for a 
candidate, counƟes can begin using the 
SVRS peƟƟon module to track signatures. 
As we’ve noted in this newsleƩer and 
other presentaƟons throughout the year, 
the clerk and the CEB are not the  
candidate police. Candidate ﬁlings can 
only be rejected for a handful of reasons 
as noted in state law.  
 
SomeƟmes a candidate may miss a ﬁeld 
on the form or include incorrect  
informaƟon. However, once ﬁled, a  
candidate form cannot be given back to a 
candidate to amend. They may complete 
a new form as an amendment for the 
same oﬃce before the ﬁling period ends, 
but if the person ﬁled for the wrong 
oﬃce, they must ﬁrst withdraw using the 
CAN‐10 form and then ﬁle the  
appropriate candidacy paperwork for the 
new oﬃce.  
 
Reasons to Reject a  
Candidate Filing 
 
1) Faxed or emailed candidacy  
paperwork. State law requires a ﬁling 
to be an original document, which 
means it cannot be faxed or emailed. 
Instead, the forms must be hand‐
delivered by the candidate or a third 
party or mailed. (IC 3‐5‐4‐1.7) 
 
2) Received aŌer the deadline. The 
deadline to ﬁle in the May primary 
elecƟon is noon, February 4, 2022. 
Any form received aŌer this deadline 
(even if it was mailed and the  
postmark was dated before the  
deadline) must be rejected.  
(IC 3‐5‐4‐1.9) 
3) Filed with the wrong oﬃce. A candi‐
date for judicial oﬃce, prosecuƟng 
aƩorney, state legislaƟve, statewide, 
or federal oﬃce must ﬁle candidacy 
paperwork with IED. Local oﬃces 
must ﬁle candidacy paperwork with 
the CEB. If a candidate for local oﬃce 
comes to IED to ﬁle, then their ﬁling 
is rejected. This would also be true if 
a prosecuƟng aƩorney or judge, for  
example, tries to ﬁle their CAN‐2 with 
the CEB. (IC 3‐5‐4‐1.2) 
 
4) Used the wrong form. Candidates 
must use the current version of the 
candidate ﬁling forms. Please see the 
Forms Master List to idenƟfy which 
version of the form is current, if there 
are quesƟons. (IC 3‐5‐4‐8) 
 
5) Failed to aƩach the CAN‐12  
statement of economic interests (or, 
for certain state oﬃces, the  
statement of economic interests  
created by the speciﬁc agency in  
statute). Failure to include the  
CAN‐12 for local oﬃce must result in 
the CAN‐2 being rejected. NOTE:  
Party oﬃces (PC and delegate) use 
the CAN‐37 and state law does not 
require the CAN‐12 to be completed. 
 
Candidate Challenges 
There are a number of reasons why a  
candidate challenge may be ﬁled. For  
example, the candidate does not meet 
the voƟng history requirements, or does 
not reside in the elecƟon district. 
 
Any voter in the elecƟon district OR the 
county chair may ﬁle a CAN‐1 challenge 
not later than the speciﬁed deadline to do 
so. (IC 3‐8‐1‐2) For the May primary elec‐
Ɵon, the deadline to ﬁle the CAN‐1 is 
noon, Friday, February 11, 2022.  
 
When ﬁled, the CEB must hold a hearing. 
The hearing must be noƟced in  
accordance with the Open Door Law. It is 
advised that best possible noƟce of the 
hearing must be given to the individual 
making the challenge and the candidate. 
 
Both parƟes will present their facts and 
evidence to the CEB, who then must  
determine if the candidate will remain on 
the ballot once they review the facts and 
apply the law. 
 
Many of the candidate qualiﬁcaƟons are 
found in the 2022 Candidate Guide, which 
may be helpful to the CEB to idenƟfy  
statutes or other issues related to  
residency or the Hatch Act, for example.  
 
For challenges made to party oﬃces (D & 
R state convenƟon delegates or D PCs in 
2022), the CEB MUST refer to state party 
rules. State law is clear that qualiﬁcaƟons 
for party oﬃces are established by the 
respecƟve state party. (IC 3‐8‐1‐32) 
 
The CEB would order the candidate oﬀ 
the ballot, if it is decided to uphold the 
challenge.

Election Division Dispatch 
 Brad King & Angie Nussmeyer, Co-Directors | February 2022  
NEWS & UPDATES 
 
AdministraƟvely Opening Campaign Finance 
Candidate CommiƩees 
A candidate running for oﬃce that pays more than 
$5,000 in a calendar year must ﬁle a CFA‐1 to open a  
candidate commiƩee 1) not later than noon, ten days 
aŌer raising or spending $100 toward running for oﬃce, 
OR 2) not later than noon, seven days aŌer the  
candidate ﬁling period ends (noon, Feb.11, 2022), 
 whichever comes ﬁrst. 
 
Not later than noon, Feb. 18, 2022, CEBs must determine 
if a candidate for an oﬃce paying more than $5,000 year 
has opened their commiƩee as required by law. If the 
candidate has not ﬁled a CFA‐1, then the CEB must  
administraƟvely ﬁle a CFA‐1 making the candidate the 
chair and treasurer of the commiƩee, and the candidate 
will be required to ﬁle all necessary reports in 2022. 
 
State ConvenƟon Delegates 
A reminder that the DemocraƟc and Republican party 
delegate plans are posted on in.gov/sos/elecƟons under 
the “Candidate InformaƟon” page. The plans specify how 
many delegates are to be elected from each county and 
if the delegates are elected at‐large or by district. While 
the poliƟcal parƟes may have “automaƟc” delegates to 
their state convenƟons, those are not included in the 
plans ﬁled with IED. Instead, the lists focus on the  
number of delegates to be elected in the 2022 primary. If 
a county chair has a quesƟon about “automaƟc”  
delegates, please refer them to their respecƟve state 
parƟes. 
 
ABS Signature Mismatch/Missing Aﬃdavit 
Several counƟes have reached out about where to access 
the ABS‐18A/ABS‐18B, which are the new forms to  
provide an absentee voter if their signature is missing or 
mismatched on their ballot envelope when compared 
with their applica
Ɵon. The new forms are incorporated 
into SVRS and a new workﬂow is being developed to  
generate those forms. CounƟes will have to ﬂag the ABS  
voter as a signature mismatch/missing signature in SVRS, 
which will move them to provisional status. CounƟes will 
be able to print the aﬃdavits in batch, along with the 
PRO‐9 noƟce to a provisional ballot voter.

Pursuant to state law, IED will cerƟfy the

Clerk on the Ballot?

Moving Voters to New Precincts & ElecƟon Districts 
From all appearances, it appears that counƟes are closing in 
on updaƟng precinct keys and moving voters to their new 
elecƟon districts and, if applicable, new or updated precincts. 
If your county was impacted by Congressional or state  
legislaƟve redistricƟng, you must ﬁle a CAF in SVRS with an 
updated precinct key requesƟng the changes to federal and 
state level oﬃces. The IED cannot change your county’s  
registraƟon database without explicit authorizaƟon, and the 
CAF serves as that approval. You will also need to ask for your 
reprecincƟng toggle to be turned on so that you can move 
voters to new districts once the key is updated. Finally, we are 
also working to amend the statewide shapeﬁle in the GIS tool 
for counƟes to check their work and idenƟfy voters that may 
be misassigned to a precinct. Look for more info soon! 
 
SAMC & Out‐of‐State Voters 
Recently the phrases “out‐of‐state informaƟon” and “IDEA” 
were added to the VR correspondence dropdown to generate 
a SAMC. The “out‐of‐state informaƟon” is used when info is 
receive that a person may have registered in a new state AND 
you do not have a signed copy of their registraƟon or other 
document that explicitly authorizes cancellaƟon. In these  
instances, a SAMC can be sent to the voter to comply with a 
recent court order. “IDEA” is the Indiana Data Enhancement 
AssociaƟon, which is a program created by statute. There are 
currently no program parƟcipants, but should that change, we 
will let you know. 
QUESTIONS OF THE MONTH 
Q. There is an elecƟon district for a local oﬃce split  
between two counƟes. Where should the candidate ﬁle? 
A. Candidates ﬁle their declaraƟon of candidacy with the 
county containing the largest populaƟon of the jurisdicƟon 
according to the 2020 Census. The “larger” county would 
cerƟfy the names to the “smaller” county so that both  
counƟes can hold their elecƟon. The “smaller” county then 
sends their cerƟﬁed results to the “larger” county, who  
cerƟﬁes the ﬁnal total. 
 
Q. Am I required to hold a primary for one or both  
parƟes if there are no contests? 
A. In 2022, yes. Because there is a contested D or R  
primary elecƟon in the state, counƟes must hold a  
primary elecƟon, even if, locally, there are no contests. (IC 3‐
10‐1‐5) However, in 2023, it is possible a primary will not be 
held in the municipal elecƟon year since there are no state 
level oﬃces on the ballot. 
 
Q. Can relaƟves run for and hold elected oﬃce in the same 
unit of government? For example, a  husband  
serving on the township board and the wife the  
township trustee? 
A. There is no statute that prohibits individuals who are relat‐
ed from serving elected oﬃce at the same Ɵme. The conﬂict 
arises when a relaƟve is an employee, but an elected oﬃcial 
would not be an employee of another elected oﬃcial.

the ElecƟon Division can serve as an interpreƟve source. However, where important legal rights are concerned, you must consult with your own aƩorney to be fully and properly advised.

Absentee & Provisional Ballots 
Each county must esƟmate the number of

voters in your county not later than March 
4, 2022. There is no speciﬁc rule of thumb 
to make the determinaƟon, though your 
2018 and 2020 primary elecƟon numbers 
might be a reasonable gauge. 
 
Your ballot printer must deliver your  or‐
der of absentee ballots not later than 
March 14, 2022. (If your county uses a 
ballot‐on‐demand printer, then the CD or

ElecƟon Day Ballots 
CounƟes using opƟcal scan paper ballot 
cards or tradiƟonal hand‐counted paper 
ballots need to order ElecƟon Day ballots. 
The print order should arrive on Ɵme for

pick‐up by Inspectors the Saturday or  
Sunday before the elecƟon. 
 
To order ElecƟon Day ballots for the May 
primary elecƟon, a county needs to  
review its 2020 Nov. elecƟon precinct  
level results and idenƟfy which D  
candidate was the top vote geƩer in each

top vote geƩer in each precinct to set 
forth the minimum ballot order. 
 
Figure 1 is an example of how many bal‐
lots and of which party type should be 
ordered for each precinct on ElecƟon Day. 
(No, state law does not permit counƟes to 
back out any ABS voters; you must follow 
this law for ordering primary ballots.) 
 
Some counƟes use a voƟng system where 
a blank ballot card is inserted into a ballot 
marking device, the voter makes their 
selecƟons, and a completed ballot card is 
printed for the voter to insert into the 
opScan tabulator. You would sƟll follow 
the ballot ordering rules, though you 
would be ordering blank ballot stock at

If you are a vote center county using  
printed ballot cards or blank ballot card

example below, each vote center would

NOTE: the ballot prinƟng rules and needs 
are diﬀerent in the Nov. 2022 elecƟon. 
 
Special Ballot Styles 
In a primary elecƟon, a county must print 
one ballot style for the Dem. Party and 
one ballot style for the Rep. Party. 
However, some jurisdicƟons will have a 
public quesƟon cerƟﬁed to them for the 
May primary, which requires its own spe‐
cial “non‐parƟsan” ballot style for those 
voters who do not want to vote in a par‐
ty’s primary elecƟon but do want to vote

If there is a public quesƟon that

1)  print the public quesƟon on the D & R

NEW! In 2021, the state’s fail‐safe  
provisions were updated that will  
impact your county if a LOCAL public 
quesƟon is cerƟﬁed in your county. If a 
voter moved out of the district where a

primary, they must be given a “17‐year 
old” ballot as voters ﬁƫng this fail‐safe 
scenario are enƟtled to nominate  
candidates for the Nov. elecƟon but  
cannot vote on the public quesƟon, as it’s 
a ﬁnal maƩer decided in this elecƟon.

CAN‐9: NoƟce of Primary ElecƟon

(Addresses must be included unless restricted under IC 36‐

 the dates, Ɵme, and locaƟons for in‐person absentee or

The date for publishing this noƟce in the newspaper in
