Every elecƟon cycle we’re all asked  
quesƟons about yard signs and when/
where/what Ɵme can they be placed. IED  
publishes a Disclaimer brochure with 
more detailed informaƟon, but here are 
some FAQs: 
1/ Is there a state law that dictates when 
yard signs can be put out before an  
elecƟon? No, state law doesn’t  
speciﬁcally address when campaign yard 
signs can go out in people’s yards. This 
decision is leŌ to local ordinance or home‐
owner associaƟon policies.  
However, there is a state law that states IF 
there is a local ordinance prohibiƟng yard 
signs, then the ordinance is not  
enforceable for 60‐days before an  
elecƟon through 5‐days aŌer. (IC 36‐1‐3‐
11) AddiƟonally, a homeowner’s associa‐
Ɵon policy prohibiƟng yard signs cannot 
be enforced 30‐days before an elecƟon 
through 5‐days aŌerward. (IC 32‐
21‐13‐4) 
2/ can yard signs be placed in the right of 
way? No. However, the county elecƟon 
board doesn’t enforce placement of yard 
signs. Instead, your county or city  
highway department, planning dept., or 
equivalent would enforce this rule. 
3/ Are disclaimers required on yard 
signs? In most cases, yes. A disclaimer in 
at least 7 size font with who paid for the 
sign is required to be included on the sign 
in indelible ink that contrasts with the  
background. (IC 3‐9‐3‐2.5) However, signs  
supporƟng or opposing a referendum do 
not require the use of a disclaimer. (IC 3‐9‐
3‐2.5)  The county elecƟon board would 
address complaints about yard signs that 
appear to not be compliant with state’s  
disclaimer law. 
4/ A non‐incumbent printed on their yard 
sign “Sam Smith Dogcatcher.” This im‐
plies they are the incumbent. Is this al‐
lowable? In the view of the Indiana Elec‐
Ɵon Commission, yes. The bi‐parƟsan IEC 
issued an advisory opinion (2015‐01) that 
interprets IC 3‐9‐3‐5. A copy of this  
advisory opinion is included in the  
appendix of the green Campaign Finance 
Manual. 
5/ A person calls to ask if she can remove 
a yard sign placed in the highway right‐of
‐way without permission. What do I tell 
her? Only those with legal authority over 
the property can remove the yard sign 
from the county right‐of‐way. Any other 
person without such authority may be 
liable for criminal conversion. She should 
ﬁle a complaint with the proper  
authoriƟes to make them aware of the 
yard sign’s placement. If the sign is  
located on the owner’s property outside 
of any right‐of‐way, then the owner may 
remove it. 
March 4, 2022, or 60‐days from the  
primary elecƟon, is the ﬁrst day a local 
ordinance for yard signs cannot be  
enforced. This is in eﬀect through May 9, 
2022. (IC 36‐1‐3‐11) 
For homeowner’s associaƟon rules, April 
3, 2022, is the ﬁrst day an HOA rule  
cannot be enforced limiƟng the display of 
poliƟcal signs on a member’s property. 
This prohibiƟon ends on May 8, 2022. (IC 
32‐21‐13‐4) 
VR CORNER 
Military & Overseas Voters VR Deadline 
Military & overseas voters using the Federal Post 
Card ApplicaƟon (FPCA) have an extended voter  
registraƟon deadline before each elecƟon. Rather 
than the standard 29‐day statewide cut‐oﬀ,  
individuals eligible to use the FPCA may use this form 
to register to vote unƟl eight days before the  
elecƟon. The  voter registraƟon cut‐oﬀ for FPCA  
eligible voters is April 25, 2022. An FPCA can be 
emailed or faxed, so it is not necessary for a military 
or overseas voter using the FPCA to be held to the 
same “wet” or original signature standard on a VR 
form as a civilian voter submiƫng the state or federal 
voter registraƟon form. 
 
Precinct Key & ElecƟon District Changes 
A reminder for county VR oﬃcials to ensure their 
precinct key is updated to reﬂect their local oﬃce 
elecƟon district changes, if applicable. The county 
commissioners (in most cases) were required to 
recerƟfy or redraw commissioner and county council 
districts in 2021. Those changes MUST be made to 
the precinct key and voters moved to their proper 
districts. IED does NOT have visibility to these local 
changes, but has been working with counƟes to 
move voters to their proper CD/HD/SD for 2022.

the ElecƟon Division can serve as an interpreƟve source. However, where important legal rights are concerned, you must consult with your own aƩorney to be fully and properly advised. 
IN FOCUS: Campaign Yard Signs  
Voters with Print Disabilities 
Last year state law created a new absentee form for voters with print 
disabiliƟes. A voter with print disabiliƟes is deﬁned as (IC 3‐5‐2‐50.3) an 
individual who is unable to independently mark a paper ballot or ballot 
card due to blindness, low vision, or a physical disability that impairs 
manual dexterity. 
 
Recently, IED released the ABS‐VPD form for download and use. Similar 
to a military and overseas voter’s FPCA, the ABS‐VPD is a combined 
voter registraƟon and absentee applicaƟon. A qualiﬁed person using 
the ABS‐VPD form would be able to request a ballot by mail or email or 
fax.  
 
As noted at the Dec. conference, the ABS‐VPD form would need to be 
ﬁled not later than 29‐days before an elecƟon to update the voter’s 
registraƟon. To request a ballot by mail, the ABS‐VPD form would need 
to be received not later than 11:59P, 12‐days from the elecƟon. The 
legislature did not include a deadline for applicaƟons to request a fax/
email ballot, though that will hopefully be remedied before the end of 
this year’s session. 
 
The form will be made available on indianavoters.com in the forms 
secƟon for download. We are working toward adding an electronic app 
aŌer the voter logs in to their “my voter portal” page on the site. The 
goal is for the electronic app submission to be available before the  
primary elecƟon. CounƟes will be informed of this update to SVRS 
funcƟonality & the public site as soon as possible, since county users 
will need to be trained on how to use the new hoppers once deployed.
 
QUESTIONS OF THE MONTH 
Q. Do candidate names appear in CAPITAL leƩers 
on the ballot? And do I use “” or () around a  
candidate’s nickname? 
A. Yes, a candidate’s name is printed in ALL CAPS on 
the ballot. (IC 3‐10‐1‐14.1) State law changed to  
require parentheses () around a candidate’s  
nickname, not quotaƟon marks. (IC 3‐5‐7‐5) 
Q. A candidate ﬁled their declaraƟon of candidacy 
but their name designaƟon is out of order. Can
 I 
change the order to comply with law? 
A. No. The ballot name as indicated on the  
declaraƟon of candidacy must be used on the ballot 
in the order requested by the candidate, unless a 
CAN‐1 challenge was ﬁled contesƟng how the  
candidate’s ballot name was ordered. More  
informaƟon about the ﬁrst, second, third, and fourth 
designaƟon can be found in the red Candidate’s 
Guide or in IC 3‐5‐7‐5. 
Q. Do I need to change a candidate’s name on their 
voter registraƟon record if their ballot name on 
their declaraƟon of candidacy doesn’t match their
 
voter registraƟon name? 
A. Yes. State law requires county VR oﬃcials to  
adjust the voter registraƟon name of a candidate to 
match the candidate’s ballot name. The declaraƟon 
of candidacy and candidate consent forms note this 
statute and give permission to counƟes to make this 
change. (IC 3‐5‐7‐6) 
Q. What’s a federal only absentee ballot? 
A. A federal only absentee ballot is ONLY used for an 
overseas voter who marks on the FPCA that they are 
an overseas voter and their return to the U.S. is  
uncertain. These voters must be registered to vote at 
the address of the county voter registraƟon oﬃce, 
even if they provide a residence address within  
Indiana  (IC 3‐11‐4‐8).  
Under federal law , these voters can vote only for 
federal oﬃces in even‐numbered general elecƟon 
years. Every Indiana county must have a federal only 
DemocraƟc and Republican ballot with the oﬃces of 
U.S. Senator and U.S House for the May 2022  
primary elecƟon. No other persons are eligible to 
use this ballot and it should not be included with 
ElecƟon Day materials used by poll workers. 
ABSENTEE BALLOT REMINDERS 
 ABS‐Mail ballots must be delivered to the county by 
their vendor not later than March 14, 2022, for the 
primary elecƟon. 
 State law and the federal MOVE Act require counƟes 
to send absentee ballots to voters with approved 
ABS‐Mail and FPCA applicaƟons not later than 45‐
days before each elecƟon, or March 19, 2022. 
 March 19, 2022, is the default “ballot ready” date in 
SVRS. CounƟes can request the deadline to be 
moved up to an earlier date by submiƫng a county 
authorizaƟon form in INSVRS. 
 Expect IED to follow‐up on the March 19, 2022, 
deadline as each state is required to report back to 
the U.S. Department of JusƟce on compliance with 
this important federal law. 
 Once counƟes begin sending absentee ballots out on 
or around March 19, 2022, state law requires an 
absentee ballot be sent on the same day the  
applicaƟon is approved. (IC 3‐11‐4‐18) 
 ABS‐Mail, ABS‐VPD, and FPCA applicaƟons for a 
mailed absentee ballot must be received not later 
than 11:59PM, April 21, 2022. 
 Absentee and FPCA forms can be mailed, hand‐
delivered, faxed, or emailed. 
UPDATE VOTING LOCATION DATA 
In April, IED will be pulling a statewide list of voƟng  
locaƟons used on ElecƟon Day and during “early” 
voƟng. This list is sent to Democracy Works, a non‐
parƟsan, non‐proﬁt organizaƟon, who updates a  
naƟonwide address‐driven voƟng site locator 
(geƩothepolls.com).  
 
If your county has any changes to “early” voƟng or  
ElecƟon Day sites, please log the changes in the polling 
place module in SVRS to ensure indianavoters.com and 
geƩothepolls.com display the correct informaƟon. 
 
New vote center counƟes will also need to submit a 
County AuthorizaƟon Form in SVRS to have their SVRS 
permissions reﬂect this change in voƟng method. If 
you’ve already done this, there is no need to request 
this again.  
 
Don’t forget! The county elecƟon board (rather than 
the county commissioners) is to publish a list of polling 
places or vote centers used on ElecƟon Day in the 
newspaper at least 10 days before the elecƟon. See IC  
3‐11‐8‐3.2 for those details.

Election Division Dispatch 
 Brad King & Angie Nussmeyer, Co-Directors | April 2022 (REVISED)  
NEWS & UPDATES 
Voters with Print DisabiliƟes Updates 
SVRS dropdown menus for the NVRA tracking code and ABS 
applicaƟon types were updated last month to include the ABS‐
VPD form. The NVRA tracking number uses the 5‐digit form 
number (53042) found in the upper leŌ corner of the form. 
AddiƟonally, the ABS‐25 secrecy waiver used for voters with 
print disabiliƟes requesƟng an emailed or faxed ballot is  
incorporated into SVRS. This form will generate like the ABS‐9 
secrecy waiver for military/overseas voters using the FPCA for 
a fax/emailed ballot. Training on these features will be held in 
April as part of the “March Build” review. Finally, the ABS‐VPD 
will be available online for voters to submit electronically.  
 
Paper Supply Inventory for November 
It is being reported that paper sources are going to be strained 
for the November elecƟon. Now is the Ɵme to discuss with 
your vendors about your anƟcipated paper supply needs for 
November, including ABS envelopes, ballot cards, and paper 
poll lists, and get those ordered as soon as pracƟcable. 
 
ABS Envelope Redesign 
The ABS incoming and outgoing envelope redesigns are before 
the state Forms Management Oﬃce for approval. However, 
the recent court order related to voters with print disabiliƟes 
being able to complete their ABS‐Mail ballots with assistance 
may require changes to the aﬃdavit language found on those 
envelopes. UnƟl we have clarity from the court later this  
summer, the redesigned envelopes are on hold. CounƟes may 
use the current form design to order more envelopes for  
November, which would require marking out “personally” in 
the one locaƟon noted in our Forms Order (2022‐110), or wait 
and see when the redesigned envelopes will be oﬃcially availa‐
ble for use. IED also plans to survey counƟes to inquire if you 
need assistance from our print vendor to tailor the ﬁnal  
version of the form to your county’s speciﬁc needs.  
 
2022 Campaign Finance Manual Error 
We were alerted to a typo in the 2022 Campaign Finance 
 Manual and uploaded a revised copy to our website. You may 
wish to manually make the change in the books used by your 
staﬀ on page 16, in the second paragraph under CFA‐11. The 
printed date for the start of the fall CFA‐11 reporƟng period is 
Oct. 25, when it should be Oct. 15, 2022. The reporƟng dates 
chart in the front of the book correctly references the Oct. 15 
date as the start of the CFA‐11 reporƟng period for the fall 
elecƟon. 
 
ABS Cure Process SOP 
Now that the ABS‐18A and ABS‐18B aﬃdavits for ABS signature 
mismatch or missing signatures are part of SVRS, counƟes may 
have process quesƟons. A new SOP is available on the County 
Portal to help navigate this new legal framework.

IN FOCUS: Election Results Reporting 
VR CORNER 
Statewide VR Deadline 
A reminder that the statewide VR deadline is Monday, April 4, 
2022. Voters can submit their applicaƟons: 
 By Hand‐Delivery to IED or County VR Oﬃce by close of 
business on April 4; OR 
 Online by 11:59P (local Ɵme) on indianavoters.com; OR  
 By Mail, though it is important to look for the postmark 
on the envelope! If the postmark is on or before April 4, 
2022, then you must process the applicaƟon for the  
primary elecƟon, if the voter is otherwise eligible. If the 
postmark is missing or illegible, then it must be received 
by Monday, April 11, 2022, to review and process for the 
primary elecƟon. 
Voters with print disabiliƟes using the new ABS‐VPD form 
must ﬁle the form by April 4, 2022, in order for it to be used 
as a voter registraƟon document to update an address out‐
side their precinct. Because it is also an absentee applicaƟon, 
a move within the same precinct can be processed at any 
Ɵme. 
 
As noted last month, military & overseas voters using the  
Federal Post Card ApplicaƟon (FPCA) have an extended voter 
registraƟon deadline, which is April 25, 2022. 
InformaƟon in this newsleƩer is provided by the Indiana ElecƟon Division as a courtesy to county elecƟon 
administrators. If a person is unclear concerning elecƟon law provisions,  
REDISTRICTING 
There is one important part of redistricƟng that may be confusing 
for voters and that is who REPRESENTS them as a currently elected 
oﬃcial aŌer elecƟon districts are redrawn. As county elecƟon  
administrators, we are focused on the next elecƟon and the “new” 
districts are used to manage the elecƟon.  
 
But, the “old” district lines remain in eﬀect for elected oﬃcials and 
the voter conƟnues to be represented by the person elected in the 
“old” district. In many cases, it’s likely the voter was drawn into the 
same district and the transiƟon from old to new districts is easy. 
However, some voters may be drawn out of their old district and 
into a new one. The person represenƟng the voter in the “old”  
district conƟnues to represent them unƟl the end of their elected 
term, but their ballot will have a diﬀerent oﬃce. 
 
For example, your “old” district is HD1 but your “new” district is 
HD2. You are currently represented by the person elected in HD1 
and consƟtuent requests would be directed there. But, your  
ballot will have HD2 on it because the “new” district is on the ballot 
for the new term. 
 
Be prepared for this quesƟon as counƟes will likely have “false” 
reports of errors when voters are drawn into new districts but  
accustomed to the old one. If your precinct key is correct, then 
your ballot and voter registraƟon records should be accurate, too. 
NOTE: Elected oﬃce vacancies are ﬁlled by a caucus of PCs within 
the “old” district lines unƟl the new lines take eﬀect. QuesƟons 
about this can be directed to IED, if help is needed!  
Unoﬃcial ElecƟon Night Results  
ReporƟng 
Recent changes to state law require counƟes 
to report UNOFFICIAL results on elecƟon night, 
beginning not later than 8P and ending at  
midnight (local Ɵme). If results are not  
complete, then counƟes must resume  
reporƟng at 9AM the day aŌer the elecƟon and 
update results hourly unƟl all unoﬃcial results 
are entered into SVRS. 
 
Two  SVRS ReporƟng Methods 
In SVRS, the precinct level reporƟng preference 
is “oﬀ” to allow for summary level results  
reporƟng unƟl the county manually changes it 
to be “on” in County Preferences (Admin > 
System > County Preferences > Precinct Level 
ReporƟng). Once turned “on,” the SVRS  
elecƟon results module will always be set‐up to 
receive precinct level results unƟl such a Ɵme 
the county manually turns the preference “oﬀ” 
and it will revert to summary level reporƟng. 
Once the results preference is set for the  
elecƟon, it should not be changed unƟl aŌer 
elecƟon results are cerƟﬁed. Once the results 
are cerƟﬁed and ﬁnal, then the county can 
change their results preference for the next 
elecƟon.  
 
Precinct Results Upload FuncƟonality. The 
upload funcƟonality requires you to “map” the 
names used in by your county’s elecƟon  
management soŌware to the ﬁxed names in 
SVRS. Think of mapping as helping SVRS  
translate the precinct, candidate, and oﬃce 
names used by your voƟng system soŌware. 
For example, the voƟng system soŌware may 
use “clerk” for an oﬃce name but SVRS has a 
ﬁxed name of “county clerk.” You are tying, or 
“mapping,” the word choice used by your 
voƟng system soŌware (“clerk”) to the ﬁxed 
SVRS oﬃce name (“county clerk”) so SVRS 
knows clerk = county clerk when results data is 
uploaded and presents accurate elecƟon  
results.  
 
There are a few things you need to do now so 
the process will work smoothly on  
ElecƟon Night:  
 
   1.Request your zero ﬁle from your voƟng 
system vendor, which can be the zero ﬁle used 
at the public test. 
 
   2. Use the zero ﬁle to  pracƟce mapping in 
SVRS Sandbox. If you do not have 
 access to INSVRS Sandbox, please contact the 
Help Desk. 
 
   3.When you are comfortable with the fea‐
ture, upload the ZERO ﬁle into SVRS  
ProducƟon to set up your mapping.  
 
Manual Data Entry. If you do not want to 
use the upload funcƟonality, then you will 
manually enter the results for each candidate 
by precinct. Or, you can opt to enter summary 
level results, which will have an impact on  
oﬃcial, cerƟﬁed results reporƟng. 
 
CerƟﬁed ElecƟon Results 
AŌer the county canvasses its results, it must 
cerƟfy its precinct level results to IED using 
SVRS. IED is no longer accepƟng elecƟon  
results by email, fax, mail, or hand‐delivery.  
CounƟes will not be able to ﬁle the CEB‐9  
report unƟl their precinct results are uploaded. 
 
If you reported your unoﬃcial results by  
precinct, then counƟes must use the upload 
funcƟonality or hand‐key to report oﬃcial  
precinct level results. If unoﬃcial results were 
entered at the summary level, then the  
precinct level results will be added as an 
aƩachment to the CEB‐9 ﬁled in SVRS.  
 
ElecƟon results are available to download from 
indianavoters.com/elecƟonresults, which is 
why it is important for oﬃcial precinct level 
results reporƟng be replaced by ﬁnal, oﬃcial 
results in SVRS. 
 
Resources 
There are recorded web training sessions and 
step‐by‐steps available on the SVRS County 
Portal. AddiƟonally, County ENR Data Entry 
training is scheduled for 4/26 and 4/28. 
QUESTIONS OF THE MONTH 
Q. Is the credenƟal number checked against BMV  
records in the DLN CorrecƟons Hopper? 
A. Yes. When a county reviews the record, SVRS pings the BMV 
system to conﬁrm the voter’s credenƟal number for you to  
review and approval. There is a step‐by‐step on processing  
records if you need a refresher. 
 
Q. Can a D or R Party Chair serve on the CEB?  
A. To serve on the CEB (or be a proxy) a person cannot be a  
candidate, elected oﬃcial, or a chair or treasurer of a candidate 
commiƩee. Lake, Porter, and Tippecanoe counƟes also require 
the CEB member be a registered voter of the county and cannot 
be related to the county chair that appoints the member.  
Assuming the county chair meets these requirements, then they 
may serve.  
 
Q. Who conducts training for absentee voter boards used for 
early voƟng and ElecƟon Day poll workers? 
A. State law requires the county elecƟon board to conduct the 
training. For ABS voter boards used at early voƟng, the training 
is to be done not later than the ﬁrst day of early voƟng. (IC 3‐11‐
10‐39) For poll worker training, the CEB must require Inspectors 
to go to training and have discreƟon if clerks, judges , or sheriﬀs 
are required to aƩend training in order to serve. (IC 3‐6‐6‐40) 
 
Q. Can a candidate or their relaƟve serve as an  
absentee voter board or central count member? 
A. Yes, if the candidate is running for an oﬃce that is not  
countywide. However, a candidate or their relaƟve may not 
handle ballots in the precincts where their name is on the ballot. 
If a candidate is unopposed, then their relaƟve may handle  
ballots in any precinct. Further, unopposed candidates for city, 
town, township, school board, or party oﬃce (delegate, PC) can 
handle ballots in any precinct. Unopposed candidates for other 
oﬃces not named above are restricted to handling ballots in 
precincts where their name is NOT on the ballot. (IC 3‐11.5‐4‐22
(c)(d)) 
 
Q. Can a candidate or their relaƟve be a poll worker? 
A. Only unopposed candidates for PC or delegate and relaƟves of 
unopposed candidates for any oﬃce can serve as an ElecƟon 
Day poll worker. Likewise, an opposed candidate or their rela‐
Ɵves cannot work in any precinct where the candidate’s name 
appears on the ballot. For example, in a non‐vote center county, 
a candidate who is running opposed for a township oﬃce  
nominaƟon in Township A and their relaƟves cannot serve as an 
ElecƟon Day poll worker in Township A. Instead, the opposed 
candidate and their relaƟves can be assigned to work in  
Township B. The result will be diﬀerent in a vote center county, 
since ballots from both Township A and Township B will be avail‐
able to voters at every ElecƟon Day vote center. Therefore, 
“opposed” candidates and their relaƟves cannot be a poll  
worker on ElecƟon Day in a vote center county. (IC 3‐6‐6‐7) 
 
Q. Can an opƟcal scan ballot card completed during early 
voƟng, whether marked by hand or a ballot marking device, be 
inserted into the tabulator by the voter or ABS voter board 
member? 
A. No. Once the voter completes their early voƟng ballot, the 
voter is to fold the card in such a way to hide their selecƟons 
and place it directly into the ABS‐7 envelope. The envelope is 
sealed and the voter & ABS voter board signs completes their 
required aﬃdavits on the envelope.
 
LEGISLATIVE UPDATES 
While a few laws passed in 2021 were amended or  
clariﬁed in 2022, the 2021 language must be followed for the 
May primary elecƟon, as the eﬀecƟve date for the changes 
made this year is July 1. This includes: 
 Provisional NoƟces to voters. CounƟes are required to 
mail the PRO‐9 to provisional ballot voters not later than 
3‐days aŌer the primary elecƟon. This statute was updat‐
ed to remove this requirement aŌer July 1, and added 
new requirements to update SVRS to ﬂag provisional vot‐
ers within a speciﬁc Ɵmeline. 
 Voters with Print DisabiliƟes requesƟng a fax or email 
ballot. AŌer July 1, 2022, state law requires the ABS‐VPD 
form to be ﬁled not later than 11:59PM, 12‐days before 
the elecƟon, regardless of the method the ballot is to be 
sent (mail, email, fax). For the primary elecƟon, the  
deadline to ﬁle an ABS‐VPD form to request a mail ballot 
is 11:59PM, 12‐days before the elecƟon; the law is silent 
on the deadline for a faxed/email ballot requested using 
the ABS‐VPD form. 
 
IED is working on a legislaƟve summary for the 2022  
session, which is tradiƟonally released before July 1.  
Reminder: ABS Changes in 2021 
Last year several state laws related to absentee voƟng were 
updated or added and were covered in the 2021 LegislaƟve 
Summary. Since this is the ﬁrst elecƟon for most counƟes  
under these new rules, here is a quick refresher: 
 Hand delivery of ABS‐Mail ballots. The law was expanded 
to permit relaƟves of the ABS voter to hand‐deliver a  
voted ABS‐Mail ballot to the CEB. State law sƟll permits 
the voter, member of the voter’s immediate household, 
aƩorney‐in‐fact, or a bonded courier to hand‐deliver an 
ABS ballot. Further, an ABS‐Mail ballot can be hand‐
delivered to an early voƟng locaƟon. Be sure early voƟng 
staﬀ is aware of this change and have a process in place to 
allow for the secure return of those ballots. If someone 
other than the voter or a bonded courier hand delivers a 
voted ABS‐Mail ballot, an ABS‐19 must be completed.
 
 Drop Boxes. Any dop box used must be under the direct 
control of the CEB. The 2021 LegislaƟve Summary has 
more details regarding noƟces to be placed on drop boxes 
used for other purposes, like parking Ɵcket payments.  
 Surrendering ABS‐Mail Ballots. A voter who requested an 
ABS‐Mail ballot can surrender their ABS‐Mail ballot at an 
early voƟng locaƟon and request a replacement ballot. 
The voter completes the ABS‐5 and then a replacement 
ballot is oﬀered, if the voter is otherwise qualiﬁed. On 
elecƟon day, a voter can surrender their ABS‐Mail ballot, 
which is rejected. Poll workers can then issue a   
replacement ballot, if the voter is otherwise qualiﬁed.   
Remember, in a primary elecƟon, the same party  
requested on the ABS‐Mail applicaƟon must be the same 
party ballot given as a replacement.

Election Division Dispatch 
 Brad King & Angie Nussmeyer, Co-Directors | REVISED May 2022 
NEWS & UPDATES 
Primary ElecƟon—Party A ﬃliaƟon Challenge 
In primary elecƟons only, a voter of the precinct may challenge 
another voter, if it is believed the voter does not aﬃliate with 
the party whose ballot the voter selected. The challenger 
would complete the PRE‐6 aﬃdavit, which all of your poll 
workers should have in their ElecƟon Day materials.  
The voter can overcome the challenge, and vote a regular  
ballot if otherwise qualiﬁed, if the voter completes their  
porƟon of the aﬃdavit which conﬁrms one of the following 
choices: 
1/ At the last general (November 2020) elecƟon, I voted for 
a majority of the nominees of the party the voter selected to 
vote in the primary elecƟon; OR 
2/ I did not vote at the last general elecƟon, but I intend to 
vote at the next elecƟon (November 2022) for a majority of 
the regular nominees of the party the voter selected to vote 
in the primary elecƟon. 
Absentees & ElecƟon Day TroubleshooƟng 
On elecƟon day, you may hear from absentee voters who want 
to deliver their ABS‐Mail ballot to you. That’s ﬁne, but the  
voter should seal their completed ballot in the security  
envelope and sign the appropriate aﬃdavit found on the  
envelope. The voter, bonded courier, aƩorney‐in‐fact, member 
of the voter’s immediate household, or the expanded list of 
family members may deliver this to the county elecƟon board, 
presumably at your central count locaƟon. Don’t forget to use 
the ABS‐19, if someone other than the voter or a bonded cou‐
rier drops oﬀ the ballot. However, a voter cannot drop oﬀ a 
completed ballot for counƟng at an ElecƟon Day polling place! 
If an absentee voter did not receive their ballot by mail, on 
ElecƟon Day, the voter can complete the PRE‐5. Or, if the voter 
wants to surrender their ballot to the Inspector, they may do 
so and poll workers would reject the voter’s ABS‐Mail ballot. In 
either case, the poll workers may issue the voter a regular  
ballot, if the voter is otherwise qualiﬁed, though the ballot 
must be from the same poliƟcal party requested on their app. 
If a voter’s absentee ballot is rejected, then an ABS‐21 can be 
issued to the voter as long as the voter appears before the CEB 
not later than 5PM on ElecƟon Day. Lastly, the ABS‐5 form is 
NOT used on ElecƟon Day. This form is used before ElecƟon 
Day for many of the issues noted above. 
ABS‐18A & ABS‐18B Aﬃdavits 
Don’t forget! An absentee voter with a missing or mismatched 
signature may return their ABS‐18A or ABS‐18B aﬃdavit to the 
Inspector at an ElecƟon Day polling place. The voter may also 
fax, email, hand‐deliver, or mail the aﬃdavit to the CEB, but it 
must be received by noon, 8‐days aŌer the primary elecƟon.

IN FOCUS: Libertarian & Minor Party and Independent Candidate Filings 
InformaƟon in this newsleƩer is provided by the Indiana ElecƟon Division as a courtesy to county elecƟon administrators. If a person is unclear concerning elecƟon law provisions,  
the ElecƟon Division can serve as an interpreƟve source. However, where important legal rights are concerned, you must consult with your own aƩorney to be fully and properly advised. 
Libertarian Candidates 
The Libertarian Party of Indiana generally  
nominates their candidates for federal, state, 
and local oﬃces at a state or county  
convenƟon. Instead of ﬁling declaraƟons of 
candidacy with the CEB, the LPIN state chair 
and secretary will cerƟfy the Party’s nominees 
to the CEB using the CAN‐22 cerƟﬁcate of  
nominaƟon along with the candidate’s CAN‐12 
statement of economic interests.  If held, the 
LPIN county convenƟon must be held not later 
than noon, July 3, 2022, and paperwork ﬁled 
with the CEB not later than noon, July 5, 2022. 
Should the LPIN not nominate candidates for 
all oﬃces on the ballot in November, the party 
may ﬁll its ballot vacancies not later than noon, 
July 3, 2022. The LPIN chair will ﬁle noƟce with 
the CEB of their party’s intent to ﬁll a ballot 
vacancy for local oﬃce, which must be ﬁled not 
later than ten days before the ballot vacancy 
can be ﬁlled. No state form is prescribed for 
this noƟce; a list of oﬃces on leƩerhead signed 
by the chair is suﬃcient.  
If ballot vacancies are ﬁlled by LPIN, the  
CAN‐32 (NEW FORM!)  and CAN‐12 must then 
be ﬁled with the CEB not later than noon, July 
5, 2022. 
Independent & Minor Party 
Candidates 
Independent and minor parƟes have two ballot 
access methods—through the peƟƟon process 
or to be a write‐in candidate. 
If an independent or minor party candidate 
wants their name printed on the ballot, then 
they must go through the peƟƟon process. 
Beginning January 5, 2022, candidates may ﬁle 
peƟƟon signatures using the CAN‐19 or CAN‐
21 forms with the county VR oﬃce. The 
CAN-21 is used for local oﬃces; the CAN‐19 is 
used for federal, state, state legislaƟve, and 
judicial oﬃces, including prosecuƟng aƩorney. 
The individual signing the peƟƟon must be a 
registered voter in the elecƟon district of the 
oﬃce the candidate is seeking a
t the Ɵme the 
peƟƟon is processed. 
In order to gain ballot access, the candidate 
must collect signatures totaling at least 2% of 
the total votes cast in the 2018 Secretary of 
State race in t
he precincts of the elecƟon  
district. This means county elecƟon oﬃcials will 
need to pull out the November 2018 precinct 
level results and calculate the signature  
t
hreshold for local oﬃces using the current 
oﬃce boundaries. (Countywide totals can be 
found in the back of the 2022 Candidate 
Guide.) State legislaƟve or federal candidates 
should contact IED for this informaƟon. 
CAN‐19 or CAN‐21 peƟƟons must be ﬁled with 
the county VR oﬃcial by noon, June 30, in  
order for the peƟƟon to be reviewed and  
cerƟﬁed. If seeking a local oﬃce, the candidate 
must also submit their CAN‐12 with the ﬁrst 
batch of peƟƟons ﬁled with the clerk’s oﬃce. 
However, in the few counƟes with a separate 
county VR oﬃce, the CAN‐12 is ﬁled with the 
cerƟﬁed peƟƟons when those are ﬁled with 
the county clerk or elecƟon board. The CAN‐20 
consent form must also be ﬁled with the cerƟ‐
ﬁed peƟƟons not later than noon, July 15, 
2022.  
The county clerk must send by cerƟﬁed mail a 
leƩer to the candidate if the individual does 
NOT achieve the signature threshold for ballot 
access. If the candidate did collect enough 
signatures, then counƟes will send the  
candidate a CAN‐5. 
Some individuals want to be a write‐in  
candidate. WRITE‐IN CANDIDATES ARE NOT 
PRINTED ON THE BALLOT! The CAN‐3 form may 
be submiƩed from January 5 through noon, 
July 5, 2022. For local oﬃces, the CAN‐12 must 
also be ﬁled with the CAN‐3. 
School Board Candidates 
Candidates for school board may ﬁle the CAN‐
34 peƟƟon and consent along with a CAN‐12 
beginning July 27, 2022, and not later than 
noon, August 26, 2022. There is no separate 
declaraƟon of candidacy; instead, the consent 
of the candidate found on the back of the CAN‐
34 is used for this purpose. A candidate can ﬁle 
mulƟple CAN‐34 forms, but only one needs to 
have a consent completed.  
Most school board candidates will need to 
collect at least ten signatures of registered 
voters within the school corporaƟon’s  
boundaries. However, there are excepƟons to 
this rule if the district is single member or  
subject to special legislaƟon. 
AddiƟonally, some school corporaƟon  
boundaries cross into more than one county. In 
these instances, the county with the largest 
populaƟon receives the CAN‐34 & CAN‐12, and 
then cerƟﬁes the signatures on the peƟƟon. 
This means the “large” county will use a 
statewide search to cerƟfy names in other 
counƟes. This process, where another county 
cerƟﬁes another county’s voters, is unique to 
the CAN‐34. 
“Small” Town Oﬃces 
Towns with a populaƟon of less than 3,500 
may move some or all of their municipal oﬃces 
to even‐numbered years through a local  
ordinance. Unless the local ordinance  
speciﬁcally requested the D/R candidates be 
nominated at the May primary elecƟon, then 
“small” towns will have town convenƟons to 
nominate D, L, and R candidates to the oﬃces 
on the ballot. This requires a candidate to ﬁle 
the CAN‐16 and CAN‐12 with the CEB not later 
than noon, Aug. 1, 2022.  
If none of the oﬃces for that parƟcular party is 
contested, then no convenƟon is held for that 
party. If an oﬃce is contested within the  
poliƟcal party, then the party will host a town 
convenƟon. There are speciﬁc procedures to 
follow, and the CEB/clerk will need to provide 
info to the party to conduct their convenƟon 
properly. The blue ElecƟon Administrator’s 
Manual covers this topic, though please reach 
out to IED if you need assistance. This type of 
nominaƟon will be more common in 2023, our 
municipal elecƟon year in Indiana. 
“Ballot Selfie” Law 
A number of counƟes have reached out in recent weeks asking about IC 3‐11‐4‐17.5, the former “ballot 
selﬁe” law that prohibited an individual from taking a photo of their completed ballot and sharing it with  
others. This statute that was found by a federal court to be unconsƟtuƟonal in 2017 and is no longer  
enforceable pursuant to court order. The statute has not been repealed, which is why it is printed in the  
Title 3 Code Book and searchable on iga.in.gov. But, the red 2022 IC Book published by IED has a notaƟon 
under the printed statute about the court case.  
Please be sure your staﬀ, poll workers, absentee voter boards, and others involved in elecƟon administraƟon 
are aware t
hat the “ballot selﬁe” statute cannot be enforced.  
VR CORNER 
US District Court Data Project 
AŌer the primary elecƟon, the Indiana ElecƟon Division will be 
distribuƟng informaƟon related to a voter list maintenance 
project. This project centers on data provided by the Northern 
and Southern District Courts, where a jury noƟce was returned 
to the courts. 
State law (IC 3‐7‐38.2‐1 6) requires county VR oﬃcials to send a 
SAMC mailer to those individuals on this list. However, our 
agency advice is to ﬁrst review the voter’s whose status shows 
“deceased” to conﬁrm if that informaƟon has already been 
shared with you through hoppers or informaƟon gathered by 
your agency. If not, you may use the tools found out in state 
law to conﬁrm the person has passed, such as ﬁnding an  
obituary or estate noƟce, before sending the SAMC. 
Here is the anƟcipate d Ɵmeline: 
Week of May 16th: IED distributes VLM data to counƟes 
Week of May 30th: Training to review the steps in SVRS to 
generate SAMC noƟces & other tools to assist with the  
project June 14, 2022: Deadline for counƟes to send SAMC to 
individuals noted on the list. 
 
More informaƟon to come! 
QUESTIONS OF THE MONTH 
Q. Do we process voters in line when our early voƟng l ocaƟons
close down each day?
A. Yes. If there are voters in line waiƟng to vote early at the
clerk’s oﬃce or other satellite locaƟon, then those individuals
are to be processed and receive an absentee ballot, if otherwise
eligible. Much like ElecƟon Day, the absentee voter board will
write down the names of all persons waiƟng in line, OR stamp
the hand of each individual, OR put a staﬀ person at the end of
the line to mark it. (IC 3‐11‐10‐29.2)
Q. How do we remake a faxed or emailed ballot on elecƟon
day?
A. Whe
n a county receives an absentee ballot returned by fax or
email, the paper ballot is stored in the ABS‐10 envelope and the
county should include the voter’s name on the envelope and
aƩach the ABS‐9 or ABS‐25 secrecy waiver to the envelope. On
elecƟon day, a bi‐parƟsan remake team should be given a blank
ballot card for the voter’s precinct and then they aﬃx their
iniƟals to the ballot card. The faxed/emailed ballot should be
given a randomized serial number and the same randomized
serial number printed on the remade ballot card. (Be sure to ask
your vendor where you can write the number to avoid
tabulaƟon issues.) The matching serial numbers are important in
a recount to ensure the voter’s choices on the faxed/emailed
ballot were remade correctly on the ballot card. Once the
remake team marks the ballot card, the ballot card is ready for
tabulaƟon. 
Q. Do candidates ﬁlling 
 ballot vacancies need to ﬁle special
campaign ﬁnance reports?
A. Yes, if the oﬃce pays more than $5,000 in a calendar year or
the candidate has an open commiƩee already then a vacancy
report will be required. AddiƟonally, those candidates
nominated at a convenƟon are required to ﬁll a pre– or post‐
convenƟon report. More info can be found in the 2022
Campaign Finance Manual.
D&R Primary Ballot Vacancies 
If a D or R did not ﬁle to run for an oﬃce in the primary elecƟon, 
the parƟes are able to ﬁll those ballot vacancies not later than 
noon, July 3, 2022. There are two opƟons for ﬁlling a local oﬃce 
ballot vacancy under IC 3‐13‐1: 
1/ Direct appointment by the chair or central commiƩee . The 
party organizaƟon may authorize the chair or central commiƩee 
ﬁrst, by passing a resoluƟon or adopƟng a moƟon at a party 
meeƟng. There is no special state form and state law does not 
provide direcƟon on what needs to be in the resoluƟon. For  
example, some parƟes give the chair limited authority to ﬁll  
ballot vacancies in a speciﬁc year, term of chair’s service, or no 
end date at all. (Note: this does NOT apply to elected oﬃce  
vacancies!) The appointments must be made by noon, July 3, 
2022, and the paperwork (CAN‐31, CAN‐12, CAN‐29) ﬁled not 
later than noon, July 5, 2022. 
2/ By holding a caucus of eligible PCs. Th e caucus must be held 
not later than noon, July 3, 2022; however, noƟce to eligible PCs 
(CAN‐30) must be sent via ﬁrst class mail not later than 10‐days 
before the caucus is held AND noƟce must be ﬁled with the  
county clerk not later than 10‐days before the caucus. The  
candidate must ﬁle their CAN‐29 declaraƟon with the chair of the 
caucus AND with the county clerk not later than 72‐hours before 
the caucus is held. (At this stage, the CAN‐12 is not required.) 
AŌer the caucus is held, the CAN‐29 cerƟﬁcate of candidate  
selecƟon and the CAN‐12 statement of economic interests for 
the selected candidate must be ﬁled with the county elecƟon 
board by noon, July 5, 2022. 
More informaƟon o n this topic can be found in the blue 2022 
ElecƟon Administrator’s Manual. 
Note: Local oﬃces include judicial oﬃce and prosecuƟng  
aƩorney; however, the paperwork noted in #1 and #2 for these 
two oﬃces is ﬁled with IED NOT with  the county clerk. State  
legislaƟve vacancies are managed by state parƟes & ﬁled with 
IED. 
Candidate Withdrawal for November 
Candidates on the November ballot may withdraw for any reason 
not later than noon, July 15, 2022. An original, signed copy of the 
CAN‐24 must be ﬁled by this deadline.  
If a D, L, or R candidate withdraws by July 15, then the poliƟcal 
party
 has 30‐days to ﬁll the vacancy under IC 3‐13‐1. AŌer noon, 
July 15, 2022, a candidate on the ballot in Nov. cannot withdraw, 
unless the candidate moves from the elecƟon district, is removed 
by the court, is convicted of a felony, or if the candidate dies, or a 
few other special cases.  
The D, L, and R parƟes are
  able to ﬁll the vacancy in those  
situaƟons; however, the procedures are a liƩle diﬀerent if the 
withdrawal happens in the ﬁnal 30‐days before the elecƟon. UnƟl 
Oct. 9, the parƟes follow IC 3‐13‐1. On or aŌer Oct. 9, 2022, this 
is considered a “late” ballot vacancy and the procedures under IC 
3‐13‐2 are followed. The 2022 Candidate Guide provides more 
details on this topic, including situaƟons where an Independent 
or minor party candidate may be able to ﬁll the ballot vacancy for 
November.

Election Division Dispatch 
 Brad King & Angie Nussmeyer, Co-Directors | June 2022  
NEWS & UPDATES 
 
US District Court VLM Project 
As noted in last month’s newsleƩer, the VLM project using 
data from the US District Court jury summonses is underway. 
County speciﬁc data was shared on May 16 and posted to the 
SVRS County Portal. Training on reviewing the data and pro-
cessing the informaƟon in SVRS will be held at the end of May 
and ﬁrst week of  June. SAMC postcards must be sent not later  
than June 14, 2022, pursuant to state law. 
 
DRE (MicroVote) CounƟes & VVPAT Compliance 
Beginning July 1, state law will require that a county elecƟon 
board using MicroVote (DRE) voƟng systems to cerƟfy to the 
SOS that the county has an inventory of VVPAT units totaling at 
least 10% of the total voƟng system inventory. If a county does 
not meet this threshold, then the county may not use the DRE 
in the November 2022 elecƟon. The deadline to cerƟfy this 
informaƟon to the SOS is August 11, 2022, and this  
informaƟon will be subsequently re-cerƟﬁed in 2023 and 2024. 
Stay tuned for more informaƟon. 
 
Local Government RedistricƟng 
State law was updated this year to limit redistricƟng (meaning  
changing elecƟon district boundaries)  to speciﬁc years  
following the decennial census. The new statutes—IC 3-5-10, 
generally—will be updated on iga.in.gov a Ōer July 1 but you 
can ﬁnd the new language when searching for HEA 1285-2022 
on this same website. 
 
What county elecƟon administrators need to know is that your 
local units of government (city and town councils, generally) 
have unƟl December 31, 2022, to pass an ordinance with their 
new elecƟon district descripƟons and have to ﬁle a copy of the 
ordinance with the county clerk where the greatest percentage 
of the city or town populaƟon resides, not later than 30 days 
aŌer it is adopted.  
 
Similar standards for redistricƟng in 2021 apply in 2022. See IC 
IC 36-4-6 for city council redistricƟng requirements or IC 36-5-2 
for town council redistricƟng requirements. AddiƟonally, case 
law has set a standard deviaƟon for populaƟon between the  
elecƟon districts to be at or under 10%. This is not in statute; 
rather, court precedent demands the standard deviaƟon be at 
this threshold number to avoid the redistricƟng being declared  
unconsƟtuƟonal. 
 
Finally, redistricƟng is a separate process from reprecincƟng. 
Many counƟes did draw new precinct lines in 2021, but later 
this summer, IED will announce another opportunity to  
modify, consolidate, or eliminate precincts in preparaƟon for 
the 2023 elecƟon.

IN FOCUS: VR Activities During “Blackout” Period After VR Deadline 
InformaƟon in this newsleƩer is provided by the Indiana ElecƟon Division as a courtesy to county elecƟon administrators. If a person is unclear concerning elecƟon law provisions,  
the ElecƟon Division can serve as an interpreƟve source. However, where important legal rights are concerned, you must consult with your own aƩorney to be fully and properly advised. 
For a period starƟng 28-days before the  
elecƟon and a few weeks aŌer the elecƟon, 
most voter registraƟon acƟvity is “closed” unƟl 
registraƟon oﬃcially re-opens. Below are some 
common acƟviƟes and more informaƟon about 
whether those acƟviƟes should be put on hold 
during this “blackout period.” 
 
New Registrants 
If an individual is not currently registered to 
vote and the county receives an online or  
paper registraƟon form during this “blackout 
period” a county can either 1/ hold the  
registraƟon or leave it in the hopper unƟl 
registraƟon re-opens or 2/ process the  
registraƟon as an incomplete and ﬁnish  
processing aŌer registraƟon re-opens. 
 
Updates to Current RegistraƟons 
A person currently registered to vote can use 
an absentee applicaƟon to update their  
registraƟon within the same precinct or to 
change their name. A move within a precinct or 
a name change would be treated as a  
correcƟon to their record. Otherwise, an  
update to a registraƟon would be held unƟl 
aŌer the elecƟon (though the voter may be 
eligible for a fail-safe upon execuƟng the VRG 
4/12). 
 
VRG 4/12 
State law recently changed to prevent the  
processing of the VRG 4/12 unƟl aŌer the 
county’s vote history has been applied in SVRS. 
CounƟes will be presented with an error if the 
county aƩempts to process a VRG-4/12  and 
vote history has not been added for the cur-
rent elecƟon. 
 
OVR & BMV Hoppers 
During this black-out period, no voter  
registraƟon request in your OVR & BMV  
hopper can be processed. CounƟes should look 
at the date/Ɵme stamp on the hopper entry 
and only review and approve those that were 
received by the statewide VR deadline.  
Otherwise, the records dated aŌer the VR 
deadline are held for processing unƟl  
registraƟon re-opens. 
 
ABS‐VPD VR Hopper 
Unlike the OVR & BMV Hopper, you may be 
able to process a registraƟon in this hopper 
ONLY IF the voter moves within their precinct 
or has a name change, as the combined form is 
considered an absentee applicaƟon and moves 
within a precinct or a name change on an  
absentee applicaƟon can be corrected on the 
voter’s record.  
 
If the record in the ABS-VPD VR Hopper is a 
new registraƟon or an update outside the  
precinct for an exisƟng registrant AND the 
record was received aŌer the statewide VR 
deadline, then you cannot process the VR re-
quest unƟl aŌer registraƟon re-opens. This also 
means the ABS request cannot be processed in 
the ABS-VPD ABS Hopper. A workaround here 
would be if the voter separately sent in a VRG 
4/12 to determine if the voter is eligible to 
vote one last Ɵme in their former precinct.  
 
VLM Hopper 
The VLM Hopper is shut down during the 90-
day freeze period before the elecƟon in even-
numbered years, and the 29-day freeze period 
in odd-numbered years. No county can move a 
voter registraƟon record into “inacƟve” status 
during the freeze periods. In this case, the 
freeze liŌs aŌer elecƟon day; however,  
counƟes should wait unƟl voƟng history is 
applied to ensure the voter did not vote in the 
elecƟon at their registraƟon address. 
 
Death & DOC Hoppers 
A voter who has passed away or one who is 
convicted of a crime and currently imprisoned 
may be cancelled throughout the year. In other 
words, the “blackout” period does not apply to 
this requirement. 
 
Federal Post Card ApplicaƟon 
Military & overseas voters using the FPCA have 
a special registraƟon period. For these voters, 
the registraƟon deadline is 11:59PM, 8-days 
before the elecƟon. AŌer this deadline, the 
FPCA cannot be processed for voter  
registraƟon changes but the voter may be  
eligible to request and receive an absentee 
ballot by email or fax, as the deadline to  
request a faxed or emailed ballot using the 
FPCA is noon, the day before ElecƟon Day. 
 
Voter CancellaƟons 
A voter’s signed, wriƩen request to cancel their  
registraƟon can be processed at any Ɵme. 
 
CerƟﬁcates of Error 
A cerƟﬁcate of error that is issued on or before 
ElecƟon Day because the voter’s record was 
not found in SVRS even though they are 
properly registered, allows for a voter’s record 
to be restored from canceled status or be  
created if the record was found not be entered 
into SVRS. This can be done anyƟme. 
QUESTIONS OF THE MONTH 
Q. Does return postage need to be included on a SAMC mailer? 
A. Yes, as this is a requirement under state law. (IC 3-7-38.2-2(f)) 
 
Q. Is there a requirement to send copies of the PRE‐4/PRO‐2 aﬃdavits to the 
SOS oﬃce aŌer the elecƟon? 
A. Yes. A county must give one set of copies to the grand jury of the county and 
send another set of copies to the SOS oﬃce aŌer each elecƟon. (IC 3-14-5-2)  
Copies should be made of all PRE-4/PRO-2 aﬃdavits, whether the ballot was 
counted or not. In a primary elecƟon, copies of the PRE-6 (party challenge) are to 
be ﬁled with the SOS. However, you cannot send the copies of the PRE-4/PRO-2 
unƟl aŌer the recount or contest period expires as provisional balloƟng  
informaƟon is conﬁdenƟal. If a recount is being conducted, then counƟes are 
advised to wait on sending copies unƟl the recount is concluded. 
 
Q. Do parƟes ﬁlling local oﬃce ballot vacancies need to include a copy of the 
resoluƟon or meeƟng minutes giving the chair the authority to do a direct  
appointment on each ﬁling? Or can the chair just submit a copy of the  
document to cover all ballot vacancy ﬁlings in 2022? 
A. A copy of the resoluƟon or meeƟng minutes must be aƩached to each ﬁling 
being made to ﬁll a local oﬃce ballot vacancy by direct appointment. 
VR CORNER 
 
VRG 4/12 Changes 
While county voter registraƟon  
oﬃcials are to have access to the 
VRG 4/12 once the elecƟon materials 
are returned to the county elecƟon 
board, a county must ﬁrst apply 
voƟng history to all voters in the 
county before the VRG 4/12 updates 
can be made and processed in SVRS.  
This was a change made in state law 
last year to ensure the voter’s voƟng 
history transfers with the voter to 
their new county, for example. The 
May 2022 elecƟon is the ﬁrst elecƟon 
where this funcƟonality is being used 
by county users, so it may be new to 
you this year.

NEWS & UPDATES

CounƟes must complete their voter list maintenance work,

IN FOCUS: Candidate Withdrawal Procedures for November Election 
InformaƟon in this newsleƩer is provided by the Indiana ElecƟon Division as a courtesy to county elecƟon 
administrators. If a person is unclear concerning elecƟon law provisions,  
Summer candidate ﬁling season is about 
at its mid‐point with school board ﬁlings 
ramping up and most other types of ﬁlings  
winding down.  Candidate withdrawals are 
part of this process that are oŌen  
overlooked and can be confusing to  
candidates, party oﬃcials, and elecƟon 
administrators. 
Vacancies ON or BEFORE Noon,  
July 15, 2022 
July 15 is the most important date for  
purposes of candidate withdrawing for the 
November elecƟon. Any candidate can 
withdraw for any reason unƟl noon, July 
15, 2022. The candidate simply ﬁles the 
CAN‐24 form with the county elecƟon 
oﬃcial (or IED, for federal, state, state 
legislaƟve, and judicial oﬃces, including 
prosecuƟng aƩorney) by this deadline and 
their name is removed from the ballot.  
It does not maƩer if this 
 candidate was 
selected to ﬁll a ballot vacancy, was  
nominated at the primary elecƟon or state 
or county convenƟon, or ﬁled a form to be 
a write‐in candidate. Again, a candidate 
needs no reason to withdraw up to noon, 
July 15, 2022. 
Should a D, R, or L candidate withdraw, 
then 
a party chair is able to ﬁll the vacancy 
not later than 30‐days aŌer the CAN‐24 
was ﬁled. The clerk does not need to give 
noƟce to the chair of the vacancy; instead, 
state law assumes the candidate is  
coordinaƟng with the poliƟcal party. 
Independent and write‐in candidates are 
not a
ble to ﬁll a ballot vacancy, but minor 
party candidates who gain ballot access by  
peƟƟon can. 
D/R party leaders follow procedures found 
in IC 
3‐13‐1, generally, to ﬁll the local 
oﬃce vacancy through direct appointment 
or caucus and use forms county oﬃcials 
are already familiar with (CAN‐29, CAN‐30, 
CAN‐31, CAN‐12). L party leaders should 
review IC 3‐13‐1‐20 for speciﬁc procedural 
details. The party chair then has unƟl 
noon, three days aŌer ﬁlling the vacancy 
to ﬁle their paperwork with the county 
elecƟon oﬃcial. 
Vacancies AFTER Noon, July 15, 2022 
AŌer noon, July 15, a candidate can only 
withdraw if they move out of the elecƟon 
district, die, are convicted of a felony, or 
ordered oﬀ the ballot by the court. 
Should this occur, then a CAN‐24 is t
 o be 
ﬁled and the ballot vacancy may be ﬁlled. 
For the D/R party, the vacancy is ﬁlled by 
caucus or direct appointment of the chair. 
With the excepƟon noted in the coming 
paragraphs, the D/R parƟes follow the 
procedures in IC 3‐13‐1, generally, and use 
the CAN‐29, CAN‐31, CAN‐30, and CAN‐12 
for a local oﬃce vacancy. An L candidate 
would withdraw using the CAN‐24, and 
their party follow procedures in IC 3‐13‐1‐
20.
Similarly, it is possible for a minor par‐
ty who gained ballot access by peƟƟon to
ﬁll a ballot vac
ancy, but an independent or
write‐in candidate cannot.
Late Ballot Vacancies 
Lastly, a ballot vacancy in the ﬁnal 30‐days 
before the elecƟon is considered a “late” 
ballot vacancy ParƟes who experience any  
vacancy occurring before October 9, or an 
“early” ballot vacancy are to follow the 
procedures in IC 3‐13‐1. Ballot vacancies 
occurring on or aŌer October 9 (that is, 
within the 30‐day window before an elec‐
Ɵon) follow the procedures under IC 3‐13‐
2, generally. 
While the party may be able to ﬁll the 
“late” ballot vacancy,  its 
possible that the 
ballot may not be reprinted, depending on 
the Ɵming.  
IC 3‐11‐3‐29.5 is 
 the guiding principle on  
whether or not a ballot is to be re‐printed. 
Further, IC 3‐12‐1‐6 notes how to tabulate 
results should a late ballot vacancy be 
ﬁlled but the ballot is not re‐printed.  
Please be in touch with our oﬃce if you 
experience a late ballot vacancy, and need 
direcƟon on next steps. 
If you would like to learn more, please 
review the blue ElecƟon A
dministrator’s 
Manual and red Candidate Guide. 
QUESTIONS OF THE MONTH 
Q. Do we have to open the same satellite early voƟng sites 
used in the May primary for the November elecƟon?
A. Yes, state law requires any “satellite” locaƟon (that is, any 
early voƟng locaƟon opened in addiƟon to the clerk’s oﬃce) 
used in the May elecƟon to be used in the November
elecƟon. In other words, at minimum your county must 
open the same satellite locaƟons for the same hours  in 
November that your county used in May. You can add more 
early voƟng sites and expand hours, either by the CEB 
unanimously agreeing to amend its vote center plan or 
passing the satellite resoluƟon, but you cannot take
locaƟons away or reduce hours. (IC 3‐11‐10‐26.3(e))
Q. Can we use the electronic adjudicaƟon features on our 
opScan voƟng systems?
A. While state law now authorizes the use of an electronic 
adjudicaƟon of scanned opƟcal scan ballots, no voƟng 
system in Indiana is currently cerƟﬁed to use this feature. 
UnƟl a system is cerƟﬁed to use this feature, it should not be 
marketed to counƟes and counƟes should not be using it.
VR CORNER 
School Board Residency & SVRS Districts 
For most school corporaƟons it is possible to create an at‐large 
district that is also divided into “districts” for purposes of creaƟng 
residenƟal “balance” on their board. This is very similar to County 
Commissioners—where there are “d istricts” to meet candidate 
qualiﬁcaƟons but all voters within the county vote for the oﬃce. 
Same idea here—the school plan may establish districts for  
purposes of candidate qualiﬁcaƟons, but all voters within the 
school corporaƟon boundaries vote on those races. 
In SVRS, the precinct key would reﬂect that the precincts within 
the school corporaƟon are assigned to that school corporaƟon, 
not the district. But, the district set‐up in SVRS should reﬂect 
which precincts make up each residenƟal district. This is helpful 
to conﬁrm which “district’ a person resides in case they want to 
run for school board, for example. 
BUT, when reviewing the CAN‐34 peƟƟon for school board, for 
most school corporaƟons, a registered voter simply needs to 
reside in the school corporaƟon boundaries. The school plan will 
provide more informaƟon about district set‐up. 
NOVEMBER BALLOT  
BUILDING REMINDERS 
1/ IED will cerƟfy a list of federal, state, and judicial  
candidates, including prosecuƟng aƩorney, to counƟes not 
later than August 26, 2022. 
2/ALL ballots MUST include a write‐in opƟon for each  
federal oﬃce (US Senate, US House in 2022), even if IED 
does not cerƟfy a declared write‐in candidate for these 
oﬃces to counƟes.  
3/ If a candidate has ﬁled a CAN‐3 to be a write‐in  
candidate for local oﬃce, then you must include a write‐in 
line for that local oﬃce only. You do NOT need to include a 
write‐in line for a local oﬃce otherwise. 
4/ DO NOT PRINT A WRITE‐IN CANDIDATE’S NAME ON 
THE BALLOT!  The write‐in line serves as a voter’s chance to 
cast a vote for a declared write‐in candidate. See IC 3‐12‐1‐
1.7 for more details on tabulaƟon. 
5/ Should a public quesƟon be cerƟﬁed to the CEB by noon, 
August 1, 2022, the public quesƟon will be the ﬁrst thing 
printed on your ballot, above the straight party secƟon. 
6/ NEW! If a school corporaƟon cerƟﬁes a public quesƟon 
to the CEB, then the CEB MUST create a ballot style that 
leaves oﬀ the public quesƟon for those precincts within the 
boundaries of the school corporaƟon. This is a result of 
recent changes in state law regarding the fail‐safe  
provisions that permit a voter who moved out of the school 
district to vote one last Ɵme in their “old” precinct for all 
candidates on the ballot, but does not permit the person to 
vote on the public quesƟon. Hence, the non‐public  
quesƟon ballot style now needed for those precincts. 
7/ Don’t forget federal only ballots! It will include straight 
party devices, candidates for US Senate, and US House  
ONLY. The ballot style is ONLY used for overseas voters who 
ﬁle the FPCA and mark “I am a US ciƟzen and my return is 
uncertain.” These voters maintain their Indiana residency in 
the county where they last lived, though are registered to 
vote at the address of your voter registraƟon oﬃce. 
8/ ALL BALLOTS used in Nov. must include the straight  
party device. At minimum, your county will display the D, L, 
and R party symbol and name. The D or R party name/
symbol will be displayed in the order on the ballot as to 
which candidate for the 2018 SOS race came in ﬁrst and 
second in the county. The L party name/device will be third. 
9/ If the county clerk is on the ballot for ANY oﬃce, then 
their signature cannot be printed on ballots and the generic 
seal must be used. All counƟes have a customized generic 
seal available on the SVRS County Portal. 
10/ The blue ElecƟon Administrator’s Manual has a chapter 
on ballot layout, including the text and proper order of the 
instrucƟons and oﬃces. Upon request, IED can review  
ballots to assist the CEB with ﬁnalizing the layout. 
QUESTIONS OF THE MONTH:  
School Board Filing Focus 
Q. Do school board candidates have to open a campaign  
ﬁnance commiƩee? 
A. Maybe. A school board candidate must open a campaign ﬁnance  
commiƩee and ﬁle required reports if and when they raise or spend more 
than $500 toward running for oﬃce. UnƟl then, there is no need to ﬁle a 
CFA‐1.  
 
Q. Who can sign a school board peƟƟon? 
A. Even though there may be a “district” to meet residency  
requirements of the candidates, in most Indiana counƟes, all  registered 
voters within the boundaries of the school corporaƟon vote on each 
school board member. (This is similar to County Commissioners.)  
Therefore, registered voters within the boundaries of the  community 
school corporaƟon would be eligible to sign the CAN‐34 peƟƟon.  
CauƟon! There are some addiƟonal requirements which apply to certain 
speciﬁc school corporaƟons listed in state law. 
 
School board informaƟon should be part of your county’s precinct key 
matrix and included in the voter’s record. If not, reach out to your GIS 
department or the school corporaƟon for a map. (Only a handful of 
school corporaƟons in Indiana are metropolitan school districts that may 
elect a school board candidate in a single member district, meaning only 
registered voters in this elecƟon district may be cerƟﬁed on a  
peƟƟon. The school’s plan will have this informaƟon.)  
 
Q. How many signatures does a school board candidate need? 
A. In nearly every school district, a candidate must have at least ten  
signatures of registered voters of the school district as cerƟﬁed by the 
county VR oﬃcial. A few school corporaƟons have a speciﬁc state laws 
requiring a diﬀerent threshold requirement, which may be in the school 
plan. PeƟƟon processing standards can be found in the purple VR  
Guidebook. 
 
Q. Does a candidate for school board need to submit mulƟple  
candidate consent forms? 
A. No. The CAN‐34 form is designed to capture the signatures of  
registered voters on the front of the form, while the back of the form 
includes the candidate’s consent. While the candidate can submit  
mulƟple CAN‐34 documents to ensure he or she has enough peƟƟon sig‐
natures, only one “back” side needs to be completed by the candidate. 
 
Q. Where is the CAN‐34 peƟƟon ﬁled? 
A. In most Indiana counƟes, the county clerk is the county’s voter  
registraƟon oﬃcial, so the CAN‐34 and CAN‐12 is ﬁled with the clerk’s 
oﬃce of the county where the greatest percentage of the populaƟon of 
the school corporaƟon is located, not later than noon, Aug. 26. 
 
In the few counƟes where the county has a separate VR board, the CAN‐
34 and CAN‐12 is ﬁled ﬁrst with the elecƟon board by noon, Aug. 26, but 
the CAN‐34 is to be forwarded to the VR Board. Only the county VR board 
can cerƟfy  the number of signatures on the peƟƟon. The cerƟﬁed  
peƟƟon is then delivered to the clerk. 
 
The clerk has a responsibility  to inform the candidate if the peƟƟon was 
approved or denied  either in person or by  cerƟﬁed mail. If denied, the 
candidate may ﬁle a CAN‐1 challenge by noon, Sept. 2 to contest the  
denied signatures.

Election Division Dispatch 
 Brad King & Angie Nussmeyer, Co-Directors | August 2022  
NEWS & UPDATES 
 
Absentee Ballot Ready Date 
All counƟes must mail (or email/fax, if applicable) absentee 
ballots to voters with approved absentee applicaƟons,  
including ABS‐VPD and the FPCA, not later than Saturday,  
September 24, 2022, or 45‐days before the date of the  
elecƟon. This date ‐ 9/24/22 ‐ is the default “issued” date in 
SVRS. However, many counƟes will begin sending absentee 
ballots ahead of the 45‐day deadline. Please submit a County 
AuthorizaƟon Form (CAF) through SVRS to request an earlier 
ballot ready date, if your county intends to send ballots out 
early. The “issued” date is an important record to maintain in 
SVRS and an accurate ballot ready date will ensure the system 
maintains the precise date the ballot was sent to the voter. 
Don’t forget that once this ﬁrst batch of absentee ballots is 
sent to voters, an absentee ballot must be sent the same date 
the applicaƟon is reviewed and approved.  
 
VSTOP Public Test Lists 
By August 26, 2022, VSTOP is to provide counƟes with a list of 
voƟng systems to pull for the public test of voƟng  
systems. Please be certain your equipment list is up to date in 
the VSTOP database! If you need assistance, please contact 
vstop@bsu.edu. CounƟes will receive one list for opScan  
systems and, if applicable, one list for DRE systems or ballot 
marking devices. For each list, the county will need to test at 
least 5% of the machines on the list, starƟng at the top and 
skipping those machines that might be in the database but not 
pulled for this elecƟon. 
 
Paper Supply Chain Updates 
CounƟes should be working closely with your vendors to     
ensure your inventory for ballot cards and other important 
paper‐based elecƟon supplies can be met for the November 
elecƟon. Ballot prooﬁng will be criƟcal in this elecƟon to limit 
ballot reprinƟngs given the strain on the paper supply chain. 
At a naƟonal conference, the co‐directors heard from supply 
chain experts that the paper shortage will persist into 2023 
and possibly 2024, so please be sure you conƟnue working 
with vendors to idenƟfy and secure inventory needs for the 
next  elecƟon cycles ‐ even while prepping for the current  
elecƟon!

InformaƟon in this newsleƩer is provided by the Indiana ElecƟon Division as a courtesy to county elecƟon administrators. If a person is unclear concerning elecƟon law provisions,  
the ElecƟon Division can serve as an interpreƟve source. However, where important legal rights are concerned, you must consult with your own aƩorney to be fully and properly advised. 
With the elecƟon just around the corner, 
county elecƟon oﬃcials are ramping up 
their absentee operaƟons. CriƟcal to its 
success are absentee voter boards. 
Each county elecƟon board must noƟfy 
the D/R county chair of the number of 
absentee voter boards needed to support 
absentee operaƟons—mail, travel board, 
and in‐person voƟng—not later than 50 ‐
days before the elecƟon, or September 
19, 2022. (IC 3‐11.5‐4‐23) 
The D/R county chairs have unƟl noon, 46‐
days before the elecƟon (Sept. 23) to ﬁle, 
in wriƟng, their nominaƟons for those 
absentee voter board posiƟons. Of course, 
CEBs can request ABS voter boards more 
than 50‐days out and county chairs can 
ﬁle nominaƟons before their noon  
deadline, but these dates are the very 
latest to make the request or nominate 
board members. 
Individuals serving as ABS voter board 
members must meet the qualiﬁcaƟons 
under IC 3‐11.5‐4‐22. A candidate to be 
voted for at the elecƟon except as an  
unopposed candidate for a city oﬃce, 
town oﬃce, township oﬃce, school board 
oﬃce, precinct commiƩeeman, or state 
convenƟon delegate may NOT be an ABS 
voter board member, unless the opposed 
candidate is assigned to work on absentee 
ballots in precincts where their name does 
not appear on the ballot.  
Family members (as deﬁned in the  
statute) of an opposed candidate may not 
be an absentee voter board member, but 
as above, can perform absentee work in 
precincts where the candidate’s name 
does not appear on the ballot.  
State law requires the CEB or the ABS  
voter board to review and approve all ABS 
applicaƟons. (IC 3‐11‐4‐17.5) AŌer the 
clerk’s oﬃce enters the apps into the 
SVRS, the D/R appointed members of the 
CEB or the ABS voter board must aﬃx 
their iniƟals to the back of the ABS ballot. 
(IC 3‐11‐4‐19) 
ABS voter boards OR the CEB also perform 
the ﬁrst absentee signature review,  
comparing the signature on the voter’s 
ABS applicaƟon against the ABS ballot 
security envelope. This work must be  
performed before ElecƟon Day and then 
the apps/ballots (sealed in the ballot  
envelope) are ﬁled by precinct in a cabi‐
net/oﬃce/receptacle with a bi‐parƟsan 
lock. The D/R CEB member or their  
designee is to maintain custody of their 
key at all Ɵmes and must make  
arrangements to be present to unlock the 
door/receptacle each day.  
Early voƟng or in‐person absentee voƟng 
is voƟng that occurs before an absentee 
voter board, much like traveling board. 
ABS voter boards are to be present during 
in‐person absentee voƟng at the clerk’s 
oﬃce or other satellite locaƟons to  
perform work like approving applicaƟons, 
checking a voter’s ID, or assisƟng voters 
with the voƟng equipment or ballot.  
AddiƟonally, the absentee voter board 
must also sign the ABS‐7 security envelope 
aŌer the voter seals their opƟcal scan bal‐
lot card inside and signs the aﬃdavit 
found on the ABS‐7. 
Traveling board is a speciﬁc funcƟon of 
the ABS voter board, where a biparƟsan 
two‐person team travels to a conﬁned 
voter, or caregiver for the conﬁned voter, 
to assist them with compleƟng a ballot or 
to bring a DRE or ballot marking device 
unit to allow the voter to vote privately 
and independently. (The DRE or BMD res‐
oluƟon has to be approved by the CEB 
ﬁrst; see IC 3‐11‐10‐26.2) 
ABS Ballot PrinƟng. Not later than 60‐
days before the elecƟon, the clerk or the 
board of elecƟons & registraƟon in Lake, 
Porter, and Tippecanoe counƟes must 
esƟmate the number of absentee ballots 
needed for the elecƟon. 
Those absentee ballots must be delivered 
not later than 50‐days before the elecƟon. 
And not later than 5‐days aŌer receiving 
the printed ballots, counƟes must begin 
mailing ABS ballots to those voters with 
approved applicaƟons. 
Using 50‐days as the rule of thumb,  
counƟes receiving their ABS ballots on day 
50 have unƟl Saturday, September 24, 
2022 (or 45‐
days before the elecƟon) to 
begin mailing ABS ballots. However, if 
your county receives ballots on day 55, 
then your deadline to begin mailing  
ballots is day 50 to comply with the “5‐
day” rule found in IC 3‐11‐4‐18(c)). More 
informaƟon can be found in the blue  
ElecƟon Administrator’s Manual.

EI-ISAC Membership 
 
The ElecƟons Infrastructure InformaƟon Sharing & Analysis Center 
(EI‐ISAC®) is a community of dedicated elecƟon oﬃcials and  
cybersecurity professionals working side‐by‐side to ensure the  
integrity of elecƟons among U.S. State, Local, Tribal, and Territorial 
(SLTT) governments. It is funded by the US Cybersecurity  
Infrastructure and Security Agency and the Center for Internet  
Security. Open to all SLTT government organizaƟons that support US 
elecƟons oﬃcials, membership is free and voluntary for eligible or‐
ganizaƟons. The co‐directors strongly encourage every county to be‐
come an EI‐ISAC member. More informaƟon, including the member‐
ship registraƟon, can be found at hƩps://www.cisecurity.org/ei‐isac 
DECLARED WRITE-IN  
CANDIDATES 
As part of the candidate cerƟﬁcaƟon IED will send to 
each county not later than noon, August 26, 2022, a list 
of declared write‐in candidates for federal, statewide, 
state legislaƟve, and judicial oﬃces,  
including prosecuƟng aƩorney. 
Write‐in candidates are NEVER printed on the  
ballot! Instead, the CEB must include a “write‐in” space  
on the ballot for each oﬃce where a person has ﬁled a 
CAN‐3 form. The one excepƟon is that a write‐in line 
MUST be included for all federal oﬃces (US Senate and 
US House), even if no declared write‐in candidate ﬁled. 
A list of write‐in candidates, which is to include those 
cerƟﬁed by IED to counƟes and those write‐in  
candidates ﬁled with the county, are to be provided to 
ElecƟon Day poll workers to assist with tallying write‐in 
votes. However, the list of write‐in candidates should 
NOT be posted inside the polling locaƟon. 
As part of canvassing aŌer the polls close, ballots or DRE 
vote total tapes are reviewed to determine if a write‐in 
candidate’s vote is to be counted. IC 3‐12‐4‐4 and IC 3‐
12‐1‐1.7 explains the procedures, which includes  
determining a voter’s intent and counƟng “write‐in” 
votes for candidates printed on the ballot. For example, 
John Smith is a D candidate for dogcatcher and printed 
on the ballot. A voter writes‐in John Smith on the  
write‐in line. The write‐in vote would be added to Mr. 
Smith’s vote total. 
QUESTIONS OF THE MONTH  
Q. Do the straight party instrucƟons go to the right of 
the party devices on the ballot? 
A. For opƟcal scan balloƟng systems and DRE voƟng  
systems, the straight party instrucƟons can go with the 
other  instrucƟons at the top OR between the public 
quesƟon (if applicable) and the straight party secƟon of 
the ballot. For opScan and DREs these instrucƟons MUST 
be printed on the ballot. CounƟes may NOT print and 
post it in the voƟng booth, for example. (IC 3‐11‐13‐11
(l), IC 3‐11‐14‐3.5(l)). 
 
Q. Do voter fail‐safes apply to absentee voters? 
A. Yes. Voter fail‐safes apply to an absentee voter in the 
same way it would apply to an ElecƟon Day voter. The 
only diﬀerence is the VRG 4/12 would be ﬁled at the 
same Ɵme as their ABS applicaƟon or during in‐person 
absentee voƟng before the voter signs an ePollbook. 
 
Q. Which county reviews the CAN‐34 (school board 
candidate peƟƟon & consent), if the school corporaƟon 
boundaries include more than one county? 
A. The candidates will ﬁle their CAN‐34 peƟƟons in the 
county with the largest populaƟon within the elecƟon 
district AND the “larger” county will review all  
signatures on the peƟƟon, even for registered voters 
not in their county. This is an excepƟon in state law that 
permits one county to cerƟfy signatures of voters in  
another county. (IC 3‐8‐2.5‐5) The “larger” county will 
then cerƟfy the  candidates for school board to the 
“smaller” county (or counƟes) ahead of the elecƟon. 
 
Q. Can a poliƟcal party ﬁll a ballot vacancy created 
when the CEB or IEC removes a candidate through the 
challenge (CAN‐1) procedures? 
A. Yes. State law was updated in 2021 to allow a ballot 
vacancy created when a challenged candidate is  
removed from the November ballot to be ﬁlled  
according to IC 3‐13‐1, generally. (Previously, the party 
could only ﬁll a ballot vacancy created when no one ran 
in the primary elecƟon such as no one ﬁling or a  
candidate removed through challenge but could not ﬁll 
the ballot vacancy post‐primary when a challenged  
candidate was removed.) See IC 3‐13‐1‐7(b).  
NOTE: An Independent candidate is not a member of a 
poliƟcal party; therefore, a ballot vacancy created by a 
successful candidate challenge cannot be ﬁlled by  
another Independent.

Election Division Dispatch 
 Brad King & Angie Nussmeyer, Co-Directors | September 2022  
NEWS & UPDATES 
 
ABS Ballot Delivery Deadline 
All voters with a reviewed and approved ABS‐Mail or ABS‐VPD 
app or FPCA must have their ballot sent to them not later than 
Sept. 24, 2022 pursuant to federal and state law. This is the 45‐
day cut‐oﬀ for sending ballots to comply with the Military & 
Overseas Voter Empowerment (MOVE) Act. The default ballot 
ready date in SVRS is Sept. 24. If you plan to send your ballots 
out earlier, please submit a CAF in SVRS to request a new date.  
 
Please be certain your county is adhering to this deadline. The 
US Department of JusƟce asks our agency to track ballot sent 
dates to ensure compliance with federal law. If ballots are sent 
late, you may be contacted by their oﬃce. A reminder that 
aŌer you make your iniƟal push to send ABS ballots, state law 
requires you to send a ballot to a voter on the same date the 
app is reviewed and approved. 
 
Early VoƟng & ElecƟon Day Site Updates 
Visitors to Indianavoters.com rely on informaƟon pulled from 
SVRS as entered by each county. If your county has ﬁnalized its 
plans for early voƟng or elecƟon day sites please make sure 
your county’s voƟng info in SVRS is updated as soon as  
possible. Later this month and into October, this data will be 
shared with our partner, Democracy Works, to display on 
geƩothepolls.com. This will increase the reach of our state’s 
voƟng informaƟon, so accurate data in SVRS is criƟcal.  
 
Scanned ABS ApplicaƟons from IED 
Beginning Sept. 26, 2022, IED will begin scanning ABS apps  
received by our oﬃce and upload them to your county’s folder 
in the IED PosƟngs secƟon of the INSVRS County Portal.  
CounƟes may download and print these requests to process 
more quickly, or wait for the hard copies to arrive by mail. 
 
New CISA Toolkit 
 
CISA has released “ProtecƟng U.S. ElecƟons: A CISA  
Cybersecurity Toolkit”, a catalog of free services and tools for 
state and local elecƟon oﬃcials. The toolkit is organized into 
broad categories: 
1. Assess risk using an Elec Ɵon Security Risk Proﬁle Tool de‐
veloped by CISA and the U.S. EAC; and  
2. Find tools related to protec Ɵng voter informaƟon, web‐
sites, email systems, and networks; and protect assets 
against phishing, ransomware, and distributed denial‐of‐
services (DDoS) aƩacks.
