InformaƟon in this newsleƩer is provided by the Indiana ElecƟon Division as a courtesy to county elecƟon administrators. If a person is unclear concerning elecƟon law provisions,  
the ElecƟon Division can serve as an interpreƟve source. However, where important legal rights are concerned, you must consult with your own aƩorney to be fully and properly advised. 
In Indiana, “elecƟoneering” is deﬁned as 
expressing support or opposiƟon to any 
candidate or poliƟcal party or expressing 
approval or disapproval of any public 
quesƟon in any manner that could  
reasonably be expected to convey that 
support or opposiƟon to another person. 
This would include the wearing of  
clothing, buƩons, or displaying signs, etc. 
that states the name of any poliƟcal party 
or includes the name, picture, photo, or 
other likeness of any candidate or current‐
ly elected federal, state, county, or local 
oﬃcial in spaces where this speech is cur‐
tailed. (IC 3‐14‐3‐16) 
Our state law speciﬁcally requires that the 
candidate be clearly idenƟﬁed. Therefore, 
slogans like “I’m with her” would not be 
considered elecƟoneering but “Sam Smith 
for Dogcatcher” would be. 
However, the elecƟoneering statute does 
not prevent a voter from receiving  
informaƟon about a candidate or public 
quesƟon or bringing in material with  
informaƟon about a candidate/PQ to  
assist them with voƟng. 
While poll workers or absentee voter 
boards, for example, would be within their 
rights to ask the voter to remove the 
clothing or cover it up, the voter follow 
that request to do so and may vote a regu‐
lar ballot if otherwise qualiﬁed to do so.  
BUT, elecƟon workers are within their 
rights to forward the issue of  
elecƟoneering to the CEB or the county 
prosecutor for violaƟng state law. 
Before ElecƟon Day “ElecƟoneering”  
cannot occur in the space where in‐person 
absentee voƟng is taking place or the 
“chute,” which is 50‐feet from the en‐
trance to the clerk’s oﬃce or satellite  
locaƟon. This is new state law, which was 
ﬁrst used in May 2022.  
AddiƟonally, the county commissioners 
would control whether yard signs can be 
posted on the courthouse lawn. This is a 
ﬁrst amendment issue, with an all or none 
approach. The Commissioners should  
consult their county aƩorney on this 
maƩer.  
No person can “elecƟoneer” to an  
absentee voter while the voter is  
compleƟng their vote‐by‐mail ballot, but 
there is an excepƟon for the person’s 
spouse or member of the voter’s  
household in state law. 
On ElecƟon Day No elecƟoneering can 
occur within the “chute” or inside the 
voƟng area. The chute is deﬁned in IC 3‐5‐
2‐10 as the 50 foot area leading to the 
entrance to where voƟng occurs. 
Unlike “early” voƟng, similar limitaƟons 
are not placed on yard signs unless the 
sign is placed within the “chute” or inside 
the polls. 
More informaƟon about yard signs can be 
found in the “Disclaimers” brochure found 
on in.gov/sos/elecƟons in the ElecƟon 
Administrator’s Portal, under the ElecƟon 
Reference Materials heading. 
IN FOCUS: ELECTIONEERING REMINDERS 
VR CORNER 
 
Forwarding Voter RegistraƟons 
A voter may ﬁle state and federal voter registraƟon 
forms or an FPCA in a county where the voter doesn’t 
reside. If that occurs, county voter registraƟon oﬃcials 
must forward the VR document to the appropriate 
county.  
 
The forwarding county is able to email the document to 
the correct county, but the hard copy must be sent to 
the correct county regardless. (IC 3‐7‐34‐9) AddiƟonally, 
IED can receive voter registraƟon forms from any  
person, and our oﬃce will forward them to the  
appropriate county.  
 
Timely Voter RegistraƟons 
A reminder that any Ɵmely voter registraƟon form  
received by IED will be sent with a “Ɵmely” memo as 
we near the statewide VR deadline. A “Ɵmely” VR form 
is either hand‐delivered by the registraƟon deadline, or  
mailed and postmarked on or before October 11, 2022.  
 
Remember, if the postmark is missing or illegible, then 
those registraƟons can be processed up to and  
including Monday, October 17, 2022. A legible  
postmark date on or before October 11 must be  
processed for the November elecƟon.  
Suggestions, Fixes & Updates 
While many elecƟon and VR procedures are changed 
through legislaƟon, IED relies on county users to idenƟfy 
correcƟons in SVRS or request changes to further enhance 
workﬂows. Here is how to use the two diﬀerent request 
form types in the SVRS module: 
 
County AuthorizaƟon Form (CAF). These are made 
through SVRS to allow county users to request and  
authorize changes to the database by state or system 
users. For example, making changes to a precinct key or 
puƫng an end date on a registraƟon when records were 
not merged correctly . 
 
Request for Service Enhancement (RSE). Similar to a CAF 
(and in the same module), an RSE allows a county user to 
suggest an improvement to SVRS. This could be a request 
to eliminate a step in processing a record, for example, or 
a suggesƟon for a new report. 
 
SVRS is used to track these requests to help us keep beƩer 
records and ensure items are being acted upon. Before, the 
CAF would come by email, fax, or mail. Centralizing the 
process gives visibility to state and county users. 
 
If a county user has a suggesƟon to improve a form, send a 
note to elecƟons@iec.in.gov. Forms are generally updated 
once a year before the next elecƟon cycle, so suggesƟons 
may wait to be considered by the IED Co‐Directors. 
QUESTIONS OF THE MONTH  
Q. What is the retenƟon policy for elecƟon materials? 
A. Federal and state law set forth a 22‐month retenƟon policy 
for all elecƟon materials. (IC 3‐10‐1‐31.1) Once the 22‐month 
period ends, counƟes may move forward with their standard 
procedures to have those records destroyed. These laws set 
forth the minimum retenƟon policy. A county can hold on to 
elecƟon materials longer, but cannot  move to destroy them 
any earlier. Please note: elecƟon materials are managed on a 
diﬀerent retenƟon policy than voter registraƟon records or 
elecƟon results, for example. The purple VR guidebook and 
blue ElecƟon Admin manual include more informaƟon about 
records retenƟon speciﬁc to each type. 
Q. Do I need to include candidate names and address 
on the CAN‐39 legal noƟce of elecƟon? 
A. No. Unlike the primary elecƟon, a county is not  
required to print the names & addresses of candidates on the 
CAN‐39. Instead, the noƟce only needs the names of the  
oﬃces and public quesƟons in addiƟon to early voƟng dates, 
Ɵmes, and locaƟons. CounƟes can generate the CAN‐39 in 
SVRS or create their own using the paper form. (For CD02 
special elecƟon counƟes, you will have a separate CAN‐60 for 
the special elecƟon only and in this case, must include  
candidate names and addresses on it.) A reminder: the  
CAN‐39 publicaƟon deadline was pushed to 21‐days before 
the elecƟon, or October 18, 2022. The CAN‐39 must also be 
discussed at a CEB meeƟng for purposes of recording it in the 
meeƟng minutes, so please be sure it is included on a future 
agenda. (IC 3‐10‐2‐2) 
Q. Can the ABS‐Mail app be modiﬁed by a printer to 
remove the party selecƟon for the primary elecƟon? 
A. Yes. The IED forms order includes a note that an ABS‐Mail 
form can be modiﬁed to remove the “party choice” secƟon on 
the applicaƟon and renumber the form secƟons. CounƟes 
may see the modiﬁed forms that exclude secƟon 3 and go 
from mailing address in secƟon 2 to the reasons box in #4. 
AddiƟonally, the forms order permits the ABS‐Mail app to be 
printed in portrait or landscape, even though the app is  
currently conﬁgured in portrait style. 
Q. Can I auto‐acƟvate pending registraƟons in batch 
before the elecƟon? 
A. To move forward with auto‐acƟvaƟng pending  
registraƟons, you must ﬁrst complete the auto‐acƟvate  
request document found on the INSVRS County Portal and 
aƩach it to your County AuthorizaƟon Request  (CAF) ﬁled 
through INSVRS. Signing this document acknowledges your 
county understands the state’s policy relaƟng to acƟvaƟng 
registraƟons in a batch seƫng. Once approved, county users 
may move forward with the batch processing. The Help Desk 
will be able to assist you with the batch process, if help is 
needed. 
“Late” Ballot Vacancies 
Occasionally there will be instances where a candidate must 
withdraw as a candidate from an elecƟon due to a felony  
convicƟon, a move out of the elecƟon district, or the candidate 
dies. Any vacancy occurring on or before October 9, 2022, is 
considered an “early” vacancy (even though this may seem 
late in the  elecƟon season to elecƟon administrators). For 
“early” vacancies, the parƟes follow IC 3‐13‐1, generally, to ﬁll 
those ballot vacancies through caucus or, if the county party 
has  authorized it or there is only one eligible PC to vote in the  
caucus, by direct appointment. 
 
However, “late” ballot vacancy procedures found in IC 3‐13‐2, 
generally, are followed for any ballot vacancy occurring on or 
aŌer October 10, 2022. The procedures to ﬁll a “late”  ballot 
vacancy are streamlined to allow for direct appointment in 
some cases. Please be sure you and the appropriate county 
chair review IC 3‐13‐2, if a vacancy occurs during the ﬁnal 30‐
days leading up to the elecƟon. The blue ElecƟon  
Administrator’s Manual  goes into more detail on the forms 
used for ﬁling with the clerk (or IED, if it’s a state or federal 
oﬃce). 
 
Ballot Re-Printing? 
Despite all the hours and eyes on ballot proofs, mistakes  
happen. In this scenario of a defecƟve ballot due to error or 
omission, the CEB can choose to 1/ reprint the ballot OR 2/ 
hold a hearing to determine if ballot re‐prinƟng is necessary. 
(IC 3‐11‐2‐16)  
 
Before the hearing, the CEB must noƟfy the party(ies) or  
candidate(s) who may have an interest in the maƩer. At the 
hearing, the CEB must discuss the number of ballots, if any, 
containing the error or omission that have been cast; the cost 
of correcƟng the error; whether the error would cause  
confusion or mistakes by the voter; and whether any voter 
objects to using the ballot. 
 
If no voter objects, in wriƟng, to using the defecƟve ballot AND 
the CEB determines that the error or omission will not cause 
confusion, then the defecƟve ballots may conƟnue to be used.  
 
However, if any voter objects, in wriƟng, to using a defecƟve 
ballot OR the CEB determines the error or omission will create 
confusion, then new ballots shall be printed.  
 
AlternaƟvely, a candidate may pass away aŌer the ballot is 
printed. In this scenario, the procedures in IC 3‐11‐3‐29.5  
apply. The CEB must re‐print ballots unless 1/ the party ﬁlls the 
ballot vacancy within the ﬁnal ﬁve days before the elecƟon OR 
2/ the candidate dies and noƟce of the death is received aŌer 
noon, the ﬁnal seven days before the elecƟon. The CEB can 
also unanimously agree a candidate has died without noƟce 
and re‐print the ballot.  
 
If the ballot is found to be defecƟve, absentee voters must ﬁle 
an ABS‐5 to have an absentee ballot reissued. While there is no 
requirement for the CEB to proacƟvely send the ABS‐5, the 
CEB could choose to send uniform noƟce to impacted voters.

Election Division Dispatch 
 Brad King & Angie Nussmeyer, Co-Directors | October 2022  
NEWS & UPDATES 
 
Fall Build 
Several improvements were made to indianaovters.com and 
SVRS in our recent Fall Build. Training covering those  
improvements will be held in October, and you can ﬁnd the 
Build Notes being covered at training on the INSVRS County 
Portal. 
 
CFA‐11 Supplemental ReporƟng Period 
The large contribuƟon supplemental reporƟng period begins 
October 15 and ends 6AM on November 6, 2022. During this 
window, any candidate on the ballot receiving a contribuƟon 
totaling $1000 or more from a single source must ﬁle the CFA‐
11 not later than 48‐hours aŌer receipt. This contribuƟon can 
be given in one lump sum or be an aggregate about from the 
single donor during this period. Remember, loans to the com‐
miƩee and in‐kind contribuƟons count! 
 
For example, Sally gives Tom’s commiƩee a $1000 contribuƟon 
on Oct. 16. Tom then must ﬁle a CFA‐11 within 48‐hours of 
receiving the contribuƟon. Ron gives Tom’s commiƩee a $300 
contribuƟon on Oct. 19 and gives $800 on Nov. 1. Because Ron 
gave $1300 between October 15 and November 6, Tom must 
ﬁle a CFA‐11 disclosing both contribuƟons within 48‐hours of 
receiving the $800 check. More informaƟon can be found in 
the 2022 Indiana Campaign Finance Manual. 
 
Accessible ABS‐VPD Forms 
Last month, IED made available to counƟes an accessible write‐
in absentee ballot (AWB) for voters with print disabiliƟes re‐
quesƟng an emailed ballot. As you know, a voter with print 
disabiliƟes is a person with temporary or permanent blindness, 
low vision, or a physical disability that impairs their ability to 
mark their ballot. The AWB works with screen reader technolo‐
gy to allow voters to vote privately and independently at 
home. 
 
A reminder that all emailed ballots are secured in the ABS‐10 
envelope, using the ABS‐10B checkbox in SVRS to create a label 
to aﬃx to the envelope to assist with sorƟng and storage by 
precinct. The ABS‐25 secrecy waiver must also be returned by 
6PM on ElecƟon Day and aƩached to the ABS‐10 envelope. 
Emailed ballots are then remade by bi‐parƟsan teams on Elec‐
Ɵon Day on ballot cards, being certain to serialize the emailed 
copy and the ballot card with the same number in case a  
recount is ﬁled and the remake team’s work needs is reviewed.

InformaƟon in this newsleƩer is provided by the Indiana ElecƟon Division as a courtesy to county elecƟon administrators. If a person is unclear concerning elecƟon law provisions,  
the ElecƟon Division can serve as an interpreƟve source. However, where important legal rights are concerned, you must consult with your own aƩorney to be fully and properly advised. 
In Indiana, candidates must ﬁle a CAN‐3 
declaraƟon to be an “oﬃcial” write‐in  
candidate. While write‐in candidates are 
never printed on the ballot and not posted 
in the polling place, the CAN‐3 must be 
ﬁled in order for the CEB to tabulate votes 
for the write‐in candidate during post‐
elecƟon canvassing. 
A write‐in line is added to the ballot for 
those oﬃces where a write‐in candidate 
has ﬁled. In addiƟon, federal law requires 
a write‐in line to be added to all federal 
oﬃces (US President, US House, US Sen‐
ate), even if no CAN‐3 was ﬁled. 
If a write‐in line is oﬀered in the race, a 
voter will make their voƟng mark and  
indicate their choice on the ballot card or 
it is hand‐keyed into the MicroVote DRE 
system. AŌer ElecƟon Day, the CEB will 
review the totals tapes generated by the 
individual voƟng system units and are  
encouraged to compare those totals to the 
report generated from the main elecƟon 
management system soŌware. 
Some voƟng systems include the names of 
the write‐in votes cast on the ballot;  
others simply include a total vote count 
any Ɵme the write‐in box was used. 
CEBs or the bi‐parƟsan write‐in team will 
need to review the ballot cards or totals 
tapes for those precincts where a write
‐in 
candidate is indicated. Then, the team will 
need to evaluate whether the person is a 
declared write‐in candidate OR a  
candidate that ﬁled for the oﬃce and was 
wriƩen in. 
For example, Donald Duck ﬁled a CAN‐3 to 
run for dogcatcher. His name is not on the 
ballot but a voter wrote his name in for 
the oﬃce, so Donald Duck gets a vote  
tallied for him. Goofy ﬁled a CAN‐2 and 
appears on the ballot for dogcatcher.  
Rather than marking Goofy’s name on the 
ballot, a voter wrote in his name. The CEB 
will count a vote for Goofy. 
State law provides guidance on  
determining when a write‐in candidate’s 
voted is counted. Generally, the CEB or the 
write‐in team will have to ascertain the 
voter’s intent when wriƟng in a  
candidate’s name. This usually means the 
name does not have to be spelled  
perfectly, BUT this is at the discreƟon of 
the individuals reviewing the ballot  
materials. For example, Mickey Mouse is a 
write‐in candidate for dog catcher. The 
voter writes in Mick Mouse. This write‐in 
vote is likely to be counted for Mickey 
Mouse if the CEB ﬁnds this was the voter’s 
intent. 
If your voƟng system includes an  
approved electronic adjudicaƟon feature 
in the system’s EMS then you can use the 
feature to assist in determining what a 
voter provide on a write‐in voƟng line and 
if the is a vote for a candidate either on 
the ballot or ﬁled as DECLARED write‐in 
candidate. (IC3‐11‐15‐13.8) 
Once counƟes complete their canvass, it is 
vitally important to make sure your  
precinct level results are adjusted and  
correctly reﬂect vote totals. Please conﬁrm 
totals posted to SVRS are updated so that 
the statements of votes cast align with 
your precinct elec
Ɵon results ﬁled with the 
state. 
IN FOCUS: TABULATING VOTES CAST FOR WRITE-IN CANDIDATES 
VR CORNER 
 
Incomplete RegistraƟons 
With the VR deadline on the horizon, counƟes will likely have 
incomplete registraƟons to address aŌer the VR deadline of 
Oct. 11. CounƟes are required to make an aƩempt to contact 
the voter to noƟfy them of the issue with the registraƟon  
request. Below are the steps to take to cure or reject the  
registraƟon. 
 
Missing Age/CiƟzenship QuesƟons 
If a voter failed to answer the aƩestaƟon quesƟons, then the 
voter has unƟl Oct.11 to ﬁle a wriƩen statement under  
penalƟes of perjury that they will be 18 on or before ElecƟon 
Day and are a US ciƟzen. This also can be done by ﬁling a new 
registraƟon form. If the voter did not ﬁx this issue, then the 
incompletes are rejected immediately following the  
registraƟon deadline (or October 12, 2022). (IC 3‐7‐34‐3(a)) 
 
Other Incomplete Fields 
All other incompletes are rejected not later than 10‐days  
before the elecƟon, aŌer a list of names of those with an  
incomplete registraƟon are provided to the CEB. (IC 3‐7‐34‐4
(b)) However, the voter does have unƟl ten days before the 
elecƟon to correct the missing informaƟon. Please see the 
FAQ secƟon of the purple VR Guidebook for more details on 
how this informaƟon can be provided. 
ABS-5 & PRE-5 
 
SomeƟmes a voter’s absentee ballot does not arrive or the voter 
changes their mind about voƟng by mail or the county corrects a 
ballot defect. Below are the common reasons BEFORE elecƟon 
day to use the ABS‐5 or ON elecƟon day using the PRE‐5. 
 
If a voter DOES NOT receive their absentee ballot, then the voter 
would complete and ﬁle the ABS‐5 for the county to reissue the 
absentee. OR, on ElecƟon Day, the voter would complete the PRE
‐5 form and be issued a regular ballot, if otherwise qualiﬁed. 
 
If a voter DOES receive their absentee but would prefer to vote in 
person during early voƟng, then the voter must surrender their 
original ballot, complete the ABS‐5, and a replacement ballot can 
be issued. OR, on ElecƟon Day, the voter can surrender their  
absentee to the Inspector and be issued a regular ballot, if  
otherwise qualiﬁed. 
 
Should a voter spoil their absentee ballot or the county ﬁnds an 
error and the original ballot is “defecƟve,” then the voter  
completes and ﬁles the ABS‐5 and a replacement ballot can be 
issued. However, on ElecƟon Day, the voter would need to bring 
in their defecƟve ballot to surrender their ballot to the Inspector 
and then a regular ballot would be issued. 
 
More details about the forms and their related processes are 
found in the blue ElecƟon Administrators’ Manual. 
QUESTIONS OF THE MONTH  
Q. Can an absentee ballot that is requested to be sent by 
email or fax be remade on a DRE machine? 
A. No. State law requires that an absentee ballot that is returned 
by fax or email be remade ON ElecƟon Day using a opƟcal scan 
ballot card designated for the voter’s precinct. A bi‐parƟsan  
remake team with determine the voter’s intent and mark the 
ballot card with the voter’s choice. It is important the team add 
a serial number to the faxed/emailed ballot and apply the same 
serial number to the ballot card in an area where the tabulator 
will not pick up stray marks. The serial number should in no way 
idenƟfy the voter, and is used in the event of a recount to match 
the voter’s original emailed or faxed ballot against the remade 
ballot card.  
Note: Only voters with print disabiliƟes using the ABS‐VPD form 
or military and overseas voters using the FPCA are enƟtled to 
receive an absentee ballot by email or fax. 
Q. Does Indiana have an automaƟc recount if elecƟons 
are close?  
A. No. A candidate or county party chair can ﬁle a recount aŌer 
the elecƟon. The deadline for a candidate to ﬁle a recount  is 
noon, Nov. 22, 2022; the deadline for a county chair to do so is 
Monday, Nov. 28, 2022. The person ﬁling the liƟgaƟon would 
need to pay the court ﬁling cost and the required bond amount, 
which is at least $100. For races separated by 1% or less of the 
total vote, the ﬁrst ten precincts are covered by the $100 bond 
and any addiƟonal precinct over the ﬁrst ten adds another $10 
per precinct to the bond fee. If the races are separated by more 
than 1%, the ﬁrst ten precincts are covered by the $100 bond 
and addiƟonal precincts are $100 per precinct. More  
informaƟon can be found in the 2022 ElecƟon Administrator’s 
Manual or in IC 3‐12‐6 for local recounts. 
Q. Can anyone be a challenger on ElecƟon Day?  
A. No. State law is clear that a poliƟcal party with a candidate on 
the ballot or an independent candidate on the ballot in the  
precinct may appoint challengers to ElecƟon Day voƟng  
locaƟons where the party or independent candidate appears, 
which can challenge a voter’s residency before the voter checks 
into the poll list. Otherwise, there is no state law that allows for 
another voter or watcher to make a challenge. The challengers 
must have credenƟals issued by the   
Q. Can media watchers really ﬁlm or take photos in a  
polling place? 
A. Yes, but they cannot do so in a way that would reveal how a 
voter voted. Remember, only a newspaper of general circulaƟon 
in the county where an elecƟon is held; a new service operaƟng 
in the county where an elecƟon is held; or a radio or tv staƟon 
operaƟng in the county where an elecƟon is held may appoint 
watchers. The media watcher must have a credenƟal, in wriƟng, 
that states the person is an appointed watcher, the name of the 
individual, and the person that appointed the watcher. 
Watchers 
Watchers are individuals appointed by the D, R, & L parƟes to 
observe, and NOT interfere in, certain elecƟon processes.  
Indiana state law authorizes party watchers for: 
Early In‐Person Absentee VoƟng. The county chair may 
have up to two people designated as watchers at each 
early voƟng locaƟon, including the clerk’s oﬃce and satel‐
lite voƟng locaƟons. 
Central Count of Absentee Ballots on ElecƟon Day. The 
county chair may have one watcher for each central count 
team reviewing absentee ballots. 
ElecƟon Day: Non‐Vote Center LocaƟons. In this instance, 
the state AND county chairs can have one watcher for 
each precinct in the county. 
ElecƟon Day: Vote Center LocaƟons. In this instance, the 
state AND county chairs can have one watcher for each 
ePollbook deployed to each vote center or the number of 
ePollbooks to be sent to each locaƟon according to their 
vote center plan, whichever is greater. 
On ElecƟon Day, a party watcher can enter the polling locaƟon 
as early as 5:30AM and stay un
Ɵl the work is complete aŌer 
the polls close. A watcher may come and go from the site as 
they please. The watcher may also ask for a copy of the totals 
tape that is printed from the voƟng system as part of the clos‐
ing procedures. The watcher can also follow the Inspector and 
Judge of the opposite poliƟcal party to ensure materials are 
turned in to the county elecƟon board. 
Party watchers MUST have, in wriƟng, a credenƟal from their 
chair that includes: the status of individual as an appointed 
watcher; watcher’s name; name of the county (or state) chair; 
and the name of the poliƟcal party. (IC 3‐6‐8‐3) There is no 
requirement for the chair to ﬁle their list with the CEB or clerk 
ahead of ElecƟon Day. 
Poll workers or absentee voter boards at early voƟng sites, or 
central count teams can request the watcher show their  
credenƟals. If the watcher does not have the proper  
credenƟal, then they must leave the polling locaƟon. 
There is no mechanism in state law to allow Independents or 
for local oﬃce to have watchers in the November elecƟon. 
However, the county elecƟon board may issue watcher  
credenƟals to watchers for school board candidates as noted 
in IC 3‐6‐9. AddiƟonally, media watchers are permiƩed under 
IC 3‐6‐10.  
Only voters in the act of voƟng, a county chair or vice chair 
with credenƟals from the CEB, and certain individuals such as 
the CEB members, watchers, challengers, poll book holders, or 
children accompanying a voter are authorized to be in a voƟng 
locaƟon. (IC 3‐11‐8‐15) 
Any unauthorized person entering the chute or voƟng area on 
Elec
Ɵon Day or during early voƟng must not be permiƩed to 
stay. CEB members should train their poll workers on this topic 
and ask that they contact the CEB immediately if there are 
issues. The 2022 ElecƟon Day Handbook also covers this  
subject area.

Election Division Dispatch 
 Brad King & Angie Nussmeyer, Co-Directors | November 2022  
NEWS & UPDATES 
 
Provisional Ballot SVRS Module Updates 
In October changes were made to SVRS to comply with  
changes to state law informing voters when the provisional 
ballot hearing is scheduled through a portal part on indianavot-
ers.com. Those changes were reviewed during the Hoƞix/Build 
training last month. CounƟes are encouraged to review these 
training materials regarding this new requirements to enter 
provisional balloƟng informaƟon into SVRS. IED is working with 
Civix to schedule a separate training on this topic to review 
again with counƟes ahead of ElecƟon Day. 
 
ENR Summary or Precinct Results SelecƟon Deadline 
CounƟes have the opƟon to enter summary level results or 
precinct level results (by hand or through upload) in SVRS, 
which is then used to display elecƟon results at  
indianavoters.com/elecƟonresults and also is used to populate 
data in the statements of votes cast used to cerƟfy the  
elecƟon. Please make sure your county’s preference is toggled 
to the method of reporƟng your county wants to use not later 
than 6PM (ET), Mon., Nov. 7, 2022. In order to avoid impacts 
with reporƟng, this toggle cannot be used aŌer this deadline to 
switch to the other method. 
 
ElecƟon CerƟﬁcaƟon  
Your county elecƟon board must process any provisional  
ballots or late arriving overseas ballots by 3PM (local Ɵme), Fri., 
Nov. 18, 2022. Please be certain your elecƟon results in SVRS 
are updated to reﬂect these changes! The CEB will then submit 
the canvassed results in SVRS using the CEB series of forms 
(except the CEB-9) not later than noon, Mon., Nov. 21, 2022. 
The CEB-9, SecƟon I along with the county’s precinct level  
results are to be ﬁled in SVRS not later than noon, Tues., Nov. 
22, 2022. Training materials on ﬁnalizing your elecƟon results 
reporƟng can be found on the INSVRS County Portal. The  
CEB-9, SecƟon II reporƟng is due by December 16, 2022, which 
is informaƟon needed to complete the state’s EAVS survey that 
is used in a report to the U.S. Congress. 
 
BMV Open on ElecƟon Eve & ElecƟon Day 
State law requires BMV branches that issue credenƟals like 
driver’s licenses or state ID cards to be open from 8:30A to 8P, 
local prevailing Ɵme, Mon., Nov. 7, 2022, and from 6A to 6P, 
local prevailing Ɵme, Tues., Nov. 8, 2022, to assist individuals in 
geƫng ID required to vote. As a reminder, state law requires a 
photo ID to include a photo of the voter, be issued by the state 
or federal government, be current or expired since 11/3/20, 
and include the voter’s name that conforms (not necessarily be 
exact!) to their registraƟon record. (IC 3-5-2-40.5)  Further, an 
address on a state ID does not need to match the person’s  
registraƟon record. ExcepƟons exist for military and veterans’ 
IDs and IDs issued by NaƟve American tribes recognized by the 
U.S. Government and state of Indiana.

InformaƟon in this newsleƩer is provided by the Indiana ElecƟon Division as a courtesy to county elecƟon administrators. If a person is unclear concerning elecƟon law provisions,  
the ElecƟon Division can serve as an interpreƟve source. However, where important legal rights are concerned, you must consult with your own aƩorney to be fully and properly advised. 
Military and overseas voters are permiƩed 
to use the Federal Post Card ApplicaƟon 
(FPCA), which aﬀords extra protecƟons to 
our men and women in the military, their 
spouses and dependents, and US ciƟzens 
living abroad. 
When using the FPCA, a military or over-
seas voter can register or update their 
registraƟon as late as eight (8) days before 
the elecƟon, or Monday, October 31, 
2022. These voters can also request a 
faxed or emailed ballot by ﬁling their FPCA 
as late as noon, November 7, 2022, or  
receive a mailed ballot if the FPCA was 
ﬁled on or before October 27, 2022. 
A faxed or emailed ballot must be received 
by the county elecƟon board not later than 
6PM on ElecƟon Day, November 8, 2022. 
(Remember, state law has changed the 
noon deadline to receive absentees to 
6PM when the polls close!) 
For overseas military and overseas voters 
ONLY, a mailed absentee ballot can be 
postmarked on or before Nov. 8, 2022, 
and received as late as noon, Nov. 18, 
2022, and be counted in the elecƟon, if the 
voter is otherwise eligible. (Note: for all 
other absentee voters, the absentee-by-
mail ballot must be received not later than 
6PM on ElecƟon Day, November 8, 2022.) 
Since overseas mail and internet connec-
Ɵvity is not always reliable, military and 
overseas voters that ﬁled an FPCA with the 
county can also ﬁle the Federal Write-In 
Absentee Ballot (FWAB) to serve as the 
voter’s “back-up” ballot in case their  
original absentee ballot sent by mail, fax, 
or email does not arrive by the deadlines 
noted above. 
To be clear, a military and overseas voter 
cannot simply ﬁle a FWAB with the county 
to have the write-in ballot count. The  
voter must also have an FPCA on ﬁle. This 
can be confusing to voters since the ﬁrst 
page of the FPCA and the FWAB look very 
similar.  
If you have a military or overseas voter 
that has simply ﬁled the FWAB with your 
oﬃce, it is recommended to reach out to 
the voter to make them aware of the FPCA 
requirement. If the FPCA ﬁling deadline 
has not passed, then the FPCA can be  
processed and an absentee ballot issued to 
the voter. And then the FWAB can be ﬁled 
as a precauƟon in case the original  
absentee ballot is not returned. 
If the military or overseas voter’s original 
absentee ballot is NOT received by the 
appropriate deadline (6P on ElecƟon Day 
for faxed/emailed ballots or noon, Nov. 18, 
if ballot mailed and postmarked by Nov. 8, 
2022 for an overseas or overseas military 
voter), then the CEB should conﬁrm 
whether the voter ﬁled a FWAB.  
If the voter ﬁled a FWAB for this elecƟon, 
then a bi-parƟsan remake team will  
determine the voter’s intent from the 
FWAB and transcribe the voter’s choices 
on an opƟcal scan ballot card. Keep in 
mind that the voter does not have to spell 
the candidate’s name correctly, or can 
simply write the poliƟcal party the voter is 
choosing for their enƟre ballot or in one 
speciﬁc contest. (IC 3-12-1-19) 
The 2022 Military & Overseas Voter’s 
Handbook has more informaƟon about the 
FWAB.

VR CORNER 
 
Voter Fail‐Safe: When & Where Voter Moved Analysis 
Indiana elecƟon law has a number of fail-safes to assist voters in several scenarios. The 
most common is a voter forgeƫng to update a registraƟon when they move. For the Nov. 
2022 elecƟon, a voter can move anywhere in Indiana and vote one last Ɵme in their old 
precinct but ONLY IF the move occurred on or aŌer Oct. 10, 2022.  
 
If the voter moved on or before Oct. 9, 2022, then more detailed analysis is required. Only 
voters that move within the same county (and in a few counƟes, the same Congressional 
district, too) are eligible to go back to their old precinct one last Ɵme to vote.  
 
For example, a voter moved from Randolph County to Wayne County on Sept. 1, 2022 and 
did not update their registraƟon to Wayne County. In this scenario, the voter would not be 
able to go back to Randolph County to vote one last Ɵme in their former county and 
should be given a VR form to complete.  But, if the voter moved on Oct. 15 to Wayne 
County, then the voter would be enƟtled to vote one last Ɵme in Randolph County be-
cause the move happened on or aŌer Oct. 10. This is why the “when” is important to ask 
the voter to determine which fail safe applies. 
 
Lastly, a voter can move within their precinct or change their name and capture that move 
or name change on the paper poll list or on a VRG-4/12 in ePB counƟes. “When” the move 
happened within the precinct or name change is not relevant here. The 2022 VR Guide-
book and the 2022 ElecƟon Day Handbook have more informaƟon about voter fail-safes, 
including a chart to help navigate the work ﬂow on the “when” and “where” analysis. Both 
books also discuss voter cancellaƟons, BMV errors, and other clerical-type errors and how 
to troubleshoot to assist the voter.

QUESTIONS OF THE MONTH  
Q. How should we manage voters who asked for an absen‐
tee ballot and now want to vote on ElecƟon Day? 
A. Because all voters who asked for an absentee are to be 
ﬂagged in the poll list, there are a couple of paths for the  
voter & CEB to address issues where an absentee voter ap-
pears in person at the polls: 
1/ Complete the PRE-5 ONLY if the voter’s absentee ballot 
was mailed and not received by the voter. AŌer compleƟng 
the PRE-5, the voter votes a regular ballot if otherwise quali-
ﬁed. 
2/ Before signing the poll list, voter surrenders their absentee 
ballot to the Inspector, who cancels it and issues a regular 
ballot to the voter, if otherwise qualiﬁed. 
3/ Before signing the poll list, voter discloses they forgot their 
ballot or it was lost at home. Voter can go to CEB before 5P 
to request an ABS-21, which will allow them to vote at their 
polling locaƟon. 
4/ If the voter signed the poll list, then oﬀer a provisional 
ballot to the voter. The CEB will determine if the voter was a 
qualiﬁed voter of the precinct. 
 
Q. Can I remake a faxed/emailed ballot on a MicroVote 
DRE?  
A. No. A faxed/emailed ballot must be remade on a ballot card 
and tabulated on the opƟcal scan voƟng system. (IC 3-12-3-5) Do 
not forget to serialize your remade ballots! The bi-parƟsan re-
make team must include a serial number of the voter’s original 
ballot and use the same number on the remade ballot. This is 
important in the event there is a recount. Those involved with 
the recount should be able to look at the original ballot and the 
remade ballot to ensure the remake team captured the voter’s 
intent appropriately. 
Q. If we have a line at the end of the day during in‐person 
absentee or “early” voƟng, are we required to allow  
individuals waiƟng in line to vote if our oﬃce is closed? 
A. Much like elecƟon day, if there are voters in line waiƟng to 
vote during any day of “early” voƟng at the clerk’s oﬃce or 
satellite locaƟon, then those individuals are allowed to vote, 
if otherwise eligible. Staﬀ should either write down each per-
son’s name who is waiƟng, mark their hands with a stamp, or 
designate a staﬀ person to wait at the end of the line when 
the polls close to mark the end. (IC 3-11-8-11 and IC 3-11-10-
29.2) 
 
Q. Does a voter’s ID need to have a matching address to 
their registraƟon record? 
A. No. The photo ID law does not require a matching address. 
Instead, the requirements are that it must be issued by the 
state of Indiana or federal government, be current or expired 
since the last general elecƟon (11/3/20), and include a photo 
and name that conforms with the registraƟon. (IC 3-5-2-40.5)

Election Division Dispatch

NEWS & UPDATES 
Commissions for ConsƟtuƟonal Oﬃceholders 
A reminder that consƟtuƟonal oﬃceholders (sheriﬀ, surveyor, 
treasurer, auditor, clerk, coroner, prosecuƟng aƩorney, judge, 
recorder) receive a Commission from the governor along with a 
copy of an oath of oﬃce. There is no cerƟﬁcate of elecƟon for 
the county clerk to issue, as a result. Commissions will be in the 
mail to the home address of the candidate by mid‐December. If 
you are alerted to an issue with the Commission, please ask the 
oﬃceholder to send an email to elecƟons@iec.in.gov for IED to 
resolve the maƩer.  
AddiƟonally, the oath of oﬃce included with the Commission or 
with the cerƟﬁcate of el
ecƟon is provided as a courtesy. While 
most oaths are ﬁled with the county clerk not later than Jan. 31, 
2023, a clerk would not reject an oath that is not on the state 
form. It is acceptable for an individual to transcribe an oath on 
leƩerhead, for example, if the person swearing in the  
oﬃceholder wants a more formal document. 
RedistricƟng Ordinances Filing Reminders 
CiƟes and towns (and other jurisdicƟons that did not redistrict in 
2022) have unƟl December 31, 2022, to pass an ordinance  
describing their new elecƟon districts OR to recerƟfy their  
exisƟng districts. Copies of the ordinances to redistrict or recerƟ‐
fy city or town elecƟons districts must be ﬁled not later than 30‐
days aŌer adopƟon. An ordinance adopted on the very last day—
December 31, 2022—would need to be ﬁled with the county 
clerk by January 30, 2023. NOTE: Some small towns may have 
previously adopted an ordinance to abolish town council districts 
and elect all members at large, and then ﬁled that ordinance with 
you. Unless the town chooses to adopt new districts, no further 
acƟon is needed by that town to keep its ordinance to abolish 
districts in eﬀect. 
Ideally, the ciƟe
 s and towns will ﬁle those ordinances ahead of  
candidate ﬁling , which opens on January 4, 2023. County  
elecƟon administrators are encouraged to reach out to  
municipaliƟes to gather the informaƟon you need to update 
precinct keys within SVRS with those new districts to ensure 
smooth candidate ﬁling for the May primary elecƟon. 
2023 Forms, Guidebooks & Manuals

the INSVRS County Portal (word and .pdf versions) or online at 
in.gov/sos/elecƟons in ﬁllable .pdf format only. The ABS form

IED has completed its updates to our manuals and guidebooks 
for 2023, including the special “Small” Town Guidebook. You can 
ﬁnd those mater
ials online at in.gov/sos/elecƟons under the 
“ElecƟon Administrator’s Portal.” Physical copies will be provided 
to registrants of the December conference along with  
supplements to the 2022 Code Book. AddiƟonal copies can be 
purchased at the conference, too.

InformaƟon in this newsleƩer is provided by the Indiana ElecƟon Division as a courtesy to county elecƟon administrators. If a person is unclear concerning elecƟon law provisions,  
the ElecƟon Division can serve as an interpreƟve source. However, where important legal rights are concerned, you must consult with your own aƩorney to be fully and properly advised. 
CANDIDATE QUALIFICATIONS 
The red 2023 Candidate Guide is an invaluable 
resource for candidates to understand the 
requirements to run for a speciﬁc oﬃce. Re‐
quirements to run may include, but are not 
limited to, residency, voter registraƟon status, 
felony convicƟon restricƟons, and other con‐
sideraƟons such as how government employ‐
ment may impact their ability to assume oﬃce 
and retain their job. 
CITY & “LARGE” TOWN OFFICES  
Candidate ﬁling in ciƟes and “large” towns 
(those with a populaƟon of 3,500 or more as of 
the 2020  census) in 2023 is similar to the pro‐
cess used in 2022. However, form names are 
diﬀerent and municipaliƟes pay for their elec‐
Ɵons. 
DemocraƟc and Republican party  candidate 
ﬁling for the 2023 primary elecƟon starts Jan. 
4, 2023, and ends at noon, Feb. 3, 2023. These 
candidates ﬁle the CAN‐42 and  CAN‐12 with 
the county clerk. (NOTE: The “two” primary 
rule to run as a D or R does not apply to candi‐
dates running for an oﬃce nominated at a 
“small” town convenƟon. This means a D or R 
candidate needs to have pulled a D or R ballot 
in the last primary in Indiana in which the per‐
son voted, if seeking a “small” town oﬃce 
nominated at a convenƟon and not a primary 
elecƟon.) 
Libertarian candidates in ciƟes and large towns 
are nominated by convenƟon in order for their  
candidates to appear on the November ballot. 
The form used here is the CAN‐22 and CAN‐12 
for local oﬃces in 2023. The deadline to ﬁle 
these forms is noon, July 3, 2023. 
ParƟes can also ﬁll ballot vacancies when no 
candidate ﬁles or a candidate withdraws from 
the Nov. ballot, which be covered later. 
 
“SMALL” TOWN OFFICES  
For elecƟon purposes, a “small” town has a 
populaƟon of less than 3,500 as of the 2020 
decennial census. By default, a “small” town 
does not hold a May primary elecƟon. Instead, 
the D/R/L candidates are nominated at a town 
convenƟon held in August if there is a contest 
within a party for a nominaƟon. The CAN‐16 
and CAN‐12 forms are used for a “small” town 
D/R/L nominaƟng convenƟon and the ﬁling 
period is Jan. 4, 2023 to NOON, Aug. 1, 2023.  
If there is a contest within the party for a par‐
Ɵcular oﬃce, then the town convenƟon is held 
for that party and voters at the convenƟon will 
nominate the candidate who will appear on 
the November ballot. If there is no contest for 
an oﬃce within that party, then no convenƟon 
is held and the candidates that ﬁled with ap‐
pear on the November ballot.  
Some town councils in a “small”  town will have 
adopted an ordinance not later than January 1, 
2023, for the county elecƟon board to conduct 
a primary elecƟon for the D and R parƟes. If so, 
then the “small” town follows the primary 
ﬁling deadlines of Jan. 4, 2023 to noon, Feb. 3, 
2023 using the CAN‐42 and CAN‐12. The Liber‐
tarian party will sƟll need to hold convenƟon 
to nominate their candidates not later than 
noon, Aug. 1, 2023. 
INDEPENDENT & MINOR PARTY 
CANDIDATES  
An independent or minor party candidate gains 
ballot access through the peƟƟon process (CAN
‐44) in order for their name to be printed on 
the ballot. Candidates must collect signatures 
of registered voters in precincts contained in 
their elecƟon district totaling at least 2% of the 
total votes cast amongst all candidates in the 
2022 Secretary of State’s elecƟon.   
The CAN‐44 may be ﬁled as early as Jan. 4, 
2023, and not later than noon, June 30, 2023. 
The CAN‐12 would accompany the CAN‐44 
peƟƟons, unless t
he county has a separate 
Board of RegistraƟon (Allen, LaPorte, Madison, 
Marion, St. Joe, Vanderburgh & Vigo counƟes 
only). Please also see note in second quesƟon 
below, if municipality covers more than one 
county. 
The county VR oﬃcial cerƟﬁes the individuals 
are registered voters of the elecƟon district. 
(More info about peƟƟon processing is found 
in the purple VR Guidebook. The candidate 
then ﬁles the CAN‐45 consent not later than 
noon, July 17, 2023, to qualify for the ballot. 
(In those counƟes with a separate VR Board, 
the CAN‐12 is ﬁled with the CAN‐45 along with 
the cerƟﬁed peƟƟons to the clerk or CEB.) 
To be a declared write‐in candidate where the 
person’s name is NOT  printed on the ballot, a 
candidate must ﬁle the CAN‐51 and CAN‐12 
not earlier than Jan. 4, 2023, and not later than 
noon, July 3, 2023. 
STATEMENT OF ECONOMIC  INTERESTS  
(CAN‐12)  
The CAN‐ 12 is required of nearly every  person 
running for a local oﬃce in 2023. (Candidates 
for judge complete the statement of economic 
interests form available through the Commis‐
sion on Judicial QualiﬁcaƟons and will need to 
print out the receipt showing it has been ﬁled 
to aƩach to their candidate form.)  
The candidate should ﬁll it out looking through 
the lens of 2022, and this should be the year 
the candidate includes near the top of the 
black box where the “20___”  appears.  
IN FOCUS: 2023 CANDIDATE FILING 
QUESTIONS OF THE MONTH  
Q. Can the clerk or staﬀ re ject a ﬁling because a candidate does not meet the qualiﬁcaƟons to run for oﬃce? 
A. NO! County elecƟon administrators are not the candidate police! Candidates must be fully and properly advised before running for oﬃce, 
and their ﬁlings are public informaƟon. There is a challenge period that ends aŌer candidate ﬁling that will allow a party chair or voter of
the elecƟon district to ﬁle a CAN‐1 challenge because a candidate may not meet the qualiﬁcaƟons to run for oﬃce or may have deﬁcient or
incomplete paperwork. The CEB must then hold a hearing, aŌer giving the candidate and complainant noƟce of the hearing to allow both
parƟes to present their facts and evidence. The CEB will then determine whether the candidate can remain on the ballot. (See separate box
in the newsleƩer about the four reasons in state law to reject a candidate ﬁling for more informaƟon.)
Q. Where does a candidate ﬁle when a municipality’s boundaries cover more than one county?
A. For most candidate ﬁlings like the CAN‐42 and CAN‐12, the candidate will ﬁle the form with the clerk in the county with the largest
percentage of the populaƟon of the elecƟon district, if the elecƟon district covers more than one county. BUT, for the CAN‐44 peƟƟons
used by independent and minor  party candidates to have their name printed on the ballot, the candidate will ﬁle the peƟƟon with the
county where the individuals signing the peƟƟon are registered to vote for that speciﬁc county VR oﬃcial to review and cerƟfy those voters
registered in their county only. The candidate would then collect and ﬁle  the cerƟﬁed peƟƟons along with the CAN‐45 consent and CAN‐12
statement of economic interests not later than noon, July 17, 2023 with the county clerk with the largest percentage of the populaƟon of
the elecƟon district. (IC 3‐8‐6‐10)
VR CORNER 
Voter RegistraƟon Record RetenƟon  
IC 3‐10‐1‐31.1(f) requires a county VR 
oﬃcial to maintain a voter’s paper  
registraƟon document unƟl such a Ɵme 
the person’s registraƟon is cancelled at 
their registraƟon address. 
   
If at any point the voter moves within or 
out of your  jurisdicƟon and cancels their 
registraƟon (or is cancelled through by 
following proper VLM procedures), paper 
VR forms  corresponding to the cancelled 
registraƟon address must be 1) scanned in 
to SVRS, if the records are not already; 
and 2) retained for at least 24‐months  
following the next general elecƟon. AŌer 
this 24‐month period, the  county may 
destroy the paper document by following 
the proper protocols. 
  
For example, Robert moves within Starke 
County from Main Street to First Avenue, 
and submits the update on a paper VRG‐7 
form on January 10, 2023. Starke County 
must scan the paper form with the First 
Avenue address into SVRS.  If there is a 
paper record for his previous address on 
Main Street, the county must also make 
sure it is scanned and in the voter’s  
document secƟon of SVRS. However, the 
paper form with the Main Street address 
becomes  eligible for destrucƟon on or 
aŌer November 5, 2026, or 24‐months 
aŌer the November 5, 2024, general  
elecƟon.  
 
Paper VR documents include, but are not  
limited to the VRG‐7, VRG‐11, federal VR 
form, Statewide Address Mailing  
ConﬁrmaƟon (SAMC) noƟce, and VRG‐6 
forms submiƩed by full‐service agencies. 
There is no requirement to print online 
voter registraƟ
on forms or electronic  
submissions from the BMV. However, if 
your county creates a paper record for the 
electronic submission, meaning you have 
printed the online registraƟon form, then 
you must follow the retenƟon schedule as 
noted above for the printed copy of the 
electronic  record.  
CAMPAIGN FINANCE REMINDERS 
 
2022 Annual Report 
ALL candidate and poliƟcal acƟon commiƩees must ﬁle their 2022 Annual  
Report with the county clerk (or, if applicable, the Indiana ElecƟon Division) not 
later than noon, January 18, 2023. If a candidate was not on the ballot in 2022, 
then the reporƟng period is January 1, 2022 (or whenever the commiƩee was 
opened) through December 31, 2022.  For PACs and candidates on the ballot in 
November, the reporƟng period for the annual report is October 15, 2022 
through December 31, 2022. 
 
ALL regular party commiƩees have unƟl noon, March 1, 2023, to ﬁle their 2022 
annual report. Party commiƩees have an extended deadline to make this  
speciﬁc candidate ﬁlings. 
 
2023 Candidates Filing in the D/R May Primary 
If an elected oﬃce pays $5,000 or more in a calendar year, then a candidate 
must open a candidate’s commiƩee by ﬁling a CFA‐1:  
 
1) not later than noon, ten days aŌer raising or spending more than $100 
toward running for oﬃce; or 
 
2) aŌer ﬁling a declaraƟon of candidacy or consent (for example, CAN‐ 42) or 
consent (for example, CAN‐ 45), not later than noon, ten days aŌer ﬁling the 
form or not later than noon, seven days aŌer the ﬁling deadline, whichever 
comes sooner. 
 
As an example, Joan ﬁles for mayor on January 9, and the oﬃce pays more than 
$5,000 a year. She needs to ﬁle the CFA‐1 no later than noon, ten days aŌer 
January 9 to comply with state law. Michael ﬁles for mayor on February 3, which 
is the candidate ﬁling deadline. He has to ﬁle his commiƩee’s CFA‐1 no later 
than noon, seven days later or Friday, February 10, 2023. 
 
If an elected oﬃce pays less than $5,000 a calendar year, then the candidate 
ﬁles a CFA‐1 no later than noon, ten days aŌer raising or spending  more than 
$500 toward running for oﬃce. For example, MarƟn ﬁles to run for dogcatcher 
on January 10, 2023, an oﬃce paying $3,000 a year. He spends $750 on t‐shirts 
on June 1. He has to ﬁle a CFA‐1 no later than noon, ten days aŌer the June 1st  
expenditure.  
LIMITS ON REJECTING CANDIDATE FILINGS 
The blue ElecƟon Administrator’s Manual covers this in more detail, but in short, 
there are four reasons to for a candidate ﬁling to be rejected: 
 
1) Candidate running for state oﬃce (federal, statewide, state legislaƟve, 
judge, prosecuƟng aƩorney) presents candidate ﬁling incorrectly to county 
(Doesn’t apply in 2023). (IC 3‐5‐4‐1.2) 
 
2) Form presented for ﬁling aŌer the noon, prevailing local Ɵme of candidate 
ﬁling deadline. (IC 3‐5‐4‐1.9) 
 
3) Filing made on a form NOT approved by the state. (IC 3‐5‐4‐8) 
 
4) DeclaraƟon of candidacy is not accompanied by the required statement of 
economic interest  (IC 3‐8‐2‐11; IC 3‐8‐9‐6) 
 
However, if the forms are ﬁled with the oﬃce and an error discovered, the ﬁl‐
ings cannot be rejected aŌer the fact. It would require a CAN‐1 challenge to be 
ﬁled by a party chair or voter within the elecƟon district. Remember, clerks & 
their staﬀ are NOT the candidate police! QuesƟons concerning a candidate’s  
qualiﬁcaƟons are managed through the CAN‐1 challenge procedures.

Election Division Dispatch 
 Brad King & Angie Nussmeyer, Co-Directors | January 2023 
NEWS & UPDATES 
SVRS Candidate Entry & CAN‐5 ConﬁrmaƟon NoƟce 
State law requires all primary and municipal candidates to be  
entered into SVRS. CounƟes will want to conﬁrm their elecƟon is set 
up and all oﬃces on the ballot in 2023 are associated to it. The Help 
Desk can provide some support and point you to the appropriate 
step‐by‐step resources if you are unfamiliar with the process to set‐
up an elecƟon. 
 
Once the candidate informaƟon is entered into SVRS, you can use it 
to create your CAN‐5 noƟce. The CAN‐5 is required to be provided to 
the candidate within one business day of ﬁling pursuant to state law, 
and it can be emailed, hand‐delivered, or mailed to the candidate. 
Keeping up on candidate entry, daily, means you can leverage SVRS 
to manage the CAN‐5 process and mail them by batch each day.  
 
Note: The CAN‐5 is now a “disconƟnued” form since it can be  
generated in SVRS, and as a result, cannot be found online or in the 
2023 forms folder on the county portal. 
 
IEC‐22 Due by Jan. 31 
Don’t forget to ﬁle your county’s IEC‐22 before Jan. 31, 2023. This is 
a state form that acknowledges the voƟng system and ePB inventory 
database managed by VSTOP is up‐to‐date with your county’s 
 inventory, and must be signed by your county elecƟon board. 
 
Changes to BMV Temporary Paper License 
Beginning Jan. 1, 2023, the BMV has made an update  to the paper 
license it issues to customers as a temporary measure unƟl the 
“original” license is received by the customer. The change simply 
prints the bar code on the front of the temporary license, when  
before it was printed on the back. This change allows the temporary 
license to be printed from self‐service kiosks. Old versions of the 
temporary paper credenƟal are “on the street” unƟl March 1, 2023. 
 
Independent Candidate Signature Threshold 
The online version of the 2023 Candidate Guide was revised to in‐
clude countywide totals for independent candidates that want their 
name printed on the ballot in any elecƟon between 2023 and 2026. 
The number is calculated from reviewing the total votes cast for all 
candidates for SOS in 2022 within the county and mulƟplying the 
total by 2%. A statewide total is included, too. 
 
However, if an elecƟon district is smaller than the enƟre county, 
then the county clerk will need to pull out the November 2022  
precinct level results, add up the total votes cast for ALL candidates 
running for SOS in those precincts making up the elecƟon district, 
mulƟple the number by 2%, and then round down, if there is a  
fracƟon of a number. (For example, 11.88 is rounded to 11.) In 2023, 
some elecƟon districts may not be a whole precinct. Our best advice 
is compute the number based on the total votes cast for SOS for the 
whole precinct.

Please verify against the training calendar. 
InformaƟon in this newsleƩer is provided by the Indiana ElecƟon Division as a courtesy to county elecƟon administrators. If a person is unclear concerning elecƟon law provisions,  
the ElecƟon Division can serve as an interpreƟve source. However, where important legal rights are concerned, you must consult with your own aƩorney to be fully and properly advised. 
Candidate ﬁlings can only be rejected for 
a handful of reasons as permiƩed under 
state law. Once ﬁled, a candidate form 
cannot be given back to a candidate to 
amend (excepƟon: missing peƟƟon carrier 
informaƟon on the CAN‐44 can be 
amended when required).  They may 
complete a new form as an amendment 
for the same oﬃce before the ﬁling period 
ends, but if the person ﬁled for the wrong 
oﬃce, they must ﬁrst withdraw using the 
CAN‐43 form in the primary or CAN‐46 for 
the general elecƟon and then ﬁle the  
correct candidacy paperwork for the new 
oﬃce.  
 
Otherwise, the clerk and CEB do not  
police candidate ﬁlings, unless a CAN‐1 
challenge is Ɵmely ﬁled, which would  
result in a CEB hearing on the maƩer. 
 
Reasons to Reject a Candidate Filing 
 
1. Faxed or emailed candidacy  
paperwork. State law requires a ﬁling to 
be an original document, which means it 
cannot be faxed or emailed. Instead, the 
forms must be mailed or hand‐delivered 
by the candidate or a third party. (IC 3‐5‐4
‐1.7) 
 
2. Received aŌer the deadline. The dead‐
line to ﬁle in the May primary elecƟon is 
noon, Feb. 3, 2023. Any form received 
aŌer this deadline (even if it was mailed 
and the postmark was dated before the  
deadline) must be rejected.  
(IC 3‐5‐4‐1.9) 
 
3. Filed with the wrong oﬃce. Candidates 
for local oﬃces must ﬁle candidacy  
paperwork with the CEB. If a candidate for 
local oﬃce comes to IED (the state) to ﬁle, 
then their ﬁling is rejected. This would 
also be true if a state legislator, for  
example, tries to ﬁle their candidacy  
paperwork with the CEB. (IC 3‐5‐4‐1.2) 
 
4. Used the wrong form. Candidates must 
use the current version of the candidate 
ﬁling forms. Please see the Forms Master 
List to idenƟfy which version of the form 
is current, if there are quesƟons. (IC 3‐5‐4‐
8) 
 
5. Failed to aƩach the CAN‐12  
statement of economic interests (or, for 
certain state or judicial oﬃces, the  
statement of economic interests created 
by the speciﬁc agency in statute). Failure 
to include the CAN‐12 for local oﬃce must 
result in the CAN‐42 being rejected in the 
primary elecƟon, for example. 
 
Candidate Challenges 
There are a number of reasons why a  
candidate challenge may be ﬁled. For  
example, the candidate does not meet 
the primary voƟng history requirement, 
or does not reside in the elecƟon district, 
or has defecƟve paperwork. 
Any voter in the elecƟon district OR the 
county chair may ﬁle a CAN‐1 challenge 
not later than the speciﬁed deadline to do 
so. (IC 3‐8‐1‐2) For the May primary  
elecƟon, the deadline to ﬁle the CAN‐1 is 
noon, Friday, Feb. 10, 2023.  
 
When ﬁled, the CEB must hold a hearing. 
The hearing must be noƟced in  
accordance with the Open Door Law. It is 
advised that best possible noƟce of the 
hearing must be given to the individual 
making the challenge and the candidate. 
 
Both parƟes will present their facts and 
evidence to the CEB, who then must  
determine if the candidate will remain on 
the ballot once they review the facts and 
apply the law. 
 
Many of the candidate qualiﬁcaƟons are 
found in the 2023 Candidate Guide, which 
may be helpful to the CEB to idenƟfy  
statutes or other issues related to  
residency or the Hatch Act, for example.  
 
At the hearing, the CEB would order the 
candidate not to be printed on the ballot,  
if it is decided to uphold the challenge. 
IN FOCUS: Candidate Filings & CAN-1 Challenges 
VR CORNER 
Several municipaliƟes in Indiana have boundaries that cover 
more than one county. For candidate ﬁling, the candidate ﬁles 
their CAN‐42 or CAN‐16 with the county clerk with the largest 
percentage of the populaƟon of the elecƟon district, according 
to the 2020 census. BUT, independent and minor party candi‐
dates using the CAN‐44 form to gather peƟƟon signatures, the 
county VR oﬃcial can only  
cerƟfy signatures of voters registered within their county.  
 
For example, Sally has a CAN‐44 with 6 signatures of voters in 
county A and 4 signatures of voters in county B. She ﬁles the 
peƟƟon with county A ﬁrst. The VR oﬃcial would determine if 
any of the 6 signatures of voters within county A should be  
cerƟﬁed and complete the cerƟﬁcaƟon for their county on the 
back of the form. The candidate could then pick up their county 
A cerƟﬁed peƟƟon and deliver it to county B for review,  
assuming the candidate has not missed the noon, June 30, 2023, 
deadline to ﬁle peƟƟons for cerƟﬁcaƟon. County B would then 
review the four signatures and complete their part of the  
cerƟﬁcaƟon on the back of the form.  
QUESTION OF THE MONTH  
Q. What can the CEB do to disband a commiƩee that no 
longer ﬁles campaign ﬁnance reports?? 
A. Not later than January 27, 2023, the CEB may review 
its campaign ﬁnance records to determine if a  
commiƩee is subject to the administraƟve dissoluƟon 
procedure. To move forward with dissoluƟon, the  
commiƩee must have not ﬁled any CFA‐4 or CFA‐11  
during the previous three calendar years AND the cash 
on hand on their last ﬁled report is $1,000 or less. If both 
condiƟons are met, then the CEB may move forward 
with the process found in IC 3‐9‐1‐12.  
 
Q. When and where do oaths of oﬃce need to be ﬁled? 
A. Most newly elected oﬃcials can take their oath of 
oﬃce as late as January 31, 2023, but it would also need 
to be ﬁled by this deadline date as well. Local elected 
oﬃcials ﬁle their oath with the county clerk; however, 
judges and prosecuƟng aƩorney ﬁle with the SOS/IED.

Election Division Dispatch 
 Brad King & Angie Nussmeyer, Co-Directors | February 2023 
NEWS & UPDATES 
Democracy Live & Accessible Online BalloƟng Tool 
As we noted at the December conference, IED and the SOS 
were working to secure an online balloƟng tool for voters with 
print disabiliƟes to vote privately and independently at home. 
We recently brought on Democracy Live to assist counƟes 
with providing this service to voters with print disabiliƟes who 
complete the ABS‐VPD form and request an absentee ballot 
by email. 
 
More informaƟon will be distributed to counƟes in the coming 
weeks, though aƩached to the newsleƩer email is more infor‐
maƟon about Democracy Live and their omni ballot soluƟon 
and the diﬀerent decision points we are seƩling on here to roll 
out training and the tool to counƟes. Stay tuned! 
 
January Hoƞix 
Civix, our statewide voter registraƟon system vendor, pushed 
a number of enhancements to SVRS at the end of last month 
and provided an online review of those enhancements. Build 
notes and training materials can be found on the SVRS County 
Portal now. 
 
UpdaƟng County Contact InformaƟon in SVRS 
SVRS has a module for counƟes to enter contact informaƟon 
for the various elecƟon duƟes managed by your oﬃces. This  
informaƟon is then displayed on indianavoters.com to help 
voters ﬁnd their local elecƟon administrators and used in re‐
ports or other documents produced in the system. Please 
make sure your county’s informaƟon is up‐to‐date by logging 
in to SVRS and selecƟng AdministraƟon, then County, then 
Directory. A new module window will display. To edit exisƟng 
informaƟon, click on the pencil on the far right. You can also 
“Add Directory LisƟng” to create more entries. Using the 
“Directory Search” link on the tool bar will let you ﬁnd and 
edit your ElecƟon Board members, which needs to be 
accurate for ﬁling certain reports in SVRS.  
 
AdministraƟvely Opening Candidate CommiƩees 
A candidate running for oﬃce that pays more than $5,000 in a  
calendar year must open a candidate commiƩee 1) no later 
than noon, ten days aŌer raising or spending $100 toward 
running for oﬃce, OR 2) not later than noon, seven days aŌer 
the candidate ﬁling period ends (noon, Feb. 10, 2023)  
whichever comes ﬁrst. 
 
Not later than noon, Feb. 17, 2023, CEBs must determine if a 
candidate for an oﬃce paying more than $5,000 year has 
opened their commiƩee as required by law. If the candidate 
has not ﬁled a CFA‐1, then the CEB must administraƟvely ﬁle a 
CFA‐1 making the candidate the chair and treasurer, and the 
candidate will be required to ﬁle all necessary reports in 2023.

InformaƟon in this newsleƩer is provided by the Indiana ElecƟon Division as a courtesy to county elecƟon administrators. If a person is unclear concerning elecƟon law provisions,  
the ElecƟon Division can serve as an interpreƟve source. However, where important legal rights are concerned, you must consult with your own aƩorney to be fully and properly advised. 
NEWSLETTER ACRONYMS 
ABS = absentee  |  CAN = candidate  |  CEB= county elecƟon board   
CFA= campaign ﬁnance act  |  FPCA = Federal Post Card ApplicaƟon  
IED = Indiana ElecƟon Division  |  VPD = voters with print disabiliƟes 
Now that the 2022 Annual Report  
deadline has passed (at least for  
candidate and poliƟcal acƟon  
commiƩees), the county elecƟon board is 
required to follow campaign ﬁnance  
enforcement laws. 
 
The ﬁrst item of business is to determine 
which candidate and poliƟcal acƟon  
commiƩees failed to ﬁle their Annual  
Report. Then, the county elecƟon board 
must noƟfy the commiƩees of their  
failure to Ɵmely ﬁle their reports not later 
than 30‐days aŌer the ﬁling deadline, or 
Friday, February 17, 2023. 
 
An example delinquency noƟce is found in 
the appendix of the 2023 Campaign  
Finance Manual, which is a template for 
counƟes to follow, if needed. 
The next step is to determine when the 
CEB will hold its county elecƟon board 
hearing. All commiƩees with a delinquent 
report must receive wriƩen noƟce of the 
hearing at least ﬁve days (not including 
weekends or holidays) before the  
hearing is held, which means counƟes 
should mail out with enough lead‐Ɵme to 
ensure proper noƟce requirements. A 
sample noƟce of hearing is also found in 
the Appendix of the Manual. 
 
The CEB will follow the open door law, 
making sure noƟce of the meeƟng is  
posted at least 48‐hours before the hear‐
ing is held. The 48‐hours does NOT in‐
clude weekends, so a Monday hearing 
should be posted not later than Thursday, 
for example.  
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
At the meeƟng, the CEB may want to  
establish ground rules for those  
requesƟng a waiver or reducƟon of their 
ﬁne and will need to administer the oath 
for any person providing tesƟmony. (The 
Manual has the oath in the Appendix.) 
 
The CEB should consider tesƟmony from 
each commiƩee to determine if their ﬁnes 
should be waiver or reduced. State law 
does require this decision to be made 
unanimously. 
 
AŌer the hearing, the commiƩees should 
receive an Order from the CEB. The  
sample Finding of Fact Order found in the 
Manual’s Appendix is a helpful template, 
which includes details like the date of the 
hearing; which report was late and by 
how many days; the assessed ﬁne OR that 
the ﬁne was waived or reduced; and the 
Order that commands the commiƩee to 
pay their ﬁne or that the maƩer was dis‐
missed because the ﬁne was waived. 
 
Don’t forget! Regular party commiƩees 
ﬁle their 2022 Annual Report not later 
than noon, March 1, 2023, which will  
iniƟate a new round of enforcement  
acƟviƟes. 
IN FOCUS: Campaign Finance Enforcement 
VR CORNER 
 
Voter Fail Safes in 2023 
The purple Voter RegistraƟon Guidebook includes helpful  
informaƟon about voter fail safes, which include the “where” 
and “when” did a voter move analysis to determine if the  
person is eligible to vote one last Ɵme in their old precinct.  
 
In 2023, this fail‐safe is more strict. First, oﬃcials need to  
determine if  the voter would be otherwise qualiﬁed to vote 
one last Ɵme in their “old” precinct. There is a ﬂow chart in 
the appendix of the VR Guidebook and in the ElecƟon Day  
Handbook that is helpful here. 
 
If the person is NOT eligible to vote one last Ɵme in their old 
precinct under this ﬁrst review, then the voter would not be 
given a regular ballot but may use a provisional ballot. 
 
If the person IS eligible to vote one last Ɵme in their old  
precinct, in 2023, there is an important second step to  
determine if the voter receives a provisional or regular ballot. 
Any voter that moves in or out of a city or town cannot vote in 
their old precinct one last Ɵme. The voter may be oﬀered a 
provisional ballot, but not a regular ballot. 
 
For example, Joan lived in Cardinal Town but moved into the 
“county” on March 1 and did not update her registraƟon. In 
2023, Joan is not eligible to vote a regular ballot in her old 
precinct in Cardinal Town because she no longer lives in the 
municipality. 
 
AlternaƟvely, Mark lived in the “county” and moved into  
Cardinal Town on April 15 and did not update his registraƟon. 
This one is a liƩle easier to assess in 2023. Assuming there is 
not a countywide elecƟon this year, no elecƟon is being held 
his old precinct in the “county” and he is not eligible to vote in 
his new “in town” precinct, even though his move was within 
the ﬁnal 30‐days before the elecƟon. 
QUESTIONS OF THE MONTH  
Q. Can we reduce early voƟng hours in the municipal 
elecƟon year? 
A. Yes! See IC 3‐11‐10‐26.5, which permits a county CEB 
to unanimously agree to reduce early voƟng hours in 
municipal elecƟon years like 2023. This can also be used 
to adjust your Saturday hours, if the board wanted to 
limit the hours or further reduce the days the sites are 
open on the two Saturdays leading up to elecƟon day. 
 
Q. If we reduce early voƟng hours, do we also wait to 
mail out absentee ballots? 
A. No. State law requires a county to send absentee  
ballots to those voters with approved ABS applicaƟons 
not later than 45‐days before the elecƟon, or March 18, 
2023 for the May 2, 2023 primary.  
 
The default ballot ready date in SVRS is March 18, so if 
your county wants to move up the deadline (to March 
17 or earlier), submit a county authorizaƟon request in 
SVRS. This date is used for reports to track when you 
sent this ﬁrst batch of ballots out, which should be  
accurate in SVRS. 
Ballot PrinƟng Orders for 
May Primary ElecƟon 
1) Be sure to esƟmate the number of 
provisional and absentee ballots your 
county will need not later than March 
3, 2023. 
2) Receive the order of absentee  
ballots not later than Monday, March 
13, 2023. (If your county uses a ballot
‐on‐demand printer, then the CD or 
equivalent with the ballot ﬁles should 
be delivered by this date.) 
3) Coun Ɵes using opƟcal scan paper 
ballot cards or tradiƟonal hand‐
counted paper ballots need to order 
ElecƟon Day ballots. The print order 
should arrive on Ɵme for your county 
to organize the ballots for pick‐up by 
Inspectors the Saturday or Sunday 
before the elecƟon. 
 
To order ElecƟon Day ballots for the May 
primary elecƟon, a county needs to  
review the precinct level results from the 
November 2022 elecƟon and idenƟfy 
which DemocraƟc candidate was the top 
vote geƩer in each precinct, and which 
Republican candidate was the top vote 
geƩer in each precinct to set the  
minimum ballot order. 
 
Figure 1 below is an example of how many 
ballots and of which party type should be 
ordered for each precinct on ElecƟon Day. 
(No, state law does not permit counƟes to 
back out any absentee voters; you must 
follow this law for ordering in the  
primary.) 
 
Some counƟes use a voƟng system where 
a blank ballot card is inserted into a ballot 
marking device, the voter makes their 
selecƟons, and a completed ballot card is 
printed for the voter to insert into the 
opScan tabulator. You would sƟll follow 
the ballot ordering rules, though instead 
of having printed ballots, you would be 
ordering blank ballot stock at this  
minimum threshold. 
 
If you are a vote center county using  
printed ballot cards or blank ballot card 
stock, then you’ll want to go through this 
same exercise and sum the minimum  
precinct order to reach a total minimum 
to deliver to each vote center. Using the 
example below, each vote center would 
be supplied with at least 237 D ballots 
(125+112) and 215 R ballots (101+114). 
 
Please note: ballot prinƟng rules and 
needs are diﬀerent for the November 
elecƟon. 
 
Special Ballot Styles 
In a primary elecƟon, a county must print 
one ballot style for the DemocraƟc Party 
and one ballot style for the Republican 
Party. 
 
However, some jurisdicƟons will have a 
public quesƟon cerƟﬁed to them for the 
May primary, which requires its own  
special “non‐parƟsan” ballot style for 
those voters who do not want to vote in a 
party’s primary elecƟon but do want to 
vote on the referendum. 
 
If there is a public quesƟon that  
appears in some or all of the precincts in 
the county, then you must 1) print the 
public quesƟon on the D & R primary  
ballots, 2) create a non‐parƟsan ballot 
with only the public quesƟon for the  
reason stated above, and 3) print special 
17‐year old D & R ballots that do NOT  
include the public quesƟon but do include 
all candidates. 
 
In addiƟon, recent changes to state law do 
not permit a voter who moved in the ﬁnal 
30‐days outside of the elecƟon district 
where a school‐related public quesƟon 
will be on the ballot to vote on the public 
quesƟon. Instead, the voter would be en‐
Ɵtled to vote only for candidates on the 
ballot, assuming they moved inside the 
municipality’s boundaries. For this small 
universe of voters, the 17‐year old ballot 
used in the primary would be the correct 
ballot to provide to the voter. 
 
Don’t forget that primary elecƟon ballots 
should have the name of each party  
printed near the top of the ballot, and it’s 
also permissible to include color coding to  
allow for beƩer visual idenƟﬁcaƟon for 
poll workers to pull the proper party’s 
ballot requested by the voter.

Does our county need to hold a primary elecƟon in May 2023? 
It depends. If there are no contested races within a party, then the county elecƟon board is not required to hold a primary elecƟon 
for that party UNLESS the county chair ﬁles a wriƩen request for a primary elecƟon to be held not later than noon, February 10, 
2023. However, you could have a situaƟon where one or both parƟes only has one contested race on the ballot in an elecƟon  
district that is smaller than the municipality. For example, a single member city council district that would not consist of the enƟre 
municipality. If that oﬃce was the only one contested within a party, then an elecƟon would only need to be conducted within 
that district. Of course, if there is a local public quesƟon on the ballot, it would be possible to have a May elecƟon just for the  
public quesƟon if there are no contested races in either party and the county chairs did not request that the county elecƟon board 
hold a primary elecƟon. Please email elecƟons@iec.in.gov if you have speciﬁc quesƟons.

Election Division Dispatch 
 Brad King & Angie Nussmeyer, Co-Directors | March 2023 
NEWS & UPDATES 
March Build 
Throughout the year a number of “hoƞixes” are pushed to 
SVRS, which tend to be smaller enhancements or bug ﬁxes. In 
March, however, a number of  SVRS improvements will be 
released, which is called a “build.” Build notes and training will 
be released toward the end of the month, so please plan to 
aƩend the online training session to understand these  
changes, which may impact how you use the system. 
 
Upcoming Public NoƟces to Publish in Newspaper 
Before each elecƟon there are three public noƟces that must 
be published in a newspaper in accordance with IC 5‐3‐1,  
generally. This would apply in those counƟes conducƟng a 
primary elecƟon and include: 
 
1) NoƟce of Public Test. NoƟce must be published in the 
newspaper not later than 48‐hours before the county’s 
public test of voƟng equipment. The CEB is required to 
pay for its publicaƟon, and there is no prescribed state 
form  (IC 3‐11‐14.5‐2; IC 3‐11‐13‐22)  
2) CAN‐9 NoƟce of Primary ElecƟon. NoƟce must be  
published not later than 21 calendar days before the  
elecƟon. The CEB is required to pay for its publicaƟon, 
and counƟes are to use the CAN‐9 form. A copy of this 
noƟce is to be ﬁled with IED not later than 10 days before 
the elecƟon. (IC 3‐8‐2‐19)  Note: If candidates were  
entered into SVRS, a CAN‐9 can be generated through the 
SVRS Reports Library. 
3) NoƟce of Polling LocaƟons (including Vote Centers). This 
noƟce must be published not later than 21 calendar days 
before the elecƟon. The CEB is required to pay for its  
publicaƟon in non‐voter counƟes; county commissioners 
are required to pay for its publicaƟon in vote center  
counƟes. There is no special state form. (IC 3‐11‐8‐3.2) 
 
Please note: unless speciﬁcally noted in statute like those 
items above, CEB meeƟngs do not need to be published in the 
newspaper, though a CEB may do so if desired. Be certain to 
follow the Open Door Law to post proper noƟce as well. 
 
Absentee Ballot Ready Date 
Don’t forget that absentee ballots for voters with approved 
ABS applicaƟons (ABS‐Mail, ABS‐VPD, FPCA) must be sent not 
later than Sat. March 18, 2023. This is a ﬁrm deadline set in 
federal and state law. Your ballot ready date in SVRS is set to 
March 18, but you can request an earlier date be programmed 
into the system. Please remember that once you send  
absentees out in this ﬁrst push, state law requires you to send 
an absentee ballot out on the same day the applicaƟon is  
approved! (IC 3‐11‐4‐18)
