InformaƟon in this newsleƩer is provided by the Indiana ElecƟon Division as a courtesy to county elecƟon administrators. If a person is unclear concerning elecƟon law provisions,  
the ElecƟon Division can serve as an interpreƟve source. However, where important legal rights are concerned, you must consult with your own aƩorney to be fully and properly advised. 
NEWSLETTER ACRONYMS 
ABS = absentee  |  CAN = candidate  |  CEB= county elecƟon board   
CFA= campaign ﬁnance act  |  FPCA = Federal Post Card ApplicaƟon  
IED = Indiana ElecƟon Division  |  VPD = voters with print disabiliƟes 
VR CORNER 
 
VR Deadline & No Primary ElecƟon 
Monday, April 3, 2023 is the voter registraƟon deadline for 
municipaliƟes holding a May primary elecƟon. Voters must 
submit their request online by 11:59PM, April 3, 2023 or hand‐
deliver their paper form before the VR oﬃce closes on April 3 
or mail the form and ensure it is postmarked on or before 
April 3, 2023.  
 
A reminder that a voter registraƟon form postmarked on or 
before this deadline date must be reviewed and processed by 
the VR oﬃce, even if it is received aŌer April 3. Those  
envelopes missing a postmark or where the postmark is  
illegible can be processed as long as the envelope is received 
by April 10, 2023. 
 
However, if a voter lives “in the county” (meaning outside a  
municipality) OR the CEB decided not to hold BOTH party’s 
primary elecƟons in a city or town because there were no  
contested races on the D & R ballots, then the VR deadline 
does not apply this spring in that county or within that city or 
town. This means voter registraƟon requests can conƟnue to 
be processed aŌer April 3 and unƟl the next VR deadline, 
which will be October 10, 2023, in those jurisdicƟons holding 
an elecƟon this November. 
QUESTIONS OF THE MONTH  
Q. Do both parƟes need to provide ABS board members, 
central count teams, and poll workers for the primary 
elecƟon, if only one party is holding a primary elecƟon? 
A. Yes! ElecƟon administraƟon is a bi‐parƟsan acƟvity. The 
CEB must send noƟce to county chairs by March 13, 2023, 
with the number of ABS boards and elecƟon day central 
count teams needed. The D/R county chairs have unƟl 
noon, March 17, 2023, to provide those names, in wriƟng, 
to the CEB. Poll worker nominaƟons from the county chair 
are due by April 11, 2023.  
 
Q. Are early voƟng sites set up like ElecƟon Day voƟng 
locaƟons? 
A. There are key diﬀerences between the two because 
early voƟng is absentee voƟng. This means you do not 
have poll workers like Inspector, Judge or Clerk at early 
voƟng sites but instead use bi‐parƟsan ABS voter boards. 
(IC 3‐11‐10‐26; IC 3‐11.5‐4‐22) Of course you can have  
other employees (full‐Ɵme or temporary) to support those 
teams, but those are not party appointments. Further, any 
disagreements between the ABS voter boards would go to 
the CEB. AddiƟonally, counƟes using opScan voƟng  
systems cannot have their voters scan their ballots on a 
tabulator during early voƟng. Instead, the voter encloses 
their ballot in the ABS‐7  envelope and signs the aﬃdavit 
before the ABS voter board. The board members then 
print and sign their name on their aﬃdavit. 
 
Q. If there is no primary elecƟon being held for one or 
both parƟes but candidates have ﬁled to be on the May 
ballot, do those candidates sƟll need to ﬁle a pre‐primary 
CFA‐4 report and comply with the 48‐hour CFA‐11  
reporƟng requirements? 
A. Yes! If a candidate has ﬁled a CAN‐42 to run in the  
primary and is required to open a campaign ﬁnance  
commiƩee, then the candidate must ﬁle a pre‐primary 
report and report any “large” contribuƟons during the CFA
‐11 reporƟng window in April. Please see the 2023  
Campaign Finance Manual for more informaƟon, including 
ﬁling dates. 
 
Q. How do we handle a situaƟon where a voter submits 
an ABS applicaƟon for the May elecƟon but the voter 
requests a ballot for a party that is not holding a primary 
or a ballot for the public quesƟon only but there are no 
public quesƟons on the ballot where they live? 
A. You would reject the ABS applicaƟon in this scenario 
and send noƟce of disposiƟon to the voter. This noƟce is 
generated in SVRS once you enter and then reject the ABS 
applicaƟon. However, you would NOT reject an ABS‐VPD 
or FPCA if the voter requests a ballot for a party not having 
a primary elecƟon or forgets to include a party choice 
 altogether or requests a public quesƟon only ballot where 
there is none on the ballot. These two types of ABS  
applicaƟons are ongoing, meaning the request to send an 
absentee ballot would be honored for November and 
needs to be recorded as such.  
Statewide VLM Project Preview 
The ElecƟon Division is required to engage in a statewide 
voter list maintenance project in each odd‐numbered year 
under state law, which means the project will launch right 
aŌer the May 2023 primary elecƟon. The project follows 
federal and state law and consists of two mailers: 
1) Card 1: Sent to the mailing address of every acƟve  
voter in Indiana via USPS non‐forwardable mail. This 
ﬁrst card should be mailed in late May. If the card is 
returned undeliverable pursuant to IC 3‐5‐2‐49.7, then 
card 2 is sent to the voter. 
2) Card 2: Sent by USPS forwardable mail to the mailing  
address of a person whose card 1 is returned  
undeliverable. Card 2 allows the person to a) conﬁrm 
their residence address is their registraƟon address or 
b) update their registraƟon within the county or c) 
cancel their registraƟon if they’ve moved out of  
county. 
Card 2 is the main focus for county VR oﬃcials since it is a 
voter registraƟon document. However, the bulk of the  
returned second cards will be scanned and sorted into 
SVRS VLM hoppers for counƟes to review and approve or 
reject. Or, if Card 2 is not returned by the stated deadline 
on Card 2, then those voters will go into the VLM inacƟve 
hopper for counƟes to review. 
More details about the project, including images of the 
cards and a more deﬁned Ɵmetable, will be shared as the 
contract is ﬁnalized.

Election Division Dispatch 
 Brad King & Angie Nussmeyer, Co-Directors | April 2023 
NEWS & UPDATES 
VIP & Polling Places 
IED partners with Democracy Works, a non‐parƟsan non‐proﬁt 
organizaƟon, to increase visibility of early voƟng and polling 
place informaƟon. Please make sure your voƟng locaƟons are 
up to date in SVRS on or before April 10 as our elecƟon  
informaƟon will be shared via geƩothepolls.com as well as our 
own indianavoters.com. Remember to update your polling 
locaƟons in SVRS promptly if they change aŌer that day! 
 
Ballot Vacancies  
Several counƟes have asked about the process for the  
DemocraƟc or Republican parƟes to ﬁll a ballot vacancy, if the 
party did not have a candidate ﬁle a CAN‐42 for nominaƟon in 
a  primary elecƟon. Details about the process to ﬁll ballot  
vacancies, including how the Libertarian Party can ﬁll ballot 
vacancies, are found on pages 43‐47 of the 2023 ElecƟon  
Administrator’s Manual.  
 
The deadline to ﬁll a ballot vacancy where no candidate ran in 
the D or R primary elecƟon is NOON, July 3, 2023 and the 
deadline to ﬁle the paperwork is NOON, July 3, 2023. This is 
not a typo! There are no extensions unless your oﬃce is 
closed on July 3, 2023, and then only the ﬁling deadline would 
roll over to noon, the next day the oﬃce is open for business. 
 
NOTE: Ballot vacancy procedures do not apply to elecƟons 
held in “small” towns that hold a nominaƟng convenƟon  
instead of a primary elecƟon. In this case, the deadline to ﬁle 
the CAN‐16 and CAN‐12 is noon, August 1, 2023. If no candi‐
date ﬁled to run for one or all oﬃces in the “small” town, then 
the D/R/L parƟes do not get to ﬁll the ballot vacancy.  
However, if a candidate nominated to run for a “small” town 
oﬃce withdraws, then the D/R/L party is able to ﬁll the ballot 
vacancy using procedures in IC 3‐13‐1 or, if it is the ﬁnal 30‐
days before elecƟon day, IC 3‐13‐2. 
 
Yard Signs 
One sign that spring is here is the popping up of yard signs 
ahead of the May primary! A reminder that the CEB only has 
jurisdicƟon over whether the yard sign contains the “Paid for 
by” disclaimer in at least 7‐point font. Otherwise, state law 
permits a local unit of government to adopt an ordinance to 
restrict when poliƟcal yard signs can be placed in yards.  
However, any local ordinance restricƟng when signs can be 
planted cannot be enforced for signs up to 4’x8’ 60‐days  
before the elecƟon and 5‐days aŌer it. There is a similar state 
law for homeowners’ associaƟons, but their rules cannot be 
enforced 30‐days before the elecƟon and 5‐days aŌer. More 
informaƟon can be found in the “Disclaimer” brochure found 
in the elecƟon administrator’s portal at in.gov/sos/elecƟons.

the ElecƟon Division can serve as an interpreƟve source. However, where important legal rights are concerned, you must consult with your own aƩorney to be fully and properly advised. 
VR CORNER 
 
Incomplete Voter RegistraƟons 
As the primary elecƟon nears in many jurisdicƟons throughout the 
state, county VR oﬃcials will need to manage their incomplete voter 
registraƟon forms. When those tasks are to be performed depends on 
the type of informaƟon missing or otherwise incomplete on the form: 
 
1/ Voter did not answer age or ciƟzenship quesƟons. Voter has 
unƟl the VR deadline of April 3, 2023 to ﬁle, in wriƟng, made  
under the penalƟes for perjury the answers to those quesƟons. If 
voter fails to ﬁx by the deadline, then the registraƟon is rejected. 
 
2/ Voter has incomplete informaƟon for required ﬁelds other 
than the age/ciƟzenship quesƟon. In most cases, the voter can 
provide the missing informaƟon over the phone (see the FAQ in 
the 2023 Voter RegistraƟon Guidebook) but has unƟl 10‐days 
before the elecƟon. If the voter does not do so, then their  
registraƟon is rejected. 
 
The county VR oﬃcial must then cerƟfy to the CEB a list of the 
voters with rejected registraƟons by April 22, 2023. 
QUESTIONS OF THE MONTH  
Q. Can an absentee voter who has an approved  
applicaƟon on ﬁle requesƟng a DemocraƟc ABS  
ballot change their mind and submit a new ABS  
applicaƟon for a Republican or public quesƟon‐only 
ballot (or vice versa)? 
 
A. No, a voter may not change their mind and request 
a diﬀerent party’s (or public quesƟon only) ballot in 
the primary elecƟon. If you issue a replacement  
absentee ballot aŌer the voter ﬁles the ABS‐5, the 
absentee ballot must be for the same poliƟcal party. 
AddiƟonally, once a voter selects their party on the 
poll book (paper or electronic), in the primary  
elecƟon, the voter cannot change their mind and  
receive the other party’s (or public quesƟon only) 
ballot. (IC 3‐11‐4‐17.7(d); IC 3‐10‐1‐24(a)(3)) 
 
Q. What is the diﬀerence between the ABS‐5 and 
PRE‐5 forms? 
 
A. The key diﬀerence is one form is used BEFORE  
elecƟon day (ABS‐5) and the other is used ON elecƟon 
day (PRE‐5). The ABS‐5 allows a voter to request a 
replacement absentee ballot if their original ballot 
was lost, spoiled, or defecƟve. Once the ABS‐5 is  
processed, then the CEB can deliver a new ballot to 
the voter or permit the voter to cast an absentee  
ballot when early voƟng commences.  
 
The PRE‐5 is used on ElecƟon Day if an absentee voter 
did not receive their absentee ballot. The voter would 
sign this aﬃdavit at their elecƟon day polling place 
aﬃrming their ballot did not arrive in order to receive 
a ballot at the polling place. 
 
SomeƟmes a voter who received an absentee ballot 
wants to surrender it during early voƟng or on  
ElecƟon Day. That’s ﬁne. However, if the voter  
surrenders their absentee ballot during early voƟng, 
then the voter should complete the ABS‐5 form and 
absentee board members mark the surrendered  
absentee ballot as “CANCELED” and store it with the  
canceled absentee ballots. On ElecƟon Day, there is 
no form for the voter to complete, but the poll work‐
ers should mark the absentee ballot as “REJECTED” 
and store it in their rejected ballot bag to be returned 
with their elecƟon materials aŌer the polls close. 
 
Q. My newspaper failed to publish our noƟce of  
public test of voƟng systems. Do I have to  
reschedule the public test? 
 
A. Not necessarily. If the paper did not publish your 
noƟce as requested, then the county elecƟon board 
can either 1) display the noƟce prominently in three 
locaƟons in the county or 2) post on the county’s 
website. (IC 5‐3‐1‐2(k))  
CONDUCTING AN ELECTION WHEN CITY OR 
TOWN IS PART OF MORE THAN 1 COUNTY 
A few ciƟes or towns in Indiana cross county lines, which does 
impact elecƟon administrators. IC 3‐6‐5‐15 states that the  
county containing the greatest percentage of the populaƟon 
according to the 2020 census may designate the polling places 
for the elecƟon, which may be located in any county in which 
the poliƟcal subdivision is located, and shall appoint poll workers 
to conduct the elecƟon upon nominaƟon by the county chair of 
the county where the precinct is located. 
 
However, each county elecƟon board must provide poll lists,  
receive and approve absentee ballot applicaƟons, issue  
cerƟﬁcates of error or other documents for the voters of that 
county, print ballots, and canvass results. For example, “Indiana 
City” has 5 precincts in Wayne County and 3 precincts in  
Randolph County, where the greatest populaƟon is in Wayne 
County.  
 
The Wayne CEB can establish polling places exclusively in Wayne 
County or in both counƟes. The Wayne and Randolph county D/
R party chairs would nominate their poll workers to the Wayne 
CEB. However, each CEB would conduct poll worker training, 
produce poll lists, build ballots, code voƟng systems, and  
manage ElecƟon Day for the precincts located in their county. 
AŌer canvassing the results, the Randolph CEB would cerƟfy 
their results to the Wayne CEB, who would then determine the 
winners and issue cerƟﬁcates of elecƟon, if required.  
 
Both counƟes would determine the cost to conduct the elecƟon, 
and “Indiana City” would need to reimburse both counƟes.

Election Division Dispatch 
 Brad King & Angie Nussmeyer, Co-Directors | May 2023 
NEWS & UPDATES 
2023 Ballot Vacancies 
AŌer May 2, the DemocraƟc and Republican parƟes can ﬁll 
ballot vacancies where no candidate ran in the primary  
elecƟon. The county chair (or central commiƩee) can ﬁll these 
vacancies by direct appointment, but this requires the party 
organizaƟon to pass a resoluƟon OR adopt a moƟon to allow 
direct appointments. This resoluƟon or meeƟng minutes must 
be aƩached to each ballot vacancy ﬁling pursuant to state law. 
(NOTE: if only one eligible PC can vote in the caucus or there is 
not a quorum at the caucus or there is a Ɵe vote at the caucus, 
then the chair can ﬁll by direct appointment without the party 
organizaƟon’s permission.) 
 
The Libertarian Party is also enƟtled to ﬁll ballot vacancies 
where no candidate was nominated at their convenƟon. The 
party must ﬁle wriƩen noƟce with the county clerk about their 
intent to ﬁll ballot vacancies and for which oﬃce not later than 
10‐days before those vacancies can be ﬁlled. 
 
The deadline for the D/R party to ﬁll a ballot vacancy where no 
candidate ran in the primary AND to ﬁle the paperwork is 
NOON, July 3, 2023. The same noon, July 3rd deadline applies 
to the Libertarian Party. More informaƟon is available in the 
2023 ElecƟon Administrators’ Guidebook. 
 
Statewide VLM Post Card Mailer 
The ﬁrst card in the statewide VLM post card mailer will be 
dropped in the mail beginning May 5 and not later than May 
17, 2023. If card 1 is returned as undeliverable, then card 2, or 
the voter response card, will start dropping by June 23.  By late 
June, counƟes will likely start seeing their VLM Hoppers popu‐
lated with records to review and approve.  
 
Civix will be hosƟng two training opportuniƟes on the SVRS 
modules related to this eﬀort. Please plan for at least one per‐
son on your team to aƩend one of these trainings, which will 
be held at 3P ET on May 15 and 11A ET May 17, 2023. 
 
Finalizing ElecƟon Results in SVRS 
Please remember to update your ﬁnal elecƟon results in SVRS 
to include late‐arriving military and overseas voters and those 
provisional ballots that were counted. It is important that the 
results entered in to SVRS match the records in your cerƟﬁed 
elecƟon results ﬁle. Please do not skip this step in cerƟﬁcaƟon! 
 
LegislaƟve Summary 
As a reminder, IED publishes a legislaƟve summary each year, 
usually around the beginning of July, which will highlight the 
statutes impacted by bills from the most recent legislaƟve  
session. Previous versions going back to 1999 can be found 
under the ElecƟon Administrator’s Portal on the IED website.

Voluntary VoƟng System Guidelines (VVSG) are 
a set of speciﬁcaƟons and requirements 
against which voƟng systems can be tested to 
determine if they meet standards under  
federal guidelines. These standards are  
developed through the support and advice of a 
diverse number of stakeholders, including 
state and local elecƟon oﬃcials.  
 
While the Help America Vote Act (HAVA)  
mandates the EAC to develop and maintain 
these standards, adhering to the VVSG is  
voluntary except in select states that require it 
by law.  In Indiana, a voƟng system is required 
to meet the standards set forth in the VVSG 
but addiƟonal tesƟng against our state laws 
related to voƟng systems is performed by 
VSTOP. Their recommendaƟons are shared 
with the bi‐parƟsan Indiana ElecƟon  
Commission, who then cerƟﬁes the equipment 
for use in Indiana for a period of Ɵme, up to 
four years. 
 
On February 10, 2021, EAC Commissioners 
adopted the newest VVSG standard, version 
2.0. EnacƟng the VVSG 2.0 is an important step 
to enhance U.S. elecƟon security, which is a 
naƟonal security imperaƟve.   
 
Currently, no voƟng system is cerƟﬁed against 
the 2.0 standard—and that is to be expected. 
It takes Ɵme for voƟng system manufacturers 
to develop voƟng equipment that comply with 
the new standard and for tesƟng laboratories 
to be federal cerƟﬁed (VSTL). As of March 
2023, one system has been submiƩed to the 
EAC that is currently being tested to VVSG 2.0.  
 
This means the “old” VVSG standards, versions 
1.0 and 1.1, are being “deprecated,” meaning 
the older voƟng systems are no longer at the 
cuƫng edge of technology. However,  
deprecaƟon does NOT mean the voƟng  
systems are decerƟﬁed. This is an important 
disƟncƟon to make, if a consƟtuent engages in 
conversaƟon about the topic. 
 
VoƟng systems cerƟﬁed in Indiana, even those 
built against the VVSG 1.0 and 1.1 standards, 
are secure and will remain cerƟﬁed. Even if a 
voƟng system vendor chooses not to reapply 
for Indiana cerƟﬁcaƟon in the future, the  
legacy equipment maintained by counƟes  
remains cerƟﬁed but no alteraƟons to the 
equipment can be made by the vendor unless 
the vendor submits an applicaƟon to renew 
the cerƟﬁcaƟon. (IC 3‐11‐7‐15; IC 3‐11‐7.5‐5) 
 
Further, voƟng systems will not be decerƟﬁed 
by the EAC as the result of VVSG deprecaƟon. 
ElecƟon oﬃcials may conƟnue to use or  
procure voƟng systems that have been  
cerƟﬁed to VVSG 1.0 and 1.1 in accordance 
with state or local law, even once depreciaƟon 
occurs.  
 
While our state does not exclusively rely on 
EAC cerƟﬁcaƟon of voƟng systems, most, if not 
all, voƟng system vendors do seek cerƟﬁcaƟon 
from the EAC and undergo tesƟng at the  
federally accredited voƟng system tesƟng  
laboratories (VSTL).  As of November 2022, the 
VSTLs are fully accredited to test against the 
2.0 standard. But, the EAC will conƟnue to 
accept applicaƟons for voƟng systems to be 
tested against VVSG 1.0 and 1.1 unƟl Nov. 15, 
2023.  
 
AŌer that point, VVSG 1.0 and 1.1 will be  
deprecated, and all applicaƟons for voƟng 
systems to be newly cerƟﬁed by the EAC must 
be for VVSG 2.0 or limited maintenance  
modiﬁcaƟons to exisƟng EAC‐cerƟﬁed systems. 
Again, this does NOT mean voƟng systems that 
meet VVSG 1.0 or VVSG 1.1 standards will be  
decerƟﬁed for use. CounƟes will be able to use 
their exisƟng voƟng systems unƟl such a Ɵme 
the Indiana ElecƟon Commission decerƟﬁes 
the equipment pursuant to our state laws.  
 
 More informaƟon, including fact sheets on the 
topic, are available through the EAC’s website: 
hƩps://www.eac.gov/elecƟon‐oﬃcials/
voluntary‐voƟng‐system‐guidelines‐vvsg‐
deprecaƟon 
IN FOCUS: Federal Voluntary Voting System Guidelines & the Deprecation of Versions 1.0 & 1.1 
VR CORNER 
Out‐of‐State VR InformaƟon 
Occasionally the IED receives informaƟon from other states 
regarding voters from Indiana that appear to have moved and 
registered to vote in the new state. InformaƟon provided by 
these out‐of‐state jurisdicƟons is not suﬃcient by itself to 
move the voter’s registraƟon record to “cancelled.” Instead, 
you can request a copy of the voter’s registraƟon in the new 
state to see if there is language that authorizes cancellaƟon at 
a previous address. Or, you can send a statewide address  
mailing conﬁrmaƟon (SAMC) noƟce from SVRS to the voter, 
which allows the individual to update, conﬁrm, or cancel their 
registraƟon. And if the voter does not respond aŌer 30‐days or 
the card is returned as undeliverable, you can move the status 
to “inacƟve,” if outside of a freeze period. Or, mail the VRG‐14 
cancellaƟon noƟce to the voter, which will allow the individual 
to cancel their Indiana registraƟon when returned to you. Re‐
member, in these instances, you must have authorizaƟon, in 
wriƟng from the voter, to move the registraƟon record to 
“cancelled” status unless you send the SAMC that may iniƟate 
the acƟve to inacƟve to cancelled workﬂow over two general 
elecƟons. 
 
RetenƟon Schedule for VR Records 
IED recently learned the state’s record retenƟon schedule for 
county oﬃces has out‐of‐date informaƟon regarding the reten‐
Ɵon of voter registraƟon records. We are working to get that 
corrected, but in the meanƟme, be sure to follow IC 3‐10‐1‐
31.1 and review pages 66 & 67 of the purple VR Guidebook. 
QUESTIONS OF THE MONTH  
 
Q. Do D & R candidates running for a small town oﬃce in 
those towns holding a town convenƟon to nominate for 
the November elecƟon also have to meet the two primary 
vote history requirement? 
A. No. When the law was updated a few years ago to require 
candidates running in the D or R primary to have a voƟng 
history where the last two primaries in Indiana in which the 
person voted be the same as the party they are aﬃliaƟng on 
the primary ballot, the “small town” candidate statutes were 
overlooked. This means candidates seeking nominaƟon in 
2023 in a small town (that is, those candidates that can ﬁle 
to run for oﬃce up to noon, August 1, 2023) only need to 
have a vote history where the last primary in Indiana in 
which the candidate voted be of the same party in which the 
candidate is seeking nominaƟon. HEA1336, once it becomes 
law, will update the “small town” candidate secƟon of the 
law to require the two primary vote history aŌer December 
31, 2023. 
 
Q. What about D & R candidates looking to ﬁll ballot  
vacancies ‐ do they need the two primary voƟng history 
requirement?  
A. No. The primary voƟng history requirement only applies 
to candidates running in the D or R primary elecƟon. The 
county party chair or party caucus ﬁlls the ballot vacancies,  
and this would be a group of individuals who would know 
which candidate would best represent their party on the 
ballot.

Election Division Dispatch 
 Brad King & Angie Nussmeyer, Co-Directors | June 2023—Revised  
NEWS & UPDATES 
Paper Supply & Upcoming ElecƟons in 2023, 2024 
IED has learned that paper supply may again be in short 
order for this fall’s elecƟon as well as next year’s elecƟon.  
CISA (Cybersecurity & Infrastructure Security Agency) is 
working with their printer partners on the Sector  
CoordinaƟng Council to understand the supply chain issues 
and compeƟƟon for resources. Please make sure you are 
engaging with your voƟng system and other paper‐related 
vendors to place orders for November and start esƟmaƟng 
for 2024. 
 
Statewide VLM Post Card Mailer Updates 
Voter Response Cards (or card 2) will start being mailed on 
or around June 23, 2023, to those voters where card 1 was  
returned as undeliverable. The postage pre‐paid card allows 
the voter to conﬁrm their registraƟon address, update their 
registraƟon within the county, or cancel their Indiana  
registraƟon. 
 
Voters receiving a card 2 will have at least 30‐days’ noƟce 
to respond before their registraƟon record status will be 
moved to inacƟve status. All VRCs must be received by Au‐
gust 31, 2023, in order for the state’s vendor to sort and 
organize the returns into SVRS hoppers for county oﬃcials 
to review and accept or reject. Expect to see data popu‐
laƟng in the VLM Hoppers in late June through the begin‐
ning of Sept. It is important to stay on top of all your hop‐
pers, especially the inacƟve hopper, because the “freeze” 
period begins on Oct. 11. 
 
May Primary ElecƟon Recounts 
AŌer the May primary, several counƟes reported to IED 
that a recount lawsuit was ﬁled. Since this is a legal  
proceeding, the CEB and clerk play no signiﬁcant role.  
However, someone is generally are on‐hand to pull records 
or other materials the three‐member local Recount  
Commission and the parƟes may need to review.  
 
The local Recount Commission will bring back their ﬁndings 
to the judge, who has unƟl the ﬁnal Friday in June (or June 
30, 2023) to ﬁnalize the recount. The judge may extend this 
deadline if there is good cause to do so. (IC 3‐12‐6‐21.9) If 
the recount cerƟﬁcate changes the cerƟﬁed results, then 
the clerk will need to make a correcƟon. This will require a 
CAF to be ﬁled in SVRS to unlock the reporƟng module to 
make those updates. AddiƟonally, a revised copy of the 
elecƟon results will need to be ﬁled with the CEB minutes at 
a future meeƟng. (IC 3‐12‐6‐30; IC 3‐6‐12‐31) 
InformaƟon in this newsleƩer is provided by the Indiana ElecƟon Division as a courtesy to county elecƟon administrators. If a person is unclear concerning elecƟon law provisions,

IN FOCUS: VLM Project SVRS Hoppers 
VR CORNER 
GIS Tool & Voter Assignments 
Summer is a good time for VR officials to evaluate whether 
voters are assigned to the proper precinct and split to prep for 
future elections. This is particularly important since the state 
and local governments have completed redistricting after the 
2020 Census. The state has partnered with GeoConvergence to 
offer a GIS module that allows counties to take data from SVRS 
and plot individual voter coordinates onto the state’s official 
precinct shapefile. Those voter “points” that are in the wrong 
precinct can then be reassigned to the correct precinct, or 
those with wrong coordinates can be assigned the correct co‐
ordinates. When all corrections are complete, the county can 
download a file from the GIS module and upload to SVRS to 
make those corrections on the voter records.  
 
If your county needs access to the GIS module, please email 
support@sess.cloud. Training materials can be found on the 
INSVRS County Portal. 
QUESTIONS OF THE MONTH  
 
Q. When a caucus is called to ﬁll a ballot vacancy, does a 
CAN‐12 (statement of economic interests) need to be 
ﬁled at the same Ɵme as the CAN‐48 (declaraƟon of can‐
didacy) to ﬁll a ballot vacancy? 
A. No. The CAN‐12 does not need to be ﬁled with the CAN‐
48 when a candidate comes to ﬁle their declaraƟon with 
the clerk’s oﬃce 72‐hours before the caucus. Instead, the 
CAN‐12 is ﬁled with the CAN‐49 (cerƟﬁcate of candidate 
selecƟon to ﬁll ballot vacancy). 
Q. Our oﬃce received undeliverable card 1s (or card 2 or 
voter response card). What should we do with those? 
A. Please mail them back to the state’s PO Box listed on 
the speciﬁc card. You should be able to write “Return to 
Sender” for those to be directed back to the PO Box. It’s 
important that the info on those cards be properly  
documented. 
Now that the ﬁrst VLM postcard has 
been mailed to more than 4.2 million 
acƟve Hoosier voters, a few hundred 
thousand of those “card 1’s” are being 
returned to the state as USPS undeliver‐
able. This return requires IED to mail a 
Card 2, which includes a detachable, 
postage‐paid voter response card (VRC).  
 
The VRC allows the voter to conﬁrm 
their registraƟon is correct (oval 1),  
authorize cancellaƟon due to a move 
out of county (oval 2), or update their 
registraƟon within the county (oval 3). 
When the VRC is received by IED on or 
before August 31, 2023, it is reviewed 
and placed in the proper data “silo” so 
that the informaƟon can be made  
available to counƟes in one of the  
following four hoppers: 
 
1) CANCEL HOPPER: if a voter has 
marked oval 2 to authorize  
cancellaƟon of their registraƟon 
record and signed the VRC, the  
person’s name will appear in the 
cancel hopper. Records in the  
cancel hopper may be reviewed  
individually or processed in a batch. 
  
2) INACTIVE HOPPER: If a voter does 
not respond to the second mailing 
by August 31, 2023, OR Card 2 is  
returned as undeliverable, OR the 
voter fails to sign the VRC to make 
their changes eﬀecƟve, the record 
will appear in the inacƟve hoper. 
This hopper will have records early 
in the process, but expect the bulk 
to come on or aŌer Sept. 1, 2023, 
as the “no response” individuals will 
be loaded in bulk. Records in the 
inacƟve hopper can be reviewed 
individual or processed in batch. 
 
3) UPDATE HOPPER: If a voter marked 
oval 3 to update their registraƟon 
address within the county,  
answered the age & ciƟzenship 
quesƟon, and signed the VRC, then 
the record is placed in the update 
hopper. Records in the update hop‐
per must be reviewed individually 
by a county user. Special aƩenƟon 
should be made to review the card 
for a name change, which was a 
new addiƟon to the VRC card for 
the 2019 mailing.  
 
4) EXCEPTION HOPPER: SomeƟmes a 
VRC will be returned with  
conﬂicƟng informaƟon, like ovals 2 
& 3 marked, or oval 3 marked for an 
update and signed, but the voter 
failed to answer the age & ciƟzen‐
ship quesƟons. Records like these 
go to the VLM excepƟon hopper 
and require a county admin to  
review the record to determine the 
best path forward based on state 
and federal law. (County  
Admins are the only persons who 
have access to this hopper) 
 
The Step‐By‐Step document includes 
the business rules adopted by the state 
to direct how a response on a VRC 
should be categorized in the data “silos” 
and may be helpful to a county user to 
beƩer understand why a speciﬁc record 
ended up in a speciﬁc hopper. 
 
So what happens to a voter who marks 
oval 1 (address conﬁrmaƟon) and signs 
the VRC? No acƟon is taken on their 
record, which will not be directed to 
any hopper for county review. Howev‐
er, you can view the VRC in the Image 
Viewer and an image of the VRC will be 
aƩached to the voter’s documents in 
SVRS. 
 
In fact, you can search the image  
viewer for scanned images of the VRC 
or cards returned as undeliverable and 
those images will be aƩached to the 
individual’s voter record in SVRS.  
However,  there will be a message 
staƟng that no image is available when 
a person does not respond to the  
second mailing.

Election Division Dispatch 
 Brad King & Angie Nussmeyer, Co-Directors | July 2023 
NEWS & UPDATES 
Statewide VLM Post Card Mailer Updates 
Voter response card data is hiƫng county VLM hoppers for 
VR oﬃcials to review and process. Voters are to return their 
response card not later than Aug. 31, 2023, to be processed 
and uploaded to county hoppers for review. CounƟes were 
also recently noƟﬁed about the dates to receive shipments 
of the physical cards later this fall and winter.  
 
2023 LegislaƟve Summary 
The 2023 LegislaƟve Summary has been released and is 
now available online under the ElecƟon Administrators’ 
Portal on in.gov/sos/elecƟons. If you did not aƩend the 
State Board of Accounts meeƟng at the end of June (or did 
and did not get a copy of the presentaƟon), you can ﬁnd the 
IED presentaƟons on the same page. 
 
Revised Absentee ApplicaƟons 
Except for the FPCA, all absentee applicaƟons ‐ Mail, Travel‐
ing Board, VPD, AƩorney General, In‐Person ‐ have been 
revised to include the new voter ID requirement to apply 
for an absentee ballot. Older versions of the form are not 
grandfathered, so only the new absentee form can be ac‐
cepted for review and approval on or aŌer July 1, 2023.  
 
“Small” Town Filing Deadline 
For those “small” towns that do not hold primary elecƟons, 
the ﬁling deadline for the CAN‐16/CAN‐12 is noon, August 
1, 2023. A town nominaƟng convenƟon, which replaces the 
primary elecƟon, is only permiƩed if there is a contest for 
an oﬃce within the poliƟcal party. More informaƟon about 
town convenƟons and its procedures are found in the  
orange 2023 Town ElecƟon Guidebook. Remember,  
candidates using the CAN‐16 form are not able to withdraw 
for any reason aŌer noon, August 1, 2023. PoliƟcal parƟes 
cannot ﬁll a ballot vacancy when no D/R/L candidate ﬁled to 
run for a “small” town oﬃce where no primary is held. 
 
2024 ReprecincƟng Now Open 
IED emailed a reprecincƟng memo to county elecƟon  
oﬃcials on June 27, which includes noƟce of two important 
deadlines. The ﬁrst is to respond to a quick survey by noon, 
July 28, 2023, to let IED know if your county commissioners 
are considering changes to precinct boundaries to be  
eﬀecƟve for the 2024 elecƟon cycle. (There is no need to 
respond if your county has no plans to reprecinct, but it is 
helpful to respond if there is a chance your county might do 
so.) Staﬀ will be assigned to counƟes that respond to the 
survey, to assist with ﬁling the IEC‐8 and other required  
paperwork by the Sept. 27, 2023, deadline. 
InformaƟon in this newsleƩer is provided by the Indiana ElecƟon Division as a courtesy to county elecƟon administrators. If a person is unclear concerning elecƟon law provisions,  
the ElecƟon Division can serve as an interpreƟve source. However, where important legal rights are concerned, you must consult with your own aƩorney to be fully and properly advised.

IN FOCUS: Legislative Changes to Absentee Voting Effective July 1 
The Indiana General Assembly made 
signiﬁcant changes to the absentee 
voƟng process, which begins on July 1, 
2023. As noted in the “News & Up‐
dates” column, IED has revised its ab‐
sentee applicaƟons and those will be 
available on in.gov/sos/elecƟons in the 
ElecƟon Forms secƟon the week of July 
1.  Several key points in the legislaƟon 
are outlined below. 
Voter IdenƟﬁcaƟon on Paper ABS App 
All paper absentee applicaƟons (Mail, 
Traveling Board, In‐Person, AG, VPD) 
are updated to include a secƟon to  
request the voter provide idenƟﬁcaƟon 
to authenƟcate the individual. Voters 
have two opƟons: 
1: Provide at least one of the following: 
 A/ Indiana Driver’s License Number 
 B/ Indiana ID Card Number 
 C/ Last four of Social Security  
Number 
 D/ SVRS –generated ID for voters 
who registered to vote without A‐C 
above; OR 
2: Include a copy of the voter’s valid 
photo ID that complies with the state’s 
photo ID law (IC 3‐5‐2‐40.5). A voter can 
aƩach an image to an emailed  
applicaƟon or include it with their fax. 
If the voter provides an ID number 
listed in opƟon #1, then the county will 
conﬁrm the number matches the vot‐
er’s registraƟon record as part of the bi‐
parƟsan review and approval process.  
If the voter provides a DLN/ID number 
or SSN and the number provided is NOT 
on their registraƟon, the ABS module in 
SVRS will allow counƟes to ping the 
BMV to validate the informaƟon. Once 
validated, this number, if not currently 
on the voter’s registraƟon record, will 
be added to it.  
(IED is working with Civix on this  
enhanced SVRS workﬂow—more details 
to come!)  
If the voter provides a copy of a valid ID 
in opƟon #2 that complies with the  
photo ID law, then there is no further 
acƟon. 
The voter ID informaƟon must be  
provided each Ɵme the voter requests 
an absentee ballot, unless the voter 
submits one of the three ongoing  
applicaƟons that need only to be sub‐
miƩed once in a calendar year (Jan. 1 to 
Dec. 31). 
Note: The voter ID requirement noted 
above applies to military and overseas 
voters requesƟng an absentee ballot on 
or aŌer July 1, 2023. The Federal Post 
Card ApplicaƟon (FPCA) is managed by 
the US Dept. of Defense and already 
includes ﬁelds for the voter’s DLN/ID 
card number and last four of the SSN to 
validate the voter’s idenƟty when  
requesƟng an absentee ballot. 
Indianavoters.com ABS Submission 
Voters accessing the ABS‐
Mail, ABS‐
Traveling Board, and ABS‐VPD forms to 
submit electronically through indi‐
anavoters.com will have expanded ID 
opƟons to access the forms. 
 
Currently, the voter is prompted to  
provide their Indiana driver’s license or 
ID card number or the last four of the 
voter’s Social Security Number (or 
prompts the voter to give one or the 
other, if both numbers happen to be on 
their record and the voter can choose 
which one to enter). If the voter does 
not have a matching number, then the 
person can provide their Indiana 
 credenƟal (DLN or ID) number, which is 
added to the voter’s record as a correc‐
Ɵon. Once that work is done on the 
county‐side, the voter can access the 
absentee applicaƟon to submit elec‐
tronically. 
New law provides that the voter can 
provide any of the four voter ID  
numbers noted above. If the number is 
not on the registraƟon record but is 
validated aŌer the BMV check, then the 
number is added to the voter’s  
registraƟon record. Once the correcƟon 
is made by county VR oﬃcials, then the 
voter can access the applicaƟon. 
Voters will not be able to upload a copy 
of their ID when using the online ABS 
applicaƟon on indianavoters.com to 
submit their request electronically. 
ABS‐Mail Defect NoƟce  
CounƟes should prepare for a slight 
change when reviewing ABS applica‐
Ɵons. All absentee ballot applicaƟons 
will conƟnue to be reviewed by the bi‐
parƟsan absentee voter board, the 
county elecƟon board, or the board’s 
designees. If the applicaƟon is  
approved, then the voter will be sent 
their absentee ballot.  
 
The change in the review process  
impacts ABS‐Mail applicaƟons that are 
rejected under the bi‐parƟsan review. If 
Example of the voter ID secƟon on revised ABS‐Mail forms 
 
an ABS‐Mail applicaƟon is rejected, 
then it is forwarded to the clerk, who 
then makes note of the defecƟve app 
and sends noƟce to the voter AND a 
new ABS‐Mail applicaƟon, IF the ABS‐
Mail applicaƟon is received not later 
than 13‐days before the elecƟon. (The 
law is silent on what happens on the 
12th day.) 
If the ABS‐Mail applicaƟon is received 
aŌer the 12th day deadline, then the 
voter’s ABS‐Mail app is simply rejected 
but a special noƟce must be sent to 
voter. 
Otherwise, if the other absentee ballot 
applicaƟon types are rejected, then 
counƟes will conƟnue to send the  
noƟce of disposiƟon to the voter, 
which is current pracƟce. 
An updated version of the ABS‐24 
(noƟce of disposiƟon for ABS apps) 
will be incorporated into SVRS to  
account for this change. 
Replacement ABS ApplicaƟons 
If a county receives an absentee app 
that is rejected or found defecƟve, it is 
possible for the county to send the 
county clerk and a bi‐parƟsan absen‐
tee voter board to the voter’s 
 residence with a replacement absen‐
tee applicaƟon and an absentee bal‐
lot, if the applicaƟon is reviewed and 
approved by the county clerk. 
 
CounƟes will need to respect the  
absentee applicaƟon deadlines. For 
example, a voter with a defecƟve ABS‐
Mail applicaƟon could not be sent a 
new ABS‐Mail applicaƟon once the 
ABS‐Mail deadline has passed. But, the 
voter may be eligible to vote by travel 
board, assuming that deadline has not 
passed. The clerk and bi‐parƟsan team 
could deliver the ABS‐Traveling Board 
applicaƟon and have an absentee  
ballot ready for compleƟon by the vot‐
er and returned by the bi‐parƟsan 
board, if the applicaƟon was approved 
on‐site. 
If a county clerk adopts this policy to 
provide replacement absentee  
applicaƟons and deliver an absentee 
ballot to the voter, then the county 
must be uniform and non‐
discriminatory in its applicaƟon. That 
is, what you do for one, you do for all! 
ConﬁdenƟal InformaƟon on ABS App 
As noted above, the validaƟon check 
of the voter ID numbers provided in 
opƟon #1 of the ABS form is pinged 
against the BMV. (The state is working 
with Civix to incorporate this  
validaƟon check in the ABS module.)
 
However, the credenƟal informaƟon 
provided by the BMV is conﬁdenƟal 
and may only be used for the purpose 
of matching the credenƟal informaƟon 
to a voter’s absentee applicaƟon, 
where it was not already exisƟng on 
the voter’s registraƟon record.  
As a result, the county voter  
registraƟon oﬃcial will need to redact 
the voter ID number provided in  
opƟon #1 on all ABS applicaƟons, if a 
public records request is made. 
Please note that the above require‐
ment does not extend to the voter ID 
number on the voter’s registraƟon 
record. Pursuant to state law, the  
voter ID number (DLN/ID number, last 
four of SSN, or SVRS‐generated ID 
number) is public informaƟon and 
would not be redacted if a request is 
made for the voter’s registraƟon rec‐
ord. The one excepƟon is to redact the 
voter’s 9‐digit SSN to the last four  
digits, if applicable. 
AddiƟonally, if the voter provides a 
copy of their photo ID with their ABS 
app in opƟon #2, the copy of their ID is 
conﬁdenƟal and would not be  
provided if requested in a public  
records request. 
Temporary Status from BMV info 
When counƟes enter  credenƟal  
number provided in opƟon #1 on an 
absentee applicaƟon, the data is sent 
to the BMV to validate. As part of this  
process, the data will include whether 
the person has a temporary credenƟal 
under IC 9‐24‐11‐5(c) or IC 9‐24‐16‐3
(f), which refers to an individual who 
holds a temporary immigraƟon status 
as described in that statute. (This 
should not to be confused with the 
temporary paper credenƟal given unƟl 
the oﬃcial driver’s license or ID card is 
sent by mail). 
 
This is a "point in Ɵme" veriﬁcaƟon, 
captured at the Ɵme of the credenƟal 
applicaƟon, and may not reﬂect the 
individual's true status or eligibility to 
register to vote. Records with this indi‐
cator reﬂect one of the following cir‐
cumstances: 
 Individuals who are not US ciƟzens 
and have temporary lawful status 
 Individuals who are not US ciƟzens 
and have lawful permanent status 
 Individuals who may be US ciƟzens 
and whose lawful status could not 
be determined at the Ɵme of the 
transacƟon and veriﬁcaƟon is 
pending. 
AddiƟonal research is required by the 
elecƟon oﬃcial to determine the  
individual's eligibility to vote. IED is 
working with the BMV to develop an 
SOP about this document type. 
Mailing ABS ApplicaƟons 
An agency of the state or a poliƟcal 
subdivision (for example, IED, county, 
city, town, township, school corpora‐
Ɵon, etc.) may only mail any type of 
absentee ballot applicaƟon to an indi‐
vidual who requests the applicaƟon 
for themselves or their family  
members (meaning their spouse, par‐
ent, father‐in‐law, mother‐in‐law, 
child, son‐in‐law, daughter‐in‐law, 
grandparent, grandchild, brother,  
sister, brother‐in‐law, sister‐in‐law, 
uncle, aunt, nephew, or niece). 
 
This limitaƟon does not apply to any 
private individual, poliƟcal party, or 
other enƟty providing an absentee 
ballot applicaƟon to another  
individual. AddiƟonally, government 
forms, like the absentee applicaƟon, 
must sƟll be made available to an  
individual, poliƟcal party, or other  
enƟty appearing in person to request 
copies of the blank form.  
IN FOCUS, con’t 
VR CORNER 
 
VRG‐21 Filing Date Changes in Odd‐Numbered Years 
The state law regarding the filing of the VRG‐21 form was up‐
dated to reflect the later freeze period before odd‐numbered 
primary and general elections; that is, 29‐days before election 
day versus the 90‐day freeze period that applies before federal 
elections, such as the 2024 presidential election. Before the 
November 2023 election, the VRG‐21 must be sent to IED by 
email, mail, or fax not later than noon, October 23, 2023. 
 
Petition Signatures & Partial Precincts 
For those Independent and minor party candidates running for 
an office where the election district is made up of one partial 
precinct, state law now sets the number of valid petition  
signatures of voters living in the district at five, since there was 
no way to calculate the required number of signatures using 
the 2% model in a partial precinct. This change applies to the 
November 2023 election! (Do not confuse this with the re‐
quirements for school board candidates, which have their own 
statutes setting for the minimum signature requirements). 
 
More Signature Types Can Be Used on VR Record 
Now counties can use more types of signatures to update the 
“main” signature on the voter’s registration record in SVRS, 
including the signatures used on a poll list, a voter registration 
application, SAMC, VRG‐14, or an absentee ballot application.  
 
Update Coming to the VRG‐4/12 
A change in state law will require the VRG‐4/12 to include an 
affidavit for the voter in cancelled status to confirm they con‐
tinue to reside at their registration address. When used with 
an absentee ballot application, this confirmation will  
return the voter’s status to “active” and an absentee ballot can 
be issued, if the voter is otherwise qualified. (On Election Day, 
current procedures are in effect; that is, the voter in cancelled 
status makes an oral or written affirmation that they continue 
to reside at their registration address and the voter is given a 
regular ballot, if otherwise qualified.) This law is effective July 
1, so look for updated forms from IED soon. 
 
Non‐Residential Address Warning in SVRS 
SVRS will include a feature that identifies potential non‐
residential addresses submitted on VR applications. However, 
this feature is not, by itself, sufficient evidence to reject a VR 
request. VR officials will need to research to determine if the 
applicant could reside at the address or if it is a non‐traditional 
address such as a recreational vehicle or a homeless shelter.  
 
Out‐of‐State Registration Information 
Our voter list maintenance statute related to receiving out‐of‐
state information was clarified to note that the letter from the 
other state is not sufficient to move the voter’s registration 
status to cancelled. The update notes that the Indiana VR  
official can request the voter’s registration in their new state 
to confirm the form used authorized cancellation in another 
state. If it does, then the voter’s  status is moved to cancelled. 
If not, or if the county does not want to perform the outreach, 
a SAMC can be sent to the voter OR the VRG‐14, which allows 
the voter to authorize cancellation in writing. 
QUESTIONS OF THE MONTH  
 
Q. If a voter has already ﬁled an approved ongoing absentee 
applicaƟon, such as the FPCA or ABS‐VPD form, are they 
required to submit a new request to comply with the voter 
ID changes? 
A. No, if the county had already reviewed AND approved the 
ongoing applicaƟon before July 1, 2023. If the ongoing form 
was received or approved on or aŌer July 1, 2023, then the 
voter will need to comply with the new voter ID requirement. 
 
Q. Are poliƟcal parƟes or other third party organizaƟons 
limited like county clerk’s oﬃces on mailing absentee  
applicaƟons just to voters and their family members? 
A. No. While state agencies and local units of government can 
only mail an absentee applicaƟon to a voter or a voter’s fami‐
ly member, poliƟcal parƟes, individuals, or other third party 
organizaƟons do not have this restricƟon. A reminder that 
disclaimer rules, including who mailed the applicaƟon and 
that it was unsolicited, do apply. The blue 2023 ElecƟon  
Administrators’ Manual has more details. 
 
Q. Can our staﬀ in the clerk’s oﬃce or elecƟon board mail 
ABS‐Traveling Board applicaƟons to nursing homes as re‐
quested by their employees for their residents? 
A. The change in state law eﬀecƟve July 1, 2023, only permits 
government oﬃces like the clerk’s oﬃce to send an absentee 
applicaƟon to the voter or a member of the voter’s family 
(spouse, parent, father‐in‐law, mother‐in‐law, child, son‐in‐
law, daughter‐in‐law, grandparent, grandchild, brother, sister, 
brother‐in‐law, sister‐in‐law, uncle, aunt, nephew, or niece). 
Unless the nursing home staﬀ person calling your oﬃce is 
related to the resident as described above, the clerk’s oﬃce 
cannot mail a packet of blank absentee applicaƟons to the 
nursing home as requested by staﬀ. They should be  
redirected to online resources or to ask the resident to con‐
tact your oﬃce directly. 
 
Q. If we use ePollbooks for early voƟng (that is, in‐person 
absentee voƟng at the clerk’s oﬃce or satellite locaƟon), do 
we need to also perform the voter ID credenƟal check as we 
would on a paper applicaƟon? 
A. No. CounƟes using ePBs for early voƟng check‐in simply 
need to review the voter’s photo ID for compliance with the 
photo ID law before processing the voter and providing them 
an absentee ballot to vote in‐person. 
 
Q. Can candidates withdraw aŌer noon, July 17, 2023 and 
the party ﬁll the ballot vacancy? 
A. Yes. A candidate can withdraw for any reason and ﬁle the 
CAN‐46 up to noon, July 17, 2023. However, any candidate 
that dies, moves out of the elecƟon district, is challenged and 
removed, convicted of a felony, or ordered oﬀ the ballot by a 
judge are required to withdraw, even if this acƟon occurs a 
day before the elecƟon. Early ballot vacancies happen up to 
30‐days before elecƟon day and allow the party to ﬁll the 
vacancy not later than 30‐days from the date the vacancy 
occurred. (IC 3‐13‐1) Late ballot vacancies occur in the ﬁnal 
30‐days and can be ﬁlled under IC 3‐13‐2.

IN FOCUS: Small Town Nominating Conventions 
In Indiana, the DemocraƟc, Libertarian, 
and Republican parƟes in “small” towns 
(populaƟon of less than 3,500 according 
to the 2020 census) may need to  
nominate candidates for the November 
ballot at a town convenƟon held in late 
summer.  
This convenƟon replaces the May primar y 
elecƟon, unless the small town’s council 
passed an ordinance for the county  
elecƟon board to conduct a primary  
elecƟon back in May. A “small” town 
nominaƟng convenƟon is not a caucus 
nor a primary elecƟon nor the municipal 
elecƟon. Instead, it’s how the DemocraƟc, 
Republican, and Libertarian parƟes  
nominate their candidates for the  
November ballot (where all candidates go 
head‐to‐head to determine who is  
elected to serve a speciﬁc term in oﬃce). 
The candidate ﬁling deadline for “small” 
town oﬃces (where no primary elecƟon 
was held) is noon, August 1, 2023. This is 
also the deadl
ine for a candidate who 
ﬁled the CAN‐16/CAN‐12 to withdraw 
their candidacy for “small” town oﬃce 
with one excepƟon noted later. 
The county’s poliƟcal parƟe s will then 
determine if a nominaƟng convenƟon is 
necessary. A convenƟon is only held if 
more individuals from the same  
poliƟcal party ﬁle to run for the same 
oﬃce than there are seats to ﬁll. For  
example, town dogcatcher is one race. 
Two Democrats ﬁled to run; one  
Republican ﬁled. The DemocraƟc Party 
must hold a town convenƟon, while the 
Republican Party will not. 
SomeƟmes more than one 
 person can be 
elected to a posiƟon, usually in at‐large 
council seats. Let’s say in a vote‐for‐three 
small town oﬃce that four Republicans 
ﬁle and two Democrats ﬁle. In this  
example, the Republican Party would 
hold a convenƟon to determine which of 
their four candidates will be one of three 
nominees; the DemocraƟc Party would 
not hold a convenƟon since fewer than 
three people ﬁled. The orange 2023 Town 
ElecƟon Guidebook contains the steps to  
conduct a small town convenƟon. In a 
nutshell, the county party chair  
nominates a registered voter of the town 
who is not a candidate or an elected  
oﬃcial of the town to serve as the town 
party chair. The town party chair then 
selects a registered voter of the town to 
serve as the party’s secretary. The  
secretary will also serve as secretary of 
the “small” town convenƟon. 
The town chair and secretary must then 
post the call 
to convenƟon (CAN‐15)  
noƟce in at least three prominent  
locaƟons, including the town clerk‐
treasurer’s oﬃce, at least three days  
before the convenƟon is to be held and 
ﬁle the CAN‐15 with the circuit court 
clerk. 
Any registered voter within the town may 
parƟcipate
 in one party’s convenƟon, as 
long as the person meets the  
requirements under state law and the 
poliƟcal party’s rules. It is a misdemeanor 
to knowingly vote in more than one town 
party convenƟon. 
The Town E
lec Ɵon Guidebook walks 
through many of the steps to help town 
party chairs conduct their convenƟon. 
The town chairs should also consult state 
party rules, as Indiana elecƟon law does 
defer to party rules in some instances.  
(Sample rules are in the orange book, but 
our best advice is to get the current  
informaƟon directly from the state party.) 
All small town nominaƟng c
 onvenƟons 
must be held not later than August 21, 
2023. AŌerward, the town party chair and 
town party secretary will cerƟfy the  
nominees to the county clerk’s oﬃce  
using the CAN‐18 form. The CAN‐18 must 
be ﬁled for each candidate not later than 
noon (local prevailing Ɵme), August 28, 
2023. 
A candidate nominated at a small town 
convenƟon m
ay withdraw not later than 
noon (local prevailing Ɵme), three days 
following the adjournment of the  
convenƟon. The poliƟcal party may ﬁll the 
ballot vacancy if this occurs, but  
generally, no other ballot vacancies for 
“small” town oﬃce can be ﬁlled. For  
example, the DemocraƟc Party only ﬁlls 
two of the three at‐large council seats. 
The party is not able to ﬁll the remaining 
open seat aŌer the noon, August 1, 2023, 
ﬁling deadline. However, there are special 
cases when ﬁlling a vacancy is permiƩed. 
See IC 3‐13‐1‐7(b). 
The county clerk must then ﬁle a copy of 
each CAN‐18 ﬁlling a ballot 
vacancy with 
the town clerk‐treasurer not later than 
noon (local prevailing Ɵme), September 5, 
2023.  
VR CORNER 
What roles does the county voter registraƟon oﬃcial play in a small town 
convenƟon? The county does not play a formal role if the county party  
determines that a convenƟon is necessary to determine who will be the  
party’s nominee for “small” town oﬃce on the November ballot. 
BUT, the county VR oﬃcial  does need to provide to the town party chair 
and town party secretary a report with the name and registraƟon date of 
each individual within the municipality. Those reportscan be pulled from 
SVRS.  
The county VR oﬃcial does not upload any voƟng history from the town  
convenƟon. This may seem confusing, but the county would not upload 
voƟng history from a state or naƟonal party convenƟon held in even‐
numbered years, and the “small” town convenƟon is a similar type of  
nominaƟng process. However, voƟng history is  a public record and availa‐
ble for inspecƟon upon request. 
QUESTIONS OF THE MONTH 
Q. Can a candidate nominated in the May primary
elecƟon be cha
llenged now?
A. No. The op
portunity to ﬁle a CAN‐1 challenge against a
DemocraƟc or Republican 
candidate who ﬁled a CAN‐42 to run
as a local candidate for the May primary elecƟon has passed.
There may be other legal opƟons to explore, b
ut the CAN‐1
hearing bef
ore the CEB is not one of them.
Q. Can candidates who ﬁlled a ballot vacancy or those who
were cerƟﬁed 
as an independent/minor party candidate be
challenged?
A
. Yes,
 though the deadlines to ﬁle a CAN‐1 challenge are
staggered depending 
on the type of ﬁling. Please consult the
yellow Ind
iana ElecƟon Calendar: ElecƟon Administrator’s
EdiƟon for those details, as some dates go into September.
Q. Does our county need to hold an elecƟon in November?
A
. Maybe. Similar to the May primary elecƟon
, a November
elecƟon may not be required. 
Please see IC 3‐10‐6‐7.5 for ciƟes
and “large” t
owns; IC 3‐10‐7‐6 for “small” towns. The CEB will
need to unanim
ously agree on a resoluƟon to not hold an
elecƟon,
 however, if there are no contested oﬃces.
Q. When does a small town council need to pass a resoluƟon
to conduct its own November 
elecƟon and when does it need
to be ﬁled?
A. A “sma
ll” town council must adopt a resoluƟon to conduct its
own November elecƟon not lat
er than August 8, 2023, and ﬁle it
with the county clerk not later than noon (local prevailing Ɵme),
August 21, 2023. (IC 3‐10‐7‐5.5) The resoluƟon expires on
December 31, 2023.
Q. Our small town adopted a resoluƟon in 2019 to conduct its
own November elecƟon. Can the same resoluƟon be used
again in 2023?
A. No. A re
soluƟon adopted by a “small” town council to
conduct its own November elecƟon expires on December 31 in
the year it was adopted. Therefore, the town council will need
to pass a new resoluƟon for 2023. An outdated resoluƟon
cannot be used by the town as jusƟﬁcaƟon to c
onduct their
November elecƟon (with the e
xcepƟon of a few small towns
that have special procedures u
nder “grandfathered” state laws).
Q. What happens if a “small” town doesn’t pass a
resoluƟon to conduct its own elecƟon by Aug
ust 8 or ﬁles it
with the clerk aŌer the noon, August 21 deadline?
A
. In this scenario,
 state law requires the county elecƟon board
to conduct the 
small town’s November elecƟon. The town will
reimburse the c
ounty for the cost of the elecƟon.
Q. Is there anything the clerk’s oﬃce needs to  do aŌer the
August 1, 2023, small town oﬃce ﬁling deadline?
A. Yes. Immediately followin
g candidate ﬁling, the county clerk
will need to p
ost a list of candidates who ﬁle for “small” town
oﬃce on your oﬃce’s public noƟce board, cerƟfy to the town
clerk‐treasurer (but only if the 
town is conducƟng its own
elecƟon) and re
lease a list to the public of each candidate who
ﬁled, and provide a copy of each CAN‐16 to the respecƟve town
clerk‐treasurer. (IC 3‐8‐5‐10.5) 
There are addiƟonal noƟce
requirements if
 a town is located in more than one county. (IC 3
‐8‐2‐6)
HOLDOVERS 
On occasion, no one ﬁles to run for an oﬃce on the November 
ballot. In these cases, the current oﬃceholder “holds over” for 
a new term of oﬃce pursuant to ArƟcle 15, SecƟon 3 of the 
Indiana ConsƟtuƟon. 
For example, Cardinal Town Council District 1 is on the ballot 
in November 2023. Julie is the currently elected councilor for 
district 1 and is currently serving a four‐year term. Not only 
did Julie not ﬁle paperwork to be a candidate, but also no one 
else in Cardinal Town ﬁled for the oﬃce. As a result, Julie  
conƟnues serving as the town council member for district 1 
for another four‐year term, unƟl her successor is elected and 
qualiﬁed. Because she is a “holdover” under state law, she 
does not ﬁle a new oath of oﬃce. 
CounƟes oŌen ask what happens if Julie didn’t ﬁle to run 
again because she doesn’t want to conƟnue serving? Julie may 
resign from elected oﬃce by ﬁling a wriƩen resignaƟon with 
the county clerk, and the elected oﬃce vacancy would be ﬁled 
according to statute. Depending on when the  
resignaƟon becomes eﬀecƟve, the individual selected as a 
“pro‐tem appointment” would serve: 
 the remainder of Julie’s current term and holdover for the
new term, if her resignaƟon was eﬀecƟve on or 
before
Decemb
er 31; OR
 The remainder of the new term of oﬃce, if Julie’s
resignaƟon wa
s eﬀecƟve on or aŌer January 1.
STATEWIDE VLM UPDATE 
The statewide VLM Mailing Project finishes this month with 
records being loaded for county review through early Dec. 
2023. The “freeze” period begins Oct. 10, 2023, and at that 
time, the VLM Inactive Hopper will be closed.  
During the first week of Sept., Civix will load the VLM Inactive 
hopp
er with those individuals that were sent a second mailing 
but did not return it by Aug. 31, 2023. Historically, about 
100,000+ individuals were in this universe so expect to see an 
increase in your VLM Inactive hopper in early September. 
Counties are strongly encouraged to complete their “inactive” 
moves by the Oct. 10 “freeze” deadline to avoid conflict with 
VRCs received after Aug. 31, which will continue to be  
uploaded to your other VLM hoppers. Because the VRC is 
treated like a voter registration form, counties can make the 
requested changes. But, it’s important that “inactive” be  
applied first so that the voter’s status can be moved back to 
active (confirming registration or updating within the county 
on the VRC) or to cancelled at the voter’s written request. 
The VLM Inactive hopper will be reopened after Nov. 7 and it, 
along wit
h other VLM Hoppers will close on Dec. 31, 2023. 
Finally, shipping deadlines previously communicated to  
counties 
are being changed and a new schedule will be shared. 
However, our vendor will contact the individual your county 
designated as their point person for delivery at least 24‐hours 
ahead of time to alert you to the delivery.

Election Division Dispatch 
 Brad King & Angie Nussmeyer, Co-Directors | September 2023 
NEWS & UPDATES 
August Build 
New features have been pushed to SVRS, including 
changes to mailing labels and to the ABS‐24 noƟce of 
disposiƟon. If you did not aƩend online training, please 
review the materials found on the INSVRS county portal, 
which includes a recording of the online training. 
 
The ABS‐24 is used to noƟfy a voter that their absentee 
applicaƟon was found defecƟve or rejected under new 
state law. This noƟce should be mailed to voters and, if 
an ABS‐Mail applicaƟon is found defecƟve, a new ABS‐
Mail applicaƟon sent to the voter. The training materials 
demonstrate the workﬂow funcƟons to ensure the prop‐
er box on the ABS‐24 is marked along with the reason 
the applicaƟon was rejected or found defecƟve. 
 
NoƟce of Public Test of VoƟng Systems 
State law requires a county elecƟon board to begin its 
test of  voƟng systems not later than the day before early 
voƟng occurs in the clerk’s oﬃce. (CounƟes are to follow 
the 28‐day start date, even if the CEB passed a resoluƟon 
to reduce in‐person absentee early voƟng hours under IC 
3‐11‐10‐26.5 for Nov. 2023 elecƟon.)  
 
NoƟce of the public test under the Open Door Law  
requires noƟce to be posted not later than 48‐hours  
before the public test, or Thurs., Oct. 5, 2023, for a test 
conducted on Oct. 10, 2023. Because the Open Door Law 
views the 48‐hours in business days and not calendar 
days, a county may not count the weekend or the holiday 
in its calculaƟon for posƟng noƟce. 
 
AddiƟonally, state elecƟon law requires noƟce of the 
public test to be published in the newspaper not later 
than 48‐hours before the test begins. This deadline is 
Oct. 8, 2023, for a public test held on Oct. 10, 2023. In 
this case, the Title 3 statute relies on calendar days, so 
the 48‐hours may include the weekend and holiday. 
There is never a penalty for publishing early! 
 
SomeƟmes a newspaper fails to publish noƟce of a public 
test, which does not require the CEB to reschedule it. 
State law permits a county where the newspaper failed 
to Ɵmely publish a noƟce to either 1) display the noƟce 
prominently in three locaƟons in the county or 2) post on 
the county’s website (IC 5‐3‐1‐2(k)).

IN FOCUS: Ballot Reprinting 
With absentee ballots being delivered to 
counƟes and mailed to voters this month, a 
common quesƟon our oﬃce receives is 
what do we do if we spot an error (or  
omission) or we have a candidate withdraw 
aŌer ballots are printed and the elecƟon 
coded on our voƟng systems. 
 
ERROR OR OMISSION 
If the CEB is alerted to an error or omission 
on a ballot, then one of two things can  
occur: 
 
1/ The CEB conducts a public meeƟng,  
discusses the issue, and agrees to correct 
and re‐print the ballot; OR 
 
2/ The CEB conducts a public hearing,  
noƟﬁes the parƟes that may have an  
interest in the error or omission, discusses 
the issue, takes tesƟmony, and decides if  
re‐prinƟng is necessary.  
 
If the hearing is conducted under #2 and no 
person ﬁles a wriƩen request to re‐print the 
ballots before the hearing ends, then the 
CEB may choose to reprint the ballots or 
not. However, if a person ﬁles a wriƩen 
request before the close of the hearing in 
opƟon #2, then the CEB must re‐print the 
ballot. 
 
There are a number of requirements to  
follow, if the county chooses to hold the 
hearing noted in opƟon #2. Please be  
certain to consult IC 3‐11‐2‐16 for those  
details. 
 
CANDIDATE WITHDRAWAL 
As noted below, ballot vacancies can be 
ﬁlled by county chairs up to the day before 
an elecƟon, if certain criteria are met. 
 
A CEB MUST re‐print a ballot if the county 
chair ﬁlls the vacancy not later than 5‐days 
before the elecƟon. If no replacement or 
“successor” candidate is found, then the 
CEB may re‐print the ballot to include the 
term “Candidate Deceased” or “No  
Candidate.”  If a ballot vacancy is ﬁlled  
within the last 5‐days before the elecƟon, 
then the CEB may re‐print the ballot but is 
not required to do so. (IC 3‐11‐3‐29.5) 
 
If a successor candidate’s name is NOT 
printed on the ballot, then only the straight 
party votes recorded for that oﬃce may be 
counted for the successor candidate. If the 
name is re‐printed on the ballot, then 
straight party votes AND the ballots where 
the successor candidate’s name appears 
may be counted. (In other words, any “old” 
ballots with the former candidate’s name 
may not be counted for the successor  
candidate, unless the voter used the 
straight party device.) 
 
This assumes the oﬃce is a “vote for 1” and 
not at‐large where more than one person 
can be elected. Straight party selecƟons do 
not apply to at‐large candidates where 
more than 1 person is elected. (IC 3‐12‐1‐7) 
 
VOTER OUTREACH 
A CEB is not required to inform voters of a 
defecƟve ballot, but are encouraged to do 
so. A voter should complete an ABS‐5 to 
request a new absentee ballot.  
 
If in‐person “early voƟng” has begun in the 
oﬃce, the voter may complete the ABS‐5, 
complete an ABS‐In Person applicaƟon (or 
sign ePollbook), and complete an in‐person 
ABS ballot. Or the person may receive a 
new ballot by mail or if needed, by travel 
board. If travel board is needed and the 
voter meets the travel board requirements, 
then the voter should complete a ABS‐
Traveling Board applicaƟon before sending 
the bi‐parƟsan team to deliver the  
replacement ballot. 
 
If the voter does not request a replacement 
ABS ballot, then the CEB may need to re‐
make the absentee ballot on ElecƟon Day, if 
the original ballot card cannot be read. 
Early Ballot Vacancy v. Late Ballot Vacancy 
 
For context, ballot vacancies are created because a person did not run for an oﬃce in the Dem. or Rep. party primaries (or, a D, R, or 
L candidate is nominated at a small town convenƟon and withdraws within the deadline), not ﬁlled by the Libertarian Party at their 
convenƟon, or a candidate withdrew for any reason up to noon, July 15 (or later, if the deadline falls on a weekend), in an elecƟon 
year. State law limits candidate withdrawal aŌer the applicable deadline to the following: the candidate dies, moves out of the elec‐
Ɵon district, was convicted of a felony, ordered oﬀ the ballot by a judge, or disqualiﬁed for other reasons. (IC 3‐8‐7‐28)  
 
Because candidate withdrawals can occur up to ElecƟon Day, state law contemplates two ballot vacancy periods: “EARLY” (any  
withdrawal up to and including 31‐days before an elecƟon) and “LATE” (any withdrawal in ﬁnal 30‐days before the elecƟon) . 
 
CounƟes are likely more familiar with early vacancies, which are ﬁlled pursuant to IC 3‐13‐1. The method by which an “early”  
vacancy is ﬁlled is for the chair to either call a caucus of eligible PCs or ﬁll by direct appointment if authorized by the party (or 
there’s only one or no eligible PC to vote in a caucus or, if applicable at the caucus, there is not a quorum or a Ɵe vote). An “early” 
vacancy must be ﬁlled within 30‐days aŌer the vacancy occurs, and the applicable paperwork ﬁled not later than noon, three days 
aŌer the vacancy is ﬁlled. Unless the candidate has passed away, the CAN‐46 form is used to withdraw, which starts the 30‐day 
clock to ﬁll the vacancy. An early vacancy can also occur due to the death of a candidate, a court order, or a successful challenge to 
a candidate. (IC 3‐13‐1‐17) 
 
The procedures in IC 3‐13‐2 are used to ﬁll a “late” ballot vacancy. For local oﬃce “late” ballot vacancies, the county chair ﬁlls it by 
direct appointment  and the cerƟﬁcate of candidate selecƟon ﬁled within three days. The Ɵming of when the cerƟﬁcate of candi‐
date selecƟon is ﬁled will impact whether or not a ballot is re‐printed. The ElecƟon Administrator’s Manual has more details. The 
CAN‐46 is used to withdraw, and other forms include CAN‐50 cerƟﬁcate of candidate selecƟon, the CAN‐48 and CAN‐12 completed 
by the candidate ﬁlling the vacancy. 
 
NOTE: Independent candidates who withdraw are not eligible to ﬁll a ballot vacancy, since independent candidates by deﬁniƟon do 
not aﬃliate with a poliƟcal party.

QUESTIONS OF THE MONTH 
Q. Where are at‐large candidates, where more than one 
person can be elected, placed on the ballot? 
A. At‐large candidates are NOW placed before the  
corresponding single member district seats, if applicable. 
This is a recent change in state law. Reminder: straight party 
selecƟons in the Nov. elecƟon do not apply for at‐large can‐
didates where more than one person is elected.  
 
Q. Do we need to put all candidates on the ballot if some 
races are uncontested? 
A. It depends. If all voters vote for an oﬃce in a city or town 
and the oﬃce is contested, then all oﬃces go on the ballot. If 
the only contested oﬃces on the ballot are NOT municipality
‐wide, then an elecƟon only needs to be held in those isolat‐
ed precincts with the contested oﬃce on the ballot if the CEB 
adopts a resoluƟon, by unanimous vote, only hold the  
elecƟon in the contested district. 
 
Q. Do we need write‐in lines on the ballot? 
A. For a municipal elecƟon year, a write‐in line for any oﬃce 
on the ballot is ONLY needed if the candidate ﬁled the CAN‐
51 form. If NO CAN‐51 Form is ﬁled for an oﬃce, then NO 
write‐in line should be included. (IC 3‐11‐2‐6(e)) 
 
Q. Do we need to include a poliƟcal party under the 
“Straight Party” secƟon of the ballot, if no candidate of the 
party has ﬁled to run in all of the vote‐for‐one oﬃces on the 
ballot for a precinct? 
A. No. See IC 3‐11‐13‐14 and IC 3‐11‐14‐14.5 
 
Q. How many ballots do we provide to each precinct or vote 
center on ElecƟon Day? 
A. For opƟcal scan counƟes, the county must provide blank 
ballot cards for ballot marking devices or printed opScan  
ballots totaling 100% of the total acƟve registered voters for 
each precinct. For DRE counƟes, the number of printed bal‐
lots necessary for emergency purposes. If your county has 
mulƟple precincts reporƟng to one polling locaƟon or are a 
vote center, then you must plan accordingly. (IC 3‐11‐3‐11) 
 
Q. Can an ABS‐Mail applicaƟon used in the Nov. elecƟon 
exclude the party choice box needed in a primary elecƟon? 
A. Yes. In the forms order signed by the co‐directors and  
noted on the Forms Master List provided to counƟes, it’s 
noted that a printer may remove the primary party choice 
box on the ABS‐Mail applicaƟon (both English and Spanish) 
used in a November elecƟon and renumber the secƟons. 
Further, the printer may print the ABS‐Mail applicaƟon por‐
trait or landscape. 
 
Q. Does the CEB enforce where or when yard signs are to be 
placed in and around our community? 
A. No but see IC 36‐1‐3‐11 and review local ordinances. The 
CEB would enforce whether or not a yard sign includes the 
proper “paid for” disclaimer language. If this is missing, then 
the CEB may ask that the signs be removed, disclaimer lan‐
guage added, or ﬁnd other approach the CEB believes is ap‐
propriate. See the “Disclaimer” brochure found at in.gov/
sos/elecƟons for more informaƟon. 
LEGAL NOTICES 
This fall counƟes need to publish the following noƟces ahead 
of the November elecƟon: 
 
1/ NoƟce of the Public Test of VoƟng Systems; 
2/ CAN‐39 NoƟce of General or Municipal ElecƟon; and 
3/ List of polling locaƟons used on ElecƟon Day 
 
The noƟce for the public test is covered extensively on page 1 
of the newsleƩer, so please refer back for those details. 
 
The CAN‐39 NoƟce includes the oﬃces on the ballot along 
with early voƟng dates and Ɵmes. Unlike the CAN‐9 NoƟce for 
the primary elecƟon, state law does NOT require the names of 
candidates and their address on the CAN‐39 form. If counƟes 
use SVRS to create the CAN‐39, they will  ﬁnd that the system 
does not include the candidate informaƟon. This noƟce must 
be published in the newspaper not later than 21‐days before 
the elecƟon! (Don’t forget that a copy of the CAN‐39 must be 
included in the CEB meeƟng minutes!) 
 
All county elecƟon boards are required to publish a list of all 
ElecƟon Day voƟng locaƟons in a newspaper not later than 21 
days from ElecƟon Day. The law recently changed to clarify 
the CEB (rather than the county commissioners) publishes 
noƟce in vote center counƟes; this has been the requirement 
for the CEB to publish noƟce in non‐vote  
center counƟes for years.  
 
Newspaper publicaƟon informaƟon is found in IC 5‐3, general‐
ly. Further, failure to publish these noƟces does not invalidate 
an elecƟon, but please do your part to ensure this important  
informaƟon is shared with voters.

Election Division Dispatch

NEWS & UPDATES 
 
September Build

enter provisional ballot informaƟon into SVRS before

are available to county users on the INSVRS County  
Portal. 
 
Annual ElecƟon Administrators’ Conference 
Don’t forget to register for the 2024 Conference!  
RegistraƟons received on or aŌer 11/17/23 will have a 
$50 per person late fee added to the conference fee. 
 
At each conference we like to recognize the good work 
of our colleagues across the state. The deadline to  
nominate in a variety of categories is Monday, November 
13, 2023. As a convenience, the nominaƟon forms are 
included with this month’s newsleƩer. 
 
Lastly, each registraƟon comes with a full set of books, 
but counƟes can submit an IEC‐7 and payment now to 
purchase addiƟonal Code Books and publicaƟons for pick
‐up at the conference. These materials will also be  
available for purchase at the conference while supplies 
last. 
 
ConƟnuity of OperaƟons Plan Resources 
The U.S. ElecƟon Assistance Commission (EAC) recently 
released a ConƟnuity of OperaƟons Plan (COOP) tem‐
plate and guidance document to assist elecƟon oﬃcials 
in creaƟng or reviewing their own COOP plans.    
ConƟngency planning acƟviƟes can help elecƟon oﬃcials 
prepare for unexpected circumstances, whether it’s a 
natural disaster, a pandemic, or something unknown. A 
COOP serves as one document that elecƟon oﬃcials can 
turn to in an emergency that has all the informaƟon 
needed to be able to carry on the essenƟal elecƟon func‐
Ɵons.  
 
For more informaƟon, templates, and resources visit 
eac.gov/elecƟon‐oﬃcials/conƟngency‐planning
