IN FOCUS: Election Equipment Delivery for Election Day 
The County ElecƟon Board is required to 
have the necessary voƟng systems and  
equipment required for a voter to cast a  
ballot not later than 6PM, the day before 
ElecƟon Day.  
 
ePOLLBOOKS 
ePollbooks are to be given to the inspector 
(or a person authorized in wriƟng by the  
inspector) on the Saturday before the  
elecƟon at the same Ɵme other elecƟon 
materials are picked up for use on ElecƟon 
Day. The CEB MUST seal ePBs  and provide a 
list of seal numbers with the PRE‐1 Oath 
Book. To assist with this process, counƟes 
can enter their seal numbers in SVRS and 
produce the Poll LocaƟon Seal Number 
tracking report out of the Reports Library. 
 
On ElecƟon Day, the inspector and opposite 
party judge will complete step #4 of the  
PRE‐1 Oath Book to conﬁrm the seal  
numbers listed in the oath book (or SVRS 
report, if applicable) are the same as the 
seal numbers on the ePBs used at their  
polling place and that the seals are not  
otherwise broken or tampered with. 
AlternaƟvely, if the county elecƟon board 
wants to secure their ePB in a diﬀerent 
manner than a plasƟc seal, state law allows 
them to unanimously agree to adopt a  
resoluƟon staƟng its policy and procedures 
for securing ePBs. However, the PRE‐1 Oath 
Book will sƟll be completed by poll workers 
to conﬁrm the ePB has not been tampered 
with prior to the polls opening. 
 
AŌer the polls close, the Inspector and 
judge of the opposite poliƟcal party are to 
complete the CEB‐1D and ﬁle it with the 
CEB to ensure the ePBs were safely and 
securely returned. 
 
VOTING SYSTEMS 
County elecƟon boards must either adhere 
to statutory requirements to seal voƟng 
systems aŌer the public test unƟl the  
elecƟon results canvass or other speciﬁc 
cases where access is necessary OR adopt a 
resoluƟon that sets forth its policy to secure 
voƟng systems from tampering throughout 
the year.  (IC 3‐11‐15‐46) 
 
VoƟng systems (DRE, opScan, ballot  
marking devices) are to be delivered by the 
CEB, a bi‐parƟsan team, OR a commercial  
delivery enƟty. (IC 3‐11‐3‐10) The teams or 
commercial enƟty delivering the equipment 
must complete the CEB‐1A and the individu‐
al at the polling place must be present  to 
sign the acceptance form. 
 
Unlike the other statutes, state law doesn’t 
give the CEB discreƟon in adopƟng an  
alternate policy as to who may deliver the 
voƟng system. However, several counƟes 
have raised quesƟons about using a county 
highway department or an inspector/judge 
combo to deliver the equipment.  
 
As long as the county highway department 
or other delivery service has bi‐parƟsan 
representaƟon approved by the enƟre 
county elecƟon board membership, then 
the standards under the law are met in the 
ElecƟon Division’s view.  
 
The CEB‐1C form is completed by the team 
noted above upon the voƟng systems  
return to the CEB aŌer the polls close. 
 
NOTE: The CEB‐1B is completed by the  
Inspector and judge of the opposite party 
when other materials are returned from the 
precinct or vote center. 
QUESTIONS OF THE MONTH 
Q. Do candidates who ﬁled a CAN‐16 for small town oﬃce 
need to ﬁle a pre‐elecƟon report? 
A. Maybe! If the oﬃce pays more than $5,000 in a calendar 
year, then a person ﬁling a CAN‐16 must open a campaign 
ﬁnance commiƩee (CFA‐1) not later than noon, 7‐days aŌer 
the candidate ﬁling deadline. Those candidates will have a 
pre‐elecƟon report due not later than noon, Oct. 20, 2023. 
 
Q. What about candidates who ﬁled to run in the primary 
elecƟon but lost? Do they need to ﬁle a pre‐elecƟon report? 
A. No. DemocraƟc and Republican candidates who ﬁled to 
run in the primary elecƟon, and ﬁled a CFA‐1, and do not  
appear on November’s ballot because they lost the May  
elecƟon, are not required to ﬁle a pre‐elecƟon report.  
Instead, they ﬁle an annual report in Jan. 2024 unless a ﬁnal/
disbands report is ﬁled before the annual report deadline. 
 
Q. How about a candidate who ﬁled to run for oﬃce who 
ﬁled a CFA‐1 but is not on the ballot because the oﬃce is 
uncontested? Do they need to ﬁle a pre‐elecƟon report? 
A. Yes. State law requires a pre‐elecƟon report to be ﬁled in 
this instance. 
 
Q. If we approved ABS applicaƟons before new features in 
SVRS were added to correct a voter’s record with addiƟonal 
voter ID numbers, can we make those correcƟons now? 
A. Yes. State law requires a voter’s registraƟon record to be 
updated with alternate voter ID numbers provided by the 
voter that can be validated using the BMV/SSA tool in SVRS. 
VR CORNER 
NEW! SVRS & ABS ApplicaƟon Voter ID Requirements 
1/ DLN/SSN CorrecƟons Hopper. This is ONLY for online ABS 
applicaƟons where a voter has been condiƟonally approved 
to access the online absentee applicaƟon using a DLN/SSN 
not previously on their record. While the number provided by 
the voter to gain entry to the online applicaƟon is validated 
by the system, county VR oﬃcials must approve it BEFORE 
the online applicaƟon can be processed in SVRS. Once pro‐
cessed out of the hopper, the number is added to the voter’s 
registraƟon record as a correcƟon. 
 
2/ ID Updates Hopper. This hopper is used for online AND 
paper apps AFTER an applicaƟon has been approved in SVRS, 
which allows addiƟonal voter ID numbers to be included on a 
voter’s record as a correcƟon. For example, a voter used their 
DLN to gain entry to indianavoters.com but wants to add the 
last four digits of their Social Security Number to their  
registraƟon record. The new feature in the ABS module will 
allow the county to view the voter’s SSN4 submission,  
validate it against the BMV/Social Security AdministraƟon 
feed, and approve the applicaƟon. Then the county VR oﬃcial 
reviews/approves the correcƟon in the ID Update Hopper.  
 
3/ Photocopy of ID. Some voters may wish to instead aƩach 
a copy of an ID to their paper absentee applicaƟon, which is 
permiƩed by state law. CounƟes need to conﬁrm the ID  
complies with the state’s photo ID law; however, counƟes 
cannot use photocopy to update a voter’s ID number in SVRS.

Election Division Dispatch

NEWS & UPDATES 
 
December Conference Reminders 
 If you haven’t registered for the December ElecƟon  
Administrators’ conference, please do so before 5PM 
(Indy Ɵme), Friday, November 3, 2023, to avoid a $50 per 
person late fee added to the registraƟon fee. 
 The WesƟn room block was expanded to include a few 
more rooms at the reduced rate, but room block is  
nearing capacity. Make your hotel reservaƟons soon! 
 IED has only received a handful of nominaƟons for

are due to IED not later than 5PM (Indy Ɵme), November

why you’ve nominated this person for consideraƟon. 
 
CerƟfying ElecƟon Results 
There isn’t much Ɵme to rest following elecƟon day! Your 
county elecƟon boards must complete the canvass of the re-
sults of your elecƟon, and also process any provisional ballots 
or late arriving overseas ballots by 3PM, ten days aŌer the 
elecƟon. You’ll then need to ﬁle the CEB series of forms using 
SVRS not later than noon, Monday, November 20, 2023. 
Most counƟes upload precinct level results directly into SVRS, 
but if your county does not, please aƩach the precinct level 
results to your CEB-9, SecƟon I submission. The CEB-9, SecƟon 
I is due not later than noon, Indy Ɵme, Tuesday, November 21, 
2023. CounƟes will need to complete the wait Ɵme infor-
maƟon in the CEB-9, SecƟon II module. This informaƟon is 
found in the PRE-1 oath book completed by your poll workers.   
 
Don’t forget! CounƟes cerƟfy elecƟon results, including those 
from small towns holding their own elecƟons. The town  
elecƟon board should be reminded to get their results to the 
county asap. Further, the town is required to ﬁle all of its  
elecƟon materials with the county elecƟon board to comply

County clerks may begin issuing cerƟﬁcates of elecƟon to

where no elecƟons need to be held) aŌer 12P local prevailing

2024 Resources

the ElecƟon Division can serve as an interpreƟve source. However, where important legal rights are concerned, you must consult with your own aƩorney to be fully and properly advised.

IN FOCUS: Quick Election Day FAQs 
Below are some topics that are asked of IED 
before many elecƟons As a reminder. IED is open 
on ElecƟon Day , so please do not hesitate to 
reach out if issues or quesƟons arise. 
 
BMV Hours 
The BMV is required to be open on ElecƟon Day 
for the same hours polls are open. If a voter 
needs an ID for voƟng purposes, they may bring 
their required materials to a BMV branch to 
secure an ID. However, a voter who signs the 
poll list cannot leave and come back. If a voter 
lacks suﬃcient ID and they sign the poll book, 
the voter must be oﬀered a provisional ballot. 
The voter then has unƟl noon, ten days aŌer 
ElecƟon Day to bring their ID to the county  
elecƟon board (or aﬃrm they are indigent or 
have a religious exempƟon) using the PRO-10 or 
PRO-11 in a small town where town elecƟon 
board is used. 
 
Ballot Remakes 
SomeƟmes a ballot cannot be read by an opƟcal 
scan ballot card tabulator. A bi-parƟsan remake 
team is responsible for capturing the voter’s 
intent from their original ballot on to a ballot 
card. It is important the voter’s original and  
remade ballot have the same serial number 
printed on it for tracking purposes in case of a 
recount AND two sets of iniƟals. A remade ballot 
CANNOT be cast on a DRE voƟng system (that is, 
the MicroVote touch screen unit). 
Firearms & Polling LocaƟons 
Except for polls located on school property, 
there is no state law that prohibits ﬁrearms in a 
polling place. If the person carrying a weapon is 
observing the general laws regarding carrying, it 
may be permissible to carry in a polling locaƟon. 
However, even one who lawfully possesses a 
ﬁrearm can run afoul of the law if they act  
carelessly (or with any other weapon for that 
maƩer). There are voter inƟmidaƟon laws on the 
books at both the federal level (18 U.S.C. §§ 241, 
245(b)(1)(A) and the state level (IC 3-14-3-21.5). 
However, mere lawful possession of a ﬁrearm 
does not violate these statutes.  
 
Voter’s in “InacƟve” Status 
Our oﬃce is oŌen asked if a voter in “inacƟve” 
status within SVRS needs to complete addiƟonal 
paperwork when voƟng in-person. The answer is 
no. All acƟve and inacƟve voters are including in 
the poll list used on ElecƟon Day. However, re-
gardless of their SVRS status, if a voter has 
moved, poll workers will need to determine if 
the voter qualiﬁes for a fail-safe to vote at their 
old precinct one last Ɵme. If they do, then the 
VRG 4/12 is used to capture the voter’s new 
informaƟon before being issued a regular ballot, 
if otherwise qualiﬁed. 
 
ElecƟoneering 
ElecƟoneering is deﬁned in IC 3-14-3-16.  
Generally, a person may not wear an arƟcle of 
clothing or otherwise express the support of a 
candidate, poliƟcal party, or public quesƟon. A 
person wearing such an arƟcle of clothing, for 
example, may be asked to cover up. However, a 
person not complying with this request may not 
be kept from voƟng, if otherwise eligible.  
Instead, the poll workers may forward the  
voter’s name to the county elecƟon board, who 
may determine if an elecƟon law violaƟon  
occurred. 
 
Ballot Selﬁe 
Although the statute has not been repealed (IC 3
-11-8-17.5) and remains “on the books,” a 
 federal court has ruled the Indiana law  
unconsƟtuƟonal and it cannot be enforced. 
Therefore, ballot “selﬁes” are permissible. 
 
Voter Assistance 
A voter may bring any material with them into a 
voƟng booth to assist them, even those  
materials created by a candidate or poliƟcal 
party. This wriƩen assistance is not considered 
elecƟoneering. (IC 3-11-8-18.5)
 A voter is also 
enƟtled to have any person, except for their 
employer or union representaƟve, assist them 
with compleƟng their ballot. The PRE-3 form 
must be completed BEFORE the voter enters 
their voƟng booth. The PRE-3 applies to judges 
who might also be asked for assistance by the 
voter to help complete their ballot.
 
QUESTIONS OF THE MONTH 
Q. Will the ABS‐7 be included in the absentee envelope  
redesign eﬀorts? 
A. All mailed absentee envelopes (ABS-6, ABS-8, ABS-10,  
ABS-18) are being redesigned in partnership with the USPS to 
ensure compliance with USPS standards. The ABS-7 is used to 
secure voted absentee ballots during early voƟng or travel 
board, and therefore, not part of the style guidelines for the 
new envelopes. However, a minor tweak was made to the 
envelope and an updated version will be released soon. Old 
stock of the absentee envelopes noted here will be  
grandfathered and can be used unƟl exisƟng stock is used.
 
Q. Do we need to complete the envelope redesign survey? 
A. The state is oﬀering free envelope design services with 
The Jackson Group. Before, IED provided a generic template 
for counƟes to build out with their print vendor with liƩle 
USPS input. Now, IED has a more robust style guideline that 
must be followed by all vendors, and IED is oﬀering support 
to create a customized print ﬁle for counƟes to take to their 
print vendor. The survey gauges your county’s interest in 
using this free service. 
Q. Can we use our own print vendor instead of the state’s 
vendor (The Jackson Group) to create the template for our 
absentee envelopes? 
A. Yes. However, your print vendor must follow the specs 
included in the design guidelines (when ﬁnalized) when 
prinƟng the ABS-6, ABS-8, ABS-10A/10B, and ABS-18. 
VR CORNER 
Voter Fail Safe “Twist” in Municipal ElecƟons 
In 2023, the voter fail safes concerning “when” and “where” a voter 
moved are sƟll in eﬀect. Meaning, a voter who moves within the 
same county and same Congressional 30-days or more before elec-
Ɵon day (or any Ɵme on or before October 8, 2023) may be eligible 
to vote at their old precinct one last Ɵme. Or, a voter who moves 29-
days or less (or on or aŌer October 9, 2023) anywhere in Indiana 
may be eligible to vote at their old precinct one last Ɵme. 
 
However, no maƩer when the voter moved in 2023, an individual 
who moved into or out of a municipality is NOT eligible to vote one 
last Ɵme at their old precinct. (IC 3‐10‐11‐4 & IC 3‐10‐12‐3.4) Poll 
workers will likely want to ask “where” the voter moved ﬁrst to  
determine if their move was within the same municipality. Then, the 
poll workers would need to know “when” the moved occurred to do 
the addiƟonal analysis noted above. 
 
VLM Records RetenƟon 
Last month revisions were made to an October memo outlining the 
next steps on materials sent to counƟes from the statewide VLM 
project. The IARA adopted a new records retenƟon policy for elec-
Ɵon records maintained by county oﬃcials. This policy requires un-
deliverable Card 1s and Card 2s, and any voter response card where 
the voter marked opƟon 1 to conﬁrm their registraƟon address, to 
be retained for two years following the next general elecƟon.  
 
For example, a returned card 1 from the 2023 statewide VLM pro-
ject must be kept unƟl aŌer the November 2026 general elecƟon. 
AŌer elecƟon day, this record would be eligible for destrucƟon fol-
lowing the required protocols from your local Records Commission.

Dec. 19 & 21  | Oﬃce, ElecƟon & Candidate Set-Up 
 
2024 Calendar is pending review and will be posted to the INSVRS County 
Portal as soon as possible. 
InformaƟon in this newsleƩer is provided by the Indiana ElecƟon Division as a courtesy to county elecƟon administrators. If a person is unclear concerning elecƟon law provisions,  
the ElecƟon Division can serve as an interpreƟve source. However, where important legal rights are concerned, you must consult with your own aƩorney to be fully and properly advised. 
CounƟes should expect 2024 to be a 
heavy peƟƟon ﬁling year. If you need a 
quick refresher before candidate ﬁling 
begins in January, the purple VR guide-
book includes a chapter on peƟƟon pro-
cessing and is very detailed. AddiƟonally, 
IED will present on this topic at the De-
cember conference and Civix will host an 
online training session to cover the SVRS 
modules that are helpful in managing peƟ-
Ɵons.  
Here are a few reminders based on  
quesƟons our oﬃce is ﬁelding from your 
colleagues: 
1) The master peƟƟon in SVRS for state 
and federal candidates will need to be 
set up by the HAVA administrator. When 
you get a peƟƟon and don’t ﬁnd it in 
SVRS, please email HAVAadministra-
tor@sos.in.gov and ScoƩ Zarazee will get 
the oﬃce set up as soon as possible. Our 
oﬃce cannot proacƟvely set up peƟƟons 
in SVRS; a county must receive at least 
one peƟƟon and share the name of the 
candidate, their poliƟcal party, and oﬃce 
sought to set up the SVRS module for 
county use. Usually several counƟes email 
us all at once - and that’s ok! It is beƩer to 
have too many emails than none at all and 
keep people waiƟng. As a reminder, the 
county is responsible for seƫng up a mas-
ter peƟƟon if an independent or minor 
party candidate is seeking local oﬃce.  
2) With one excepƟon related to school 
board oﬃces, the county VR oﬃcial may 
only review signatures of voters  
within their county. 
3) IC 3‐5‐6, generally, is the chapter in 
Indiana Code that sets forth the stand‐
ards to cerƟfying documents signed by  
registered voters, including substanƟal 
and minor variaƟon in a person’s name or 
address. Remember, IC 3-5-6-2 notes that 
resoluƟon of reasonable doubt is to be in 
favor of the registered voter.  
4) A person’s residence address on the 
peƟƟon must conform to their registra‐
Ɵon address at the Ɵme the peƟƟon is  
processed by county VR oﬃcials.  
SubstanƟal and minor address variaƟons 
are covered in IC 3-5-6-4 & IC 3-5-6-5. 
5) Please do NOT forget to complete the 
county VR oﬃcial’s cerƟﬁcaƟon on the

out of each Congressional district be not-

with a separate board of registraƟon or

Ɵons (Allen, Lake, LaPorte, Madison,  
Marion, Porter, Tippecanoe, Vanderburgh,

oﬃcials. Otherwise, the clerk or their

6) Please try not to mark through a

nature is rejected. The form has an “oﬃce 
use only” secƟon that allows you to add

for the Congressional District, to make it 
easier to complete the cerƟﬁcaƟon refer-
enced in #5 above. The Indiana ElecƟon 
Commission may need to review the peƟ-
Ɵon forms if a challenge is ﬁled, and mark-
ing through a name may prevent the com-
missioners from performing their due dili-
gence. 
7) PeƟƟons may be mailed to the county 
VR oﬃce for review and cerƟﬁcaƟon. 
However, you must receive and ﬁle stamp 
the peƟƟon form by the stated deadline. 
Any peƟƟon received aŌer the noon

8) Make sure the peƟƟon is on the cur‐
rent version of the form. You can ﬁnd the

which will note the current version of the

9) Before a peƟƟon ﬁler leaves the oﬃce, 
take a moment to review the aﬃdavit of 
peƟƟon carrier. If the requested  
informaƟon of the peƟƟon carrier is miss-
ing or incomplete, the county VR oﬃcial 
may not process the peƟƟon. BUT, the 
county VR oﬃcial must aƩempt to reach 
out to the peƟƟon carrier to alert them of 
their omission. The person has unƟl the 
ﬁling deadline (noon, Jan. 30, 2024 for the 
CAN-8 form for D/R US PresidenƟal candi-
dates; noon, February 6, 2024 for the CAN
-25 peƟƟon for D/R Governor  
candidates and CAN-4 peƟƟon for D/R US 
Senate candidates) to correct the error. 
Failure to perfect the peƟƟon carrier aﬃ-
davit by this deadline will result in the 
peƟƟon being rejected by the county VR 
oﬃcial. 
10) Candidates may wish to make ar‐
rangements to pick up cerƟﬁed peƟƟons, 
since the originals must also be ﬁled with 
IED/SOS by noon, February 9, 2024. It is 
recommended to ask the person ﬁling the 
peƟƟon if campaign is picking up the com-
pleted peƟƟons. If not, the county may 
mail the cerƟﬁed peƟƟons to IED, but it 
must be received by IED not later than 
noon, February 9, 2024 to be accepted. 
IN FOCUS: CANDIDATE PETITION PROCESSING REMINDERS 
LIMITS ON REJECTING CANDIDATE FILINGS 
The blue ElecƟon Administrator’s Manual covers this in more detail, but in short, there are at least four main reasons for a  
candidate ﬁling to be rejected when presented: 
 
1) Candidate running for state oﬃce (federal, statewide, state legislaƟve, judge, prosecuƟng aƩorney) presents candidate 
ﬁling incorrectly to county or vice versa, a candidate for local oﬃce or party oﬃce trying to ﬁle with IED/SOS. (IC 3-5-4-1.2) 
 
2) Form ﬁled aŌer the noon, prevailing local Ɵme of candidate ﬁling deadline. (IC 3-5-4-1.9) 
 
3) Filing made on a form NOT approved by the state. (IC 3-5-4-8) 
 
4) DeclaraƟon of candidacy is not accompanied by the required statement of economic interest  (IC 3-8-2-11; IC 3-8-9-6) 
 
However, if the forms are ﬁled with the oﬃce and an error discovered , the ﬁlings cannot be rejected aŌer the fact. It would  
require a CAN-1 challenge to be ﬁled by a party chair or voter within the elecƟon district. Remember, counƟes are NOT the  
candidate police! QuesƟons about candidate qualiﬁcaƟons are managed through the CAN-1 challenge procedures. For example, 
if you discover a candidate does not have the required vote history to run as a D/R candidate, you cannot reject the candidate 
ﬁling. A CAN-1 must be ﬁled and the CEB must hold a hearing aŌer giving proper noƟce to the parƟes involved.  
HOLDOVER REMINDERS 
SomeƟmes no one ﬁles to run for an elected oﬃce during an elecƟon 
cycle. The state consƟtuƟon has a remedy: holdovers.  
 
Generally, if no one ﬁles to run for an oﬃce OR an individual who was 
elected does not qualify to assume oﬃce for the new term, then the 
previous oﬃceholder “holds over” and conƟnues in oﬃce unƟl such a 
Ɵme their successor is elected and qualiﬁed or the holdover oﬃcial 
resigns (which would allow for the elected oﬃce vacancy to be ﬁlled  
under IC 3-13, generally).  
 
Determining who holds over when more than one person can be  
elected to the posiƟon is a liƩle more complicated. Depending on the 
unit of government,  the legislaƟve body holds a meeƟng to determine 
which of the incumbent “at-large” members will hold over. This year, 
city common councils or town councils may make this determinaƟon.  
 
These details can be found in IC 3-13, but you’ll have to ﬁnd the correct 
arƟcle that corresponds to the unit of government. IC 3-13-9, for  
example, are procedures for elected oﬃce vacancies for town oﬃces.  
 
Finally, a person who holds over does not need a cerƟﬁcate of elecƟon 
and does not complete a new oath of oﬃce. (IC 5-4-1-1.2)  
VR CORNER 
Vote History Updates 
If you haven’t already, counƟes may begin up-
daƟng SVRS with informaƟon from the Nov. 7, 
2023, elecƟon. State law requires vote history 
updates be completed not later than 60-days 
aŌer the elecƟon or Jan. 8, 2024. However, in 
those areas where a recount is being conducted, 
this deadline is 60-days from when the judge 
concludes the legal maƩer.  
 
Voter List Maintenance  
State and federal law allow for VLM acƟvity to 
begin aŌer the general, municipal, primary, or 
special elecƟon. If your county has work in the 
statewide VLM mailing hoppers or statewide 
address mailing conﬁrmaƟon noƟces (SAMC) 
sent by your oﬃce that were put on hold, then 
VLM acƟvity may resume up to Feb. 7, 2024, 
which is the last day to complete VLM work be-
fore the primary elecƟon. 
QUESTIONS OF THE MONTH  
Q. When do we need to complete the CEB‐35 (precincts) or CEB‐39 (vote center) and 
ﬁle with the county auditor? 
A. Unless a small town entered into a ﬁxed price agreement with the county 
elecƟon board, the county auditor must submit the elecƟon expenses  
calculated by the CEB to the town ﬁscal body not later than 30-days aŌer the 
November 7, 2023, elecƟon, or December 7, 2023. 
 
Q. Do we have to issue cerƟﬁcates of elecƟon? 
A. The statute says that you only have to issue a cerƟﬁcate of elecƟon when 
requested by a candidate. However, our oﬃce encourages you to do provide 
each elected oﬃcial with the documentaƟon. (IC 3-12-5-2) SVRS was recently 
updated to use informaƟon counƟes entered for the elecƟon to generate the 
cerƟﬁcates of elecƟon within the system. Therefore, paper forms are not  
available. NOTE: City and town judges do not receive a cerƟﬁcate of elecƟon; 
instead, they will receive a commission from the governor. 
 
Q. Do elected oﬃcials have to submit the oath of oﬃce included with the 
state form such as the CEB‐27? 
A. No. The oath of oﬃce included with the cerƟﬁcates of elecƟon prescribed by 
IED is provided as a convenience. An oath of oﬃce is to be in wriƟng, which 
could be on leƩerhead from an elected oﬃcial or another person authorized to 
give the oath of oﬃce (see IC 33-42-9-7). The text of the oath is to be  
substanƟally similar to the text found on page 54 of the blue  
ElecƟon Administrator’s Manual. 
 
Q. Who can give an oath of oﬃce? 
A. A person who is authorized to perform notarial acts may give an oath of 
oﬃce. See IC 33-42-9-7 for the full list. 
 
Q. What is the deadline to ﬁle an oath of oﬃce? 
A. The deadline to take and ﬁle an oath of oﬃce with the county clerk is Jan. 
31, 2023. This includes elected oﬃcials in small towns where a town elecƟon 
board conducted the November elecƟon. NOTE: City or town judges ﬁle the 
oath of oﬃce with the Secretary of State. 
 
Q. What happens if a person fails to ﬁle the oath of oﬃce by the deadline? 
A. The oﬃce becomes vacant when an oath of oﬃce has not been properly 
ﬁled by the deadline. (IC 5-4-1-1.2) The incumbent oﬃceholder would then 
“holdover” pursuant to the Indiana ConsƟtuƟon. This would include city and 
town judges because those oﬃces are created by statute. (ConsƟtuƟonal oﬃce 
holders such as superior or circuit court judges, prosecuƟng aƩorney, county 
clerk, etc. are exempt from this rule.) 
 
Q. Are oaths of oﬃce public records? And how long are those to be retained? 
A. Yes, oaths are public records and available for public inspecƟon. Please refer 
to the county’s general retenƟon policy established by State Archives as to 
when you may move or otherwise destroy oaths of oﬃce.  
USPIS & EI-ISAC 
Last month, there were headlines related to 
suspicious substances found in mail sent to 
elecƟon oﬃces in several states. Members of 
the EI-ISAC (ElecƟon Infrastructure InformaƟon 
Sharing & Analysis Center) received helpful re-
minders from the US Postal InspecƟon Service 
(USPIS), including the informaƟon sheet on the 
next page of this newsleƩer and PublicaƟon 
166—”Guide to Mail Center Security,” which 
can be found at hƩps://about.usps.com/
publicaƟons/pub166.pdf  
 
Joining the EI-ISAC is free for county elecƟon and 
voter registraƟon oﬃcials. To learn more, visit  
www.cisecurity.org/ei-isac and click the orange “Join 
the EI-ISAC” buƩon on the main landing page. 
 
Remember, if you believe you have a  
suspicious leƩer or package, isolate it  
immediately, do not open it, and call 911.

Election Division Dispatch 
 Brad King & Angie Nussmeyer, Co-Directors | January 2024 
NEWS & UPDATES 
Don’t Forget the CAN‐5! 
When a candidate ﬁles to run for oﬃce, counƟes must 
hand‐deliver or mail the CAN‐5 (Candidacy Filing  
ConﬁrmaƟon for 2024) not later than one day aŌer 
receiving the candidate’s ﬁling. You can use the form 
found on the INSVRS County Portal or use SVRS to 
generate the document aŌer creaƟng the candidate’s 
proﬁle in the system. QuesƟons? Contact the Help 
Desk or visit the online training portal for a step‐by‐
step guide. 
2023 Annual Report 
ALL open candidate and poliƟcal acƟon commiƩees 
are required to ﬁle a 2023 Annual Report not later 
than noon, January 17, 2024. Regular party  
commiƩees are the excepƟon to this deadline; these 
commiƩees have unƟl noon, March 1, 2024, to ﬁle the 
annual report. 
AdministraƟve Disbanding of CommiƩees 
Not later than January 26, 2024, the CEB must review 
its campaign ﬁnance records to determine if a  
commiƩee is subject to the administraƟve dissoluƟon 
procedure. To move forward with dissoluƟon, the 
commiƩee must have not ﬁled any CFA‐4 or CFA‐11 
during the previous three calendar years AND the cash 
on hand on their last ﬁled report is $1,000 or less. If 
both condiƟons are met, then the CEB may move  
forward with the process found in IC 3‐9‐1‐12,  
including providing noƟce by cerƟﬁed mail to the 
treasurer and making addiƟonal ﬁndings by the CEB.  
Accessible ElecƟons Resources 
The US ElecƟon Assistance Commission recently  
released an on‐demand training series on making  
elecƟons more accessible to voters with disabiliƟes. 
The videos are now available on the EAC’s YouTube 
Channel. More resources, including a link to their 
training videos, can be found at eac.gov/voƟng‐
accessibility. 
To that end, stay tuned for more informaƟon related 
to the OmniBallot Portal, the online ballot marking 
device for voters with print disabiliƟes. 2024 will be 
the ﬁrst full statewide implementaƟon of the tool.

InformaƟon in this newsleƩer is provided by the Indiana ElecƟon Division as a courtesy to county elecƟon administrators. If a person is unclear concerning elecƟon law provisions,  
the ElecƟon Division can serve as an interpreƟve source. However, where important legal rights are concerned, you must consult with your own aƩorney to be fully and properly advised. 
IN FOCUS: AUTHORIZED VOTING METHODS  
Indiana state law authorizes a county  
elecƟon board to determine how ballots 
are to be cast in their county: using a direct 
record electronic voƟng system (DRE) or an 
opƟcal scan voƟng system or tradiƟonal 
hand‐counted paper ballots (or a combina‐
Ɵon of those methods.) However, the DRE 
or opScan voƟng systems must be cerƟﬁed 
by the Indiana ElecƟon Commission to be 
selected for use in a county. 
For example, counƟes using the MicroVote 
system use the DRE, generally, for all  
in‐person voƟng but use an opƟcal scan 
paper ballot card for absentee by mail 
voƟng, for example. Those counƟes may 
also have hand‐counted paper ballots used 
for provisional ballots. 
In counƟes using ES&S, Hart, or Unisyn 
opƟcal scan voƟng systems, only one 
voƟng method (opƟcal scan ballot cards) is 
likely being used (the ballot marking device 
is not a DRE since it does not store votes 
on the equipment). 
OŌen, the term “paper ballot” is used as a 
generic catch‐all term. However, Indiana 
state law makes a disƟncƟon between a 
“ballot card” and “paper ballot.” Ballot 
cards, while on paper, are only used with 
opƟcal scan voƟng systems to be tabulated 
by the voƟng equipment. 
On the other hand, paper ballots are  
tradiƟonal, hand‐counted ballots that are 
not used with an opƟcal scan voƟng  
system.  CounƟes using an opƟ
cal scan 
voƟng system also could not use their elec‐
Ɵon management soŌware to create their 
hand‐counted paper ballot as the ballot 
layout standards for hand‐counted paper 
ballot are diﬀerent than ballot cards and 
the opƟcal scan voƟng system would not 
be used to tabulate votes.  
IC 3‐12‐2, generally, directs counƟes how 
to count paper ballots should the county 
elecƟon board opt to use hand‐counted 
paper ballot cards. The procedures under 
IC 3‐12‐2 ARE NOT the procedures for 
counƟng a ballot card used with an opƟcal 
scan voƟng system.  
The canvassing and tabulaƟon procedures 
for an opƟcal scan voƟng systems are  
covered under IC 3‐12‐3, generally. (And 
for DRE systems, under IC 3‐12‐3.5) 
The ballot layout requirements for hand 
counted paper ballots can be found in IC 3‐
11‐2, for opƟcal scan ballot cards in IC 3‐11
‐13, and DRE systems in IC 3‐11‐14. In  
addiƟon when using opƟcal scan ballot 
cards or a DRE system, there are speciﬁc 
requirements for the delivery or return of 
those voƟng systems’ equipment. The  
delivery of both OPSCAN and DRE equip‐
ment to the polls can be found in IC 3‐11
‐3
‐10. Returning OPSCAN equipment from 
the polls to the CEB can be found in IC 3‐12
‐3‐2.2. For DRE systems, see IC 3‐12‐3.5‐4.5 
If tradiƟonal hand counted paper ballots 
are used, then a ballot box must be  
provided at the polls. Procedures on using 
and returning the ballot box can be found 
in IC 3‐11‐11 and IC 3‐12‐2. 
Upcoming VLM Projects 
County voter registraƟon oﬃcials 
will have access to at least two  
pieces of informaƟon from other 
county oﬃcials to assist with vot‐
er list maintenance at the end of 
January. 
At minimum, the county sheriﬀ 
must ﬁle on a quarterly basis a list 
of each Indiana resident who has 
been convicted of a crime and 
placed in a county correcƟonal 
facility during the previous quar‐
ter. The ﬁrst list for 2024 is due to 
the county VR oﬃcial not later 
than January 31, 2024. The VRG‐1 
cover sheet is to be aƩached to 
any list provided to the county 
from the sheriﬀ’s oﬃce.  
Using the sheriﬀ’s list, the county 
VR oﬃcial is to move a person’s 
registraƟon status to “cancelled” 
if the person is currently impris‐
oned following convicƟon of a 
crime. If the individual is no long‐
er imprisoned, then the person’s 
registraƟon is not to be moved to 
“cancelled” status. (IC 3‐7‐46‐6; IC 
3‐7‐46‐1) 
AddiƟonally, the local health  
department ﬁles a copy of death 
records with the county Auditor 
pursuant to IC 16‐37‐3‐9(d). 
CounƟes may request this list 
from the auditor and use it to 
move a registered voter’s status 
to “cancelled” as the individual is 
cerƟﬁed as deceased. (IC 3‐7‐45‐
2.1(d); IC 3‐7‐45‐1) 
Later this spring counƟes will be 
hearing from IED about a project 
using data from the U.S. Northern 
and Southern District Courts. Stay 
tuned!
 
Voting Systems & ePB Inventory Due Jan. 31! 
Each year county elecƟon boards must cerƟfy to SOS that the inventory the  
county enters and maintains in the VSTOP voƟng system and electronic poll 
books inventory database is accurate. This review must be completed not later 
than Jan. 31, 2024, which is the deadline to send the IEC‐22 to VSTOP@bsu.edu. 
(IC 3‐11‐16‐5) 
 
Ensuring an accurate inventory is important for elecƟon administraƟon,  
especially the public test of voƟng systems. If you have quesƟons about the 
VSTOP inventory database, please email VSTOP@bsu.edu. Their team can assist 
counƟes with logging in to the system.
 
Most of the quesƟons noted below were submiƩed at the 
2024 ElecƟon Administrators’ Conference. Most presentaƟons 
are now available on the “ElecƟon Administrator’s Portal” at 
in.gov/sos/elecƟons. Thank you to everyone who aƩended! 
Q. I’m the elected Clerk and plan to run for re‐elecƟon or for 
another oﬃce in 2024. What, if any, special steps do I need to 
take to manage elecƟons? 
A. The only restricƟon you should be concerned about relates 
to absentee ballots. A county clerk running for re‐elecƟon or 
another elected oﬃce on the ballot may not print their signa‐
ture on the absentee ballot and must instead use the generic 
county seal on it. (Your county’s generic seal can be found on 
the SVRS county portal in the “Shared Documents” folder.) 
State law does not require the clerk’s signature or county seal 
be printed on elecƟon day ballots, but if the county does so, 
then it’s our best advice to apply the same ballot prinƟng rule. 
Q. Do candidates for U.S. House need to collect peƟƟon  
signatures? 
A. It depends. DemocraƟc, Libertarian, and Republican  
candidates do not, but Independent and minor party  
candidates who want their names printed on the general  
elecƟon ballot do. The independent and minor party candi‐
dates must collect signatures of registered voters within their 
Congressional district totaling 2% of ALL votes cast in the 2022 
Secretary of State’s race in that district. 
Q. Does a Republican running for precinct commiƩeeman 
need to ﬁle a separate CAN‐37 to run for state  
convenƟon delegate? 
A. Because she is running for two diﬀerent party oﬃces, a Re‐
publican who wants to seek both posiƟons must ﬁle two sepa‐
rate CAN‐37 forms—one for each o ﬃce—as noted in the  
instrucƟons on the CAN‐
37 form.. 
Q. I want to minimize the Ɵme necessary to search the Indi‐
ana ElecƟon Code. Is there an ability to search “words” or 
“phrases” in the elecƟon code book or on a website? 
A. The Title 3 Code Book published by IED does contain an  
Index in the back of the book with keywords to idenƟfy poten‐
Ɵal code cite matches. AddiƟonally, the Indiana General As‐
sembly’s website (iga.in.gov) has a code search feature that 
will allow you to do a code word search within that database 
Another opƟon is to ﬁnd the relevant chapter in the table of 
contents of one the handbooks published by IED like the cur‐
rent version of Voter RegistraƟon Guidebook or Campaign Fi-
nance Manual, as most passages do include the relevant code 
cite. This cite can be used by your CEB to cross reference in the 
code book, whether online or the paper version. 
Q. Are D & R county chairs responsible for assigned ABS voter 
board, central count, and precinct workers to speciﬁc roles? 
Or just give a list of names? 
A. The county elecƟon board should be requesƟng the number 
of ABS voter boards and ElecƟon Day central count teams 
needed to perform absentee work on or before elecƟon day. 
This request would separate the funcƟonaliƟes of ABS voter 
board and central count, since those duƟes and “work days” 
are disƟnct in state law. Beyond requesƟng the number of 
team members needed, it would be up to the CEB to  
determine how granular the Board would like to be to assign 
people to speciﬁc days or work funcƟon, such as absentee ap‐
plicaƟon review or travel board. IC 3‐11.5‐4‐22 and  
IC 3‐11.5‐4‐23. 
For poll workers, the statute does not require the same 
wriƩen no
Ɵce to the party chairs by the CEB. However, the 
chair’s nominaƟons should include which posiƟon the person 
is being nominated and, for the posiƟons of judge, clerk, assis‐
tant clerk, and sheriﬀ, if the individual is serving a full day or 
half day (poll opening to noon and noon to poll closing). The 
CEB must appoint the individuals to the poll worker posiƟons, 
if otherwise qualiﬁed. IC 3‐6‐6‐9; IC 36‐6‐10; IC 3‐6‐6‐11. 
Q. When does the CEB review the ABS‐18A or ABS‐18B for 
missing or mismatched signatures on absentee balloƟng  
materials—before Elec Ɵon Day, on ElecƟon Day, or at the 
provisional hearing? 
A. Because absentee voters with a missing/mismatched  
signature issue are made provisional, the CEB must make the 
determinaƟon whether to count the provisional ballot at the 
county’s provisional ballot hearing. CounƟes are not limited to 
hold only one provisional hearing; it is possible to have  
mulƟple hearings as long as CEB properly noƟces them.  
Regardless, the CEB must make its determinaƟon whether to 
count a provisional ballot not later than 3PM, ten days aŌer 
each elecƟon. 
Q. If an exisƟng voter fails to mark the age/ciƟzenship  
quesƟons to update their registraƟon to a new residence 
address, do we send it back to the voter? 
A. The county would not send the original document back to 
the voter. Instead, this would be treated as an incomplete  
registraƟon (see IC 3‐7‐34) and the voter would need to  
submit, in wriƟng under a penalty of perjury statement, the 
answer(s) to the missing quesƟon(s). This is usually done by 
submiƫng a new registraƟon document. The voter would 
need to perfect their incomplete registraƟon not later than 29‐
days before elecƟon day. (For any other incompletes, the 
deadline to correct is 10‐days before the elecƟon.) CounƟes 
would handle this process in SVRS the same as they would a 
new registrant whose applicaƟon was marked as incomplete 
for any reason. QuesƟons on using SVRS to ﬂag an incomplete 
registraƟon request should be directed to the Civix Help Desk. 
Q. Who is the best one to speak with about a Driver’s License 
that does not match the voter? 
A. It depends. It could be the voter mis‐entered the infor‐
maƟon, so the ﬁrst person to check with is the voter. Rarely, a 
voter sharing a smartphone or iPad, even in the same home, 
can mistakenly autoﬁll a DLN with a number that is not theirs, 
for example. If the DLN on their request corresponds to the 
VR CORNER/QUESTIONS OF THE MONTH GRAB BAG 
voter’s informaƟon, then send a note to elecƟons@iec.in.gov 
and we can check with our IN BMV contact and conﬁrm if there 
was a transmission error on the back‐end. 
Q. Is the travel board for people who can mark their own  
ballot? 
A. A voter that is conﬁned to their own home due to illness or 
injury, their caregiver, or a person with a disability who believes 
their polling place is inaccessible to them is enƟtled to use the 
ABS‐Traveling Board applicaƟon and vote by this absentee  
method. The voter would decide whether they need assistance 
or not from the bi‐parƟsan absentee voter board team.  
However, a voter who cannot personally mark their own ballot is 
required, by law, to vote by travel board unless the person  
qualiﬁes to use the ABS‐VPD form, which would allow the  
individual to use adapƟve technology to complete their  
absentee ballot, such as the Democracy Live online marking  
device oﬀered by the State for counƟes to use. Illness or injury 
can also be temporary and may not be a visible disability. A  
voter aﬃrms, under penalƟes of perjury, they meet one of these 
qualiﬁcaƟons and must not be used by voters who simply want 
to vote on a paper ballot or opƟcal scan ballot card. 
Q. We are starƟng to see voter registraƟons from the BMV 
with name change and sex changes. How do you verify this 
informaƟon from the voter? 
A. A voter does not need to provide a court order to make a 
name change on their voter registraƟon form or absentee  
applicaƟon. Further, marking the person’s sex is opƟonal on the 
voter registraƟon form and has no bearing on whether to reject 
the form. Both forms are signed under the penalƟes of perjury 
and act as the voter’s sworn statement to permit the changes to 
their voter record. 
Q. So much of our conference was on cybersecurity. Our IT is 
oﬀ‐site and private. This is so important. Do you have a confer‐
ence for our IT Department or third parƟes? 
A. IED is required, by state law, to cover a number of topics at 
our annual conference, including cybersecurity. Your IT profes‐
sionals are welcome to aƩend, though are not speciﬁcally cov‐
ered for reimbursement for aƩendance. This would be a local 
decision. Otherwise, the key persons from the Cybersecurity and 
Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) at the conference would be 
a good point of contact for your IT professionals. AddiƟonally, 
state law requires the county IT point of contact to be “on ﬁle” 
with the SOS oﬃce, who works directly with those individuals on 
implemenƟng FireEye, for example. Lastly, the Governor’s  
Council on Cybersecurity may have  more informaƟonal re‐
sources beneﬁcial to local IT professionals: hƩps://www.in.gov/
cybersecurity/execuƟve‐council/ 
Q. Can there be some type of training to get elecƟon staﬀ and 
auditors on the same page in regard to poll worker pay? 
A. State Board of Accounts created resources on this very topic. 
You can ﬁnd links to presentaƟons in the SBOA Resource Library 
(in.gov/sboa) like this one: hƩps://www.in.gov/sboa/ﬁles/
HoĬerr_ElecƟon‐Payroll_2022_Clerks.pdf . Otherwise, SBOA 
would be your best resource to answer technical payroll  
quesƟons. The state’s elecƟon laws set forth basic parameters in 
terms of the type of pay elecƟon day poll workers, absentee 
voter boards, absentee ballot counters, provisional ballot  
counters, write‐in vote counƟng teams, assistants to CEB when 
canvassing votes, and which county body sets that pay. 
Q. Can we use an “iniƟal stamp” to sign the ballots to be sent 
out on the ballots? Both the D/R members have other jobs and 
at Ɵmes, Ɵme is limited. 
A. No, IC 3‐11‐4‐19 is clear that the iniƟ
als on the back of an  
absentee ballot to be mailed must be iniƟaled by hand in ink. 
The appointed members of the CEB can designate a proxy to 
iniƟal absentee ballots or the D/R absentee voter board team is 
authorized by state law to perform this duty. 
Q. What do you do when a husband signs his wife’s ballot and 
vice versa? 
A. All absentee ballots undergo a ﬁrst signature review  
performed by the CEB or an absentee voter board. A second 
signature review is performed by a central count team on  
ElecƟon Day, which applies to all absentees unless the CEB 
adopts a resoluƟon to only perform this second review on ABS‐
Mail ballots. If during either review, a signature is mismatched 
(or missing) the county must send the ABS‐18A or ABS‐18B  
within 2 business days from making the determinaƟon. The  
voter has unƟl noon, eight days aŌer the elecƟon to return the 
aﬃdavit by email, mail, hand‐delivery, or fax. This applies to a 
situaƟon where a married couple mistakenly signs the other’s 
ballot security envelope—this is a mismatch that should be  
idenƟﬁed through the bi‐parƟsan review process noted above. 
Q. If, aŌer the elecƟon, you have leŌ over ballots that clerks 
have iniƟaled but were not voted on by a voter—what are you 
to do with them? 
A. Unvoted ballots would be sealed and stored with other elec‐
Ɵon materials under IC 3‐10‐1‐31.1. Unvoted ballots may be de‐
stroyed aŌer the recount/contest deadline expires, but at least 
one ballot from each township in the county and one provisional 
ballot from any precinct in the county must be retained in the 
elecƟon board meeƟng minutes in perpetuity. Please note—
counƟes should not have leŌover absentee ballots that are pre‐
marked by absentee voter board members or the appointed CEB 
members. (IC 3‐11‐10‐27(d)). On ElecƟon Day, however, a poll 
clerk can iniƟal a new opƟcal scan ballot card once the ballot 
before it in the stack has been given to the voter. (IC 3‐11‐13‐
28.5) 
Q. When a potenƟal voter is under the age of 18 and registers 
at the BMV and will not turn 18 unƟl aŌer the current elecƟon, 
do we reject them automaƟcally or do we keep them in the 
incomplete hopper unƟl they do turn 18? 
A. To start, an underage voter may register to vote as long as 
they turn 18 on or before the November elecƟon, generally 
speaking. The voter registraƟon form is a liƩle confusing  
because it asks if the person will be at least 18 by ElecƟon Day. 
In this case, ElecƟon Day is the date of the November general or  
municipal elecƟon. Or, in rare instances, the date of a special 
elecƟon. If the voter is otherwise eligible and turns 18 on or be‐
fore the elecƟon date, then the registraƟon form is  
processed. If the voter does not turn 18 by the date of the gen‐
eral, municipal, or special elecƟon, then a county would reject 
the applicaƟon.  
Q. What happens to voters in a nursing home or assisted living 
facility that no longer have a valid driver’s license within 
expired Ɵme or no longer have a valid state idenƟﬁcaƟon card 
within expired Ɵme. Can they sƟll vote without those forms of 
ID? What needs to happen to ensure our elders can sƟll vote?
A. State law does not require a voter voƟng by travel board or 
by mail or by using the VPD form to provide a valid photo ID to 
vote their ballot. And, if the nursing home or assisted living facil‐
ity is used as an ElecƟon Day polling place or an early voƟng 
locaƟon, then the photo ID law does not apply to residents of 
those residenƟal care faciliƟes.
Now, voters are to provide a voter idenƟﬁcaƟon number on 
their absentee ballot applicaƟon or a photocopy of the valid 
photo ID as deﬁned in IC 3‐5‐2‐40.5. The photocopy of the ID 
must be current or expired since the last general elecƟon 
(November 8, 2022). But, the voter can instead provide a voter 
ID number that corresponds to the number on their voter regis‐
traƟon record. If the voter provides a DLN that is not on their 
registraƟon record and the query on the ID is returned as ex‐
pired by the BMV, the credenƟal number itself is sƟll valid and 
can be added to the voter’s registraƟon and used, assuming it is 
a match to their absentee applicaƟon. Expired just means their 
driving privileges have expired; the credenƟal number is theirs 
(generally speaking) for life.  
Q. Did you say that we need to send the electronic ﬁle of new 
envelope set‐up and a physical sample envelope to USPS for 
approval before ordering? OpƟonal or required?
A. Our absentee security envelope template was reviewed with 
USPS and the style guide includes their suggested placement for 
speciﬁc elements like the “oﬃcial elecƟon mail logo.” However, 
we believe the USPS will sƟll recommend a review by their 
design analyst aŌer your county speciﬁc envelope is ﬁnalized. 
The USPS presentaƟon from the Conference is found under the 
ElecƟon Administrator's Portal on in.gov/sos/elecƟons under 
Tuesday, December 12, 2023 with the ﬁle name of “UPSP Mail 
Design Guidelines and Postage.” Slide 26 includes informaƟon 
for our Indiana USPS contacts if you wish to get a deﬁniƟve 
answer.
Q. If an ABS applicaƟon gets turned in, then is found to have a 
problem such as no reason selected, do we scan the “problem” 
app in SVRS now or wait to scan it in unƟl ﬁxed?
A. There is no state law that requires counƟes to scan an absen‐
tee applicaƟon and upload into SVRS. Instead, state law requires 
absentee ballot applicaƟon informaƟon to be entered into SVRS 
by the clerk’s staﬀ. AddiƟonally, absentee applicaƟons except 
those used for early voƟng or the ABS‐AƩorney General form, 
are to be scanned or otherwise copied for public inspecƟon be‐
fore the approved absentee applicaƟon is aƩached to the ballot 
security envelope. (IC 3‐11‐10‐8.5) All absentee materials such 
as the oiginal approved applicaƟon, original rejected applica‐ 
Ɵon, photocopies of approved applicaƟon, etc, are maintained 
as elecƟon materials under IC 3‐10‐1‐31.1 for a period of at least 
22‐months aŌer the elecƟon. A county may, but is not re‐
quired, to upload the voter’s ABS applicaƟon (rejected or ap‐
proved) to the voter’s documents in SVRS. Some counƟes 
choose to do so; others do not. At minimum, the county is 
 responsible for entering data into SVRS about an approved or 
rejected absentee applicaƟon or absentee ballot and to make 
copies or scan into a digital ﬁle certain absentee applicaƟons 
before the applicaƟons are stored under bi‐parƟsan key with 
their ballot, which makes ﬁlling public records requests for  
absentee applicaƟons diﬃcult. 
Other quesƟons? Please ask! Send an email to  
elecƟons@iec.in.gov

Election Division Dispatch 
 Brad King & Angie Nussmeyer, Co-Directors | February 2024 
NEWS & UPDATES 
January Build 
In mid‐January, important updates and enhancements 
were made to SVRS. Updates include changes in  
handling correcƟons to voter registraƟon records, add‐
ing “proof of residency” to the types of documents 
being uploaded to a voter proﬁle, and reﬁnements to 
the absentee module. Build Notes and training videos 
are now available on the INSVRS county portal.  
 
CISA Resource on GeneraƟve AI 
Last month the Cybersecurity & Infrastructure Security 
Agency (CISA) released a new fact sheet on generaƟve 
AI (arƟﬁcial intelligence) and its potenƟal impact on 
the 2024 elecƟon cycle. This resource provides an 
overview of relevant AI‐enabled capabiliƟes, how they 
can be used by bad actors to target elecƟon infrastruc‐
ture, and basic acƟons elecƟon oﬃcials can take to 
miƟgate these risks. To download this fact sheet, visit: 
hƩps://www.cisa.gov/resources‐tools/resources/risk‐
focus‐generaƟve‐ai‐and‐2024‐elecƟon‐cycle 
 
IED CerƟﬁcaƟon of Federal & State  
Candidates for May Ballot 
IED will cerƟfy the list of DemocraƟc and Republican 
candidates running for federal, statewide, state  
legislaƟve, and judge oﬃces in the primary elecƟon to 
counƟes not later than Friday, February 23, 2024. It’s 
important to note the iniƟal list provided may not be 
ﬁnal. The Indiana ElecƟon Commission (and county 
elecƟon boards, too) have unƟl NOON, Thursday,  
February 29, 2024, to determine the outcome of any 
candidate challenges, so it is possible an amended list 
may be sent to counƟes depending on the challenges 
ﬁled. 
 
Please do NOT rely on lists you ﬁnd on websites, even 
those found on the IED website. The cerƟﬁed lists 
from IED will contain the oﬃcial informaƟon for you to 
use for ballot‐building purposes. 
CALENDAR 
Feb. 6, 2024 (NOON): Deadline for CAN‐4 (D/R US Senate) and 
CAN‐25 (D/R Governor) peƟƟons to be ﬁled with COUNTY for 
cerƟﬁcaƟon of signatures 
Feb. 7, 2024: Last day for county VR oﬃcials to complete VLM 
acƟviƟes before “freeze” period begins on Feb. 8, 2024 
Feb. 9, 2024 (NOON): Candidate Filing closes 
Feb. 16, 2024 (NOON): Candidate withdrawal deadline for May 
primary (CAN‐10) for all candidates but US President 
Feb. 16, 2024 (NOON): Deadline to challenge a candidate who 
ﬁled to run in May 2024 primary (CAN‐1) 
Feb. 16, 2024 (NOON): Deadline for a candidate running in D/R 
primary for an oﬃce paying more than $5,000 in a  
calendar year to open a campaign ﬁnance commiƩee (CFA‐1) 
Feb. 16, 2024 (NOON): Deadline for D/R member of CEB to 
request unopposed candidates for delegate or PC to be placed 
on the ballot; otherwise, unopposed candidates for party oﬃce 
are not included on the ballot 
Feb. 20, 2024 (NOON): Deadline for county VR oﬃcial to ﬁle 
VRG‐21 with IED 
Feb. 22, 2024 (NOON): Deadline for D/R candidate for US Presi‐
dent to withdraw from the primary elecƟon (CAN‐10) 
Feb. 23, 2024 (NOON): Deadline for a public quesƟon to be 
cerƟﬁed to the CEB for the May primary elecƟon 
Feb. 23, 2024: Deadline for VSTOP to provide counƟes with list 
of voƟng systems to test at public test 
Feb. 29, 2024: Deadline for CEB to determine CAN‐1 challenges 
Mar. 1, 2024 (NOON): Deadline for party commiƩees to ﬁle 
2023 Annual Report 
Mar. 1, 2024: Deadline for CEB to provide wriƩen noƟce to D/R 
county chair and, if a public quesƟon is on the ballot, to the 
school superintendent that sample ballots are ready to review 
Mar. 18, 2024: Deadline for ABS ballots to be delivered to CEB 
Mar. 18, 2024 (NOON): Deadline for CEB to noƟfy D/R chairs of 
number of ABS voter boards, counters, couriers needed for 
May primary 
Mar. 22, 2024 (NOON): Deadline for D/R chairs to nominate 
individuals  to ABS voter board, courier, counter posiƟons 
Mar. 23, 2024 (NOON): Deadline to send ABS ballots to those 
with approved apps 
Mar. 29, 2024: IED Closed (Good Friday) 
April 8, 2024: Statewide VR Deadline 
April 8, 2024: Deadline for CEB to conduct public test of voƟng 
systems 
April 9, 2024: First day of early voƟng 
April 12, 2024: End of pre‐primary report period 
April 18, 2024: Travel Board appointments begin 
April 19, 2024 (NOON): Deadline to ﬁle pre‐primary report 
April 25, 2024 (11:59PM):  ABS‐MAIL/ABS‐VPD Deadline 
FEBRUARY WEB TRAINING 
Feb. 6 & 8 | Reports Overview 
Feb. 13 & 15 | User Account Management in SVRS 
Feb. 20 & 22 | APS‐VPD Overview 
Feb. 27 & 29 | Absentee FPCA Overview 
 
2024 Calendar is posted to the INSVRS County Portal but is subject to revision.  
InformaƟon in this newsleƩer is provided by the Indiana ElecƟon Division as a courtesy to county elecƟon administrators. If a person is unclear concerning elecƟon law provisions,  
the ElecƟon Division can serve as an interpreƟve source. However, where important legal rights are concerned, you must consult with your own aƩorney to be fully and properly advised. 
IN FOCUS: CANDIDATE CHALLENGES & HEARINGS 
Candidate ﬁling for the DemocraƟc 
and Republican party primaries closes  
at noon (prevailing local Ɵme), Friday, 
February 9, 2024, and candidates have 
unƟl noon, Friday, February 16, 2024, 
to withdraw their name from  
placement on the ballot. (Note: presi‐
denƟal candidates have a liƩle extra 
Ɵme to withdraw.) 
The candidate challenge period ends 
at noon, Friday, February 16, 2024. A 
voter in the elecƟon district or a  
DemocraƟc or Republican county chair 
within the elecƟon district may ﬁle a 
challenge using the CAN‐1 form.  
The form requires the person making 
the challenge to provide facts   
indicaƟng why the candidate is not 
qualiﬁed to run for oﬃce. The CAN‐1 
challenge form must have an original 
“wet” signature (in other words, it 
can’t be faxed or emailed). 
Once your oﬃce receives a CAN‐1 
form, it’s important that wriƩen  
noƟce be sent to the challenger and 
the challenged candidate. The noƟce 
should include the day, Ɵme, and  
locaƟon of the County ElecƟon Board 
meeƟng and it is recommended a copy 
of the CAN‐1 be enclosed. 
Our best advice is to mail the wriƩen 
noƟce in a way that includes postal 
service tracking like cerƟﬁed or  
priority USPS mail. However, keep in 
mind that cerƟﬁed mail travels very 
slowly. Tracking informaƟon is oŌen 
helpful to CEB members if either  
person fails to a
Ʃend the hearing. 
(Sending addiƟonal noƟce by email 
can be a helpful back‐up, too, if the 
person acknowledges receipt.) 
At the hearing, the county elecƟon 
board may establish procedures that 
can help move along the challenge 
hearing and, at the same Ɵme, give 
each side the opportunity to present 
their arguments to the board. While 
each side is enƟtled to be heard on 
the challenge, it may be best pracƟce 
to have rules that each side get an 
equal amount of Ɵme to present their 
case and rebut claims made by the 
other party.  
AŌer each side makes their  
arguments, the county elecƟon board 
should debate the challenge and vote 
to uphold or dismiss the challenge. 
Since candidate challenge hearings 
have to be conducted at a public  
hearing of the elecƟon board, all  
debate on the challenge and any votes 
on the challenge have to be conducted 
in public. 
For the May 2024 primary elecƟon, 
the CEB has unƟl Leap Day, Thursday, 
February 29, 2024, to determine to 
uphold a ﬁled challenge or not. 
VR CORNER 
Receiving VRG‐6 Apps from Full Service Agencies 
Federal law designated certain state enƟƟes as a “full 
service” agency, which requires voter registraƟon to be 
oﬀered for speciﬁc transacƟons.  
In Indiana, the VRG‐6 is a uniform VR form across all full 
service agencies using it EXCEPT that the form number is 
customized to the agency. This is the number counƟes 
enter for the NVRA tracking number. The VRG‐6 is not 
available online, since it is a specialized form that may 
only be used by full service agencies. If your local agency 
needs the VRG‐6 ﬁle, please have them contact IED at 
elecƟons@iec.in.gov 
While those geƫng a driver’s license or ID card from the 
BMV have their VRG‐6 transmiƩed electronically 
through SVRS, other full service agencies submit their 
VRG‐6 paper applicaƟons by mail or hand‐delivery.  
When a paper VRG‐6 is transmiƩed to your oﬃce, the 
VRG‐9 cover sheet is to be included, which tells the 
county how many applicaƟons and declinaƟons are  
included. The county VR oﬃcial is to then provide the  
VRG‐8 receipt to the full service agency. 
QUESTIONS OF THE MONTH 
Q. Do I have to put uncontested candidates for precinct 
commiƩeeman or state convenƟon delegate (party  
oﬃces) on the ballot? 
A. No—but the Democra Ɵc or Republican member of the 
county elecƟon board can submit a wriƩen request to print 
names of uncontested party oﬃce candidates on the ballot. 
The deadline to do so is noon, Friday, February 16, 2024. (IC 
3‐10‐1‐5(d)) 
Q. Can I use the list on the IED website to build my ballot 
for federal and state candidates? 
A. No. This is not recommended. The cerƟﬁed list of  
candidates for federal, statewide, state legislaƟve, and  
judicialoﬃces will be sent to counƟes not later than Febru‐
ary 23, 2024. This is the oﬃcial list of candidates that are to 
be printed on your ballots, and this list may be diﬀerent 
from what is posted online. 
Q. What can or can’t we do during the VLM “freeze”? 
A. All counƟes need to complete their voter list  
maintenance acƟvity to move voters records to “inacƟve” 
status not later than Feb. 7, 2024, or 90‐days before the 
May primary. Otherwise, counƟes may conƟnue to update 
or add new registraƟons, cancel registraƟon records at the 
wriƩen request of the voter or due to death or  
disenfranchisement following criminal convicƟon. 
Timeline 
CounƟes must esƟmate the number of 
provisional and absentee ballots your 
county will need not later than March 
8, 2024. 
 
Then, your county must receive the 
order of absentee ballots not later 
than Monday, March 18, 2024. (If your 
county uses a ballot‐on‐demand  
printer, then the CD or equivalent 
with the ballot ﬁles should be  
delivered by this date.) 
 
Lastly, counƟes using opƟcal scan  
paper ballot cards or tradiƟonal hand‐
counted paper ballots need to order 
ElecƟon Day ballots. The print order 
should arrive on Ɵme for your county 
to organize the ballots for pick‐up by 
Inspectors the Saturday or Sunday 
before the elecƟon. 
 
To order ElecƟon Day ballots for the 
May primary elecƟon, a county needs 
to review its 2022 November elecƟon 
precinct level results and idenƟfy 
which DemocraƟc candidate was the 
top vote geƩer in each precinct, and 
which Republican candidate was the 
top vote geƩer in each precinct to set 
forth the minimum number of ballots 
to order. 
 
Figure 1 below is an example of how 
many ballots and of which party type 
should be ordered for each precinct 
on ElecƟon Day. (No, state law does 
not permit counƟes to back out any 
absentee voters; you must follow this 
law for ordering in the primary.) 
 
Some counƟes use a voƟng system 
where a blank ballot card is inserted 
into a ballot marking device, the voter 
makes their selecƟons, and a  
completed ballot card is printed for 
the voter to insert into the opScan 
tabulator. You would sƟll follow the 
ballot ordering rules, though instead 
of having printed ballots, you would 
be ordering blank ballot stock at this 
minimum threshold. 
 
If you are a vote center county using 
printed ballot cards or blank ballot 
card stock, then you’ll want to go 
through this same exercise and sum 
the minimum precinct order to reach 
a total minimum to deliver to each 
vote center. Using the example below, 
each vote center would be supplied 
with at least 237 D ballots (125+112) 
and 215 R ballots (101+114). 
 
Please note: the ballot prinƟng rules 
and needs are diﬀerent for the  
November general elecƟon. 
 
Special Ballot Styles 
In a primary elecƟon, a county must 
print one ballot style for the  
DemocraƟc Party and one ballot style 
for the Republican Party. 
 
However, some jurisdicƟons will have 
a public quesƟon cerƟﬁed to them for 
the May primary, which requires its 
own special “non‐parƟsan” ballot style 
for those voters who do not want to 
vote in a party’s primary elecƟon but 
do want to vote on the referendum. 
 
If there is a public quesƟon that  
appears in some or all of the precincts 
in the county, then you must 1) print 
the public quesƟon on the D & R  
primary ballots, 2) create a non‐
parƟsan ballot with only the public 
quesƟon for the reason stated above, 
and 3) print special 17‐year old D & R 
ballots that do NOT include the public 
quesƟon but do include the  
candidates. 
 
In May, the “17‐year‐old” ballot would 
also be used for those voters who 
moved out of the school corporaƟon 
district in the ﬁnal 30‐days before the 
elecƟon, if a public quesƟon for the 
school was on the ballot. These voters 
are enƟtled to vote for candidates to 
elected or party oﬃce, but not  
permiƩed to vote on the school  
corporaƟon’s public quesƟon. 
 
Don’t forget that primary elecƟon  
ballots should have the name of each 
party printed near the top of the  
ballot, and it’s also permissible to  
include color coding to allow for 
beƩer visual idenƟﬁcaƟon for poll 
workers to pull the proper party’s  
ballot requested by the voter.

Election Division Dispatch 
 Brad King & Angie Nussmeyer, Co-Directors | March 2024 
NEWS & UPDATES 
Democracy Live 
Felicia Erlich, the COO and corporaƟon counsel for Democ-
racy Live, is our state’s point of contact to provide an online 
ballot marking tool to voters with print disabiliƟes who re-

Solar Eclipse & VR Deadline 
Many counƟes are reporƟng that their oﬃces will be closed 
on Monday, April 8, 2024, because of the interest in the 
total solar eclipse. This isn’t just a special day for space  
enthusiasts—it’s also our statewide VR deadline!  
 
If your oﬃce is closed on April 8, 2024, then the deadline to 
receive paper voter registraƟon forms rolls over to noon, 
April 9, 2024, but online applicaƟons sƟll must be received 
by 11:59PM, April 8, 2024 since the state is not closed.  
Therefore, it will be important to pay special aƩenƟon to 
the Ɵme/date stamp in your OVR and BMV hoppers. Also 
note that early voƟng is NOT delayed due to the ﬁling  
deadline rollover. It must begin when the clerk’s oﬃce 
opens on April 9, 2024, which means your public test must 
be completed by April 8, 2024. 
 
If your county is not closed on “eclipse day” then it’s  
business as usual and there are no changes to your calendar 
or procedures.

IN FOCUS: CANDIDATES AS ABSENTEE OR ELECTION DAY WORKERS 
Several counƟes have reached out to 
ask if candidates, whether opposed or 
unopposed, can serve as an absentee 
board member or ElecƟon Day poll 
worker. The short answer is that it 
depends.  
 
ABS Voter Board Members 
The general qualiﬁcaƟons to serve as a 
D or R on the absentee voter board or 
as a central count team member are 
found in IC 3-11.5.4-22. Some  
candidates may be eligible to serve in 
these posiƟons. 
 
An unopposed candidate can serve, if 
the person is running for a city, town, 
township or school board oﬃce or for 
a party oﬃce (PC or delegate). A  
family member of any unopposed  
candidate can serve in these posiƟons. 
However, if a candidate is opposed for 
any oﬃce, including for party oﬃce, 
then the candidate and their family  
members may not serve in these  
posiƟons if the candidate is running 
countywide.  
 
Iif the candidate is opposed and is not 
running countywide, then the  
candidate and their family members 
can be assigned to handle absentees 
in precincts where the candidate’s 
name does not appear on the ballot. 
 
For example, there are nine townships 
in Cardinal County. John is an opposed 
candidate for township board in town-
ship 1. This means John and his family 
can handle absentees in townships 2-
9, but cannot handle an absentee in 
township 1. 
 
ElecƟon Day Poll Workers 
The requirements to work the polls on 
ElecƟon Day are found in IC 3-6-6-7. 
Unless a person is only running for PC 
or delegate, no candidate—whether 
opposed or unopposed—can be a poll 
worker.  
 
The party oﬃce excepƟon noted 
above allows unopposed candidates 
for PC or delegate and their family 
members to serve as poll workers. 
Recent changes in state law also allow 
opposed candidates for PC and  
delegate and their family members to 
work the polls but only if the CEB 
unanimously supports a resoluƟon 
under IC 3-6-6-7(c). 
 
While family members of opposed 
candidates for elected oﬃce cannot 
work the polls on ElecƟon Day, it is 
possible for family members of  
unopposed candidates to work. 
 
There is one ﬁnal workaround, but it 
only applies to non-vote center  
counƟes. It is possible for an opposed 
candidate and their family members 
to work on ElecƟon Day IF the  
candidate is not running countywide. 
These individuals must be assigned to 
a precinct where the candidate’s 
name does not appear on the ballot. 
 
For example, if Sally is running in  
district 2 of Tulip Tree Town Council, 
then she or her family members can 
be assigned to a precinct that does not 
include her elecƟon district. This is not 
possible in vote center counƟes, since 
all precincts vote at every locaƟon.  
VR CORNER 
Federal Post Card ApplicaƟons & RegistraƟon 
Military and overseas voters are encouraged to use the Feder-
al Post Card ApplicaƟon (FPCA), as it oﬀers special protecƟons 
to these individuals. Below are just a few of the beneﬁts: 
 
A US ciƟzen who resides overseas can maintain their “nexus” 
to their last known US address when using the FPCA. If they 
last resided in Indiana for at least 30-days before heading 
overseas, the voter should complete secƟon 2 of the form 
with their former Indiana address. However, if the overseas 
ciƟzen marks the box indicaƟng their “return is uncertain” 
then the voter’s residence address in SVRS is changed to the 
address of your VR oﬃce. This “return uncertain” designaƟon 
allows the voter to receive a “federal only” ballot to vote on 
President, US House, and US Senate. 
 
SecƟon 3 of the FPCA is the voter’s overseas mailing address, 
which counƟes will use to update the voter’s mailing address 
in the SVRS registraƟon module and absentee module. 
 
Lastly, the voter registraƟon deadline is extended for voters 
using the FPCA to 7-days before the elecƟon and in some cas-
es, can be extended up to elecƟon day. See the 2024 Military 
and Overseas Handbook for more details. 
QUESTIONS OF THE MONTH 
 
Q. Do candidate names appear in CAPITAL leƩers on the ballot? 
And do I use “” or () around a candidate’s nickname? 
A. Yes, a candidate’s name is printed in ALL CAPS on the ballot. (IC 
3-10-1-14.1) State law also requires parentheses () around a  
candidate’s nickname, not quotaƟon marks. (IC 3-5-7-5) 
 
Q. Can we use the Democracy Live tool the state provides to 
counƟes to email ballots to military and overseas voters? 
A. The state’s contract with Democracy Live only covers voters 
with print disabiliƟes. If you have a military or overseas voter  
using the Federal Post Card ApplicaƟon (FPCA) that asks for an 
emailed or faxed absentee ballot, then you will need to send to 
the voter the ABS Voter Bill of Rights, MOVE InformaƟon Sheet, 
ABS-9 (generated from SVRS), and a copy of the voter’s ballot 
iniƟaled by bi-parƟsan ABS voter board or CEB.  
 
The voter then has to return the ABS-9 secrecy waiver and their 
marked ballot. County oﬃcials will print oﬀ the returned ballot 
and seal it in the ABS-10B (or ABS-10, if using old stock) envelope 
and aƩach the ABS-9 and voter’s ABS applicaƟon to it. On ElecƟon 
Day, if the voter is found to be a qualiﬁed voter of the precinct, a 
bi-parƟsan team will remake the voter’s emailed ballot on an  
oﬃcial ballot card for tabulaƟon.

If your county has any changes to “early” voƟng or

New vote center counƟes will also need to submit a

you’ve already done this, there is no need to request

Don’t forget! The county elecƟon board (rather than

YARD SIGNS 
It’s spring and yard signs will be popping up before 
you know it. The good news is that the CEB only has 
enforcement jurisdicƟon over disclaimers, but you 
are oŌen asked about other statutes related to 
yard signs. Below are some answers to frequently 
asked quesƟons: 
 
1/ Is there a state law that dictates when yard signs 
can be put out before an elecƟon? No, state law 
doesn’t speciﬁcally address when campaign yard 
signs can go out in people’s yards. This decision is 
leŌ to local ordinance or homeowner associaƟon 
policies. However, there is a state law that states IF 
there is a local ordinance prohibiƟng yard signs, then 
the ordinance is not enforceable for 60-days before 
an elecƟon through 5-days aŌer elecƟon day. (IC 36-
1-3-11) AddiƟonally, a homeowner’s associaƟon  
policy prohibiƟng yard signs cannot be enforced 30-
days before an elecƟon through 5-days aŌerward.  
(IC 32-21-13-4) 
2/ Are disclaimers required on yard signs? In most 
cases, yes. A disclaimer in at least 7 size font with 
who paid for the sign is required to be included on 
the sign in indelible ink that contrasts with the  
background. (IC 3-9-3-2.5) However, signs supporƟng 
or opposing a referendum do not require the use of 
a disclaimer. (IC 3-9-3-2.5)  The CEB would address 
complaints about yard signs that appear to not be 
compliant with state’s disclaimer law. 
3/ A non‐incumbent printed on their yard sign “Sam 
Smith Dogcatcher.” This implies they are the  
incumbent. Is this allowable? In the view of the  
Indiana ElecƟon Commission, yes. The bi-parƟsan IEC 
issued an advisory opinion (2015-01) that interprets 
IC 3-9-3-5. A copy of this advisory opinion is included 
in the appendix of the green Campaign Finance 
Manual. 
4/ A person calls to ask if she can remove a yard 
sign placed in the highway right‐of‐way without 
permission. What do I tell her? Only those with legal 
authority over the property can remove the yard 
sign from the county right-of-way. Any other person 
without such authority may be liable for criminal 
conversion. She should ﬁle a complaint with the 
proper authoriƟes to make them aware of the yard 
sign’s placement. If the sign is located on the  
owner’s property outside of any right-of-way, then 
the owner may remove it. 
For more informaƟon, IED publishes a “PoliƟcal Signs 
& Disclaimer Requirements” brochure that is  
available on in.gov/sos/elecƟons.

Election Division Dispatch 
 Brad King & Angie Nussmeyer, Co-Directors | April 2024 
NEWS & UPDATES 
Democracy Works & Poll LocaƟon Data 
Each elecƟon cycle the state provides early voƟng and ElecƟon

The week of April 15, Democracy Works will begin sharing

just for our partners but also indianavoters.com. If you have

reasons for provisional ballots; an auto‐save feature to save

gaƟng between pages within each mapping category; a new

maƟon to voters when deadlines pass; and an update to the ABS
‐24 to include the voter’s name and precinct and update the text 
on the “Ɵmely” received porƟon of the form to reﬂect changes

CAN‐9: NoƟce of Primary ElecƟon 
For the May primary elecƟon, each CEB must compile a list of 
DemocraƟc and Republican candidates for federal, state, and 
local oﬃce along with their address and oﬃce sought. 
(Addresses must be included unless restricted under IC 36‐1‐

Ɵmes and locaƟons of early voƟng sites. In some counƟes, the

AŌer entering candidate details in SVRS, the CAN‐9 can be

The CAN‐9 must be ﬁled in the minutes of a CEB meeƟng and

Candidates for party oﬃces (PC and delegate) do not need to be

Note: ElecƟon Day voƟng locaƟons are published separately
