IN FOCUS: Election Results Reporting  
Unoﬃcial ElecƟon Night Results  
ReporƟng 
CounƟes are required to report UNOFFICIAL 
results on elecƟon night, beginning not later 
than 8P and ending at midnight (local Ɵme). If 
results are not complete, then counƟes must 
resume reporƟng at 9AM the next day and 
update results hourly unƟl all unoﬃcial results 
are entered into SVRS. Results are displayed on 
indianavoters.com/elecƟonresults. 
 
Two SVRS ReporƟng Methods 
In SVRS, there are two ways to enter results: 
summary or precinct level. Your reporƟng  
preference can be turned “oﬀ” or “on” by  
manually changing the seƫng to be “on” or 
“oﬀ” in County Preferences (Admin > System > 
County Preferences > Precinct Level  
ReporƟng).  
 
“Oﬀ” mode means your county is manually 
reporƟng summary level results in SVRS. When 
in the “on” posiƟon, counƟes will be reporƟng 
results by precinct. The default seƫng for  
precinct level reporƟng is to use the uploader; 
if you want to manually enter precinct results, 
you must toggle the “Precinct Level Hand  
Entry” on, too. (See image below) 
 
Once the results preference is set for the  
elecƟon, it cannot be changed unƟl aŌer  
elecƟon results are cerƟﬁed. CounƟes may 
change their results reporƟng preference for 
the next elecƟon aŌer cerƟﬁcaƟon. 
 
The upload funcƟonality requires you to “map” 
the names used in by your county’s elecƟon  
management soŌware to the ﬁxed names in 
SVRS. Think of mapping as helping SVRS  
translate the precinct, candidate, and oﬃce 
names used by your voƟng system soŌware.  
 
For example, the voƟng system soŌware may 
use “clerk” for an oﬃce name but SVRS has a 
ﬁxed name of “county clerk.” You are tying, or 
“mapping,” the word choice used by your 
voƟng system soŌware (“clerk”) to the ﬁxed 
SVRS oﬃce name (“county clerk”) so SVRS 
knows clerk = county clerk when results data is 
uploaded and presents accurate elecƟon  
results.  
 
 
There are a few things to do now so the  
process will work smoothly on ElecƟon Night:  
 
1.Request your zero ﬁle from your voƟng  
system vendor, which can be the zero ﬁle used 
at the public test. 
 
2. Use the zero ﬁle to  pracƟce mapping in 
SVRS Sandbox. SVRS Sandbox was refreshed in 
March, so elecƟon informaƟon should be  
reasonably updated. If you need access to 
INSVRS Sandbox, please contact the Help Desk. 
 
3.When you are comfortable with the feature, 
upload the ZERO ﬁle into SVRS ProducƟon to 
set up your mapping.  
 
CerƟﬁed ElecƟon Results 
AŌer the county canvasses its results, it must 
cerƟfy its precinct level results to IED using 
SVRS. IED is no longer accepƟng elecƟon  
results by email, fax, mail, or hand‐delivery.  
CounƟes will not be able to ﬁle the CEB‐9  
report unƟl their precinct results are uploaded. 
 
If unoﬃcial results were entered at the  
summary level, then the ﬁnal precinct level 
results will be added as an aƩachment to the 
CEB‐9 ﬁled in SVRS. For those counƟes that 
entered results by precinct in SVRS and ﬁnal‐
ized them in the system, there is no need to 
add an aƩachment to the CEB‐9. 
 
Before ﬁnalizing results, don’t forget to update 
unoﬃcial results in SVRS with any absentees or 
provisionals that were counted and to update 
voter turnout staƟsƟcs. 
 
ElecƟon results are available to download from 
indianavoters.com/elecƟonresults, which is 
why it is important for oﬃcial precinct level 
results reporƟng be replaced by ﬁnal, oﬃcial 
results in SVRS. 
 
Resources 
There are recorded web training sessions and 
step‐by‐steps available on the SVRS County 
Portal. AddiƟonally, County ENR Data Entry 
training is scheduled for April 16 & 18. 
VR CORNER 
US District Court Data VLM Project Preview 
In even‐numbered years, the state is required to request jury 
duty USPS returns from the Northern and Southern US  
District Courts. This informaƟon must be shared with counƟes 
aŌer the May primary elecƟon and counƟes must send the 
SAMC noƟce, if applicable, not later than June 18, 2024. 
 
The list is not housed within SVRS hoppers; instead,  
spreadsheets will be posted on the INSVRS County Portal in 
the Special Projects folder. The spreadsheet will include voters 
whose jury duty summons was returned with “deceased” or 
“returned as undeliverable” designaƟons. 
 
Before sending a SAMC to the voter where “deceased” is  
indicated, we recommend looking for obituaries in the  
newspaper or funeral home websites, for example. If your 
county VR oﬃcial is reasonably saƟsﬁed the person in the  
obituary and the spreadsheet are the same, then you can 
move the voter’s registraƟon status to “cancelled” and  
Include the source info for the cancellaƟon. 
 
More informaƟon will be shared next month, and online  
trainings by Civix on SVRS modules will take place in June. 
QUESTIONS OF THE MONTH 
 
Q. Do we use the PRE‐5 at early voƟng locaƟons? 
A. No. The PRE‐5 is used on ElecƟon Day only for those voters 
whose absentee‐by‐mail ballot did not arrive. The voter  
completes the PRE‐5 and then can vote a regular ballot, if  
otherwise qualiﬁed. BEFORE ElecƟon Day, the ABS‐5 is used for 
this scenario or if the voter wants to surrender their absentee 
ballot and request to vote in‐person, for example. 
 
Q. Can voters hand‐deliver an absentee ballot by mail to an  
early voƟng locaƟon? 
A. Yes. A voter, a member of the voter’s household, aƩorney in 
fact and certain relaƟves may hand‐deliver a voter’s completed 
absentee ballot to an early voƟng locaƟon. Please be sure to have 
the ABS‐19 form handy for any person, other than the voter, 
hand delivering their absentee ballot. Absentee voter boards 
should also receive training on managing this scenario. 
 
Q. Are County Commissioners elected at large? 
A. Except for Lake, Marion and St. Joe counƟes, all county  
commissioners are elected at‐large, meaning every voter of the 
county votes for the candidates. However, candidates must  
reside in one of the three districts to meet duraƟonal residency 
requirements to qualify to run for the oﬃce and while holding 
elected oﬃce.

### Indiana Election Division Dispatch — May 2024

Election Division Dispatch 
 Brad King & Angie Nussmeyer, Co-Directors | May 2024 
NEWS & UPDATES 
Primary ElecƟon—Party A ﬃliaƟon Challenge 
Our oﬃce is oŌen asked if Indiana has a “closed” or “open” 
primary. A closed primary, generally speaking, means the voter 
registers to vote indicaƟng a party aﬃliaƟon, which voters do 
not do in Indiana. Instead, the voter develops a voƟng history 
based on which party’s primary ballot was chosen by them. An 
open primary usually means there are no restricƟons on who 
can vote in the primary. 
 
Indiana strikes a balance between the two and is closer to a 
closed primary than an open one. Our state law (IC 3‐10‐1‐6) 
notes that a voter may vote in a party’s primary elecƟon: 
 (1) if the voter, at the last general elecƟon (Nov. 2022),  
voted for a majority of the regular nominees of the party 
holding the primary, or  
 
 (2) if the voter did not vote in the last general elecƟon (Nov. 
2022) but intends to vote for a majority of the party’s  
candidates in the next general elecƟon (Nov. 2024). 
 
In fact, in primary elecƟons only, a voter of the precinct may 
challenge another voter on ElecƟon Day, if it is believed the  
voter does not aﬃliate with the party whose ballot the voter 
selected. The challenger would complete the PRE‐6 aﬃdavit, 
which all of your poll workers should have in their ElecƟon Day 
materials.  
 
The voter can overcome the challenge and vote a regular  
ballot, if otherwise qualiﬁed, if the voter completes their  
porƟon of the aﬃdavit which conﬁrms they meet one of the two 
qualiﬁcaƟons in IC 3‐10‐1‐6 to vote in the party’s primary. 
 
Ballot “Selﬁes” & Smartphones 
A reminder that the former “ballot selﬁe” law (IC 3‐11‐8‐17.5)
prohibiƟng an individual from taking a photo of their completed 
ballot and sharing it was found by a federal court to be  
unconsƟtuƟonal in 2017 and is no longer enforceable pursuant 
to court order. However, the statute has not been repealed, 
which is why it is printed in the Title 3 Code Book and searchable 
on iga.in.gov. Please be sure your staﬀ, poll workers, absentee 
voter boards, and others involved in elecƟon administraƟon are 
aware that the “ballot selﬁe” statute cannot be enforced.  
 
Voters are permiƩed to use their smartphone or other  
electronic device or wriƩen materials to assist them with  
compleƟng their ballot. This does not consƟtute elecƟoneering 
under IC 3‐14‐3‐16 as long as the materials or images are not  
displayed in a way for others to see. (IC 3‐11‐8‐18.5) 
 
CEB‐9: County ElecƟon Report 
State law requires the CEB‐9 to be ﬁled in SVRS. While the form 
includes lines for your CEB members to sign, this was added as a 
request by counƟes to keep with their records. There is no need 
to email or fax the signed form to our oﬃce, or to aƩach it to 
your completed CEB‐9 in SVRS. 
CALENDAR 
May 4, 2024: All county clerk’s oﬃces must be open for 
early voƟng; vote center counƟes must also open one  
addiƟonal vote center used on elecƟon day for early 
voƟng  
May 6, 2024 (NOON): Deadline for FPCA to be ﬁled to  
request faxed/emailed ballot; Deadline for ABS‐Traveling 
Board to be ﬁled; Early voƟng ends 
May 7, 2024: Primary ElecƟon Day; polls open from 6A to 
6P (local Ɵme); ABS‐Mail ballots due by 6P (local Ɵme) 
May 15, 2024 (NOON): Deadline for ABS voter to return 
ABS‐18A, ABS‐18B to cure mismatched or missing  
signature 
May 17, 2024 (NOON): Deadline to receive an ABS ballot 
issued to an overseas or overseas military ballot by mail, 
which must be counted if the envelope is postmarked on 
or before May 7, 2024 
May 17, 2024 (NOON): Deadline for a provisional ballot 
voter with ID issues to bring their ID to the CEB or sign an 
aﬃdavit (PRO‐10) that the voter is indigent or has a  
religious objecƟon to having their photo taken for an ID 
May 17, 2024 (3PM): Deadline for CEB to determine 
whether or not to count a provisional ballot 
May 20, 2024 (NOON): Deadline for CEB to cerƟfy oﬃce‐
level elecƟon results to IED; must be done in SVRS 
May 21, 2024 (NOON): Deadline for counƟes to ﬁle CEB‐9; 
must be done in SVRS 
May 21, 2024 (NOON): Deadline for candidate to ﬁle  
recount/contest acƟon following primary elecƟon 
May 21, 2024: Voter RegistraƟon re‐
opens; ﬁrst day an 
ABS app can be ﬁled for November elecƟon 
May 21, 2024: First day a school board candidate can ﬁle 
CAN‐34 peƟƟon & CAN‐12  
May 24, 2024: First day, aŌer noon, to issue a cerƟﬁcate 
of elecƟon to a PC (CEB‐14) or delegate (CEB‐15) (no other 
cerƟﬁcates of elecƟon would be issued aŌer the primary) 
May 24, 2024 (NOON): Deadline for state or county party 
chair to ﬁle recount/contest acƟon following the primary 
elecƟon 
May 27, 2024: IED Closed (Memorial Day)  
MAY WEB TRAINING 
May 2 & 9| Post‐ElecƟon Processing 
May 14 & 16 | CEB Form GeneraƟon Overview 
May 12 & 23| PeƟƟons Overview 
May 28 & 30 | US District Court Data Processing 
 
2024 Calendar is posted to the INSVRS County Portal but is subject to revision.  
InformaƟon in this newsleƩer is provided by the Indiana ElecƟon Division as a courtesy to county elecƟon administrators. If a person is unclear concerning 
elecƟon law provisions, the ElecƟon Division can serve as an interpreƟve source. However, where important legal rights are concerned, you must consult with 
your own aƩorney to be fully and properly advised. 
IN FOCUS: Summer Candidate Filings 
More candidate ﬁling deadlines will be upon us 
this summer, as ballot vacancies will be ﬁlled, 
convenƟons held, and more peƟƟons ﬁled for 
minor party, independent, and school board 
candidates to gain ballot access. 
 
D & R Ballot Vacancies 
If a D or R did not ﬁle to run for an oﬃce in the 
primary elecƟon, the parƟes are able to ﬁll 
those ballot vacancies not later than noon, July 
3, 2024. There are two opƟons for ﬁlling a local 
oﬃce ballot vacancy under IC 3‐13‐1: 
 
1/ Direct appointment by the chair or central 
commiƩee. The party organizaƟon may  
authorize the chair or central commiƩee ﬁrst, 
by passing a resoluƟon or adopƟng a moƟon at 
a party meeƟng. There is no special state form 
and state law does not provide direcƟon on 
what needs to be in the resoluƟon. For  
example, some parƟes give the chair  
limited authority to ﬁll ballot vacancies in a 
speciﬁc year, term of chair’s service, or no end 
date at all. (Note: this authorizaƟon DOES NOT 
apply to elected oﬃce vacancies!) The  
appointments must be made by noon, July 3, 
2024, and the paperwork (CAN‐31, CAN‐12, 
CAN‐29) ﬁled not later than noon, July 3, 2024. 
 
2/ By holding a caucus of eligible PCs not later 
than noon, July 3, 2024. NoƟce of the caucus 
(CAN‐30) must be sent to eligible PCs by ﬁrst 
class mail not later than 10‐days before the 
caucus is held AND noƟce must be ﬁled with 
the county clerk not later than noon, 10‐days 
before the caucus is held. The candidate must 
ﬁle their CAN‐31 declaraƟon with the chair of 
the caucus AND with the county clerk not later 
than 72‐hours before the caucus is held. (At 
this stage, the CAN‐12 is not required.) AŌer 
the caucus is held, the CAN‐29 cerƟﬁcate of 
candidate selecƟon and the CAN‐12 statement 
of economic interests must be ﬁled  not later 
than noon, July 3, 2024. 
 
Note: Local oﬃces include judicial oﬃce and 
prosecuƟng aƩorney; however, the paperwork 
noted in #1 and #2 for these two oﬃces is ﬁled 
with IED NOT with  the county clerk. The CAN‐
12 is also not used; instead, the candidate must 
ﬁle the statement of economic interests  
prescribed by the Commission on Judicial  
QualiﬁcaƟons using their portal. 
 
Note 2: State legislaƟve vacancies are  
managed by state parƟes & ﬁled with IED. 
 
Libertarian Candidates 
The Libertarian Party of Indiana generally  
nominates their candidates for federal, state, 
and local oﬃces at a state or county  
convenƟon. Instead of ﬁling declaraƟons of 
candidacy with the CEB, the LPIN county 
convenƟon chair and secretary will cerƟfy the 
Party’s nominees to the CEB using the CAN‐22 
cerƟﬁcate of nominaƟon along with the candi‐
date’s CAN‐12 statement of economic inter‐
ests.  If used, the LPIN county convenƟon must 
be held not later than noon, July 3, 2024, and 
paperwork ﬁled with the CEB by the same 
deadline. 
 
Should the LPIN not nominate candidates for 
all oﬃces on the ballot in November at their 
convenƟon, the party  has unƟl noon, July 3, 
2024, to ﬁll a ballot vacancy. The LPIN chair will 
ﬁle noƟce with the CEB of their party’s intent 
to ﬁll a ballot vacancy for local oﬃce, which 
must be ﬁled not later than ten days before the 
ballot vacancy can be ﬁlled. No state form is 
prescribed; a list of oﬃces on leƩerhead signed 
by the chair is suﬃcient.  
 
If ballot vacancies are ﬁlled by LPIN, the  
CAN‐32 and CAN‐12 must then be ﬁled with 
the CEB not later than noon, July 3, 2024.  
 
Note:  L candidates ﬁlling a vacancy for judge 
ﬁle paperwork with IED and use the statement 
of economic interests created by the Commis‐
sion on Judicial  QualiﬁcaƟons not the CAN‐12. 
 
Independent & Minor Party  Candidates 
Independent and minor parƟes have two ballot 
access methods—through the pe ƟƟon process 
or to be a write‐in candidate. 
 
If an independent or minor party candidate 
wants their name printed on the ballot, then 
they must go through the peƟƟon process. 
Beginning January 10, 2024, candidates may 
ﬁle peƟƟon signatures using the CAN‐19 or 
CAN‐21 forms with the county VR oﬃce. The 
CAN‐21 is used for local oﬃces; the CAN‐19 is 
used for federal, state, state legislaƟve, and 
judicial oﬃces, including prosecuƟng aƩorney. 
 
The individual signing the peƟƟon must be a 
registered voter in the elecƟon district of the 
oﬃce the candidate is seeking at the Ɵme the 
peƟƟon is processed. 
 
In order to gain ballot access, the candidate 
must collect signatures totaling at least 2% of 
the total votes cast in the 2022 SOS race in the 
precincts of the elecƟon district. This means 
county elecƟon oﬃcials will need to pull out 
the November 2022 precinct level results and 
calculate the signature threshold for local oﬃc‐
es using the current oﬃce boundaries. 
(Countywide totals can be found in the back of 
the 2024 Candidate Guide.) State legislaƟve or 
federal candidates should contact IED for this 
informaƟon. 
 
CAN‐19 or CAN‐21 peƟƟons must be ﬁled with 
the county VR oﬃcial by noon, July  1, 2024, for 
the peƟƟon to be reviewed and cerƟﬁed. If 
seeking a local oﬃce, the candidate must also 
submit their CAN‐12 with the ﬁrst batch of 
peƟƟons ﬁled with the clerk’s oﬃce. However, 
in the few counƟes with a separate county VR 
oﬃce, the CAN‐12 is ﬁled with the cerƟﬁed 
peƟƟons when those are ﬁled with the county 
clerk or elecƟon board. The CAN‐20 consent 
form must also be ﬁled with the cerƟﬁed  
peƟƟons not later than noon, July 15, 2024.  
 
The county clerk must send a leƩer by cerƟﬁed 
mail to the candidate if the individual does 
NOT achieve the signature threshold for ballot 
access. If the candidate did collect enough 
signatures, then counƟes will send the  
candidate a CAN‐5. 
 
Some individuals want to be a write‐in  
candidate. WRITE‐IN CANDIDATES ARE NOT 
PRINTED ON THE BALLOT! The CAN‐3 form may 
be submiƩed from January 10 through noon, 
July 3, 2024. For local oﬃces, the CAN‐12 must 
also be ﬁled with the CAN‐3.   
School Board Candidates 
NEW! Candidates for school board may ﬁle the 
CAN‐34 peƟƟon and consent along with a CAN‐
12 beginning May 21, 2024, and not later than 
noon, June 20, 2024. There is no separate dec‐
laraƟon of candidacy; instead, the consent of 
the candidate found on the back of the CAN‐34 
is used for this purpose. A candidate can ﬁle 
mulƟple CAN‐34 forms, but only one needs to 
have a consent completed.  
 
Most school board candidates will need to 
collect at least ten signatures of registered 
voters within the school corporaƟon’s  
boundaries. However, there are excepƟons to 
this rule if the district is single member or  
subject to special legislaƟon. 
 
AddiƟonally, some school corporaƟon  
boundaries cross into more than one county. In 
these instances, the county with the largest 
populaƟon receives the CAN‐34 & CAN‐12, and 
then cerƟﬁes the signatures on the peƟƟon. 
This means the “large” county will use a 
statewide search to cerƟfy names in other 
counƟes. This process, where another county 
cerƟﬁes another county’s voters, is unique to 
the CAN‐34. 
 
“Small” Town Oﬃces 
Towns with a populaƟon of less than 3,500 
may move some or all of their municipal oﬃces 
to even‐numbered years through a local  
ordinance. Unless the local ordinance  
speciﬁcally requested the D/R candidates be 
nominated at the May primary elecƟon, then 
“small” towns will have town convenƟons to 
nominate D, L, and R candidates to the oﬃces 
on the ballot, if there is a contest in that party 
for nominaƟon to an oﬃce. This requires a 
candidate to ﬁle the CAN‐16 and CAN‐12 with 
the CEB not later than noon, Aug. 1, 2024.  
 
More informaƟon on this topic can be found in 
the blue 2024 ElecƟon Administrator’s Manual 
or 2024 Candidate’s Guide. 
MISSING BALLOT VACANCY DEADLINES 
As noted in this newsleƩer there are various ﬁlling deadlines that the 
county party chairs and candidates must observe when ﬁlling an 
 early ballot vacancy.  
 
Per IC 3‐13‐1‐21 if the CAN‐30 caucus noƟce or Libertarian noƟce, 
CAN‐31 candidate declaraƟon form, or CAN‐29 cerƟﬁcate of candi‐
date selecƟon is oﬀered for ﬁling aŌer the deadline then that speciﬁc 
form cannot be accepted according to IC 3‐5‐4‐1.9 and the cerƟﬁcate 
of candidate selecƟon placing the candidate on the ballot cannot be 
accepted. The poliƟcal party would need to re‐do the process to ﬁll 
the ballot vacancy if there is Ɵme remaining. 
QUESTIONS OF THE MONTH 
 
Q. Can we use jail inmates to deliver voƟng systems? 
A. No. State law explicitly forbids the use of inmates to deliver voƟng 
systems (IC 3‐11‐3‐10(e)). Instead, state law requires a bi‐parƟsan 
team to deliver the equipment OR the CEB OR a commercial delivery 
service. (IC 3‐11‐3‐10(d)) The CEB lacks home rule authority to adopt 
delivery procedures contrary to state law. 
 
Q. Do we use the ABS‐5 on ElecƟon Day? 
A. No. The ABS‐5 is used to troubleshoot absentee issues before 
ElecƟon Day. On ElecƟon Day, if a voter did not receive their ABS 
ballot, then they can complete the PRE‐5 at the voƟng locaƟon and 
vote a regular ballot, if otherwise qualiﬁed. A voter can also  
surrender their ABS to the Inspector, which allows them to be issued 
a regular ballot if otherwise qualiﬁed. Should the voter’s ABS be  
rejected on ElecƟon Day, then the individual may request the ABS‐21 
from the CEB not later than 5PM on ElecƟon Day. This allows the 
voter to go to their voƟng locaƟon to cast a regular ballot if  
otherwise qualiﬁed. 
 
Q. Can the ABS‐18A/ABS‐18B be delivered to the Inspector at an 
ElecƟon Day voƟng locaƟon? 
A. Yes. The aﬃdavits used for a missing or mismatched signatures on 
ABS materials can be hand‐delivered to the Inspector on ElecƟon 
Day. However, voters have unƟl noon, 8‐days aŌer the elecƟon (May 
15, 2024 for the primary) to ﬁle the aﬃdavit by email, fax, hand‐
delivery or mail. 
 
Q. Can we use INcite to verify a voter’s Indiana driver’s license 
number or SSN4 for VR or ABS purposes? 
A. No. CounƟes are to use SVRS to validate Indiana DLN numbers 
using the direct connecƟon to BMV and SSA records. INcite leverages 
court data that may not be accurate or validated by the BMV. More 
importantly, federal and state law do not authorize its use for this 
validaƟon feature and instead relies upon the informaƟon sourced 
directly from BMV/SSA. 
 
Q. Can a CAN‐1 challenge for a local candidate that won the  
primary elecƟon be ﬁled? 
A. No. For local oﬃces, the challenge period for those ﬁling to run in 
the primary elecƟon has passed. If there are concerns about a  
candidate’s qualiﬁcaƟons, a contest lawsuit may be ﬁled by certain 
persons under IC 3‐12‐8. 
Summer Nominating Conventions 
This summer the DemocraƟc and Republican parƟes will 
host their state convenƟons to nominate candidates for 
AƩorney General and Lt. Governor candidate. Their  
nominaƟng paperwork is ﬁled with IED not later than noon, 
July 15, 2024. (The Libertarian Party held their state conven‐
Ɵon in March 2024.) 
 
All three parƟes—D, R, L—will host a na Ɵonal convenƟon to 
nominate their PresidenƟal and Vice‐PresidenƟal Ɵckets. 
For Indiana, the nominaƟon paperwork is to be ﬁled not 
later than noon, September 10, 2024. 
 
There will be a statewide public quesƟon on the ballot this 
November to amend the state’s consƟtuƟon. 
 
The state will cerƟfy to counƟes info for all federal (except 
for D/R/L President/VP candidates), statewide, state legisla‐
Ɵve, and judicial candidates on the ballot to counƟes not 
later than noon, August 23, 2024. The presidenƟal Ɵcket for 
the D/R/L parƟes will be cerƟﬁed to counƟes not later than 
noon, September 12, 2024.  
 
Note: PresidenƟal Ɵckets for minor parƟes or those running 
as independents follow the same deadlines of submiƫng 
peƟƟons to counƟes for cerƟﬁcaƟon by noon, July 1, 2024, 
and then ﬁling cerƟﬁed peƟƟons with IED not later than 
noon, July 15, 2024. 
Filling Ballot Vacancies for Nov. 
Due to Candidate Withdrawals 
Candidates on the November ballot may withdraw for any 
reason not later than noon, July 15, 2024. An original, 
signed copy of the CAN‐24 must be ﬁled by this deadline. If 
a D, L, or R candidate withdraws by July 15, then the  
poliƟcal party has 30‐days to ﬁll the vacancy under IC 3‐13‐1 
for an early ballot vacancy. This process is touched upon in 
the feature arƟcle on page 2. 
 
However, aŌer noon, July 15, 2024, a candidate on the  
ballot in November can only withdraw for limited reasons. 
For example, the candidate  moves out of the elecƟon  
district, is removed by court order or is convicted of a  
felony, or a few other special cases, including death of the 
candidate.  
 
The D, L, and R parƟes are sƟll able to ﬁll the ballot vacancy 
created due to these situaƟons; however, the procedures to 
do so are a liƩle diﬀerent depending on the Ɵming. Between 
noon, July 15, and October 5, 2024, the early ballot vacancy 
procedures in IC 3‐13‐1 are followed.   
On or aŌer Oct. 6, 2024,the parƟes follow “late” ballot  
vacancy procedures under IC 3‐13‐2. The 2024 Candidate 
Guide provides more details, including situaƟons where a 
minor party candidate may be able to ﬁll the ballot vacancy 
for November.

Election Division Dispatch 
 Brad King & Angie Nussmeyer, Co-Directors | June 2024 
NEWS & UPDATES 
Vote History & Get Winners 
Unless a county is involved in a recount, vote history must be posted 
not later than 60‐days aŌer the primary elecƟon, or July 8, 2024. The 
state has to pull “winners” from the primary elecƟon but has to wait 
unƟl recounts are concluded at the state level. This means counƟes 
may not see those oﬃces and judicial retenƟon quesƟons listed cor‐
rectly on reports unƟl later this summer. AddiƟonally, US Senate Class I 
and Class III are “new” oﬃces in SVRS to reﬂect the two seats are u 
sually elected in diﬀerent elecƟon cycles. This is intenƟonal. The “old 
oﬃce” will appear along with the two “new” oﬃces and should clear up 
once federal and state oﬃces are pulled over to the November elecƟon 
in SVRS. 
 
May Primary ElecƟon Local Oﬃce Recounts 
AŌer the May primary, several counƟes reported to IED that a recount 
lawsuit was ﬁled. A judge will appoint a local Recount Commission to 
review materials along with candidates and their representaƟves. Their 
ﬁndings to the judge, who has unƟl the ﬁnal Friday in June (or June 28, 
2024) to ﬁnalize the recount. The judge may extend this deadline if 
there is good cause to do so. (IC 3‐12‐6‐21.9) If the recount cerƟﬁcate 
changes the cerƟﬁed results, then the clerk will ﬁle a CAF in SVRS to 
unlock the reporƟng module to make those updates. AddiƟonally, a 
revised copy of the elecƟon results will need to be ﬁled with the CEB 
minutes at a future meeƟng. (IC 3‐12‐6‐30; IC 3‐6‐12‐31) 
 
Campaign Finance & Ballot Vacancy Reports 
Candidates who ﬁll a ballot vacancy have the same requirements to ﬁle 
a statement of organizaƟon as those who ran in the primary. That is, if 
the oﬃce pays more than $5000 in a calendar year, then a candidate’s 
commiƩee must be opened not later than noon, 7‐days aŌer the ﬁling 
deadline OR, if they’ve raised or spent more than $100 toward running 
for oﬃce, then the CFA‐1 is ﬁled not later than noon, 10‐days aŌer this 
threshold amount is met, whichever comes sooner. 
 
This group of candidates also has a special ballot vacancy report that is 
due not later than noon, three weeks aŌer the CAN‐29 statement of 
candidate selecƟon is ﬁled. The reporƟng period is the date the person 
became a candidate and ends two weeks aŌer the CAN‐29 is ﬁled. The 
report is then due by noon, at the end of the third week. For example, 
Sally becomes a candidate on July 3, 2024. Her reporƟng period is July 3 
through July 17, 2024, and the CFA‐4 report is due by noon, July 24. Her 
CFA‐1 to form the commiƩee would be due not later than noon, July 
10, 2024. Sally then will ﬁle the pre‐elecƟon report with a reporƟng 
period of July 18, 2024, through October 11, 2024. The pre‐elecƟon 
report is due the same as all other candidate commiƩees—noon, Octo ‐
ber 18, 2024. 
 
If a candidate is running for an oﬃce paying less than $5000 in a  
calendar year OR the person is a school board candidate, a CFA‐1 only 
needs to be ﬁled when the candidate raises or spends more than $500 
toward running for oﬃce.

IN FOCUS: New Election Laws Effective By July 1, 2024 
QUESTIONS OF THE MONTH 
 
Q. Is there a requirement to send copies of the PRE‐4/PRO‐2 and PRE‐6 aﬃdavits 
to the SOS oﬃce aŌer the elecƟon? 
A. Yes. A county must give one set of copies to the grand jury of the county and send 
another set to the SOS oﬃce aŌer each elecƟon. (IC 3‐14‐5‐2) Copies should be 
made of all PRE‐4/PRO‐2 aﬃdavits, whether the ballot was counted or not, and any 
PRE‐6 ﬁled in a primary elecƟon. However, you cannot send the copies unƟl aŌer the 
recount or contest period expires as provisional balloƟng informaƟon is conﬁdenƟal. 
If involved in a recount, counƟes are advised to wait on sending copies unƟl it is 
concluded. These procedures will change in some ways aŌer July 1, 2024. See the 
2024 LegislaƟve Summary for more info. 
 
Q. When a caucus is called to ﬁll a ballot vacancy, does a CAN‐12 (statement of 
economic interests) need to be ﬁled at the same Ɵme as the CAN‐31 (declaraƟon 
of candidacy) to ﬁll a ballot vacancy? 
A. No. The CAN‐12 does not need to be ﬁled with the CAN‐31 when a candidate 
comes to ﬁle their declaraƟon with the clerk’s oﬃce 72‐hours before the caucus. 
Instead, the CAN‐12 is ﬁled with the CAN‐29 (cerƟﬁcate of candidate selecƟon to ﬁll 
ballot vacancy). 
 
Q. Can a party chair ﬁll a ballot vacancy by direct appointment without their party 
organizaƟon’s consent through a resoluƟon or moƟon? 
A. Yes but only if there are fewer than two (that is, one or no) eligible PCs to vote in 
a caucus to ﬁll the ballot vacancy. The CAN‐29 form includes a check box on it for 
this scenario. Otherwise, a ballot vacancy can be ﬁlled by direct appointment only if 
the party has given the chair or central commiƩee the ability to do so. A resoluƟon 
or meeƟng minutes must be aƩached to each ballot vacancy ﬁling in this scenario. 
 
Q. Do we enforce deadlines to ﬁle paperwork concerning ballot vacancies? 
A. Yes. For example, if a CAN‐30 noƟce to ﬁll a ballot vacancy is not ﬁled with the 
clerk not later than noon, ten‐days before the caucus is held, then it must be reject‐
ed pursuant to state law. (IC 3‐5‐4‐1.9) 
VR CORNER 
SAMC Reminders 
With the US District Court Data Project underway, 
counƟes have asked IED a few quesƟons about 
the Statewide Address Mailing ConﬁrmaƟon 
(SAMC) noƟce created by SVRS: 
 
1/ Do we need to include return postage on the 
SAMC? Yes  ‐ return postage must be provided. (IC 
3‐7‐38.2‐2(f)) 
 
2/ Do we send a SAMC to a voter on the list if we 
cannot conﬁrm the address or name on the VLM 
list against a VR record? No. If you cannot match a 
voter’s name or address between the list and 
SVRS, then there is no way to generate a SAMC 
and aƩach it to a voter’s record in SVRS. 
 
3/ Can we send a SAMC to the address on the  
District Court data list in cases where it does not 
match? No. State law requires the SAMC to be 
sent to the voter’s mailing address on ﬁle, though 
the form is to be sent by forwardable mail to the 
voter. (IC 3‐7‐38.2‐2(d)& (f) & IC 3‐7‐38.2‐16) 
 
4/ Should we send a SAMC to a voter already in 
inacƟve status? No. Doing so will “reset the clock” 
on the process to move to the voter to cancelled if 
he or she fails to vote or update their registraƟon 
over two federal elecƟon cycles. 
Last month, IED emailed counƟes the 
2024 LegislaƟve Summary, which summa‐
rized changes made to state law through a 
variety of bills passed and signed into law 
earlier this year. Updates are made to the 
statutes found online on the General  
Assembly’s web page (iga.in.gov) on or 
around July 1, the eﬀecƟve date of many 
code changes. Here are a few highlights: 
 
1/ First Ɵme voters who register to vote in
‐person at any voter registraƟon agency 
will need to provide proof of residency, if 
their VR applicaƟon does not include an 
Indiana credenƟal number or last 4 of 
their Social Security Number that can be 
validated by SVRS. CounƟes will follow the 
same procedures with this group of ﬁrst 
Ɵme voters as they do with those ﬁrst 
Ɵme voters who register to vote by mail. 
Several forms like the ABS‐12, PRO‐9 & 
VRG‐7 will be updated as a result. 
 
2/ The “sore loser” law, eﬀecƟve now, 
clariﬁed that a candidate who ran for an 
oﬃce in the primary elecƟon cannot run 
for the same or diﬀerent oﬃce for the 
opposite poliƟcal party. However, the 
“losing” candidate can conƟnue to ﬁll a 
ballot vacancy for any oﬃce within their 
own poliƟcal party. 
 
3/ Early voƟng locaƟons used in the  
primary elecƟon can be changed for the 
general or municipal elecƟon conducted 
later in the year. This requires unanimous 
consent of the CEB, whether in the coun‐
ty’s vote center plan or resoluƟon adopt‐
ed under IC 3‐11‐10‐26.3.The county clerk 
conƟnues to designate one locaƟon of the 
clerk’s oﬃce for early voƟng under IC 3‐11
‐10‐26. 
 
4/ The deﬁniƟon of “chute” in IC 3‐5‐2‐10 
now includes early voƟng locaƟons and 
clariﬁes the area extends as a radius from 
the entrance of the area or room where 
voƟng occurs rather than a line or  
pathway from the door. 
 
5/ EﬀecƟve on March 13, 2024, it is a level 
6 felony to threaten an elecƟon worker, 
which includes a member of the CEB, poll 
workers, and absentee board members, 
among others. 
 
6/ Indiana ProtecƟon and Advocacy  
Services Commission is enƟtled to be  
present at early voƟng and ElecƟon Day 
polling locaƟons related to voƟng access 
program authorized under federal law. 
IPAS must provide these individuals with 
credenƟals. 
 
7/ The CEB of non‐vote center counƟes 
must establish a method and Ɵming for 
providing ABS reports to persons enƟtled 
to receive them under state law. (Vote 
center counƟes already must include this 
in their vote center plan.) 
 
8/ Previously, a CEB was required to adopt 
a uniform, non‐discriminatory policy  
permiƫng access to the full countywide 
registraƟon list. Now, state law has added 
to that policy all records in SVRS, including 
elecƟon administraƟon records and ABS 
acƟvity reports. This policy does not apply 
to individual VR records or other reports 
required by law to be provided to the  
poliƟcal parƟes. 
Indiana Officials Win EAC Clearinghouse Awards! 
CongratulaƟons to the Lake County Board of ElecƟons and RegistraƟon and the Knox County Clerk’s oﬃce on being 
recognized by the US ElecƟon Assistance Commission for their work to improve local elecƟons. To read more about all 
the winners, visit www.eac.gov/elecƟon‐oﬃcials/eac‐clearinghouse‐award‐winners‐2023#HAVA 
 
Lake County Board of ElecƟons and RegistraƟon, Indiana 
ElecƟon EducaƟon and Quick Guide 
 
ElecƟon integrity has taken center stage in America and conﬁdence in the electoral process is of criƟcal importance. 
OŌen, there is a lack of accurate informaƟon for voters and insuﬃcient training for elecƟon staﬀ. This erodes voter 
conﬁdence and increases the chance of human error by elecƟon oﬃcials. To address this need, the Board of ElecƟons 
developed the Voter EducaƟon Module to provide accurate and veƩed informaƟon from subject maƩer experts in the 
form of a quick guide booklet. The Poll Worker Quick Guide has a lay‐ﬂat design, index, and uncovered tabs to provide 
fast answers to the most popular quesƟons. The guide works with the county’s exisƟng Poll Worker Quick Guide and 
contains informaƟon to help elecƟon employees respond to voter and poll worker quesƟons. A HAVA grant covered 
professional prinƟng. QR surveys provide feedback loops for quanƟﬁable results. This branded biparƟsan project  
improves public sector engagement through educaƟonal components speciﬁcally designed for four target audiences: 
voters, poll workers, elecƟon oﬃcials, and elecƟon administrators. Both guides can be easily adapted for use in other 
jurisdicƟons.   
 
Knox County Clerk, Indiana 
Electronic Sample Ballots 
 
Before July 2023, all Indiana CounƟes were required to post paper sample ballots at every voƟng locaƟon. In Vote  
Center CounƟes, this could mean thousands of pages of sample ballots. Knox County received permission from the  
Indiana ElecƟon Division to test the use of electronic sample ballots for the November 2022 General ElecƟon. By using 
electronic sample ballots, voters had every ballot at their ﬁngerƟps in an accessible format to review prior to voƟng. 
Images and content in the electronic sample ballots could be enlarged to assist voters with vision impairment. The 
feedback from the 2022 general elecƟon was extremely posiƟve. A legislaƟve proposal was created for the 2023  
General Session, which was approved, making it the only Clerk‐related bill to pass in that session. The bill also  
permiƩed, for the ﬁrst Ɵme, the use of repurposed e‐poll books for this program. This has decreased e‐waste, prinƟng 
costs, and paper consumpƟon throughout Indiana. The state law that allowed the use of electronic sample ballots can 
be found under Indiana Code 3‐11‐3‐25.  
 
Knox County Clerk, Indiana  
ePoll Book Encoder Stabilizer Bracket 
 
The County Clerk’s Oﬃce created and produced an ePoll Book Encoder Stabilizer Bracket to respond to a known  
elecƟon administraƟon need. With KNOWiNK ePoll Books, an encoder is used to pre‐program a vote card to pull up the 
correct ballot for a voter. The connecƟon point of the encoder was not stable, causing encoding errors and diminishing 
the public conﬁdence in our elecƟons. Weaknesses idenƟﬁed included both the connecƟon point of the encoder into 
the ePoll book, as well as the power connecƟon to the encoder itself. The stabilizer bracket eliminated the connecƟvity 
issues and encoding errors. An Indiana company, Shelton SpecialƟes, LLC, was created to produce, market, and sell the 
brackets, iniƟally in Indiana. The Shelton SpecialƟes Encoder Stabilizer Bracket is patent pending. The Stabilizer Bracket 
was used in two Indiana counƟes in 2023 and has been uƟlized by 15 counƟes across the state. 
QUESTIONS OF THE MONTH, con’t 
 
Q. Can a candidate sign their own peƟƟon, such as a school board candidate signing their CAN‐34? 
A. Yes. The signature would be counted, assuming the individual is a registered voter at the address on the peƟƟon and their residence is within 
the elecƟon district. 
Q. Can a power of aƩorney execute a voter registraƟon form? 
A. If the voter is a person with a disability and needs assistance compleƟng their VR form or signing their name, then anyone, including their POA, 
can assist them with compleƟng it and, if necessary, print the voter’s name on the signature line. (IC 3‐7‐32‐7) The aﬃdavit of assistance must be 
completed. However, a POA does not have the authority to execute a VR form on a voter’s behalf without unless requested by the voter. 
 (IC 30‐5‐5‐14(a)(6)) 
InformaƟon in this newsleƩer is provided by the Indiana ElecƟon Division as a courtesy to county elecƟon administrators. If a person is unclear concerning elecƟon law provisions, the ElecƟon Division can serve as an interpreƟve source. However, where important 
legal rights are concerned, you must consult with your own a Ʃorney to be fully and properly advised.

Election Division Dispatch 
 Brad King & Angie Nussmeyer, Co-Directors | July 2024 
NEWS & UPDATES 
July 1, 2024 Deadline for DRE Units to Have VVPAT 
Beginning July 1, 2024, all counƟes using the MicroVote Direct Record 
Electronic (DRE) voƟng unit must have a voter veriﬁable paper audit 
trail (VVPAT) unit Ɵed to it pursuant to state law. (IC 3‐11‐15‐13.3(c)) If 
the county does not have a VVPAT unit for each DRE component, then 
the county cannot use the voƟng equipment in future elecƟons. This 
requirement means that any DRE unit deployed for ElecƟon Day, in‐
person early voƟng, or if authorized by the CEB, travel board, must 
have a VVPAT unit aƩached to it. 
 
MicroVote is the only DRE voƟng system IEC‐cerƟﬁed for use in Indiana. 
Some counƟes use opƟcal scan voƟng systems exclusively that may 
have a ballot marking device (BMD) unit to allow voters with disabiliƟes 
to vote privately and independently, though any voter can use it. A 
blank ballot card is inserted into the unit BMD, the voter’s choices 
printed upon it, and then the voter casts it on a separate opƟcal scan 
tabulator. OpƟcal scan voƟng systems are already “VVPAT compliant” 
because the ballot card, whether hand‐marked or produced by the 
BMD, is paper documentaƟon of the voter’s choices and can be used in 
a risk‐limiƟng audit or recount. The VVPAT unit on the DRE machine 
now serves that same purpose ‐ to document the voter’s choices on 
paper ‐ and why it is necessary for each DRE unit to have a VVPAT 
aƩachment. 
 
June Build 
Several enhancements were made to SVRS at the end of last month. If 
you weren’t able to aƩend the June 27 webinar to review those  
changes, Civix is hosƟng another session on July 2 at 1PM ET.   
 
A few changes include being able to print a voter acknowledgement 
card to send to voters who had correcƟons made to their registraƟon 
rather than a full update; idenƟfying those voters who may have a  
temporary credenƟal issued by the BMV on the registraƟon and  
absentee modules; updaƟng the date of birth report (those aged 115 
and over) to reﬂect changes in state law; and ensuring the voter ID 
number hierarchy is followed when adding numbers to a voter’s record 
(that is, IN DLN number ﬁrst; SSN4 second; and SVRS‐issued ID number 
third). Training materials are available to county users on the INSVRS 
County Portal. 
 
Federal Agency Updates 
CISA, FBI, DHS Intelligence and Analysis, and the EAC released a  
resource on insider threats, including recommendaƟons for  
miƟgaƟng the risk.  
 
CISA and the EAC released a public communicaƟons guide enƟtled 
“Enhancing ElecƟon Security through Public CommunicaƟons” to assist 
locals with creaƟng a public communicaƟons plan. 
 
The US Postal InspecƟon Service (USPIS) – the law enforcement agency 
aﬃliated with USPS responsible for invesƟgaƟng crimes commiƩed by 
mail – shared an updated list of ElecƟon Crimes Coordinators.  These 
are your primary POCs in the event of criminal issue involving the 
mail. The updated list is posted in the “Shared Documents” folder on 
the INSVRS County Portal. 
 
USPIS also shared this poster that will be posted in about 32,000 post 
oﬃces naƟonwide.

IN FOCUS: Special Ballot Vacancy Campaign Finance Reports 
QUESTIONS OF THE MONTH 
 
Q. Our county has a school corporaƟon where the boundaries extends into 
a neighboring county. How do we manage the elecƟon? 
A. The county with the largest percentage of populaƟon of the school  
corporaƟon handles candidate ﬁling, whether the candidate uses the CAN‐
34 peƟƟon (deadline has passed) or the CAN‐26 form to be a write‐in  
candidate (deadline is noon, Aug. 23, 2024). The “larger” county will need to 
share the candidate ﬁlings with their “smaller” county so that the county can 
enter the candidate name informaƟon into SVRS and build their ballot. Each 
county manages their voters within the elecƟon district and enters results 
into SVRS. SVRS is now designed to share the elecƟon results data from the 
“smaller” county to the “larger” county, as the “larger” county’s elecƟon 
board will cerƟfy the winner. 
Q. Can a candidate on the November ballot withdraw from the elecƟon 
aŌer noon, July 15, 2024? 
A. Yes, but for limited reasons such as death, felony convicƟon, move out of 
the elecƟon district, or disqualiﬁed by a judge. The party then has 30‐days to 
ﬁll the ballot vacancy under IC 3‐13‐1 (early ballot vacancies up to the ﬁnal 
30‐days before the elecƟon) or IC 3‐13‐2 (late ballot vacancies in the ﬁnal  
30‐days before the elecƟon). 
Q. Can candidates ﬁlling a ballot vacancy or a school board candidate be 
challenged?  
A. Yes. A voter of the elecƟon district or a county chair within the elecƟon 
district can ﬁle a CAN‐1 challenge not later than noon, Aug. 23, 2024. (Note: 
the deadline to challenge a write‐in candidate for school board is noon, Aug. 
30, 2024). The CEB has unƟl noon, Sept. 6, 2024, to hold the hearing and 
decide the maƩer. 
Q. Will there be a statewide public quesƟon on the ballot?  
A. Yes. Oﬃcial language will be cerƟﬁed to the counƟes by August 23, 2024. 
The quesƟon asks whether Superintendent of Public InstrucƟon should be 
removed from the order of succession to the Governor’s oﬃce in our state’s 
consƟtuƟon.  
VR CORNER 
VRG‐6 & First Time Voter Changes 
Changes in state law now require a ﬁrst‐Ɵme voter who registers 
to vote using a VRG‐6 from a full‐service agency such as FSSA, 
DWD, ISDH, BMV for speciﬁc types transacƟons or when applying 
for a handgun license with local law enforcement to provide proof 
of residency, if the voter does not provide an Indiana driver’s 
license or state ID card number or the last four digits of their  
Social Security Number in the voter ID secƟon of the form OR the  
number provided cannot be validated.  
 
As a result, IED updated the VRG‐6 forms and shared them with 
their respecƟve full‐service agency. The revised versions are to be 
used aŌer June 30, 2024. However, it is possible county VR  
oﬃcials will receive the older versions of the VRG‐6 form during 
this transiƟon period from full‐service agencies. 
 
Because federal and state law consider a full‐service a “voter  
registraƟon agency” counƟes are advised to accept the older  
version of the VRG‐6 form, if it was received by the full‐service 
agency on or before June 30, 2024, and transmiƩed to your oﬃce 
not later than 5‐days aŌer the agency received the form. It will be 
important for staﬀ to review the date on the VRG‐9 transmiƩal 
cover sheet to conﬁrm if the VRG‐6 was submiƩed on or before  
June 30, 2024. 
 
A reminder that the VRG‐6 is NOT a public‐facing form since it 
was developed speciﬁcally for full‐service agencies for use with 
speciﬁc types of transacƟons. The state’s point of contact with 
each agency received the new form types; however, if you learn 
of a local full‐service agency oﬃce that does not have the new 
forms, please email elecƟons@iec.in.gov and IED will coordinate 
delivery.
 
As noted in last month’s Dispatch, candi‐
dates ﬁlling a ballot vacancy may have a 
special ballot vacancy CFA‐4 report due in 
your oﬃce. (IC 3‐9‐5‐8.5) To make this 
determinaƟon, the ﬁrst part of this  
analysis hinges on whether the oﬃce pays 
more than $5,000 in a calendar year.  
 
If the answer to the salary quesƟon is 
“no” (or,  the person is running for school 
board), then the candidate does not need 
to open a campaign ﬁnance commiƩee 
unƟl the individual raises or spends more 
than $500 toward running for oﬃce and 
will not have a special ballot vacancy  
report. 
 
If the answer to the salary quesƟon is 
“yes,” then you will have to ﬁrst deter‐
mine whether the candidate has opened 
their campaign ﬁnance commiƩee (CFA‐1) 
or not. Candidates in this scenario who 
have not yet opened a commiƩee must 
ﬁle their CFA‐1 not later than noon, ten 
days aŌer the CAN‐29 (cerƟﬁcate of  
candidate selecƟon) was ﬁled or by noon, 
seven days aŌer the ﬁling deadline.  
 
The next step is determining the reporƟng 
period for the ballot vacancy report. The 
start of the reporƟng period is either the 
date the candidate ﬁled the CFA‐1, which 
is one way a person becomes a candidate 
for campaign ﬁnance purposes, or, the 
date the CAN‐29 was ﬁled. (Note: If a  
candidate opened their commiƩee before 
2024, then the start of their reporƟng 
period is January 1, 2024.)  
 
The end of the reporƟng period is two 
weeks aŌer the nominaƟon date (that is, 
the date the CAN‐29 is ﬁled) and the  
special ballot vacancy CFA‐4 report due 
not later than noon, seven days aŌer the 
end of the reporƟng period. 
 
For example, Josh ﬁlls a ballot vacancy for 
an oﬃce paying more than $5,000 in a 
calendar year. He has not ﬁled a CFA‐1 
and the CAN‐29 was ﬁled on July 3, 2024. 
 
This is the most straighƞorward example. 
Josh has to ﬁle a CFA‐1 not later than 
noon, July 10, 2024, and has a CFA‐4 ballot 
vacancy report due not later than noon, 
July 24, 2024, with a reporƟng period of 
July 3 through July 17, 2024. 
 
On the other hand, Laurie ﬁlls a ballot 
vacancy for an oﬃce paying more than 
$5,000 in a calendar year. She ﬁled her 
CFA‐1 on June 1, 2024, and the CAN‐29 
was ﬁled on June 21, 2024. 
 
Her CFA‐4 ballot vacancy report will cover 
the period of June 1, 2024 (the date she 
ﬁled her CFA‐1), through July 5, 2024 (or 
two weeks from her June 21, 2024,  
nominaƟon date). This report must be 
ﬁled not later than noon, July 12, 2024, or 
one week aŌer the end of the reporƟng. 
 
Similar requirements for a “special” CFA‐4 
report exist for those ﬁling as a write‐in 
candidate (IC 3‐9‐5‐8.4) or as a minor  
party or independent candidate ﬁling a 
peƟƟon for ballot access (IC 3‐9‐5‐8.2), 
assuming the oﬃce pays more than 
$5,000.

the ElecƟon Division can serve as an interpreƟve source. However, where important legal rights are concerned, you must consult with your own aƩorney to be fully and properly advised.

Election Division Dispatch 
 Brad King & Angie Nussmeyer, Co-Directors | August 2024 
NEWS & UPDATES 
November 2024 Ballot CerƟﬁcaƟon 
IED will cerƟfy the oﬃcial list of candidates, judicial retenƟon  
quesƟons, a state consƟtuƟonal amendment quesƟon, and the straight 
party devices (that is, the image used on the ballot in November for 
straight party voƟng) to counƟes not later than Aug. 23, 2024—EXCEPT 
for the presidenƟal Ɵckets for all parƟes. These Ɵckets will be cerƟﬁed 
to counƟes not later than Sept. 12, 2024. Please do not rely on spellings 
that you might ﬁnd on websites—even our candidate list posted to the 
elecƟon division website! The cerƟﬁcaƟon documents are the ballot 
names provided by the candidates and reviewed by staﬀ. 
 
elecƟonmail.org 
As you begin planning for the November elecƟon, please bookmark 
elecƟonmail.org ‐ a website speciﬁcally for elecƟon administrators to 
report speciﬁc issues with the USPS related to their elecƟon mail. Your 
fact‐speciﬁc scenarios are used to help troubleshoot issues within the 
USPS workﬂow and is shared with the state. 
 
US EAC Social Media Toolkit 
The US ElecƟon Assistance Commission has a number of toolkits  
available for local elecƟon administrators on their website: 
hƩps://www.eac.gov/elecƟon‐oﬃcials/toolkits 
 
Most recently their agency launched a Social Media Toolkit, which  
includes over 150 images that are organized into 17 diﬀerent categories 
from "Community Engagement" to "VoƟng OpƟons." Each image  
includes links to two versions of the image in Canva ‐ one square and 
one horizontal ‐ that can be fully customized to meet your needs. 
Here’s a link to this kit: hƩps://www.eac.gov/sites/default/ﬁles/2024‐
05/ElecƟon_Oﬃcial_Social_Media_Toolkit_508_Final.pdf 
 
VSTOP Public Test Lists & Reminders 
By August 23, 2024, VSTOP is to provide counƟes with a list of voƟng 
systems to pull for the public test of voƟng systems. Please be certain 
your equipment list is up to date in the VSTOP database! For those 
counƟes using the MicroVote DRE, you must have your DRE, VVPAT, 
AND OpScan units in the database. If you need assistance, please  
contact vstop@bsu.edu.  
 
CounƟes will receive one VSTOP list for opScan systems and, in  
MicroVote counƟes, one list for DRE systems. For each list, the county 
will need to test at least 5% of the machines on the list, starƟng at the 
top and skipping those machines that might be in the database but not 
pulled for this elecƟon.  
 
Public tests must be completed by October 7, 2024. This is a public 
meeƟng conducted by the county elecƟon board, which requires the 
CEB to follow the Open Door Law to give proper noƟce. AddiƟonally, 
state law requires counƟes to publish, at least 48‐hours before the 
public test, noƟce of the public test in the newspaper in accordance 
with IC 5‐3‐1. 
 
MicroVote counƟes will submit both the IEC‐9 (DRE Public Test Aﬃda‐
vit) AND the IEC‐10 (OpScan Public Test Aﬃdavit) to the ElecƟon  
Division, since both the DRE units and the OpScan units must be tested. 
All other elecƟon systems used by counƟes are exclusively OpScan. 
Therefore, only the IEC‐10 needs to be ﬁled with the Division by those 
counƟes. State law changed this year and now permits the IEC‐9 and 
IEC‐10 to be ﬁled by email (elecƟons@iec.in.gov).

With the elecƟon just around the corner, 
county elecƟon oﬃcials are ramping up 
their absentee operaƟons. CriƟcal to its 
success are absentee voter boards. 
Each county elecƟon board must noƟfy 
the D/R county chair of the number of 
absentee voter boards needed to support 
absentee operaƟons—mail, travel board, 
and in‐person voƟng—not later than 50 ‐
days before the elecƟon, or September 
16, 2024. (IC 3‐11.5‐4‐23) 
 
The D/R county chairs have unƟl noon, 46‐
days before the elecƟon (Sept. 20) to ﬁle, 
in wriƟng, their nominaƟons for those 
absentee voter board posiƟons. Of course, 
CEBs can request ABS voter boards more 
than 50‐days out and county chairs can 
ﬁle nominaƟons before their noon  
deadline, but these dates are the very 
latest to make the request or nominate 
ABS workers. 
 
Individuals serving as ABS voter board 
members must meet the qualiﬁcaƟons 
under IC 3‐11.5‐4‐22. While contested and 
uncontested candidates cannot work in 
this capacity, it may be possible to assign 
their family members to work with ABS 
ballots in those precincts where their 
“candidate” family member is not on the 
ballot. 
 
State law requires the CEB or the ABS  
voter board to review and approve all ABS 
applicaƟons. (IC 3‐11‐4‐17.5) AŌer the 
clerk’s oﬃce enters the apps into the  
system, the D/R appointed members of 
the CEB or the ABS voter board must aﬃx 
their iniƟals to the back of the ABS ballot. 
(IC 3‐11‐4‐19) 
 
ABS voter boards OR the CEB also perform 
the ﬁrst absentee signature review,  
comparing the signature on the voter’s 
ABS applicaƟon against the ABS ballot 
security envelope. This work must be  
performed before ElecƟon Day and then 
the apps/ballots (sealed in the ballot  
envelope) are ﬁled by precinct in a  
cabinet/oﬃce/receptacle with a bi‐
parƟsan lock. The D/R CEB member or 
their designee is to maintain custody of 
their key at all Ɵmes. 
 
Early voƟng or in‐person absentee voƟng 
is voƟng that occurs before an absentee 
voter board, much like traveling board. 
ABS voter boards are to be present during 
in‐person absentee voƟng at the clerk’s 
oﬃce or other satellite locaƟons to  
perform work like approving applicaƟons, 
checking a voter’s ID, or assisƟng voters 
with the voƟng equipment or ballot. 
 
Traveling board is a speciﬁc funcƟon of 
the ABS voter board, where a two‐person 
team travels to the voter to assist them 
with compleƟng a ballot or to bring a DRE 
unit or BMD unit to allow the voter to 
vote privately and independently. (The 
DRE or BMD resoluƟon has to be  
approved by the CEB ﬁrst; see IC 3‐11‐10‐
26.2) 
 
ABS Ballot PrinƟng. Not later than 60‐
days before the elecƟon, the clerk or the 
board of elecƟons & registraƟon in Lake, 
Porter, and Tippecanoe counƟes must 
esƟmate the number of absentee ballots 
needed for the elecƟon. 
 
Those absentee ballots must be delivered 
not later than 50‐days before the elecƟon. 
And not later than 5‐days aŌer receiving 
the printed ballots, counƟes must begin 
mailing ABS ballots to those voters with 
approved applicaƟons. 
 
Using 50‐days as the rule of thumb,  
counƟes receiving their ABS ballots on day 
50 have unƟl Saturday, September 21, 
2024 (or 45‐days before the elecƟon) to 
begin mailing ABS ballots. However, if 
your county receives ballots on day 55, 
then your deadline to begin mailing  
ballots is day 50 to comply with the “5‐
day” rule found in IC 3‐11‐4‐18(c)). More 
informaƟon can be found in the blue  
ElecƟon Administrator’s Manual. 
IN FOCUS: ABSENTEE VOTER BOARDS & ABS-Mail PRINTING DEADLINES 
HOLDOVERS & UNCONTESTED RACES ON THE NOV. BALLOT 
HOLDOVERS. On occasion, no one ﬁles to run for an oﬃce on the November ballot. In these cases, the current oﬃceholder 
“holds‐over” for a new term of oﬃce pursuant to ArƟcle 15, SecƟon 3 of the Indiana ConsƟtuƟon. 
 
For example, County Surveyor is on the ballot in November 2024. Mia is the currently elected county surveyor, who is serving 
her second four‐year term*. No one—not even Mia— ﬁled for the oﬃce. Therefore, Mia will conƟnue serving as the county  
surveyor for another four‐year term, unƟl her successor is elected and qualiﬁed. Because she is a “holdover” under state law, 
Mia does not ﬁle a new oath of oﬃce and will not receive a Commission from the Governor. 
 
CounƟes oŌen ask what happens if Mia didn’t ﬁle because she doesn’t want to conƟnue serving ? Mia may resign from  
elected oﬃce by ﬁling a wriƩen resignaƟon with the Governor (as she is a consƟtuƟonal oﬃce holder), and the elected oﬃce 
vacancy would be ﬁled according to statute. (IC 3‐13‐3 through IC 3‐13‐11, generally) The individual selected is a “pro‐temp 
appointment” for the remainder of the term. 
 
UNCONTESTED RACES. Unlike the odd‐numbered municipal elecƟon years, ALL candidates appear on the November general 
elecƟon ballot, even if only one person ﬁled. CounƟes may use “No Candidate Filed” on the ballot for races where no person 
ﬁled to run OR for those parƟes that did not ﬁnd a candidate to run for a speciﬁc oﬃce.  
 
*The posiƟon of county surveyor is NOT a state consƟtuƟonal oﬃce with a term limit, so the person holding this oﬃce will hold-
over. Think of the holdover as a conƟnuaƟon of her service rather than a “new” four-year term. She’ll serve unƟl December 31, 
2028, unless she resigns OR unƟl her successor is elected and qualiﬁed in the 2028 elecƟon. HOWEVER, other county consƟtu-
Ɵonal oﬃceholders such as county clerk or recorder have term limits. No person can serve more than 8 years in a 12 year peri-
od. (Gosman v. State) 
InformaƟon in this newsleƩer is provided by the Indiana ElecƟon Division as a courtesy to county elecƟon administrators. If a person is unclear concerning elecƟon law provisions,  
the ElecƟon Division can serve as an interpreƟve source. However, where important legal rights are concerned, you must consult with your own aƩorney to be fully and properly advised. 
QUESTIONS OF THE MONTH  
Q. Anything else special to include in the instrucƟons in a 
presidenƟal elecƟon year? 
A. Yes. Every ballot must contain a statement in the  
instrucƟons found at the top of the ballot that a vote for 
the presidenƟal Ɵcket is a vote for the electors. See IC 3‐
10‐4‐3 for speciﬁc details. 
Q. Do voter fail‐safes apply to absentee voters? 
A. Yes. Voter fail‐safes apply to an absentee voter in the 
same way it would apply to an ElecƟon Day voter. The 
only diﬀerence is the VRG 4/12 would be ﬁled at the same 
Ɵme as their ABS applicaƟon or during in‐person absentee 
voƟng before signing an ePollbook. 
Q. What is the presidenƟal only ballot? 
A. This ballot is ONLY used for voters who moved out of 
the state of Indiana aŌer October 6, 2024, and did not 
register to vote in their new state. Federal and state law 
allow this speciﬁc voter to return to their old state and 
vote for president only one last Ɵme at their old  
polling place (or by absentee ballot). The voter completes 
the VRG‐15 form at the polling place or, if requesƟng an 
absentee ballot, the VRG‐15 form should be ﬁled with 
their ABS applicaƟon. The voter is then given the  
presidenƟal only ballot to complete and return to elecƟon 
oﬃcials. AŌer the elecƟon, the voter’s registraƟon is  
cancelled, as authorized by the VRG‐15 form. NOTE: 
Please do NOT instruct your poll workers or absentee vot‐
er boards to use this ballot for voters who simply express 
interest in only voƟng for president. This is not the proper 
use for this ballot! 
Q. When will we be able to pull a list of candidates for 
the November 2024 elecƟon that is complete, including 
the D/R candidates that won the primary? 
A. The State Recount Commission meets on Aug. 7, 2024, 
to make its ﬁnal determinaƟon on two House district  
primary recounts. Once this work is complete, IED can 
cerƟfy primary elecƟon results online and in SVRS. This 
will then “get winners” from the primary and make all 
candidate lists whole. IED may need a day or two to  
complete this work, so lists should be in good shape 
around Aug. 12, 2024. 
Q. What is the deadline to challenge candidates who 
ﬁlled a ballot vacancy or ﬁled to run for school board? 
A. A voter of the elecƟon district or a county chair has 
unƟl noon, Aug. 23, 2024, to ﬁle a CAN‐1 challenge 
against those ﬁlling a ballot vacancy or ﬁling a CAN‐34 to 
run for school board. 
 
It is possible to have a write‐in candidate for school board. 
The CAN‐1 challenge deadline for these candidates using 
the CAN‐26 form is noon, Aug. 30, 2024. If you had a small 
town that followed a convenƟon model to nominate D/R/
L candidates, the CAN‐1 challenge deadline is noon, Sep‐
tember 4, 2024. 
 
Note: Local candidates who won the primary elecƟon can 
no longer be challenged. Instead, individuals should  
consult with their aƩorney on ﬁling a lawsuit. 
VR CORNER 
FPCA & Voter Residency 
On the FPCA, military and overseas voters are asked to  
provide the last address where the person last lived in Indiana 
before moving overseas or being deployed.  In some cases, the 
voter may not intend to return to this address. However, there 
are special allowances in state and federal law that permit the 
person’s registraƟon address to be listed as the last locaƟon 
where they personally lived in Indiana. 
 
In Indiana, an overseas voter may mark “I am a US ciƟzen, but my 
return is uncertain.” These voters must have lived in Indiana for 
at least 30 consecuƟve days at some point in their life from birth 
to their current age. Wherever they formerly lived, state law re‐
quires the county VR oﬃcial to register the person to vote at their 
VR oﬃce address. Remember, overseas voters who mark “my 
return is uncertain” are provided the Federal Only ballot style! 
More informaƟon can be found in the 2024 Military & Overseas 
Handbook found on in.gov/sos/elecƟons 
President/VP & Electors 
On November 5, 2024, voters are not selecƟng their  
presidenƟal and vice presidenƟal candidates, who run as a Ɵcket. 
Technically, voters are voƟng for the 11 Indiana electors who will 
cast their vote for the Ɵcket at a meeƟng of the electoral college 
held in December 2024.  The electors of the state’s winning  
presidenƟal Ɵcket then cast their votes, which are recorded and 
are the oﬃcial elecƟon results for the oﬃce of president and vice‐
president for our state. Please remember your ballot  
instrucƟons MUST include “electors” language found in IC 3‐10‐
4‐3 this year! 
CHANGES TO THE “CHUTE” 
New for November 2024 is an adjustment to the deﬁniƟon of 
“chute.” Not only does it now apply to elecƟon day and early 
(absentee) voƟng locaƟons, it also changed from a 50 foot line 
from the entrance to the room where voƟng occurs to a 50 foot 
radius from the entrance.  
 
CounƟes may want to consider how 
to best mark the chute area to ensure 
individuals do not elecƟoneer inside 
it; no one can elecƟoneer inside the 
room where voƟng occurs.  
 
Here is a mock‐up to help  visualize 
what this might look like. The doƩed 
lines are the 50 foot radii and 
the yellow area then becomes 
the chute or the area where  
elecƟoneering is prohibited. It 
almost looks like a basketball key ‐ 
perhaps telling folks they can’t cam‐
paign inside the three foot line would 
resonate with sports fans?

Election Division Dispatch 
 Brad King & Angie Nussmeyer, Co-Directors | September 2024 
NEWS & UPDATES 
Early VoƟng & ElecƟon Day Site Updates 
Visitors to Indianavoters.com rely on informaƟon pulled from 
SVRS as entered by each county. If your county has ﬁnalized its 
plans for in‐person absentee voƟng or locaƟons for elecƟon day 
voƟng, please make sure your county’s voƟng info is  
updated as soon as possible in INSVRS. Later this month and into 
October, this data will be shared with our partner,  
Democracy Works, to display on geƩothepolls.com. This will 
increase the reach of our state’s voƟng data, so having  
accurate informaƟon in SVRS will be even more criƟcal. 
 
ABS Voter Boards/Central Count Teams 
Don’t forget! CEBs must noƟfy the D/R county chairs not later 
than noon, Sept. 16 of the number of ABS voter board teams the 
county needs to assist with ABS‐Mail, Travel Board, and  
In‐Person absentee voƟng AND the number of ElecƟon Day  
central count teams (and, if applicable, couriers) needed. The 
chairs have unƟl noon, Friday, Sept. 20 to recommend or  
nominate individuals to these posiƟons. The CEB appoints those 
who are qualiﬁed pursuant to IC 3‐11.5‐4‐22 and ﬁlls any  
vacancy that might exist aŌer noon, Sept. 20. 
 
Public Test: IEC‐9 & IEC‐10 
AŌer conducƟng your public test of voƟng equipment, don’t 
forget to send in your IEC‐9 & IEC‐10 forms to IED. All counƟes 
will submit the IEC‐10, since an opScan tabulator is needed in all 
counƟes for absentee ballots, at minimum. MicroVote counƟes 
must also submit the IEC‐9 in addiƟon to the IEC‐10. Please 
email those to elecƟons@iec.in.gov to ﬁle with our oﬃce. 
 
New CISA PublicaƟon on Swaƫng 
CISA recently shared this important reminder as we head into 
the criƟcal months before elecƟon day. As noted in recent  
public reporƟng, elecƟon oﬃcials across mulƟple states have 
experienced swaƫng incidents in August. As a reminder, 
swaƫng is an illegal acƟvity where an actor makes a false report 
designed to elicit an armed law enforcement response to a  
targeted individual’s locaƟon.  
 
ElecƟon oﬃcials can take proacƟve steps to miƟgate the impacts 
of a swaƫng incident targeƟng their homes, oﬃces, or other 
elecƟon‐related sites. This year, CISA and FBI released the 
“Swaƫng PrevenƟon and Response Guide for ElecƟon Workers 
and Law Enforcement,” which provides recommended pracƟces 
for prevenƟng and responding to these incidents. 
 
ADA Accessibility Checklist for Polling Places 
A few counƟes have reached out to request the Americans with 
DisabiliƟes Act polling place checklist. This is not a state check‐
list; instead you’ll ﬁnd the informaƟon you need at the US Dept 
of JusƟce website: hƩps://www.ada.gov/resources/polling‐

VR CORNER 
Forwarding Voter RegistraƟons 
A voter may ﬁle state and federal voter registraƟon forms or an FPCA in a county where the voter doesn’t reside. If that occurs, 
county voter registraƟon oﬃcials must forward the VR document to the appropriate county. The forwarding county is able to email 
the document to the correct county on an expedited basis (IC 3‐5‐2‐23.2), but the hard copy must be sent by mail to the correct 
county (IC 3‐7‐34‐9) AddiƟonally, IED can receive voter registraƟon forms, and our oﬃce will forward them to the correct county.  
 
Incomplete Voter RegistraƟons 
SomeƟmes a voter misses boxes on their VR form before turning it in. In these cases, county VR oﬃcials are to call the voter, if a 
number is available, and mail noƟce to a voter if their VR form is incomplete. Voters not checking the age/ciƟzenship quesƟon have 
unƟl Oct. 7, 2024, to put in wriƟng the answer to those quesƟons made under the penalƟes of perjury (such as on a new VR form). 
For any other reason, the voter can cure the incomplete applicaƟon not later than 10‐days before the elecƟon, when the VR oﬃcial 
must reject the applicaƟon and send those names to the CEB. (IC 3‐7‐34‐4) More info is in the purple 2024 Indiana VR Guidebook. 
 
Timely Voter RegistraƟons 
A reminder that IED will send any Ɵmely received voter registraƟon form with a “Ɵmely” memo as we near the statewide VR  
deadline. A “Ɵmely” VR form is either hand‐delivered by the registraƟon deadline, or postmarked on or before October 7, 2024. If 
the postmark is missing or illegible, then those registraƟons can be processed up to and including Tuesday, October 15, 2024 
(deadline moved due to holiday). A legible postmark date on or before October 7 must be processed for November’s elecƟon. If a 
registraƟon is Ɵmely received by IED and your oﬃce receives it aŌer the registraƟon deadline, your oﬃce will process it. 
 
Pending RegistraƟons & Auto‐AcƟvate FuncƟonality 
CounƟes may choose to auto‐acƟvate pending voƟng registraƟons before each elecƟon. You’ll want to sign the auto‐acƟvate  
request document found on the INSVRS County Portal and aƩach it to your County AuthorizaƟon Request ﬁled through INSVRS. 
Signing this document acknowledges your county understands the state’s policy regarding pending voter registraƟon applicaƟons 
(IC 3‐7‐33.5) relaƟng to acƟvaƟng registraƟons in a batch seƫng. 
State law is very speciﬁc about the people 
permiƩed into an early voƟng or ElecƟon 
Day polling site besides a voter. You can 
ﬁnd the full list in state law: IC 3‐11‐8‐15. 
 
ElecƟon Day poll workers are nominated 
by the D/R county chairs not later than 
noon, 21‐days before the elecƟon, or Oct. 
15, 2024 for the upcoming elecƟon. AŌer 
the deadline, vacancies are to be ﬁlled by 
the CEB. All poll workers must meet the 
qualiﬁcaƟons found in IC 3‐6‐6‐7. 
 
Generally, ElecƟon Day party watchers are  
appointed by the state and county party 
chair of the D/R/L parƟes. See IC 3‐6‐8‐2.5 
for party watcher qualiﬁcaƟons, including 
being a registered voter of the county. 
 
At ElecƟon Day voƟng sites in non‐vote 
center counƟes, the state and county  
party chair can each independently  
appoint one watcher at each precinct. (IC 
3‐6‐8‐1) For example, if there are three 
precincts reporƟng to one polling locaƟon, 
the D/R/L parƟes can have up to 6  
watchers each at this speciﬁc locaƟon.  
 
In vote center counƟes, a state and county 
party chair can appoint one watcher for 
each ePB at the vote center on ElecƟon 
Day, as indicated on their plan or actually 
deployed, whichever is greater. For  
example, 10 ePBs are at an ElecƟon Day 
vote center. Therefore, the D/R/L parƟes 
can have up to 20 watchers each at this 
one locaƟon on ElecƟon Day. 
 
Some minor party and independent candi‐
dates might be able to appoint watchers, 
though the statutory procedures are a  
liƩle diﬀerent. See IC 3‐6‐8‐1 for details. 
 
Before elecƟon day, only the county D/R/L 
parƟes can appoint up to 2 watchers at 
each early voƟng locaƟon. On ElecƟon 
Day, watchers can be present on the 
“ﬂoor” of the central count: one watcher 
nominated by the state and county chair 
for each bi‐parƟsan team counƟng ballots. 
(IC 3‐11.5‐3‐2) 
 
The media can also appoint watchers,  
generally following the same rules as 
above for party watchers. Before elecƟon 
day, a media watcher can enter an early 
voƟng locaƟon and on elecƟon day, enter 
a polling place or central count “ﬂoor.” 
More details about media watchers can be 
found in IC 3‐6‐10, generally, and IC 3‐6‐10
‐5.5 and IC 3‐11.5‐3‐4. 
 
Challengers are appointed by the county 
parƟes for ElecƟon Day only. They can 
challenge a voter if they have facts a per‐
son is not a qualiﬁed voter of the precinct. 
(IC 3‐11‐8‐21) If a challenge is made, then 
the challenger ﬁlls out the PRE‐4 and once 
the voter completes their aﬃdavit on the 
PRE‐4, the poll workers issue the voter a 
provisional ballot. The voter then places 
their provisional ballot into the PRO‐2 en‐
velope and signs the aﬃdavit found on it. 
 
Poll book holder credenƟals allow a  
person to enter the polling place and mark 
who has voted already at the precinct on 
what’s oŌen called a “scratch” list. A poll 
clerk cannot be a pollbook holder for a 
party, but can keep a scratch list for poll 
book holders to see. See IC 3‐6‐7, general‐
ly, for the qualiﬁcaƟons for serving in ei‐
ther of these roles. This posiƟon is less 
common, now that CEBs can provide data 
from ePB check‐ins to the poliƟcal parƟes. 
 
All persons other than a voter must have 
a credenƟal to enter a polling site! Poll 
worker credenƟals are issued by the CEB. 
In most cases, watchers, challengers, and 
poll book holders have credenƟals issued 
by their poliƟcal party or in the case of 
media watchers, by their news organiza‐
Ɵon. (Note: if a news organizaƟon is in 
more than one county, IED issues the cre‐
denƟals). AddiƟonally, Indiana ProtecƟon 
and Advocacy Service can issue credenƟals 
to individuals evaluaƟng elecƟon day and 
early voƟng sites for accessibility require‐
ments. 
 
CEBs should read the statutes noted above 
closely, as they may be required to issue 
credenƟals in cases where there is a public 
quesƟon on the ballot, for example. 
IN FOCUS: POLL WORKERS, WATCHERS, CHALLENGERS & POLL BOOK HOLDERS 
QUESTIONS OF THE MONTH  
Q. Can a voter cancel their absentee ballot applicaƟon 
once submiƩed to the county? 
A. No. State law does not address cancelling an ABS appli‐
caƟon once received by the county. For that reason, the 
absentee ballot must be sent to the voter, assuming the 
applicaƟon is reviewed and approved. A voter can surren‐
der their absentee ballot to the absentee board during 
early voƟng or to the Inspector on ElecƟon Day and vote a 
regular ballot, if qualiﬁed. Or, if the voter’s absentee ballot 
is lost, spoiled, or defecƟve, it can be re‐issued aŌer the 
voter ﬁles an ABS‐5. Or, if the voter never received their 
absentee ballot, on ElecƟon Day, the voter completes the 
PRE‐5 and votes a regular ballot, if qualiﬁed. 
 
Q. We’re a non‐vote center county. Are we able to  
consolidate polling locaƟons for November? 
A. Yes. In non‐vote center counƟes, state law allows  
adjoining precincts to be co‐located at the same site. See 
IC 3‐11‐8‐4.3 for more details. 
 
Q. Can we modify in‐person “early” absentee voƟng 
hours in the clerk’s oﬃce? 
A. At minimum, early voƟng must be oﬀered for the same 
hours as the clerk’s oﬃce is open. If the clerk’s oﬃce is 
open 8A to 5P, for example, then early voƟng must be 
oﬀered from 8A to 5P during the weekday. State law sets 
forth minimum hours on the two Saturdays before  
elecƟon day. See IC 3‐11‐10‐26 for more informaƟon. 
 
Q. Could a family member or other individual complete a 
PRE‐3 and assist a voter with compleƟng their absentee‐
by‐mail ballot? 
A. No. State law requires the voter to be able to  
personally mark their own vote‐by‐mail ballot. If they  
cannot, then state law speciﬁcally requires the person to 
vote before a travel board. See IC 3‐11‐10‐24(b).  
AlternaƟvely, if the individual has a “print disability” (that 
is, they are blind, have low vision, or lack manual dexterity 
to complete their ballot) they may request an accessible 
ballot to complete independently at home.  
 
If a voter does not want to use the travel board and can 
vote in‐person on ElecƟon Day or an early voƟng site, then 
any person other than the voter’s employer or union rep‐
resentaƟve can assist a voter with disabiliƟes or who can‐
not read or write the English language if the PRE‐3 form is 
ﬁlled out before going to the voƟng booth. (IC 3‐11‐9‐2) 
 
Q. We don’t have a write‐in candidate for a US House 
seat on the ballot. Do we need the write‐in line on the 
ballot? 
A. Yes. Any Ɵme there is a federal oﬃce (US President/Vice 
President, US House, US Senate) on the ballot a write‐in 
line must be included on the ballot, even if no one ﬁled to 
be a declared write‐in candidate for any of these oﬃces. 
However, a write‐in line is only included for statewide, 
state legislaƟve, local, and school board when a candidate 
ﬁles a CAN‐3 for that parƟcular oﬃce.  
Q. Can the county parƟes appoint watchers during early voƟng? 
A. Yes. The D/R/L state or county party chairs (or both) can each 
appoint up to two watchers at each early voƟng locaƟon. (IC 3‐6‐8‐
7; IC 3‐11‐10‐26.3) 
 
Q. Can independent candidates appoint watchers for ElecƟon Day? 
A.  Only statewide or federal candidates can appoint watchers, who 
must meet the qualiﬁcaƟons under state law to be appointed. (An 
independent candidate running for local oﬃce is not enƟtled to 
watcher credenƟals.) The chair of the candidate’s campaign ﬁnance 
commiƩee would issue the credenƟal. See IC 3‐6‐8‐1 and IC 3‐6‐8‐3.  
 
Q. Can independent candidates appoint poll book holders or  
challengers? 
A. Yes. The poll book holder and challenger may be nominated by 
the independent candidate who is on the ballot, but again, these 
individuals must meet the qualiﬁcaƟons under state law to serve. 
See IC 3‐6‐7‐1 for details. 
 
Q. Can school board candidates appoint watchers? 
A. Yes. A school board candidate or a group of school board  
candidates can appoint watchers by ﬁling a wriƩen statement with 
the clerk. The contents of this statement must include their  
aƩorney‐in‐fact and the list of precincts where the watchers will be 
present. The clerk then issues the credenƟal to the individuals on 
the wriƩen request.  See IC 3‐6‐9, generally, for the speciﬁc  
procedures. NOTE: School board candidates are not enƟtled to  
appoint challengers or poll book holders. 
 
Q. Can a commiƩee supporƟng or opposing a public quesƟon  
appoint watchers? 
A. Yes. The chair of the PAC can appoint watchers, but must ﬁrst 
collect signatures equal to 2% of the total votes cast for SOS in 2022 
and ﬁle the peƟƟon with the county elecƟon board. Once the num‐
ber of signatures determined to equal this threshold is met, the CEB 
will issue a credenƟal to the watchers. See IC 3‐6‐8, generally. 
 
Q. Can a candidate be a poll worker? 
A. It depends. In a non‐vote center county, a candidate may be a 
poll worker in a precinct where their name does not appear on the 
ballot. In a vote center county, a candidate may not serve as a poll 
worker since all precincts vote at each vote center. This applies to 
unopposed candidates as well as opposed candidates, except for 
unopposed candidates for a party oﬃce (PC or delegate). See IC 3‐6‐
6‐7 for details. 
 
Q. My newspaper failed to publish my noƟce for a public test. Do I 
have to reschedule? 
A. Not necessarily. State law permits a county where the newspaper 
failed to Ɵmely publish a noƟce to allow the county to either 1) dis‐
play the noƟce prominently in three locaƟons in the county or 2) 
post on the county’s website (IC 5‐3‐1‐2(k)). 
 
Q. Do counƟes provide the PIN numbers to voters with print  
disabiliƟes using the Democracy Live website? 
A. Democracy Live has updated its mulƟ‐factor authenƟcaƟon  
services to provide PINs to voters who are given access to  
complete an accessible ballot. Indiana counƟes no longer need to 
provide a PIN to the voter; instead, aŌer entering a credenƟal to log‐
in, the unique PIN is sent to the email address provided by the voter 
on the ABS‐VPD app and entered into SVRS by the county. 
InformaƟon in this newsleƩer is provided by the Indiana ElecƟon Division as a courtesy to county elecƟon administrators. If a person is unclear concerning elecƟon law provisions,  
the ElecƟon Division can serve as an interpreƟve source. However, where important legal rights are concerned, you must consult with your own aƩorney to be fully and properly advised.
