Election Division Dispatch 
 Brad King & Angie Nussmeyer, Co-Directors | October 2024 
NEWS & UPDATES 
 
ElecƟon Day Poll Workers 
D & R county chairs have unƟl noon, Oct. 15, 2024, to nominate 
individuals to serve as an ElecƟon Day poll workers. Unless the 
person is a 16 or 17‐year‐old student, poll workers must be a  
registered voter of the county. In a non‐vote center county, a  
candidate can be a poll worker in a precinct where their name 
does not appear on the ballot. However, in a vote center county, a 
candidate cannot serve as a poll worker since all precincts vote at 
each vote center. See IC 3‐6‐6‐7 and IC 3‐6‐6‐39 for details, includ‐
ing limitaƟons on a candidate’s family members from serving.  
 
CFA‐11 Supplemental ReporƟng Period 
The large contribuƟon supplemental reporƟng period begins Oct. 
12, 2024, and ends 6AM on Nov. 3, 2024. During this window, any 
candidate on the ballot receiving and accepƟng a contribuƟon 
totaling $1000 or more from a single source must ﬁle the CFA‐11 
not later than 48‐hours aŌer receipt. This contribuƟon can be  
given in one lump sum or be an aggregate from the single donor 
during this period. Remember, loans to the commiƩee and in‐kind 
contribuƟons count! 
 
For example, Sally gives Tom’s commiƩee a $1000 contribuƟon on 
Oct. 16. Tom then must ﬁle a CFA‐11 within 48‐hours of receiving 
and accepƟng the contribuƟon. Ron gives Tom’s commiƩee a 
$300 contribuƟon on Oct. 19 and gives $800 on Nov. 1. Because 
Ron gave $1100 between October 12 and November 3, Tom must 
ﬁle a CFA‐11 disclosing both contribuƟons within 48‐hours of  
receiving and accepƟng the $800 check. More informaƟon can be 
found in the 2024 Indiana Campaign Finance Manual. 
 
Ballot Selﬁes 
While there is a statute “on the books” (IC 3‐11‐8‐17.5) that  
prohibits a voter from taking a picture of their ballot, it was found 
unconsƟtuƟonal by a federal court and cannot be enforced by 
counƟes. (ICLU v. IN SOS)  
 
This is diﬀerent from a media watcher, who is permiƩed under 
state law to photograph a voter unless the voter objects to the 
photograph, and the media watcher cannot capture how the voter 
voted. More informaƟon about media watchers can be found in IC 
3‐6‐10, generally, including the requirement to have a wriƩen 
credenƟal. If a media watcher is covering more than one county, 
then a request for a watcher credenƟal is to be ﬁled with IED. 
 
Timely/UnƟmely VR and ABS applicaƟons 
A reminder that if a VR or ABS app is Ɵmely received by IED or 
another county, then it is considered Ɵmely when transferred to 
the correct county ‐ even if it is received by the correct county 
aŌer the form‐speciﬁc deadline. IED will include a “Ɵmely” or 
“unƟmely” memo in its mailed packets to assist with this  
determinaƟon.

VR CORNER 
Forwarding Voter RegistraƟons in SVRS 
Voters registering to vote online select their county of resi‐
dence; the county is not automaƟcally pre‐populated. For 
this reason, your county from Ɵme‐to‐Ɵme may receive a 
registraƟon request for another county. Rather than re‐
jecƟng the registraƟon, state law requires you to forward 
the registraƟon as expediƟously as possible. The OVR and 
BMV Hopper both have a transfer funcƟon to direct the reg‐
istraƟon to the proper county. Transferring records between 
hoppers is an overnight process, so the “new” county will 
not see the record unƟl the next day. See the “Processing 
BMV and OVR Hopper Records” Step‐by‐Step on the INSVRS 
County Portal for more details.  
 
 
FPCA & RegistraƟon 
A military or overseas voter using the federal postcard appli‐
caƟon (FCPA) does not need to have previously been regis‐
tered to vote in Indiana to be considered for registraƟon. 
Instead, the voter must meet the general requirements un‐
der state and federal law such as being a US ciƟzen who will 
be 18 by Nov. 5, 2024. The FPCA provides special dispensa‐
Ɵon for residency at their last IN address, assuming the vot‐
er lived there for at least 30‐days before being deployed or 
moving overseas. 
In Indiana, candidates must ﬁle a CAN‐3 
declaraƟon to be an “oﬃcial” or declared 
write‐in candidate. While write‐in candi‐
dates are never printed on the ballot and 
a list is not posted in the polling place or 
included with absentee ballot materials, 
the CAN‐3 must be ﬁled in order for the 
CEB to tabulate votes for the write‐in  
candidate during post‐elecƟon canvassing. 
 
A write‐in line is added to the ballot for 
those oﬃces where a write‐in candidate 
has ﬁled. In addiƟon, federal law requires 
a write‐in line to be added to all federal 
oﬃces (US President, US House, US Sen‐
ate), even if no CAN‐3 was ﬁled. 
 
If a write‐in line is present for a parƟcular 
race, the voter will select the write‐in op‐
Ɵon and either hand‐write or type in the 
name of their preferred candidate,  
depending on the voƟng system. Then, 
aŌer the polls close, a tally tape is generat‐
ed from the machine. Again, depending on 
the system, this tape will either include a 
grand total for the “write‐in” selecƟon 
type only or include the candidate speciﬁc 
informaƟon typed in by the voter. 
 
The CEB or the bi‐parƟsan write‐in team 
will need to review the ballot cards or to‐
tals tapes for those precincts where a 
write‐in candidate is indicated. Then, the 
team will need to evaluate whether the 
person is a declared write‐in candidate OR 
a candidate who ﬁled for oﬃce and ap‐
pears on the ballot in that parƟcular race. 
Only these two candidate types can have 
votes tabulated by the CEB.  
 
For example, Donald Duck ﬁled a CAN‐3 to 
be a declared write‐in candidate for dog‐
catcher. A voter wrote “Donald Duck” on 
the write‐in line for the oﬃce; therefore, 
Donald Duck gets a vote tallied for him.  
 
On the other hand, Goofy ﬁled a CAN‐2
(declaraƟon of candidacy) and appears on 
the ballot for dogcatcher as the R candi‐
date. Rather than voƟng for Goofy in the 
area provided on the ballot, a voter in‐
stead wrote Goofy’s name in on the write‐
in line for dogcatcher. The CEB will count a 
vote for Goofy because he ﬁled to run for 
that oﬃce and appears on the ballot. 
 
Or, a voter writes in “Minnie Mouse” for 
dogcatcher. Minnie did NOT ﬁle a CAN‐3 
to be a declared write‐in candidate and 
she is not a candidate already on the bal‐
lot in the dogcatcher race. The CEB cannot 
tally a vote for Minnie. 
 
State law provides guidance on counƟng 
write‐in votes. Generally, the CEB or the 
write‐in team will have to ascertain the 
voter’s intent. This usually means the 
name does not have to be spelled  
perfectly, BUT this is at the discreƟon of 
the individuals performing the canvass. 
For example, Mickey Mouse is a declared 
write‐in candidate for dog catcher. The 
voter writes in Mick Mouse. This write‐in 
vote is likely to be counted for Mickey 
Mouse if the CEB ﬁnds this was the voter’s 
intent. 
 
If your voƟng system includes an  
approved electronic adjudicaƟon feature 
in the system’s EMS then you can use the 
feature to assist in determining what a 
voter provided on a write‐in voƟng line 
and if it is a vote for a candidate either on 
the ballot or ﬁled as a DECLARED write‐in 
candidate. (IC3‐11‐15‐13.8) 
 
Once counƟes complete their canvass, it is 
vitally important to make sure your  
precinct level results are adjusted to  
correctly reﬂect vote totals. Please  
conﬁrm totals posted to SVRS are updated 
so that the statements of votes cast align 
with your precinct elecƟon results ﬁled 
with the state. 
IN FOCUS: TABULATING VOTES CAST FOR WRITE-IN CANDIDATES 
ABS-5 & PRE-5 
SomeƟmes a voter’s absentee ballot does not arrive or the voter 
changes their mind about voƟng by mail or the county corrects a 
ballot defect. Below are the common reasons BEFORE elecƟon day 
to use the ABS‐5 or ON elecƟon day to use the PRE‐5. 
 
If a voter DOES NOT receive their absentee ballot, then the voter 
would complete and ﬁle the ABS‐5 for the county to reissue the 
absentee. OR, on ElecƟon Day, the voter would complete the PRE‐5 
form and be issued a regular ballot, if otherwise qualiﬁed. 
 
If a voter DOES receive their absentee ballot but would prefer to 
vote in person during early voƟng, then the voter must surrender 
their original ballot, complete the ABS‐5, and a replacement ballot 
can be issued. OR, on ElecƟon Day, the voter can surrender their  
absentee to the Inspector and be issued a regular ballot, if  
otherwise qualiﬁed. 
 
Should a voter spoil their absentee ballot or the county ﬁnds an 
error and the original ballot is “defecƟve,” then the voter  
completes and ﬁles the ABS‐5 and a replacement ballot can be  
issued. However, on ElecƟon Day, the voter would need to bring in 
their defecƟve ballot to surrender their ballot to the Inspector and 
then a regular ballot would be issued. 
 
More details about the forms and their related processes are found 
in the blue ElecƟon Administrators’ Manual. 
Q. If we have a line at the end of the day during in‐person  
absentee or “early” voƟng, are we required to allow voters waiƟng 
in line to vote when our oﬃce closes? 
A. Much like elecƟon day, if there are voters in line waiƟng to vote 
during any day of “early” voƟng at the clerk’s oﬃce or satellite  
locaƟon, then those individuals are allowed to vote that day, if  
otherwise eligible. Staﬀ should either write down each person’s 
name who is waiƟng, mark their hands with a stamp, or designate a 
staﬀ person to wait at the end of the line to mark the end. (IC 3‐11‐8
‐11 and IC 3‐11‐10‐29.2) 
 
Q. If a voter comes to early voƟng and doesn’t have the correct 
photo ID, do they vote provisionally? 
A. The voter should be issued a provisional ballot, and given the PRO
‐9 form. The voter then has unƟl noon, ten days aŌer the elecƟon to 
bring their ID to the CEB or sign the PRO‐10 to indicate the person is 
indigent or that their religion bars them from being photographed. 
 
Q. Does a voter’s ID need to have an address that matches their 
registraƟon record? 
A. No. The photo ID law does not require a matching address be‐
tween the ID and registraƟon record. Instead, it must be issued by 
the state of Indiana or federal government, be current or expired 
since the last general elecƟon (11/8/22), and include a photo and 
name that conforms with the registraƟon. (IC 3‐5‐2‐40.5) However, 
a ﬁrst Ɵme voter with a proof of residency ﬂag can use their Indiana 
driver’s license as their proof of residency if the name and address 
do match. They could also provide a bank statement, uƟlity bill,  
government document, or paycheck stub if the name and address 
match. 
 
Q. Can we remove ballot cards from the ABS security envelope 
before elecƟon day to prepare for tabulaƟon? 
A. No. State law does not permit an absentee ballot envelope to be 
opened prior to the start of the central count of absentee ballots. 
State law also explicitly states that a ballot card cannot be  
tabulated prior to elecƟon day. (IC 3‐11.5‐4‐6(b)) 
 
 
Q. Why is there a reason on the ABS‐Mail form for IN NaƟonal 
Guard members? Would they not be eligible to use the FPCA? 
A. It depends. If a NaƟonal Guard member is deployed within the 
state of Indiana, then the voter would not be eligible for the FPCA 
and would use the ABS‐Mail form. If the NaƟonal Guard member is 
deployed outside of Indiana or overseas, then the FPCA would be 
the best form for them. However, a member of the armed services 
(Army, Navy, Air Force, Marines, Space Force) is always eligible to 
use the FPCA, even if they are deployed within Indiana. 
 
Q. Can anyone hand‐deliver a VR form or ABS applicaƟon to the 
CEB or VR oﬃce? 
A. Yes. Any person can hand‐deliver a VR form or ABS applicaƟon to 
a county oﬃce, and the county will review and process the request 
if the voter is otherwise eligible. If another person takes custody of a 
voter’s state VR form, then the receipt is to be completed and given 
to the voter and the cerƟﬁcate of acceptance on the lower secƟon 
completed. On the ABS form, there is a line to include the date the 
person took custody of another’s form. State law requires a person 
taking custody of another voter’s state or federal VR form to submit 
it by noon, ten days aŌer taking custody of it or by the deadline 
date, whichever is sooner. If late, the county sƟll processes it but the 
maƩer is to be brought to the CEB for invesƟgaƟon. 
QUESTIONS OF THE MONTH  
Q. Are we able to process the state or federal VR form if 
the envelope is postmarked on or before Oct. 7, 2024? 
A. If the postmark is legible and is dated on or before Oct. 
7, 2024, then yes, counƟes must process the registraƟon 
for the Nov. 2024 elecƟon if the voter is otherwise quali‐
ﬁed. If the postmark is missing or illegible, then counƟes 
are to process
 a VR request for the Nov. 2024 elecƟon if it 
is received by Oct. 15, 2024. 
 
Q. Are we able to process ABS‐Mail or ABS‐VPD applica‐
Ɵons if the envelope is postmarked on or before Oct. 24, 
2024, but received aŌer the deadline? 
A. No. State law requires any absentee ballot applicaƟon 
to be received not later than the speciﬁed deadline. Any 
ABS app that is received aŌer the deadline for ﬁling ‐ even 
if the envelope has an pre‐deadline postmark—is  rejected. 
 
Q. Can a voter receive assistance compleƟng their  
absentee applicaƟon? 
A. Yes. State law permits anyone ‐ other than the voter’s 
employer or union representaƟve ‐ to assist a voter with 
compleƟng their ABS applicaƟon on paper or online at 
indianavoters.com. AddiƟonally, if the voter has a disabil‐
ity, then the assistor can print the voter’s name on the 
signature line. In either case, the aﬃdavit of assistance 
must be completed on the boƩom of the form. If the per‐
son is also POA, the POA should be aƩached. The use of an 
aﬃdavit of assistance is not a reason for a county to reject 
an absentee applicaƟon. 
 
Q. Do we have to organize our ABS applicaƟons and  
ballot envelopes by precinct before elecƟon day? 
A. YES! State law requires this organizaƟon of apps and 
ballots in advance to perform the central count of absen‐
tees on elecƟon day. See IC 3‐11.5‐4‐5 for details. CounƟes 
might also consider running the ABS Ballot AcƟvity Report 
to use as a checklist for the central count teams to conﬁrm 
all ballots received are present in their precinct pack. 
 
Q. Do we have to make copies or scan original absentee 
applicaƟons? Do those need to go into SVRS? 
A. State law requires a county to scan or make copies of 
original absentee applicaƟons, since the originals are 
stored with the ballot security envelope and unavailable 
for public records requests. If scanned, the absentee appli‐
caƟon does not need to be added to SVRS documents un‐
less the applicaƟon made a change to the voter’s record. 
ABS applicaƟons can be used to update a registraƟon  
address within a precinct or make a name change. 
 
Q. Can a voter or member of their household or family 
member drop oﬀ a completed ABS‐Mail ballot to an early 
voƟng site? 
A. Yes! Please be sure your ABS voter boards are prepared 
to receive ballot security envelope and request the ABS‐19 
to be completed by anyone other than the voter. The CEB 
should develop a chain‐of‐custody protocol for the return 
of the envelopes to be stored according to state law.

Election Division Dispatch 
 Brad King & Angie Nussmeyer, Co-Directors | November 2024 
NEWS & UPDATES 
BMV Open on ElecƟon Eve & ElecƟon Day 
State law requires BMV branches that issue credenƟals like  
driver’s licenses or state ID cards to be open from 8:30A to 8P, 
local prevailing Ɵme, Mon., Nov. 4, 2024  and from 6A to 6P, 
local prevailing Ɵme, Tues., Nov. 5, 2024, to assist individuals in 
geƫng ID required to vote.  
 
As a reminder, state law requires a photo ID used for voƟng pur-
poses to include a photo of the voter, be issued by the state or 
federal government, be current or expired since 11/8/22, and 
include the voter’s name that conforms (not necessarily be an 
exact match!) to their registraƟon record. (IC 3-5-2-40.5)   
Further, an address on a state ID does not need to match the 
person’s registraƟon record. ExcepƟons exist for military and 
veterans’ IDs and certain NaƟve American Tribal IDs. 
 
ENR Summary or Precinct Results SelecƟon Deadline 
CounƟes have the opƟon to enter summary level results or  
precinct level results (by hand or through upload) in SVRS, which 
is then used to display elecƟon results at indianavoters.com/
elecƟonresults and also is used to populate data in the  
statements of votes cast used to cerƟfy the elecƟon.  
 
Please make sure your county’s preference is toggled to the 
method of reporƟng your county wants to use not later than 
6PM (ET), Fri. Nov. 1, 2024. In order to avoid impacts with  
reporƟng, this toggle cannot be used aŌer this deadline to 
switch to the other method. 
 
ElecƟon Results ReporƟng 
Unoﬃcial Results: State law requires county elecƟon oﬃcials to 
report in SVRS their unoﬃcial results at 8PM, 10PM and 12AM. 
If work conƟnues into the next day, then unoﬃcial results are to 
be updated in SVRS hourly beginning at 9AM. Of course, coun-
Ɵes will need to add to their unoﬃcial results any valid provi-
sional ballots as determined by the CEB at their hearing, write-in 
votes that can be counted, and any valid mailed absentee bal-
lots sent by overseas military or overseas civilian voters by mail. 
Please be certain your elecƟon results in SVRS are updated to 
reﬂect these changes!  
 
The CEB will then submit the canvassed results in SVRS using the 
CEB series of forms (except the CEB-9) not later than noon, 
Mon., Nov. 18, 2024. The CEB-9, SecƟon I along with the coun-
ty’s precinct level results are to be ﬁled in SVRS not later than 
noon, Tues., Nov. 19, 2024. Training materials on ﬁnalizing your 
elecƟon results reporƟng can be found on the INSVRS County 
Portal. The CEB-9, SecƟon II reporƟng is due by Dec. 13, 2024, 
which is informaƟon needed to complete the state’s EAVS  
survey that is used in a report to the U.S. Congress regarding 
outcomes from federal elecƟons.

NOVEMBER WEB TRAINING 
 
Nov. 7 | Post ElecƟon Processing 
Nov. 12 & 14 | CEB Form GeneraƟon 
 
2024 Calendar is posted to the INSVRS County Portal but is subject to revision.  
OVERSEAS VOTERS 
Military members and their spouse or de-
pendents residing overseas or overseas US 
ciƟzens that requested a mailed absentee 
ballot using the Federal Post Card Applica-
Ɵon (FPCA) have an extended deadline for 
the CEB to receive their completed ballot. 
If the ballot security envelope is post-
marked on or before Nov. 5, 2024, and 
received not later than noon, Nov. 15, 
2024, then it is considered Ɵmely and 
counted, if the voter is otherwise quali-
ﬁed. A reminder that faxed or emailed 
ballots requested by a military or overseas 
voter are due by 6P, Nov. 5, 2024, to be 
counted. 
 
Federal Write‐In ABS Ballot (FWAB) 
Any military or overseas voter using the 
FPCA can have a FWAB on ﬁle with the 
CEB. The FWAB is the voter’s “back-up” 
ballot should the original absentee re-
quested by the voter is not returned by 
the state’s deadline.  
 
If the voter ﬁled a FWAB for this elecƟon, 
then a bi-parƟsan remake team will  
determine the voter’s intent from the 
FWAB and transcribe the voter’s choices 
on an opƟcal scan ballot card. Keep in 
mind that the voter does not have to spell 
the candidate’s name correctly, or can 
simply write the poliƟcal party the voter is 
choosing for their enƟre ballot or in one 
speciﬁc contest. (IC 3-12-1-19). 
 
PROVISIONAL BALLOTS  
(IC 3‐11.7, generally) 
Reminder! State law requires counƟes to 
noƟfy voters when the provisional ballot 
hearing is scheduled through a portal part 
on indianavoters.com. Training materials 
regarding how to enter this informaƟon 
into SVRS is available on the SVRS County 
Portal. 
 
The provisional ballot hearing must be  
conducted not later than noon, ten days 
aŌer the elecƟon (or Nov. 15, 2024) and 
the CEB must make a determinaƟon to 
count provisional ballots not later than 
3PM that same day. Voters received no-
Ɵce of the hearing when they were given 
the PRO-9 by elecƟon workers. 
 
The board will need to review the facts 
and apply the law to determine if a voter’s 
provisional ballot is to be counted. Some 
issues are easier to adjudicate. For exam-
ple, a voter was challenged for not having 
valid photo ID. The voter has a hard dead-
line of noon, ten days aŌer the elecƟon to 
present their ID to the CEB or aﬃrm they 
are indigent or have a religious exempƟon 
when compleƟng the PRO-10 form. 
 
Or, an absentee voter was found to have a 
missing or mismatched signature and the 
ABS-18A or 18B was sent. The voter has 
unƟl noon, eight days aŌer the elecƟon to 
return the aﬃdavit by email, mail, fax or 
hand-delivery. If not, then the CEB cannot 
count the voter’s provisional ballot. 
 
Generally, if the voter is found not to be a 
qualiﬁed voter of the precinct, then the 
provisional ballot should not be counted. 
However, if the voter is found to be a 
qualiﬁed voter of the precinct by the CEB, 
then the provisional ballot is to be count-
ed unless the provisional ballot was cast 
as a result of: 
1/ a court order extending polling locaƟon 
hours (court will provide direcƟon on this 
group of voters); 
2/ being omiƩed from a poll list and the 
voter provided a receipt documenƟng that 
the voter Ɵmely applied at a voter regis-
traƟon agency like the BMV or FSSA;  
3/ failing to produce required ID by the 
noon, ten-day post elecƟon deadline;   
4/ failing to provide proof of residency if 
required to do so not later than 6PM on 
elecƟon day; or 
5/ not submiƫng the ABS-18A or 18B by 
noon, eight days aŌer the elecƟon.  
 
LOCAL RECOUNTS (IC 3‐12‐6, generally) 
All CEBs must cerƟfy their elecƟon results 
to IED not later than noon (Indy Ɵme), 
Nov. 18, 2024, using SVRS.  (The CEB-9, 
SecƟon I is due by noon, Nov. 19, 2024.) A 
candidate can ﬁle for a recount not later 
than noon, Nov. 19, 2024, and a county 
party chair can ﬁle for a recount by noon, 
Nov. 22, 2024. 
 
There are no automaƟc recounts in  
Indiana! Instead, the vote margin  
between the candidates dictates the 
amount of the bond the individual pays. 
The person ﬁling the recount, at mini-
mum, must pay the ﬁling fee for a civil 
court case and a bond amount of at least 
$100.  
 
The $100 bond allows for up to ten pre-
cincts to be recounted. If the vote margin 
is 1% or less, then each addiƟonal precinct 
is $10. If the vote margin is more than 1%, 
then the price per precinct is $100.  
 
For example, the person ﬁling the lawsuit 
wants to recount 15 precincts. If the vote 
margin is 1% or less, her bond will be 
$150. If the vote margin is more than 1%, 
then her bond is $600. 
 
The judge assigned to the civil miscellane-
ous case will set up a recount commission 
made up of one D and one R member and 
a technician, or a person familiar with the 
voƟng system. The local recount commis-
sion manages the process and brings the 
ﬁndings back to the judge, who makes the 
ﬁnal determinaƟon. 
 
Statewide and state legislaƟve candidates  
use diﬀerent procedures, so please direct 
those inquiries to IED. More informaƟon 
on these topics can be found in the blue 
2024 ElecƟon Administrators’ Manual. 
IN FOCUS: Overseas ABS Voters, FWABs, Provisional Ballots & Recounts 
CERTIFICATES OF ELECTIONS, COMMISSIONS & OATHS  
County clerks may begin issuing cerƟﬁcates of elecƟon to newly elected oﬃcials aŌer 12P local prevailing Ɵme on Nov. 22, 2024.  
As a reminder, the cerƟﬁcates of elecƟon contain an oath of oﬃce in the packet. However, candidates are not required to use this 
oath form. Sample text for the oath of oﬃce can be found in the blue ElecƟon Administrator’s Manual, if you have newly elected 
oﬃcials that wish to have an oath of oﬃce put on leƩerhead or fancier paper at a swearing-in event organized by their party, for 
example.  
 
Remember, consƟtuƟonal oﬃceholders (ProsecuƟng AƩorney, Judge, Sheriﬀ, Clerk, Auditor, Treasurer, Recorder, Coroner,  
Surveyor) will NOT receive a cerƟﬁcate of elecƟon from the county clerk. Instead, this group will receive a Commission from the 
governor, which also includes an oath form. Except for prosecuƟng aƩorney and judges, who ﬁle their oaths with the SOS, all other 
newly elected oﬃcials are to ﬁle their oath of oﬃce with the county clerk not later than Jan. 31, 2025. 
QUESTIONS OF THE MONTH  
Q. Can media watchers really ﬁlm or take photos in a polling place? 
A.Yes, but they cannot do so in a way that would reveal how a 
voter voted. Remember, only a newspaper of general circulaƟon in 
the county where an elecƟon is held; a news service operaƟng in the 
county where an elecƟon is held; or a radio or tv staƟon operaƟng in 
the county where an elecƟon is held may appoint watchers. The  
media watcher must have a credenƟal, in wriƟng, that states the  
person is an appointed watcher, the name of the individual, and the 
person that appointed the watcher. 
 
Q. Are watchers enƟtled to receive a totals tape printed out from 
our voƟng equipment aŌer the polls close? 
A.Yes. See IC 3-6-8-4; IC 3-6-9-13; IC 3-6-10-5.5. 
 
Q. Are we required to give state or county party chairs ePollbook 
data on ElecƟon Day or during early voƟng? 
A. Yes. State and county party chairs, who are enƟtled to appoint 
watchers under our state’s ElecƟon Code, are enƟtled to receive 
ePollbook data upon request. Further, vote center counƟes should 
have the cadence of the Ɵmes when these reports are to be made 
available in their vote center plan. 
 
Q. Can an absentee ballot that is requested to be sent by email or 
fax be remade on a DRE machine? 
A. No. State law requires that an absentee ballot that is returned by 
fax or email be remade ON ElecƟon Day using a opƟcal scan ballot 
card designated for the voter’s precinct. A bi-parƟsan remake team 
will determine the voter’s intent and mark the ballot card with the 
voter’s choice. It is important the team add a serial number to the 
faxed/emailed ballot and apply the same serial number to the ballot 
card in an area where the tabulator will not pick up stray marks. The 
serial number should in no way idenƟfy the voter. It is used in the 
event of a recount to match the voter’s original emailed or faxed 
ballot against the remade ballot card. Note: Only voters with print 
disabiliƟes using the ABS-VPD form or military and overseas voters 
using the FPCA are enƟtled to receive an absentee by email or fax. 
 
Q. Can we start our central count of absentee ballots before Elec‐
Ɵon Day? 
A. Yes, if the county unanimously agrees to follow the procedures 
found in IC 3-11.5-4-11.5, This allows the central count team to per-
form their required review under IC 3-11.5-4-12 & IC 3-11.5-4-13. 
However, NO ABSENTEE BALLOT can be scanned or tabulated  
before ElecƟon Day. Results also cannot be released to any person, 
even CEB members, before 6PM, ElecƟon Day, including those absen-
tees counted throughout the day. 
 
Q. Do we have to perform the second signature review  for  
absentee ballots during the central count? 
A.State law allows a county elecƟon board to unanimously agree to 
forego the second signature review on travel board and in-person 
absentee (early voƟng) ballots only. See IC 3-11.5-4-12 for details. If 
such a policy is adopted, then only MAILED absentee ballots are to go 
through a second signature review by central count teams. If no such 
policy is adopted, then all absentee ballots, regardless of method, 
must go through a second signature review. Details are found in the 
blue ElecƟon Administrators’ Handbook. 
InformaƟon in this newsleƩer is provided by the Indiana ElecƟon Division as a courtesy to county elecƟon administrators. If a person is unclear concerning elecƟon law provisions,  
the ElecƟon Division can serve as an interpreƟve source. However, where important legal rights are concerned, you must consult with your own aƩorney to be fully and properly advised. 
VR CORNER 
VRG 4/12’s 
State law permits the county VR oﬃcial to access  
elecƟon materials “upon delivery of the poll lists” to 
retrieve the VRG 4/12 to update the voter’s registraƟon 
record. (IC 3-10-1-31.1(d))  Once work is complete with 
the 4/12, including scanning into SVRS, the VRG 4/12’s 
are to be stored with the elecƟon materials from this 
elecƟon for a period of at least 22-months. 
 
VoƟng History 
County voter registraƟon oﬃcials can begin updaƟng 
vote history from the Nov. 5, 2024 elecƟon once the poll 
lists are returned to the CEB. If a state or local recount is 
going to be conducted, your elecƟon materials will be 
impounded. For those counƟes using paper poll lists, 
this means you will not have access to the poll lists to 
make updates. However, you can make copies of the 
poll lists if copies are made in the presence of the agen-
cy impounding the materials. (IC 3-12-6-19) Vote history 
must be uploaded to SVRS not later than sixty days fol-
lowing the elecƟon. Should a recount be conducted, this 
deadline is extended to sixty days following the conclu-
sion of the recount. (IC 3-10-1-31.2) 
 
DON’T FORGET! 
Voter RegistraƟon Re‐Opens Dec. 2, 2024

CISA prepared an on-demand training video to help

Security ConsideraƟons for ElecƟon Workers & a guide-

AcƟon Guide,   
 
#Protect2024 Sub‐Page on ElecƟon Threats 
CISA published the ElecƟon Threat Updates sub-page on

shop for ﬁnding recent reporƟng from the Intelligence 
Community on the threat environment (including ODNI,

updates; FBI and CISA PSAs). 
 
Electionmail.org 
Don’t forget! ElecƟon administrators can log MAIL issues 
at elecƟonmail.org, which can help troubleshoot issues 
you are experiencing. The Indiana USPS lead, Trina 
Webb, also sent invites to counƟes to hop on a bi-
weekly call with her to discuss speciﬁc USPS issues. The

Election Division Dispatch 
 Brad King & Angie Nussmeyer, Co-Directors | December 2024 
NEWS & UPDATES 
Thank You! 
CongratulaƟons on a successful elecƟon year! For those of you  
reƟring at the end of 2024, thank you for your service. We are  
grateful to your commitment to Hoosier voters and wish you the 
very best for whatever comes next! The last page of the newsleƩer 
has some important reminders to aid in the transiƟon.  
 
Filing Provisional Ballot Aﬃdavits with SOS 
State law requires copies of all PRE‐4 aﬃdavits, regardless if the pro‐
visional was counted, to be ﬁled with the SOS following the elecƟon. 
Now that the recount and contest deadline has passed and assuming 
your county does not have a pending local or state recount or con‐
test, a copy of the provisional ballot PRE‐4/PRO‐2 aﬃdavits (sealed 
or unsealed) are to be delivered to your county prosecutor. You 
must also make a third set of copies for your records in case a public  
records request is ﬁled, so that the originals can be preserved should 
the prosecutor want to share them with a grand jury. See IC 3‐14‐5‐2 
for more informaƟon. 
 
ElecƟon Materials 
A reminder all elecƟon materials are to be retained for at least 22‐
months following the elecƟon. While ballots and provisional ballots 
are conﬁdenƟal and cannot be accessed, other materials like provi‐
sional ballot aﬃdavits, poll lists, tally tapes, etc. are public record 
once the recount and contest deadline has expired. (IC 3‐10‐1‐31.1) 
Please note voter registraƟon documents follow a diﬀerent sched‐
ule. The purple VR Guidebook has more informaƟon starƟng on page 
74. State Archives also has a more succinct chart available here: 
hƩps://www.in.gov/iara/ﬁles/county_clerk.pdf 
 
CEB‐9, SecƟon II 
Rather than send mulƟple surveys to counƟes over the holidays, 
several years ago SecƟon II was added to SVRS to collect data to 
complete the biennial ElecƟon AdministraƟon and VoƟng Survey 
(EAVS) report. Published by the US ElecƟon Assistance Commission, 
EAVS creates the framework for our state’s report to Congress about 
the current state of elecƟons. The deadline to submit the CEB‐9, 
SecƟon II is December 13, 2024. Baker Tilly may be reaching out to 
counƟes aŌer your submission to reﬁne data points, if necessary. 
 
Save the Date for Next Year’s Conference! 
A reminder that IED will not be holding a December conference this 
year and new publicaƟons will not be published unƟl late 2025 in  
anƟcipaƟon of next year’s conference. However, the yellow Calen‐
dar Guidebook does have a few key dates for 2025, though new  
publicaƟons—and a new Code Book—will be made available at next 
year’s conference to be held December 15‐17, 2025, at the HyaƩ 
Regency in downtown Indianapolis. For your 2025 budget planning 
purposes, we anƟcipate the per person registraƟon fee will increase 
but not to exceed $400, subject to other approval.

Dec. 17 & 19 | December Build Review 
 
2025 Calendar is pending review and will be posted to the INSVRS County 
Portal as soon as possible. 
CANDIDATE COMMITTEES 
With the elecƟon now behind us,  
candidates may be approaching you 
about campaign ﬁnance next steps. 
 
Whether a candidate is elected or  
defeated, the commiƩee can remain 
open or be disbanded. Unless a  
candidate disbands their commiƩee, 
their campaign ﬁnance commiƩee is 
considered to be open and acƟve. This 
will require the candidate’s commiƩee 
to ﬁle an annual report EACH YEAR, at 
minimum, unƟl their commiƩee is  
disbanded. 
 
CANDIDATE COMMITTEES ARE NOT 
CLOSED AUTOMATICALLY OR  
REQUIRED TO BE CLOSED BY THE 
CANDIDATE AT THE END OF THE  
ELECTION CYCLE!  
 
To disband a campaign ﬁnance  
commiƩee, their ﬁnal CFA‐4 report 
MUST have a $0 balance and may NOT 
have any debts or loans owed to or by 
the commiƩee.  
To reach a zero dollar balance,  
commiƩee funds can be donated to 
another regular party commiƩee,  
another candidate’s commiƩee, the 
elecƟon division, or certain non‐
proﬁts. AlternaƟvely, contribuƟons 
can be returned to donors on a pro 
rata basis. (More details are found on 
pages 32‐33 of the green Campaign 
Finance Manual.) 
 
To communicate their commiƩee is 
disbanded, commiƩees will need to 
mark on their ﬁnal CFA‐4 summary 
sheet the “Final/Disbands” box under 
the “Type of Report” SecƟon.  
It is possible for a commiƩee to mark 
both “Annual” and “Final/Disbands” to 
saƟsfy both their annual report  
ﬁling and their ﬁnal report ﬁling. 
 
REGULAR PARTY/PACs 
Similar to candidate commiƩees, it is 
possible for a regular party commiƩee 
or PAC to disband. The same  
procedures—$0 balance, no debts or 
loans, mark “ﬁnal/disbands” ‐ apply to 
these commiƩee types, too.  
 
If the commiƩees remain open, then 
their reporƟng requirements are 
diﬀerent in that PACs & regular party 
commiƩees ﬁle a pre‐primary, pre‐
elecƟon, and annual report. However, 
in 2025, commiƩees are only required 
to ﬁle an annual report since there are 
no scheduled elecƟons held. 
 
ALL OPEN CANDIDATE COMMITTEES 
& PACs MUST FILE THEIR 2024  
ANNUAL REPORT NOT LATER THAN 
NOON, JANUARY 15, 2025!   
 
REGULAR PARTY COMMITTEES MUST 
FILE THEIR 2024 ANNUAL REPORT 
NOT LATER THAN NOON, MARCH 3, 
2025! 
 
Failure to do so is a $50 per calendar 
day ﬁne, up to $1,000. County elecƟon 
boards must enforce delinquent  
campaign ﬁnance reporƟng. 
IN FOCUS: Disbanding Committees & 2024 Annual Report Reminders 
VR CORNER 
Processing VRG 4/12’s aŌer an ElecƟon 
AŌer elecƟon day, state law requires county voter  
registraƟon oﬃcials to make updates to a voter’s 
registraƟon records as requested by a voter who ﬁled a 
VRG‐4/12 during elecƟon season.  
 
However, BEFORE you can make the change to a voter’s 
record within your county OR forward the original docu‐
ment to the voter’s new county, you MUST apply vote 
history. (IC 3‐10‐1‐31.2) In fact, SVRS business rules now 
keep you from processing a VRG 4/12 unƟl absentee, 
elecƟon day, and provisional vote histories are uploaded 
to ensure compliance with this recent change in state 
law. 
 
Some voters might have moved to a new county but sƟll 
qualiﬁed for a fail‐safe to allow them to vote one last 
Ɵme at their former registraƟon address. If the voter has 
moved to a new county, the voter’s “old” county must 
ﬁrst apply vote history to the voter’s registraƟon record 
and then forward the original VRG 4/12 to the “new” 
county not earlier than the deadline to ﬁle a recount or 
contest acƟon (IC 3‐10‐1‐31.1(b) and not later than 30‐
days aŌer registraƟon reopens (IC 3‐7‐43‐4). 
 
QUESTIONS OF THE MONTH  
Q. What happens if an oﬃceholder fails to take and ﬁle 
their oath of oﬃce by February 1? 
A. For non‐commissioned local oﬃce holders (that is, any 
local elected oﬃcial besides a consƟtuƟonal oﬃceholder 
such as the clerk or sheriﬀ), their oﬃce would be considered 
vacant for failure to be sworn into service (IC 5‐4‐1‐1.2)  
unless they are enƟtled to hold over under the Indiana Con‐
sƟtuƟon. Any dispute would be resolved by a judge ruling on 
a court case. 
 
Q. Can a new oﬃceholder be sworn in and ﬁle their oath 
before January 1? 
A. Yes. See IC 33‐42‐9‐7 for who can perform swearing‐in. 
 
Q. Does the oath included with the state’s CerƟﬁcate of 
ElecƟon form need to be used or can it be created on a 
separate document? For example, can the oath be printed 
on a judge’s leƩerhead? 
A. The oath found with commissions or with the cerƟﬁcate 
of elecƟon is included as a courtesy. It’s OK if a new oﬃce‐
holder wants to create their own document using the text 
found on pages 57 & 58 of the blue ElecƟon Administrator's 
Manual. 
 
Q. Where are oaths ﬁled? 
A. Judges and prosecuƟng aƩorney  ﬁle their oath with SOS/
IED. All other oﬃces, even commissioned local oﬃceholders, 
ﬁle their oath with the county clerk.  
STATEWIDE VOTER REGISTRATION SYSTEM (SVRS) RESOURCES FOR NEW STAFF  
 
SVRS “Start‐Up” Checklist  
 Do you have access to SVRS (or at least know which staﬀ have access)? 
 Do you know your SVRS county admins? 
 Do you know how to access the SVRS county portal? 
 Do you have enough tokens for your staﬀ to access SVRS? 
 
Civix Help Desk 
Don’t know the answers to the checklist quesƟons? Contact the Civix Help Desk. Civix is our vendor partner that  
manages our statewide voter registraƟon system. You can email insvrshelpdesk@gocivix.com or call 1‐888‐467‐8771. 
 
New User Training for SVRS 
Civix will be scheduling new user training in 2025. Please contact the Help Desk later for those dates and Ɵmes, as the 
training calendar was not released at the Ɵme of this wriƟng. This training can last a few hours and will walk through 
key features of SVRS. The webinars highlight key processes and walk through the training materials on the various 
modules within the system. The 2025 web training calendar, when available, will be posted to the INSVRS County Por‐
tal. County elecƟon administrators that are transiƟoning out of the oﬃce in December are encouraged to print a copy 
of the calendar to share with their new colleagues, if available. 
 
On‐Site SVRS Training 
Want a hands‐on demonstraƟon? Reach out to the Civix Help Desk to assist you with compleƟng a county authorizaƟon 
form that is available through SVRS. This form is submiƩed to the state for their review. Once approved, Civix staﬀ will 
coordinate on a visit to the county in‐person or virtually. 
OTHER KEY RESOURCES 
 
ElecƟon Forms 
Forms can be found in two places: 
1) SVRS County Portal. County SVRS users can ﬁnd state elecƟon forms in the “Shared Documents” folder on the  
portal, and the forms are available in word and Adobe .pdf. This folder can be downloaded in its enƟrety and saved 
to your work computer. If you need assistance in learning how the portal works, please contact the Civix Help 
Desk. 
2) Indiana Elec Ɵon Division website: in.gov/sos/elecƟons. Navigate to the “ElecƟon Administrator’s Portal” and you 
will ﬁnd the ﬁllable .pdf versions of the forms there. The web page is public facing, so it will be a helpful resource 
to candidates and other public and party oﬃcials. 
NOTE: There will be very few form updates for 2025 since there are no regularly scheduled elecƟons in most  
jurisdicƟons. However, there may be changes required by new state laws. 
 
Brochures & PublicaƟons 
CounƟes can order addiƟonal printed guidebooks by submiƫng an IEC‐7 form with the required payment. Those same 
publicaƟons can be accessed through the IED website at in.gov/sos/elecƟons under the “ElecƟon Administrator’s  
Portal.” Please note: no new publicaƟons are released for 2025. 2026 publicaƟons will be available at the December 
2025 Conference, which is scheduled for December 15‐17, 2025, at the HyaƩ Regency in downtown Indianapolis. 
 
“ElecƟon Day” Outreach Materials 
Materials produced by the Help America Vote Act (HAVA) Administrator like the 2024 ElecƟon Day Handbook oŌen 
used by poll workers, Military & Overseas Voters Guide, and other materials like the Voters’ Bill of Rights can be found 
on the IED website in the HAVA Outreach Library. Printed versions of these materials will be  
available to county elecƟon administrators in the spring of 2026.  
 
Email IED Staﬀ 
You can ﬁnd a list of contact informaƟon for IED staﬀ here: hƩps://www.in.gov/sos/elecƟons/ied‐staﬀ/ 
Or, you can email elecƟons@iec.in.gov, which is a shared email for the co‐directors and their general counsel.

Election Division Dispatch 
 Brad King & Angie Nussmeyer, Co-Directors | January 2025 
NEWS & UPDATES 
RedistricƟng Amnesty 
Last year the Indiana General Assembly passed a bill containing a 
“redistricƟng amnesty” period for those jurisdicƟons that failed to 
draw new or recerƟfy exisƟng elecƟon district boundaries follow-
ing the 2020 Decennial Census as required by law. This special 
“amnesty” period ends on Oct. 31, 2025. However, a member of 
any redistricƟng authority who fails to recerƟfy or redistrict before 
June 30, 2025, will not be enƟtled to receive a salary unƟl the local  
governing redistricƟng authority complies with the law. 
 
This does NOT apply to Congressional or state legislaƟve district 
boundaries, as that work was completed in 2021 by the Oﬃce of 
Census Data and the Indiana General Assembly. This process only 
applies to local government redistricƟng authoriƟes, such as a 
county or town council or school board, who failed to complete 
required redistricƟng work in 2021 or 2022.  
 
The county clerk or county elecƟon board (CEB) is not responsible 
for this acƟvity. However, there is a direct impact as you assign 
voters to the proper elecƟon districts and manage elecƟons for 
those jurisdicƟons. You may want to look for paperwork ﬁled in 
2021 or 2022 to conﬁrm a local redistricƟng authority ﬁled a copy 
of an ordinance or resoluƟon that either recerƟﬁed exisƟng elec-
Ɵon districts for the current 10-year period OR adopted new 
boundaries (and ﬁled a copy of the maps). If you cannot ﬁnd such 
documentaƟon, you may wish to reach out to the appropriate 
redistricƟng authority or their aƩorney to conﬁrm their intent to 
meet their obligaƟons under state law. (IC 3-5-10-7; IC 3-5-10-7.1) 
 
ReprecincƟng 
Not to be confused with redistricƟng (or the drawing of elecƟon 
district boundaries), reprecincƟng involves changing the bounda-
ries of precincts, the building blocks of an elecƟon district. This 
process is detailed in state law (IC 3-11-1.5, generally). Since 2025 
is a non-elecƟon year, counƟes have a liƩle more Ɵme to consider 
this process ahead of the 2026 elecƟon cycle. 
 
Under state law, the county execuƟve (that is, the county commis-
sioners in all counƟes except for Marion, Lake, and Porter) is in 
charge of reprecincƟng unless they have delegated the authority 
to the CEB. Now is a good Ɵme to “take inventory” of your pre-
cincts and look at recent annexaƟons or other precinct splits 
where adjusƟng the boundary or creaƟng a new precinct might 
make the most sense for elecƟon administraƟon purposes. Look 
for more informaƟon from IED later this year.

Assembly

endum to be held on May 6, 2025

Campaign Finance: AdministraƟve Disband 
As you and your county elecƟon board (CEB) become more famil-
iar with the state’s campaign ﬁnance act (CFA), you’ve likely 
found commiƩees who failed to ﬁle required reports  
despite best eﬀorts to contact them about delinquent reports. 
Each year, not later than the last Friday of January (January 31, 
2025) state law requires the CEB to review its list of open  
commiƩees and determine if any commiƩee has not 1) ﬁled a 
CFA-4 report of receipts and expenditures (CFA-4) in the last  3 
years; 2) has $1000 or less cash on hand; AND 3) has no  
outstanding debts noted on their most recent CFA-4 ﬁling.  
 
If those three things are true, then the CEB can send noƟce of a 
hearing to the chair and treasurer of the commiƩee (by cerƟﬁed 
mail) that the CEB intends to administraƟvely disband the com-
miƩee. At the hearing the CEB will make its determinaƟons and 
follow the procedures found in IC 3-9-1-12 to disband the  
commiƩee.

The VRG-6 is a special voter registraƟon 
form used by the BMV and other full  
service agencies to register individuals 
during speciﬁc transacƟons. For example, 
a person can register to vote when geƫng 
a driver’s license at the BMV. The 
“declinaƟon” is part of the form and rec-
ords if the person declines to register vote.  
 
A “full service” agency is deﬁned by state 
law and includes not just the BMV but also 
FSSA, DWD, and law enforcement agen-
cies that handle handgun permits.  
 
The VRG-6 form is the same across all 
agencies with one notable diﬀerence. The 
ﬁve-digit state form number (found in the 
upper right corner under the form Ɵtle/
state seal) is diﬀerent and is the “NVRA 
code type” assigned in SVRS to each full 
service agency. (Note: This form is also 
only available through the ElecƟon Divi-
sion, so if a WorkOne oﬃce asks you for 
the VRG-6, please have them email elec-
Ɵons@iec.in.gov) 
 
How your oﬃce receives the VRG-6 form is 
determined by state law. The BMV is re-
quired to send the VRG-6 form electroni-
cally through SVRS. The registraƟon comes 
through the BMV Hopper; the declinaƟons 
come through the BMV DeclinaƟons Hop-
per.  
 
All other full service agencies are required 
to mail or hand-deliver the completed 
paper declinaƟon or registraƟon to your 
oﬃces not later than 5-days aŌer the form 
or declinaƟon is completed. The VRG-9 is 
submiƩed with the VRG-6 forms/
declinaƟons; the county VR oﬃce provides 
the VRG-8 form as a receipt to the full ser-
vice agency submiƫng paper forms. 
 
Regardless of the delivery method 
(through the BMV declinaƟon hopper or 
on paper VRG-6 form ﬁled with your 
oﬃce), counƟes can send a statewide ad-
dress mailing conﬁrmaƟon (SAMC) noƟce 
generated through SVRS to a voter if the 
address on the declinaƟon is not the same 
as the residence address on their registra-
Ɵon record. 
 
CounƟes have asked what “the same” 
means regarding address matches. The 
two don’t have to be an exact match. For 
example, maybe the declinaƟon uses the 
full ZIP + four but their registraƟon does 
not include the “+4”. This would be a 
“minor variaƟon” similar to how peƟƟon 
signatures are processed. Minor variaƟons 
between addresses would not necessarily 
lead to a “match” for purposes of sending 
a SAMC.  
 
CounƟes have also asked what to do when 
the voter’s name on the declinaƟon does 
not match their registraƟon. This is not a 
reason to send a SAMC and counƟes 
should refrain from sending one. Instead, 
the voter can update their name at any 
Ɵme during the voƟng cycle whether by 
ﬁling a new registraƟon or absentee appli-
caƟon or by making the change when they 
go vote in-person. 
 
A reminder that declinaƟons are conﬁden-
Ɵal and can only be shared with the voter. 
Now that BMV declinaƟons are sent 
through SVRS, the declinaƟon database 
will conƟnue to grow. This will be helpful 
in future elecƟons if a voter believes they 
registered at the BMV but their registra-
Ɵon was not updated. Using the SVRS tool 
allows you to conﬁrm if a declinaƟon was 
recorded for the parƟcular voter. 
IN FOCUS: VRG-6 Declination Reminders 
VR CORNER 
 
Records Management 
2025 should be a reasonably quiet year for counƟes, at least in 
terms of running elecƟons. This is a good opportunity to do 
some clean-up and organizaƟon ahead of the next three-year 
elecƟon cycle. 
 
For example, counƟes may want to use the GeoConvergence 
GIS tool to ensure voters are assigned to their correct pre-
cinct. More informaƟon about the GIS tool and how it works 
with SVRS can be found here: Geoconvergence—Mapping Sup-
port Tools for ReprecincƟng 
 
If a voter ﬁles a paper registraƟon form or your county prints 
registraƟon records out of the SVRS OVR or BMV Hoppers, the 
current paper voter registraƟon form must be kept unƟl such a 
Ɵme the voter cancels their registraƟon at the address on the 
form. Then, it must be retained for at least 24-months from 
the date of the general elecƟon immediately following the can-
cellaƟon. 
 
For example, Sally Smith’s registraƟon was cancelled on Aug. 1, 
2023. The county must hold the paper record unƟl at least 
Nov. 2026, which is 24-months following the most recent 
general elecƟon (Nov. 5, 2024). AlternaƟvely, John Doe’s  
registraƟon was cancelled on Oct. 1, 2024.  His cancellaƟon 
occurred just before the 2024 general elecƟon, so his paper 
record would be eligible for destrucƟon in Nov. 2026, too. 
QUESTIONS OF THE MONTH  
Q. Are there voter registraƟon deadlines in 2025? 
A. For most counƟes, no. There is at least one town in 
Wayne County (Cambridge City) where there may be a 
municipal elecƟon in November, and some counƟes 
may hold a special elecƟon if public quesƟons are cerƟ-
ﬁed to the CEB by a parƟcular deadline in February or 
August. If that applies to your county, then the registra-
Ɵon deadline for those impacted precincts is 29-days 
before the elecƟon in May or November. 
 
Q. Can an underage voter register to vote in 2025 
ahead of the 2026 elecƟon cycle? 
A. Yes. The underage voter would need to turn 18 on or 
before November 3, 2026, to register and be eligible to 
vote in 2026. However, if a jurisdicƟon holds a special 
elecƟon in 2025, an underage voter residing in an im-
pacted precinct would need to turn 18 on or before the 
date of the special elecƟon in May or November 2025. 
 
Q. Do all commiƩees ﬁle an annual campaign ﬁnance  
report in January 2025? 
A. All OPEN candidate and poliƟcal acƟon commiƩees 
are required to ﬁle a 2024 Annual Report not later than 
noon, January 15, 2025. The green Campaign Finance 
Manual goes in to more detail on this subject. Regular 
party commiƩees (i.e. your county, district, and state 
parƟes) have an extended deadline: noon, March 3, 
2025.

Election Division Dispatch 
 Brad King & Angie Nussmeyer, Co-Directors | February 2025 
NEWS & UPDATES 
May Special ElecƟons 
Most Indiana counƟes will not be holding an elecƟon in 2025, as it is 
an “oﬀ‐year” where no elecƟons are regularly scheduled. However, 
it is possible for certain types of public quesƟons to be cerƟﬁed to 
the county elecƟon board, who would have the responsibility of 
conducƟng the elecƟon. IED publishes a “referendum brochure” 
available on our website, which provides more detail on the topic. 
The Indiana Department of Local Government Finance (DLGF)  
website is also a terriﬁc resource (in.gov/dlgf). 
 
School corporaƟons most commonly use referendums to help raise 
money for their school or a capital improvement project. Using it as 
an example, the school board would need to adopt a resoluƟon to 
move forward with a referendum quesƟon and cerƟfy it to the CEB 
not later than noon, Feb. 21, 2025, for a May 6, 2025 special elec‐
Ɵon. Once the quesƟon is cerƟﬁed, then the CEB is to meet and 
discuss plans for conducƟng the elecƟon. 
 
The elecƟon calendar or procedures do not change signiﬁcantly for 
a special elecƟon. However, the CEB can adopt a resoluƟon by 
unanimous consent to reduce the days of in‐person early voƟng (IC 
3‐11‐10‐26.5) The enƟty requesƟng the special elecƟon does have 
to pay for the elecƟon held in an oﬀ‐year though there is a liƩle 
nuance if a city or town elecƟon is held at the same Ɵme. (IC 3‐5‐3‐
12)  
 
Please note: IED does not publish an elecƟon calendar brochure for 
2025. Many key dates are included in this newsleƩer. If you have 
speciﬁc quesƟons, please email elecƟons@iec.in.gov   
January Hoƞix 
Civix, our statewide voter registraƟon system vendor, pushed a 
number of enhancements to SVRS at the end of last month and  
provided an online review of those enhancements. Build notes and 
training materials can be found on the SVRS County Portal. 
 
UpdaƟng County Contact InformaƟon in SVRS 
SVRS has a module for counƟes to enter contact informaƟon for the 
various elecƟon duƟes managed by your oﬃces. This informaƟon is 
displayed on indianavoters.com and used in reports or other  
documents produced in the system. To update or conﬁrm county 
contact info, log in to SVRS and navigate to AdministraƟon, then 
County, then Directory. You can then edit (click the pencil on the far 
right) or add a directory entry. To edit your elecƟon board  
members, use the “Directory Search” link on the tool bar. For more 
assistance, please contact the INSVRS Help Desk.

IN FOCUS: Campaign Finance Enforcement by the CEB 
VR CORNER 
 
Sheriﬀ’s Department Quarterly Reports 
State law sets forth a requirement that your county sheriﬀ 
provide a list of individuals who are currently imprisoned ‐
following convicƟon of a crime. The VRG‐1 should be aƩached 
to the report as well. The reports, at minimum, should be ﬁled 
with your oﬃce on Jan. 31, April 30, July 31, and Oct 31. See IC 
3‐7‐46‐6 for more details. 
 
A person’s name on the list is not an automaƟc move to a  
cancelled registraƟon status!  This is why it is important that 
the sheriﬀ’s report give the county VR oﬃcial insight if the  
person is currently imprisoned following convicƟon of a crime.  
 
For example, a person who was imprisoned and released  
before the date of the report would no longer meet the 
threshold requirement of being currently imprisoned to be 
disenfranchised under state law. Further, a person being held 
but not yet convicted also does not meet the threshold analy‐
sis of being imprisoned AND convicted of a crime. 
 
County Department of Heath Reports 
Your county health department is likely ﬁling quarterly reports 
with your county Auditor. You can request these quarterly  
reports and use this informaƟon to move deceased voters to 
cancelled status within SVRS, assuming the county VR oﬃcial 
agrees the person on this list is the same on the registraƟon 
record. See IC 3‐7‐45‐2.1(e) 
QUESTIONS OF THE MONTH  
Q. Can we destroy 2022 elecƟon materials? 
A. Yes, you can destroy materials related to the 2022 elec‐
Ɵon but keep in mind that voter registraƟon form retenƟon 
is on a diﬀerent schedule. A retenƟon schedule and related 
procedures are found on the State Archives website under 
the “record management” tab. 
 
Q. An elected oﬃcial ﬁled their resignaƟon with our oﬃce, 
and now the county party is planning their caucus to ﬁll it. 
Does the candidate need to ﬁle the CEB‐5 declaraƟon of 
candidacy with the county clerk? 
A. No. Unlike ballot vacancies, the candidate’s declaraƟon of 
candidacy (CEB‐5) is ONLY ﬁled with the chair of the caucus 
not later than 72‐hours before a caucus is held. 
 
Q. What paperwork needs to be ﬁled with our oﬃce aŌer a 
caucus is held for an elected oﬃce vacancy? 
A. The CEB‐3 or the CEB‐4, depending on how the elected 
oﬃce was ﬁlled. The CEB‐3 is ONLY used if there was only 
ONE or NO eligible precinct commiƩeeman to vote in a  
caucus or a Ɵe vote at the caucus. (The ballot vacancy law 
has diﬀerent rules on direct appointment!) The CEB‐4 is ﬁled 
if a caucus was held. The CEB‐3 or CEB‐4 is to be ﬁled not 
later than noon, ﬁve days aŌer the elected oﬃce vacancy is 
ﬁlled. 
 
Q. When is the CAN‐12 statement of economic interests 
due aŌer a person ﬁlls a local elected oﬃce vacancy? 
A. The CAN‐12 is to be ﬁled with the clerk not later than 60‐
days aŌer the person assumes the elected oﬃce. 
All OPEN candidate and poliƟcal acƟon 
commiƩees had an annual report due not 
later than noon, January 15, 2025. All  
regular party commiƩees have unƟl noon, 
March 3, 2025, to ﬁle their annual report. 
 
Every county elecƟon board (CEB) must 
enforce the campaign ﬁnance act, which 
includes holding a hearing CEB to give late 
or delinquent ﬁlers the chance to ask for a 
reduced penalty. 
 
First, what’s an OPEN COMMITTEE? An 
open commiƩee is one that has not 
marked the ﬁnal/disbands box on the CFA
‐4 Summary Sheet aŌer spending down 
their funds to $0 and has no debts owed 
to or by the commiƩee. The commiƩee is 
open unƟl it meets these legal require‐
ments and ﬁles a “ﬁnal/disbands” report. 
 
Unlike other elecƟon‐related ﬁlings, a 
campaign ﬁnance report is only rejected if 
it’s on an old version of the form. (You can 
use “Forms Master List” found on the 
SVRS County Portal to see which forms or 
current.)  
 
Instead, a report received by the CEB aŌer 
the noon deadline is considered  
DELINQUENT and incurs a $50 per  
calendar day ﬁne, up to $1,000.  
 
The ﬁrst $50 is assessed on the deadline 
date, if the commiƩee did not ﬁle by 
noon. Let’s say the commiƩee ﬁled the 
Monday aŌer the Wednesday deadline. 
This is a six‐day period (W, R, F, S, S, M), 
so the total assessed ﬁne is $300. 
 
Not later than 30‐days aŌer the ﬁling 
deadline (for 2024 Annual, this is Feb. 14, 
2025), the CEB must send noƟce to each 
commiƩee that ﬁled a later report or 
failed to do so. (IC 3‐9‐4‐14)  
 
Next, the CEB MUST hold a campaign  
ﬁnance hearing. NoƟce of the hearing 
must be sent to all commiƩees with a late 
report to be aﬀorded the commiƩee’s 
right to due process.  
 
At the hearing, the CEB will listen to tesƟ‐
mony, review the facts, and apply the law. 
It can unanimously agree to waive or re‐
duce the ﬁne for each commiƩee that 
requests one.  
 
AŌer the hearing, the CEB must send or‐
ders to each commiƩee that was assessed 
a full ﬁne or received a waived or reduced 
ﬁne. This is the document the commiƩee 
should keep for its records and use to pay 
their ﬁne, if applicable. 
 
When paid, campaign ﬁnance ﬁnes go into 
a non‐reverƟng county fund that can be 
used by the CEB for elecƟon purposes. 
See IC 3‐9‐4‐17(k) for those details. 
 
More informaƟon about the CEB’s duty to 
enforce the state’s Campaign Finance Act 
along with sample noƟces and orders  are 
found in the CFA Enforcement Toolkit in 
appendix of the green 2024 Campaign 
Finance Manual available on campaign‐
ﬁnance.in.gov.

Election Division Dispatch 
 Brad King & Angie Nussmeyer, Co-Directors | March 2025 
NEWS & UPDATES 
  
SAMC Update To Be Made in SVRS 
Later this month Civix is updaƟng the statewide address mailing 
conﬁrmaƟon (SAMC) noƟce in SVRS. AŌer the push is made, noƟce 
will be sent to counƟes along with a copy of the revised form. There 
is nothing for counƟes to act upon; the SAMC simply needed a date 
refresh for the voter list maintenance (VLM) cycle applicable to this 
version of the form. Don’t forget! If you are able to send a SAMC 
using one of the permiƩed reasons under state law (IC 3‐7‐38.2‐2
(e)), your county must aﬃx pre‐paid postage on the voter response 
card. This is a requirement under federal and state law. 
 
PoliƟcal Party ReorganizaƟon 
The DemocraƟc and Republican parƟes are going through party 
reorganizaƟon in March. CounƟes have reached out to ask what, if 
anything, the parƟes need to ﬁle with the EB aŌerward. If the party 
selected a new chair or treasurer, then the party needs to amend 
their CFA‐3 statement of organizaƟon to provide the  
updated contact informaƟon and ﬁle it by noon, ten days aŌer the 
change in leadership. 
 
If a new treasurer is selected, then the OLD treasurer needs to ﬁle 
an outgoing treasurer’s report not later than noon, 30‐days aŌer

IN FOCUS: Statewide VLM Postcard Mailing 
VR CORNER 
 
Special ElecƟons & VR Deadlines 
For most counƟes in 2025, there are no voter registraƟon 
deadlines as there are no regularly scheduled elecƟons. How‐
ever, a few counƟes are holding a special elecƟon in May and, 
it’s possible there will be a few special elecƟons in November. 
 
CounƟes juggling a special elecƟon in 2025 must impose a VR 
deadline for only those precincts holding a special elecƟon.  
For the May 6, 2025, special elecƟon, the VR deadline is April 
7. This means counƟes will need to review records in SVRS 
hoppers to determine if the voter lives in a precinct where the 
special elecƟon is being held. If so, then they must conﬁrm the 
registraƟon was submiƩed electronically on or before April 7.  
 
Paper registraƟons for voters living within the special elecƟon 
district must be hand‐delivered before your oﬃce closes on 
April 7, OR postmarked, if sent by mail, on or before April 7, to 
be processed. Remember, if a postmark is missing or illegible, 
then a mailed registraƟon for a voter living in the special elec‐
Ɵon district can be processed if it is received by April 14, 2025.  
 
Of note, if an underage voter submits a VR form AND lives 
within the special elecƟon district, then the individual must 
turn 18 on or before the date of the special elecƟon. Outside 
the special elecƟon district, the underage voter needs to be 18 
on or before the date of the November 2026 elecƟon.  
 
Voters living outside of the special elecƟon district are not  
impacted, and the form can be processed for qualiﬁed voters. 
QUESTIONS OF THE MONTH  
Q. Are there any requirements a CEB should follow when 
audiƟng campaign ﬁnance reports? 
A. State law says that a CEB will audit reports from “Ɵme‐to‐
Ɵme” but does not set forth parameters to conduct the au‐
dit. Instead, it is up to the CEB to develop and adopt uniform 
and non‐discriminatory procedures to perform this work. 
Please note that this is diﬀerent from enforcement acƟons, 
where a commiƩee has not ﬁled or ﬁled a delinquent report. 
All CEBs must track and determine which commiƩees have 
not Ɵmely ﬁled their CFA‐4 or CFA‐11 reports and follow 
state law to hold a hearing and assess a ﬁne. The 2024 Cam-
paign Finance Manual has more informaƟon on conducƟng 
enforcement proceedings. 
 
Q. A few folks have asked when candidate ﬁling for 2026 
will start. Is there an updated elecƟon calendar with that 
informaƟon? 
A. Not yet. Keep in mind that the state legislature is consid‐
ering bills that may aﬀect these dates. AŌer ﬁnal acƟon by 
the governor, then IED will update forms and publicaƟons 
ahead of the December ElecƟon Administrators’ Conference. 
PeƟƟons for certain candidates and the calendar brochure 
for the next cycle are released early, usually in early July.  
Since it may be a while for updated materials to be released, 
you can pencil in on your calendar the following 2026 dates: 
 Jan. 7, 2026: First day of candidate ﬁling 
 NOON, Feb. 6, 2026: Deadline to ﬁle for D/R Primary 
 May 5, 2026: Primary ElecƟon Day 
The ElecƟon Division is required to 
engage in a statewide voter list 
maintenance (VLM) project in each 
odd‐numbered year under state law. 
This year, the project is expected to 
launch in mid‐May 2025 and follows 
VLM procedures found in federal and 
state law. 
 
Indiana’s program consists of two 
mailers. Card 1: is sent to the mailing  
address of every acƟve voter in Indi‐
ana via USPS non‐forwardable mail. 
This ﬁrst card is anƟcipated to be 
mailed in mid‐May. If the card is re‐
turned undeliverable by mail pursuant 
to IC 3‐5‐2‐49.7 or is marked “return 
to sender” , then card 2 is sent to the 
voter. 
 
Card 2, or the Voter Response Card, is 
sent by USPS forwardable mail to the 
mailing address of a person whose 
card 1 is returned undeliverable. Card 
2 allows the person to a) conﬁrm their  
registraƟon address or b) update their 
registraƟon within the county or c) 
cancel their registraƟon if they’ve 
moved out of county.  
 
Card 2 is very similar to a SAMC in 
look and feel. The response card has 
pre‐paid postage aﬃxed, and needs to 
be received by the state by a cut‐oﬀ 
date in late August for the voter to 
avoid having their registraƟon status 
moved to “inacƟve” outside of a 
freeze period.  
 
Card 2 is the main focus for county VR 
oﬃcials, as the voter response card 
(VRC) is treated like a voter registra‐
Ɵon document. Our vendor will scan 
and sort the returned VRC informaƟon 
into VLM Hoppers in SVRS. This allows 
the counƟes to review and make the 
ﬁnal determinaƟon if the voter has 
updated or cancelled their registraƟon 
based on the response.  
 
If Card 2 is not returned by the late 
August cut‐oﬀ date or is returned as 
undeliverable, then those records will 
be loaded into the VLM Hopper for 
counƟes to move their status to 
“inacƟve” outside of the freeze  
period.  
 
Two years ago our vendor conƟnued 
to scan “late arriving” card 1 and card 
2s and loaded them to VLM Hoppers 
once all counƟes cleared their work 
statewide. This is an important step, 
as voter records need to be acted on 
to capture the changes in chronologi‐
cal order. 
 
More details, including images of the 
cards, will be shared with counƟes in 
the near future once our contract with 
Civix and The Jackson Group is ﬁnal‐
ized. IED will also have an info page on 
our website (in.gov/sos/elecƟons) to 
help voters understand this eﬀort  
before the project is launched. 
InformaƟon in this newsleƩer is provided by the Indiana ElecƟon Division as a courtesy to county elecƟon administrators. If a person is unclear concerning elecƟon law provisions,  
the ElecƟon Division can serve as an interpreƟve source. However, where important legal rights are concerned, you must consult with your own aƩorney to be fully and properly advised.

Election Division Dispatch 
 Brad King & Angie Nussmeyer, Co-Directors | April 2025 
NEWS & UPDATES 
  
“Oﬀ‐year” Pay for Clerk, CEB 
In a county where the circuit court clerk serves as voter  
registraƟon oﬃcer, the clerk is enƟtled to per diem compensaƟon, 
which is paid out of the general fund. (IC 3‐7‐12‐22) In other words, 
the county council would determine what, if any, pay can be provid‐
ed to the clerk for serving as the chief VR oﬃcial and the county 
commissioners would approve the budget line item. (IC 3‐5‐3‐1) 
Also, the clerk, serving as the county VR oﬃcial, is enƟtled to a  
sƟpend of not more than $2,500 each year a general elecƟon is 
held. (IC 3‐7‐12‐22) 
 
For the County ElecƟon Board (CEB), the county ﬁscal body deter‐
mines the pay schedule for the two appointed members and secre‐
tary of the CEB. (IC 3‐6‐5‐9) There is no statute that prohibits pay in 
an “oﬀ‐year;” in fact, many counƟes are busy with administraƟve 
tasks put oﬀ during the busy elecƟon cycles. Further, the CEB is  
required to propose its budget esƟmate each year (IC 3‐6‐5‐16), 
which may be an opportunity to explore changes to compensaƟon. 
Be sure to check in with the State Board of Accounts to get their 
perspecƟve, too. 
 
Don’t Forget! ReprecincƟng Request Deadline  
In February, IED sent an email to counƟes explaining the steps and 
deadlines for counƟes to take to adjust precinct boundaries ahead 
of the 2026 elecƟon cycle. The ﬁrst step in the process is for  
counƟes to noƟfy IED of their intent to reprecinct by April 25, 2025, 
and IED staﬀ is assigned to you to assist with paperwork. 
 
QuesƟons? The reprecincƟng memo is found on the County Portal 
in the Shared Documents folder under “2026 Precinct Change  
Process” or send an email to elecƟons@iec.in.gov. 
 
Statewide VLM Postcard Project Update 
The web page for the state’s VLM project was updated and is now 
available to voters on the IED website (in.gov/sos/elecƟons) or  
using indianavoters.com/VLM. The page includes general infor‐
maƟon about the project and sample cards that voters will receive. 
 
Beginning May 16, 2025, we anƟcipate the ﬁrst wave of card 1’s to 
be mailed to Indiana voters with a registraƟon status of “acƟve”. 
These cards are not forwardable so that any undeliverable address 
will be returned to iniƟate the mailing of a second card (similar to 
the SAMC) to voters in June. We should complete the card 1 mailing 
by May 30, 2025. Training sessions on processing card 2 responses 
will be held in early June, ahead of when we expect to begin  
receiving informaƟon back from the second mailing.

IN FOCUS: Elected Office Vacancies 
VR CORNER 
 
Voter List Maintenance (VLM) Concepts 
Federal and state law sets forth voter list maintenance rules 
and procedures. In federal law, you’ll ﬁnd the VLM statues in 
52 USC sec. 20507; in state law, these requirements are found, 
generally, in IC 3‐7‐38.2. 
 
VLM is conƟnual work, using resources from the Department 
of Health, Social Security AdministraƟon, Department of  
CorrecƟon, and other valid sources like this summer’s 
statewide postcard mailer or your statewide address mailing 
conﬁrmaƟon (SAMC) noƟces. 
 
Before each elecƟon in even‐numbered years, VLM work to 
move registraƟons to “inacƟve” status must “freeze” 90‐days 
before the elecƟon. This means you cannot move any voter’s 
registraƟon to “inacƟve” status during this period and must 
wait unƟl you apply vote history in that elecƟon before making 
the change. In odd‐numbered years, the “freeze” starts 29‐
days before the elecƟon. Unless your county has a special elec‐
Ɵon in 2025, there is no “freeze” period this year.  
 
Certain list maintenance  tasks to move registraƟon records to 
“cancelled” status may occur at any Ɵme, like cancellaƟon due 
to death or incarceraƟon following convicƟon of a crime or at 
the voter’s wriƩen request. 
 
Updates to a registraƟon made by the voter can be processed 
almost any Ɵme, except when registraƟon closes ahead of 
each elecƟon and when it reopens aŌer each elecƟon. 
QUESTION OF THE MONTH  
 
Q. Can we use other state informaƟon to move a  
registraƟon to “cancelled” status? 
A. Maybe. If you receive or request a copy of the voter  
registraƟon form completed in the other state AND it is  
dated aŌer the Indiana registraƟon AND the form has the 
“magic words” from the voter to authorize cancellaƟon of 
the voter’s record at a previous address, then yes, you can 
cancel the Indiana registraƟon. 
 
If the form does NOT include the “magic words” to authorize 
cancellaƟon or you just receive basic informaƟon about the 
voter from the other state, then you can send a SAMC to the 
voter or the VRG‐14 form to the individual. Sending the 
SAMC will allow the voter to go through the acƟve to inac‐
Ɵve to cancelled workﬂow if they fail to respond or the card 
is returned as undeliverable. AlternaƟvely, the voter can also 
conﬁrm their Indiana registraƟon or update it within the 
county.  
 
Sending the VRG‐14 requires the voter to sign the document 
and return it to you. You cannot use an undeliverable VRG‐
14 as the basis to cancel a registraƟon or move it to inacƟve 
status. This process is based on a federal court order and is 
reﬂected in our state law (IC 3‐7‐38.2‐5.5). More details are 
found in the purple 2024 Voter RegistraƟon Guidebook. 
Occasionally an elected oﬃcial in a local 
oﬃce will resign from oﬃce before their 
term ends and the oﬃce will need to be 
ﬁlled as a pro tempore appointment. 
 
NoƟce of resignaƟon and procedures to 
noƟfy chairs of a death of an oﬃce holder 
can be found in IC 5‐8‐3.5 and IC 5‐8‐6, 
respecƟvely. Most local oﬃce holders will 
ﬁle their resignaƟon leƩer with the county 
clerk (and several countywide oﬃcials 
with the governor), who then must noƟfy 
the chair in wriƟng within 72‐hours. 
 
CerƟfying the death of a local oﬃceholder 
is a responsibility of the clerk, once she 
receives informaƟon and is reasonably 
saƟsﬁed it is true. However, in some  
cases, the governor must receive noƟce of 
the death and send noƟce to the chair. A 
caucus cannot occur unƟl the chair  
receives noƟce of the death from the  
appropriate oﬃcial. However, this rule 
does NOT apply to a resignaƟon. 
 
IC 3‐13‐6 is the ﬁrst chapter in the vacancy 
statutes that directly applies to local  
oﬃces. While it is important to read the 
enƟre chapter, beginning with IC 3‐13‐7, 
the ﬁrst secƟon notes that a vacancy in a 
local oﬃce that was last held by a person  
elected or selected as a candidate of a 
major poliƟcal party (D or R) of the state 
shall be ﬁlled by a caucus under IC 3‐13‐
11. 
  
The other procedures outlined in the rest 
of the chapter usually apply only if the 
oﬃcial was elected as a Libertarian,  
Independent, or other minor party. In 
these instances, a unit of government will 
hold a public meeƟng to ﬁll the vacancy, 
though there are special excepƟons with 
some local oﬃces where the unit is able 
to ﬁll the vacancy if the D or R chair fails 
to ﬁll it within the 30‐day period. 
 
A caucus is required for D or R elected 
oﬃce vacancies with three excepƟons: 
     1/ there is only ONE (or no) eligible PC  
     that can parƟcipate in the caucus (IC 3‐ 
     13‐11‐5(c); IC 3‐13‐11‐5(a) sets forth PC  
     eligibility requirements);  
     2/ there is a Ɵe at the caucus (IC 3‐13‐ 
     11‐8(a)); OR  
     3/ quorum at the caucus is not  
     established (IC 3‐13‐11‐8(b)). 
 
For elected oﬃce vacancies, there is no 
state form for noƟce of a caucus. Instead, 
chairs send wriƩen noƟce under IC 3‐13‐
11‐4, which includes the date, Ɵme,  
locaƟon, purpose, and name of the caucus 
chair, to all eligible PCs by ﬁrst class mail. 
 
Candidates are required to submit the  
CEB‐5 to the caucus chair not later than 
72‐hours before the caucus is held (IC 3‐
13‐11‐7), and must meet the same gen‐
eral qualiﬁcaƟons to run for the elected 
oﬃce. The caucus adopts rules of proce‐
dures, such as establishing the deﬁniƟon 
of quorum or requiring a secret ballot if 
only one candidate ﬁles. See IC 3‐13‐11‐
10. 
 
The chair ﬁles the CEB‐4 (if it’s a direct 
appointment, the chair uses the CEB‐3) 
not later than noon, ﬁve days aŌer the 
caucus. Clerks are to give the new oﬃcial 
the CEB‐22. The oath is ﬁled not later than 
30‐days aŌer assuming oﬃce while the 
CAN‐12 is ﬁled not later than 60 days.

Election Division Dispatch 
 Brad King & Angie Nussmeyer, Co-Directors | May 2025 
NEWS & UPDATES 
  
May 2025 Special ElecƟon Reminders 
A few Indiana counƟes are holding a special elecƟon on May 6, 
2025, to conduct an elecƟon for local public quesƟons. These  
counƟes must cerƟfy the results of their elecƟon in SVRS not later 
than noon, May 19, 2025. The CEB‐9, SecƟon I is due not later than 
noon, May 20, 2025. There is no need to ﬁle paper copies with IED; 
complete the cerƟﬁcaƟon in SVRS, please.  
 
However, once the elecƟon is cerƟﬁed, you will need to also cerƟfy 
the results “immediately” to the Department of Local Government 
Finance for both a controlled project (that is, construcƟon) and an 
operaƟng referendum (that is, a school tax levy). For controlled  
projects, you must also cerƟfy the results of the elecƟon to the 
county auditor of each county in which the poliƟcal subdivision is 
located. 
 
One thing that will be diﬀerent this year is that the state’s elecƟon 
night reporƟng website (indianavoters.com/elecƟonresults) will not 
be refreshed or otherwise available. You may have voters reaching 
out to your oﬃce as a result. 
 
ReprecincƟng Next Steps 
Many counƟes signed up to draw new precinct boundaries by the 
survey deadline of April 25, 2025. CounƟes will be assigned a staﬀ 
person (Lori Clark or Stephanie Davidsen) who are reaching out to 
these counƟes now. The next step is to complete IEC‐8 forms and 
aƩach the required paperwork such as annexaƟon orders, maps, 
and an email noƟng you informed the county party chairs of the 
changes. Lori or Stephanie will support you through each step of the 
process. The deadline to ﬁle the IEC‐8s is noon on August 27, 2025. 
 
QuesƟons? The reprecincƟng memo is found on the County Portal 
in the Shared Documents folder under “2026 Precinct Change  
Process” or send an email to elecƟons@iec.in.gov. 
 
Minor SAMC Update 
Later in May a hoƞix is going to be pushed to add the print date of

counƟes asked for this enhancement, which not only helps them

spond. More informaƟon, including a sample, will be sent when the 
hoƞix is released. There is no need for training, as the update is

VRG‐1: Sheriﬀ Report of Incarcerated Individuals 
At least quarterly the county Sheriﬀ must send a list of individuals 
who are convicted of a crime and aƩach the VRG‐1 to the list. (IC 3‐
7‐46‐6) The Sheriﬀ can send you this informaƟon more frequently, 
but at minimum, it must be done quarterly. Remember, a person 
must be currently imprisoned following convicƟon of a crime to 
have their registraƟon moved to “cancelled.” If the person has 
been released or not yet convicted, then their registraƟon remains 
as‐is.
