VR CORNER 
 
Incomplete VRG‐6 Forms 
On occasion, counƟes will receive incomplete VRG‐6 
voter registraƟon forms from a full‐service agency 
such as FSSA or DWD. County voter registraƟon  
oﬃcials treat an incomplete VRG‐6 the same as any 
other registraƟon form. That is, make an aƩempt to 
contact the voter by mail and, if a phone number is 
provided, by phone. The voter has unƟl 29‐days before 
the next elecƟon to complete a new registraƟon form 
to answer the age/ciƟzenship quesƟons, if that infor‐
maƟon was missing. Any other incomplete informaƟon 
must be provided not later than 10‐days before the 
date of the next elecƟon. If the voter fails to respond 
by those deadlines, depending on their error, then the 
registraƟon request is rejected. 
 
There is an extra step if the incomplete form used is a 
VRG‐6. Because a full‐service agency is a covered 
agency of the NaƟonal Voter RegistraƟon Act (NVRA), 
missing or incomplete informaƟon on the VRG‐6 re‐
quires your oﬃce to noƟfy IED. It is helpful if you send 
the incomplete registraƟons and, if possible, which full 
service agency and their address delivered the incom‐
plete applicaƟons. This allows us to properly noƟfy the 
full‐service agency and request that they correct their 
procedures to avoid this problem in the future.  (IC 3‐7
‐34‐7) 
QUESTION OF THE MONTH  
 
Q. Can we transfer our voƟng systems or ePollbooks to our vendor 
before the IEC‐6 is approved by IED? 
A. No. IEC‐6 is the form that must be completed and signed oﬀ by 
the county elecƟon board for a county to request that their voƟng 
system or ePollbooks can be transferred, sold, or destroyed under 
IC 3‐11‐15‐59. This form can be emailed, mailed, faxed or hand‐
delivered to IED. But, before the voƟng equipment can leave the 
county’s possession, the co‐directors must approve the plan. Please 
read the form closely and provide speciﬁc details, such as the pro‐
posed date of destrucƟon or transfer of equipment, who is receiv‐
ing the equipment and/or destroying it, etc. This will make the re‐
view process go more quickly . 
 
Q. Can a candidate thinking about running for elecƟon in 2026 or 
beyond, open a campaign ﬁnance commiƩee? 
A. Yes! In fact, the candidate may be required to do so if they raise 
or spend $100.01 or more toward running for an oﬃce paying more 
than $5,000 in a calendar year, even if there is no elecƟon in 2025. 
(For oﬃces paying less than $5,000 a calendar year or school board, 
the threshold amount to trigger acƟon is $500.01 or more.) In 2025, 
a candidate who exceeds this threshold must ﬁle the CFA‐1 state‐
ment of organizaƟon not later than noon, ten days aŌer raising or 
spending this dollar amount. Candidates running for local oﬃce, 
including judge or prosecuƟng aƩorney, ﬁle campaign ﬁnance pa‐
perwork with the CEB. Statewide or state legislaƟve candidates ﬁle 
electronically with IED. 
Beginning May 16, the ﬁrst batch of “card 1” mailers will be sent 
to every Indiana voter with an “acƟve” registraƟon status, or 
about 4 million or so individuals. The last batch is expected to 
drop on or around May 30, 2025. 
 
A sample of the front and back of this card is presented here. 
You’ll note that the back of the card explains to the voter that if 
they are the individual addressed on the card, then the voter 
does not need to do anything else. But, if they receive a card at 
their home and the person on the card is not in the household, 
then we recommend wriƟng “Return to Sender” and placing it 
back in their mailbox for the USPS to return to IED. No postage is 
required to “return to sender.” 
 
We do anƟcipate receiving calls where a voter tried to “return to 
sender” but the mail piece came back to them (or never leŌ their 
mailbox). If you hear of that happening, please email elec‐
Ɵons@iec.in.gov. Baker Tilly and Civix work closely with the 
USPS, as we need their approval on the cards but also meet rou‐
Ɵnely to ensure as smooth a program as possible. 
 
You can direct voters to our oﬃce email or visit indianavot‐
ers.com/VLM for more informaƟon, including details on the sec‐
ond part of our mailing the voter response card. SVRS training is 
scheduled for June, so please be sure to mark your calendars!

the ElecƟon Division can serve as an interpreƟve source. However, where important legal rights are concerned, you must consult with your own aƩorney to be fully and properly advised.

QUESTION OF THE MONTH  
Q. Can a voter’s Power of AƩorney (POA) register the  
individual to vote and sign the form on behalf of the voter? 
What about an absentee ballot applicaƟon or absentee  
ballot security envelope? 
 
A. Before we get to the answer, keep in mind that a voter 
with a disability or a person who cannot speak or read the 
English language can have assistance from nearly any person 
except for their employer or union representaƟve for many 
elecƟon procedures. AddiƟonally, when a POA provides this 
support, a copy of the POA is to be aƩached to the record. 
These general rules are assumed in the explanaƟon below. 
 
For voter registraƟon, the voter’s POA does not give the indi‐
vidual the power to determine where and whether the per‐
son receiving assistance should be registered to vote. State 
law (IC 30‐5‐5‐14) makes it clear that POA’s do not have au‐
thority to execute a person’s voter registraƟon applicaƟon. 
However, certain voters may have help compleƟng their reg‐
istraƟon applicaƟon, including signing the voter’s name, if 
the aﬃdavit of assistance is ﬁlled out.  
 
Similar rules apply to an absentee ballot applicaƟon. Certain 
voters may have assistance in ﬁlling out the applicaƟon, in‐
cluding signing the voter’s name, if the aﬃdavit of assistance 
is completed.    
When it comes to the absentee ballot to vote itself, support 
is more restricted under state law. Only the voter can com‐
plete their own ballot, enclose it in the ballot security enve‐
lope, and sign their name or make their mark on the voter’s 
aﬃdavit. A POA does NOT have authority to complete an 
absentee ballot on another person’s behalf!  
 
Instead, a POA can aƩest to the voter’s signature or mark on 
the absentee ballot aﬃdavit, or seal the envelope on the 
voter’s behalf. AddiƟonally, any person but those noted 
above can also assist with sealing the envelope. The aﬃdavit 
of assistance must be completed by the individual providing 
this support.   
 
Voters who cannot personally mark their own ballot are to 
vote by travel board. AlternaƟvely, a voter with print disa-
biliƟes can request an accessible ABS ballot. A voter can also 
vote in-person before or on ElecƟon Day and request assis‐
tance from persons noted above or ABS voter board mem‐
bers or ElecƟon Day judges aŌer compleƟng a PRE‐3 form 
before entering the voƟng booth.

IN FOCUS: Statewide VLM Project Continues 
Last month we touched on card 1 of the statewide postcard mailing. Those cards entered the mail stream on or around May 27, 
2025, with the ﬁnal batch being dropped by the end of May. These cards were sent by non‐forwardable ﬁrst class mail to all Hoosi‐
er voters in “acƟve” status. This means cards that cannot be delivered by the USPS will “return to sender” (that is, IED) and iniƟate 
the process to send the card 2 to those impacted voters. 
 
On or around June 20, 2025, the Voter Response Card (VRC or Card 2) will be mailed to those voters where Card 1 was returned by 
the USPS as undeliverable to the state. This second card is sent as forwardable, ﬁrst‐class mail and includes a postage pre‐paid 
“response card” for the voter to conﬁrm, update, or cancel their Indiana registraƟon. IED must receive this card not later than  
August 29, 2025, to avoid the voter’s registraƟon being moved to “inacƟve” status. (Note: The instrucƟons note that the state rec‐
ommends the voter drop the card in the mail by August 22, 2025, to ensure IED receives it by August 29, 2025. However, the voter 
can sƟll send the card back aŌer August 22, 2025, though acƟons taken on their record will depend on when the response card was 
received.) 
 
A voter receiving the VRC can conﬁrm their registraƟon address is accurate; update it within their same Indiana county; or cancel 
their registraƟon if they moved out of their Indiana county. The voter must sign the response card to make their response eﬀecƟve. 
AddiƟonally, if the voter wants to update their registraƟon address within their same county, then they must answer the age and 
ciƟzenship quesƟons. 
 
CounƟes will begin receiving card 2 data to act upon someƟme aŌer June 20, 2025. Please make sure you are working through your 
list maintenance hoppers rouƟnely, as counƟes need to complete the ﬁrst round of hopper work by September 9, 2025. This will 
allow Civix to upload “late‐arriving” response cards into the VLM hoppers for counƟes to process out as a registraƟon form. 
 
More informaƟon, including training materials and detailed memos, will be shared as the project moves forward. Please be sure to 
add one of the two SVRS training dates to your calendar: June 3 and June 5. Lastly, informaƟon about this project is available at 
indianavoters.com/VLM. Please direct consƟtuents to this website or they can email or call our oﬃce (elecƟons@iec.in.gov or 317‐
232‐3939) with quesƟons. In some cases, however, we may need to direct the voter back to the county, as county registraƟon oﬃ‐
cials make the ﬁnal determinaƟon on how to process the VRC. 
InformaƟon in this newsleƩer is provided by the Indiana ElecƟon Division as a courtesy to county elecƟon administrators. If a person is unclear concerning elecƟon law provisions,  
the ElecƟon Division can serve as an interpreƟve source. However, where important legal rights are concerned, you must consult with your own aƩorney to be fully and properly advised.

Election Division Dispatch 
 Brad King & Angie Nussmeyer, Co-Directors | July 2025 
NEWS & UPDATES 
 
New Title 3 Chapter (IC 3-5-2.1) for DeﬁniƟons 
During the 2025 legislaƟve session, some clean-up work was 
made to our elecƟon law deﬁniƟons, formerly under IC 3-5-2. 
Those deﬁniƟons have moved to IC 3-5-2.1 and are reor-
ganized. Now, each deﬁniƟon will have a clean secƟon num-
ber, unƟl more deﬁniƟons are added in the future. Since we 
rely on these deﬁniƟons on a nearly daily basis, we wanted to 
call this out to look up IC 3-5-2.1 when visiƟng iga.in.gov. AŌer 
July 1, 2025, the General Assembly’s website (iga.in.gov) is 
updated with the new statutes. Click the magnifying glass in 
the upper right corner to pop up the search bar. Then click 
“Search Indiana Code” in the boƩom right of the bar. This al-
lows you to enter the Title (T), ArƟcle (A), Chapter (C), and 
SecƟon (S) you want to review. 
 
 
VoƟng System RecerƟﬁcaƟon 
State law requires all voƟng systems to go through recerƟﬁca-
Ɵon in the year aŌer the presidenƟal elecƟon, meaning the 
voƟng system cerƟﬁcaƟons expire on Oct. 1, 2025. If the ven-
dor applies to have the cerƟﬁcaƟon issued for the next four 
year period, then IEC will hold a hearing to consider recerƟfy-
ing exisƟng systems. If the vendor chooses not to, counƟes 
can conƟnue to use the “legacy” systems but the vendor can-
not market, sell, or lease those voƟng systems anymore. 
 
EAVS: ElecƟon AdministraƟon & VoƟng Survey 2024 Report 
Remember compleƟng the CEB-9 SecƟon II last winter? Well, 
the answers your county provided were shared with the US 
ElecƟon Assistance Commission and compiled into the bi-
annual report to Congress that is now available here: hƩps://
www.eac.gov/research-and-data/studies-and-reports 
 
Disclosure of AppoinƟng AuthoriƟes 
HEA 1509 took eﬀect on July 1, 2025, which requires the dis-
closure of the term and appoinƟng authority for certain 
boards and commissions. This requirement applies to the 
County ElecƟon Board. State law is clear under IC 3-6-5-4 that 
in most counƟes, the county clerk appoints the individual to 
serve on the CEB aŌer receiving nominaƟons from the party 
chair. For Lake and Porter counƟes, however, IC 3-6-5.2-4, IC 3
-6-5.4-4, and IC 3-6-5.6-4 require the county chair to make the 
direct appointment.  
 
State law is also changing to note that the appointed CEB 
member elected to serve as chair of the CEB has a term that 
ends on January 1 of the year immediately following the elec-
Ɵon of the county clerk. For example, if the Cardinal County 
clerk’s term of oﬃce ends on January 1, 2027, then the chair’s 
term also ends and a new elecƟon for CEB chair will need to 
be conducted at the next CEB meeƟng aŌer the new clerk’s 
term of oﬃce begins. 
CALENDAR 
Note: This calendar includes dates to assist counƟes who 
have a special elecƟon on November 4, 2025. These dates do 
not apply to a county if no elecƟon is being conducted. 
 
June 20, 2025: First wave of card 2’s (voter response cards) 
mailed to voters whose card 1 was returned as undeliverable 
June 30, 2025: Deadline for a school corporaƟon to adopt a 
resoluƟon under IC 20-46-1-8 to place a school operaƟng ref-
erendum on the ballot as a special elecƟon on Nov. 4, 2025 
July 4, 2025: Independence Day, IED Closed 
July 11, 2025: Last wave of card 2’s (voter response cards)

IN FOCUS: Highlights of Some Legislative Changes Effective July 1, 2025 
In early June, IED completed the 2025 LegislaƟve Summary and shared it with county elecƟon and voter registraƟon oﬃcials. This 
document, along with slide decks covering this topic at the summer Clerk’s AssociaƟon meeƟng, are available on the ElecƟon Ad-
ministrator’s Portal at in.gov/sos/elecƟons. Below are a few noteworthy changes: 
 
Candidate CommiƩees Required for Elected Oﬃcials: All elected oﬃcials in an oﬃce paying more than $5000 a year must open 
and maintain a candidate commiƩee unƟl such a Ɵme the oﬃcial no longer holds oﬃce or is not a candidate for elecƟon. If an 
elected oﬃcial does NOT have a CFA-1 on ﬁle with the CEB (or, if required, IED) already, then a CFA-1 must be ﬁled not later than 
noon, July 11, 2025. Failure to ﬁle by this deadline results in a $50 per calendar day ﬁne, up to $1,000. If the oﬃcial does not ﬁle a 
CFA-1 aŌer the maximum ﬁne is reached, the CEB must administraƟvely open a campaign ﬁnance commiƩee, making the elected 
oﬃcial the chair and treasurer of the commiƩee.  
 
There is an excepƟon to this rule, of course. If an elected oﬃcial holds an oﬃce paying a salary of less than $5,000 a calendar year 
OR if the person holds a school board oﬃce, then a candidate commiƩee does NOT need to be opened unƟl such a Ɵme the com-
miƩee raises or spends more than $500 toward running for the oﬃce. 
 
Below are some commonly asked quesƟons our oﬃce is receiving related to this change: 
 Under state law, a separate bank account must be opened when the commiƩee spends or raises more than $200 (IC 3-9-2-9
(c)); therefore, a candidate’s commiƩee that does not intend to raise or spend any money would not need to open an bank 
account unless they exceeded this threshold and can leave this blank on the CFA-1. 
 Some currently elected oﬃcials plan to seek another elected oﬃce and already have a CFA-1 on ﬁle. There is no need to open 
a second candidate’s commiƩee, if the candidate is seeking another local oﬃce.  
 Judges and ProsecuƟng AƩorneys are included in this change of law, and their CFA-1 is ﬁled with the CEB (not IED!). There is no 
need to ﬁle a courtesy copy with IED. In three counƟes (Lake, Marion, St. Joseph), some or all of their judges face retenƟon 
instead of elecƟon. In these limited circumstances only, this subset of oﬃceholders do not ﬁle a CFA-1. Instead, if they “face 
opposiƟon” then a PAC (CFA-2) can be created. IED recommends that judges review the Code of Judicial Conduct, speciﬁcally 
Canon 4.4, to determine the best way to handle this requirement. 
 At minimum at the local level, all candidate commiƩees will have an annual report due. The 2025 Annual CFA-4 report for can-
didate commiƩees is due at noon, January 21, 2026. If the oﬃceholder is a candidate on the ballot for local oﬃce, then the pre
-primary and pre-elecƟon CFA-4 report or CFA-11 large contribuƟon report may be due, if applicable. 
 
New Direct Appointment Authority for Filling Elected Oﬃce Vacancies. Beginning July 1, 2025, if only one candidate ﬁled a CEB-5 
to ﬁll an elected oﬃce vacancy, the caucus must be held but the chair may choose to make a direct appointment instead of holding 
a vote at the caucus. The CEB-3 form will be used in the case of a direct appointment, and not the CEB-4 form. Remember, an 
elected oﬃce vacancy caucus is called when a currently elected oﬃcial has resigned from oﬃce or passed away, for example. This 
rule does NOT apply to ballot vacancy caucuses. Updated versions of the CEB-3 and CEB-5 are available as of July 1. 
 
Two Primary Rule Requirement for Candidates Filling Elected Oﬃce Vacancies. Beginning July 1, 2025, any person seeking to ﬁll 
an elected oﬃce vacancy (NOT a ballot vacancy!) must meet the primary voƟng history requirement (the last two primary elecƟons 
in Indiana in which the candidate voted must be of the same party the person is seeking to aﬃliate with on the ballot) OR aƩach 
the chair’s cerƟﬁcaƟon to the CEB-5 form ﬁled with the chair of the caucus. As a result, the CEB-5 form is being updated. 
 
Updates to Party DelegaƟon of Direct Appointment Authority to Fill Ballot Vacancies. Under state law, a county party organiza-
Ɵon may delegate direct appointment authority to the county chair or central commiƩee to ﬁll ballot vacancies (for example, when 
no one ﬁled to run for an oﬃce in the primary elecƟon or withdraws ahead of the November elecƟon). The resoluƟon or moƟon 
adopted for these purposes will expire on primary elecƟon day in 2026 (May 5, 2026) for the DemocraƟc Party and for the Republi-
can Party, on primary elecƟon day in 2028 (May 2, 2028). Each county party organizaƟon will then need to adopt a new resoluƟon 
or moƟon, which will expire the next Ɵme the parƟes elect their precinct commiƩeemen in 2030 (Ds) and 2032 (Rs). Of course, the 
parƟes can shorten the length of Ɵme to apply to one elecƟon, for example, but it cannot extend beyond the four-year period. 
 
School Board Candidates & Party AﬃliaƟon. StarƟng in the 2026 elecƟon cycle, school board candidates can aﬃliate with a poliƟ-
cal party (D/R/L or other minor party), or be an Independent candidate, or leave the aﬃliaƟon box blank. The CAN-34 will be updat-
ed to reﬂect these changes. No other part of the process changes for school board candidates - peƟƟon signature requirements are 
the same, any D/R school board candidate is NOT on the May primary ballot, the straight party device sƟll does not apply to this 
oﬃce. CounƟes will want to work with the voƟng system vendors to ensure the party aﬃliaƟon/Independent/Blank box is added to 
this oﬃce. AddiƟonally, there is no limit on the number of D/R/L candidates who can ﬁle for school board, meaning it is possible for 
4 Ds, 5 Rs, and 3 Ls to ﬁle for a school board seat where voters can only vote for one person. Please make sure your voƟng system 
vendor is aware of this possibility. 
 
Ballot RetracƟon. Like their DRE counterparts, opƟcal scan voƟng systems may use a ballot retracƟon feature on ballot cards. No 
opƟcal scan voƟng system in Indiana is cerƟﬁed to use this feature, though it is expected to be reviewed this fall when all voƟng 
systems must be re-cerƟﬁed for the next four-year period.  
InformaƟon in this newsleƩer is provided by the Indiana ElecƟon Division as a courtesy to county elecƟon administrators. If a person is unclear concerning elecƟon law provisions,  
the ElecƟon Division can serve as an interpreƟve source. However, where important legal rights are concerned, you must consult with your own aƩorney to be fully and properly advised. 
VR CORNER 
Proof of CiƟzenship 
Beginning July 1, 2025, voters idenƟﬁed as receiving a tem-
porary credenƟal from the BMV (that is, temporary creden-
Ɵal = T or true, as displayed in SVRS) must be sent the VRG-
26, a noƟce generated out of SVRS to inform the voter that 
they must provide the VR oﬃcial with one of ﬁve types of 
ciƟzenship documentaƟon before their applicaƟon can be 
reviewed. The noƟce lists the ﬁve types of documentaƟon 
that can be accepted under state law (See IC 3-7-38.2-7.3). 
This documentaƟon must be received by the county not later 
than 30-days aŌer the person receives the VRG-26. 
 
There will be two diﬀerent data sets provided to counƟes—
potenƟal matches against exisƟng registraƟon records where 
temporary credenƟal = true (as required by HEA 1264 from 
2024) and ongoing matches as new applicaƟons or updates 
are ﬁled (as required by HEA 1680 from 2025). 
 
The “one-Ɵme” ﬁle review records will go into a hopper 
called “CiƟzenship Maintenance.” All work will be processed 
out of this one hopper. However, “ongoing” work will have 
two disƟnct hoppers.  
 
The “CiƟzenship ValidaƟon” hopper will be loaded with elec-
tronically received records from the BMV and indianavot-
ers.com (OVR, ABS-VPD) where temporary credenƟal = T. 
(RegistraƟons where temporary credenƟal = F will load into 
current hoppers (BMV, OVR) for the usual processing.) 
 
When the VRG-26 is printed and sent to the voter, the elec-
tronically received record will move into a “CiƟzenship 30-
Day Hold” hopper. For paper VR applicaƟons, counƟes will 
do their manual review with the ﬁrst step to validate wheth-
er the individual has a temporary credenƟal or not. If tempo-
rary credenƟal = T, then the VRG-26 must be sent and the 
record moves into the “CiƟzenship 30-Day Hold” hopper.  
 
The voter must provide the proof of ciƟzenship to the county 
VR oﬃcial not later than 30-days aŌer receiving the VRG-26. 
If the voter does meet this deadline and provides acceptable 
documentaƟon, then the county conƟnues its usual review 
of the applicaƟon. However, if the voter fails to respond to 
the noƟce or the noƟce is returned as undeliverable as de-
ﬁned by state law, then the voter’s registraƟon status is 
moved to cancelled, if the voter is currently registered, OR 
their registraƟon applicaƟon is rejected, if a new registrant, 
aŌer more than 30-days has lapsed from sending the VRG-
26. 
 
FuncƟonality for these new workﬂows was released on July 
1, 2025, with training to be provided by Civix on July 2, 3, and 
9, 2025, on these new tools and reporƟng features. CounƟes 
are strongly encouraged to aƩend. 
 
A voter whose registraƟon was cancelled or rejected by this 
process can appeal the decision by requesƟng a hearing, 
which the CEB must honor and determine if the voter’s regis-
traƟon should be reinstated. SVRS tools, including a new 
hearing noƟce (VRG-27) and scheduling module is expected 
in August. Updates to indianavoters.com will be made at that 
Ɵme to provide hearing details to the voter. 
QUESTIONS OF THE MONTH  
Q. Can we restrict the public’s ability to ﬁlm or record a 
CEB meeƟng? 
 
A. No. From the state’s Public Access Counselor’s Hand-
book:  
A person has the right under the ODL (Open Door Law) to 
be present at a public meeƟng, other than an execuƟve 
session, and to record the meeƟng by videotape, short-
hand, or any other method of recording, subject to reason-
able restricƟons as to equipment and use that may be im-
posed by the governing body. Rules and regulaƟons prohib-
iƟng the use of cameras, tape recorders or other recog-
nized means of recording a meeƟng are void. 
 
Q. Are we required to live stream (or record and post the 
video online) CEB meeƟngs on or aŌer July 1, 2025? 
A. Generally speaking, no. However, if your CEB is holding 
its meeƟng in a room with equipment available to 
livestream or record, then your CEB is required to do so. In 
the end, it depends on the room your board books to hold 
its meeƟng.  
NEW FORMS & COUNTY UPDATES 
A number of legislaƟve changes require updates to exisƟng 
forms and even a few completely new forms for 2025. A 
forms order is expected to be released on or around July 1, 
2025, with more detailed informaƟon about the changes, 
along with an updated Forms Master List. 
 
A few notable changes to exisƟng forms include: 
 CFA-2 (Statement of OrganizaƟon for PACs) 
 CFA-4 (Report of Receipts & Expenditures) 
 CEB-3 (Chair’s Appointment to Fill Elected Oﬃce Vacancy) 
 CEB-5 (DeclaraƟon of Candidacy to Fill Elected Oﬃce Vacancy) 
 IEC-9 & IEC-10 (Public Test CerƟﬁcaƟon Forms) 
 
Several candidate forms, including the peƟƟons of nomina-
Ɵon for independent, minor party, and school board candi-
dates, will be part of this release and then updated online 
under the Candidate’s InformaƟon and ElecƟon Administra-
tor’s portal. 
 
To help facilitate changes on the county contact informaƟon 
found on the ABS-Mail and VRG-7 forms, IED is asking for 
your help. A survey has been sent to counƟes to conﬁrm if 
the contact informaƟon on the back of these forms is accu-
rate or not. Changes can then be shared through this survey 
so that IED can make the necessary updates. 
 
A reminder that forms can be found online on forms.in.gov or 
in.gov/sos/elecƟons OR on the SVRS County Portal. Using the 
portal allows you to download all forms directly from the fold-
er, including the Word and .pdf versions. Lastly, please review

grandfathered. Any outdated version must be rejected, so

Election Division Dispatch 
 Brad King & Angie Nussmeyer, Co-Directors | August 2025 
NEWS & UPDATES 
 
New Round of 2026 ElecƟon Forms 
The IED co-directors released another round of forms used in 
the 2026 elecƟon cycle in late July with IED Order 2025-102. 
Most are candidate forms, which should complete the candi-
date forms list for the 2026 cycle aŌer IED Order 2025-102. A 
few forms sƟll need to be updated, including the state VR 
forms to reﬂect a minor legislaƟve change and the ABS-Mail 
forms to eliminate confusion with the current form used in 
any November special elecƟon. Absentee forms for the 2026 
primary elecƟon cannot be received unƟl December 1, 2025, 
so expect the revised forms to be available aŌer the Novem-
ber elecƟon date. Current forms are available under the 
“ElecƟon Administrator’s Portal” on in.gov/sos/elecƟons and 
on the legacy SharePoint site available to counƟes unƟl the 
new site is made available. 
 
 
RedistricƟng Amnesty Reminder 
CiƟes and towns that failed to redistrict or cerƟfy elecƟon dis-
tricts following the 2020 decennial census have unƟl October 
31, 2025 to complete their work and ﬁle the ordinance and 
map with the county clerk. As a reminder, any redistricƟng 
authority who failed to ﬁle a redistricƟng ordinance by June 
30, 2025 cannot receive a salary. Further, the redistricƟng 
authority must use precinct boundary lines that are already 
established. It may be necessary to make changes to precinct 
lines as a result of “split” elecƟon districts, if the County Com-
missioners wish to do so. But a few proposals received by 
counƟes have contained precincts that do not currently exist, 
which creates an administraƟve issue for county elecƟon 
boards. 
 
 
Statewide VLM Project Updates 
Hoosiers receiving a voter response card, the second card sent 
to a voter when the ﬁrst card was returned to the state as 
undeliverable, have unƟl August 29, 2025, for IED to receive 
the card for processing. CounƟes should expect to see a sig-
niﬁcant upƟck in hopper loads on or aŌer Labor Day for pro-
cessing. Keep in mind that counƟes need to process out the 
VLM hoppers as quickly as possible so that any voter response 
cards received aŌer August 29, 2025, can be shared with 
counƟes for updaƟng. More details will be shared in the com-
ing weeks. 
 
A reminder that if the USPS mistakenly sends any card 1s or 
card 2s to your oﬃce to please mail them to the PO Box 
found on the postcard, NOT the IED oﬃce. Mailing the VLM 
cards to the post oﬃce box will ensure the records are pro-
cessed correctly. It would also help to email elec-
Ɵons@iec.in.gov and let the oﬃce know if your county is mis-
takenly receiving these cards directly. We can work with our 
USPS contacts to make adjustments, where necessary.

IN FOCUS: Campaign Finance Enforcement Matters 
Several counƟes have reached out in re-
cent weeks about how to enforce the re-
quirement for elected oﬃcials to open 
and maintain a candidate’s commiƩee 
(CFA-1) beginning July 1, 2025 with the 
recent change in state law. 
 
Enforcement procedures for failing to 
Ɵmely open a commiƩee are the same as 
the procedures for failing to Ɵmely ﬁle a 
CFA-4 or CFA-11 report.  More detailed 
informaƟon can be found in the 2024 
Campaign Finance Manual, which includes 
an enforcement toolkit in the appendix. 
 
If a commiƩee ﬁles their CFA-1 (or CFA-2 
for PACs or CFA-3 for party commiƩees) 
aŌer the noon deadline, then the com-
miƩee accrues a $50 for each calendar 
day or part of a day ﬁne, up to $1000. 
Should a candidate (or in this case, an 
elected oﬃcial) fail to open their com-
miƩee aŌer the “$1000 ﬁne clock” has run 
out, then the CEB is responsible for open-
ing the commiƩee. 
 
AddiƟonally, the CEB is responsible, not 
later than 30-days aŌer the deadline to 
ﬁle the statement of organizaƟon or cam-
paign ﬁnance reports, to send a delin-
quency leƩer to each commiƩee alerƟng 
them of their late ﬁling or failure to ﬁle. 
See form 1 in the appendix of the 2024 
Indiana Campaign Finance Manual for a 
sample noƟce. 
 
Before determining if a CFA statement or 
report is delinquent and commiƩee is sub-
ject to a civil penalty, the county elecƟon 
board must hold a hearing. 
 
The commiƩee alleged to have to not 
have ﬁled a Ɵmely CFA statement or re-
port or ﬁled it late must be sent a noƟce 
of hearing staƟng the Ɵme, place, and 
purpose of the hearing. (See Form 3 in the 
appendix of Indiana Campaign Finance 
Manual.) 
 
The county elecƟon board will then con-
duct the hearing, giving representaƟves of 
the commiƩee the opportunity to speak 
and request a waiver or reducƟon of their 
ﬁne. Each person who tesƟﬁes before the 
board at the hearing should be sworn in. 
(See Form 4 in the appendix of the Indiana 
Campaign Finance Manual for a copy of 
the oath.) 
 
Following the hearing the county elecƟon 
board can proceed to discuss the alleged 
violaƟon, determine if a violaƟon did oc-
cur, and issue the appropriate civil penalty 
under law. This can be done at the same 
board meeƟng as the hearing or at a fu-
ture meeƟng.  
  
The county elecƟon board, by unanimous 
vote of the enƟre board, may vote to 
waive or reduce the imposed civil penalty 
under IC 3-9-4-19. 
 
However, if the county elecƟon board 
majority votes that a commiƩee did vio-
late state campaign ﬁnance law and did 
not ﬁle a Ɵmely report, the board must 
complete and sign a Finding or Facts and 
Final Order to impose the appropriate civil 
penalty. (See Form 5 in the appendix of 
the Indiana Campaign Finance Manual.) 
InformaƟon in this newsleƩer is provided by the Indiana ElecƟon Division as a courtesy to county elecƟon administrators. If a person is unclear concerning elecƟon law provisions,  
the ElecƟon Division can serve as an interpreƟve source. However, where important legal rights are concerned, you must consult with your own aƩorney to be fully and properly advised. 
VR CORNER 
115+ Year Olds 
At least once a year, counƟes must review a list containing 
registered voters that the system has calculated have a 
date of birth of 115-years-old or older. The SVRS reports 
library contains a report of those individuals, and counƟes 
should use this informaƟon to perform their own list 
maintenance work. This can include ﬁnding an obituary 
published in the newspaper or on a licensed funeral home 
website or a noƟce of estate administraƟon or any other 
legally permissible informaƟon to conﬁrm the person’s 
death. (The 2024 VR Handbook provides more details.) If 
counƟes idenƟfy such a valid piece of informaƟon, they 
may move the voter’s registraƟon status to “cancelled.” 
 
Complete VLM Tasks Within 48-Hours 
Beginning July 1, 2025, state law now requires counƟes to 
perform voter list maintenance work not later than 48-
hours aŌer receiving informaƟon that triggers a list 
maintenance requirement. AddiƟonally, the list of infor-
maƟon that can be used to send a statewide address mail-
ing conﬁrmaƟon (SAMC) noƟce has expanded to include 
the county receiving informaƟon a voter has moved to 
another state and when a voter’s absentee ballot is return 
as undeliverable due to unknown or insuﬃcient address. 
(IC 3-7-38.2-2) IED’s 2025 LegislaƟve Summary (found on 
in.gov/sos/elecƟons) has more informaƟon. 
QUESTIONS OF THE MONTH  
Q. We’re having a special elecƟon in November. Are the pro-
cedures any diﬀerent than a typical elecƟon? 
 
A. For the most part, everything operates in the special elec-
Ɵon the same as any other elecƟon. The one excepƟon is that 
the CEB can adopt a unanimous resoluƟon to reduce the num-
ber of early voƟng days and hours (see IC 3-11-10-26.5). Oth-
erwise, absentee ballots must be sent to those with an ap-
proved applicaƟon not later than 45-days before the elecƟon 
(or 5-days aŌer receiving the absentee ballots, whichever is 
sooner) and ElecƟon Day voƟng locaƟons are open from 6AM 
to 6PM. The 2024 ElecƟon Administrator’s Manual remains a 
good resource to walk counƟes through the ﬁner points—and 
IED is happy to help with any quesƟons. 
 
Q. How do we handle a death of an oﬃceholder? 
A Before a poliƟcal party can ﬁll an elected oﬃce vacancy for 
a local oﬃce under IC 3-13-11, the county clerk must receive 
informaƟon about the local elected oﬃcial’s death and be 
“reasonably saƟsﬁed” the informaƟon is true. If so, within 72-
hours of receiving the informaƟon, the clerk must noƟfy the 
county party chair, in wriƟng, about the oﬃceholder’s death. 
Only then can the party begin the process to ﬁll the elected 
oﬃce vacancy. More informaƟon is in the 2024 ElecƟon Ad-
ministrator’s Manual and the relevant statutes can be found 
in IC 5-8-6, generally, including which oﬃcial (governor, SOS, 
clerk) receives noƟce of an oﬃceholder’s death.

IN FOCUS: YARD SIGNS 
Though it seems a liƩle early to be talking about yard signs, be-
lieve it or not, the topic has come up a few Ɵmes this summer as 
candidates for elected oﬃce are starƟng to put them out for the 
2026 elecƟon cycle. 
 
Local ordinances control the Ɵming of when yard signs can be 
planted, if adopted. Otherwise, state law places no restricƟon on 
the yard sign season “starts”. So it is possible for candidates to 
put yard signs out for next year, now.  
 
But, if there is a local ordinance restricƟng the Ɵme when signs 
can be placed, then local rules must be followed. However, state 
law “suspends” any local ordinance for signs up to 32 square 
feet to be placed no earlier than 60 days before the elecƟon and 
not later than 5 days aŌerward. Otherwise, poliƟcal yard signs 
can be out any Ɵme. (IC 36-1-3-1) 
 
For neighborhoods with a Homeowner’s AssociaƟon, the HOA 
can restrict the placement of yard signs to the last 30 days be-
fore the elecƟon through 5 days aŌerward. Homeowners should 
consult the rules of the HOA to determine any restricƟon on po-
liƟcal yard signs. (IC 32-21-13-4) 
 
Yard signs cannot be placed in the public right-of-way. Com-
plaints should be directed to the street department, not the CEB, 
for removal. AddiƟonally, no person has the right to remove a 
sign from a person’s yard, which can be considered conversion 
and subject to a criminal invesƟgaƟon. 
 
The CEB does enforce the disclaimer rule on yard signs, even 
homemade ones. If the sign is missing the “Paid for by” language 
in at least 7 point font in a color that contrasts from the back-
ground, then a wriƩen complaint may be ﬁled. The CEB can then 
hold a hearing to invite both parƟes to present facts and evi-
dence for the body to determine if an elecƟon law violaƟon oc-
curred.  
 
PACs supporƟng a public quesƟon, however, do not need to 
place any “paid for by” disclaimer on yard signs, if it is expressing 
the support or defeat of the public quesƟon only. 
InformaƟon in this newsleƩer is provided by the Indiana ElecƟon Division as a courtesy to county elecƟon administrators. If a person is unclear concerning elecƟon law provisions,  
the ElecƟon Division can serve as an interpreƟve source. However, where important legal rights are concerned, you must consult with your own aƩorney to be fully and properly advised. 
VR CORNER 
Non-ResidenƟal Address Review 
Not later than August 1 of each year, state law requires the county voter registraƟon oﬃcial to idenƟfy potenƟal nonresidenƟal 
addresses submiƩed on voter registraƟon applicaƟons and voter registraƟons in the statewide voter registraƟon system that 
list a potenƟal non-residenƟal address. (IC 3-7-33-5.7(c)) 
 
If the county VR oﬃcial comes across such an address and there are no notes or other ﬁndings as researched by the county, 
then the county VR oﬃcial must determine if it is possible for the person to reside at the address or if it is a non-tradiƟonal ad-
dress. Any ﬁndings should be recorded in SVRS for the county’s next review. 
 
Should the county VR oﬃcial conﬁrm the registraƟon address appears to be at a non-residenƟal locaƟon, then a SAMC must be 
sent to the voter under IC 3-7-38.2-7.4. 
QUESTIONS OF THE MONTH  
Q. The CAN-16 form no longer includes D/R can-
didates for the 2026 elecƟon cycle. Was there a 
change in state law? 
 
A. Yes. State law changed in 2024 and now re-
quires that “small” towns (that is, those with a 
populaƟon of less than 3500) that moved their 
town (municipal) elecƟon to the even-numbered 
years (2026, 2028, and so on) must nominate their 
D/R candidates at the primary elecƟon (or ﬁll the 
ballot vacancy in the tradiƟonal way aŌer the May 
elecƟon). (IC 3-8-5-2.5) This means D/R candidates 
for the “small town” oﬃces will use the CAN-2/
CAN-12 forms in 2026 and ﬁle within the Jan. 7 to 
noon, Feb. 6, 2026 window. Libertarian Party can-
didates will use the CAN-16/CAN-12 forms and 
hold their convenƟon and ﬁle paperwork, if neces-
sary, by noon, Aug. 28, 2026. Independent or oth-
er minor party candidates will use the CAN-21 pe-
ƟƟon (and CAN-20/CAN-12) to appear on the No-
vember ballot, geƫng at least enough signatures 
of registered voters in their elecƟon district to 
total at least 2% of the total vote cast for SOS in 
2022 in the precincts making up their elecƟon dis-
trict. Write-in candidates for “small town” oﬃces 
will use the CAN-3/CAN-12 forms, though their 
name does not appear on the Nov. ballot.  
 
Q. Does an individual who was recently selected 
to ﬁll an oﬃce vacancy (that is, when a currently 
elected oﬃcial dies or resigns from oﬃce, for 
example) need to open a campaign ﬁnance com-
miƩee under the new law? 
A. Yes, if the oﬃce pays $5000 or more in a calen-
dar year and the individual does not already have 
an open campaign ﬁnance commiƩee, then it is 
necessary for the individual to ﬁle a CFA-1. Their 
statement of organizaƟon must be ﬁled not later 
than noon, ten days aŌer a copy of their oath of 
oﬃce is ﬁled.

IN FOCUS: Voting System Renewals 
On October 1, 2025, the four year cerƟﬁcaƟon for voƟng sys-
tems approved by the Indiana ElecƟon Commission will expire 
and those systems become “legacy” unƟl the cerƟﬁcaƟons are 
renewed. So what does this mean for county elecƟon oﬃcials? 
 
Under Indiana law, a “legacy” voƟng system may sƟll be used in 
federal, state, and local elecƟons. However, the vendor may no 
longer market, sell, or lease a “legacy” system in Indiana and 
cannot modify its hardware, soŌware, or ﬁrmware. CounƟes are 
authorized under state law to conƟnue using the “legacy” sys-
tem, being mindful that their vendor is limited on the “sales” 
side of their relaƟonship with local oﬃcials. 
 
The Commission approved an amended protocol to the 2021 
voƟng system standards at its September meeƟng. Recent 
changes to state law requiring the addiƟon of a “no public ques-
Ɵon” style ballot in the November elecƟon for voters using a fail 
safe when certain public quesƟons are on the ballot and adding 
party aﬃliaƟon to school board oﬃces were added to the tesƟng 
protocols for voƟng system renewals for the next four-year peri-
od. 
 
Several vendors have applied for renewal or recerƟﬁcaƟon. IED 
will send leƩers to those counƟes informing them of their appli-
caƟon. VSTOP will review their documentaƟon and perform a 
ﬁeld test to conﬁrm the systems meet the requirements of state 
law under the amended 2021 protocols. 
 
IEC will meet later this fall to hear reports and recommendaƟons 
from VSTOP on the renewals. If approved, the voƟng systems 
will become cerƟﬁed in Indiana for the next four years through 
October 1, 2029. This means the vendor will be able to market, 
sell, or lease their equipment in Indiana but also can improve the 
voƟng system through modiﬁcaƟons that are approved by IEC. 
 
The renewal process cannot consider “new” features on a sys-
tem. VoƟng system vendors can seek modiﬁcaƟons whether mi-
nor (or “de minimis”) or not aŌer their renewal request is ap-
proved by the Commission. This is a separate applicaƟon process 
and those systems will be reviewed using an updated 2025 
tesƟng protocol that will be approved at a future Commission 
meeƟng. 
 
The 2025 tesƟng protocol uses the amended 2021 protocol as its 
foundaƟon, but also includes the new ballot retracƟon feature 
that opƟcal scan voƟng systems may use once approved by the 
Commission.  
 
While the MicroVote DRE (or any other DRE approved for use in 
the future) is required to have ballot retracƟon under state law, 
opƟcal scan systems do not. RetracƟon is an opƟonal feature for 
opScan systems, as absentee ballots can remain sealed in an en-
velope to reject without the need for scanning. This is not possi-
ble on a DRE system, as those votes are stored electronically in 
the system itself. (The VVPAT tape is NOT a ballot.) 
InformaƟon in this newsleƩer is provided by the Indiana ElecƟon Division as a courtesy to county elecƟon administrators. If a person is unclear concerning elecƟon law provisions,  
the ElecƟon Division can serve as an interpreƟve source. However, where important legal rights are concerned, you must consult with your own aƩorney to be fully and properly advised. 
VR CORNER 
VR & Nursing Home Residents 
A few counƟes have reached out to ask where a per-
son living in a nursing home or other care facility 
should be registered to vote - at their home address 
or the facility. The answer boils down to the voter’s 
intent. Residency is incredibly fact sensiƟve. IC 3-5-5, 
generally, states the residency standards for register-
ing to vote or being a candidate or elected oﬃcial. 
This can be helpful to the voter to make the best deci-
sion for their circumstances.  
 
For example, if the voter intends to return to their 
home, (whether or not such a return is likely) then 
they may conƟnue to be registered at their home 
address. If they don’t wish to remain registered at a 
former address, then the voter may choose to be reg-
istered at the care facility.  
QUESTIONS OF THE MONTH  
Q. Can a PAC disband their commiƩee at any Ɵme? 
Or are they bound by the same rule as a candidate’s 
commiƩee? 
 
A. A poliƟcal acƟon commiƩee, or PAC, is not part of 
the state’s deﬁniƟon of “candidate”. For this reason, 
a PAC can disband at any Ɵme, assuming there is a $0 
cash on hand, no debts owed to/by the commiƩee, 
and the “ﬁnal/disbands” box is checked.  
 
Q. Does the new law permiƫng a school board can-
didate to aﬃliate with a poliƟcal party mean that 
the oﬃce is going to be on the May primary ballot? 
A. No. School board elecƟons are sƟll held at the No-
vember elecƟon. There is no primary elecƟon nomi-
naƟng process; however, the D and R candidates do 
have to meet the “vote history” requirement or 
aƩach a chair’s cerƟﬁcaƟon to their peƟƟon of nomi-
naƟon and consent form. AddiƟonally, the parƟes are 
not limited to ﬁelding candidates that equal the num-
ber of seats to be voted upon. For example, if the 
school board seat is a “vote for 1” elecƟon, the D or R 
party can have an inﬁnite number of candidates and 
are not bound to only one. Or, if it’s a seat that you 
select “not more than 3”, the party is not bound by 
this number and can ﬁeld an inﬁnite number of can-
didates. The same is true for the Libertarian or other 
minor party candidates and Independents. 
 
Q. What about straight party voƟng - will that apply 
to school board races now? 
A. No. Straight party voƟng will NOT apply to school 
board races, even though a candidate may have a 
party aﬃliaƟon associated with them.

IN FOCUS: Filing Petitions for Ballot Access in 2026 
Believe it or not it’s Ɵme to start preparing for 
the next elecƟon cycle, if you haven’t already. 
Unlike 2024, there are no statewide D/R candi-
dates on the ballot in the primary elecƟon. This 
means counƟes will not have peƟƟons to pro-
cess on a compressed Ɵme frame ahead of the 
May elecƟon.  
 
However, Independent and minor party candi-
dates may begin ﬁling peƟƟons to appear on 
the November ballot as early as January 7, 
2026.  
 
To have their name printed on the ballot, these 
candidates must collect peƟƟon signatures of 
registered voters within their elecƟon district 
that total at least 2% of the total votes cast for 
all candidates running in the 2022 SOS race.  
 
Countywide totals are  compiled in the back of 
the 2026 Candidate Guide. If the elecƟon dis-
trict is smaller than the county,  then the clerk 
will need to pull the 2022 SOS precinct level 
results to add up all votes cast among all SOS 
candidates in the precinct making up the elec-
Ɵon district and then mulƟply that number by 
2%.  
 
If the math results in a decimal point, then you 
round down. For example, the calculated  
number is 10.76. In this case, the candidate 
must have at least 10 cerƟﬁed signatures of 
registered voters within their elecƟon district 
to have their name printed on the ballot. 
 
Minor party or independent candidates  
running for federal, statewide, or state  
legislaƟve oﬃce should contact IED at  
elecƟons@iec.in.gov to have the minimum 
number of cerƟﬁed signatures needed to be on 
the ballot. 
 
Federal, state, state legislaƟve, and candidates 
for judge or prosecuƟng aƩorney who wish to 
run as an Independent or other minor party 
use the CAN-19 form. For all other local oﬃces, 
the CAN-21 form is used.  
 
(Note: an independent or minor party candi-
date can ﬁle a CAN-3 to be a write-in, but their 
name is NOT printed on the ballot.) 
 
School Board Candidates 
Most school board candidates gain access to 
the November ballot by collecƟng signatures of 
10 registered voters in their elecƟon district. In 
most instances, the elecƟon district is the en-
Ɵre school corporaƟon. In limited cases, there 
are smaller elecƟon districts within the bound-
aries of the school corporaƟon. The school plan 
or the school corporaƟon’s aƩorney would be 
the best resource if a candidate is unsure 
about how the districts are structured.  
 
Remember, the law changed in 2025 and 
school board candidates may aﬃliate with the 
DemocraƟc, Republican, Libertarian parƟes or 
run as an Independent or other minor party 
candidate or leave the party aﬃliaƟon box 
blank. However, D/R school board candidates 
do NOT run in the May primary and straight 
party voƟng will NOT apply to these oﬃces. 
 
Libertarian Candidates 
Reminder: ballot access rules for Libertarian 
candidates do not require peƟƟons. Instead, 
candidates are nominated at convenƟon or 
through ballot vacancy procedures.

paperwork

Party candidates to ﬁle peƟƟon for county

the ElecƟon Division can serve as an interpreƟve source. However, where important legal rights are concerned, you must consult with your own aƩorney to be fully and properly advised. 
VR CORNER 
PeƟƟon Processing Reminders 
Here are a few reminders about peƟƟon processing, which 
will be covered in more detail at the December conference: 
 
1/ The person signing a peƟƟon must be registered to vote 
at the address noted on the peƟƟon at the Ɵme the peƟƟon 
is processed. If Sally signs the peƟƟon in Nov. 2025 at an 
address on Main Street and she updates her registraƟon in 
Dec. 2025 to First Avenue, then her entry on the peƟƟon 
will not be counted as she is no longer registered at the 
Main Street address when the county reviews the peƟƟon 
in Jan. 2026. 
 
2/ PeƟƟon carriers can be anyone; there is no legal require-
ment that they be registered voters in Indiana, for example. 
However, the carrier MUST complete the aﬃdavit found on 
the peƟƟon of nominaƟon form. No informaƟon can be 
missing. If it is, then the county must try to contact the 
peƟƟon carrier and cannot process the peƟƟon unƟl that 
aﬃdavit is perfected. If the ﬁling deadline passes and the 
aﬃdavit remains incomplete, then the peƟƟon is rejected. 
 
3/ PeƟƟon processing may be impacted if Congressional 
lines are redrawn and adopted during special session, spe-
ciﬁcally for those Independent or minor party candidates 
running for one of the seats. Stay tuned for more info! 
QUESTION OF THE MONTH  
Q. Can the county clerk run for elected oﬃce in 2026, either to be re-
elected as clerk or to another oﬃce, and manage elecƟons for the 
county? 
A. Yes, the clerk can run for oﬃce and conƟnue to manage local elec-
Ɵons. State law does not require a county clerk to set aside their re-
sponsibiliƟes to manage the county’s elecƟons under Title 3, even if 
their name appears on the ballot for elected oﬃce.  
 
However, state law does require the county to use the generic seal on 
its absentee and provisional ballots, if the clerk is running for elected 
oﬃce. The generic seal can be found on the SVRS County Portal under 
“IED PosƟngs” in your county-speciﬁc folder. 
 
Further, the clerk’s signature cannot appear on the absentee or provi-
sional ballots, again, if the clerk is running for elected oﬃce. No signa-
ture will appear on the ballot. 
 
Anecdotally, our oﬃce hears from some clerks who choose to step back 
from some elecƟon duƟes when on the ballot. There are ways to dele-
gate some “clerk” responsibiliƟes to the CEB or to staﬀ using procedures 
found in IC 3-6-5, generally. Or, the clerk could appoint a proxy to act on 
their behalf during CEB meeƟngs, for example. 
 
Lastly, party oﬃces—delegate and precinct commi Ʃeeman—are NOT 
elected oﬃces. The clerk can run for these oﬃces, and the county would 
use the “regular” county seal and place the clerk’s signature on the ab-
sentee and provisional ballots.

IN FOCUS:  
Clerk’s Oﬃce Closure on ElecƟon Day 
During this last session, legislators passed a 
new law that requires the clerk’s oﬃce to be 
closed on ElecƟon Day but for their duƟes to 
manage the elecƟon along with their board 
members. (IC 3-5-4-14) 
 
This applies only to the May and Nov. elecƟons  
held in even-numbered years, meaning it does 
not apply to the municipal or special elecƟon 
years. 
 
SubsecƟon (b) of the statute makes it clear that 
the clerk is not required to perform any “clerk” 
responsibiliƟes but for elecƟon administraƟon. 
This would extend to any clerk oﬃce staﬀ that 
supports elecƟon work. 
 
However, other clerk staﬀ who focus on other 
work with the courts, for example, would not 
be required to be at work on the primary and 
general elecƟon day. Of course, clerk staﬀ can 
be a poll worker, assist staﬀ, etc. but they 
would not need to focus on other duƟes of the 
clerk’s oﬃce that day.  
 
 County commissioners have general authority 
over county oﬃces and property, so these 
oﬃcials would determine if the enƟre court-
house was closed, rather than just an individu-
al oﬃce. But, even if the courthouse is closed 
for elecƟon day, the clerk’s oﬃce or wherever 
the CEB is meeƟng needs to be accessible to 
the public. 
 
“Small” Town ElecƟons in 2026 
Several counƟes have asked when the CAN-16 
for DemocraƟc and Republican candidates for 
2026 is being released. In short—it’s not. 
 
State law changed in 2024 to require all “small” 
towns who moved some or all of their elec-
Ɵons to the even-numbered year to require D/
R candidates to ﬁle for the May primary elec-
Ɵon, even if they small town did not pass an 
ordinance making that change. 
 
This means all D/R candidates running for 
“small” town oﬃce will ﬁle the CAN-2/CAN-12 
from Jan. 7 to noon, Feb. 6, 2026, like other D/
R candidates running for federal, state, or oth-
er local oﬃces. The D/R parƟes can ﬁll ballot 
vacancies on or aŌer May 8, 2026, for “small” 
town oﬃces, the same as other oﬃces. 
 
Independent and minor party candidates run-
ning for a “small” town oﬃce conƟnue to sync 
up with the same ﬁling deadlines as other can-
didates. This means a CAN-3 to be a write-in 
candidate for “small town” oﬃce and CAN-12 
must be ﬁled by noon, July 6, 2026 (the July 3 
deadline rolls to July 6 due to a state holiday). 
 
If an independent or minor party candidate for 
small town oﬃce wants their name printed on 
the ballot, then CAN-21 peƟƟons must be ﬁled 
with the county VR oﬃce by noon, June 30, 
2026, with the candidate consent due by noon, 
July 15, 2026. 
 
However, Libertarian candidates achieve ballot 
access through convenƟon, generally speaking. 
This means the CAN-16 will be used by Liber-
tarian candidates for “small town” oﬃce in 
2026, with a ﬁling period of Jan. 7 to noon, Aug 
1, 2026. A “small” town convenƟon would only 
be held to nominate a Libertarian candidate for 
the Nov. ballot if more than one Libertarian 
candidate ﬁled for a parƟcular “small” town 
oﬃce. 
 
“Small” towns holding some or all of their elec-
Ɵons in 2027 will revert back to the town con-
venƟon model for D/R/L candidates unless the 
town council passed an ordinance requiring a 
primary for D/R parƟes to nominate their can-
didates for the Nov. 2027 elecƟon.

the ElecƟon Division can serve as an interpreƟve source. However, where important legal rights are concerned, you must consult with your own aƩorney to be fully and properly advised. 
VR CORNER 
Prepping for 2026 
Last month, Civix held two training sessions to help coun-
Ɵes get ready for the 2026 elecƟon cycle. These sessions 
focused on voter address points and assignments along 
with  voter excepƟons. If you were not able to aƩend 
these trainings, you can access materials and recordings 
on the County Portal. 
 
County VR oﬃcials will also want to keep up with VLM 
acƟviƟes, including reviewing SVRS reports such as the 
one idenƟfying voters who are more than 115 years old or 
lack a birth date on their record. At least once a year 
counƟes must review this informaƟon and use the BMV 
link in SVRS to drawn down a birth date, if available, to 
correct the registraƟon. 
 
Making sure your voters are properly assigned to the right 
precinct and elecƟon district is key to a relaƟvely smooth 
elecƟon. CounƟes are encouraged to review their precinct 
key to ensure each precinct has the correct elecƟon dis-
tricts assigned to it. If there is a correcƟon to be made, 
submiƫng a County AuthorizaƟon Form (CAF) through 
SVRS along with a marked up precinct key is how updates 
can be made, followed by Batch RedistricƟng to refresh 
exisƟng voter records. 
 
Of course, counƟes need to review oﬃce assignments for 
accuracy in SVRS. You may need to reference the 2022 
elecƟon cycle to ensure every oﬃce on the ballot is pre-
sent with two excepƟons. US Senate is not on the ballot in 
2026 in Indiana and judges elected in 2022 will not be the 
same ones on the ballot in 2026, since they serve six year 
terms. Not only is the oﬃce set-up important for candi-
date ﬁling, but also results reporƟng. 
QUESTIONS OF THE MONTH  
Q. Must counƟes provide an accessible voƟng system at travel board  
appointments? 
A. While encouraged, the CEB determines whether to bring a direct record 
electronic voƟng system (DRE) or ballot marking device (BMD) to travel 
board appointments through a resoluƟon. IC 3-11-10-26.2 permits the CEB 
to unanimously agree to use these voƟng systems for travel board purposes. 
Remember, if a county uses a BMD for travel board, the ABS-7 envelope 
must be used to store the absentee ballot. The travel board team must wit-
ness the voter’s signature on the security envelope or aƩest the voter was 
not able to  sign their name or make a mark.  
 
The travel board members then sign and print their name on their porƟon of 
the aﬃdavit. Otherwise, a voter voƟng by travel board would use a hand-
marked paper ballot card, where the voter can receive assistance from the 
bi-parƟsan travel board team. 
 
Q. Is the CEB required to accept public comment at its meeƟngs? 
A. Not necessarily, with some excepƟons. State law changed in 2024 to per-
mit a local governing body, like the CEB, to designate a period for public 
comment before ﬁnal acƟon is taken. If the CEB adopts a rule or policy on 
public comment or removing aƩendees disrupƟng a meeƟng, then it must 
be announced before taking public comment at the meeƟng or by posƟng 
the rules at the entrance of the meeƟng. (IC 5-14-1.5-3.3) Hearings are an-
other maƩer, where the parƟes involved would be permiƩed to speak and 
provide facts to the CEB to consider when making decisions on candidate 
challenges or campaign ﬁnance issues, for example. 
 
Q. Is there a state form for the D or R chair to cerƟfy that a candidate is a 
member of their poliƟcal party, if the candidate does not have the proper 
voƟng history to run in the May primary elecƟon? 
A. No. There is no oﬃcial state form. However, IED has a sample cerƟﬁcaƟon 
document available for county use. Otherwise, the county chair may use 
party leƩerhead, for example, to sign oﬀ of the candidate.

Election Division Dispatch 
 Brad King & Angie Nussmeyer, Co-Directors | January 2026 
NEWS & UPDATES 
Don’t Forget the CAN-5! 
When a candidate files to run for office, counties must
 hand-deliver or mail the CAN-5 (Candidacy Filing Confirmation 
for 2026) not later than one day after receiving the candidate’s 
filing. You can use the form found on the INSVRS County Portal 
or use SVRS to generate the document after creating the 
candidate’s profile in the system. Questions? Contact the Help 
Desk or visit the online training portal for a step-by-step guide. 
2025 Annual Report 
ALL open candidate and political action committees are 
required to file a 2025 Annual Report not later than noon, Jan. 
21, 2026. Regular party committees are the exception to this 
deadline; these committees have until noon, March 2, 2026, to 
file the annual report.  
As a reminder, party committees file with IED or the CEB, 
depending on where the CFA-3 statement of organization is 
filed; party committees are not required to file in both places. If 
you are unsure if a party committee files with the CEB or IED 
visit campaignfinance.in.gov and do a committee search.  
If the party committee files with IED, their name will appear 
along with the term “active.” If a party committee closed with the 
state, the name will still appear but the term “disbanded” will be 
noted on the record. 
Administrative Disbanding of Committees 
Not later than January 30, 2026, the CEB must review its cam-
paign finance records to determine if a committee is subject to 
the administrative dissolution procedure. 
To move forward with dissolution, the committee must have not 
filed any CFA-4 or CFA-11 during the previous three calendar 
years AND the cash on hand on their last filed report must be 
$1,000 or less. 
If both conditions are met, then the CEB may move forward with 
the process found in IC 3-9-1-12, including providing notice by 
certified mail to the treasurer and making additional findings by 
the CEB.  
Dissolution of a committee does not resolve any past fines. The 
committee members can be held personally liable for any fine 
assessed against the committee.

their 2025 annual report as late as noon, March 2, 2026)

to the administrative dissolution procedure (IC 3-9-1-12) 
Feb. 2, 2026: Deadline for county sheriff and local health officer to pro-
vide quarterly reports related to imprisonment following conviction or 
death, respectively

begins on Feb. 5, 2026

SAMC or move a voter’s status to inactive now through  
election day, May 5, 2026

ry

IN FOCUS: CANDIDATE FILING REMINDERS  
General Tips 
- Candidate filings must be original  docu-
ments with a “wet” signature. Candidate fil-
ings cannot be filed by email or fax! If ailed, 
the CEB must receive the candidate forms 
by noon, Feb. 6, 2026. The form must be 
rejected if received after the deadline, even if 
the envelope is postmarked on or before the 
deadline. 
- Clerks and their deputies are considered 
notaries under state law and must provide 
this service free of charge to candidates for 
their candidate filings. (IC 33-42-14-1(f)) 
- Any person can file candidacy paperwork 
on behalf of a candidate. However, the can-
didate must have their forms notarized head 
of time. Notaries witness the person signing 
the document; therefore, it is not permissible 
for the form to be notarized after it is signed. 
- Do not allow a person to alter their filing 
once it is notarized and file stamped. If an 
error is discovered on the filing and the filing 
deadline has not yet passed, the candidate 
can submit a second form to amend their 
first filing. We recommend adding “amended” 
to the top of the form. 
- In 2026, the D Party has PC/delegates on 
the ballot in May. Any D who wants to run for 
BOTH offices must file two CAN-37 forms; 
one for PC and one for delegate. A reminder 
that party offices do NOT file a CAN-12 or 
need to open a campaign finance committee. 
Limits on Rejecting a Candidate Filing 
Clerks, their staff, or the election board are 
NOT the candidate police at the time the 
form is presented for filing but for the rea-
sons noted below. If you need more infor-
mation, The Election Administrator’s  
Manual covers this in more detail: 
1) Candidate running for state oﬃce 
(federal, statewide, state legislative, 
judge, prosecuting attorney) presents 
their candidate ﬁling incorrectly to county 
when they should file with IED/SOS, or 
when a candidate for local office or party 
office tries to file with IED/SOS instead of 
the CEB. (IC 3-5-4-1.2) 
2) Form ﬁled after the noon, prevailing 
local time of candidate ﬁling deadline. For 
2026, the period to file for the May prima-
ry is Jan. 7 through noon, Feb. 6, 2026. 
(IC 3-5-4-1.9) 
3) Filing made on a form NOT approved 
by the state. (IC 3-5-4-8) 
4) Declaration of candidacy is not accom-
panied by the required statement of eco-
nomic interest. (IC 3 -8-2-11; IC 3-8-9-6) 
5) Candidate form improperly filed by 
email or fax. (IC 3-5-4-1.7) 
However, if the forms are filed with the office 
and an error discovered, the filings cannot 
be rejected after the fact. A CAN-1 challenge 
must be filed by a party chair or voter within 
the election district.  
Candidate Challenges 
Questions about candidate qualifications are 
managed through the CAN-1 challenge pro-
cedures. For example, a candidate does not 
have the required vote history to run as a D/ 
R candidate in the primary election or is not 
a registered voter of the election 
district. The CEB must accept the candidate 
filing, unless there is a deficiency as noted 
above. Then, a CAN-1 can be filed not later 
than noon, Feb. 13, 2026. This prompts the 
CEB to hold a hearing after giving proper 
notice to the parties involved. Challenges 
must be resolved by noon, Feb. 26, 2026. 
Voting Systems & ePB Inventory Due Feb. 2, 2026! 
Each year county election boards must certify to SOS that the inventory the county enters 
and maintains in the VSTOP voting system and electronic poll books inventory database is 
accurate. This review must be completed not later than Jan. 31, 2026 and the deadline to 
file the IEC-22 to VSTOP@bsu.edu rolls to noon, Monday, Feb. 2, 2026. (IC 3-11-16-5) 
Ensuring an accurate inventory is important for election administration, especially the public 
test of voting systems. If you have questions about the VSTOP inventory database, please 
email VSTOP@bsu.edu. Their team can assist counties with logging into their 
system. 
Upcoming VLM Projects 
County voter registration officials will 
have access to at least two pieces of 
information from other county officials to 
assist with voter list maintenance at the 
end of January. 
At minimum, the county sheriff must file 
on a quarterly basis a list of each Indi-
ana resident who has been convicted of 
a crime and placed in a county correc-
tional facility during the previous quarter. 
The list for the period of Oct. to Dec. 
2025 is due to the county VR official not 
later than Feb. 2, 2026. The VRG-1 cov-
er sheet is to be attached to any list pro-
vided to the county from the sheriff’s 
office. 
Using the sheriff’s list, the county VR 
official is to move a person’s registration 
status to “cancelled” ONLY IF the per-
son is currently imprisoned following 
conviction of a crime. If the individual is 
no longer imprisoned by the time the list 
is received, then the person’s registra-
tion is not to be moved to “cancelled” 
status. (IC 3-7-46-6; IC 3-7-46-1) 
Notice of disposition must be mailed to 
the voter if their registration is cancelled 
due to imprisonment following convic-
tion. If a voter’s status is cancelled due 
to disenfranchisement, the person may 
re-register to vote even if they are on 
probation, parole, home detention, or 
enrolled in a community correction pro-
gram. 
Additionally, the local health department 
files a copy of death records with the 
county auditor and NOW with the county 
clerk pursuant to IC 16-37-3-9(d) on a 
quarterly basis. Filing directly with the 
county VR official is a relatively new 
requirement for the local health depart-
ment, so you may want to reach out to 
their office to make them aware of this 
change. Counties then use this list to 
move a registered voter’s status to 
“cancelled” as the individual is certified 
as deceased. (IC 3-7-45-2.1(d); IC 3-7-
45-1) 
Later this spring counties will be hearing 
from IED about a project using data from 
the U.S. Northern and Southern District 
Courts. Stay tuned!

POST-CONFERENCE FEEDBACK 
A reminder that the survey to share your feedback about the 2026 Election Administrators’ conference is available now through end of 
day, Jan. 9, 2026 (please email our office if you need the link re-upped in your inbox). We appreciate you taking a few minutes out of 
your day to help us improve for the next event! 
We have started to review your feedback. Several people shared their concerns about slide decks, breakout sessions, and the loca-
tion/timing. To specifically address those concerns, up until a few years ago, we did print out each slide deck to provide with the con-
ference materials. However, county feedback asked that the slide decks be formatted in color or black or white or three slides per 
page or just one slide per page. We were not going to be able to accommodate everyone’s request, so a decision was made to post 
them online and let counties decide how to print their decks (or not). We also acknowledge that having presentations available a week 
before the conference is ideal. This year the four of us responsible for those decks were supporting legislators during an unprecedent-
ed special session and responding to discovery requests in the three lawsuits the agency is involved at the same time as we were 
working on our materials that then go through bi-partisan review before they are shared with counties. We certainly do try our best to 
provide the information in advance; this year it was a little out of our hands with competing priorities. Lastly, we have no plans to print 
and bind the presentations ahead of conference. 
We have offered breakout sessions in the past. But, the overwhelming feedback was that counties preferred general sessions. The 
biggest concern conveyed was that the information discussed in breakout sessions, namely the question and answer period, would 
not be heard by everyone. The request was to keep everyone in the same space to hear everything to not miss out on information. 
Counties often ask for networking opportunities. If a county wants to organize one, please email our office. We can work with the hotel 
to secure space before or after each conference day to meet. Our time with you is limited, so the preference is to focus on sharing 
information with everyone at the same time. 
Lastly, the location—downtown Indianapolis. Feedback on hosting conferences downtown is always mixed. Some people love it; oth-
ers hate it. Our office is trying to find the location that offers the most “bang for your buck.” This last solicitation went to event spaces 
or hotels downtown but also outside of Marion County. Our conference hovers around 450 attendees, which is too large for most ho-
tels and too small for most event spaces, so some locations will simply not respond. The choice to be downtown this year was based 
on the most competitive bid; the spaces outside of Indianapolis were more expensive.

Election Division Dispatch 
 Brad King & Angie Nussmeyer, Co-Directors | February 2026 
NEWS & UPDATES 
Filing Deadlines & Office Closure Reminders 
With the recent winter weather that closed the IED office and 
some county offices in late January, several counties reached 
out to ask how that would affect candidate filing. Candidate 
filing is NOT extended for the days the offices are closed for 
any reason. However, if the closure happens on the filing dead-
line, then state law pushes the filing deadline to noon, the next 
day the office is open. For example, if a county office is closed 
on the statewide filing deadline for the primary election— 
February 6, 2026—then only in that county is the filing deadline 
moved to noon, Monday, February 9, 2026. But, if the office 
was closed on February 5, but open on February 6, then the 
deadline remains noon, February 6, 2026. Note: This law only 
applies to the filing of documents. It does not impact deadlines 
where a county party would need to act to hold a caucus to fill 
an elected office vacancy, for example, or to send out absentee 
ballots by the MOVE Act deadline of 45-days from Election Day. 
Friday the 13th… 
...isn’t just an “unlucky day” to start a project, but it also 
happens to be an important deadline in the primary election 
calendar: 
 Deadline for the D or R member of the CEB to file a 
written request for uncontested PCs and delegates to 
appear on the ballot. Without this request, only contested 
candidates for party offices will appear on the ballot. 
 Deadline for candidate to withdraw from the primary 
election ballot for any reason, using the CAN-10 form. 
In most cases, if a candidate is nominated in May to ap-
pear on the November election, then they can withdraw 
from the general election ballot by noon, July 15, 2026, for 
any reason. After this deadline, the options to withdraw 
become limited. 
 Deadline for a voter in the election district (or a county 
chair within the election district) to file a CAN-1  
challenge to dispute a candidate’s qualifications to run 
for an elected or party office. In most cases, this is the 
only opportunity for a candidate to be challenged where the 
CEB is involved. If a candidate challenge is not filed and 
it’s determined by the CEB that the person is not qualified, 
then it becomes a matter for the courts to decide and a 
person with standing would file a lawsuit. 
 Deadline for a candidate running for an office paying 
$5000 or more to open their candidate’s committee 
(CFA-1). See “Questions of the Month” feature for more 
details. 
CALENDAR

quarterly reports related to imprisonment following conviction or death, 
respectively 
Feb. 4, 2026: Deadline to complete VLM work before freeze period begins on 
Feb. 5, 2026 
Feb. 5, 2026: VLM “freeze” period begins; counties cannot send a SAMC or 
move a voter’s status to inactive now through election day, May 5, 2026 
Feb. 6, 2026 (NOON): Candidate filing for primary closes 
Feb. 13, 2026 (NOON): Deadline for candidate to withdraw from the primary 
election 
Feb. 13, 2026 (NOON): Deadline for a voter in the election district or county 
chair to file a CAN-1 challenge against a candidate who filed for the May 
primary election 
Feb. 13, 2026 (NOON): Deadline for D or R appointed CEB member to file a 
request that uncontested candidates for party offices (PC, delegate) must 
appear on the ballot 
Feb. 13, 2026 (NOON): Deadline for a candidate seeking an office paying 
more than $5000 in a calendar year to open a candidate’s committee (CFA-1) 
unless they’ve already done so 
Feb. 17, 2026: Deadline for VR official to file VRG-21 with IED to confirm 
completion of VLM tasks 
Feb. 20, 2026: Deadline for CEB to notify candidate committees or PACs that 
did not file or filed late their 2025 annual report (see related entry on Mar. 2) 
Feb. 20, 2026: Deadline for VSTOP to provide random list of voting systems 
to use at their public test 
Feb. 20, 2026: Deadline for IED to send the certified list of federal, state 
legislative, and judicial candidates to CEB (see related entry on Feb. 26) 
Feb. 26, 2026: Deadline for CEB (or IEC) to determine the outcome of a 
CAN-1 candidate challenge 
Feb. 27, 2026: Deadline for CEB to share a draft ballot with the D/R county 
party chairs for their review

annual report

provisional ballots needed for the May primary election 
Mar. 6, 2026: Deadline for chairs to provide feedback on the ballots; if no 
feedback received, CEB may proceed with ballot printing 
Mar. 16, 2026: Deadline for CEB to receive ABS print order/blank stock/

IN FOCUS: Ballot Printing Orders for May Primary Election 
Absentee & Provisional Ballot Orders 
Each county must estimate the number of provisional and absentee  
ballots need by voters in your county not later than Mar. 6, 2026. There 
is no specific rule of thumb to make the determination, though your 2022 
and 2024 primary election numbers might be a reasonable gauge. 
Your ballot printer must deliver your order of absentee ballots not later 
than Mar.16, 2026. (If your county uses a ballot-on-demand printer, then 
the CD or equivalent with the ballot files must be delivered by this date.) 
This includes the absentees needed for mail, travel board, and in-person 
absentee or early voting. If a county uses a ballot marking device (BMD) 
with their opScan system, then your vendor must deliver the estimated 
blank card stock by this deadline date. 
Election Day Ballot Orders 
Counties using optical scan paper ballot cards or traditional hand-
counted paper ballots must order Election Day ballots. There is no dead-
line to receive the ballot, other than the print order should arrive on time 
for your county to organize the ballots for pick-up by Inspectors the  
Saturday or Sunday before the election. 
To order Election Day ballots for the May primary election, a county 
needs to review its precinct election results from the 2024 November 
election and identify which D candidate was the top vote getter in each 
precinct, and which R candidate was the top vote getter in each precinct 
to set forth the minimum ballot order. 
Figure 1 is an example of how many ballots and of which party type 
should be ordered for each precinct on Election Day. (No, state law does 
not permit counties to back out any ABS voters; you must follow this law 
for ordering primary ballots.) 
Some counties use a voting system where a blank ballot card is inserted 
into a ballot marking device, the voter makes their selections, and a com-
pleted ballot card is printed for the voter to insert into the opScan tabula-
tor. You would still follow the ballot ordering rules, though you would be 
ordering blank ballot stock at this minimum threshold. 
If you are a vote center county using printed ballot cards or blank ballot 
card stock, then you’ll want to go through this same exercise and sum 
the minimum precinct order to reach a total minimum to deliver to each 
vote center. Using the example below, each vote center would be sup-
plied with at least 237 D ballots (125+112) and 215 R ballots (101+114). 
NOTE: the ballot printing rules are different in the Nov. 2026 election. 
Special Ballot Styles 
State law was updated recently and no longer permits the “common” 
type of public questions to be placed on the May primary ballot. Howev-
er, there are a few “rare” types of questions, such as expanding the size 
of a town council, that can appear on the May ballot. If your CEB must 
place a public question on the May ballot, then you will need to create a 
special “17-year old” ballot that eliminates the public question from the 
ballot. “Underage” voters can register and vote in the May primary elec-
tion, as long as they turn 18 on or before the Nov. 3, 2026, general elec-
tion. While they can nominate candidates for the Nov. ballot in May, they 
cannot participate in an election that is “final,” like a public question. 
Certified List of Candidates from IED 
Candidates for US House, state legislative offices, and judicial offices, 
including prosecuting attorney, file their candidacy paperwork with the 
state; NOT the county. Do NOT rely on the candidate lists found on the 
state’s website OR any courtesy filings. 
The official list of federal and state candidates will come from IED not 
later than Feb. 20, 2026. This certification may change depending on the 
outcome of any challenge hearings, but the initial list will be shared to 
the IED Postings section of the INSVRS County Portal. 
Primary Election Ballot Layout Reminders 
Don’t forget that primary election ballot cards should have the name of 
each party printed near the top of the ballot. It’s also permissible to in-
clude color coding to allow for better visual identification for poll workers 
to pull the proper party’s ballot requested by the voter. This applies to 
opScan ballot cards and DRE or BMD screens. 
All ballot cards must be printed with their precinct designation. (IC 3-10-1 
-13(b)) Further, a line must appear on the ballot to allow for the absentee 
voter board members or poll clerks to affix their initials. 
All candidates within a specific office must appear in the same column 
on the ballot card or screen of a DRE or BMD. There is an exception for 
party offices. PC and delegate names can spill over into a new column or 
screen, if it is not feasible to group them under the same column or 
screen. 
Ballot Proof Review by Third Parties 
The CEB must notify the D and R county chairs (AND, if applicable, 
school superintendents) aware that a ballot proof is ready for their  
review. The deadline to notify these individuals is Feb. 27, 2026. If  
feedback is not received by Mar. 6, 2026, then the CEB can move  
forward with their ballot printing. 
If an error is discovered after the ballots are printed, there are proce-
dures in statute to cure the problem. See the 2026 Election Admin 
Manual at in.gov/sos/elections for details.
